Happy Friday from sunny San Diego. This is Jonathan Wosen, West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. We’ve got a strong lineup to help you kick off the weekend, featuring the lively final day of our STAT Summit, a pharmacist’s insights into why patients sometimes stop taking medication, and a recap of the highlights (or, depending on your perspective, lowlights) of STAT’s coverage of Elizabeth Holmes, for those looking to refresh their memory before watching a newly released documentary of the former Silicon Valley wunderkind’s fall from grace.
STAT Summit, Day 2
Thursday marked the second and final day of our annual flagship STAT Summit in Boston, and the event ended on a high note, with timely sessions on vaccine hesitancy, cutting-edge tools to study the brain, and the future of biotech. Here are some highlights:
- A PSA to health care firms. If you’re an executive at a health care company that may have violated the law, the Department of Justice has a message for you: Please report yourself. The justice department, which has announced plans to expand investigations into corporate wrongdoing, is creating new incentives for both companies and whistleblowers to report offenses such as providers billing for unneeded services and the fabrication of patient records. Read more from STAT’s Isabella Cueto.
- Merck and Moderna go exploring. Merck and Moderna made headlines when they announced in August that their cancer vaccine, which uses messenger RNA, significantly delayed cancer recurrence and metastatic disease in melanoma patients. Their next challenge? Proving this approach can transform other tumors. Read more from STAT’s Jason Mast about where the company’s execs think their next best opportunities may lie.
- A Congressional representative’s thoughts on China. The head-spinning rise of China’s biotech sector has some policymakers endorsing protectionist measures. Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.) has a different idea: Be better than China. Auchincloss plans to introduce a bil that would allow early-phase trials to bypass pre-approval evaluation, speeding up clinical development. He also warned that Trump administration moves to politicize science funding decisions could undermine the nation’s biomedical preeminence. Read more from my colleague John Wilkerson.
What to read before you go see that new documentary on Elizabeth Holmes
We’re leaving room for popcorn and intrigue tonight: The new A24 documentary, “You Can See Everything,” hits theaters today. Its subject is fallen Silicon Valley golden child Elizabeth Holmes, who invited a film crew into her home days before she was about to start her years-long prison sentence.
But STAT, of course, has been covering Holmes for years. We documented Theranos’ halcyon unicorn days. We were at the American Chemical Society meeting back in 2016, for instance, when Holmes was finally to reveal the company’s secretive and dubious data (and, turns out, basically didn’t).
“Would you have Al Capone come and talk about his novel accounting practices?” one clinical pathologist at ACS said at the time. “Is it acceptable to allow someone to talk about science if they’ve used that science so horribly inappropriately?”
It’s been a wild ride: Holmes was convicted in 2022 of defrauding investors and sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison. STAT last year published an op-ed from Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz, which notes the suspicious familiarity between Holmes’ original efforts and her partner’s new diagnostic company, Haemanthus.
Over the years, we tracked the company’s layoffs, legal woes, and eventual shutdown — and kept on top of everything in between with regular Readout dispatches. (Sign up here!) Read up if you need a primer before movie night! — Meghana Keshavan
Why do patients stop taking medication? The answers can be complicated
As a clinical pharmacist, Marcela Gottschald thought she understood why patients usually stop taking medication: They forget, grow tired of dealing with side effects, or don’t understand the severity of their condition. But Gottschald has learned that beneath those initial explanations often lie more complicated concerns. In a STAT First Opinion, she writes about meeting patients worried that taking medication meant they were losing control over their own bodies, and how stopping treatment was a way for them to prove they could still function unaided.
One case left an especially strong impression on her: A young man who’d been on immunosuppressants after he received a kidney transplant. After his body’s immune system attacked the donated kidney, he told Gottschald that he’d simply forgotten to take his medication. But he later shared that his girlfriend was pregnant, and that he’d stopped taking immunosuppressants because he felt he needed to “become a man.”
“This conversation changed the way I understood adherence,” she writes. “Medication can become entangled with the way people see themselves, and the kind of people they believe they need to be.”
A possible silver lining in Pope Leo XIV’s cancer diagnosis
This week, surgeons removed the lower lobe of Pope Leo XIV’s right lung to treat his lung cancer. The Vatican said the surgery was successful with no complications, though it didn’t provide details on the cancer’s stage or whether additional treatment is needed. But some experts are inferring that the cancer was likely caught early, noting that surgery is often prescribed when the entire tumor can be removed.
“The decision to proceed with surgery is encouraging because it suggests the treating physicians believed the cancer could be completely removed. However, successful surgery alone does not necessarily mean the cancer has been cured,” Mohamed Abazeed, a lung cancer physician at Northwestern Medicine, said in a statement.
Lung adenocarcinoma, the type of lung cancer that the pope underwent treatment for, is the most common type of lung cancer and a serious illness. That being said, the 5-year survival rate for localized non-small cell lung cancer is 67%, according to the American Cancer Society. At the absolute earliest stages, 5-year survival can rise to more than 90%. In some cases, surgeons might even do surgeries called a segmentectomy, or a wedge resection, which takes less tissue than one of the five lobes of a lung, to preserve more lung function. — Angus Chen
An FDA policy that made getting a hearing aid easier and cheaper has had mixed results
Four years after the Food and Drug Administration legalized over-the-counter hearing aids, it’s easier and cheaper than ever to get one. So why are companies leaving the market?
Many experts heralded the FDA’s decision in 2022, saying it made it possible for adults with mild-to-moderate hearing loss to get hearing aids over-the-counter rather than through a prescription or professional fitting.
The regulation succeeded in making it cheaper. Prescription aids typically run about $3,400, while over-the-counter aids are roughly $500, according to a JAMA article published Thursday. The majority of first-time buyers are choosing these over-the-counter devices.
But there are some caveats. It’s unclear how many people who need the devices are actually buying, clinicians are struggling to figure out how to refer patients to over-the-counter devices, and it’s tough to know you’re buying a sound product. Researchers found that only 25% of the hearing aids listed on Amazon could be verified with the FDA.
These challenges have forced some of the earliest companies who released over-the-counter hearing aids to flee the market after struggling to gain a foothold. Read on for the solutions proposed by the researchers. — O. Rose Broderick

Quick answers to key questions
Delhi Police detained Dipke on Friday while he was on his way to join the CJP’s ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ march at Connaught Place. Police cited restrictions in force there and preventive action to maintain peace.
Dipke was detained under Sections 126 and 170 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). Section 126 concerns security for keeping the peace, while Section 170 allows preventive arrest to stop a cognisable offence.
One notice directed Dipke not to visit Central Park because restrictions under BNSS Section 163 were in force. The other referred to a previous undertaking requiring him and others not to disturb public peace for one year.
Section 163 was in force in Connaught Place as a preventive measure. Under the provision, gatherings of five or more people, processions and demonstrations were prohibited without prior written permission.
CJP’s legal head said Dipke’s location was unknown and that lawyers had not been able to meet him. She said he was expected to be produced before the Special Executive Magistrate court around noon on Saturday.
According to Bar and Bench, Dipke was detained under Section 126/170 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
Section 126 pertains to the security for keeping peace, and Section 170 allows “arrest to prevent commission of cognisable offences.”
The Delhi Police issued two notices to Abhijeet Dipke, citing restrictions under Section 163 of BNN and a previous undertaking related to maintaining peace, according to PTI.
“We are placing you under preventive detention. Section 163 is in force in Connaught Place. You are being detained," a police official said while informing Dipke about the detention.
Section 163 of the BNSS is a preventive provision invoked by law enforcement (replacing the former Section 144 of the CrPC) to maintain public order and prevent imminent threats or dangers.
Under BNSS Section 163, public gatherings or assemblies of five or more people, processions, demonstrations, picketing and dharnas are prohibited without prior written permission.
According to PTI, one of the two notices was issued by the New Delhi district under the Delhi Police Act, directing Dipke not to visit Central Park in view of the restrictions imposed under Section 163 of the BNSS.
The second notice was issued by the South-West Delhi district and referred to a previous preventive action involving Dipke, Ashutosh and Saurav, who were detained at the airport ahead of the October 10 protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The notice referred to the bond that they should not disturb public peace for a period of one year.
A day after CJP leaders' detention on October 10, the outfit's legal head informed that the Executive Magistrate court released Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on the condition: “no breach of peace for one year." The Delhi Police said a “surety bond” of ₹50,000 was also signed.

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
- Published
The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.
Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.
For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.
This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.
France's prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.
The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.
"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.
So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?
Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.
Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?
"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.
She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.
"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."
"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.
"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."
"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.
Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.
But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.
France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.
I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.
They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.
"France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."
None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.
The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.
- France's school protests: What lies behind the anger 
  - Published8 October
They are part of a defiant French tradition.
Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."
("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")
Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."
Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.
Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.
This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.
France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.
Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.
At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.
"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."
Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the biggest general strike in French history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.
Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.
"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.
"This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu.
But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.
Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.
For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's €11bn contribution to the EU's budget.
There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.
France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Persian Gulf.
Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.
In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.
Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.
But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.
"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.
"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."
For France to progress, she says, that has to change.
The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."
In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me.
"Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity."
Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier.
She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology.
Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard".
"Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately."
I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country."
"My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris."
"That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics."
It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year.
But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply.

Amid intense competition in the quick home services market, Snabbit incurred a net loss of ₹167.8 Cr in the financial year ended March 31, 2026 (FY26) as against a loss of ₹5.7 Cr in FY25. Important to note that FY26 was Snabbit’s first full financial year of operations following its service launch in August 2024. Thus, comparability of the two fiscals is limited. Snabbit posted an operating revenue of ₹12.2 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹26.3 Lakh in FY25. Platform services generated ₹10.8 Cr in revenue, while uniform sales to service professionals contributed the remaining ₹1.4 Cr. The startup recognises platform service revenue net of discounts it bears. Including other income of ₹14.8 Cr, the startup’s total income for the fiscal stood at ₹27 Cr. Interest on bank deposits contributed ₹14.1 Cr, with the remainder largely coming from gains on mutual fund sales. Snabbit held ₹292.2 Cr in cash and bank balances and ₹26.6 Cr in mutual fund investments, totalling ₹318.9 Cr. This balance predates its $56 Mn Series D funding round in April. Founded in 2024 by former Zepto executive Aayush Agarwal, Snabbit connects users with trained domestic help for cleaning, dishwashing, and other household chores, promising arrivals within 10-15 minutes. The April funding round took the startup’s total funding to $112 Mn. It is backed by the likes of Susquehanna Venture Capital, Mirae Asset Venture Investments, Bertelsmann India Investments, Nexus Venture Partners, Lightspeed Ventures, among others. Snabbit currently operates in five cities, including Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad. It intends to expand its operations to 10 cities, with Kolkata and Chennai as priorities. The startup is focusing on penetrating deep into a handful of existing markets, rather than aggressive geographical expansion. Even within cities, it is doubling down on ‘micro-markets’, or certain neighbourhoods where it can ensure quick delivery, rather than the whole city. It was present in 140 micromarkets by May this year, and had onboarded 40,000 professionals on its platforms, with an average order value of ₹169-₹199. Where Did Snabbit Spend In FY26? Snabbit’s total expenses rose to ₹194.8 Cr from ₹6.8 Cr in FY25. Employee Benefit Expenses: These rose to ₹46 Cr from ₹3.3 Cr, including salaries and wages, provident fund contributions, employee stock options, and staff welfare expenses. Expert Service Cost: Its largest expense head stood at ₹63.1 Cr, compared with ₹27 Lakh in FY25. Marketing Expenses: Spending on marketing increased to ₹48.7 Cr from ₹82.1 Lakh in the previous year. Service Fulfillment Expenses: Spending under this head stood at ₹23.8 Cr compared with ₹84.5 Lakh in FY25. Snabbit’s Loss Per Job Falls Below ₹200 In a statement issued today, Snabbit’s CEO Agarwal said the startup closed FY26 with a run rate of 35,000 daily jobs, up 70X from around 500 jobs a day at the beginning of the fiscal year. It acquired nearly 10 Lakh customers and onboarded more than 20,000 service professionals during the year. He attributed the growth to investments in customer acquisition, workforce training, technology, infrastructure and geographical expansion. Agarwal said the startup deliberately invested ahead to scale into the competitive quick home services category. The startup said it closed the fiscal with approximately ₹319 Cr in cash and investments, zero borrowings and a net worth of ₹312.4 Cr. He also argued that its annual financial statements do not fully reflect the underlying economics or maturity of the business. In a separate statement, Snabbit claimed that its losses per job declined from approximately ₹1,500 at the beginning of FY26 to below ₹200 in September 2026, indicating an improvement in unit economics as its operations scaled. Its Q2 FY27 metrics show that the platform completed 64.5 Lakh jobs, up 61% QoQ, and recorded a net transaction value (NTV) of ₹73 Cr, up 34%. House help accounted for 64 Lakh jobs, while more recently launched verticals — home cooking and home salon services — accounted for 50,000 and 10,000 jobs, respectively, in the fiscal. The startup reported an EBITDA loss of ₹145 Cr, equivalent to 199% of NTV. Snabbit also claimed to be the largest high-frequency home services platform by jobs completed and NTV, and the most capital-efficient at the job level. Its strategy centres on building density within fewer cities and micromarkets rather than expanding its geographical footprint aggressively. Competition Heats Up In Quick Home Services Snabbit competes with Pronto and listed home services company Urban Company’s InstaHelp in the instant household assistance market. Pronto closed its $45 Mn Series B round in May at a $200 Mn valuation, adding to the capital flowing into the segment. However, profitability remains a challenge: all three platforms are loss-making due to intense competition, deep discounting, and rising operational costs. Urban Company posted a ₹174 Cr EBITDA loss from InstaHelp in Q2 FY27, over 4X jump from ₹44 Cr in the same quarter last year. InstaHelp fulfilled 6.2 Mn orders, marking a 63% QoQ increase, while its net transaction value (NTV) rose 34% to ₹71 Cr. However, net order value declined to ₹114 from ₹138 in the previous quarter, which it attributed to competitive intensity and introductory pricing for new users. In the past, Urban Company has claimed that it does not expect InstaHelp to meaningfully contribute to its bottom line over the next 4-5 years. The quick home services segment also faces scrutiny over working conditions. Inc42’s reporting documented workers’ concerns about earnings, strict logged-in hour requirements, and inadequate access to waiting areas and washrooms.

Sixteen years since FirstCry began its journey, what began as a kidswear marketplace has spawned a massive multi-channel ecommerce and retail empire, and a house of brands that’s grown well beyond kids today. Today, FirstCry is not just a listed kidswear retailer, but also the engine dragging the Globalbees house of brands and a budding education business that will become hard to ignore soon. But how exactly do each of these engines work? Before we dive in, here’s a look at where FirstCry stands after the last quarter, ahead of its Q2 FY27 results. The first quarter (Q1) of FY27 saw its consolidated revenue climb 13.1% year-on-year to ₹2,106.2 Cr, while its overall net losses were slashed by nearly 34%, dropping to ₹44 Cr from ₹66.5 Cr in Q1FY26. According to founder Supam Maheshwari, this milestone marks the company's strongest baseline revenue expansion over the last five years on a consolidated level. It builds cleanly on the momentum of the previous financial year, where FirstCry closed its books at ₹8,548 Cr in total sales while narrowing its statutory consolidated net loss down to approx ₹204 Cr. However, beneath those headline numbers, take a closer look at the business structure and a different story will unfold. While its top-line revenue signals absolute category dominance, FirstCry’s true bottom line is being heavily squeezed by a highly rigid corporate framework and expensive side-bets. For starters, GlobalBees, FirstCry's D2C brand aggregation subsidiary, contributed ₹1,894.3 Cr, or roughly 22% of its consolidated operating revenue in FY26 while revenue from international businesses in the UAE and Saudi Arabia grew 10% to ₹947.4 Cr. However, together these two businesses accounted for ₹148.5 Cr in segment losses. Further, in Q1FY27, while India multichannel revenue grew 17.7% and international business rose 12%, GlobalBees remained largely flat. The fastest growth, at 47%, came from the much smaller 'Others' segment, primarily comprising the FirstCry Intellitots preschool business. Notably, the segment growing fastest is contributing hardly 1% to the overall consolidated revenue, underscoring the uneven economics behind FirstCry's expanding revenue base. The Overburdened India Goliath A majority 70% of FirstCry’s consolidated operating revenue comes from its India multi-channel business. In Q1FY27, the segment generated around INR 1456 Cr in revenue, up 17.7% YoY. However, despite operating across 10+ categories for mothers, babies, and kids from conception up to approximately 12 years of age, this revenue channel is continuously losing out on gross margin. In Q1FY27, the gross margin fell to 35.2% from 37.8% in Q1FY26. In other words, FirstCry was selling significantly more but retaining less from every rupee of revenue before accounting for delivery, marketing and other operating expenses. A major pressure point is the diapers business, which although just a 15% contributor to GMV, acts as the primary top-of-funnel customer acquisition gateway. It is a high-volume category hit heavily by quick-commerce and private-label discounting, which temporarily drags down the overall multi-channel gross margins. FirstCry's parent company, Brainbees Solutions Limited, holds a 76.59% stake in Swara Baby Products Limited, which gives it a promoter status in the company, which is about to go for an ₹1,000 Cr IPO separately. This will allow FirstCry to further vertically integrate its supply chain for the diapers category. To combat the short-term pressures on the diapers segment, Firstcry has been pushing on its private labels particularly Babyhug, Pine Kids, Cute Walk and Babyoye, to gain greater control over product pricing, sourcing and margins. At the same time, FirstCry has been actively pushing efforts around three initiatives. First, it is rapidly deploying internal logistics networks. Its in-house logistics platform RocketBees has scaled rapidly to 72 cities and covers around 50% of total online shipment as of June 2026. In Q1FY27 earnings call, Maheshwari also pointed out a 20% improvement in turnaround time from delivery perspective. The under-3-hour delivery pilot, FC Qwik, is also live across 12 cities completing approximately 1.25 Lakh shipments in June 2026 alone. Founder and MD Maheshwari said, “We had an overall ambition of growing to 10% of our overall shipment onto the FC Qwik platform. Now, we will aim to grow to 20% of our volumes.” He also highlighted that the FC Qwik TAT has been reduced from three to two hours in selected cities and the team is working on further reducing it. As its third pillar, the company continues to be bullish on its physical retail network, which had grown to around 1,190 stores by FY26. Its offline business recorded approximately 15% year-on-year GMV growth in Q1FY27, with management targeting another 90-100 net store additions during FY27. This gives FirstCry an advantage in product discovery and customer reach, particularly beyond large metropolitan markets, but also requires it to manage the costs of an extensive physical network alongside faster online fulfillment. The trade-off is becoming increasingly visible. Despite the 17.7% revenue growth in Q1FY27, the India business's adjusted EBITDA declined from approximately ₹107 Cr to ₹84 Cr. Its adjusted operating margin consequently contracted from around 8.6% to 5.8%. This suggests that higher sales volumes have yet to compensate for the combined pressure of product margins and operating costs. The company expects some relief as higher raw material and currency-related costs are gradually passed on through product pricing, with a fuller recovery anticipated from Q3FY27, as per management disclosures after Q1. However, competitive pressure in diapering could take longer to ease. In essence, the India multichannel goliath is growing faster, but whether that growth can translate into stronger profits remains the bigger test. The Q2 results will clear up some questions around which direction this key business is headed in. Globalbees’ Drag Effect If the India multi-channel business is FirstCry’s heavy brick-and-mortar anchor, GlobalBees is its high-stakes venture capital pivot. In FY26, Globalbees registered a solid 20% y-o-y growth in overall revenue, however, the momentum doesn't seem to continue. In Q1FY27, the revenue remained almost flat with marginal reduction, while core categories revenue saw only 2% year on year growth. GlobalBees has been a significant capital allocation bet for FirstCry. Parent Brainbees Solutions earmarked ₹169 Cr from the IPO proceeds for GlobalBees to gain further control of its portfolio under the house of brands model. By March 2026, it had deployed ₹104.81 Cr of this allocation. Separately, in March 2025, Brainbees approved a further infusion of up to ₹146 Cr. Despite this capital backing GlobalBees has not acquired a single new brand since September 2022. During the FY26 earnings call, CEO Anuj Jain acknowledged that the company rationalised its portfolio, cutting off brands struggling with slower growth and persistent losses. Instead, the focus has shifted towards four core categories spanning home improvement, appliances, personal care and lifestyle. Thanks to this, even on flat revenue, the segment delivered a remarkable 308% year-on-year surge in Adjusted EBITDA, jumping from ₹4.1 Cr to ₹16.7 Cr, and operating margins grew from 1% to 3.9%. Jain said the cutbacks are a temporary and planned transition that should be completed in the second quarter and growth should bounce back in the winter months. Globalbees can unlock more growth in these categories, but how profitable will this model remain in the long run? Investors will undoubtedly be looking at the next three quarters keenly. The International & Preschool Hedge The other two parts of FirstCry’s business are part of its vision of targeting customers early and making a global retail giant. The company entered the UAE in 2019 and Saudi Arabia in 2022, betting on far higher spending per child than in India. While average spend per child on its Indian platform is around ₹9,280–₹9,350, the corresponding figures are approximately ₹61,000–₹71,000 in Saudi Arabia and ₹1,60,000–₹1,70,000 in the UAE. But converting that premium opportunity into profits has proved difficult amid aggressive discounting by larger ecommerce rivals. FirstCry has reduced its proposed allocation for the international business after the IPO. The move raises questions about the pace and capital demands of its overseas rollout, even as management maintains that the region remains a long-term opportunity. And to be fair, international revenue growth is in line with the overall topline. International revenue rose 12% year on year to ₹232.1 Cr in Q1FY27, from ₹207.2 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA losses narrowed 22% to ₹16.7 Cr. The adjusted EBITDA loss margin improved from about 10% to 7%. For now, management is prioritising unit economics over a breakneck expansion push and has avoided committing to a break-even quarter. The premium-spending thesis remains attractive, but the international business still has to prove it can turn that opportunity into sustainable profits. Away from the bruising battles of babycare retail and overseas expansion, FirstCry harbors a smaller, highly lucrative engine quietly gathering momentum. Its preschool operations, housed under the 'Others' segment, are emerging as an unlikely margin champion in a sprawling consumer empire historically plagued by cash burn. The numbers present a striking contrast. In Q1 FY27, the Intellitots preschool business saw net revenue surge 47% year-on-year to ₹19 Cr, while its adjusted EBITDA improved 65% to hit ₹5 Cr. Operating at a 26% adjusted EBITDA margin, this division outperforms FirstCry's primary retail segments. With management aiming to scale the network to 1,000 preschools over the next few years, this asset-light education bet offers a clear blueprint for high margin revenue beyond traditional retail operations. But the ₹19 Cr quarterly revenue base is small and the preschool business accounts for less than 1% of FirstCry’s consolidated topline. The profitability offers little immediate relief to the group as a whole. But it could become a bigger lever if and when the core business matures. Is FirstCry Stuck In The Past? When you zoom out, FirstCry's consolidated revenue model reveals a business in a state of transition, which has not really been solved by its IPO and the funds raised through the listing. It is caught between defensive strategies for margin recovery and an aggressive push for growth. It’s not a crisis by any means but it is a time for the company to reassess its strengths once again and push for growth in that direction. FirstCry is increasingly feeling the weight of over 1,000 physical storefronts, which have saddled the company with fixed, unyielding operational overheads like high commercial rent and retail payroll. The ecommerce moat is also rapidly eroding under a fierce, industry-wide quick commerce frenzy led by Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart and Flipkart Minutes as well as specialised players, which we had reported in detail here. Having gone beyond kidswear and babycare, the harder question in front of FirstCry is whether its disparate pieces can start to show an ecosystem effect to generate enough operating leverage to sustain the business without another major funds infusion, as has been the major trend in the public markets this year for new-age listed companies.

Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
- Published
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.

In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."

Vedanta Resources Chairman Anil Agarwal expressed his awe at the rapid pace of technological innovation following Tesla CEO Elon Musk's latest showcase of advanced robotics and flying vehicles.
Musk’s redesigned Tesla Roadster, developed in collaboration with SpaceX, demonstrated the electric sports car performing aerial manoeuvres using rocket-style thrusters.
Tesla unveiled the redesigned Roadster on Thursday, showcasing a white two-seater vehicle that performed a series of dramatic manoeuvres, including turning in mid-air and jumping over other vehicles.
Quick answers to key questions
Agarwal said flying cars and running robots had once been concepts from science fiction, but were now becoming real. He praised the combination of risk-taking entrepreneurship and cutting-edge science.
He saw it as an example of rapid innovation in mobility and technology. Agarwal said bold business leadership combined with scientific development can change the world.
The redesigned Roadster was demonstrated using rocket-style thrusters developed with SpaceX. It performed aerial manoeuvres, including turning in mid-air, before landing.
The demonstration showed short aerial manoeuvres, but did not establish a practical flight range or routine. It does not show that the Roadster can replace conventional road or air transport.
Tesla said production of the redesigned Roadster would begin in 2028. The company has not specified a target price for the model at the latest event.
Developed in collaboration with Musk’s rocket company SpaceX, the vehicle features rocket-style thrusters that were demonstrated during the event.
Taking to X, the billionaire industrialist highlighted how rapid advancements in mobility and artificial intelligence are bringing futuristic concepts into the mainstream.
“Flying cars and running robots! Not long ago, we saw these in science fiction movies and books. Today, they are real,” Agarwal wrote, reacting to the tech billionaire's latest showcase.
For Agarwal, whose own conglomerate operates in the traditional, capital-intensive sectors of mining and metals, the leap in autonomous and futuristic tech represented a broader triumph of business innovation.
He praised the synergy between scientific development and bold business leadership, adding: “What an amazing time we live in. When risk-taking entrepreneurship and cutting-edge science combine, they change the world.”
Tesla said production of the redesigned Roadster would begin in 2028, more than a decade after the company first unveiled a prototype of the next-generation electric sports car.
Tesla vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said the Roadster could accelerate from zero to 60 mph (97 kph) in less than one second and reach a top speed of more than 230 mph (370 kph).
"Definitely much faster than that," Musk said, adding, "I think you've got to crack halfway to the speed of sound."
The vehicle is also expected to offer a range of more than 300 miles (480 km) on a single charge. That is less than half the range Musk promised in 2017, when Tesla first revealed a prototype of the second-generation Roadster and said deliveries would begin in 2020.
Tesla has not specified a target price for the redesigned model at the latest event. Nearly a decade ago, the company quoted a base price of $200,000 for the vehicle.
The original Roadster, launched in 2008 and sold until 2012, was Tesla’s first electric vehicle and used a Lotus Elise chassis. The model helped establish the company’s early credentials in electric sports cars before it expanded its lineup to include the Model S and Model 3 sedans and Model X and Model Y SUVs.

She registered her dog to vote in California. Her punishment is one she will remember ‘furever’
At least one ballot from Maya Jean was successfully counted
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Join today
Already a member? Log in
A California woman who registered her own dog to vote has learned her fate - and it’s certainly a little ruff.
Laura Lee Yourex, 64, was charged with five felonies after investigators determined that she registered her dog, Maya Jean, to vote and submitted five mail-in ballots during the 2021 state recall election and the 2022 primary election, according to KTLA.
She recently reached a plea deal in the case that saw the charges dismissed after she agreed to a unique punishment.
Yourex agreed to pay $1,500 to fund four billboards in Orange County to warn voters about fraud and have her dog featured in the ad.
Prosecutors noted that the dog’s vote was successfully counted in the 2021 recall election, but was not for the 2022 primary.
The billboards featured a photo of Maya Jean with an “I voted” sticker and carried the message “Don’t be a dog,” KTLA noted. They remind residents that voting fraud is a crime and anyone not eligible should not vote.
Voters are also reminded that fraud can be reported to the District Attorney’s office.
The billboards are currently up and will remain in place through the November election, according to the report.
The investigation started after a woman called the Orange County Registrar of Voters and said she registered her dog to vote. Yourex also made social media posts about her scheme.
Yourex pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor case earlier this year, which prosecutors dismissed this week after the billboards went up.

Nova Scotia to host massive data centre to power Anthropic's AI assistant Claude
EverWind Fuels will own it, AI giant Anthropic will lease it
A massive data centre to provide computing power for the artificial intelligence giant Anthropic is under pre-construction just outside Port Hawkesbury in Cape Breton.
EverWind Fuels will build and own the facility, while Anthropic will lease the first phase for a term of at least 20 years. Anthropic said in a news release the data centre "will power Claude models and serve growing demand from Canadian and global customers."
EverWind, headed by Australian-American private equity veteran Trent Vichie, had previously confirmed it has data centre ambitions, but said little else.
On Friday, EverWind released more information about its plans.
The company said it will build the facility in two stages, with the first phase to come online by the end of 2027 and the second in 2028.
The first phase will have a capacity of 95 megawatts and the second, 325 megawatts, for a total of 420 megawatts. Nova Scotia’s current electrical generating capacity is close to 3,000 megawatts.
EverWind and Anthropic said they will pay for any required upgrades to Nova Scotia’s electricity system.
EverWind raising $8 billion for project
EverWind said it is raising $8 billion in private capital to fund the project and an additional $2 billion for four of the onshore wind farms it is planning to build.
"This is investment that is in the ground here, supporting Nova Scotians, not only its energy economy but its knowledge economy as well," Vichie said at an announcement in Point Tupper, the industrial park where the facility is to be built.
Land clearing is underway and officials said they hope to have foundations poured before winter.
Trent Vichie, CEO of Everwind, spoke at the event. (Tom Ayers/CBC)
EverWind's four wind farms would eventually support the data centre’s electricity needs, but existing generation on the provincial grid would be the primary supply to begin.
The Independent Energy System Operator, which manages the provincial grid, told CBC News it studies all new projects to ensure the grid can handle them, before allowing them to connect. It did not answer specifically whether there is capacity to connect this data centre, although EverWind officials said they've been assured there is capacity, at least for phase 1.
Anthropic was not at EverWind's Friday announcement and Vichie was initially mum about which AI company he was partnering with. Anthropic issued a news release later in the day.
But EverWind did have a large contingent of supporters at its event. Politicians from every level of government were on hand to praise the project.
Premier Tim Houston thanked Vichie for bringing such a large sum of money to Nova Scotia, and said it demonstrates "what is possible in our province."
"Please don't stop, keep moving, we'll be here to support you in that," he said, directing his remarks to the EverWind CEO.
EverWind's data centre will be in Point Tupper, just outside Port Hawkesbury. (Tom Ayers/CBC)
Kings-Hants MP Kody Blois, who is parliamentary secretary to the prime minister, said the data centre aligns with the Liberal government's priorities.
"Today is an example of how we're building a stronger Canada," he said.
Richmond County Warden Lois Landry noted there has been some skepticism in the community in recent weeks as people have been speculating about the project's specifics, but she said she feels optimistic after learning more information.
"We're hearing about potential construction and long-term employment, opportunities for local businesses and infrastructure investment that could support future growth," she said.
EverWind has been trying to develop renewable energy projects in Nova Scotia for several years. It says those plans remain unchanged.
The data centre is to be built at the same site as one of EverWind’s other proposed projects — a green hydrogen and ammonia facility.
Data centre controversies
Data centres have become a flashpoint across Canada, especially those that power AI, because they can have huge footprints and require vast amounts of energy and water for cooling. Concerns about AI’s potential impacts on jobs and dire warnings about risks to human existence also have some people pushing back.
There are some proposed data centres that would dwarf this one in size, including the Wonder Valley data centre in Alberta — the first phase of which is meant to be more than a gigawatt — but this project is still on the larger end of facilities that have been recently announced in Canada.
EverWind and Anthropic have signed on to Ottawa’s responsible data centre development principles — a set of non-binding guidelines the federal government released last month.
Houston recently laid out similar guidelines. Both levels of government say they expect any data centre to have local benefits, minimal environmental impact and minimal water use, and for there to be no resulting power rate spikes.
“We applaud the federal and provincial governments for setting high standards for responsible development,” Vichie said in a news release. “And we will continue to work with communities to ensure that our work meets their expectations.”
EverWind said it will use a closed-loop water-glycol system. The company’s preliminary estimate for water usage is an average of 100,000 litres per day for the first phase and 500,000 litres of water per day including both phases.
Water would be drawn from nearby Landrie Lake. The provincial regulator has approved the Landrie Lake Water Utility to withdraw 34 million litres from the lake each day, which would make EverWind’s daily requirements about one per cent of the total safe withdrawal volume.
The company promised the data centre would come with a community benefit program worth tens of millions of dollars. A specific dollar figure was not provided. Local communities and Anthropic would consult on how to spend the money.
A consortium of Mi’kmaw communities, fronted by Membertou First Nation, is negotiating a nine per cent equity stake in the project.
But not everyone is ready to endorse the project.
Nova Scotia's Ecology Action Centre (EAC) said it poses more questions than it answers.
Thomas Arnason McNeil, policy advocate on grid decarbonization at the EAC, raised concerns about the project's scale.
"There will need to be analysis and work that is done in terms of quantifying ... the impact on ratepayers and understanding what the environmental impacts of the project will be," he said.
McNeil added that while the group is reserving judgment for now, thorough impact assessments are essential before moving forward.
MORE TOP STORIES

Some Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses were recording people’s conversations without the wearer knowing. The recordings occurred without users saying the prompt phrase (“Hey, Meta”), in a bug that Meta says has been fixed.
This week, some users reported online that their Ray-Ban Metas were recording without their consent. A person going by Kindly-Audience-137 on Reddit, for example, said this happened to them across three Meta Ray-Bans and that they had the “Respond without Hey Meta” setting turned off. The person said the Meta AI app “saves audio recordings and text transcripts of these conversations in my conversation history.”
“I believe this deserves a serious technical investigation. Customers should not have to wonder whether their private conversations are being captured when they have not intentionally activated their glasses’ AI assistant,” the Reddit user said.
Android Authority reported the discussions on Tuesday. Later that day it published a response from Meta that read:
“This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review, and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.”
Although Meta’s brief message suggests that the bug is fixed, the broader privacy problem remains.
Unanswered questions
Meta hasn’t said what caused the Ray-Ban Metas to record people without user consent. Reddit user Kindly-Audience-137 said they “first noticed this behavior after a recent firmware update,” but Meta hasn’t confirmed if a faulty update caused the bug.
We also don’t know how many Meta smart glasses were affected. There are a few reports online, but Android Authority said it was unable to replicate the problem before Meta said it fixed it.
Ars Technica sent Meta a message asking what it’s doing to prevent future bugs like this from happening again and how many devices were affected. We’ll update this article if we hear back.
Even a handful of affected devices is cause for concern, though.
Before reports of this bug, privacy advocates had already expressed widespread concerns about Meta’s smart glasses, as well as those from other vendors. Beyond the fear that naturally accompanies the release of new technology that features a microphone and camera, Meta’s glasses pushed the boundaries of privacy further with their more inconspicuous look, prompting concern about how easy it could be for someone to secretly record another person.

Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network
- Published
US President Donald Trump has denied limiting Ukraine's access to Starlink's sister internet network Starshield after it restricted drone speed, hampering Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.
"It wasn't me and I don't think it was [Starlink owner] Elon [Musk]," Trump said, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed had yet to be restored.
Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions, while Reuters news agency reported on Thursday that the order had come from inside the White House.
Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes on Tuesday after the network slowdown.
Starlink is a civilian-use high-speed internet network operated by Musk's SpaceX. Starshield - which relies on Starlink- is its military-grade sister service that was designed for the Pentagon.
The US had previously warned it could withhold sharing intelligence, crucial for Kyiv's defences, if Ukraine did not stop hitting Russian oil refineries.
Tension has been brewing between Washington and Kyiv for days over a recent controversial diesel deal between Russia and the US.
Zelensky - angered by the deal - resumed targeting Russian oil refineries this week in a move criticised by Trump after he announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it would only stop the strikes if Moscow did the same.
"If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" Zelensky asked EU leaders at a summit on Friday.
Trump had also said that Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".
But speaking to reporters as he left the White House on Friday, the US president said he had a good relationship with his Ukrainian counterpart.
Asked about Starshield, he said he was "not sure" it "ever came down".
Musk earlier explained that Starshield was managed by the US government, and that the Pentagon could have been responsible.
In its report about the alleged order regarding Starshield, Reuters quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.
On Tuesday night, Starlink restricted speed limits to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
Some 600,000 in Ukraine were left without power as communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military were also hit in the deadly attacks.
A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an investigation into the disruptions to the network.
"Restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure," the letter read.
On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron vowed that EU states would not abandon Ukraine.
Speaking at the end of the two-day summit in Brussels attended by Zelensky, Macron said it was Europe's job to hold the line in the face of some people's "ambiguities". That was apparently a reference to signs of wavering US support for Ukraine.
Funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the summit's agenda.
The war will cost €155bn (£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least €70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons.
Macron said Europe was working to help Ukraine with its satellite and early warning systems, and Ukraine's friends would look at its request for further aid.

Prime minister to speak at pro-Confederation rally in Edmonton
Prime minister set to deliver remarks in support of Canadian unity ahead of referendum
Prime Minister Mark Carney will speak at Edmonton's Expo Centre on Friday night to urge Albertans to vote to stay in Canada in a provincial referendum.
Earlier in the day, Carney spoke at a pro-unit event in Red Deer.
Alberta and Canada don't agree on everything, but they're on the same page when it comes to staying in Confederation, Premier Danielle Smith told a crowd in Red Deer Friday.
"We often disagree quite publicly on several things," she said. "But today we can all agree that on Question 10, we are voting for Option 1 to remain in Canada."
Albertans are set to get to polls on Monday for a 10-question referendum. On Question 10, Albertans will choose either Option 1, to remain in Canada, or Option 2, to begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on separation.
Smith joined Prime Minister Mark Carney at a brewery in Red Deer, as he passed through on his way from Thursday's Forever Canadian rally in Calgary and the one set to take place in Edmonton Friday.
"This is now a time, a moment in Canadian history, where we are going to be able to work side by side," Smith said. "I feel for the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together."
Carney said Alberta's trust in the federal government has been tested, but their interests are now aligned.
"As a country, we are co-operating again," he said. "Canada is working again. We are coming together. "
Both leaders urged Albertans to vote and listed examples of what their recent co-operation has achieved, including the announcement of the Pacific Link pipeline and agreements on water, housing and defence.
There are more shared wins to come, Smith said, noting the Supreme Court of Canada agreed Thursday to hear an appeal of the federal ban on single-use plastics.
While Carney and Smith agree on a united Canada, Smith wants Albertans to vote "yes" on nine referendum questions that would give the province more control over immigration and a mandate to pursue constitutional changes to wrest power from Ottawa.
Prime Minister Mark Carney attends a national unity rally in Red Deer alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)
Carney, meanwhile, has urged Albertans to say “no to the nine.”
Smith said Friday she will work to change his mind.
Near the end of his brief comments, Carney held up a pair of red, knitted mittens, calling them a symbol.
They were made in Red Deer with a pattern by an Ontario designer and yarn from New Brunswick. He cited the mittens as an example of the “threads that link us as a country.”
“What we're facing on Monday is, in part, a reflection of that.”
Both leaders called out notable politicians in the crowd, including former Alberta premier Ed Stelmach and former MP Monte Solberg from Stephen Harper's cabinet. Matt Jeneroux, the MP for Edmonton Riverbend, was also there.
A number of current and former municipal leaders also attended the event, like Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas, former Edmonton mayor Amarjeet Sohi, Sylvan Lake Mayor Megan Hanson, Airdrie Mayor Heather Spearman and Red Deer Mayor Cindy Jefferies.
"I don't think Red Deer's seen this kind of attention for some time," Jefferies said.
She added that when she attended a Liberal caucus retreat a month ago, she told federal politicians at the time that she has noticed them paying more attention to Alberta recently and that she doesn't want that to stop when the referendum is over.
Prime Minister Mark Carney is seen at a national unity rally at a brewery in Red Deer, Alta., on Oct. 16, 2026. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC News)
Jefferies had co-signed a statement with Edmonton Centre MP Eleanor Olszewski last month calling for Albertans to vote for Option 1 on Question 10.
"I hesitated to take a position on it," she told CBC News. "But listening to businesses in the community, many of them were having concerns around recruiting and retention of staff because of the uncertainty created in our province with respect to this referendum and the discussion that's going on.
"I want stability."
While the brewery was filled with people who support Alberta staying in Canada, some people could be seen across the road waving an "Alberta strong" flag and one person told CBC News they support the idea of an independent Alberta.
Red Deer resident Kelsie Petersen said she came because she "never had a chance to see a prime minister before." She said she will vote for Option 2 on Question 10 because even though she "wants a better deal for Alberta," she would rather not separate.
Pro-remain supporters gather outside of Red Hart Brewing in Red Deer, Alta., on Friday, Oct. 16. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith spoke inside the brewery, making a pitch for unity before the Alberta referendum on Monday. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC)
Carney is scheduled to speak later Friday at a Forever Canadian rally in Edmonton, while Smith is headed to Calgary to speak at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference. Earlier Friday, Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre made his pitch for unity at the same conference.

Katie Zacharia's first briefing as President Donald Trump's press secretary was on Tuesday. By Friday, the White House confirmed she was out.
The record five-day tenure came after days of missteps by Zacharia, and amid two watchdog groups filing complaints with the State Bar of California on Wednesday, asking it to investigate whether she violated California law by calling herself a lawyer.
While the longest-serving press secretary was Stephen Early, who held the post for 12 years under Franklin D. Roosevelt, only four press secretaries have lasted under two months.
Here's a closer look at White House press secretaries with the shortest tenures.
Katie Zacharia
Katie Zacharia made her White House press briefing debut on Tuesday and quickly came under intense scrutiny over her legal credentials.
Shortly after Tuesday's briefing, she was asked which state she passed the bar exam in and replied: "When I moved to China."
On Thursday in an interview with right-wing provocateur Jack Posobiec, Zacharia said she took the bar exam but failed, and never retook it.
Zacharia moved to China after earning her law degree in 2011, and told Posobiec she had already preregistered for the bar exam before moving to Beijing, where her husband was working at an American private equity firm.
"I didn't want to withdraw from that," Zacharia said of the bar exam. "And we knew we would be moving out to China, and I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I had been long-distance from for at least a year."
She served as press secretary between October 12 and October 16.
Stephen Early
Stephen Early is both the longest-serving press secretary in US history and the press secretary with the second-shortest tenure.
He was President Franklin D. Roosevelt's press secretary for 12 years, from 1933 to March 1945.
Early then briefly returned as acting press secretary under President Harry S. Truman in December 1950 after the death of press secretary Charles Ross.
Early was in the position for 14 days, from December 5 to December 18, 1950.
Jerald TerHorst
Jerald TerHorst served as President Gerald Ford's press secretary for over one month, from August 9 to September 8, 1974.
He resigned in protest of Ford's pardon of former President Richard Nixon following the Watergate scandal.
TerHorst said he could not defend Ford's decision in good conscience, despite his long-standing friendship with the president.
Jonathan Daniels
Jonathan Daniels served a short tenure as press secretary at the end of Franklin D. Roosevelt's presidency and at the beginning of Harry S. Truman's.
That brings his tenure to 48 days, from March 29 to May 15, 1945.
He was appointed shortly before Roosevelt's death and stayed on temporarily to help Truman transition into the presidency.
Truman then selected Charles Ross as Daniels' replacement.

Employers in England are to be forced to pay more to train an older worker than a youth apprentice under plans being drawn up by the government to tackle the youth jobs crisis.
The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training by 25% for a worker over the age of 25 in order to encourage businesses to train young people instead.
Aiming to reverse a 40% drop in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade, the proposal is being developed as part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are out of work.
With his final report delayed until after the budget, the former Labour cabinet minister this week signalled that boosting access to apprenticeships would be critical for fixing the first rungs of the career ladder for young people.
The chancellor, John Healey, is preparing to include measures to tackle soaring youth unemployment in his highly anticipated tax and spending statement to the Commons in less than a fortnight’s time.
After a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training to almost 1 million, Andy Burnham has made supporting youth job opportunities central to his agenda for power, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and apprenticeships.
Ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the apprenticeship system back towards younger people. More than half of new starts are now for over-25s and the number of under-19s enrolling has almost halved in a decade.
Under the changes being planned to the growth and skills levy – the £4bn a year tax used to fund the national apprenticeship system – employers in England will face a new “co-investment” rule restricting the funding they can access.
Aiming to tip the balance to incentivise youth apprenticeships, the change is controversial because employers have for years been told by successive governments they were free to spend their levy funds on training as they saw fit.
“Employers are not going to like it,” said one senior policy expert close to the government. “They were told ‘it’s your money, you get to decide’. But the system is not working at the moment.”
Earlier this year Labour revamped the apprenticeship levy introduced by the Conservatives in 2017, with changes handing more flexibility to employers over the types of training the system can be used for – including new foundation apprenticeships and shorter courses.
Under the levy, large employers (those with yearly wage costs totalling more than £3m) must pay 0.5% of their total annual pay bill into a dedicated digital pot that they can draw from to fund training and assessment costs.
Following the proposed change, money from the pot would still be available to cover eligible training costs for apprentices aged 16 to 24. However, for older apprentices, the funds would cover only 75% of the cost and employers would need to pay for the remainder. It is believed the measure is under consideration for a phased launch from the start of the next academic year, in September 2027.
Labour has been warned that its skills strategy to tackle youth unemployment risks failure without a change in course. Official figures show its flagship foundation apprenticeship scheme has enrolled just 160 young people in the first eight months, against an ambition for 30,000 starts over the course of the parliament.
This month the Fabian Society thinktank called on ministers to increase the rate of the growth and skills levy to 0.7% to raise an additional £2.5bn, which could be used to target more funding towards youth apprenticeships.
However, it is understood that ministers are wary of heaping additional costs on businesses after the backlash suffered over employer national insurance contributions and as firms press for budget support to help them hire more young people.
Alongside tight constraints on the public finances, this has shifted the focus to restricting levy funds as a way to support young people without further adding to the costs for the public purse.
A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “We remain determined to address the 40% decline in apprenticeship starts among young people and give them the skills they need to succeed.
“We are already pivoting the system towards the next generation, including by creating 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people, and introducing a new hiring payment of £2,000 for SMEs who take on a 16-24-year-old apprentice.
“The Milburn review is due in the autumn. We will not pre-empt its findings.”

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has asked all medical colleges and medical institutions across the country to constitute patient safety committees/cells and designate nodal officers to strengthen patient safety practices and reduce avoidable harm in healthcare settings.
In a recent communication to the heads of medical institutions, NMC has asked institutions to share the composition and details of their patient safety committees, along with the particulars of the designated patient safety nodal officer, with the National Patient Safety Secretariat (NPSS) at the Directorate-General of Health Services (DGHS).
As per the direction, the proposed committee is to be chaired by the director, head of the institution or medical superintendent, with representation from relevant specialties and patient safety domains.
Patient safety framework
According to the NMC, the patient safety framework covers 11 domains, including medication and surgical safety, blood and medical device safety, laboratory and diagnostic safety, and infection prevention and control. Other areas include patient and family engagement, vaccine and injection safety, operational research in patient safety, facility safety covering biomedical waste management, fire safety, structural safety and environmental safety, along with safety in AYUSH services.
The Commission notes that the move places responsibility on medical institutions to establish an institutional mechanism for monitoring safety practices rather than treating patient safety as an isolated clinical responsibility.
According to the latest order, institutions should comply with the directions and communicate the required details to the NPSS.

Patients in chains rescued from suspected illegal rehab centre in South Africa
- Published
A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in the north-eastern part of the country.
The facility, operated from a church in Mpumalanga province, was discovered during an operation by officials in the area on Thursday.
Authorities said they uncovered "gross inhumane conditions" when they raided the facility, with some patients found with "sores all over their bodies" and "others chained to each other".
Police have since charged the couple, who were running the facility, with kidnapping but could add more charges. They have not yet commented.
Illegal rehabilitation centres have mushroomed in South Africa in recent years as drug use spirals in the country.
Last year, the department of social development said it had uncovered over 100 unlawful facilities operating across the country, mostly in Gauteng province.
This is where some of those found at this facility come from, the department said in a statement on Friday.
The couple running the centre told officials they were housing 60 people, but upon inspection, a higher number was found, which included two minors and 30 women.
The group, mostly believed to be drug addicts, were found in crowded rooms and without access to functioning bathrooms or running water.
"Some [of them had] been at the alleged illegal centre for a while," the department said.
The couple charged a monthly fee of 3,000 rand ($182; £137) to house the patients, of which almost a half would go to the church.
Fourteen of those found at the centre have since been taken to hospital for further medical treatment, police said.
The couple is expected to appear in a local court on Monday.
