Mr Ingo Behnel, Ambassador Dr Katharina Stasch, Dr Gesa Miehe-Nordmeyer and Dr Catharina Boehme. ©WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
In a meeting on 3 November, Germany reaffirmed its support for WHO as the Organization takes on wide-ranging global health challenges and advocated prompt action to establish a pandemic accord – an international agreement that would pave the way for better collaboration on emergencies, science and research.
A German delegation that included Dr Katharina Stasch, UN Ambassador in Geneva; Ingo Behnel, Director-General of European and International Policy Issues at the German Ministry of Health; and Dr Gesa Miehe-Nordmeyer, Director General of the German Chancellery’s Department for Social, Health, Labor Market, Environment and Social Policy, met with WHO representatives including Assistant Director-General Dr Catharina Boehme, Emergencies Programme Executive Director Dr Michael Ryan and Chief Scientist Dr Jeremy Farrar.
During the meeting Germany also reaffirmed its support for flexible, sustainable funding to carry out WHO’s 14th General Programme of Work for 2025-28 (GPW14) towards vital objectives such as withstanding pandemics, responding to health emergencies, and confronting the threats to health posed by climate change and drug-resistant infections.
“Germany is very supportive of WHO, and also supportive of the pandemic agreement,” Dr Miehe-Nordmeyer said, adding that Member States have a clear window of opportunity to establish the pandemic agreement in time for the World Health Assembly next May.
Dr Ryan praised Germany for having been a “huge supporter of global health security over many years,” cited the country’s voluntary contributions to WHO’s Contingency Fund for Emergencies, its support during the COVID-19 pandemic for technology, science, innovation and operations, and for its hosting of the World Health Summit, a leading strategic forum for global health advocacy.
Germany is the largest donor to the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), which enables WHO to respond without delay to health emergencies worldwide.
Dr Ryan called the Germany-supported WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence in Berlin “a physical manifestation of Germany’s commitment” to global health security. The Hub was launched in 2021 to provide the world with better data and analytics to detect and respond to health emergencies.
@WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
At the meeting Germany and WHO signed funding agreements to support emergency responses in Libya (€1 million) and Yemen (€3 million).
An afternoon session with WHO Chief Scientist Jeremy Farrar touched on embedding science and research action across the Organization, helping countries develop ecosystems for health research and science, and supporting the international community with a digitalization agenda.
Dr Farrar also discussed WHO’s aim to add WHO collaborating centres, particularly in the Global South, and branch out into new research areas. WHO has 847 collaborating centers in more than 80 countries.
“We’d like to see collaborating centres on digital, on A.I., on trust, or on horizon scanning for the future of science,” Dr Farrar said. “We would like to work more closely with the collaborating centres and for them to see themselves very much as a part of WHO,” Dr Farrar said.

For a long time, the finance function in organisations has been a back-office job — close the books, stay compliant, keep enough cash in the bank to survive the quarter. The job rewarded accuracy over foresight, and a CFO’s standing was measured by how few surprises were brought to the table. The job description no longer holds today, particularly for SaaS businesses, where a small dip in quarterly retention can snowball into a much larger problem. The role has grown to include almost everything under its ambit, from market research to product R&D and even deciding pricing of products or services, once exclusive to the CEO’s role. Simply put: finance leaders are today involved in deciding which market deserves more investment, which product line is worth the losses, and whether a pricing model could open doors to the next big opportunity. In all odds, the CFO today is an organisation’s sounding board. LeadSquared, a SaaS platform focused on sales execution and marketing automation, is also witnessing this shift under the aegis of its CFO, Chandra Sahal, who joined the company in November 2025 after a 12-year stint at Wipro as its head of finance. Prior to joining Wipro, Sahal held key finance positions at Infosys, CRISIL, Vee Healthtek and GOAT Brand Labs. In the 11 months since joining LeadSquared, Sahal has helped the company transition its finance department from a paper pusher (closing books and preparing for audits) to a strategic business partner, where it now has a say in building product roadmaps and driving AI investment decisions. For Inc42’s latest initiative, The CFO Code, we spoke with Sahal about LeadSquared's finance function, his take on AI, and how finance leaders can become the CEO’s guiding light towards growth and profitability. Assuring Real-Time Visibility Into LeadSquared’s Financial Health Finance teams have long relied on month-end reports to comprehend the financial health of their respective businesses. Sahal has always been obsessed with changing this. At traditional companies, he found it quite difficult to renovate systems that had been embedded for years and brought no benefit. He saw an opportunity at LeadSquared to build systems and processes agile enough to scrutinise the business on the go. For this, he researched and experimented extensively, eventually zeroing in on using SAP, a leading ERP platform, for core financial records, alongside a CRM to track sales and an in-house system to manage the process from order placement to billing and payment. On top of these three layers, he built an internal analytics cum audit system that compiles relevant data to give management a real-time view of what’s happening underneath. “When an invoice is received, it is then looked at by the controller from a revenue recognition perspective and used by the financial team for reporting. All of this happens in real time. We do not wait until month-end to figure out what the revenue is going to look like,” Sahal said. With this, management gets a view into roughly 30% of the month's revenue in just week 1, 50% by week 2 and 75% by week 3. Therefore, the final week can be spent checking unusual cases and following up with the sales team, instead of trying to scrap the entire month’s numbers, which could be a process prone to errors. Scrapping numbers at the eleventh hour could also jeopardise the finance team’s productivity and create mockery of everyone’s efforts before the CEO. “By month-end, our systems give over 95% visibility into what the final numbers are going to be. This near-real-time reporting assists us in closing books much earlier and getting the management information report (MIS) ready by the eighth of the month,” Sahal said. From Letting AI Do The Grunt Work To Calling The Shots Speaking about how AI has helped Sahal streamline his operations, he shared that everything that is finance at LeadSquared, including reconciliations, identification of journal-entry gaps, variance analysis and budgeting, now has AI behind the wheel. This has helped Sahal do a rolling forecast for the full year by the 10th of every month “So, when I enter a board meeting, I have 80-85% visibility into full year numbers,” he said. So, as someone who keeps an eye on every penny spent in the organisation, how does he analyse the ROI on the company’s AI investments? Sahal has a simple thesis: the return should show up in the team’s productivity. “Faster deployment, faster code checks, quicker product launches and reducing the time spent collecting and reconciling information is where I feel the real ROI lies,” Sahal said. At a time when most organisations think it is a good idea to hire specialised AI talent while bloating token costs, Sahal begs to differ. “The more practical approach here is to train existing employees by investing in their upskilling, be it AI or any other technologies. We, at LeadSquared, have the industry’s best token optimisation practices,” said Sahal. Amid all the AI brouhaha, Sahal does not see AI as a magic bullet but a tool to speed up routine finance work. Tasks that once took days, he said, can now be completed in hours. Similarly, a board presentation that previously took about three days can now be prepared in a few hours. But the bigger shift, according to Sahal, is the unclogged bandwidth his team uses to interpret numbers, challenge assumptions, and focus on decisions that move the needle. Over more than a decade in finance, he has seen several tech cycles emerge and perish. But one thing remains: CFOs need to stay ahead of the tech learning curve. A tech-savvy CFO is a guiding force many organisations lack and don't even know about. “It is the endeavour of such finance leaders that the finance function today has a say at the table,” he said, while illustrating his role as a tech-savvy CFO in the organisation. And ever since the arrival of AI, tracking token usage, the technology stack and utilisation across teams has also become a diligent part of CFOs’ job role, something nobody would have fathomed would be the case a few years ago, according to Sahal. Becoming CEO’s Guiding Force To Defend Margins All said and done, the last 11 months have been anything but a walk in the park for Sahal. He said that when he joined LeadSquared, the company was ailing with challenges that were only patched and never really got solved. Like any other startup, LeadSquared’s focus was centred around growth at all costs. Somewhere along the way, the balance between growth and profitability went for a toss. While such a growth strategy can work for a wide array of startups, the problem is that these fads are hardly sustainable. "Any dollar of new revenue that costs $3 to acquire and churns in a year is not growth. It's a subscription to losing money," Sahal said, suggesting the Rule of 40 as a useful gut check for whether a company's growth rate and profit margin together still make sense. According to the Rule of 40, a company's combined annual revenue growth rate and profit margin should equal or exceed 40% The second major challenge, he noted, sat outside the company’s control. Sahal shared that LeadSquared was once too exposed to geopolitical unpredictability, which often made its decision-making uncertain while investing in a particular market. “A case in point is our US operations that are averse to rupee volatility. With the INR inching closer to the 100 mark, the onus to defend margins falls on us,” said Sahal. To combat such uncertainties in regional compliance, Sahal has helped LeadSquared partner with vendors that either operate locally in those regions or are based in India with expertise in specific markets. This helps the company cut compliance and other expenses, offsetting INR depreciation in many cases. CFO As A Strategic Business Partner When asked about the mistakes that startups on a hyper-growth path often make, Sahal said that for today’s new-age businesses, an integrated tech stack connecting ERP, CRM, order-to-cash, and an analytics layer is a must. Without an integrated stack connecting the ERP, CRM, order-to-cash, and analytics layers, a new invoice flow could derail projections and create chaos. So, does that mean businesses should build a highly stacked finance function from day one? Sahal argued that early stage startups, with a single product and one geography, have the legroom to operate comfortably on Excel and Tally for a couple of years. “The trigger for upgrading should be complexity, whether that comes from multiple entities, products or geographies,” he added. Finally, when we asked what the future holds for CFOs, especially in this time and age of AI, Sahal said the role is undergoing a churn and has become too demanding. Finance leaders who can act and play as strategic business partners will define the next phase of finance. The era of just reporting numbers is over, and finance leaders' new job is to chart the best course for the CEO.

A Suffolk County jury on Friday awarded $6 million in damages to ousted star scientist and former MIT professor David Sabatini, whose career imploded after he was accused by a much younger colleague of inappropriate sexual conduct in his Cambridge research lab.
The verdict was a stark rejection of a high-profile #MeToo claim from Kristin Knouse, a fellow scientist who said Sabatini had subjected her to a coercive relationship and fostered a hostile and sexualized workplace environment in his lab at the world-renowned Whitehead Institute.
The jury of seven women and six men directed Knouse — who had brought her own suit against Sabatini — to pay the $6 million verdict, plus interest, finding she had defamed him and interfered with his ability to make a living.

On 22 November 2021 Paul Bekkers, Ambassador and Permanent Representative of the Netherlands to the United Nations Office at Geneva and Jane Ellison, Executive Director for external relations and governance, met to sign an amendment increasing the Netherlands’ core voluntary contribution (CVC) to the World Health Organization (WHO).
Core voluntary contributions are fully flexible funds that allow WHO to be both agile and strategic in its efforts to achieve the Triple Billion targets and support countries in improving the health and well-being of their populations. Through this increase, the Netherlands raises its core voluntary contribution from US$ 5 million to US$ 10.917 million in 2021. This consolidates its position as a leading donor of flexible funds with with the Netherlands ranking as the 4th largest WHO CVC contributor for 2020 – 2021.
Thanking Ambassador Bekkers for this contribution, Ms Ellison commented “WHO appreciates the longstanding partnership that the Netherlands has with WHO, and we welcome the decision of the Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation to increase the contribution of fully flexible funds to WHO". Reflecting on the current Member States working group on sustainable financing, Ms Ellison noted that the Netherlands has shown by example how providing flexible funds can enable WHO to better fulfil its mandate and work most effectively for the health benefit of all.
The Netherlands is a long-time supporter and partner of WHO. Through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport, the Netherlands funds crucial activities in the areas of water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, tuberculosis, sexual and reproductive health in emergencies, One Health, emergency preparedness, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with a number of top Dutch institutions.

India’s supreme court has demanded accountability from the government and the senior election body over a controversial exercise that has led to the deletion of tens of millions of voters from the electoral roll and prompted mass protests.
Demonstrations have erupted across the country in recent days as opposition parties, student groups and the youth-led Cockroach movement have demanded the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of the Election Commission of India (ECI).
They have accused Kumar of overseeing a direct attack on India’s democracy through an exercise to verify and “purify” the electoral roll in states across the country, which so far has led to 130 million names being removed. In Delhi, hundreds of people were detained as they tried to protest over the weekend.
On Monday, the supreme court issued notices to Narendra Modi’s government, the ECI and Kumar to demand answers over concerns raised about the voter list revision, saying they expected all “to respond in a clear, transparent manner”.
The ECI has claimed the exercise is simply cleaning electoral rolls of duplicate, dead and ineligible names, as well as removing “illegal infiltrators”. However, large numbers of people in Delhi and states such as Bihar and West Bengal say they have been wrongly stripped of their vote and have struggled to get it back.
There are accusations that revision of the electoral rolls particularly targets minorities such as Muslims, who are traditionally not voters of Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The opposition alliance, led by the Congress party, have accused the ECI of being hand in glove with the government over alleged vote “chori” or cheating. Kumar was chosen to head the ECI by a panel headed by Modi.
While the exercise, known as the special intensive revision (SIR), began last year, widespread outrage only recently erupted after a report in the Indian Express newspaper revealed multiple irregularities in the process, which were flagged in more than a dozen internal objections.
The two petitions taken up by the supreme court on Monday alleged that the credibility of the ECI was now in question and called for an independent inquiry into the decisions taken by Kumar in how the SIR process was conducted.
“Deletions of voters have been made in the largest democracy,” said Menaka Guruswamy, a lawyer acting for one of the petitioners. “We have grown up with free and fair elections, that is not the case now.”
Another advocate told the supreme court judges that if action was not taken to ensure that India’s electoral rolls remained fair, “this country will burn”. Another hearing in the cases will be held next week.
The controversies over the ECI have once again driven India’s young people on to the streets in protest, amid rising frustration at the Modi government.
The Cockroach Janata party (CJP), which led massive unrest over the summer that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister, have once again mobilised and called for the resignation of Kumar. Thousands of CJP supporters took to the streets of Mumbai last Friday in protest and another demonstration was held on Saturday in Delhi.
In Delhi, police have been criticised for their heavy-handed approach to stopping any student groups protesting in the heart of the capital. Officers have been accused of sexually assaulting three journalists at the protests over the weekend and hundreds of young people were forced on to police buses. Delhi police said it was investigating the assault claims.

When drugmakers Merck and Moderna announced promising results in August from a late-stage trial of adding an mRNA cancer vaccine to immunotherapy, it was heralded as potentially powerful new way of fighting tumors. But the data don’t show what such a treatment can mean for an individual patient.
At the STAT Summit in Boston on Thursday, a patient in the clinical trial for the treatment, intismeran autogene, told his story virtually. Gary Keblish, a schoolteacher, was diagnosed with melanoma and felt lucky to be in the trial for intismeran and to be in the treatment arm.
We’re including his prepared remarks, including references to the children’s television show “The Magic School Bus” and its teacher, Ms. Frizzle.
My name is Gary Keblish. I am a public school teacher. I guide students on their individual pathways through secondary school and beyond. If their idea is to graduate high school, then I am here to help achieve a successful result. “To the bus!” as Ms. Frizzle would say.
I am here today to uncover my pathway to a successful outcome after a high-risk melanoma diagnosis in 2019.
Mine was a bit of a roller coaster ride, an emotional and physical adventure. My emotional bandwidth started out broad and steadily narrowed as neuropathy issues grew and then widened again as they resolved.
I walked into my dermatologist’s office not exactly holding my head high — I had been remiss. It had been a couple of years since my last visit, and I felt ashamed.
Two excisions later, and I was worried. But a referral to a surgical oncologist left me feeling hopeful. “This time, they’ll get it all,” I thought.
A subsequent referral to an oncologist had me questioning, “What’s all this about?”
After my initial meeting with Jeffrey Weber, deputy director of the Perlmutter Cancer Center at NYU Langone and co-leader of its Clinical Melanoma Program, I was trepidatious. Would I, or wouldn’t I? Should I, or shouldn’t I?
Relief and excitement soon followed. I was lucky; my name was drawn from the hat to be a participant in a clinical trial for a combination of the immunotherapy drug Keytruda and the mRNA cancer vaccine developed by Merck and Moderna. “To the bus!” I found myself thinking.
Undergoing mRNA cancer vaccine and immunotherapy treatment is like a ride on “The Magic School Bus.” It’s an adventure full of emotions and physical changes. “Seatbelts, everyone!”
I am supported in life by happy, healthy, nurturing family and friends. The contingent of medical professionals and support staff, serving during the Covid-19 pandemic no less, proved to be no different, and to them I bow down!
Ongoing visits with Dr. Weber and his colleagues provided me with the guidance and support needed on my journey to renewed health. Together, they set a clear path and encouraged me to maintain focus on the proverbial light at the end of the tunnel. I always knew that I would come out the other end.
What I didn’t anticipate, however, was the physical and mental tension that comes with neuropathy. Tincture of time to the rescue; eventually, I wasn’t discouraged from sitting down for fear of having to get up. But I had to make a conscious decision to be happy again, because neuropathy daily affected my outlook. It taught me to feel less.
It rendered me less physically active than I might have been, and it clouded my judgement. Fortunately, both Dr. Weber and my family were able to read between the lines and push me in the right direction. Oof! That must not have been easy.
At the end of every episode of “The Magic School Bus,” all the students returned safe to the classroom, even after navigating intestines, nostrils, and Mars. So did I.
I’m back in the classroom teaching. In truth, I never had to leave, and it has been six years since my tumor was removed.
I’m thrilled that I got the treatment!
Keep doing what you do best and let the excellent adventures continue. To the bus, everyone!

A major new Lancet Commission has listed 17 interlinked catastrophic threats that could shape global health through 2100. Zooming out to take a bird’s eye view of the possible threats, the Commissioners have counted amongst them — pandemics, obesity, antimicrobial resistance, nuclear conflict, and artificial intelligence.
Driven by the motive to move away from the intense focus on certain domains, the default mode that health care governance and activism has taken so far, the Commission took upon itself the task of freeing the world from being bogged down with single issues, though the benefits of that have been aplenty, the time had come to go beyond.
Launched at the recent World Health Summit in Berlin, the report urges global leaders to stop treating these issues in isolation, and start viewing them as deeply interconnected economic, environmental, and national security challenges. The Commission, “composed of 37 experts in health, economics, security, and technology, uses a foresight-driven, health-focused approach to identify 17 priority threats to human health.” Not a crystal ball gazing exercise, it reportedly assessed threats by calculating the expected cumulative disease burden — measured as amenable disability-adjusted life-years from 2025 to 2100 — that can be reasonably altered through policy intervention. It lists two of these major catastrophic threats: nuclear conflict and malicious use of AI: as having extinction potential. Additional threats include climate change, air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, childhood malnutrition, conventional conflict, declining development assistance for health, high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics, obesity, poor mental health, smoking, and unhealthy ageing.
While the report seeks to identify the threats to human health and survival, and could been seen as doomsdayist, in principle, it is not an apocalyptic forecast of unavoidable doom. The model it uses, as described here earlier, is “amenable” Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) — meaning it measures how many years of healthy life can still be saved if take decisive policy action is launched today. It predicts that high-income nations will see dominant health losses from non communicable risks such as obesity and poor mental health. On the other hand, low-income regions will bear the brunt of childhood malnutrition and the collapse of international aid.
The Commission analysed hundreds of risks across 204 countries and territories. A threat was classified as “catastrophic” if it could account for at least 1 billion DALYs (healthy years lost to illness, disability, or premature death) by 2100. These 17 threats were then categorised into a pyramid of severity, with extinction potential right on top (nuclear conflict and malicious AI) at Category 1, and then cascading down to Category 2 (major catastrophic threats) and Category 2 (environmental, social and health risks).
Although the likelihood of Category 1 dangers remains low, the report says, the scale of harm, should they be realised, would be apocalyptical. The bulk of the threats come under category 2, and include obesity, which represents the largest single potential health loss identified in the report. Addressing high body mass index (BMI), poor diet, and physical inactivity could prevent a massive 23.1 billion DALYs, the report says.
Similarly, improving global access to education could avert 16.1 billion DALYs, it claims. The income gap between the rich and poor represents an amenable health burden equivalent to 25 COVID-19 pandemics, it avers.
The report flags poor mental health rapidly rising in the higher income countries, as also the pressures on societies from ageing populations without adequate health support systems. While smoking, high blood pressure, antimicrobial resistance, alcohol use, child malnutrition and naturally-occurring pandemics are conventionally connected with health; climate change, conventional conflict and air pollution also find a place in the list. The withdrawal of international aid has been flagged: severe cuts to health aid from wealthy nations could cause 1.5 billion DALYs, with sub-Saharan Africa bearing 70% of this blow.
A key, central argument of the report is that these threats amplify one another. For instance, climate change directly exacerbates childhood malnutrition, air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, and mental health issues. Focusing on climate mitigation alone, without strengthening local healthcare infrastructure, again, will fail to stop the downstream health fallout. It also indicates that the estimated 1.89 billion DALYs saved by meeting climate targets is a conservative underestimation, accounting for direct heat and pollution harms. It advises nations to plan for unmodeled “invisible” consequent threats such as mass displacement, geopolitical instability, and drought.
However, the primary criticism against the Commission report is that it skirts acknowledging the current geopolitical crisis, the growing rise of intolerant governments, and the collapse of international collaboration between nations. Even recently, the terse flow of information from Russia where a suspected case of pneumonic plague death was reported highlights the frigidity between nations that prevents seamless global co-operation.
Though it does have a cascade of priorities, in effect the Commission does not attempt to present “a fixed ranking of threats or policy priorities.” Instead, it makes it very clear that the analysis is a dynamic process and findings are amenable to change as and when evidence shifts. But the most important contribution that can be attributed to the Commission is how it managed to pivot the global approach to health threats — to move it from attention and focus on individual subjects to move to a larger consideration of all the complex factors impacting human health. Whether the global axis will now swivel on this pivot remains to be seen, given how complex a task this report has laid out for the world.

Over the summer, I brought the Eye Q along for a couple of weeks of family time in New Hampshire, where we were often eight or more around the table, tweens to octogenarians. Most everyone was intrigued by the toaster, and encouragingly, nobody needed coaching on how to use it.
During the months I had it, it almost always did an acceptable job. It wasn't hard to get the toast right, but—and this is a big but—compared to a regular toaster, the quality of the toast it made was comparable, not superior. To generalize, especially if you compared front to back on a slice, or piece to piece, the Eye Q's toasting was a little uneven and the top of the toast tended to come out darker than the bottom. A noticeable thing, but nothing a polite person would complain about if you set a couple buttery slices in front of them.
On BLT day, I took my nephew Eli on as intern for the afternoon and had him toast seven consecutively darker batches of toast, one per setting, then line them up in order on a sheet pan. The lowest setting was very light, settings two and three were pretty identical, settings four and five were excellent, setting six was mysteriously lighter than setting four, and setting seven was very dark and a little burnt. Two-slot toasters aren't designed for seven back-to-back cycles of toasting, but it did well enough. Store-bought bagels didn't fare particularly well.
Back in Seattle, I unpacked a new Eye Q, and that one had a bad habit of making lighter shades darker than most people would appreciate, so Breville sent another one along to close out the testing. It worked fine, though it tended to get the edges a little toastier than the center; this seemed to be getting worse as testing wound down, so if you’re thinking about buying one of these, perhaps watch the comments for a couple months before pulling the trigger.

A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.
The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.
While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.
The negatives were found more than a decade ago by Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.
Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.
What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, filled with false leads.
A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.
The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.
This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll has been visited dozens of times.
In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said severe weather had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.
“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.
Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said: “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience. This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”
The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is a true MacBook Pro competitor for Windows—if only it weren't for the lack of battery life.

Rating:
7/10

WIRED
The brightest laptop display ever made. MacBook-like design and build quality. Magnetic USB-C port is clever. Performs well unplugged. Music-ready speakers.
TIRED
Battery life can’t compete with the MacBook Pro. Some very popular games aren’t supported yet. Lower-tier RAM options limit AI capabilities.
A new fleet of Windows laptops has arrived, and the Surface Laptop Ultra is its flagship vessel. Ever since it was announced, it's been one of my anticipated laptops of the year. It not only promises to be a beefed-up evolution of the Surface Laptop (a laptop I already really liked), but also debuts a brand-new piece of silicon: the Nvidia RTX Spark N1X "superchip."
The goal is a single laptop that can handle on-device AI, gaming, content creation, and nearly anything else you might throw at it. If that sounds a bit like a MacBook Pro, you're on the right track. But unlike previous attempts to dethrone Apple, the Surface Laptop Ultra is trading blows with the very best. I just wish it had the battery life to truly keep up with the MacBook Pro.
Killer Looks and Sounds
This isn't Microsoft's first foray into a more powerful laptop. The company first tried that in 2021 with the Surface Laptop Studio. At the time, it was the company's answer to the MacBook Pro: a laptop-tablet hybrid oriented toward the growing class of content creators and media professionals. It even came with a discrete graphics card (though not a particularly good one).
The Surface Laptop Ultra rejects the Studio's form-factor experimentation and opts for a more straightforward but polished approach. It's a powerful clamshell laptop that's designed for people who need the extra performance—whether for gaming, content creation, or on-device AI workflows. The ideal demographic, I suppose, is someone who does some of all of that.
At 4.4 pounds, the Surface Laptop Ultra is lighter than the 16-inch MacBook Pro but slightly thicker. It's actually the thickest of all the new N1X laptops, with HP's OmniBook Ultra being the thinnest. The Surface Laptop Ultra appears thinner than it actually is, though, thanks to the inventive way it hides its side vents—so discreet that it's hard to photograph them. The design has just enough small touches like that to make it stand out. There's also a soft dip into the keyboard well, with a unique look that matches the curved lip of the underside vents. I appreciate the modern vibe of the rounded screen corners, though some apps don't account for them well and nearly cut off elements of the Title Bar. One other minor annoyance is that there's no lip for your finger when the device is closed. You can slide your fingernail in between, but in most cases, you'll need two hands to open it.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
But once opened, the Surface Laptop Ultra gets mostly compliments from me. The keyboard is fantastic, as is the extra-large touchpad with haptic feedback. I still dislike the power button placement (why not put it in the top right like every other laptop, as an obvious button, instead of between keys?), and the keycaps could be a bit larger. But overall, I was very happy and comfortable typing and swiping on the laptop.
I was also very pleased with the audio. The aforementioned underside vents also hide the four speakers, which sound fabulous. I was really impressed by how loud, rich, and full these sound, perhaps only second to the 16-inch MacBook Pro (and 15-inch MacBook Air). There's even a hint of bass!
Next to those speakers are lots of useful ports. You have the usual for a laptop of this type, including HDMI, USB-A, a headphone jack, an SD card slot, and three USB4 Type-C ports. The system can support up to three 4K external monitors or a single 5K display. Regardless of the resolution, you're maxed out at a 120 Hz refresh rate. This is slightly behind the latest MacBook Pro, which can support two 5K displays at a 120 Hz refresh rate. But overall, I'm really happy with this mix of connectivity—in fact, it just might be the most well-rounded offering I can imagine.
The Surface Laptop Ultra has a trick up its sleeve involving magnets. The Surface Laptop has long used the Surface Connect, a proprietary magnetic power port that can also plug into Microsoft's Surface Dock. The Surface Laptop Ultra now uses USB-C, and how Microsoft engineered it to make it magnetic is impressive. Disappointingly, only the USB-C port on the right side has this magnetic feature, but all USB-C ports deliver power. You've always been able to buy third-party add-ons that do something similar, but it's a really neat bit of innovation.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
Shines Bright
What I appreciate most about all the Surface Laptop designs is the 3:2 aspect ratio display. I often find that more vertical space comes in handy, especially if you frequently work with documents, spreadsheets, and websites. Combined with the smaller 15-inch touchscreen (compared to the typical 16-incher), this makes for a more compact laptop to carry. At a full inch narrower than the 16-inch MacBook Pro, it fits in a laptop bag a bit more easily.
The screen is extremely sharp, with a pixel density of 257 pixels per inch, just barely exceeding the 16-inch MacBook Pro. Like the MacBook Pro, the Surface Laptop Ultra's display uses Mini-LED backlighting. OLED is far more commonly used in Windows laptops, though, which make up for their lack of brightness with extreme contrast and stronger color performance. But here, the Surface Laptop Ultra clearly has its targets on the MacBook Pro. That may change soon with the rumored launch of the OLED MacBook Pro.
With 1,344 dimming zones, it's the brightest laptop screen ever made. Using my colorimeter, I measured 987 nits of brightness in SDR and 1,945 nits in HDR in a 9 percent window. The result is pretty stunning HDR performance. Games and movies look spectacular on this screen, even without the perfect black levels OLED would provide. Add in the 120-Hz refresh rate, and you have a beautiful display for gaming—especially in more visually immersive, single-player games.
But the screen is highly reflective. This was also true of the standard Surface Laptop, but it's noticeably more reflective than a MacBook. Even with the brightness fully maxed, I still found myself staring at my reflection when viewing websites with dark backgrounds—and that's despite this being unquestionably the brightest screen ever put in a laptop. The reflections are really my only complaint. Otherwise, it's one of my favorite displays I've tested.
The 1080p webcam isn't particularly impressive. It struggles in low light, and the image is pretty noisy. The MacBook Pro webcam has better image processing, brightening faces without overexposing.
The Nvidia N1X Arrives
The Nvidia N1X is a first-of-its-kind chip in Windows laptops. Qualcomm broke open the floodgates in 2024 with its Snapdragon X chips, of which the Surface Laptop was an early adopter. These were primarily an answer to the MacBook Air, and later to what would become the MacBook Neo. But Qualcomm's chips never scaled up to the performance needed to match something like the M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro. That's where the Nvidia N1X steps in.
Both the Snapdragon X and N1X use a System on a Chip (SoC) design, which packages the CPU, GPU, and memory together. It's the same design Apple Silicon chips use, and—importantly—it lets both the CPU and GPU access local memory. This is crucial for enabling the much faster local AI processing, which needs to feed that GPU as much memory as possible. The N1X comes in two configurations: an 18-core system (5,120 GPU cores) and a 20-core system (6,144 GPU cores). Think of these like Apple's M5 Pro and M5 Max, with the main differences being GPU performance and configuration options. For example, if you want 128 GB of memory to hammer home that AI performance, you have to go with the 20-core N1X. In fact, the 18-core model is limited to just 24 GB or 32 GB of RAM (and from what I've seen so far, the Surface Laptop Ultra is the only N1X laptop to be sold with only 24 GB of memory).
I tested the 32 GB model, paired with the higher-end 20-core CPU. In terms of core count, the graphics card in this configuration of the N1X sits right in between the mobile RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 5080. That sounds promising on a laptop this thin, but the core count alone doesn't mean you should expect it to perform at the same level in games. The N1X is capped at 80 watts, which puts a serious limit on in-game frame rates. Gaming as a whole, however, is also handicapped by the nature of this being an Arm-based system. In nearly every game you play, the Surface Laptop Ultra will need to rely on app emulation, which does reduce performance. As Nvidia points out, though, emulation has its biggest impact on the CPU. So, even if applications like games aren't optimized for Arm, they should still run OK. That's exactly what I experienced with the handful of games I tried. You'll need to play most games at medium settings or lower to get decent frame rates, and usually you'll want to play at 1920 x 1200 resolution.
Despite scoring lower than the M5 Max MacBook Pro in 3DMark tests, the Surface Laptop Ultra delivers up to 20 percent faster frame rates in games like Cyberpunk 2077. That's one of the few titles where I could directly compare the two systems. I also tested games like 007: First Light, Marvel Rivals, and Black Myth: Wukong. Seeing so many popular titles run on an Arm system is exciting, and Nvidia is clearly investing heavily in the future of gaming on Arm. However, a list of fairly high-profile multiplayer games aren't compatible yet due to anti-cheat systems, including PUBG, Valorant, and League of Legends. Those are some heavy hitters to be missing at launch, but Nvidia says support is coming. I did run into some glitches, though, such as in 007: First Light, where I couldn't adjust the display resolution in the options menu. That's frustrating as the game otherwise plays well on the system.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
Regardless, these are the most powerful integrated graphics we've seen in a Windows laptop, leaving Intel's Panther Lake X9 in the dust. But if you want the best bang-for-your-buck gaming performance, you're much better off buying a dedicated gaming laptop. The RTX 5060 in a Lenovo LOQ 15, for example, can draw up to 115 watts and deliver up to 22 percent better performance in games like Cyberpunk 2077 and Marvel Rivals. It's also around a thousand dollars cheaper. If gaming were the main point of the Surface Laptop Ultra, that would feel like a disappointment.
But AI performance is the real reason this laptop (and the N1X as a whole) exists, and that's where it shines most. I ran it through Procyon's latest AI benchmarks, which include text generation, image generation, and computer vision. The Surface Laptop Ultra is around 25 percent faster than the Dell XPS 14 at generating text in these lighter models, which only range from 3.5-billion parameters up to 12-billion. Nice to see, but not exactly a dramatic leap ahead. Meanwhile, the Razer Blade 16 with an RTX 5090 (and 32 GB of RAM) posts nearly twice the scores in these tests. That's a more expensive laptop, of course, but it also doesn't go around claiming to be designed for AI.
Clearly, these entry-level configurations of the Surface Laptop Ultra are more for AI dabblers than true enthusiasts. Adding more memory doesn't necessarily solve that problem. I'm also testing a 128-GB version of the HP OmniBook Ultra right now (with the same N1X chip), and I was hoping to see it run some larger models. And while you can certainly load up a 70-billion parameter model in LM Studio, performance on it is very slow. Without more raw GPU compute on hand to speed things up, these more impactful models feel too slow to use daily work. They can, however, still be used in situations that require more complex reasoning, such as for coding, when it's worth waiting for the actual correct answer.
Running local AI models as a computing task that lots of people will want to do is still a question mark for me. As long as free cloud-based models are faster and more useful, I have a hard time seeing people spend extra cash on a computer just to run a model locally. This will undoubtedly change as models improve, but right now, it'll have a limited appeal in that regard. The real benefit might be in agentic AI that gives you access to your local files on your computer and lets you do things that aren't possible in a basic ChatGPT session. I ran a very basic test in LM Studio Bionic, asking it to analyze a folder of local text files and generate a comprehensive summary using Gemma 4 E4B, a 4.5-billion-parameter model. It took 8 minutes to process the request and another 2 minutes to deliver the 853-word response. There's enough performance here to explore and experiment with on-device AI—but the speed may get frustrating. I say all that less to criticize the Surface Laptop Ultra and more just to set expectations on what laptops can do right now.
If the N1X has one serious weakness, it's the CPU. The N1X is 20 to 24 percent slower in CPU benchmarks, in both single-core and multi-core performance tests. Switching from Balanced to Performance Mode in the Windows Settings, however, makes a big difference. It's a 20 percent increase in single-core performance when enabled, a bigger delta than on other laptops. It's fast enough not to be a major bottleneck, but I'd expect to see improvement in future generations of the N1X chip.
At What Cost?
Photograph: Luke Larsen
The Surface Laptop Ultra is not the only RTX Spark laptop launching today. Many of them major Windows laptop manufacturers has one, and they all lean into high-end hardware, including nearly every premium feature possible. I'm still testing some of these models, including the closest competitor, the Lenovo Pro 9n. It has a 15-inch screen, the same N1X chip, and 32 GB of RAM. From what I can tell so far, these laptops perform fairly similarly, within a few percentage points.
But against something like the Razer Blade 16, the Surface Laptop Ultra faces a closer rival. You can buy the RTX 5070 model of the Blade 16 with 32 GB of RAM and a terabyte of storage for $2,999—a similar configuration and price to the Surface Laptop Ultra. They are a similar size and are both well-built. The Surface Laptop Ultra has a sharper and brighter screen, but the Blade 16 has a faster refresh rate. Higher-end configurations of the Razer Blade 16 with the Intel Core Ultra 9 386H even match the Surface Laptop Ultra's battery life, which lasted only 12 hours in a local video playback test. Both devices are what I'd call “do-it-all” laptops. I think the Surface Laptop Ultra is the better overall laptop, largely because of its better keyboard and touchpad. It also has the option to configure it with up to 128 GB of memory, whereas the Blade 16 maxes out at 64 GB. But if you'll spend more time gaming than running local models, the Surface Laptop Ultra (and any of the N1X devices) is the wrong choice.
The Surface Laptop Ultra is also priced nearly the same as the 16-inch MacBook Pro. For $2,999, you get 24 GB of RAM and a terabyte of storage. Both offer a lower-tier performance option, either the M5 Pro or the 18-core N1X. The Surface Laptop Ultra lets you configure the system with 128 GB of memory with only a terabyte of storage, whereas the MacBook Pro forces you into 2 TB. The MacBook Pro still has the edge in polish, whether that's better speakers and a webcam, a less reflective screen, or more comprehensive app support. The major disadvantage, however, is battery life. The MacBook Pro offers a full nine or ten more hours of battery life than the Surface Laptop Ultra. No getting around that. The MacBook Pro also tends to stay a bit quieter. That's part of the magic sauce of what makes the MacBook Pro feel special. The problem has never been that we don't have powerful-enough laptops. The difficulty is in not having to make compromises to achieve that performance, and battery life has always been the most challenging to overcome. Unfortunately, the Surface Laptop Ultra (and the other N1X laptops for that matter) still don't quite make the cut.
And yet, I'm drawn to the brighter screen and taller aspect ratio of the Surface Laptop Ultra, as well as its 15-inch size. I've always found the 16-inch MacBook Pro to be a bit unwieldy. We may be just weeks away from seeing what Apple has in store for a lighter MacBook Pro with a touchscreen. But for now, if you want to dabble in gaming, content creation, and AI workflows, it's probably the best laptop you can buy that isn't a MacBook Pro. And even more importantly, I foresee it starting a new era in Windows laptops that will grown into something truly special in the not-so-distant future.

A British father has avoided a prison sentence for causing the death of his toddler son, who fell from a window in Cyprus.
Joshua Foster appeared at Paphos District Court on Friday for sentencing, where he was fined €3,000 (£2,500).
The 37-year-old, a senior accountant at KPMG, had previously pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.
The two-year-old boy fell nearly 40 feet from the fourth-floor window of the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July.
Prosecutor Chryso Perganti earlier said that the toddler was pronounced dead in hospital a couple of hours after his fall, having suffered multiple skull and bone fractures and damage to his vital organs.
Foster wore a light blue shirt and held back tears as his sentence was read out on Friday by District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.
After the 25-minute hearing, Foster hugged his lawyer before embracing his parents.
The court previously heard that Foster thought the window was closed when he placed the boy on a sill to show him the view and “lost control” of him.
“That fraction of a second will haunt him for the rest of his life,” his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou told judge Froso Christodoulidou during mitigation proceedings.
“This is punishment he and his family will carry with them for the rest of their lives.”
Foster, his wife, two children, and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus in the early hours of 12 July.
After spending the day doing activities, the family returned to their rooms to get ready to go out for dinner.
Foster, his father-in-law and son left their rooms and walked towards the elevator at around 6pm.
As they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside, Mr Alexandrou told an earlier hearing.
Foster pushed the elevator button, placed the child on the windowsill, the boy looked out, and the “inconceivable” happened before Foster had a chance to react, the court was told.
After the incident, Foster was taken to Paphos General Hospital and a blood sample to detect drugs and alcohol was taken.
It was said that during the time of the incident – by this point around six hours earlier – the alcohol concentration in his blood was an estimated 124mg.
The alcohol consumption did not form a significant part of the case against the defendant, and his lawyer said there was no testimony that he was drunk.
The lawyer told the court that Foster has no previous convictions and his remorse “is clear”.
He said he was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident, adding that while grieving his child, he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.

A court in Delhi on Friday sentenced former AAP councillor Tahir Hussain to two years' rigorous imprisonment for abetting rioting during the 2020 northeast Delhi riots, saying he had used his position as an elected representative to facilitate violence instead of maintaining peace and harmony.
Hussain was convicted on October 10 under IPC Section 147 (rioting) read with Section 109 (abetment).
In the Friday verdict, Additional Sessions Judge Parveen Singh held that "the aggravating circumstances substantially outweigh the mitigating circumstances urged on behalf of the convict. No mitigating circumstance of sufficient weight has been established which would justify a lesser sentence".
Special Public Prosecutor Madhukar Pandey sought the maximum sentence for Hussain, arguing this was his second conviction in a riot-related case.
He submitted that Hussain, an elected representative at the time, had a responsibility to maintain peace but instead facilitated the riots by allowing rioters to use his house to attack the public.
The court noted the submission and said Hussain was expected to act as a restraining influence on people in a communally charged environment.
"Instead of discharging this responsibility, the convict has been found to have abetted the riots by providing his house, which was the highest point in the locality, as a place from where the rioters could attack people and damage property," the judge said.
The court said Hussain's position, which ought to have been used to prevent violence, was instead used to facilitate it, warranting a sentence that reflected the gravity of the offence, and served as a deterrent.
Rejecting the defence's plea for leniency, the court said the absence of Hussain's physical participation in the rioting mob could not substantially reduce his culpability. "The mere fact that the prosecution did not prove active participation of the convict in the riot, does not dilute the gravity of his conduct, for the hand that guides is as guilty, if not more, as the hand that acts."
The court also rejected Hussain's claim that he was helpless when a mob allegedly forcibly occupied his house and that he had made several calls to the police control room. It noted that he had failed to prove the alleged calls or produce other evidence in support of his defence.
The judge further noted that Hussain had not filed any complaint against known or unknown persons alleging they had forcibly occupied his house and used it to attack people during the riots.
The court said the aggravating circumstances substantially outweighed the mitigating circumstances put forward by the defence, sentencing him to two years' rigorous imprisonment, and imposing a fine of ₹10,000.
Hussain was convicted for allowing a mob to use the terrace of his house on Main Karawal Nagar Road to pelt stones at passersby and nearby properties on February 24, 2020.
In its October 10 judgment, the court had acquitted him of more serious charges, including rioting while armed with deadly weapons, theft, mischief and trespass. It also acquitted nine other accused, holding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case against them.
This is Hussain's second conviction in connection with the February 2020 riots. On July 31, a Delhi court sentenced him and four co-convicts to life imprisonment for the murder of Intelligence Bureau officer Ankit Sharma.
Hussain was expelled by the AAP in February 2020, hours after an FIR was registered against him in connection with the riots. He joined the AIMIM in 2024 and contested the 2025 Delhi Assembly elections on its ticket, but lost.
The riots in northeast Delhi in February 2020 left 53 people dead and caused extensive damage to property.

Journalist to be crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
- Published
Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country.
For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster.
But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country.
Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.
Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34.
The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned.
A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast.
He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king.
But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward.
According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne.
But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma.
The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son.
Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected.
However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions.
The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome.
Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family".
"As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay".
The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute".
"No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X.
But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind".
While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan".
A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources.
Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965.
Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs.
According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.
After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development.
"I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said.
Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead.
The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala.
The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s.
The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty.
Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him.
The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend.
The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X.
Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage.
His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum".
The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer.
Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300 km (186 miles) from Kampala.
He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999.
He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation.
The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader.
After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people".
His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition.
"I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC.
She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it."
She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man".

EV sales stalled in 2026 but not because Americans don’t want them, researcher says
The data doesn’t support the claim that electric vehicle sales stalled in 2026 because Americans don’t want them

Within three months of the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, 2026, the average price of gasoline for American drivers climbed from US$2.94 to $4.35 a gallon. If there was ever a moment for Americans to switch to electric vehicles, this was it.
From March to May 2026, in fact, sales of hybrid electric vehicles were 18% higher than over the same months in 2025.
But sales of fully electric vehicles were 16% lower from March to May 2026 compared with the same months in 2025. Some observers took that as evidence that high gas prices alone wouldn’t push Americans toward fully electric cars, but that conclusion misses half the story.
I study car buyers and their preferences, and there is an important distinction between what consumers want and what they can actually buy. Sales reveal what cars people actually bought, but not necessarily what they actually wanted.
When the supply of some kinds of cars can’t keep up with demand, prices rise, and that’s exactly what happened for electric vehicles in 2026.
An industry in retreat
In 2026, hybrids and all-electric vehicles faced the same jump in demand from the oil crisis. While there were plenty of hybrids available to meet that demand, the same was not true for EVs.
Hybrid production had been growing for years, led by Toyota, which sells about half of the hybrids bought in the United States. As a result, even as sales surged, hybrid inventories on dealer lots were 19% higher in March 2026 than they had been a year earlier.
However, EV production had been in retreat since the tax and spending law President Donald Trump signed in July 2025 ended federal tax credits for EVs. Buyers had been able to get up to $7,500 for new EVs and $4,000 for used ones, but that ended after Sept. 30, 2025.
Automakers responded by cutting back their EV production. General Motors laid off more than 3,400 workers at its EV and battery plants and shifted its Tennessee plant to make batteries for energy storage, not cars. Ford wrote off $19.5 billion from its EV business, ended production of the all-electric F-150 Lightning and converted a Tennessee EV plant to build gas-powered trucks.
Buyers, for their part, rushed to beat the tax credit deadline, pushing EVs to 11.3% of new vehicle sales in September 2025. But by November 2025, after the tax credits ended, their share dropped to 4.3%.
As 2026 progressed and gas prices began to rise, so did EV demand. New EV inventories declined, shrinking from about 130 days of supply in the first quarter of 2026 to 78 days by August – just two days above the supply level of gas-burning cars.
Discounts on new EV models shrank too. My analysis of online listings from marketcheck.com shows the median new EV was listed 9.8% below sticker price in February. By April, the median discount was 6.6%, and 4.7% in June. That’s a sign that dealers saw rising demand, not inventory to clear.
A run on used electric vehicles
Before the war, prices for used electric vehicles were still drifting down in the wake of the expired used EV federal tax credit. After the war began, they climbed 13% through late June 2026. For a typical used electric vehicle, that’s about $3,500 more.
Other data sources point in the same direction. Recurrent, a company that reports on batteries and used EVs, found that the price of a used 2023 Chevrolet Bolt rose almost 20% from January to June 2026.
And inventories of used electric vehicles dropped too, with only 31 days of supply in May, 23% below the year before.
A costly misreading
None of this means the electric vehicle market is healthy. High prices and uncertain access to charging stations are real stumbling blocks for people who are thinking about buying an EV.
But the data doesn’t support the claim that electric vehicle sales stalled in 2026 because Americans don’t want them. Rather, the sales stalled because there weren’t enough EVs available to buy – and there were plenty of hybrids as an alternative.
The distinction matters because automakers have treated a change in the policy landscape as a change in consumer demand, leading to shortages with real costs.
The average new car now sells for about $50,000 and the average new electric vehicle for about $55,000, according to Kelley Blue Book, a company that tracks car prices.
The current situation leaves drivers exposed to the volatility of oil prices with fewer alternatives. The U.S. is the world’s largest oil producer, yet a war in the Persian Gulf raised gas prices significantly in just three months. Oil trades on a global market, so American drivers pay global prices.
Seven months into the war, the pressure on drivers is still going full throttle. Oil was still above $100 a barrel in mid-October, and diesel hit a record $6.52 a gallon on Sept. 22.
Electric vehicle sales haven’t caught up. Argonne’s data show 86,000 of them sold in August, fewer than the 101,000 sold in May, while hybrid sales stayed above 216,000 a month all summer.
A look ahead
Rather than move to increase electric vehicle supply and make them more affordable, federal policy continues to hinder the U.S. electric vehicle sector.
The fuel economy rule released Sept. 28, 2026, loosens efficiency requirements for gas-powered vehicles and in 2028 ends a system that let automakers that beat the standards – mostly EV makers – earn credits for exceeding them and sell those to automakers that fell short. That means automakers will have fewer regulatory incentives to produce EVs going forward.
Regulators say buyers will save $1,289 on the purchase price of a new gas-powered vehicle from reduced engineering and manufacturing costs to make less efficient engines. But the same analysis estimates drivers will spend about $1,600 more on gas over the life of the car, and that’s using fuel price forecasts well below today’s prices. Economists say the administration’s math does not properly account for those fuel costs.
The U.S. has also effectively shut out Chinese automakers, even though nearly three-quarters of the world’s electric cars are built in China. In 2024, Chinese car buyers could choose from over 130 EV models priced under $40,000; American buyers had just four EV models under that threshold. Beyond tariffs of more than 100% on EVs made in China, a Commerce Department rule bars cars from Chinese-linked automakers starting with model year 2027, even if they are built in the U.S. A bill pending in Congress would widen the ban, blocking Chinese investment in U.S. auto factories altogether.
As long as gas stays expensive, the gap between the electric vehicles Americans want and the electric vehicles dealers can sell them is likely to remain. Decisions such as ending the tax credit, rolling back fuel economy standards and banning Chinese technology all make it harder to build them, which means Americans will continue to have fewer affordable electric vehicles to choose from.

Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall

A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window at a hotel in Cyprus has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.
The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.
Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced on Friday morning.
He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."
The auditor, his wife, two children and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident.
They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.
At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son walked towards an elevator and was playing with his son, said his lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou.
The court was told that as they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
It was said that Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react.
Alexandrou told an earlier hearing, which took place on October 6, that Foster's life "changed forever" from that moment.
Police were called to reports of a child falling "under unknown circumstances" at about 18:40.
The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".
While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him - and his lawyer said there was no testimony he was drunk.
Alexandrou said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
The court heard the window was 2.85m (9.3ft) wide and 1.2m (3.9ft) high.
In a statement outside court, Alexandrou described his client as an "incredible father".
"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."
He added Foster was "very emotional" after the sentencing and the family needed time to grieve properly.
"They have been in a defence mode during this procedure," Alexandrou said.

During her Oct. 13 debut, new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia answered three questions from outlets typically friendly to U.S. President Donald Trump, stumbling over parts of those answers, and ended the press conference after just 14 minutes.
Many social media users mocked Zacharia's performance afterward. Some posts included a video of a young beauty pageant contestant (archived), supposedly Zacharia, struggling to answer a question.
The video, along with the claim that it showed Zacharia, was shared in several popular X posts (archived) and on Instagram (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and sent emails wondering if the video really was of Zacharia.
The woman in the video was not Zacharia, but instead a 2007 Miss Teen USA contestant, Caitlin Upton. Therefore, we've rated this claim miscaptioned.
The video has gone viral before, as the internet culture website Know Your Meme has documented, and many of those who shared it with a caption identifying the woman as Zacharia appeared to have done so jokingly. However, responses to the posts indicated that at least some people unfamiliar with the video believed the captions were serious.
The question Upton, who was Miss South Carolina Teen USA that year, struggled to answer was about a large number of Americans being unable to identify the U.S. on a world map. She didn't really answer the question; Upton stumbled over her words while referencing people in the U.S. who didn't have maps, education, South Africa, Asian countries and building up the future.
Video of Upton's attempt to answer the question has been available on YouTube (archived) since Aug. 24, 2007, the date of the competition.
A few days later, Upton appeared on the "Today" show and said she was overwhelmed when she was asked the question and made a mistake. While on the show, she gave a more focused answer to the question she was originally asked during the contest:
Personally, my friends and I, we know exactly where the United States is on a map. I don't know anyone else who doesn't. If the statistics are correct, I believe there should be more emphasis on geography in our education so people will learn how to read maps better.
Several years later, Upton spoke publicly about how Upton struggled following the viral fame of her appearance in the Miss Teen USA contest. In 2015, she told Teen Vogue that she suffered from depression and even suicidal thoughts due to bullying, harassment and hate directed her way both online and offline.
In 2024, Vice President JD Vance, then a candidate for the office, posted the clip again to X to mock then-Vice President Kamala Harris for her performance in a CNN interview. At that time, Vance was criticized for bringing attention back to a moment that had Upton contemplating suicide for a time, according to Vanity Fair.
At the time Upton competed in the pageant, she was 18 years old.
In 2007, Zacharia was graduating from Pepperdine University, putting her outside the age range of the Miss Teen USA contest for that year.

Ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party-led protest in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, and on the day of the protest on October 10, Hindu Rakhsha Dal (HRD) chief Pinky Chaudhary and its members posted a series of videos on social media platforms inciting violence against the demonstrators. Strikingly, several such videos were made in the presence of police.
In the clips, Chaudhary and other HRD members urged “Hindutva supporters” to “set the protesters’ minds right” while using communal and inflammatory rhetoric. He described those planning to demonstrate as “anti-national” and “anti-Hindu”.
Despite reports claiming that Chaudhary was placed under house arrest, he continued to issue calls for HRD members and other “kattar Sanatanis” to reach Jantar Mantar and confront the protesters ahead of Saturday’s protest and on the very day.
Moreover, a video posted by News Capsule on October 10, the day of the protest, showed a group of men dragging, beating and physically assaulting young protesters near Kamla Market. Alt News identified one of the alleged assailants as Ravindra Govinda, a member of Hindu Raksha Dal.
Govinda shatred a clip on his Facebook account in which he declared “support for the Delhi police in treating the protesters” while identifying himself as a member of HRD. “…As we, the Hindu Raksha Dal, had declared, we will stand with Delhi police in treating these cockroaches…,” he says, while continue to issue threats against the agitators.
Govinda was also seen in a video posted by Pinky Chaudhary, claiming that HRD members were fighting against CJP protesters to “protect Sanatanis”.
One of the goon seen beating the kid is Ravindra Govinda. Member of Hindu Raksha Dal. He was detained in the morning. Look how Police is handling the goons. https://t.co/nONEQVhY4f
— Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear) October 10, 2026
‘We Will Beat Them With Sticks’
On October 9, Chaudhary posted a video in which he stood alongside a group of men carrying batons and openly threatened physical violence against protesters expected to assemble at Jantar Mantar the following day.
Chaudhary declared in the video: “Laath bajake inke pichwade thik karne, dimag thik karne jayenge” (We will beat them with sticks and set their minds right). He added: “Jo log iss desh ko Islam meh le jane ki galat fehmi rakhte hai” (Those who are under the misconception that they can turn this country into an Islamic nation.) He said HRD members and staunch Sanatani believers will “handle” all those who have the “insect of secularism” in their head.
