Threats Continued Despite Police Intervention
A few hours later on October 9, Chaudhary uploaded another video claiming that police had arrived at his residence and placed him under house arrest. However, even as he stood in front of several police personnel, he continued to issue threats.
In this video, he declared that several members of HRD had already reached Delhi and were prepared to confront the demonstrators. Referring to Jantar Mantar as an “adda of terrorists”, he reiterated that HRD members would use their batons against those he described as opponents of Sanatan Dharma. “Jitne Sanatani virodhi hai, unke pichwade laal karke hi wapas ayenge” (We will return only after making the backsides of all those who oppose Sanatanis red), he said. He further described HRD members as warriors who are “neither afraid to die nor to kill.”
Chaudhary portrayed the outfit as pro-police and pro-nationalist, claiming that its members wanted to teach the protesters a lesson for allegedly misbehaving with police personnel. He also accused CJP supporters of insulting Hindu deities, attempting to establish an Islamic state, and acting against the nation. “India is safe till date, only because Sanatani warriors are here,” he said.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Friday said the whereabouts of its founder Abhijeet Dipke remained unknown following his detention by Delhi Police, while the All India Students’ Association (AISA) said its president Neha Bora had been traced to the RK Puram police station after hours of uncertainty over her location.
The detentions took place ahead of the ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ protests called by the CJP against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls and voter lists.
AISA alleged that Bora had been moved between multiple locations across Delhi for around five hours before she was traced to RK Puram police station. The organisation further claimed that lawyers who reached the police station around midnight were not allowed to meet her and that police had refused to provide her medicines despite knowing she had been unwell for several days.
Quick answers to key questions
They were detained ahead of the CJP’s ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ protest in central Delhi. Police cited restrictions in force in Connaught Place, while CJP and AISA said the activists were on their way to join the protest.
AISA said Bora was traced to the RK Puram police station after being moved between locations in Delhi. The organisation also said lawyers who went there were not allowed to meet her.
CJP said Dipke had been taken to an undisclosed location and that party members had lost contact with him. The party asked Delhi Police to disclose his whereabouts and the grounds for his detention.
Police cited prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS in Connaught Place and said the march had not received permission. Central Park was also closed to the public on October 16 and 17.
Delhi Police said around 150 people had been detained as part of efforts to maintain law and order and ensure smooth traffic movement.
“Why is Delhi Police holding Neha until midnight in a police station? When will Neha be released? Why is a women student leader being put in a police station at midnight?” AISA asked.
The CJP alleged that Dipke had been taken to an undisclosed location and that party members had lost contact with him. It also claimed he was not being allowed to speak to lawyers.
“The Delhi Police has taken Abhijeet Dipke to an undisclosed location. We have lost contact with him. He is not being allowed to talk to lawyers,” the party said in a post on X.
“Abhijeet was just walking out of his home with a Tiranga in his hand! How can walking with a tiranga be a crime?” it asked, adding that the detentions would not deter people from joining the protests.
The party also wrote to the station house officer of Mandir Marg police station, seeking information about Dipke’s location and the legal provisions invoked for his preventive detention.
In the letter, CJP leader Rohan Deshpande said the party had received no information about the police station or facility where Dipke was being held.
He urged Delhi Police to disclose Dipke’s whereabouts, the grounds for his detention and the identity of the officer responsible for his custody. The party also sought assurances that he would be allowed to contact colleagues and access legal counsel.
CPI(ML) Liberation said in a statement on Friday night that Bora was initially taken to an Anti-Narcotics Task Force facility in the South-West district before being shifted elsewhere. The party said it had deployed a legal team to follow up on her detention and demanded the release of Bora, Dipke and other detained protesters.
CPI(M) Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas said an AISA representative had informed him that Bora was picked up at Mandi House while travelling to join the protest.
“Taken away alone, without her phone, her whereabouts are now unknown,” Brittas said in a post on X.

CJP legal head Ratna Singh also demanded that police disclose the whereabouts and legal status of both activists and inform their families and lawyers.

Central Park was closed for two days amid heavy barricading and the deployment of security personnel.
Despite police denying permission for the CJP’s ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ march at Connaught Place, hundreds of party supporters and student activists staged flash protests in central Delhi on Friday evening. Carrying the national flag and raising slogans of “Jai Hind”, protesters walked through parts of Connaught Place before dispersing and regrouping at different locations. Some also sang the national anthem.
Meanwhile, AISA and Left party members demonstrated near Mandi House, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, a rollback of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the withdrawal of the 2023 Election Commissioner Appointment Act.
The CJP had called the march after party activists Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to five days of judicial custody for allegedly trespassing at Jantar Mantar, which has been denotified as a designated protest venue.

Zelensky warned Trump’s diesel deal puts money in ‘Putin’s pocket’ and can never offset the impact of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz

Volodymyr Zelensky’s relationship with Donald Trump reached a new low on Friday after the US president repeatedly criticised the Ukrainian president and agreed new trading deals with Russia.
In a thinly veiled swipe at Trump, Zelensky thanked the “real leaders” in Europe for their backing of Ukraine, adding it was crucial to count on support from allies who had stood by his country since the beginning of the conflict.
It came after the US president announced a new diesel deal with Vladimir Putin, US Starlink intelligence feeds were restricted in Ukraine and Trump claimed it was easier to deal with the Russian president than Zelensky.
Trump also described the Ukrainian bombing of Russia oil refineries as a “disgrace”, despite the fact that Russia has been targeting Kyiv and other cities all week after the US president’s so-called “energy ceasefire”.
Speaking a European Union summit in Brussels, Zelensky said he had heard “support and only support” from his partners in Europe after relations with the US president deteriorated. He added that Putin was only playing games and his attempts to end the war were nothing more than “parody”.
Zelensky was blindsided by Trump’s announcement that Washington would lift sanctions on Russia to trade diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices ahead of the midterm elections next month.
"This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets,” the Ukrainian told a press conference. “But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”
Zelensky has also said his military advisers received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future, and reported on Friday that Starlink services are still not fully restored.
Ukraine’s leadership has been alarmed by disruptions to the satellite system, reporting trouble flying terminals with a vital role in intercepting Russian attacks.
A US official has denied that Trump ordered a deliberate slowdown of Starshield, and Trump said this week intelligence sharing with Ukraine continued, but Musk took to X to say any limits on the system would be controlled by the US government, not him.
It also emerged on Friday that Trump is reportedly considering lifting sanctions on Russia’s so-called “shadow fleet” of oil tankers in another to the Ukrainian war effort.
A Treasury department official told the FT that the administration was considering allowing the sale of blacklisted vessels to “legitimate” operators and lifting sanctions so they could trade in the global market.
And Vladimir Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said on Friday that Russia and the US will soon announce new joint initiatives beyond the recently agreed diesel deal.
Dmitriev said the two countries were discussing joint data centre projects, including facilities that could use electricity generated by Russian nuclear power plants.
In Brussels, Zelensky was asked by a reporter whether he believed Trump was scapegoating him for issues in the US. The Ukrainian president only looked down at his podium, grimaced and said: “That is my answer.”
Earlier, Trump hit out at Zelensky for resuming strikes on Russian oil refineries this week, after Kyiv accused Moscow of not complying with Trump’s so-called ceasefire.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace,” the US president told Newsmax.
Three people were killed in Kharkiv on Friday as Russian drone strikes continued to pound the city, while attacks elsewhere left hundreds of thousands of people without power.
Zelensky said at the EU summit that the war would likely cost Ukraine another €155bn next year, and that Kyiv would need €70bn in support from Europe.
Estonian prime minister Kristen Michal told Reuters that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.
“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” he said. "We have a lot of gaps to fill, and this is a European mission to fill the gaps that Ukraine needs.
“Because always, at the start (and) at the end of every conversation, people need to be reminded that we are sitting in a warm room, lights are on, heating is on, the coffee is warm, and we cannot get tired of the war in Ukraine, because they are fighting ... for us.”

Judge throws out child sex abuse charges against actor Timothy Busfield
- Published
A judge in the US state of New Mexico has thrown out charges against Emmy-winning actor Timothy Busfield on Friday, saying there were issues with how prosecutors presented the case.
The West Wing and Field of Dreams actor was indicted in February on four counts of criminal sexual contact of a child. Busfield has denied all allegations.
The charges stemmed from accusations brought by child actors he worked with on the Fox series The Cleaning Lady, which he directed and produced.
The judge said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner". The district attorney's office said it is evaluating options on how to move forward.
- Actor Timothy Busfield indicted on child sexual contact charges 
  - Published6 February
State District Judge Joseph Montano granted the defence's motion to dismiss the indictment on Friday, citing mistakes that undermined the grand jury process.
"Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed," a spokesperson for the Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney in Bernalillo County told the BBC on Friday.
The BBC has contacted a legal representative for Busfield.
The actor surrendered to state authorities in January when a warrant was issued for his arrest. A judge later ordered his release pending trial.
Busfield had originally been taken into custody in Albuquerque on two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and one count of child abuse.
The indictment against him, reviewed by the BBC, said that on or between 19 October 2022 and 10 September 2023, Busfield "touched or applied force to the intimate parts" of one of the unnamed boys when he was under the age of 13.
The Thirtysomething actor's defence team submitted more than 70 letters from people vouching for his character and said that he underwent and passed a polygraph test pertaining to the allegations against him.
In a warrant for Busfield's arrest, prosecutors had said the parents of the boys alleged that he groomed and sexually abused the youngsters while working on The Cleaning Lady.
Authorities claimed the boys referred to Busfield as "Uncle Tim" and alleged that he "would tickle them on the stomach and legs". Both boys told authorities they were touched inappropriately for years, his arrest affidavit stated.
Busfield's lawyers had said the actor was being accused as an act of revenge after the children were fired from the series, which angered their mother.

Elon Musk has quietly financed a major canvassing operation to help Republican candidates in the midterm elections that rivals his effort in the 2024 presidential election, according to federal filings posted Thursday night. To monitor the trillionaire’s overall influence on November’s elections, WIRED created a live-updating tracker that pulls federal filings daily.
The Musk-aligned America PAC has spent $76.7 million in the third quarter of 2026, $35.8 million of which has been spent on a field operation to drive turnout among President Donald Trump's core base across all seven Senate battleground states and a number of House races, the filings show.
That compares with the roughly $45 million America PAC had spent on putting together a field operation at the same point in the 2024 cycle, when the super PAC effectively ran the vast majority of canvassing for Trump's presidential campaign.
In short, Musk has assembled a presidential-level field operation this midterm cycle, underscoring the extent to which he has taken over the get-out-the-vote effort for the party and created something of a shadow Republican National Committee. With three weeks until Election Day, the total contributions are only set to rise even higher.
Canvassing has been America PAC’s largest expense, ahead of the $23.7 million it spent on a combination of digital ads mostly attacking Democrats, campaign literature, and phone bank efforts.
But in an effort to save Republicans' Senate majority, Musk also gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting the GOP's candidates in that chamber. The same amount appears to have been funneled into Texas PAC, which was registered with the FEC in August 2026 and is backing embattled Republican candidate and Texas attorney general Ken Paxton.
Musk has been particularly focused on the Senate race in Texas this midterm cycle, where he has extensive personal and business interests. Musk lives near Austin and his businesses SpaceX and Tesla are based in the state. Musk accounted for nearly 60 percent of the $273 million that the Senate Leadership Fund raised for Texas PAC.
The stunning war chest that Musk has unleashed into all seven battleground Senate races and, to a lesser degree, a number of competitive House races, makes him the largest known donor in the midterms among both Republicans and Democrats.
Since its inception, America PAC has relied primarily on outside firms to conduct paid canvassing, in which people are hired to knock on the doors of likely Trump or Republican voters to remind them to register to vote and vote early.
The super PAC has used mostly the same contractors as in the 2024 cycle, the filings show. The biggest canvassing contract went to Blitz Canvassing, a subsidiary of the political affairs firm GP3 Partners, which helped stand up America PAC.
The other vendors listed in America PAC’s filings were the firms Patriot Grassroots LLC, The Synapse Group, In Field Strategies, Echo Canyon Group, Threshold Strategies, and GEG Strategies LLC. All but the last two also worked for America PAC in 2024.
Going into the final stretch of campaigning, America PAC has more than $12 million remaining, though Musk, the richest man in the world, may contribute more to his PAC as required.
America PAC has spent in 40 races in 17 states since July. The Texas Senate race drew the largest share, in which Musk’s team has spent $15.3 million attacking Democrat James Talarico and $3.5 million supporting Paxton.
The super PAC has also spent about $5.3 million attacking Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio’s Senate race against Republican Jon Husted and $3.5 million attacking Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running against Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, according to the WIRED tracker.

On Oct. 8, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth confirmed (archived) reports that the U.S. military was planning to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, which is currently set for Dec. 3.
A military jury sentenced Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, to death in 2013 after it found him guilty of killing 13 people and injuring 30 more during a shooting rampage at the Army's Fort Hood post in Texas in 2009. U.S. President Donald Trump approved (archived) Hasan's death sentence on Oct. 2, clearing the path for his execution.
On Oct. 8, Hegseth shared an X post by CBS News that read:
The U.S. military plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, when he faces a firing squad on Dec. 3, a Pentagon official said.
Hegseth wrote, "Correct."
One day later, on Oct. 9, the Associated Press reported that Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on whether the Pentagon would actually livestream the execution. "I don't know that that's actually going to happen," he reportedly said. About a week after Hegseth's initial confirmation, on Oct. 15, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that Hasan's execution would go ahead "but this event will not be streamed."
Following Hegseth's confirmation, discussion abounded online about whether executing Hasan in such a public manner was legal (archived, archived, archived). Snopes readers also contacted us about the legality of the planned livestream.
The military justice system, which is separate from the civilian justice systems in the U.S., carried out Hasan's trial and sentencing in 2013. On Oct. 5, Hegseth's assistant secretary for public affairs Sean Parnell wrote on X (archived) that the Army's firing squad would execute Hasan, meaning his execution would be governed by Army regulations.
At the time of this writing, the U.S. Army did not have regulations explicitly allowing it to livestream an execution. Rather, Army Regulation 190–55, which covers procedures for military executions, included requirements that would likely hinder the Army's ability to provide a public livestream.
Trump wrote on Truth Social on Oct. 15 that the "immediate families" of Hasan's victims could still view the execution in person in accordance with current Army regulations.
Gary Barthel, a former U.S. Marine Corps officer and managing partner at the Military Law Center, told Snopes on Oct. 9 that if the Army wanted to legally livestream Hasan's execution, officials would have to either seek an exemption to regulation 190-55 from the Office of the Provost Marshal General as laid out in the regulation itself or amend the existing regulation to allow livestreaming. 
We contacted the Department of the Defense to ask if it was planning to do either of these things and await a reply.
Because the legality of livestreaming Hasan's execution was potentially subject to change, we leave this claim unrated.
What Army regulation says
Chapter 2-5 of regulation 190-55 lists who may and may not witness a military execution. According to the chapter, no person younger than 18 years old may witness an execution and the Army must approve the list of witnesses beforehand.
Those two stipulations could make it difficult for the Army to provide a public livestream without violating its own regulations because it would have to vet the audience's age. Hosting a truly public livestream would make it impossible to approve a list of "witnesses" ahead of the execution because people might log in to watch on the day without registering beforehand.
Barthel told Snopes via phone on Oct. 9:
The Army is required to follow its regulations. If the Army wants to stream this execution they need to change the regulations to allow it. And, either way, I would anticipate that there is going to be some efforts to stop it.
Barthel said that Hasan's defense team could still ask a civilian court to stop the execution and live stream by filing a habeas corpus petition. Such a petition allows a detainee to challenge their detention in court.
Would public execution be 'cruel and unusual punishment'?
Daniel Maurer, an associate professor at the Claude W. Pettit College of Law at Ohio Northern University, told Snopes that livestreaming Hasan's execution could raise constitutional concerns that would ultimately play out in court.
Hasan's defense could bring up such constitutional concerns as part of a habeas petition. Maurer said via email on Oct. 9 that Hasan's defense could argue that being executed on livestream amounted to "cruel and unusual punishment," which is banned by the U.S. Constitution's 8th Amendment. Maurer wrote (links ours):
The remaining legal issue is maybe more complicated and would need courts to resolve it: does such a practice violate Hasan's 8th Amendment protection from "cruel and unusual punishments?" - this protection is also stated in the UCMJ, article 55, and Army Regulation 190-47 ("The Army Corrections System") so it applies to prisoners already confined, not just defendants at court-martial sentencing.
In order to establish whether livestreaming Hasan's execution amounted to cruel and unusual punishment, the courts might apply the "Evolving Standard" test, according to Maurer. The test allows courts to consider whether a punishment is cruel and unusual under current societal standards, rather than according to standards at the time the Constitution was written.
Cornell Law School's Legal Information Library wrote that "in the context of capital punishment, the Court has generally viewed the Eighth Amendment to prohibit punishments that 'involve the unnecessary and wanton infliction of pain.'"
Though livestreaming may not inflict "unnecessary and wanton" pain, Maurer said there are other factors at play:
Given that federal law prohibits photographic or other visual or audio recording of an execution of any other civilian federal prisoner, this is strong evidence that our own federal government (of which the DoD is of course a part) would consider it to be "cruel and unusual," and thus would be an 8th Amendment violation.
Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law, called the decision to livestream Hasan's execution "sick-making" when speaking to Snopes on Oct. 9. He previously told DRM News that a habeas petition could postpone Hasan's execution past the end of the Trump administration as it progressed through the civilian court system. That means Hasan's execution and any potential livestream could be halted by an administration without "the same penchant for executions," Fidell reportedly told the Associated Press.
It was unclear whether Hasan would file a habeas petition. The Associated Press reported that Hasan had begun his 2013 trial by firing his lawyers and telling jurors that he was the gunman in the 2009 shooting. The outlet reported that this move "convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan's only goal was to get a death sentence." It remained unclear whether Hasan's goal remained the same in 2026.
The nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center wrote that Hasan's execution would be the first military execution in the U.S. since 1961.
The Washington Post, citing the center, reported that the last high-profile public execution of any type in the U.S. took place in 1936. Another public execution took place the year after.
For further reading, Snopes compiled 17 claims about the death penalty that we've investigated over the years.

The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”
Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.
Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.
She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”
Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.
“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”
Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.
Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.
The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”
Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.
Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.
“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”
Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.
In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”
Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

Mauritius reels from worst riots in decades after woman shot by police
- Published
Police in Mauritius imposed an overnight curfew overnight to quell the worst riots to break out on the Indian Ocean island in decades.
Peaceful protests over water shortages and the high cost of living that started a week ago erupted into violence on Friday when a woman was shot and wounded by police at a roadblock.
The circumstances of the shooting are not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody.
Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam ordered the curfew on Tuesday, warning against those "acting against the interests of the country", which is a tourism and financial services hub.
"Those who have carried out these actions will have to face the very heavy consequences warranted by their anti-patriotic acts," he said in an address to the nation.
Protesters burned tyres and blocked roads as the unrest escalated over the weekend, with police stations and other public infrastructure properties being vandalised.
The mayhem prompted the closure of schools and public transport, with foreign embassies issuing alerts warning its nationals to be cautious.
Despite the curfew, police said there had been several incidents overnight and some arrests.
But the police assured people that by Wednesday morning traffic was again moving throughout the island and said people should resume their normal activities.
When protests over the shortage of water initially started, the government had responded proactively by providing more water to households, according to Zoë McCathie, an analyst at South Africa-based Signal Risk.
The escalation had presented a more "unusual situation for the country's security situation", with the government resorting to closing schools and imposing a curfew, she told the BBC's Newsday programme.
"Protests to this scale and to this extent haven't been seen… since around 1999. So the government's response to this in that case is logical and is necessary," she said.
While the government had managed to "curtail the worst of the unrest" there was still a possibility that protests could return in some areas, with water shortages expected to persist until the rainy season in December, she said.
The cabinet is due to meet on Wednesday afternoon to reassess the situation and decide on the next steps.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Fourteen boxes are piled in front of my desk, stacked around me like a cardboard fort. Inside one is a Form Studio 1, the new, affordable, consumer-focused 3D printer Formlabs just announced.
David Lakatos, chief product officer at the 3D printer manufacturer, assured me that the Form Studio 1 has a very economical size. “It doesn't take a lot of space,” Lakatos said. “If you have a desk, then I think you should be good to go.” I have a desk. It’s covered in boxes sent by his company.
Formlabs is one of the biggest 3D printer producers, with nearly 200,000 printers in service. The company’s customers are primarily professional businesses, like assembly shops or dentists, able to shell out $2,500 or more for a printer. (Its last affordable printer was $2,300.)
But the Form Studio 1 is Formlabs’ first consumer-oriented device. It prints with SLA (stereolithography) resins—a common 3D printing material that hardens into solid plastic when exposed to ultraviolet light—and can use Formlabs-branded products or third-party resins. It costs $699 and is now on sale; individual resin bottles start at $29.
The Studio 1 takes up roughly the same space as a minifridge. You’ll also likely need a wash unit, sold separately for $199 with a similar footprint (it removes uncured liquid resin from the surface of models). Then you’ll need room for all the tools and resin cartridges. Getting all that stuff can pile up. Or at least it did when Formlabs sent more than a dozen boxes to the WIRED office for testing. Your pileage may vary.
The front touchscreen lets you troubleshoot and ready prints. When the printer starts, it’s relatively quiet and odor-free. 3D printing with resin can be stinky, but Formlabs-branded resins are UL GreenGuard–certified, the same standard used to ensure baby products aren’t harmful from skin contact or off-gassing. Lakatos says the idea is that the Studio 1 can be used anywhere without the room being overwhelmed by resin stank.
“We know that some people are going to put it in their bedrooms,” Lakatos says. “I don't sleep with my printers, but you could if you really wanted to.”
After going through the stack of boxes, I set up the Form Studio 1 and the Form Studio Wash+Cure. They’re stylish, with translucent orange cases that conjure old-school iMac aesthetics. The printing process itself is supposedly quick. Lakatos says you can print a casing for a Raspberry Pi setup in around eight minutes.
I’ve only printed a couple of things so far, but have had a good experience with the orders. (Full review coming soon.) I printed a clear cover for the toolbox that comes with the Studio 1. It took about 17 minutes and came out clean and intact. The process was relatively quiet. The resin smell was there, but really only when lifting the hood after the process was done. I’m excited to use it more and see what kind of very detailed unholy abominations I can make.
The SLA printing enables very detailed constructions. In Formlabs’ internal testing, the company says it has had a roughly 2 percent failure rate for its prints. If that holds in the real world, it’ll be a big jump over competitors. That’s if you use its own resins, though.
“You can use any material,” Lakatos says. “If you want to use the toxic resin on Amazon, you can do it. We don't recommend it, but you can do it.”
Formlabs also has an app called Form Mobile that can control prints or send designs to the Form Studio 1. The overall printer experience feels surprisingly straightforward.
“It’s great if you want to mess around with some stuff,” Lakatos says. “For serious, beautiful things and projects that really require better material properties, beautiful resolution, stuff like that—it's hard to compete with it.”

The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

The Japanese government will focus on efforts to raise young people’s awareness about a territorial issue involving the four Russian-held islands claimed by Japan, the new minister for Okinawa and Northern Territories affairs has said.
Such efforts will include attracting school trips to areas close to the islands, called the Northern Territories in Japan, and sharing related information on social media, the minister, Yasuhiro Hanashi, said in an interview on Thursday.
“We’ll also promote the dissemination of information (about the issue) abroad, in cooperation with the Foreign Ministry,” Hanashi said.
Describing the territorial dispute as “the biggest pending issue” between Japan and Russia, Hanashi said that Japan is determined to resolve the issue and conclude a peace treaty with Russia.
The four islands — Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai group of islets — were seized by former Soviet troops in the closing days of World War II.
Resolving the territorial dispute is “an issue for the entire nation,” Hanashi emphasized. “It’s essential for the whole nation to work together to solve the problem.”
“Resuming a bilateral exchange program, including visits by former residents to their ancestors’ graves on the islands, is also one of our priorities,” he said, promising to “persistently call for the program’s resumption.”
Regarding the southernmost prefecture of Okinawa, Hanashi said, “Addressing the burden (on Okinawa) of hosting U.S. bases is an important policy task.”
“We will do our utmost for Okinawa’s development,” including the use of former U.S. base sites returned to Japan, the minister said.
On the possibility of increasing the Okinawa development budget for fiscal 2027, starting next April, Hanashi said, “Compiling measures genuinely helpful for this purpose one by one is more important than a specific budget figure.”
He added that the Japanese government “will address (the matter) appropriately in the budget compilation process while listening to Okinawa Governor Genta Koja,” who took office last month.

India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
- Published
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August.
But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention.
Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said.
A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage.
"The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said.
Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment.
But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes?
India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control.
But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat.
Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods.
Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important.
A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period.
Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online.
Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau.
The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily.
And the dangers extend beyond flooding.
A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms.
While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau.
The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress.
The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations.
Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas.
In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet.
Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project.
But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort.
"One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute.
"What happened after that no one knows," he added.
Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet.
But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022.
China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said.
Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes.
"These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group.
But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved.
One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value.
"What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank.
Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders.
The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow.
"There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD.
He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks.
Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay.
"Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says.
Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain.
For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat.

The Washington Post has hit back at Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu's account of an attack on one of its photojournalists by masked settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Footage of the attack, including video shared by the Post, shows masked men beating and kicking veteran conflict reporter Heidi Levine as she lay on the ground.
Witnesses told Reuters that about 80 masked people carrying gas canisters descended on the olive harvest in Abu Falah, burning olive trees and throwing rocks at Palestinians.
Matt Murray, the newspaper's executive editor, replied on X on Friday after Netanyahu's office said the circumstances of the attack on Levine near Abu Falah were “unclear”.
Netanyahu’s office had written on X: “The facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation.”
"To be clear: Some facts are neither in dispute nor unclear,” Murray wrote in his reply on X.
“Our photographer was clearly marked as Press. She was clearly beaten. These are not partisan or risible statements, but indisputable. We urge a thorough investigation and accountability."
Netanyahu said in the same statement: "Israel unequivocally condemns violence against anyone – Jews, Arabs, Christians or journalists. Those responsible will be held accountable."
He also said that "reports indicate some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths" and that other recordings appeared "to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual".
He concluded: "The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence."
The Post said earlier on Friday that Levine was wearing "visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist".
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from the authorities," the paper added in a statement shared on X.
Speaking from a hospital bed, Levine said she was "brutally attacked", pushed to the ground and robbed of her camera gear, bag and phone.
"Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me," she said.
The Israeli military said it and the Border Police were sent to the area after "reports of a violent confrontation" and that forces "acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means".
"All details of the incident will be examined," It said. The military said soldiers at another location "fired toward a suspect who ran toward them, carrying a sharp object and posed a threat to them".
Palestinian medics said two people were injured and taken to hospitals in the Ramallah area.
Levine was among a group of journalists covering the harvest in a year of record settler violence. Yesh Din, an Israeli settlements monitoring group, has recorded at least 234 attacks related to the olive harvest since 27 September, and it said soldiers were documented as present in more than a quarter of them. The United Nations has reported that Israeli forces and settlers have killed more than 1,140 Palestinians in the West Bank over the last three years.

NY congressman to introduce bill protecting video game ownership
Representative Ritchie Torres wants the FTC to establish regulations ensuring you can play the games you've purchased.
Representative Ritchie Torres (D-NY) has announced plans to introduce a bill calling on the Federal Trade Commission to protect people's ability to own and play the video games they've purchased. The Power to the Players Act hasn't been introduced in Congress yet — but at least in spirit, it sounds like it lines up with the Stop Killing Games campaign, a movement lobbying for protecting game ownership in a landscape dominated by digital software licenses that can be revoked at a moment's notice.
The announcement for Torres' bill specifically mentions NBA 2K25, which serves as a good example of what's at stake. The basketball game launched in 2024 for $70, and is now being removed from digital storefronts on October 30, just two years after it was released. While games getting delisted isn't uncommon, 2K's decision to also shut down the servers supporting the game's online modes in December effectively means players won't own the same game they paid for by the end of the year.
The Power to the Players Act would direct the FTC to prevent similar situations from happening by making it so players own games rather than license them, and forcing companies to offer an offline mode if a game's servers are being taken down. In an interview with Kotaku, Torres said enforcing the protections would be a "restoration to the historical norm" that existed before games were primarily sold digitally. He suggested it could also inspire calls for similar protections to be extended to digitally purchased books, movies and music.
Of course, there are several potential obstacles that could get in the way of that happening. Torres' bill could die in committee, just like a California bill that offered similar protections at the state level did in June. Relying on the FTC to regulate is also far less of a sure thing than it used to be. Following a 2024 Supreme Court decision to overturn Chevron deference, a legal doctrine that directed courts to defer to federal agencies' interpretation of potentially ambiguous legislation, the FTC and other agencies have far less power. Under this new understanding of the law, the commission's attempts to regulate the game industry could be blocked in the same way its ban on noncompete clauses was — by one judge deciding it lacks the authority to set rules.
Engadget has asked Torres to share a draft of the bill and comment on the possibility of the FTC being blocked by the courts. We'll update this article if we hear back.

The brother-in-law of a man who died after being flung from the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia has shared his final words before boarding the ride.
Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old teacher, fell to his death Monday after being thrown from the coaster, which reaches a height of 200 feet.
An investigation is underway into the incident at the park, located about 20 miles from Atlanta. The park has since reopened, while a growing number of theme parks across the U.S. have suspended operations on some roller coasters to ensure they are safe.
Speaking to local outlet Atlanta News First, Kariem’s brother-in-law, Joshua Nelson, described the family outing and its devastating aftermath. Nelson said Kariem had visited the park with his wife, daughter and niece for a birthday celebration and was eager to get on the ride, which travels up to 70 mph.
“His last words were to my daughter, and they were: This is my favorite ride. I’m so excited to be here,” Nelson said. His daughter called him crying afterward, asking what had happened to her uncle.
Kariem struck parts of the roller coaster several times before landing on the roof of a nearby haunted house, according to witness reports.
“He fell and hit the car three different times,” one witness told an NBC News affiliate. “A young Black male was ejected from the vehicle…The vehicle hit him, and then he flew back up again, and it hit him again,” a witness also told 11Alive.
The incident also left several others injured.
Nelson said his daughter, who was riding with her uncle, told him Kariem appeared to faint and that his body moved up and down as the coaster continued forward.
“The third or fourth time that happened, the latch came undone, and that’s when he fell out,” Nelson told Atlanta News First.
Nelson, who had known his brother-in-law for 15 years, described him as “a big brother I never had.” He said: “He just had a great heart, always thoughtful, always kind.”
Kariem had survived cancer as well as a “freak” accident where his car caught fire just weeks before he died, Nelson said.
The Cobb County Police Department said Tuesday that its Major Crimes Unit was investigating the incident and that the investigation remained “active and ongoing.”
“Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interviews indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction,” police said.
"We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” Six Flags Over Georgia said in a statement Tuesday. “Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends, and loved ones.”
“We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected," the statement continued. "The park team and local authorities responded immediately, and we are cooperating fully with local authorities as they complete their investigation.”

Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music
If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
Writer Yiyun Li does not talk about "grief" or the "grieving process." To her, those words make it sound that at some point you emerge from grief. Instead, Li prefers to use the word "abyss," which, she says, is where she expects to be for the remainder of her life.
Li's teenage sons both died by suicide six years apart, Vincent in 2017 at age 16, and James in 2024 at age 19. Her Pulitzer Prize-winning 2025 memoir, Things in Nature Merely Grow, chronicled the loss of her sons and her effort to go on.
"James' death taught me to suffer better," she says. "To say, 'I can do it, and I can live with my pain and sorrow without ever wanting to stop feeling.'"
Li's new novel, Music Against the Night, is set in the late 1700s and early 1800s and centers on two prodigies who are brought together by music, and drawn apart because of their aspirations. The novel focuses on music, which sits outside of words.
"I think I've had the feeling both times after my children's death that words often fall short, and falling short doesn't mean not succeeding, falling short doesn't mean failing," she says. "But when I start a new project, I would like a subject [where] words naturally fall short. So music is that choice."
Li grew up in China and served a year in the Chinese military before coming to the U.S. to study immunology. She eventually left her Ph.D. program to become a writer. Li is now a professor in the creative writing program at Princeton University.
Interview highlights
On the decision to set Music Against the Night in a different time period
I was in the middle of the novel when James died. This is a novel far from my usual interests or concerns, and the reason I think I went back to history is I would like to live again through history, through historical figures, through my characters living in the late 18th and early 19th century. ... I'm making the past into a new now for myself and possibly for my readers.
On how playing piano connects to her grief
I began my piano lessons at the end of 2023, purely to get to know how to play the piano. And James died in February 2024, so two months into my piano lessons he died, and it occurred to me that piano or music is a good way for me to count time — because music is about time. It's about counting the measure, counting the rhythm. And also music is about ... be[ing] engaged with something else. You can sit in your sadness all day long, do nothing, or crying. Or, like me, I could just sit there and just play the same drill again, and again, as a way to know I was, in a way, staying in touch with the world. ...
I'm not a concert pianist, but somehow I find it liberating and healthy to do something that you absolutely love but cannot do well. Every time I go to my piano lesson, I'm so intimidated. I'm sweating because I just can't do it. I can hear other people do it, I cannot do it myself. But I think that's, again, acknowledging the limit of my capacity.
On raising two gifted children
Both my children could be called prodigies, but James, my younger son, especially was extraordinarily odd and brilliant. ... We were greatly baffled. I remember he was 5 or 6, he said, "Mommy, you will never see the world. I see it full of dots and squiggly lines." And that again was a strange perception of the world [that] we adults did not have access to. …
What is the responsibility or the difficulty of bringing up a child [who is] very brilliant? … Some people would say, well, you really have to train him to be the next Einstein, but we did not want him to be the next Einstein, we want him to be a normal, happy boy living in an ordinary life.
On her son Vincent
He was a brilliant painter and we still have all his paintings around the house. He was an oboist and when he wanted to learn the oboe, the oboe teacher said he was a bit young, because he was 8 when he want to learn oboe, but he was certain. ... [He had] started on the piano and he could articulate that piano was not his instrument. He wanted to play the oboe. But mostly, he wrote beautiful poetry. He was a great poet. And he was a greater reader. I wouldn't call him an outlier, as James was, but he was brilliant and fun and interesting.
On struggling with suicidal ideation
Sometimes I think people have all sort of thoughts about or against people who have chosen suicide, and people who've chosen or attempted suicide are often called selfish. But my experience is oftentimes people [are] in great pain, whether it's great mental pain or great physical pain. And sometimes people in deep depression cannot tell the difference between mental pain and physical pain, because everything together is a great kind of suffering. I think it's not that people who experience that kind of suicidal urge, it's not that they want to die or they want [to] use this to hurt other people.
On becoming a writer
I was born with innate curiosity and also sensitivity to things that did not quite make sense. So I grew up in China. And for instance, when I was little, all the adults would say, since you're a child, you have no right to decide who you want to be or what you want to do. And my mother even had a saying, something along the [lines] that an adult decides and the child follows. I was quite young, you know, 4 or 5. I just couldn't make sense of all of these teachings because I thought I was as capable of thinking as the adults, and why did I have to follow them? So I think that sort of sensitivity to things that are very, very nonsensical, I think maybe that's one thing that made me into a writer.
Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.
