Essential items to stock in your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Is your household ready if you get hit with a stomach bug tomorrow? Sniffles on Saturday? The flu in a month or two?
Life Kit
How to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season
In the United States, cold and flu season occurs in the fall and winter, starting in October and stretching all the way through May, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The combination of dropping temperatures and drier climates makes us more susceptible to common respiratory viruses like the common cold, the flu, RSV or COVID-19, and "back-to-back illnesses," says pediatrician Mona Amin.
Get ready now by creating a cold and flu prep kit. "Have things readily available so that you're not scrambling or depending on someone else to run to the drugstore for you when you become sick," says pharmacist Alisha Reed. That includes fever and pain relievers, hydration supplements and monitoring tools to help manage symptoms.
Many viruses and fevers can be managed at home, says Amin. And the common cold and the flu are viral infections, so they can't be treated by prescription antibiotics anyway.
Below, you'll find a list of items for the whole family, recommended by Amin and Reed. Put the products in one designated place, like a shelf in your medicine cabinet or a handy "sick day" box.
You'll also want to take preventative measures like disinfecting frequently touched surfaces, getting vaccinated and washing your hands. But remember, says Reed, no prevention strategy is foolproof.
What to include in your cold and flu prep kit
Over-the-counter medications
When you're dealing with cough, congestion, sore throat, fever, fatigue or other common cold and flu symptoms, you may be tempted to reach for a medication that hits multiple symptoms.
But those meds often include extra unnecessary ingredients that can sometimes put you at risk of accidentally overmedicating yourself, says Reed. Instead, opt for medications that target individual symptoms.
These items all come with a price tag, of course. So if you don't have something like a flexible spending account to help cover costs, consider purchasing your personal sick day must-haves to start, then building from there as you're able.
Reed and Amin suggest these medications:
Pain relievers. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen can help relieve pain and discomfort from headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation, says Reed.
- For kids: Don't use children's ibuprofen for children under 6 months old; naproxen is only approved for children 12 years and older.
Fever reducer. Medications like acetaminophen and ibuprofen can safely reduce body temperature, though acetaminophen is usually the better choice for fevers.
- For kids: Look for a children's version for 12 years and under. Be sure to follow this dosing chart when using children's acetaminophen.
- For pregnant people: Acetaminophen is the recommended OTC pain reliever for pregnant people, according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
Antihistamine. Yes, the same thing you take for spring allergies! Colds and allergies have similar symptoms like sneezing, runny noses and watery eyes, which is why they can both be treated by a histamine-blocking medication that can help dry up your sinuses.
- For kids: Some OTC allergy medicines are approved for children as young as 6 months, but not all — and some have more side effects than others, says Amin. Check in with your care provider first if you have questions.
Decongestant. Pseudoephedrine pills or nasal spray can relieve a stuffy nose or sinus pressure by restricting blood vessels and opening airways in your nasal passages.
- For kids: Pills are not recommended for kids under 4 and medicated sprays are not recommended for kids under 6.
Cough suppressant for a dry cough. Dextromethorphan — often referred to as "DM" on the cough syrup box — can temporarily suppress the signal in the brain that triggers your cough reflex, says Reed.
- For kids: Not recommended for children under 4; do not use for children under 2, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Cough expectorant for a congested cough. Guaifenesin may help relieve chest congestion by thinning mucus in your airways, says Reed. But before you buy, try just staying hydrated first. "Water is a natural expectorant," she says.
- For kids: Cough medicine is not recommended for children under 4; do not use for children under 2, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Read the label on the box or bottle of OTC products carefully to make sure that what you're taking isn't expired and will treat the ailment it's intended for. And always stick to the recommended dosage and usage to avoid unnecessary risks or side effects, says Reed.
Honey
Honey is a great sick day remedy for all ages, but is especially helpful for small children not yet old enough for cough medicine, says Amin. "Honey is an anti-inflammatory that also helps with coating the throat, which can help with that cough trigger that children will have."
Note: honey isn't safe for children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.
Thermometer
This is a basic, must-have tool to check your temperature on those days you suspect you or your little one are running a fever, says Amin.
Rectal thermometers are preferred for children 3 and under; oral and digital infrared thermometers are both fine choices for anyone older than that. (But oral thermometers are usually more accurate.)
Nasal saline treatment
The dryness of winter can dehydrate your nasal passages and make it easier for viruses to attach and replicate in your nose and throat.
One easy solution is to irrigate your nose with a saline spray or rinse, says Amin. This can be both preventative by helping to keep the mucous membranes in your nose moist, as well as symptom-relieving by loosening thick mucus if you have a cold.
Research even suggests that using saline drops at the first sign of a cold can reduce symptoms in small children by up to two days.
Other comfort items
Chest rub. Vapor rubs containing combinations of camphor, eucalyptus and menthol oils may provide some relief for nighttime cough and cold symptoms when applied to the chest and neck.
Use with caution, says Amin. Though a lot of families use this homeopathic remedy, there's not a lot of research supporting its effectiveness, and it can be harmful if used improperly. Vicks VapoRub, for example, should be applied only to the chest and throat and never heated up. And be sure to check age restrictions before using any products on children — baby and child chest rubs will be formulated with gentler ingredients.
Disposable vomit bags. These are useful to have, easy to store and a great replacement for sitting by the toilet if the stomach flu should hit your house this year, says Amin.
Humidifier. A humidifier adds moisture to the air, which can help loosen mucus stuck in your sinuses. Reed suggests using a cool-mist humidifier when sick, which can help ease stuffiness during a cold.
Pedialyte, apple juice, water, Gatorade. Diarrhea or vomiting, common symptoms of the flu or COVID-19, can sometimes lead to dehydration. Make sure to have a few favorite drinks handy that can help replace those lost liquids for you or your little one, Amin says.
When to call your doctor
As long as your symptoms are improving — and responding to treatment — many viruses can be dealt with from the comfort of your home.
However, if you're seeing these concerning symptoms, reach out to your doctor.
- A fever in infants younger than 3 months; above 102 F for children; 103 F for adults; or any high fevers that last longer than 1-2 days and/or don't respond to fever-reducing medicine.
- Shortness of breath or erratic breathing
- Extreme thirst, inability to drink liquids, trouble urinating or producing tears, dark urine, severe or persistent vomiting
- Confusion, disorientation, extreme irritability or weakness
These aren't the only signs to look for, so when in doubt, reach out, says Reed. "Don't be afraid to call your doctor or talk to a pharmacist about what's going on. It doesn't hurt to double check," she says.

Afcon move to every four years under review by Caf
- Published
The Africa Cup of Nations could continue to be held every two years, with discussions under way to reverse its proposed switch to a four-year cycle.
Speaking on Friday at a Confederation of African Football (Caf) strategy conference in Cape Verde, president Patrice Motsepe said: "We've discussed it over the last few days.
"We are looking at everything, including having the Afcon coming back every two years. We are very clear, the matter is being reviewed."
The tournament has taken place every two years since 1968, bar a one-year gap between the 2012 and 2013 editions.
However, in December 2025 CAF announced it would shift to being staged every four years after the 2027 Afcon in East Africa and a 2028 edition.
That planned alteration to the schedule had received widespread criticism across the continent.
National associations had raised concerns about the visibility of their teams, the commercial implications and where Africa's biggest competition would sit in the international football calendar.

Japan retracts mistaken magnitude 9.9 quake alert
The alert set off loud emergency alerts on millions of mobile phones in Japan. Japan's weather agency clarified later that a 6.9-magnitude quake occurred near Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula at a depth of 160 kilometres (100 miles).
TOKYO: Japan's weather agency withdrew an erroneous alert for a magnitude 9.9 earthquake minutes after issuing it, apologising for the warning that disrupted transport.
The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) had initially warned on Friday (Oct 16) that a magnitude 9.9 earthquake occurred near the Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Chishima Islands, setting off loud emergency alerts on millions of mobile phones.
The JMA clarified later that a 6.9-magnitude quake occurred near Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula at a depth of 160 km just after midday.
"We deeply apologise for the significant inconvenience and concern caused to the public," JMA official Shinya Tsukada told reporters.
The alert did not cause widespread panic, but briefly disrupted public transport.
According to the JMA, the error stemmed from an anomaly in calculating the earthquake's epicentre.
The estimated magnitude was based on an incorrect assumption that the epicentre was about 680 kilometres farther from Japan than it actually was, the weather agency said.
Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing around 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.
A 9.9-magnitude tremor would have released about 22 times as much energy as the 2011 quake, according to local media.

The promise of GLP-1 drugs has always depended on people being able to afford them. These drugs still cost hundreds of dollars per month if you’re paying cash, at which point access becomes a privilege: The higher-income executive who wants to trim a few pounds might be able to afford them either way, but the low-income worker who needs the drug to lose significant weight might not be able to afford them — unless their health insurance covers it.
Why your health insurance is dropping GLP-1 coverage
Coverage for these anti-obesity drugs was finally becoming more common. Not anymore.
For a while, the trend lines for GLP-1 insurance coverage were positive. As of 2026, roughly two-thirds of private employer plans, which insure half of Americans, were covering GLP-1 medications for weight loss to treat obesity. Over the summer, Medicare launched a new $50-per-month prescription program. The US has struggled with an obesity epidemic for decades, but it looked like powerful drugs to treat it were finally starting to be more seamlessly integrated into the health system.
At least that’s how things appeared earlier this year. But now, private plans are pulling back from GLP-1 coverage. People are being left in the lurch, debating whether to try to pay for these drugs on their own or stop taking medicines they feel are making a real difference for their health.
The dilemma reveals one of the structural flaws in American healthcare. For working-age adults, your insurance depends on your job. Unfortunately, because people no longer stay at the same job for decades, there is not a strong financial incentive for employers to make investments that will benefit your health in the long term — but there is a strong incentive to minimize short-term costs as much as possible. It’s the kind of perverse rationale that could compel employer-sponsored health plans to stop covering a drug that, if taken over the full course of a person’s life, could help them not only lose weight but ultimately reduce their risk of heart disease, kidney disease and other chronic health problems, improving their health and saving all of us money as they get older.
“An employer or an insurer making coverage decisions doesn’t necessarily care if they’re saving Medicare money,” said Dan Sacks, a healthcare economist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. “That’s a classic problem with the American health insurance system, and it’s certainly salient here.”
This mismatch between what’s good for people’s health and what’s good for the corporate bottom line has long been one of the underlying flaws in the US health system. Now access to GLP-1 drugs is shrinking just as these drugs were starting to make a real dent in the US obesity crisis. The stakes couldn’t be higher.
Why employer-sponsored health plans are suddenly dropping GLP-1 coverage
From the beginning, insurance coverage was the big question hanging over GLP-1s and their potential to revolutionize US healthcare. But recently, it looked like we’d turned a corner.
When I attended the Aspen Ideas: Health festival over the summer, pharmaceutical reps seemed visibly relieved that GLP-1 coverage had been picking up among private insurers. In 2026, about two out of every three employer-sponsored plans were covering some of these drugs for weight management, up from about 20 percent just the year before.
“They’re recognizing that this is an investment in their workforce,” said Laura Steele, who leads the cardiometabolic health unit at Eli Lilly, which manufactures Zepbound and Foundayo. “Yes, there is a budget, and there is a benefit design that every employer has. That’s real. That’s not going away. But they’re also recognizing the overall cost that they’re experiencing by not dealing with this too.”
But as employers and private insurers make coverage decisions for next year, they are suddenly pulling back. At least 10 percent of employer plans that currently cover GLP-1s for weight loss say they are likely to discontinue coverage in 2027, according to one survey by the Business Group on Health — and that number may still increase. A Mercer survey of large employers found that 6 percent had dropped coverage in 2026 and another 5 percent were planning to in 2027 or actively considering it. A separate report from the Health Policy Commission in Massachusetts found that the number of commercially insured people in the state taking a GLP-1 drug had fallen by 50 percent between 2025 and the first quarter of 2026 as private coverage started to drop off.
Some of the biggest brands in the US are reportedly eliminating or reducing their coverage: PepsiCo, Starbucks, and Lowe’s among them. And their reasons are simple: It’s too expensive. The drugs still carry a high net price tag — $600 or more for a 30-day supply — and potential demand is high (two in every five American adults have obesity).
When a lot of people start taking an expensive medication all at once, it’s going to raise costs for employer insurance plans — and they have to figure out how to adapt. Insurers set premiums at the start of each year, based on how many people are on the plan and how much healthcare they are expected to need. But if those estimates are off — say, if more people take an expensive GLP-1 drug than the insurer expected — they have to offset those costs somehow, and raising premiums the following year is a common solution. According to one estimate, premiums are projected to grow by 5 to 13 percent due to GLP-1 costs — and the burden of paying those higher premiums is likely to fall on the workers. The employer can also try to limit GLP-1 use by, for example, asking workers to pay more out of pocket for these drugs; according to Mercer, 27 percent of large US employers instituted some kind of utilization controls for GLP-1 drugs over the past year or plan to next year.
They also have the option to simply stop covering these drugs for weight loss altogether — and that’s the route more and more of them are deciding to take. The abrupt reversal has even caught economists like Sacks off guard.
3 big reasons employer health plans are dropping GLP-1 coverage
- Employers aren’t invested in people’s long-term health: As Americans switch jobs more often, companies want to cut short-term costs.
- GLP-1 prices are still high, upward of $600 per month per person for insurers.
- A lot of people are eligible to take them for weight loss; two in five US adults have obesity.
“I was surprised that anyone would do an about-face because I thought they understood the trade-offs well,” Sacks said. “My guess is that it turned out to be more expensive than they anticipated: Take-up is higher, and possibly more people are sticking with it. That’s one reason that you might not want to continue to offer it.”
For employers, the short-term costs of covering a drug often outweigh the long-term benefits that medication may confer, at least from the employer’s POV. One analysis — notably produced by Blue Cross Blue Shield Kansas — concluded that covering GLP-1s for weight loss increased average employee health costs by $7,000 in the first year and another $4,200 in the second, largely due to the cost of the drugs themselves. And yet at the same time, there were no decreases in obesity-related medical events in that time period. Another study from Sacks and his colleagues at Indiana University and the University of South Carolina found that GLP-1 use did not lead to any cost savings over five years.
So in the short term, these employers are arguably making an economically rational decision — but one that may still come at their employees’ expense. “I’m completely screwed,” said one person on Reddit about Cigna’s plans to drop GLP-1 coverage for their own employees. They’re looking at at least $300 for one month’s supply at cash prices.
They weren’t alone either: “I’m devastated,” said another person, commenting on Starbucks’s decision to stop covering GLP-1 drugs. They said they had an autoimmune condition that had made it difficult to lose weight — until this new class of medicines came along.
Where GLP-1 coverage goes from here
How could we end up here, where it makes good business sense for companies to make a decision that could potentially harm their workers’ health in the long term? It is at least in part a result of the haphazard way the US has ended up insuring people.
When employer-sponsored insurance started to arise in the mid-20th century, eventually becoming the primary way to cover the working-age population, people tended to stay at the same job for a long period of time. In theory, there was a synergy: Companies wanted their workers to stay productive, and so it was worth it for the company to invest in their long-term health via their insurance benefits. And research has found that people who stay with the same company — and the same insurance plan — tend to have better health than those who switch a lot.
But these days, people change jobs all the time or work various gigs to piece together an income. You probably don’t expect to stay at your job for 10 years — and your employer doesn’t expect you to either. Instead, they want to keep their own costs as low as possible in the short term. This leads them to cut GLP-1 coverage, even though doctors do believe that people could benefit tremendously long term from the weight loss these drugs help them achieve and all of its potential health benefits.
“There are very real health benefits of these drugs,” Sacks told me. “The fact that we don’t find offsets or they’re even more expensive than we thought doesn’t necessarily mean that we shouldn’t cover them.”
Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American healthcare policy. Sign up here.
In theory, the market is supposed to fix the price problem: Drug companies get a period of exclusivity for the drugs they develop, and then, once that time elapses, cheaper generic versions can come onto the market. But generic semaglutide won’t be available in the US until at least 2031 — and for some versions, the generic competitors aren’t going to debut until the 2040s. Offering GLP-1 coverage could become a competitive advantage for employers, a perk they can offer to entice potential workers as part of their benefits package.
Beyond that, though, the path to more affordable GLP-1s is not immediately obvious right now. A lot of people are already willing to pay cash for these drugs — and that may continue as long as people can afford to do it. But with inflation still steadily rising, these drugs could slip out of reach for more and more Americans.
The government could get involved, but, for now, the federal government’s negotiating authority only covers Medicare, not the private plans that are dropping coverage. Serious healthcare reform is probably off the table until at least 2028, and then only if Democrats win both Congress and the White House and decide to make a healthcare package their legislative priority.
But the lesson of these recent developments is that, at some point, the US may have to look seriously at the underlying problem creating this mess in the first place. A patchwork method of insuring people that privileges short-term cost-cutting over people’s long-term health isn’t a real healthcare system.

In 2025, the DOE finalizetd a rule change saying that it will no longer require new building or renovation projects to meet the standards of accessibility that comply with the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which requires new buildings and renovations to remove "architectural and transportation barriers."
The final rule has not yet been implemented. On July 1, 2026, the DOE delayed its effective date to Dec. 28, 2026. The rule change would also not affect other federal or local accessibility requirements, only the DOE's rules for funding.
Advocacy organizations that oppose the change have sent the DOE adverse comments, and it's unclear how these will affect the rule's implementation.
In October 2026, a rumor spread that the U.S. Department of Energy was changing federal law to rescind a requirement that buildings should be accessible for people with disabilities.
Posts sharing the claim multiplied on social media, including on Facebook and Instagram. "The Trump administration's Department of Energy has moved to eliminate federal regulations requiring accessibility in certain newly constructed and renovated facilities receiving federal financial assistance," an Oct. 15 Facebook post read (archived):
The rumor was not new. The claim began to circulate in 2025, as one Reddit post indicates.
In 2025, the DOE finalized a rule change saying that it will no longer require new building or renovation projects to meet the standards of accessibility that comply with the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which requires new buildings and renovations to remove "architectural and transportation barriers." However the final rule had not yet been implemented. On July 1, 2026, the DOE delayed its effective date to Dec. 28, 2026. The rule change would also not affect other federal or local accessibility requirements, only the DOE's rules for funding.
For this reason, we rated the claim a mixture of true and false information.
We have reached out to the DOE seeking more information about its delayed implementation. We will update this story should we receive a reply.
In May 2025, the DOE published a direct final rule "rescinding" a rule that new construction projects that sought funding support from the DOE needed to comply with the Uniform Federal Accessibility Standards for accessibility for people with disabilities. The UFAS, in turn, follows requirements from the 1973 Rehabilitation Act.
"Upon further evaluation, and for the reasons explained subsequently, DOE has determined this provision to be unnecessary and unduly burdensome," the May 2025 proposed rule read.
However, in July 2025, the DOE delayed its implementation because it "subsequently received significant adverse comments on that direct final rule." The implementation of that rule was then delayed several more times, most recently in July 2026, and as of this writing it was slated to take effect on Dec. 28, 2026.
In other words, the rule has yet to take effect, and it's unclear how the adverse comments the DOE has received will affect its implementation.
Opposition to the rule change
After the DOE first published the rule change, several organizations representing the rights of people with disability sent adverse comments.
If the requirements are rescinded, "covered entities will be misled into believing they need not make their facilities accessible when, in fact, there is no other way to avoid discriminating against people with disabilities. As a result, they will violate the law and be forced to remediate accessibility barriers after construction is completed, likely at significant cost," said the National Federation of the Blind in a June 6, 2025, letter.
New York Lawyers for the Public Interest also filed an adverse comment that said the rule was "unlawful":
The proposed rules are unlawful. "Direct final rules" must be routine or noncontroversial. Here, the proposed changes are neither. Instead, the proposals would delete foundational provisions implementing Section 504 [of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973] in contradiction of Congress's clear understanding of the law.
The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights said in a June 16, 2025, adverse comment that the direct final rule process was not designed for such changes:
The direct final rule process is intended for noncontroversial rules that are unlikely to raise objections. Erecting new barriers to accessibility, as the direct final rule would do, is clearly controversial.
Snopes found no evidence that this rule change would prevent other agencies, federal, state or local, from imposing such requirements on new constructions or renovations.
For further reading, Snopes confirmed the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development updated its policy to effectively remove untrained "emotional support animals."

Daniil Medvedev overcame a wobble to beat a fighting Tommy Paul on Friday and reach the semifinals of the Shanghai Masters, setting up a showdown with rising star Rafael Jodar.
At age 20, the Spaniard is the youngest player to reach the Shanghai semifinals since the tournament’s inaugural edition in 2009.
Medvedev, the 2019 Shanghai champion, overcame inconsistent serving to beat Paul 6-3, 1-6, 6-3.
The 30-year-old saved seven break points to hold back the American in a marathon sixth game, giving little away as he broke to take the first set when Paul fired long.
READ | Jodar says he is ‘still learning’ after swearing at ballboy
But the 18th-ranked Paul returned inspired in the second set, displaying fantastic defence as Medvedev drove him around the court.
He was rewarded when Medvedev double-faulted twice in a must-win game to tumble into a decider.
The Russian, ranked sixth, cruised to a 2-0 lead in the third set and carried that momentum to the end, breaking again to win on his second match point.
“I think today I was a tiny bit off,” Medvedev said afterwards, though he credited his opponent for making it a “tight” battle.
“I managed to regroup,” he said. “If I’m playing well, I’m tough to beat.”
Earlier, 13th-ranked Jodar beat Norway’s Casper Ruud 4-6, 6-4, 6-3 -- recovering from a set down for the fourth time in a row this week.
Both players were tested but held serve to start with until Ruud capitalised on a break point, taking the first set with a searing forehand into the corner.
But Jodar’s brilliance shone through, dazzling the crowd with a gorgeous over-the-shoulder smash in the fourth game of the second set.
Despite losing that game, the Spaniard held his nerve and won a crucial break point to go up 5-4 before closing out the set at the first time of asking.
Ruud, ranked 24th, saved three match points in the third set but double-faulted to hand Jodar victory.
“Casper is a very tough player,” Jodar said afterwards. “I had to give my best level today to win this match.”

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) announced a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police denied permission and detained thousands of protesters, including three CJP leaders. With Jantar Mantar barricaded, some protesters gathered elsewhere. On 12 October, opposition leaders also marched to the Supreme Court against the SIR exercise, but police stopped them (here, here, here, here).
In this context, visuals showing crowds are being shared on social media with the claim that they show gatherings at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and outside Parliament House (here, here, here). Let’s verify these videos.
Claim: Visuals showing anti-CEC protestors gathering outside Parliament and Jantar Mantar.
Fact: These videos are AI-generated, not real visuals. No media reports mentioned the viral video or any protest by the public against the CEC inside the Parliament premises. Hence, the claims made in these posts are FALSE.
Video 1: 
Upon closer examination, we noticed a Gemini logo, associated with Google’s AI tool, in the bottom-right corner of the video, suggesting that it may have been AI-generated. We further analysed a keyframe from the viral video using SynthID, which also detected AI-generated content in the clip.
Video 2:
On performing a relevant keyword search, we found that no media reports mentioned the viral video or any protest by the public against the CEC inside the Parliament premises. We analysed the viral video using Hive’s AI-detection tool, which indicated that the video was AI-generated.
Furthermore, PIB Fact Check and Delhi Police also clarified that the viral video was fake and had been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).
To sum up, these videos are AI-generated and do not show a protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar in Delhi.

Embattled White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is out of the job after just five days, making her the shortest-tenured person to hold the role in history.
President Donald Trump said on Friday that he told Zacharia to reconsider taking on the high-profile job.
Shortly after his statements, The New York Times and CNN reported that Zacharia had been fired after less than a week in the role. A White House official told Business Insider that she is "transitioning out" of the role.
"I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want,'" Trump told reporters at the White House, adding that Zacharia responded that the job is "a lot tougher" than she thought.
"I said to her, 'Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider,'" Trump said.
A conservative commentator who has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer, Zacharia made her White House press briefing debut on Tuesday and quickly came under intense scrutiny over her legal credentials.
She was widely panned after the roughly 14-minute briefing, most of which was spent on reading from prepared remarks. After the briefing, while alongside Trump, Zacharia was asked which state she passed the bar exam in and replied, "When I moved to China," raising eyebrows.
National headlines soon followed reports that Zacharia had not been licensed to practice law in any US jurisdiction.
On Thursday, Zacharia said she took the bar exam but failed, and never retook it.
Trump told reporters on Friday that Zacharia had been treated "very badly" and "very unfairly" by the media.
"She's been treated very rough, and she's a nice person, very nice person," the president said. "I've watched her for years on television, but I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because, honestly, you don't need this.'"
"She's been treated, I would say, very nastily," he said.
A rocky start
Following her first briefing, CNN reported that "several White House officials" were questioning how long she could remain in the role.
The news of Zacharia's ouster means Trump will be searching for a top spokesperson again after Karoline Leavitt left the role in August.
Previously, Jonathan Daniels held the record for shortest tenure. Daniels served as White House press secretary for just 19 days before President Franklin D. Roosevelt died in office. (He briefly served in an interim capacity for President Harry Truman.)
In the modern era, press secretaries have historically served roughly a year in the role, a fact that CNN noted when Trump's first-ever White House press secretary, Sean Spicer, departed after 182 days in August 2017.
During the first Trump administration, Anthony Scaramucci famously spent just 11 days as the White House communications director before he was booted from the position.
Scaramucci, known as "The Mooch," weighed in on Zacharia's departure in an X post, writing, "Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."
Before becoming press secretary, Zacharia worked for Trump Media, the parent company of Truth Social, and served a brief stint at the Department of Homeland Security.
Compared to her predecessors, her résumé was void of the campaign and Capitol Hill experience that previous White House press secretaries brought to the challenging role.

Popular Nigerian gospel singer Toluwanisings dies aged 41

One of Nigeria's most popular gospel singers, Olayemi Bayonile Bolaji, known as Toluwanisings, has died, his family has announced.
In a statement posted on the deceased's Instagram page, the family said the singer had "said goodbye to the world" in the early hours of Wednesday, 14 October. He was 41.

Toluwanisings was known for his beautiful voice and energetic praise performances that encouraged audience participation, according to some of the tributes paid by his fans on social media.

There was panic among thousands of his fans on social media after news first emerged of his death on Wednesday before it was later confirmed by the family.
Toluwanisings' death comes months after he was involved in a road accident alongside members of his band.
Tributes have continued to pour in from colleagues and fans following the announcement of his death.
Among those who reacted are prominent lawyer Pelumi Olajengbesi and comedian Woli Agba, who had earlier called for prayers for the singer.

A rumor that legendary comedian and satirist George Carlin once performed a comedy bit that involved jokes about televised public executions circulated online in October.
Carlin, who died in 2008, was known for his scathing political takedowns and clever wordplay.
People on social media shared a clip that appears to be from one of Carlin's standup comedy TV specials, in which the comic allegedly waxed poetic about using public executions to help balance the United States' budget.
The clip circulated as the Pentagon announced its plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was sentenced to death in 2013 for killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 during a shooting at the Army's Fort Hood post in Texas.
Some users suggested Carlin "predicted" the Pentagon's move with his comedy bit from decades earlier.
The video was authentic and clipped from Carlin's 1996 HBO special, "George Carlin: Back in Town," recorded at The Beacon Theater in New York City on March 30 of that year. The special is available to stream for free on Tubi and was also released as an album on Sept. 17, 1996.
The clip in question is part of a segment titled "Capital Punishment," which begins around the 14:30 mark in the full special. The clip was also available to viewon Carlin's official website.
During the special, Carlin joked about performing crucifixions during "Monday Night Football" in a satirical bit about executing white collar criminals facilitating the laundering of drug money.
The joke leads into the moment shown in the viral clip, beginning around the 15:15 mark. Carlin said (emphasis ours):
I don't care about capital punishment one way or another, because I know it doesn't do anything. It doesn't do anything except maybe satisfy a Biblical need for revenge. You know, if you read the Bible, you see that it's full of retribution and revenge. So really, capital punishment is kind of a religious ritual. It's a purification rite. It's a modern sacrament. And as long as that's true, I say, let's liven it up a little!
I honestly believe that if you make the death penalty a little more entertaining, and learn to market it correctly, you just might be able to raise enough money to balance the stupid f***ing budget!
And don't forget, the polls show the American people want capital punishment and they want a balanced budget. And I think even in a fake democracy people ought to get what they want once in a while. Just to feed this illusion that they're really in charge.
Let's use capital punishment the same way we use sports and television in this country, to distract people and take their minds off how bad they're being f***ed by the upper 1 percent. Now, unfortunately, "Monday Night Football" doesn't last long enough. What we really need is year-round capital punishment on TV every night with sponsors! Gotta have sponsors. I'm sure as long as we're killing people, Marlboro cigarettes and Dow Chemical will be proud to participate.
To say Carlin "predicted" the Pentagon's planned livestream of an execution was a stretch, but it's accurate to say he joked about televised capital punishment 30 years earlier.
The special also featured Carlin's takes on other hot-button issues that continue to be part of the national discourse in 2026, including abortion and the prison system.
"Back in Town" was Carlin's ninth HBO comedy special, of which he would do 14 before his death in 2008.

From the Iran war to rising geopolitical tensions across the globe, conflicts are driving demand for advanced defence technologies, from thermal imaging and missile guidance to systems that can counter drone swarms. Against this backdrop, Tonbo Imaging’s ₹852.18 Cr IPO offers investors a chance to bet on India’s growing defence tech sector. Bengaluru-based defence tech company’s IPO remained in strong demand on the second day of bidding, garnering 6.29x subscription by 1:30 PM on October 16, according to BSE data, while its grey market premium (GMP) surged to as high as 71%. The Bengaluru-based company has fixed its price band at ₹665-700 per share, valuing it at around ₹4,010 Cr at the upper end. The IPO closes on October 19. The offer-for-sale-only issue comprises 1.22 Cr equity shares by existing shareholders. Investors can bid for a minimum of 21 shares, translating into an investment of ₹14,700 at the upper end of the price band. The company is expected to list on the BSE and NSE on October 23. Founded in 2003, Tonbo enters the market with a specialised portfolio of imaging and sensing systems used by defence forces and security agencies. Its products range from thermal imaging systems and weapon sights to missile seekers and high-power microwave systems designed to counter drone swarms. It claims to have deployed more than 28,000 systems across 24 countries, building a presence in both domestic and international defence markets. However, its recent financial performance has been unimpressive. Revenue from operations fell 22.7% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹362.65 Cr in FY26, while net profit declined around 30% to ₹50.88 Cr. The company also reported a net loss of ₹17.74 Cr in Q1 FY27. CEO Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar attributes the FY26 decline to delays in executing international programmes rather than a fundamental change in the business. He argued that defence technology companies need to be assessed over longer periods, given the nature of procurement and delivery cycles. So, can Tonbo turn its tech advantage and order pipeline into sustained growth, while meeting the expectations built into its IPO valuation? But first... A Sneak Peek Into Tonbo’s Tech Tonbo designs and develops electro-optical and infrared (EO/IR) systems, embedded electronics and imaging technologies. Its products help users detect, observe, identify and track objects in difficult visibility conditions. The portfolio spans thermal imaging cores, handheld thermal binoculars, weapon sights, targeting systems, fire-control systems, missile seekers and missile-guidance systems. Tonbo’s technology focuses on reducing the size, weight and power consumption of thermal imaging systems, potentially allowing them to be deployed across a wider range of military applications. “Thermal imaging has been around for 30-40 years. But it has always been heavy, expensive and consumed a lot of power, which limited the applications in which it could be used. What we have been able to do is build components that allow us to reduce the size, weight and power usage of thermal imagers,” Lakshmikumar said. This, he added, creates opportunities to deploy the technology across smaller weapons, helmets and other military equipment. The CEO also sees considerable headroom in India's thermal sights market as the armed forces expand their procurement of such systems. “India has around 30,000 thermal sights, of which Tonbo has supplied approximately 20,000,” Lakshmikumar said. The company’s RHP, citing a Frost & Sullivan report commissioned by Tonbo, estimates that it accounted for 51% of thermal imaging units supplied to the Indian government between April 2024 and March 2026. Beyond thermal imaging, Lakshmikumar identified missile seekers and high-power microwave technology as two other potential growth drivers. Tonbo is working on a missile seeker programme with Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL). According to the CEO, India has a significant requirement for missiles and Tonbo is the sole-source supplier to BDL for an uncooled missile seeker. The third area is high-power microwave technology designed to counter drone swarms. Lakshmikumar said Tonbo is among a small number of companies globally with the capability to take down drone swarms at ranges exceeding three kilometres. He cited early customer interest, including a letter of intent from Europe and requirements from the Indian Navy, while indicating that deliveries from these opportunities are expected only in FY29-FY30. These programmes offer Tonbo multiple potential avenues for growth, but they are at different stages of development and procurement. Their contribution to revenue will depend on how quickly customer interest translates into firm orders and deliveries. Tonbo’s business model also distinguishes it from a conventional defence manufacturer. The company retains control over product design, engineering and intellectual property while outsourcing large-scale manufacturing to external vendors. According to its red herring prospectus (RHP), it works with manufacturing partners including Kaynes and Avalon. Its international footprint provides another avenue for growth. The company serves customers across more than 24 countries, with deployments spanning markets such as Armenia, Morocco, the UAE, Australia, Europe, the US and Israel. Lakshmikumar said Tonbo approaches international markets with two objectives: using deployments in developed markets to demonstrate technological performance, and entering emerging markets to establish that its products can be scaled at appropriate price points. “We sell to customers such as the Mossad and the US Navy SEALs to show that the products can be technically superior,” he said. Revenue Slows But Recovery On The Cards Tonbo’s financial performance presents an important consideration for investors. Revenue from operations rose from ₹428.19 Cr in FY24 to ₹469.08 Cr in FY25, before falling to ₹362.65 Cr in FY26. PAT rose from ₹68.54 Cr in FY24 to ₹72.76 Cr in FY25 and then declined to ₹50.88 Cr in FY26. The company’s EBITDA fell to ₹104.62 Cr in FY26 from ₹139.06 Cr in FY25. However, its EBITDA margin remained relatively resilient at around 28.9%, compared with 29.6% in FY25. The fall in earnings was therefore accompanied by a much smaller contraction in EBITDA margin, suggesting that the decline in revenue was a key factor behind the lower absolute profit. Lakshmikumar said the revenue decline was primarily caused by international programmes that could not be completed within FY26 and have consequently moved into FY27. “Defence businesses need to be looked at over a three-to-five-year window, and even more so for a defence technology products business,” he said. The CEO cited a programme in Morocco that was expected to be delivered in March but was delayed because equipment required for the contract could not be shipped from the UAE amid the West Asia crisis. Lakshmikumar also pointed to an ongoing programme in Armenia, where Tonbo has delivered systems worth $55 Mn over the past three years. He said the next phase had been delayed because guns supplied by an Indian public sector company were held up, with the shipment route affected by the regional situation. Despite the lower export contribution in FY26, Tonbo delivered gross margins above 51%, compared with the roughly 40% gross margin it typically forecasts for its domestic business. The CEO attributed this to the delivery of a different mix of higher-margin platform systems during the year. The company’s order book provides some visibility into future business. Tonbo had an order book of ₹314.24 Cr as of June 30, 2026, comprising ₹231.87 Cr in domestic orders and ₹82.37 Cr in overseas orders. It also received new orders worth ₹118.15 Cr between July and September, according to the RHP. The June-end order book was equivalent to around 87% of FY26 revenue. While this does not guarantee near-term revenue, it gives investors a base against which to track execution in the coming quarters. Cash generation and working capital are other moving parts of the financial picture. Tonbo reported negative operating cash flow of approximately ₹136 Cr in FY25 and ₹63 Cr in FY26, despite remaining profitable at the PAT level. Inventory rose from ₹219.49 Cr at the end of March 2026 to ₹319.63 Cr at the end of June 2026, while short-term borrowings increased from ₹116.06 Cr to ₹129.72 Cr over the same period. These figures warrant attention, particularly as the company prepares to execute delayed and new programmes. Lakshmikumar, however, argues that the reported working-capital days do not fully reflect the company’s underlying operating cycle because revenue is heavily concentrated in the second half of the financial year. A ₹4,010 Cr Valuation Reflects The Promise Of Deep Tech Defence Tonbo’s IPO offers investors exposure to a specialised defence technology business with proprietary products, international deployments and potential growth opportunities across thermal imaging, missile seekers and counter-drone systems. The company’s position in select thermal imaging categories, along with its existing relationships with domestic and international customers, gives it a platform from which to pursue further programmes. The broader opportunity lies in the growing importance of indigenous defence technology and advanced sensing systems. Lakshmikumar said investors should assess the company on the strength of its demonstrated technology and its ability to sell to demanding international customers. Meanwhile, the company’s high valuation means investors expect it to keep growing quickly. At the upper end of the price band, Tonbo is valued at around ₹4,010 Cr, or nearly 79X of the FY26 PAT. The grey market premium of around 71% points to strong investor enthusiasm, with the market appearing willing to look beyond the recent earnings decline and bet on the company’s longer-term opportunity. For investors, the key indicators to watch will be the execution of delayed international programmes, the conversion of new orders into revenue, the contribution of higher-value products and the improvement in cash generation. For now, Tonbo’s proposition combines a specialised technology base with a potentially expanding market. Its ability to turn that promise into consistent financial performance will determine whether the IPO marks the beginning of a new phase of growth.

Miley Cyrus kicked off her “Miley: Bass Persuades – Live at the Hollywood Bowl” shows on Friday night at the famed Los Angeles venue, giving her first headlining performance in years.
The pop star, who is going mononomously as just Miley for this era, announced this pair of Friday and Sunday shows in early September along with the news that her new album, “Bass Persuades,” would be released on September 18 via Atlantic Records. “It’s been a while,” said Cyrus of the shows at the time on Instagram. “The Hollywood Bowl is my favorite place to experience music and see my favorite artists. Twelve years ago, Vermont Democrats tried to make their state the first in the nation to have a single-payer government-financed healthcare system — a bold experiment to push the limits of American health coverage when Obamacare was just being launched.
Vermont once dreamed of universal healthcare. This Democrat wants to try again — with a twist.
Amanda Janoo has a plan to gradually advance single-payer care if she becomes governor.
Their plan failed, and rebooting it became politically impossible, even in Vermont: The Democrats lost the governorship to Republican Phil Scott for what turned out to be a decade.
This year, that could finally change. A progressive political newcomer named Amanda Janoo is taking on Scott in what polls show is a tight governor’s race.
And if she wins, the state could be poised to try a whole new national experiment: one of Janoo’s central campaign promises is to create a pioneering health system where the state pays the full tab for primary and preventive care, while leaving the rest to the existing system.
Key takeaways
- Amanda Janoo, the Democratic nominee for governor of Vermont, wants to move primary and preventive healthcare to a single-payer system — where the state would pay providers for such care, make it free for patients, and cut insurers out.
- Previous attempts to pass or enact full single-payer systems have failed at the state level, including in Vermont in 2014.
- Janoo is trying to focus first on this one relatively smaller slice of the health system, but hopes it could be a starting point to full single-payer reform eventually.
- Yet even this more limited reform faces difficult political and practical challenges.
Janoo’s candidacy is an example of the policy experiments that are becoming possible nationwide in a projected “blue wave” year, when Democrats could sweep into power in a number of states. But in the healthcare universe, her plan is also an example of how even progressive policy idealists are trying to learn from past failures and focus on what they think can actually be achieved.
Compared to the sweeping ambition of Vermont’s 2014 effort, or Bernie Sanders’s signature “Medicare-for-All” idea, Janoo’s proposal for single-payer has very specific limits. Under Janoo’s proposal for “universal primary and preventive care” (she typically avoids the term “single-payer”), the state government would pay for Vermonters seeing primary care providers such as doctors and nurse practitioners. This government coverage would be universal and free for patients, and insurance companies would be cut out.
However, other parts of the health system – such as hospitals, specialists, and prescription drug companies – would remain under the existing insurance system, for now.
Every effort so far to enact full single-payer at the state level has failed — even in blue states, bills and ballot initiatives have regularly gone down to defeat. Vermont’s previous single-payer experiment made it the furthest — it was signed into law but abandoned before being implemented, when the governor concluded it was unworkable. Wherever it’s gained steam, politicians and voters have blanched at the high costs of moving their health systems onto state budgets, and the high taxes that would be necessary to fund them.
Now, Janoo is making an attempt to refurbish single-payer as something more achievable, by cutting off a smaller slice of it.
“I think it’s clear at this point that a profit-oriented healthcare system is a terrible idea,” Janoo told me in an interview Monday. But after assessing that the state budget made it “unrealistic” to do single-payer immediately, she concluded, “we could do universal primary and preventive care,” financed by a tax on the wealthiest.
Indeed, single-payer for primary care seems more achievable precisely because primary care is a relatively less expensive part of the healthcare system. But Janoo hopes it will pay major dividends — that better preventive care will improve Vermonters’ health, reducing costs elsewhere in the system by, for instance, making some hospital visits unnecessary.
In speaking to health policy experts about this idea, I heard much sympathy for the goal of universal primary care, but many questions about the details. Would Janoo’s plan be sufficient to bring more primary care doctors to Vermont — and, not unrelatedly, would it pay them more? Would her hoped-for cost savings from preventive care actually materialize? Is picking up the tab for a relatively less expensive part of the healthcare system the best use of sparse state funding?
These questions are becoming national ones, as healthcare gains traction as a political issue again. It isn’t just Vermont where primary care reform ideas are gaining steam: Democrats in Minnesota, Washington state, and elsewhere have discussed them. “There is growing interest in a number of states across the country in doing a universal primary care for all program,” Kevin Grumbach, a family physician and a professor of family and community medicine at the University of California San Francisco, told me. Even Gov. Scott, Janoo’s opponent, signed a law calling for a study of universal primary care.
One dividing line emerging, though, is whether to keep insurers involved, or to clear them out with a single-payer system, as Janoo wants. Insurers are unpopular with the public, but they can be a formidable political opponent when they argue that the benefits voters currently enjoy might be lost. Scott has said that the idea of universal primary care is appealing — but that if universal is “just code for single payer, I’m not interested. We’ve already been through that.”
Yet Janoo is hoping that single-payer for primary care will be a stepping stone – a trial run for eventually making the rest of the state’s health system single-payer down the road.
“I think about this often,” Janoo told me. “How do you build the new system as you transition the old — or hospice the old?”
Amanda Janoo is tired of “corporate neoliberal bullshit”
Janoo has long been an unorthodox economic policy thinker. Her rise is part of a broader trend in which progressives and leftists are winning primaries and gaining influence in the Democratic Party – but she doesn’t fit the prototype of the democratic socialist candidates in New York City, Colorado and elsewhere who’ve gotten much attention this year. Instead, she comes from a different strand of the left, a movement based on a dissident strain of economics and openly skeptical of the benefits of economic growth.
Dating back to when she graduated from college in 2010, in the aftermath of the financial crisis, she was part of a younger cohort rebelling against what seemed the glaring failures of the economic establishment. “The one thing coming out of university I was clear on was that neoliberalism was the worst,” Janoo said on a podcast last year. “This whole idea that governments should just take a hands-off approach to the economy and trust in sort of the disciplinary powers of the global free market to lead them to infinite growth seemed highly problematic and very anti-democratic.”
So for graduate school, Janoo attended Cambridge to study development economics under the “heterodox” economist Ha-Joon Chang. She then spent several years working abroad in international development for the United Nations and other organizations, before moving back to Vermont and working as an economic policy consultant.
In recent years, Janoo became deeply involved with the “well-being economy” movement: an international group of advocates, academics, and experts who criticize what they deem modern capitalism’s obsession with economic growth, and say the “well-being” of humans and the environment should be prioritized instead. They overlap with the “degrowth” movement, which outright argues economic growth should be reduced; last year, Janoo led a workshop at a DeGrowth Institute event on “Degrowth Policy Design.”
Trump’s return to power horrified Janoo. “I’m feeling angry about the rise of fascism and the growing threat of world war, because I feel like we don’t have time for this shit,” she said in a speech at an environmental event last year. ”The planet is on fire and ecosystems are collapsing, and that should really be the focus of all of our attention.” But, she said, “I believe I was born in this moment of history for a reason” and vowed “to fight for democracy – for life.”
So Janoo decided to jump in the race for governor of Vermont. While she is not running on a degrowth platform, her campaign is deeply informed by aspects of the movement’s thought: skepticism about growth’s benefits, a sense that untrammeled capitalism is leading the world to disaster, and that localism provides a better way. For instance, candidates for governor typically pledge that they’d help bring business investment in, but Janoo said in a July debate: “A lot of the problems we’re facing is because we focus so much on attracting external business.”
“Our economy is not super-diversified, and it is not really centered in the most essential kinds of goods and services you want to make sure people have access to no matter what happens — because honestly, things are bad now and they’re going to get worse,” Janoo told me. “I feel a little bit like a collective prepper right now. My motto is, protect what we love, produce what we need.”
In the Democratic primary, Janoo’s opponent, Aly Richards, had closer ties to the party establishment and led in fundraising. But Janoo ran as a progressive outsider; she promised to advance a “more economically populist vision” instead of “corporate neoliberal bullshit.” Her health plan became a point of contrast with Richards, who said she wouldn’t run on “magical thinking,” and that she wanted a version of universal primary care that would keep insurance companies involved. Janoo won the primary by 2.5 percentage points.
Now, she’s facing Governor Scott, who’s long been viewed as politically untouchable in the state – in 2024, he won his fifth two-year term by a margin of 52 points. But polls show a much closer race this time around, and Janoo could have a national blue wave at her back. If that wave helps carry her into the governor’s mansion. And if she makes it there, Vermont will have its first Democratic trifecta in a decade – and with it, the opportunity for major progressive policy change.
Amanda Janoo’s plan: single-payer for primary care
Advocates for primary care reform argue that it should be at the top of Democrats’ agenda, in Vermont and elsewhere, because the system is in crisis.
Primary care providers are overwhelmed and underfunded, they say – and, as a result, there aren’t enough. Grumbach, the family physician and UCSF professor, said “the workload, the lack of resources, and the gap in compensation” — as compared to more highly paid specialists — “has made it very hard to recruit people coming out of medical school to want to be family doctors like me.”
Patients, then, are having trouble finding doctors they like, and aren’t getting sufficient access to preventive care that could help them be healthier. “The emergency rooms are functioning and doing a lot of the work that normally primary care would do,” Janoo told me. “People are waiting a really long time to see anyone, and so often health issues that could have been caught sooner become more serious and dangerous.”
Finally, both providers and patients complain that insurance companies make the preceding problems worse, by adding administrative burdens and bureaucratic hassle.
So what would Janoo’s plan do?
First, her plan would guarantee free, government-paid primary and preventive healthcare for all in the state, by cutting insurers out of that part of the system.
Second, she wants to phase out the “fee-for-service” model of care, where primary care providers are paid based on specific services. She’s suggested, instead, either government-paid annual salaries, or per-patient per-month payments.
Third, she wants to try and try and make sure there are more primary care providers in the state, via more spending. “We would need some relocation incentives, so maybe $100 grand if you want to move here, or a student loan repayment program,” she told me. “My hope would also be that we could be a place for foreign-trained medical professionals to come here and be safe and accepted and to bring some cultural diversity,” she added.
As for how it would be paid for, Janoo proposes an income tax increase on the wealthiest Vermonters that, she said, would be comparable to the tax break they got in President Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” last year. Though she hasn’t settled on a final amount, she hopes these new taxes would raise hundreds of millions of dollars.
Would Janoo’s plan work in practice?
In speaking with health policy experts both inside and outside Vermont, though, I heard various questions and doubts about Janoo’s plan.
Some of the problems mix the practical and political. For instance, under this plan, primary care visits would be free, but tests such as MRIs would likely still require the existing insurance system, as would most prescription drugs. Janoo acknowledged to me that deciding how many things the government should pay for would “always be a challenge,” but said her first priority was access to getting people at least some healthcare.
There are also questions about whether this primary spending is really targeted at patients’ most urgent problems. Erasing the copay for your doctor visit might be nice, but those copays weren’t driving people into medical bankruptcy. Janoo’s reform plan leaves the bulk of hefty health spending from hospitals and treatments for very sick people untouched.
Other questions are about whether Janoo’s hoped-for benefits from better preventive care — she’s said the state could save as much as $300 million a year — will materialize.
“There’s no question that better access to primary and preventive care makes people healthier in the end,” Larry Levitt, executive vice president of the health policy nonprofit KFF, told me. “But advocates have long tried to sell prevention as saving money. I think it’s more likely that it costs money, but keeps people healthier.” One reason for this, he said, is that better preventive care could help identify more underlying illnesses and conditions in patients, and spur more spending to try and address them.
The shift to a salaried model for providers could bring other practical challenges. Though Janoo hopes that ditching fee-for-service will free up providers to see more patients, others suspect a guaranteed salary might incentivize them to see fewer, and wonder what role the government would play in trying to hold such providers accountable.
Finally, I also heard some disconnect between what providers said they wanted, and what Janoo thought they wanted. When we talked, she told me her impression was that primary care providers were most eager for changes in their work environment. “I’ve asked them, ‘If you could get paid a good annual salary – like, average for the nation – and you didn’t have to deal with insurance and the fee-for-service structure, would you do that?’ They say, ‘Absolutely.’”
Yet Grumbach told me that, for the primary care system, “Problem number one is not enough money, problem two is not enough money, and problem three is not enough money.” In his telling, it’s more money that’s the real key to incentivize more new doctors to practice primary care, and help pay other staff and health workers who could actually deliver good preventive care.
If so, the core challenge to Janoo’s reform will be the one that has dogged single-payer reform attempts everywhere: money.
If the government takes on the responsibility of paying primary care providers and setting salaries for them, providers will want those salaries to be high. If they aren’t high enough, the shortfall in primary care providers will worsen. But the higher such salaries are, the higher the taxes the state would need to raise to pay them. Essentially, taxpayers would be asked to shore up doctors’ salaries to keep them in the state — turning the healthcare argument from one kind of difficult political issue to another.
Getting the balance right would be a challenge for the government, with much at stake. But Janoo says her background in industrial policy has convinced her that it’s possible. Furthermore, she hopes, it will be just a starting point for the full single-payer system she still thinks is urgently needed.
“My hope is, when I’m governor, that I can start to work with some of our neighboring states. Because if we could create a New England-wide system, we could move to universal healthcare really quickly,” Janoo said. “I think it’s a moment where people recognize we need a universal healthcare system.”
And, she added, “If we had done it previously, it would be much cheaper than it is now.”

Katie Zacharia leaving her White House role less than five days on the job
- Published
Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, the BBC has confirmed, as the fallout from her shaky public debut appears to have reached its climax.
Speaking to reporters moments before news of her exit dropped on Friday, President Donald Trump said he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".
Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing in the role on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.
She spent the days after playing defence, answering tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.
Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during a press gaggle outside Marine One.
"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this," Trump said.
"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media.
The BBC confirmed she was leaving the job a few hours later.
As the country draws closer to the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House.
"The White House Press Secretary is gone. MAGA extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.
Zacharia's tumultuous week began on Tuesday, after she appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing that lasted 14 minutes, where she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions, and referred to her husband as the president.
During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practice law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam.
She replied: "When I was in China."
After intense scrutiny and digging by the press, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.
She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".
Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity from conservative-leaning Fox News lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.
When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"
Zacharia also described for Hannity how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"
When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.
She told the show's hosts she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney, because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one.
Host Lawrence Jones, asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?"
She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."
Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.
In his first term, Anthony Scaramucci, left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days.
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories.
Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform, for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win.
This summer, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates.
Even odder? “Nearly all of it—about $284 million—came from pairs of accounts repeatedly buying and selling with each other,” says former Polymarket trader Chris Park, who now runs the prediction-market forensic analysis firm MSR Decode.
Such a high volume of seemingly pointless back-and-forth transactions has raised eyebrows among experts. “It’s obviously some form of volume manipulation,” says Rajiv Sethi, a Barnard College economics professor who researches prediction markets.
When asked about these markets, Shana Bautista, Polymarket’s head of global intelligence and investigations, told WIRED that the team “immediately flagged this activity, investigated, and blocked the accounts from trading.” Polymarket did not respond to follow-up questions about why the accounts were able to trade such a high amount of volume before it took action.
The timing of these trades made things even weirder. Polymarket’s rules stipulated that the Ethiopia market would be resolved in October after the prime minister was formally appointed and sworn in, which meant that it stayed open for several months after Ahmed’s victory was all but a foregone conclusion. For 123 days after the election, bursts of seemingly irrational trading continued, prompting Polymarket users to leave comments like “THIS NOT RESOLVED?” and “fuckkkk.”
Sethi calls the phenomenon a “zombie market,” where people can buy and trade on events that have already taken place or are no longer happening.
Another market about a 2024 election in Romania facilitated what Sethi described as “even more dramatic” trading anomalies. The initial election was called off due to fears about foreign interference. A new race was held several months later, but instead of closing the original market in the meantime, Polymarket kept it running alongside the new option.
It was during this period that Sethi first noticed something weird appeared to be happening with the older market. An algorithm Sethi and his colleagues created to flag potential wash trading on Polymarket identified nearly all of the volume as suspicious. “99.6 percent of volume in this market for certain weeks has been wash trading,” Sethi says.
Wash trading is a type of market manipulation in which accounts repeatedly buy and sell assets to create the illusion of heavy trading activity, when in reality, money is simply moving back and forth. It’s banned on regulated financial exchanges in the United States and is specifically prohibited in Polymarket’s terms of service. An earlier study conducted by Sethi and colleagues found evidence of widespread wash trading on Polymarket’s offshore platform.
Wash trading could explain what happened with the Ethiopian and Romanian political markets, but because the identities of the traders is unknown, uncertainty remains. “What appears to be wash trading isn’t always wash trading,” says Sethi.
MSR Decode ran an analysis of the Ethiopian market for WIRED, which found that the most likely explanation for the anomalous trading is “activity farming,” which is when people try to artificially inflate their trading volumes. The firm suspects that traders may have been interested in boosting their volume because they believed that they could benefit if Polymarket launched a cryptocurrency token. In 2025, Polymarket chief marketing officer Matthew Modabber told the hosts of a crypto-themed podcast that there “would be a token” but did not provide specifics. Sethi also finds it plausible that traders could be motivated by potential “token allocation” to higher-volume accounts.
This type of behavior has been observed before in the cryptocurrency industry. “These are textbook examples on how market participants farm a potential airdrop,” says Andre Guettler, the director of Ulm University’s Institute of Strategic Management and Finance, who researches the structure of prediction markets.
When MSR Decode analyzed the Ethiopian election market, it found that it was highly unlikely that the trading volume could be attributed to sophisticated traders using algorithms to eke out profits. It analyzed over 38,000 “trade loops” that took place after the election (instances where individual wallets bought and sold to each other in quick succession) and found that over 98 percent resulted in neither side losing or gaining money. The median time that the accounts held onto the contracts they purchased before selling them again was nine seconds.
These types of unusual trading patterns are not a new phenomenon on Polymarket. Earlier this year, Barron’s reported that much of the activity on markets predicting the 2028 US presidential election centered on unlikely candidates such as Elon Musk and New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, neither of whom is eligible to run because they were born outside of the country.
Both Polymarket and its chief rival, Kalshi, have been publicly scrutinized for unusual market activity in recent months. Furor over suspicious activity on its recently launched perpetual futures market for cryptocurrency grew so intense on X that Kalshi published a blog post denying allegations of wash trading on it. (Sethi agrees with Kalshi that the allegations were unfounded. He argues that the unusual volume could instead be explained by Kalshi’s incentives for market makers, which create opportunities for other traders to profit from small price discrepancies.)
Polymarket recently raised an over $1 billion round of funding led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. The company is now valued at an estimated $21 billion, and earlier this summer, it announced that its annualized revenue was now over $1 billion. Polymarket’s explosive growth is often measured in volume traded, since it’s a metric that can point to how active users are.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets in the United States, declined to comment on whether it is looking into these election trades. The CFTC previously investigated a number of suspected instances of market manipulation on Polymarket, including several exclusively reported by WIRED, but they usually involved potential insider trading rather than wash trading or other suspicious activity.
In the past, the agency has issued hefty fines for wash trading in other sectors. “It seems to me that the CFTC would want to know about weird activity in a very large market,” a former CFTC employee tells WIRED.
