On 29 November 2022, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Netherlands and the World Health Organization (WHO) signed a new multi-annual agreement for US$ 36.68 million in core voluntary contributions for the period 2022-2025.
| Core voluntary contributions are funds that WHO can use and allocate as needed to address health priorities and challenges. Flexible funding such as this allows the Organization to keep pace with the ever-changing demands of global health and achieve what the world expects of it to improve the health and well-being of all, including those in the most vulnerable situations. Over the last four years, the Netherlands allocated US$ 26 million in core voluntary contributions to WHO and ranked as its 4th most flexible donor for the period 2020-2021. Through this new multi-year agreement, the Netherlands will further strengthen its position as a global leader in providing flexible funding for WHO. Reflecting on this new allocation, Mr Joris Jurriëns, Head of the Health and AIDS Division at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs stressed that “we need a strong and agile WHO as a central, technical and coordinating actor in the global health architecture to face today’s complex, global health challenges”. |  | 
This increased support from the Netherlands is essential to the work of WHO.
It provides the catalytic resources enabling WHO to fulfill its mandate where and when action is most needed: to assist countries in achieving better access to high-quality essential health services, including sexual and reproductive health and mental health services; improving prevention, preparedness and response to health emergencies; boosting access to essential medicines, vaccines, diagnostics and devices for primary care and leading its partners to improve planet health – including One Health and antimicrobial resistance.
Increased strong, predictable and flexible support to WHO is a powerful example of The Netherlands’ commitment to scale up its role in global health through the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030: “Working together for health worldwide”. The Strategy aims to contribute in a coordinated and targeted way to improving public health around the world, and thus also in the Netherlands.
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO. It funds key activities and brings expertise in the areas of sexual and reproductive health and rights, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating WHO’s cooperation with major health and health-related Dutch institutions.

OpenAI has updated its ChatGPT extension to be able to do more browser-based tasks.
OpenAI has updated its ChatGPT extension for Chrome, giving it the power to look at your tabs so it can come up with more personalized and useful answers to your queries. The company used to have a browser of its own, but it retired the product on August 9. It did, however, roll out upgrades to the Chrome extension that made ChatGPT a more viable alternative to Gemini in the browser. With these latest updates, ChatGPT can now do even more tasks inside Chrome.
If you're in ChatGPT Chat, you can ask the AI assistant to take a look at your open tabs on Chrome to conjure answers that would personally be useful. You can, for instance, ask it to compare couches opened on three different tabs by their dimensions, prices, delivery time and return policy.
Meanwhile, if you're using ChatGPT Work, OpenAI's agent designed for complex multi-step tasks, you can ask the assistant to send messages, fill out forms, organize tabs and fill out forms for you. You can ask ChatGPT to fill out a form for your new dentist and then add your schedule to the calendar, for instance. Another example is to get the chatbot to analyze several contractors' terms open in multiple tabs and then draft an email to the provider that fits your needs the most.
In addition, ChatGPT in Chrome's sidebar now has access to your whole history, so you can talk to it and give it tasks without having to tab away from what you were doing. You can get the ChatGPT extension, no matter what plan you have. OpenAI says that aside from Chrome, the extension is also compatible with other Chromium-based browsers, including Microsoft Edge, Brave and Opera.
Next up: using ChatGPT right within a Chrome tab got a major upgrade – the full power of ChatGPT is now in your browser.
Your entire ChatGPT history is right there, and you can ask question in Chat or get things done in Work – side by side while you're on a site. pic.twitter.com/ABiwzLvNnD

Germany deepened its longstanding engagement with WHO on Thursday with two new agreements: one to contribute a further €40 million to WHO’s work in health emergencies, and a second to host the Berlin-based WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence.
With the new contribution, Germany has provided €53.5 million so far this year to support WHO’s response to more than 50 active health emergencies.
“This is important because climate disasters, conflicts, and the ongoing pandemic demand urgent action,” said Susanne Baumann, State Secretary of the Federal Foreign Office for Germany (GFFO), whose delegation met with WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. “Our support is flexible and vital for saving lives around the globe.”
Through the GFFO, the country provides substantial funding to humanitarian crises in Afghanistan, Libya, Ukraine, Yemen, and to Ebola responses in Africa.
Germany is an all-time top donor to WHO’s Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), having contributed €115 million since the CFE’s inception in 2015. The contributions have made a significant impact on the health of people caught up in humanitarian crises; this year alone, CFE funding allowed WHO to bring immediate, lifesaving support to victims of floods in Libya, conflict in Sudan, cholera and diphtheria outbreaks, and earthquakes in Türkiye and Syria.
Of the new €40 million contribution, €20 million goes to the WHO Health Emergencies Appeal 2023, €10 million to the Ukraine emergency, €10 million for emergencies in Africa.
Thursday’s meeting also featured the signing of a host agreement for the WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence. The Hub was established with Germany’s support in Berlin in September 2021 to provide the world with better data, analytics and decisions to detect and respond to health emergencies.
Coinciding with the signing of the host agreement in Geneva, the German government held in Berlin a high-level forum “Pandemics: no time for neglect,” which focused on political priorities and actions on pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response, along with financing for resilient health systems. WHO’s Chief Scientist, Dr Jeremy Farrar, and Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu, WHO’s Assistant Director-General for Health Emergency Intelligence and Surveillance Systems, addressed the Forum.
“After last week’s historic political declaration at the UN General Assembly committing to stronger collaboration, investments, and governance to prevent, prepare, and respond to future pandemics, I am appreciative of Germany’s leadership leveraging the political momentum to host this high-level forum,” Dr Tedros said. “We must continue the dialogue to align on strengthening and financing health systems.”
In the coming weeks, Germany will join with WHO in two more Berlin-based events:
- Breaking Barriers: Advancing the One Health Agenda with a Focus on Environment (12-13 October).
- The World Health Summit 2023 (15-17 October) will gather stakeholders from more than 100 countries under the theme: “A Defining Year for Global Health Action.”
In a whole-of-government investment approach, Germany commits funds from its federal ministries: the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development, as well as the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ), the German Development Bank (KfW), the Ministry of Food and Agriculture, and the Ministry for the Environment.

WHO and Switzerland have announced the renewal of their cooperation strategy for the period 2024-2028. In 2013, Switzerland became the first high-income country in the WHO European Region to pilot a cooperation strategy with WHO (hereafter referred to as the WHO-Switzerland Cooperation Strategy). In 2022, WHO and Switzerland jointly decided to update and renew this cooperation strategy, which was done on 4 March 2025 at the Regional Office of the WHO in Copenhagen, Denmark.
Visit the WHO/Europe website to read the news release and learn more about the WHO—Switzerland country cooperation strategy 2024—2028.

A rumor (archived) that a member of the Norwegian Nobel Committee published a letter discussing why it did not award the Nobel Peace Prize to U.S. President Donald Trump circulated in October.
For example, an X user praised the letter from the alleged committee member about its deliberations for the 2026 Peace Prize, writing "This is amazing!!"
An excerpt from the alleged letter read:
Now. This year. I will not say the name, because we never say the name, but you know the name.
A certain head of state wanted this prize the way a child wants a thing in a shop window, which is to say loudly, and in public, and with the full belief that wanting it was itself the argument. He said he deserved it. He said he'd ended eight wars, a number that grew most times he said it, like a fish. He had other heads of state phone us. Israel's prime minister posted it on the internet, "Give him the Nobel." The leaders of Cambodia and Pakistan announced they'd nominated him, as though announcing it were part of it, as though we tally mentions. A man flew around the globe collecting endorsements for a Norwegian committee the way you'd collect signatures for a petition to the council about a noisy dog.
The rumor spread as the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 2026 Peace Prize to South African lawyer Navanethem Navi Pillay. Claims had circulated in late 2025 about whether Trump might be in contention for the next year's prize.
People on Facebook also shared the letter from the alleged Norwegian Nobel Committee member (archived, archived). Some users seemed to interpret the letter as authentic, though others identified it as satire. Snopes readers searched our site to investigate the letter's legitimacy.
We identified the alleged letter's original source: an X account reportedly based in Austin, Texas, that describes its owner as a "Reader. Writer. Satirist. Hacker." Therefore, we find the letter originated as satire.
The "Peter Girnus" account on X first shared the alleged letter on Oct. 12 (archived). Though the account described itself as satirical in nature, it did not include markings in its post making it obvious that the content was satire.
Aside from the account's self-classification as satire, several other details made it obvious the letter was not written by a real member of the real Norwegian Nobel Committee, which awards the Nobel Peace Prize.
The five committee members' names are publicly available on the Nobel Peace Prize's website. None of them are named "Peter Girnus."
Additionally, Snopes previously reported that Nobel Peace Prize nominations are strictly confidential until 50 years after the committee awards a prize. Therefore, a committee member would not be allowed to discuss Trump in 2026 if he made it onto the official nominations list for that year's prize. Trump received at least one nomination for the 2026 prize, as Snopes previously reported.
After sharing the initial letter on Oct. 12, the "Peter Girnus" account also shared a follow-up letter and a fake Trump Truth Social post about the fabricated letter (archived, archived).
The "Peter Girnus" account contained other fictitious letters. For example, the account included posts where the writer posed as "the United States Ambassador to a warm, strategically vital ally on the Aegean," a "Director for Energy and Sanctions at the National Security Council" and a "Joint Secretary in the Ministry of External Affairs, Government of the Republic of India."
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' descriptions of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

The sale of books has emerged as the latest political flashpoint in West Bengal, with under-construction book stalls run by Left parties allegedly vandalised in Kolkata’s Dhakuria and elsewhere, amid chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s call to deny the CPI(M) space at Durga Puja venues.
The alleged attack in Dhakuria on Wednesday left senior activists of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation and local Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), workers injured. The structure of a book stall being set up by the Communist Party of India (CPI) was also vandalised.
The incidents come weeks after Adhikari, on September 10, urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for book stalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated the position two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Left-wing parties have been setting up book stalls during Durga Puja and other festivals in Bengal for decades. The practice dates back to 1954, when the undivided CPI set up the first festive book stall in Park Circus under the leadership of communist leader Muzaffar Ahmed.
Despite repeated electoral setbacks since 2011, the CPI(M) continues to have a network of festive book stalls across the state. The CPI, CPI(ML) Liberation and the Socialist Unity Centre of India (Communist), or SUCI(C), also set up stalls according to their organisational strength. Such stalls are set up during Kali Puja, Christmas and Eid as well.
In recent years, the Trinamool Congress, the BJP, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and its affiliated organisations have also begun setting up book stalls. However, the public call by a sitting chief minister to deny Left parties space at festive venues marks an unprecedented escalation in the dispute.
Attack on Book Stall in Dhakuria
According to eyewitness accounts, the CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI have been setting up book stalls near the Dhakuria bus stand during Durga Puja for decades. On Wednesday, around 5.30 pm, a group of 10 to 12 men arrived while CPI(ML) Liberation workers were supervising the construction of their stall. The men allegedly ordered them to stop work, identified themselves as BJP-RSS workers and demanded that the site be vacated, claiming they intended to set up their own stall at the same location.
Manas Chatterjee, also known as Babun, a member of the CPI(ML) Liberation’s Kolkata district committee, said the party had been operating its book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since at least 1985.
“From the very beginning, the body language of the group was extremely hostile. They said that beef is consumed at our book stall and that they would not allow us to set up our stall this time,” Chatterjee said.
According to him, the group claimed to have permission from the police to set up a stall at the same location and demanded that the Left workers produce their own permission. “When I confronted them, asking who they were to demand such permission, they said that their ‘Raj’ had started and that now everything had to be done according to their whims,” he said.
Chatterjee alleged that the group repeatedly claimed to have permission from the joint commissioner of Kolkata Police and said this entitled them to set up a stall wherever they wanted.
When Chatterjee tried to prevent the group from tearing down a hammer-and-sickle flag, he was allegedly assaulted. Between 10 and 15 youths pinned him to the road and kicked and punched him on his waist and chest, he said. The under-construction stall was subsequently ransacked and uprooted.
Chatterjee alleged that police personnel were present near the site, but left when the assault began.
Amalendu Bhushan Chowdhury, an 89-year-old CPI(ML) Liberation activist, was also allegedly assaulted when he tried to protect Chatterjee.
As the confrontation escalated, local CPI(M) leader Achyut Chakraborty intervened. He alleged that members of the group splashed hot tea on him and assaulted him.
Chakraborty said the CPI(M) had been setting up a book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since 1977, with the CPI and CPI(ML) Liberation subsequently joining the practice.
“What happened this year is unprecedented,” he said. According to Chakraborty, the group aggressively demanded to see police permission for the stalls and began assaulting Left workers when questioned about its authority to do so.
He alleged that the BJP workers initially outnumbered the Left activists after mobilising around 40 to 50 people over the phone. Party workers and local residents then gathered at the spot, but the Left workers tried to prevent the confrontation from escalating further.
“Book stalls during the puja have always been a defining feature of the festive season in West Bengal. The BJP’s fascist brigade is vandalising such stalls. At a book stall near Dhakuria bridge in Kolkata, our local committee secretary and State Committee member Comrade Babun Chatterjee has been seriously injured by the fascist goons. Veteran octogenarian Comrade AB Chowdhury has also been beaten up. Condemn this fascist assault on comrades and on the progressive cultural tradition of West Bengal,” CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya said in a Facebook post.
Police Permission Becomes a Point of Contention
Following the incident, CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI workers approached Lake police station to lodge a complaint. According to the Left parties, police said the stalls did not have the required permission and that, since the parties had only informed the police about their plans to set them up, and not sought formal permission, the police could not intervene.
Chakraborty said the police repeatedly asked whether the parties had obtained permission from the joint commissioner of police. “It intrigued us that the tone of the BJP workers and the police sounded similar on this issue,” he said.
The Left parties maintain that the land belongs to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), to which they have paid the required fees to set up their stalls. They said the established practice has been to inform the local police station rather than obtain police permission, and that this arrangement has been followed for close to 50 years.
Chakraborty said police were unable to produce a notification establishing that the rules had changed and that prior police permission was now mandatory.
According to CPI(M) and CPI(ML) Liberation leaders, the issue of police permission has not arisen in other parts of Kolkata, where stalls have been set up after informing the police.
On Thursday, Left party workers marched from the Dhakuria bus stand to Lake Police Station. The rally was attended by CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh, former CPI councillor from KMC Ward 92 Madhuchanda Deb and CPI leader Prabir Deb, among others.
Police, however, maintained that the stalls lacked the required permission and that they could not assist the parties because the joint commissioner had not approved them.
“It won’t be an overstatement to say that the Lake Police Station tried using the BJP workers, who are mostly outsiders, to heckle us so that the stalls would not come up,” he said.
Alt News contacted Lake police station, but officials declined to comment. The Left parties said their stalls would be inaugurated on Friday despite the dispute.
Voice of Opposition Should not be Suppressed: HC
The Dhakuria incident is not the only controversy involving Left party book stalls. The CPI(M) has also reportedly faced opposition to setting up stalls in other places in the state. According to a report in Anandabazar Patrika, similar incidents have been reported from Behala and Kasba in Kolkata, Shibpur in Howrah, Naihati in North 24 parganas and elsewhere.
The CPI(M) approached the Calcutta high court on Wednesday in this regard. In their petition, the party mentioned an incident of October 6 in Bongaon. As the party started work for building a book stall there, people allegedly from Hindu Jagran Mancha stopped them. Left workers were allegedly assaulted and threatened against putting up the stall.
Justice Sougata Bhattacharya, hearing the petition, sought the police’s response and observed that the state could not “pick and choose” while granting permission. The opposition could not be denied permission in a manner that effectively stifled its activities, the court said.
“It is not right to allow one party and deny permission to others. The voice of an Opposition political party should not be suppressed in this manner. They are not setting up a lottery shop; they want to sell books. What is the problem?” Justice Bhattacharyya observed.
The state subsequently approached a division bench, arguing that the proposed stall was to be set up on Public Works Department land without permission and that a report should be sought from the department rather than the police. On Thursday, the division bench sent the matter back to Justice Bhattacharya.
Later that day, Justice Bhattacharya directed that the CPI(M) be allowed to set up its book stall within 100 metres of the intended location. The court held that the police would be responsible for dealing with any untoward incident and assigned responsibility for maintaining law and order around the stall to the superintendent of police of Bongaon Police District and the inspector-in-charge of Bongaon.
In its order, the court observed that if other people were allowed to set up stalls selling different items during the festive season, the CPI(M) should not be prevented from selling books.
It added that the dissemination of different political thoughts and ideologies was welcome in a democracy because it made democracy “fruitful, deep-rooted and matured”. The court also said it expected the ruling dispensation to create an atmosphere in which people aligned with different political ideologies would not hesitate to express their views.

Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in UK after Palestinian Action support
Irish author Sally Rooney has long been described as "the voice of a generation" for her best-selling novels that are ostensibly about millennial relationships but also explore deeper questions of class, gender and politics.
Now the 35-year-old writer's books will no longer be sold in the UK because of her own closely-held political beliefs. She had promised to donate the revenues to a pro-Palestinian group that the UK has designated a terrorist organization.
In a statement this week, her publisher explained: 
"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher,"
"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber said.
The move comes after Rooney – who has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza – announced last year she would be donating funds from the proceeds of her books to Palestinian Action, which was controversially banned in the UK under terrorism legislation.
Israel vehemently denies allegations of genocide.
UK-based Palestinian Action says on its website it uses "disruptive tactics" to target "corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex and seeks to make it impossible for these companies to profit from the oppression of Palestinians."
It has targeted facilities linked to an Israeli weapons manufacturer and, in a major security breach, last year managed to break into Britain's largest air force base. The activists spray-painted two aircraft at the base blood red, in what the group said was a protest against Britain's military support for Israel.
Palestinian Action was also responsible for vandalizing one of President Trump's golf courses in Scotland in March last year, when activists painted the course with the words "Gaza is not 4 sale." Reacting on social media, Trump called those responsible "terrorists."
When the British government banned the group in July last year, it said it was on the grounds that Palestinian Action is responsible for "serious damage to property." It was the first time a terrorist designation had been given to an organization that does not call for violence against people.
"Its activity has increased in frequency and severity since the start of 2024 and its methods have become more aggressive, with its members demonstrating a willingness to use violence," the British government said at the time.
The government also said that the group's "activities meet the threshold of being concerned in terrorism as set out in the Terrorism Act 2000.," adding that it assessed "that Palestine Action commits and participates in acts of terrorism."
Free speech concerns
But critics questioned this assessment, saying it raised concerns about freedom of speech.
UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk urged the UK government to rescind the decision, saying it "appears disproportionate and unnecessary."
"It limits the rights of many people involved with and supportive of Palestine Action who have not themselves engaged in any underlying criminal activity but rather exercised their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association," Türk said.
Amnesty International UK also raised concerns, saying "the UK has a deeply flawed and overly broad definition of terrorism."
Under the UK law, anyone who provides financial assistance to the group could face up to 14 years in prison.
For fear of arrest, Rooney says she has stopped travelling from her home in Ireland to the UK to attend award ceremonies and other events since the law came into force.
But the novelist has defended her support of Palestinian Action, saying in an opinion piece in The Irish Times last year: "if this makes me a 'supporter of terror' under UK law, so be it."
It was in that op-ed that she announced she would use the British proceeds of her work "as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can."
Now however, her books won't be sold in Britain at all, so there will be no further proceeds.
The Normal People author was undeterred, saying in a statement shared with NPR: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."
Since the ban on Palestinian Action, several thousand people in the UK have been arrested for supporting them, mainly for carrying placards and wearing T-shirts.
The ban has been challenged in the courts, with the UK's high court ruling against it in February. A court of appeal later overturned that decision. Next month, the case heads to Britain's highest court.
In August, the U.S. Department of the Treasury followed the UK's lead in sanctioning Palestinian Action, calling them "far-left terrorists."

'Our roots are Man Utd' - but FC United ethos 'more important than ever'
- Published
FC United of Manchester striker Adam Le Fondre spent Tuesday lunchtime working with a group of players from the club's academy on a 3G pitch next to the club's 4,900-capacity Broadhurst Park stadium.
The dozen lads are probably not going to get anywhere near the Premier League, as Le Fondre once did, but the Northern Premier League club want to try and create a pathway to senior football, while ensuring the teenagers continue in education through their partnership with Manchester College.
Getting to train with the 39-year-old Le Fondre, scorer of more than 300 goals in professional football including 14 in his sole Premier League season, is the kind of community initiative that goes on at non-league clubs across the country.
For the people who run FC United, it is a world away from the club they once supported.
Just as it is 21 years since the Glazer family bought Manchester United and dropped £600m of debt on the club, it is 21 years since a group of fans decided to stop joining protests against the Americans and instead form their own supporter-owned club.
This weekend, while Michael Carrick takes his team to Leeds, desperate for a win to quieten the noise around him and his club, FC United have a short trip to Altrincham for an FA Cup fourth qualifying round tie that could be worth £25,000.
"We didn't stop loving Manchester United," said chairman Nick Boom. "We started FC United because we loved it.
"Our roots are Manchester United. The songs, the humour, the traditions and shared history still run through FC United.
"But after 21 years, we have also got our own identity. We have a sense of place in North Manchester. We're unmistakably a Manchester club. We have Manchester United fans coming here that have been priced out of Old Trafford. We have fans who feel disassociated with Premier League football.
"We think football, in a sense, has lost its way at the top level. Football should be somewhere you can go with your friends and family, stand or sit together, with a sense of community. Somewhere you can get some decent food and drink at an affordable price, where you can have a beer on the terraces, have a sing-song and forget your troubles for a couple of hours.
"Fewer people are able to do that at the very top level, on the grounds of affordability and accessibility. We believe we're more important than ever with everything that's going on at the moment."
'Supporter ownership isn't easy'
FC United distribute a monthly board meeting summary to their 1,528 adult members which explains the minutiae of club operations.
The solar power generation at Broadhurst Park is going to be increased, which the club think will save up to £4,000. A £5,000 donation has been received from one fan and there was also an update on the 'own your own football club for £5-a-month initiative' and comparisons made with other supporter-owned clubs, including Bury, whose relaunch has taken them into the same league as FC United.
The pair meet on Boxing Day in a game likely to attract a huge attendance at Broadhurst Park.
Yet, like Manchester United, FC United has a significant debt.
"Supporter ownership isn't easy," said Boom. "There's no billionaire ready to write a cheque at the end of the month to make up any shortfalls.
"The debt did get out of control for a period. It absolutely did, because the clamour was to have our own ground; somewhere we could truly call home.
"But we overextended and the ground wasn't as well managed as it could have been. We've learned some harsh lessons from that about the level of expertise you need, even at a club at this level, to run it."
Members still don't want FC United to have a front of shirt sponsor but naming rights for the stadium which 'is showing wear and tear', is being discussed.
A recent change of personnel at senior level has led to a 'review of the club's relationships' with existing commercial backers. The club pride themselves on linking up with local and independent businesses when they can.
Sadness at Man Utd decline
Boom's employment background is in finance. He is trying to ensure the financial side of the club is in order.
A profit in excess of £100,000 is forecast for the current year, a £350,000 improvement. But it is felt an annual surplus of £200,000 is needed to ensure funds can be found for essential work on and around the ground, as well as to allow the club to meet its loan repayments.
He estimates he spends 70 hours a week on club business, not bad for a volunteer who lives in West Yorkshire.
You can tell he loves it though. Whereas once Boom watched Manchester United win Premier Leagues, FA Cups and European trophies, now he is looking forward to a trip to Altrincham, currently in the National League play-off places.
The winners pocket £9,375 and would be guaranteed at least another £15,800 in prize money by reaching the first round. The loser gets £3,125. That money is important, although Boom says once the whistle blows, his focus will be on football not finance.
Twenty-four hours later, Manchester United head to Leeds, the next stop in a season of turmoil, which has triggered the type of fierce protests he was once a part of but now observes, even if a close relationship has developed with the 1958 Group, who have been at the forefront of recent protests.
"What has happened to Manchester United is an absolute tragedy," he said.
"This is one of the world's great sporting institutions, a football club with an extraordinary history, built on the achievements, sacrifices and loyalty of generations of people.
"Yet for more than 20 years it's been treated increasingly as a financial asset by owners who appear completely disconnected from what the club means to its supporters.
"The Glazers' ownership has been disgraceful. They acquired Manchester United through a leveraged takeover, burdened it with debt and have benefited enormously from something they did nothing to create. Meanwhile, the club has suffered years of decline and its relationship with supporters has been steadily eroded.
"I see very little evidence that Jim Ratcliffe and INEOS represent a fundamentally different philosophy. Ratcliffe might talk about restoring Manchester United but you cannot rebuild a football club by dismantling the very culture and community that made it great."
Ratcliffe has implemented a number of controversial measures since agreeing a minority stake in United in December 2023, including two lots of redundancies. He has defended the action, saying it was essential to return the club to profitability.
"We have enormous respect for anyone continuing to protest," added Boom. "It was particularly pleasing that, after more than 20 years, The 1958 Group reached out to FC United.
"We've developed a good relationship, and while we've taken different paths, we're united by a belief that Manchester United and its supporters deserve better."

Govt defends Jaishankar-Rubio meet in Mumbai amid Oppn criticism: 'Practice for last decade or so'
As the Opposition questioned why the US envoy had announced Jaishankar's meetings, Rahul Gandhi said “Rubio has summoned his employee to Mumbai”.
The government on Friday sought to address the opposition’s criticism of external affairs minister S Jaishankar travelling to Mumbai to meet US secretary of state Marco Rubio next week and said it has been a practice over the past decade for foreign dignitaries to be hosted outside New Delhi.
Congress leaders had earlier criticised the government after US ambassador Sergio Gor said at a public event that “we expect…Jaishankar to be joining us [in Mumbai]” for Rubio's visit. Rubio is set to travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar, and the capital is not part of his itinerary.
Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Jairam Ramesh had questioned why the US envoy had announced the external affairs minister’s meetings, with Gandhi saying “Rubio has summoned his employee to Mumbai”.
Responding to questions on the opposition’s criticism that the external affairs minister had been “summoned” to Mumbai by the US, external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said Jaishankar is set to host the United Arab Emirates (UAE)’s deputy prime minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Mumbai between October 19 and 20 before holding talks with Rubio.
Noting that Jaishankar will also attend a celebration in Mumbai of the 250th anniversary of the independence of the US as the guest of honour, Jaiswal said: “It has been the practice for the last decade or so that we have hosted foreign dignitaries outside Delhi.”
In this context, he said Prime Minister Narendra Modi hosted his Spanish counterpart in Baroda, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Ahmedabad, and the Mauritius PM in Varanasi, while the external affairs minister hosted the foreign ministers of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in Goa, the Botswana foreign minister at Kevadia in Gujarat, and the Heart of Asia conference in Amritsar.
Jaiswal said UAE PM'visit is an opportunity to review all aspects of India-UAE cooperation under their comprehensive strategic partnership. “The two delegations will assess and take forward initiatives in the areas of energy, trade and investments, fintech, defence and connectivity,” he said.
They will also have a detailed discussion on the situation in West Asia and global and multilateral issues.
Rubio’s visit will allow both sides to review India-US ties and discuss ways to strengthen the bilateral comprehensive global strategic partnership. “Discussions are expected to cover key areas of bilateral cooperation, including energy, trade and investment, defence, critical and emerging technologies, and other areas of mutual interest,” Jaiswal said.
The two sides will discuss regional and global developments, and the visit will be an opportunity to sustain high-level engagement between the two countries and advance shared priorities, he said.
During his last visit to India in May, Rubio had participated in a Quad foreign ministers’ meeting and hosted a reception in New Delhi to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence.
People familiar with the matter said Rubio will travel to Jamnagar for a few hours to visit facilities of energy major Reliance, which has partnered on the construction of America First Refining in Texas, the first new major oil refinery in the US in almost five decades. Reliance is also a major purchaser of energy from Venezuela, sales of which are controlled by the US administration.

He extensively covered Pakistan’s domestic politics and the life of the common people, as well as the fallout of the 2008 Mumbai attacks on India-Pakistan relations and the subsequent trial in Pakistan of the suspects involved in the attack. As part of his reportage in Pakistan, he travelled the breadth of the country, from the Swat Valley to Balochistan. High-profile legionnaire apologizes following profanity-laced outburst at Carbonear, N.L., wedding reception
Bride was about to throw her wedding bouquet when Berkley Lawrence erupted
A high-profile legionnaire is apologizing and pondering his future with this century-old veteran support and community service organization following an angry outburst at a wedding reception in Carbonear, N.L., earlier this month.
The Oct. 3 wedding reception at Legion Branch 23 for newlyweds Justin and Janell Clarke came to an abrupt end after Berkley Lawrence, who was the top legionnaire in Canada until this summer, lost his temper and angrily confronted the bride and other members of the wedding party.
The bride said she was afraid and humiliated, and described Lawrence's behaviour as "aggressive, erratic, unprofessional and very, very disrespectful.”
When contacted Friday by CBC News, Lawrence admitted he crossed the line.
“I handled it completely wrong. I lost control of my emotions. I swore at her, I swore at a few other people that tried to calm me down. I was loud, and it was not a good scene," Lawrence said by telephone.
Not a happy day
Clarke said Lawrence ruined her wedding day, and the days that followed the incident.
“We cannot look back on that day now and say that was a great day. That it was the best day of our lives. When we look back on that day now, we don't look back on a happy day. The only thing I look back on when I think of that night was an unfamiliar man charging [at me] and verbally assaulting me."
Lawrence is no ordinary legionnaire. Up until August, he was the dominion president of the Royal Canadian Legion, which is the Legion's top post in the country.
Justin and Janell Clarke pose with their dog after exchanging wedding vows on Oct. 3. Their dream wedding day ended on a sour note, however, following an angry outburst by a high-profile member of the Carbonear Legion during the couple's wedding reception. (Facebook/Justin Clarke)
He served in the army for 33 years, has played leading roles at Branch 23 for more than two decades, and two years ago he was a key figure in the establishment of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the war memorial in St. John's.
On the night of the wedding reception, Lawrence was attending a separate event at the Legion, and said he drank about five beer. As he left, he witnessed people outside the building holding alcoholic beverages, which is not permitted.
Lawrence was worried that liquor corporation inspectors or police officers might witness the behaviour, and that the Legion might lose its licence to sell beer and alcohol. He said the branch has long struggled to stay within the rules of its licence.
"People treat us … like a private club and [believe] they can do whatever they want," said Lawrence.
'He just kept screaming'
He admitted he lost his cool, stormed back into the Legion, and came face-to-face with the bride, just as she was about to perform the traditional newlywed ritual: the throwing of the bouquet.
"He never did say what it was about. He just kept screaming," said Clarke, adding she was unaware that guests were drinking alcohol outside the building.
For about a minute, Lawrence shouted profanities, angrily pointed his finger at the bride and others, and threatened to shut down the party.
Lawrence left after another legionnaire intervened.
Clarke said she was too shaken to carry on, and never tossed the bouquet. The party, she said, fizzled out.
“I was, as you can imagine, crying and humiliated in front of all my wedding guests," she said.
Oct. 3 started out as expected for the couple. They exchanged vows at a church in nearby Salmon Cove, and then hosted about 100 people at the Legion.
'Ruined my life'
The decorations were elaborate, the meals were tasty, and the dance floor was hopping for most of the evening. But the fun ended abruptly with Lawrence's outburst just before midnight.
On Thursday night, Clarke told her story on Facebook, with her post shared nearly 600 times as of Friday afternoon.
The wedding reception at the Carbonear Legion on Oct. 3 for Justin and Janell Clarke ended early following an outburst by Legion member Berkley Lawrence. As a result, Janell Clarke did not get to throw her wedding bouquet. (Janell Clarke)
On Friday morning, she received a letter of apology from Lawrence.
“All I can do is apologize to everybody involved in the situation, to the bride, to the groom, to the people upstairs, to my Legion, to my wife. It's not the way I behave normally. This incident has absolutely ruined my life," said Lawrence.
Five people, including Clarke, who witnessed the incident, wrote letters to the Legion executive.
Clarke had asked for Lawrence to be suspended from the Legion, and she also wanted to be compensated for having her reception cut short by Lawrence's outburst.
The branch executive met on Wednesday night and decided an apology was sufficient, and that's when Clarke decided to go public.
Branch president defends Lawrence
Branch president Mike Butt chaired Wednesday's special meeting, but said he was not able to vote on the decision to have Lawrence apologize.
Butt admitted, without offering any specifics, that he was not entirely happy with the executive's decision to limit their response to an apology.
"I may have went a little bit different," Butt said, adding "we are deeply sorry this happened."
But the president also defended Lawrence, saying "I don't think he should be made to suffer for 45 seconds or 60 seconds of a lapse."
Butt described Lawrence as "number one in the Legion and he will always be number one."
Clarke, meanwhile, said her perfect wedding day ended on a sour note, and now she gets emotional every time she glances at her wedding dress in the closet.

Horror movies are reliably successful at the box office — just look at "Obsession" and "Backrooms" this year.
They often have relatively low budgets, deliver strong box-office returns, and can create IP that leads to sequels and spin-offs for years to come. Plus, when Halloween rolls around, costumes and masks provide another bump to a studio's bottom line.
But creating a completely original, compelling, and terrifying horror story can be challenging. That's why some of the most iconic and successful scary movies are based on real-world events.
For example, "The Conjuring" franchise is based on the case files of real paranormal investigators Lorraine and Ed Warren. In total, the films have made almost $3 billion at the box office.
These are the real stories and crimes that influenced some of the most classic horror films of all time, including "The Exorcist," "Nightmare on Elm Street," and "Jaws."
"The Conjuring" is about the Perron family and the traumatic experiences they're having in their new Rhode Island home.
The Perrons (husband Roger, wife Carolyn, and their five daughters) moved into what was known as the Old Arnold Estate in 1971, The Providence Journal reported.
Almost immediately, the family reported paranormal activity, such as floating or moving furniture, doors opening and closing, disembodied sounds, and even being pushed, pulled, and hurt by unseen spirits.
Upon calling in paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren, they found that the property was haunted by various ghosts, but that one particularly malevolent spirit, Bathsheba, was preying on them.
Bathsheba Sherman, who lived on the property in the 1800s, has been described as a suspected Satanist who was charged with the violent murder of her first child, though historians say she was never convicted of a crime or accused of witchcraft.
The property sold for $1.5 million in 2022. It has since been acquired by "Ghost Hunters" star Jason Hawes for $1.3 million, according to land records.
"The Conjuring 2" is about a girl being possessed by a demon in London.
The Hodgson family reported experiencing unusual phenomena in their London home in August 1977, such as furniture flying through the air, and objects hurling toward witnesses, The Daily Mail reported.
Most famously, however, Janet, one of four Hodgson children, claimed she was being possessed by a man named Bill Wilkins — it was later confirmed that a man by that name did, in fact, live in the house and died there of a brain hemorrhage, People reported.
While Janet later said that around "2%" of the haunting was made up, she maintains that the Enfield Poltergeist was real.
You can listen to audio of her while she claimed she was possessed to make up your own mind.
The third film is "The Conjuring: The Devil Made Me Do It," which is about the real trial of Arne Cheyenne Johnson.
In the third "Conjuring" film, Ed and Lorraine are tasked with helping a young man, Arne, who murdered his landlord after getting possessed by a demon, which Ed witnessed. In his trial, the Warrens supported Arne using the defense of demonic possession, a first in the United States.
This is based on the real case of 19-year-old Johnson, who really did murder his landlord in 1981 and subsequently claimed he was innocent because he'd been possessed, as reported at the time by The New York Times.
Johnson (and the Warrens) claimed that a demon was exorcised from the body of 11-year-old David Glatzel and then moved to Johnson. His girlfriend claimed she heard Johnson challenge the demon itself to leave Glatzel and possess him instead.
Several months after Johnson's encounter with Warrens and the Glatzels, he stabbed his landlord to death, and then claimed he had no memory of the crime and was possessed.
In reality, this defense was rejected; his lawyers then pivoted toward the self-defense strategy, and he was convicted of manslaughter. He served five years in prison.
The fourth main film, "The Conjuring: Last Rites," is based on the Smurl haunting in the '70s and '80s.
In what's supposed to be the final cinematic appearance of Patrick Wilson and Vera Farmiga as the Warrens, "Last Rites" is a loose adaptation of the alleged Smurl haunting, which took place in West Pittson, Pennsylvania.
Per The Times Leader, Jack and Janet Smurl, played by Elliot Cowan and Rebecca Calder, respectively, called the Warrens to their home in 1986 to address claims that a demon had slammed their 75-pound German shepherd into a wall, threw one of their children down the stairs, and even bitten Jack's ear.
"The Smurls are truly a family coming under a visual attack," Ed Warren said at the time. "The ghost, devil, demon — or whatever you call it — is in that home."
An exorcism was performed in that year, but it was, apparently, unsuccessful.
Of course, the Smurls had plenty of doubters, including a priest who stayed in their home for two nights and reported nothing suspicious. The Smurls eventually left West Pittson and moved to Wilkes-Barre, about 10 miles away.
The film dramatizes this story, but is mainly focused on passing the demon-hunting torch from Ed and Lorraine to their daughter, Judy (Mia Tomlinson).
"Annabelle," "Annabelle: Creation," and "Annabelle Comes Home" tell the story of an evil doll that terrorizes her owner.
Annabelle is a doll believed to be imbued with an evil spirit. While the real-life Raggedy Ann doll (viewable at The Haunted Warren Museum in Salem, Massachusetts) is much less creepy-looking than her movie counterpart, she is said to have terrorized her owner.
According to The New Haven Register, the story of the doll begins in 1970, when a nurse received it as a birthday gift from her mother. She soon began to notice that the doll would change positions by itself. She then started finding creepy notes with messages like "Help me" written on them. And she claimed she once found the doll leaking blood.
Once again, the Warrens were contacted for help. According to them, the doll wasn't possessed, but it was being manipulated by a spirit. They cleansed the home and took the doll to their museum, where it remains to this day.
"The Amityville Horror" connects the murders of the DeFeo family with a demonic presence in the house.
On November 13, 1974, at 3:15 a.m., Ronald DeFeo Jr. stole his father's gun and murdered his family in their home in Amityville, New York, claiming that voices in the house made him do it, according to PIX11.
He was later convicted and sentenced to 25 years to life in prison. He died in 2021.
A year after the murders, in 1975, the Lutz family moved into the home and claimed to experience paranormal activity almost immediately, per ABC News.
George — the patriarch of the Lutz family — claimed to wake up frequently at 3:15 a.m. (the time of the murders) and hear gunshots. His daughter Missy gained an imaginary friend named Jodie. Missy says she did not know anything about the murders at the time.
The Lutz family fled their home only 28 days after moving in, sparking one of the greatest debates in paranormal history: Is the Amityville home haunted?
"The Haunting in Connecticut" is about a family that moves into a former funeral home, which turns out to be haunted.
"The Haunting in Connecticut" is based on the plight of the Snedeker family. Their name was changed to Campbell in the movie.
NBC Connecticut reported the Snedekers moved into a new home in the '80s to be closer to the University of Connecticut's hospital, since their son Phillip was undergoing treatment for cancer. The family soon realized that the house they had moved into used to be a funeral home.
According to his mother, Carmen, Phillip quickly became withdrawn and angry and started seeing a ghostly man who would tell him to lash out.
He was later committed due to a schizophrenia diagnosis. But after Phillip left, things reportedly got a lot worse for the rest of the family.
They eventually called in a priest — as well as the Warrens — to perform an exorcism.
"Veronica" is about a Spanish teenager who used an Ouija board to contact a dead loved one with disastrous consequences.
The film is based on a real Spanish teenager whose death was never solved, as Business Insider previously wrote.
In 1992, a student named Estefania Gutierrez performed a "makeshift séance" at her high school. A few months later, she died in the hospital after experiencing seizures and claiming to see shadowy figures.
The story gets even stranger: A year after Gutierrez died, her parents called the police because they were experiencing paranormal activity, similar to the shadowy figures their daughter had reported.
The police were skeptical until they, too, heard disembodied noises. According to Newsweek, the official report called the home "a situation of mystery and rarity."
"The Strangers" is a terrifying look into the mindset of monsters who commit crimes just because they can.
The poster for "The Strangers" claims that the film was "inspired by true events," though it's more of an amalgam of a few terrifying true tales.
Director Bryan Bertino said he drew his main inspiration from an experience from his childhood, according to the film's production notes.
"As a kid, I lived in a house on a street in the middle of nowhere. One night, while our parents were out, somebody knocked on the front door and my little sister answered it. At the door were some people asking for somebody that didn't live there. We later found out that these people were knocking on doors in the area and, if no one was home, breaking into the houses," said Bertino.
Fans of the film have also compared it to the Manson murders and the unsolved murders of the Sharp family, known as the Keddie Cabin Murders.
"The Exorcist," one of the most beloved horror films of all time, is about a preteen girl who becomes possessed by a demon.
"The Exorcist," is based on the story of a 14-year-old boy known as Roland Doe, who began exhibiting strange behavior in 1949, according to The New York Post. His family reported furniture moving on its own, scratches all over Doe's body, and loud, disembodied voices.
After a cross-country move and no change in Doe's strange behavior, his family enlisted the help of the Catholic church. One of the priests involved in the Doe case, Father Raymond Bishop, kept a diary, per The Daily Mail.
One of his entries stated, "At midnight, the Fathers planned to give (Roland) Holy Communion, but Satan would have no part of it. Even while the institution of the Blessed Sacrament was explained, his body was badly scratched and branded. The word 'HELLO' was printed on his chest and thigh."
Eventually, after multiple attempts, the "demon" was exorcised, and Doe returned to normal. He never spoke of the incident publicly.
His real identity was revealed by The Skeptical Inquirer in 2021: Ronald E. Hunkeler. Hunkeler died in 2020 at the age of 86. Before that, he'd been an engineer at NASA and, according to The New York Post, was always afraid his colleagues would find out about his past.
"The Exorcism of Emily Rose" is also about a girl possessed by a demon.
The story of Anneliese Michel, a young German woman — renamed Emily Rose in the film — is tragic.
When Michel was a teenager, she experienced the first symptoms of her alleged possession. She was diagnosed with epilepsy, and given medication to help treat the disease, according to The Washington Post.
But the meds didn't help. Michel continued to have seizures, and she began to claim she was having visions and hearing voices telling her she was a sinner. She became depressed and turned to religion: At her peak, she was genuflecting (kneeling) 600 times a day, eventually rupturing her knee ligaments.
By the time Michel was 23, she had been treated with dozens of different medications (nothing helped), and had undergone 67 exorcisms in 10 months, the Post reported.
She eventually stopped eating and died of starvation in 1976. She weighed 68 pounds.
Her parents and two of her priests were later found guilty of negligent homicide for allowing her to starve, per the German outlet DW.
"The Texas Chain Saw Massacre" is about a group of hitchhikers who pick the wrong family to catch a ride from — they end up being cannibals.
The main villain of "The Texas Chain Saw Massacre" is Leatherface, who was based on real-life killer Ed Gein.
Gein, who grew up in La Crosse, Wisconsin, in the early 1900s, was obsessed with his mother; he rarely interacted with anyone besides her, and when she died, he spiraled, per Encyclopedia Britannica.
Known as "the Butcher of Plainfield," he confessed to killing two women, but, more disturbingly, he took to robbing the graves of recently buried women.
He used their body parts to create something like a woman suit that he wore, pretending to be his mother, according to the book "Deviant." He also had lamps, belts, and bowls made out of human body parts.
Gein's story also partly inspired "Psycho" and "The Silence of the Lambs."
"Poltergeist" tells the story of a family who buys a haunted house built on top of a Native American burial ground.
The plot of 1982 classic "Poltergeist" was based on the Hermann family of Long Island, New York, who claimed to be haunted by a poltergeist that made objects fly through their home, according to Life Magazine.
The Hermann family eventually moved away, but they maintained that the house was haunted.
"When a Stranger Calls" is about a babysitter who's being terrorized by a mysterious caller inside the house with her.
The film is based on the real unsolved murder of 13-year-old Janett Christman in 1950.
As the Columbia Daily Tribune wrote, Christman was babysitting 3-year-old Greg Romack when she called the Columbia Police Department and told them to "come quick," but she hung up before the police could trace her call.
When the Romacks returned home, they discovered Christman's body in a pool of blood. She had been raped and strangled with a cord. The police eventually ruled that it had been an "inside job" — the killer knew the house and its layout well.
"Dead Ringers" explores the mysterious deaths of a pair of co-dependent twin brothers.
The Marcus twins shared a gynecology practice, an apartment in New York City, a house in the Hamptons — and eventually their deaths.
Apparently, 45-year-old Stewart and Cyril Marcus were addicted to barbiturates; when their decomposing bodies were found, their mysterious deaths were first ruled as being caused by an overdose, then by withdrawal (they may have been attempting to wean themselves off the drugs), The New York Times wrote.
The medical examiner told The New York Times that Cyril outlived his brother by a couple of days, and continued to live in the apartment before eventually dying himself.
The film received a TV reboot on Prime Video in 2023, starring Rachel Weisz.
"Jaws" is the story of a small beachside town that's being terrorized by a vengeful shark.
The terrifying tale of the most famous great white shark ever is based upon a string of shark attacks on the Jersey Shore in 1916.
According to Smithsonian Magazine, 25-year-old Charles Vansant bled to death from a bite in Beach Haven, New Jersey. Five days later — and 45 miles north — a bellhop from Spring Lake also bled to death from a shark bite.
The story only gets more terrifying. The same shark then swam 30 miles north and 10 miles inland, killing both a boy and a man trying to save the boy in a creek, NJ.com wrote.
Finally, the fifth victim was attacked 30 minutes later in the same creek — he survived.
According to NJ.com, George Burgess, an ichthyologist (a scientist who concentrates on the study of fish), called it the "most unique set of shark attacks that have ever occurred. "
"The Girl Next Door" is about a boy who tries to save his neighbor from her twisted adopted family.
The murder of Sylvia Likens is known as the "worst crime in Indiana history," the Indy Star reported. Likens was just 16 when she was found dead in the basement of her temporary home.
Her carnival-worker parents left Sylvia and her sister in the care of Gertrude Baniszewski, a mother of seven, paying Baniszewski by the week.
Three months later, on October 26, 1965, police found Sylvia's emaciated corpse, apparently covered in hundreds of wounds, Indianapolis Monthly wrote. Baniszewski — with the help of some of her children and a few neighborhood kids — had tortured the girl to death.
Baniszewski was sentenced to 21 years in prison, but she was eventually released on parole. The rest of the children who were involved served between two and seven years.
"The Possession" is the tale of a family being tortured by a demon inside a dybbuk box.
Jason Haxton bought the dybbuk box on eBay after an earlier owner posted a chilling account of the events that allegedly befell him after he bought it at an estate sale, My San Antonio reported.
He claimed that he bought the box for his mom's birthday and that she almost instantaneously had a stroke upon receiving it, Riverfront Times reported.
He also claimed that the final straw that inspired him to get rid of the box was when his sister, brother, and brother's wife all stayed over, and each one reported having the same exact nightmare, according to a reposting of the original eBay listing.
You might be wondering what exactly a dybbuk is. According to Encyclopedia Britannica, it's a "disembodied human spirit that, because of former sins, wanders restlessly until it finds a haven in the body of a living person," originating in Jewish folklore.
"The Rite" is based upon the life of a real priest, Father Gary Thomas, and his time at the Vatican while training to become an exorcist.
"The Rite" is based on the life of Father Gary Thomas, a priest who is one of 14 Vatican-certified exorcists who works in the US, the Los Angeles Times reported. Thomas told the Times he's exorcised the demons from five people, and that he receives multiple requests for exorcisms daily.
Father Thomas trained for three months in Rome to become a certified exorcist, completing his training in 2005, The Telegraph wrote.
Similarly, the 2023 film "The Pope's Exorcist" is based on the life of real-life priest Father Gabriele Amorth.
Russell Crowe played Amorth in the 2023 film "The Pope's Exorcist," which was based on Amorth's memoirs, "An Exorcist Tells His Story" and "An Exorcist: More Stories."
Smithsonian Magazine wrote that Amorth said he'd performed over 100,000 exorcisms before his death in 2016. He was still performing them that year — and he even let "The Exorcist" director William Friedkin observe one.
Friedkin, who died just a few months after the film's release, wrote about the experience in Vanity Fair. "Out of a hundred people who seek my help," Amorth told Friedkin, "one or two at the most may be possessed."
"Wolf Creek" is about three backpackers in the Australian Outback who unknowingly hitch a ride from a sadistic murderer.
The horrifying tale of the backpackers in "Wolf Creek" is based on a real string of murders in Australia's Belanglo State Forest in the '90s at the hands of Ivan Milat, aka "the Backpacker Killer."
Milat maintained that he was innocent until his death in 2019, The Daily Mail wrote, but was convicted for torturing and killing at least seven people, all backpackers and hitchhikers. Some think that he killed even more.
"Eaten Alive" is about the owner of a Texas hotel who feeds people to his pet crocodile.
Eccentric bootlegger Joe Ball owned a Texas bar called the Sociable Inn in the early 1900s. He also kept multiple alligators in an enclosure near the saloon.
A known ladies' man, Ball had relations with various waitresses, bartenders, and hostesses — three of whom went missing. Turns out, Ball had murdered two of them, reported Texas Monthly.
Many believe he then fed them to his pet alligators, though there was never any evidence — his keeping them as pets was enough to cause concern and create rumors.
When the police came around for questioning in 1938, however, he shot himself in the heart, the San Antonio Express-News wrote.
"Open Water" tells the harrowing tale of a couple fighting to stay alive after their boat leaves them behind in the middle of the ocean.
Tom and Eileen Lonergan were scuba diving at the Great Barrier Reef in Australia in 1998 when they were left behind by their boat after someone messed up the head count. They were never heard from again, The Independent wrote.
According to the outlet, the diving company didn't even realize they were missing until two days later, when their passports and other personal effects were found on the boat.
Months after their disappearance, Tom's dive slate was found 100 miles north of their original disappearance. He had written "We have been abandoned" by the diving company, adding "Help!"
Their dive jackets and one of Eileen's fins eventually washed ashore, but there were no signs of a shark attack or any other violent activity.
Some believe they were eaten by sharks, while others maintain that it was a murder-suicide pact.
Their bodies were never found.
"A Nightmare on Elm Street" is best known for bringing Freddy Krueger, a serial killer who murders people in their dreams, into the mainstream.
The idea for this iconic franchise came from a Los Angeles Times article that Wes Craven, the film's writer and director, read about a boy who was too terrified to sleep after surviving the Killing Fields in Cambodia.
Here's what Craven said to Vulture about his inspiration: "He told his parents he was afraid that if he slept, the thing chasing him would get him, so he tried to stay awake for days at a time."
Craven continued, "When he finally fell asleep, his parents thought this crisis was over. Then they heard screams in the middle of the night. By the time they got to him, he was dead. He died in the middle of a nightmare. Here was a youngster having a vision of a horror that everyone older was denying. That became the central line of 'Nightmare on Elm Street.'"

Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
- Published
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.
Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.
Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.
As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.
BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.
Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.
Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.
The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".
Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks
The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.
The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.
Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".
Oil shipments stall
Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.
About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.
The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.
Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.
So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.
Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".
"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.
The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.
Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.
A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.
Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.
Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.
Additional reporting by Becky Dale

Afcon final to play out in court - when will Morocco or Senegal be crowned champions?
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes but, in its own way, the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) has been playing out for nearly nine months.
Now, finally, one team or the other - either Morocco or Senegal - willl grab the winner. Only that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.
On Thursday, Sport's highest legal authority - the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) - will hear Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they had won back in January against the hosts in Rabat.
But those hungry for a resolution have already been warned it will not arrive on the same day.
So how did we get here? And what happens next?
What happened in the Afcon final?
In front of 66,000 home fans creating an electric atmosphere inside Rabat's Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco appeared set for a date with destiny as they chased their first Afcon title since 1976.
Instead, the final descended into chaos deep into stoppage time.
With the match still goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had already blown for a Moroccan free-kick.
The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a VAR review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.
Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.
Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Real Madrid's Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the grateful arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.
Or so they thought.
- 'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Senegal's triumph 
  - Published19 January
- Senegal decries imprisonment of fans after Afcon clashes 
  - Published24 February
Why was the Afcon final result overturned?
Unsurprisingly the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing Senegal had breached competition regulations.
Article 82, contained within a chapter titled "Withdrawals", states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team… leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" they shall be "considered the loser and shall be eliminated from the current competition".
In March, a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.
While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, others, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.
The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.
- Afcon final 'deficiencies' dealt with - Motsepe 
  - Published13 May
- Denounce 'abject' Afcon decision - senior Caf member 
  - Published19 March
What is the Court of Arbitration for Sport?
Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.
For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.
More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.
The appeal will be heard by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.
In this instance, the panel will be led by 76-year-old Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
If the panel fails to come to a consensus, its president will make the final decision.
- How does Cas work and why can't Man City appeal to it? 
  - Published28 September
When will we get a verdict?
While the hearing, which will be heard in private at the request of the parties involved, is expected to end on Thursday afternoon, Cas have already warned that this is merely the starting point of the panel's deliberation.
In a statement, the court warned it "cannot state when a final decision will be rendered but it will not be on the day of the hearing".
Having already waited nearly nine months to get to this stage, the bad news is that the Cas code states that appeal verdicts should be delivered a maximum of four months after a hearing, though guidelines also say panels should aim for less than three months.
The good news is that it can be quicker.
In 2020, Manchester City appealed to Cas over Uefa's decision to ban them from European club competitions for breaching financial fair play regulations.
The hearing took place on 8 June with the verdict landing in City's favour on 13 July.
What could the long-term fallout be?
Even though Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has already been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe said back in March that they will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.
The Teranga Lions' walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at a referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, back in April.
"This new rule will also apply to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Thiaw has already been given his marching orders by Senegal, having lost his job following the team's last-32 World Cup exit, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Moroccan dugout back in January, was dismissed in March.
Both men will no doubt still view success with Cas as a moral victory.
Whatever the outcome, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.
The FMRF's senior hierarchy were furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.
The FSF and the Senegalese government have, meanwhile, leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.
Other incidents also irked them, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which eventually led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.
With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.
But while the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

Selma Blair's representatives say she didn't intend to hurt anyone on flight that led to her arrest
Selma Blair's representatives have stated she did not intend to harm anyone during a recent flight incident
