Actor Selma Blair did not intend to harm anyone during a flight and its aftermath where she is alleged to have assaulted two flight attendants, a police officer and a nurse, according to a statement Friday from her representatives.
The long statement sought to push back against what it said were inaccurate and unsympathetic portrayals of Blair, 54, and the Delta flight from Los Angeles to New York on Sunday that led to her first arrest.
“Selma Blair experienced a medical emergency on the flight,” the statement said. “There was no attempt to open the door of the aircraft. Selma did not intend to harm anyone.”
A previous statement along with her lawyer's remarks in court had said briefly that a medical emergency was behind all that happened, but the new statement gave a more detailed defense.
Blair has multiple sclerosis, and without specifying she had done so, the statement said it is “outrageous” that anyone would suggest she doesn't.
“Her diagnosis has been public since 2018,” the statement said. “What Selma has been able to do physically in the years since is nothing short of a miracle. She still has bad days, and she lives with pain daily. Selma also has pseudobulbar affect, a neurological condition secondary to her MS, which bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her.”
The statement added: “For the same reason, she travels with a service dog who doesn’t leave her side, and the authorities took her dog from her.”
The statement said she has been a relentless advocate for disability rights and the MS community.
Blair was accused of injuring two flight attendants on the plane bound for John F. Kennedy Airport, then kicking a police officer taking her to the hospital and kicking a nurse once she got there, according to a statement from the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey.
She pleaded not guilty Monday to two counts of assault on state charges involving the officer and the nurse, and a judge issued a protective order for them. She is free on bail, and her next court date is in January.
The FBI also issued Blair a notice charging her with assault related to her actions aboard the aircraft, according to a federal law enforcement official who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly about the matter.
Authorities have released few details of what happened aboard the plane.
In air traffic communications, the Delta pilot asked the tower to have medical personnel waiting at the gate to treat bite marks and a bloody nose, but said ambulances were not necessary.
The Michigan-born Blair began acting in New York in her early 20s. Her major film roles have included 1999’s “Cruel Intentions,” 2001’s “Legally Blonde” and 2004’s “Hellboy.”
In 2016, Blair apologized for making statements she later regretted during a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles. She said she had mixed alcohol with medication, causing her to black out.
Friday's statement said the public version of the more recent events has “been built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline.”
“A handful of journalists have taken the time to report on Selma as a human being rather than a headline, and we are grateful to them,” the statement said. “But fair reporting has been the exception, and in the space left by our silence, speculation has hardened into something being treated as fact.”

Tesla's redesigned Roadster has a cold-gas thruster option, but you'll need $250,000 just to reserve it
The automaker has unveiled the vehicle with some crazy stunts.
Tesla has unveiled the next-generation Roadster, nine years after the company showed off its concept prototype and after years and years of launch delay. Elon Musk and the Tesla team introduced the vehicle during an event at the SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas with a stunt. It drove up a C-shaped ramp and stopped in the middle of the part perpendicular to the ground while it was hanging upside-down. Then the vehicle repeated the action and jumped off the ramp from the top and flipped, its thruster system kicking in so it could safely hover to the ground.
When they opened up the door to the driver's seat, an Optimus robot was seating there. It was, however, only for show, and the stunts were programmed into the vehicle. They explained later on that the Roadster has a suction system at the bottom of the car that enabled it to stick upside-down to the ramp. On its website, Tesla said that its multi-mode fan and ground sealing system pulls air out from beneath the vehicle to act as a downforce generator, providing suction that make holding the vehicle upside-down possible even when it's stationary.
Meanwhile, it could jump off the ramp and safely land on the ground, thanks to its attitude-control thrusters and thrusters in the rear, which use technology borrowed from SpaceX. These advanced cold-gas thrusters use all-electric actuators that enable precise thrust and can perform "micro adjustments within a fraction of a second."
Musk said the new Roadster will go into production in 2028.
Tesla first started taking pre-orders for the Roadster way back when it was first announced. Those who didn't get the chance can now reserve a unit for $5,000, with $45,000 to follow within the next 10 days for the base vehicle. As you'd expect, the thrusters and air suction system cost extra. For the "Thrust" package, which comes with the suction system and acceleration thrusters, buyers are expected to pay an additional $245,000 within 10 days of reservation. The "Rocket" version, which comes with the full-flight system, is invite-only and probably something we'll see a lot of in influencers' videos.

Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X processor is finally here, and we’ve been collectively testing a small fortune’s worth of powerful laptops sporting this new “superchip.” RTX Spark is designed to be a high-performing Arm-based SoC for laptops and small desktop computers, rivaling the best from Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. It has loads of cores, Nvidia RTX Blackwell graphics, and enough power and unified memory to run sizable local AI models.
A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops
Nvidia’s new Arm-based laptop chip is an exciting new challenger, but exclusively for the high-end.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The flagship placement is inside Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra with a staggering 128GB of unified memory, which our own Tom Warren fully reviewed. Sean Hollister has been testing a 64GB version of the Asus ProArt P16, which I’ve also been testing in its top-spec 128GB config. Since I’m the most spoiled of the lot, I also have a 64GB Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 and a 32GB HP OmniBook Ultra in for testing.
All of these laptops have the same N1X chip with 20 CPU cores and 6,144 GPU CUDA cores, and they’re all wildly expensive — ranging from the HP OmniBook at $3,199.99 to the Asus ProArt’s $6,999.99. There’s an 18-core / 5,120 CUDA N1X chip in lower cost configs, but that only gets as cheap as $2,599.99 for a Surface Laptop Ultra or a smaller Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM.
These are big and expensive laptops built on new chips. They’re meant for developers, coders, and content creators who might also want the ability to use local AI and even play games using the latest Nvidia tech like DLSS 5. There’s a lot to test, and we have not had a ton of time to test it all. So below you won’t find an exhaustive scored review of any one laptop, but instead our impressions and thoughts from three writers using five laptops for a week.
Is Nvidia’s “superchip” really all that super? Are Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm officially on notice? Have any of us gotten any sleep?
Does it just work?
Antonio Di Benedetto: Windows on Arm is no longer a wholly subpar experience like it was a few years ago. Thanks in large part to the push around Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, lots of development has been put into native Arm-based apps for Windows. And many x86 apps work fine via Microsoft’s Prism emulation layer.
Adobe has had native Arm versions of Photoshop and Premiere for some time now, and even though my precious Lightroom Classic is still an x86-based app I don’t notice any issues using it on Arm. At this point, you’ve gotta be relying on specialized software that’s exclusively x86 based for Windows on Arm to be a non-starter — or you want to freely play any games out there without any worry of incompatibilities.
Sean Hollister: Every so often, there’s that moment when an app takes longer to load than it should, and I wonder whether it’ll load at all. Even then, it typically loads. Occasionally, it takes more than one try. My Evernote notes disappeared a few times one day when I alt-tabbed away, but a force refresh fixed that. And apps don’t seem to respect my system preference for dark mode.
But I largely agree with Antonio. I made an RTX Spark my daily driver, with all my typical work and personal apps — Signal, Discord, Audacity, CapCut and Evernote, Irfanview, Slack, ScreenToGif and more — and nothing has failed me so far. I never once needed to think whether I was running an Arm or an x86 app. The real hitches came with gaming and AI, as you’ll read below.
Tom Warren: I’ve been using a Windows on Arm laptop with a Qualcomm chip daily for the past two years and things have improved to the point that I can’t tell if an app is native or not anymore. That’s the same story on the RTX Spark laptops, and I feel like Nvidia’s entry into this category will only improve the story for creative apps and gaming.
Can it game?
TW: Windows on Arm never looked like a serious gaming platform before now. While there still aren’t many native Arm games, Nvidia’s GPU helps bruteforce through the emulation layer. Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games.
I mostly game on my desktop, where I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. I was able to run Black Myth: Wukong at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in Cyberpunk 2077 and averaged 66fps, and Forza Horizon 6 managed an average of 57fps.
In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go.
SH: Like Tom says, the GPU power is there — but the CPU might hold back some of your games. I had plenty of power for a smooth 60fps in Returnal (at 1440p with high settings), Expedition 33 (at a DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with high settings), Jedi Survivor (DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with medium settings), and Shadow of the Tomb Raider (at native 1800p and highest spec).
But when I fired up Helldivers 2, even dipping down to a DLSS-upscaled 1080p was no guarantee of 60fps in the highest difficulty missions. There are just too many enemies on screen for the Spark to keep up. Star Wars Zero Company is even more CPU-bound — the Spark didn’t care whether I was maximizing or minimizing the graphics and screen resolution. No matter what I tried, I typically saw my framerate capped between 37fps and 39fps in battle.
Even ancient and low-powered games can have quirks. I tried the 2003 title Max Payne 2 and saw situations where framerate dipped to 50fps. I even saw a few hitches in the excellent UFO 50, a collection of 2D games, though a couple other 2D games ran great.
I’m also not sure if RTX Spark is suitable for VR yet. The excellent Titanfall 2 VR mod worked, and it seemed to run fine at first, but lost a little stability after a few minutes. That could be my Wi-Fi, because the driver for Valve’s Steam Frame wireless adapter wouldn’t install on the Spark. Neither did Steam’s streaming audio solution, so the audio came out of the Nvidia laptop instead of the headset.
Just so we’re clear, all of this is assuming you want a laptop maxing out its fans and positively dumping heat on your desk or lap. That’s not unusual for thin gaming notebooks, but it’s way louder and hotter than a good desktop or handheld.

AD: I’ve wanted a MacBook Pro-like laptop with full PC gaming chops for as long as I can remember, so I was hyped for these laptops to deliver the goods in graphics. The first night, I set up the Asus ProArt P16, with all 128GB of its ridiculously large pool of memory, and when I booted up Big Walk for my planned online evening with some friends my first thought was, “Well, that looks okay. I guess.” I know Big Walk isn’t some triple-A graphical titan, but it has some fairly demanding graphics for the “friend slop” genre. I expected the N1X to max it out, or at least get close, but not really.
I had to bump the P16’s 4K display down to 2560 x 1600, and instead of Big Walk’s Highest or Very high graphics presets, I brought it down to High to maintain a decently solid 60-ish fps. Does any of that really matter for this silly co-op game about solving puzzles with your buddies? Of course not. It looked fine, after all. But it was a sobering reminder that this “superchip” is no graphical magician.
As Tom and Sean point out, RTX Spark can do some decent gaming, but temper your expectations for medium or even low settings in some cases, and be ready to rely on DLSS and frame gen. There’s no denying that cheaper desktops and even laptops with discrete Nvidia graphics cards can easily beat out an N1X. Nvidia claims it’s like having an RTX 5070 Laptop GPU in an SoC, but in my testing it was somewhere between that and an RTX 5060 Laptop GPU — not a slouch, for sure, but if you’re a gamer first your money goes much further with traditional Nvidia graphics cards.
How’s the battery life?
SH: Nvidia’s partners saw fit to equip their first wave of RTX Spark laptops with some of the biggest batteries you can bring on an airplane with no questions asked — but even with a 99.9 watt-hour pack like the one in my Asus ProArt P16, these laptops won’t be winning awards for longevity. While Tom and Antonio spent their days testing every use case under the sun, I made the P16 my daily driver for normal work while watching the battery meter like a hawk. That mostly means writing stories in a web browser, and it’s not quite lasting the day.
My best run was 5 hours and 40 minutes of real-world work at 50 percent brightness, including an hour-long video call with Tom and Antonio to strategize our RTX Spark coverage plan. The next day, I got only about 5 hours from a full charge because I spent two of them editing this video in Capcut. The third time I drained the battery, it took 5 hours, too.
With web work, I’m typically seeing 13-17 watt battery drain on the laptop’s default settings, but that climbs to 20-30 watts with light video work, up to 50 watts during the (brief) Capcut video export, and I made it jump all the way to 120 watts playing Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. The battery couldn’t keep feeding at that rate — it slowly went down, and at 30 percent charge I saw a big performance hit as it dropped dramatically to 60 watts.
The good news is the Asus charges fast from a 140W USB-C PD power source. It took 20 minutes to go from dead to 50 percent battery, another 15 minutes to get to 70 percent, and a total of 1 hour, 15 minutes to reach 95 percent charge.
AD: I’ve had to run lots of benchmarks while plugged in, so I haven’t been able to spend as much time testing battery life as I’d normally like. Anecdotally, in lots of fits and starts, battery life seems solid. As Sean saw, you’re unlikely to get through a full eight hour work day unless you’re going out of your way to be efficient. And if you fire up anything heavy, like a local AI model (more on that in a minute), you won’t even make it to lunch. I’ll eventually do more thorough battery testing as I continue using these laptops, including our usual rundown tests for a bit of 1:1 comparisons.
Does local AI seem useful?
TW: Not yet. It all feels like a beta aimed at developers right now: from the install experience of AI agents flashing up command prompts and Visual Studio, to the fans blasting away for the most basic of queries.
I struggled to come up with many compelling use cases for the power of these chips for local AI work. A lot of tasks could simply be done far more quickly and without the laptop fans spinning up by using a free cloud model. The power here is really in leaving the agent running at full throttle to build something overnight, running tasks that developers would favor.
It’s also nice to have this all on a local device, without having to share emails and files with a cloud service and worry about the privacy aspects. Still, I would regularly close OpenClaw or Hermes and not let them run in the background all day, especially if I had given them permissions to access local files. I’m just not ready to trust AI fully, local or not.
Microsoft and Nvidia both envision a future where AI agents automate things on your PC, but I’m still not fully convinced. While there are some mundane tasks I could certainly automate, I like using my PC to edit photos or videos, write, and play games. I don’t want to sit there and watch a robot do all of that for me. That’s part of the joy of computing to me.
SH: I walked out of Nvidia’s Editor’s Day thinking I might finally have a reason to fire up local AI. I asked Hermes, running Qwen3.8-27B, to build me a daily news briefing much like the one in Nvidia’s on-stage demo. It took 10 minutes, and 10 percent of my entire 99.9 watt-hour battery, to finally produce a list of stories that took the cloud-based Claude (Opus 5.5) half as long — while utterly monopolizing my GPU and dramatically heating up the Spark laptop. The laptop stayed hot and a little sluggish as long as I kept Hermes open.
Claude also produced better results, with more detail and better sourcing. I guess I got the local AI tokens for “free,” I wouldn’t trust Claude with my email, and I probably could have used a smaller, lighter model. But I went with what the program recommended, and that was the result. I tried a clean reinstall of Hermes to make sure it wasn’t a misconfiguration, but this time, the prompt took even longer and used 60 percent of my battery. Ouch.
AD: I’m still early in my journey of learning to use local AI, and these RTX Spark laptops are obviously a viable — albeit, expensive — option. But even if you have 128GB of memory to use some chunky models, it’s still not a user-friendly experience for beginners. Microsoft’s Get Started intro in Windows 11 gives you easy one-click installs for Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, and Perplexity. (Which all have ESRB ratings for some reason?) But after that, you’re kind of on your own. I stuck with Hermes, since that’s what I was already using on the Mac Studio, but if you’re using it on a system with 32GB of RAM or less it just tells you there isn’t enough memory for its recommended local Qwen models — either routing you towards the cloud or fully relying on you to go fetch a smaller model on your own.
Using local AI has major privacy advantages over cloud models, but it’s definitely less convenient since local LLMs are much slower to process and more taxing on your system. Churning a local model through your laptop’s memory tears through any of these laptops’ large batteries, and the results from LLMs are still mixed. I burned through 30 percent of the Lenovo Yoga 9n’s battery in 36 minutes to get a Qwen 3.8 27B model to resize and add a white background to five product images in PNG format — and it cropped the images wrong and cut off the products. I got it to do it right after a couple follow-up prompts, and grabbing the power cable to prevent Hermes from killing the laptop in the process.
Is the hardware truly great?
AD: These laptops are very expensive, but that also means the manufacturers are mostly bringing their A-games. Across the Asus, HP, Lenovo, and what I gathered from Tom’s thoughts on the Surface, the RTX Spark line is awash in great-to-excellent haptic trackpads, keyboards, screens, and speakers. The metal builds of the three I’m testing feel great to the touch. The OLED displays all look fantastic. And each of these are decently thin for the kind of workstation-class laptops that they are.
If I had to pick one for myself based on hardware alone I’d probably choose the Asus ProArt. It ticks the most boxes for me with its three USB-C ports, super bright display, superior inverted-T arrow cluster, and full SD card slot. The HP actually feels the nicest, with an impressively rock-solid chassis, but at nearly five pounds it’s the heaviest of the bunch, and its microSD card slot is much less useful to me.
As for the Lenovo, it’s actually been my sleeper favorite. It’s the only 2-in-1 in this crop I’ve been testing, and that just makes it more flexible (pun intended) and fun. You can use its large stylus on either the screen or the large trackpad, giving it lots more potential for graphics and design work. And tent mode with a large 16-inch 120Hz OLED is a delight for the occasional gaming session or watching shows and movies — it’s just not as bright as the Asus.
SH: I’ve only truly driven the Asus P16 so far, but I was impressed with the build quality of the whole spectrum of RTX Spark launch laptops at Nvidia’s Editor’s Day. The Asus P16 probably wouldn’t be my pick personally because of its extra glossy screen and oversensitive touchpad. I like to use my laptops in rooms with lots of ambient light, and find I have to crank up the brightness of this machine’s otherwise excellent calibrated OLED screen. Meanwhile, my palms keep tapping my mouse cursor on things I didn’t mean to tap, just because they accidentally brush the touchpad while typing.
The speakers and webcam also leave something to be desired, but the Windows Hello face login and proximity sensing are excellent. As soon as I walk away, the screen dims, and I’m logged right back in just by looking at my laptop. Despite the heat, Asus’ fans aren’t shrill — they’re very loud and noticeable but at least it’s whoosh rather than whine.
TW: While I ran into some weird bugs with the Surface Laptop Ultra during testing, I can’t fault the hardware. The look and feel is very similar to a MacBook Pro, and the magnetic USB-C port really feels like something Apple should have done — it’s that good. The large haptic trackpad carries on the tradition of great Surface trackpads, with the added benefit of subtle haptic feedback when you move windows around or align objects in apps like PowerPoint.
I would have preferred an OLED display on the Laptop Ultra, but I found switching away from the default “Vivid” color option to “Enhanced” improved the contrast on the MicroLED panel. I also really appreciate the port section on the Laptop Ultra, especially that there’s a full SD card reader and even a USB-A port. Check out my full review for more thoughts.

AD: Yes, the RTX Spark N1X is a powerful chip. These high-end laptop configurations we’ve been testing with lots of unified memory are meant to compete with the Pro and Max chips in Apple’s MacBook Pros. And while they can hang in some GPU performance tests, like tying the top spec M5 Max in a Blender render, Apple’s CPUs are much more powerful.
Apple has put lots of development into its in-house processors and the extra-fast “super cores” of its M6, M5 Pro, and M5 Max chips. And, frankly, nothing competes with those chips in single core performance — not even Nvidia’s “superchip.” (Seriously, can we stop with the word super?) But the part that stings most about the RTX Spark’s 20-core CPU is that even a lowly 12-core M6 Mac Mini competes with it in multicore performance — and a Mac Mini starts at just $900.
It’s awesome to see this kind of graphics performance without the need for a discrete GPU, allowing for thinner system designs with less noisy fans. I’m into it, just as I was with AMD’s Strix Halo APU — but like Strix Halo, Nvidia’s RTX Spark is a pricey part. And there’s no denying that Apple’s offerings are more well-rounded performers, so long as you don’t care as much about games.
TW: It’s definitely up there, but I think Qualcomm comes closer to Apple’s M-series chips on the CPU side. Qualcomm also had years of experimentation with Windows on Arm before it acquired Nuvia and managed to create a competitive chip with the Snapdragon X series.
I think Nvidia will need a similar amount of work to catch up on the CPU side for future RTX Spark chips. The development of the RTX Spark took at least three years, and I had heard from sources familiar with Nvidia’s plans that the chips were supposed to launch last year. So work has been ongoing, but the CPU side is still a little disappointing.
Nvidia picked MediaTek for its Arm-based CPU, a chipmaker that is better known for the Wi-Fi hardware in laptops, not the CPUs. I sure hope the next-generation is more powerful. The whole time I’ve been testing the Surface Laptop Ultra I couldn’t help but think the forbidden dream would be a combination of a Qualcomm CPU and Nvidia GPU. I can’t see that ever happening in reality, but it would certainly be interesting to see.
So what’s our take on RTX Spark so far?
TW: I think it will elevate interest in Windows on Arm for creative and gaming tasks, simply because we haven’t had Arm-based Windows laptops that are really capable of running games until now. Nvidia is targeting creators and developers with its first round of RTX Spark laptops, but there’s definitely a gap here for a more affordable version focused on gaming. Perhaps that’s the N1 chips we’ve heard rumors about.
SH: Nice, but too pricey. Too hot and loud when you’re doing the things that would theoretically justify that price. I care what they stand for, and the direction they’re pointed, far more than I care to own one.
AD: I love that there is now even more competition in the laptop space, but the super high prices makes RTX Spark laptops mostly unattainable. I want to see lower cost options come around, as well as an eventual second generation with higher CPU performance to hopefully close the gap further with Apple. I also hope this helps push development for Arm-based and Arm-compatible games forward. Maybe it could even one day mean easier porting of games to macOS. Wouldn’t that be a fun outcome?
As cool as it will be to keep testing these super high-end RTX Spark models, I’m most hyped to get my hands on a base Surface Laptop Ultra or Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM and see how they stack up to the entry-level 14-inch M5 MacBook Pro. That’s my personal sweet spot for Apple’s lineup — the people’s MacBook Pro. (Well, okay, less these days now that it starts at two-grand.)
It’s an exciting time in computing when it comes to chip choice, but it’s also an absolutely cursed time thanks to RAMageddon and sky high prices. I’m constantly wondering what laptops like these RTX Sparks or even Googlebooks might have cost if AI demands didn’t drive up the prices of RAM and storage. I have no idea who is going to spend up to $7,000 on these laptops when PC sales as a whole seem on a downward trend, but it’s cool they exist.

Work starts on Bundaberg's first hotel development in 20 years
In short:
Work has started on Bundaberg's first hotel development in 20 years.
A recent report into the region's accommodation needs showed it was 800 beds short every night.
What's next?
Construction on the new hotel on Airport Drive is due to finish by the middle of next year.
It has taken two decades, but Bundaberg's next hotel development is underway.
Four hours north of Brisbane, the city is a key tourism destination for the southern Great Barrier Reef but has not attracted significant short-term accommodation development in 20 years, according to Bundaberg Regional Council.
The 4.5-star, three-storey hotel, situated across the road from the Bundaberg Airport, will offer 97 rooms.
Mayor Helen Blackburn said the demand for accommodation was constantly growing.
"The hotel demand study showed us that we were 800 beds short every night in our region," she said.
"This is just one step towards bridging that gap."
Cr Blackburn said it had been difficult to attract hotel developers to the region due to the current stock of aging motels.
"Those older motels sell their rooms at a cheaper rate, which then doesn't give investors the confidence to think that if they build a new hotel, they can get the price for the rooms that they need," she said.
Developer MVP said the new hotel would refresh the hospitality offering in Bundaberg.
"We hope that it will be a destination of choice for travellers to the region and will bring more travellers to the region," a spokesperson said.
The hotel has been funded by investor MyState Limited, with chief executive Brett Morgan saying the demand was clear.
"Every time you go down the street in Bundaberg, there's no-vacancy signs everywhere," he said.
Mr Morgan said the hotel would also create about 50 ongoing jobs.
Hopes for more operators, airlines
Bundaberg Tourism chief executive Duncan Littler said the development would cater to leisure and business travellers.
"Already, there's more than 750,000 people that choose to visit the beautiful Bundaberg region each year and they stay for more than 2 million nights," he said.
"We hope that investments like this will also encourage other [tourism] operators, potentially even airlines, to consider investing in the region."
Cr Blackburn said other accommodation applications were in the pipeline but did not elaborate.
"We have definitely been encouraging accommodation providers in terms of hotels, student accommodation and even aged care accommodation to set up in our region because we know that we need that here," she said.
Construction on the Airport Drive hotel is due to finish by mid-2027, with the first guests expected later next year.

Police in the Croatian city of Split on Friday arrested at least a dozen fans of HNK Hajduk Split a day after unruly supporters held an anti-Semitic rally, clashed with officers and interrupted a match against Ajax.
Ahead of the game on Thursday evening, thousands of fans shouted insults against Jews and chanted in praise of Nazi leader Adolf Hitler as they marched behind a car with the mockup of a coffin on top emblazoned with the name of the Ajax team, which has long been associated with Amsterdam’s Jewish community.
The outburst drew widespread condemnation in Croatia, with President Zoran Milanovic and the conservative government harshly criticising the fans and demanding punishment. Police said on Friday that they had arrested 12 of the fans on charges of inciting violence and hatred, but indicated that they may arrest more suspects.
The Hajduk fans clashed with police and forced a 12-minute interruption of the match when they threw flares and other objects onto the field.
ALSO READ: Spain to appeal to CAS over punishment for Islamophobic chants in Egypt friendly
Hajduk eventually beat Ajax 2-1 in the home team’s first major European match for 16 years, in the UEFA Conference League.
The Croatian Football Association said in a statement that the incident damaged the country’s football image, calling the behaviour completely opposed to “the basic values of sports: mutual respect, tolerance and togetherness.”
Milanovic urged “measures and sanctions that will show that there is no place for glorification of Nazism in Croatia.”
The Hajduk Split team could face Union of European Football Associations disciplinary action over the game disruption, apologised for the fan behaviour, but said it reflected only some of the club’s fans.
“Despite all efforts, things happened that we are not proud of, but we are ready to take the consequences as a club,” the team said in a statement.
The Croatian government long has been accused of turning a blind eye to rising nationalist and extremist sentiments in the country related to the country’s World War II regime that collaborated with the Nazis. The government has denied this.
Milorad Pupovac, the political leader of ethnic Serbs in Croatia, who were the victims of the WWII pro-Nazi regime in Croatia, said “it was just a question of time before we will reach this point that happened in Split yesterday.”
Tens of thousands of ethnic Serbs, Jews, Roma and anti-fascist Croats perished in the WWII concentration camps in Croatia. But nationalist Croats have used the WWII pro-Nazi chant as a symbol of Croatia’s struggle for independence from the Serb-led former Yugoslavia.
The Split incidents also were condemned by the Israeli Embassy in Zagreb, which said it was “deeply shocked” and urged a government response.
The Hajduk Split team, which could face Union of European Football Associations disciplinary action over the game disruption, apologized for the fan behavior, but said it reflected only some of the club’s fans.
“Despite all efforts, things happened that we are not proud of, but we are ready to take the consequences as a club,” the team said in a statement.

On 15 November 2021, the State of Qatar and WHO convened their first Strategic Dialogue, building on their strong partnership and their commitment to work jointly in addressing global health challenges. The overall objective of the meeting was to create a platform to facilitate regular dialogue with WHO leadership and technical experts on WHO programmes and policies. This event also provided an opportunity to review the key areas supported by Qatar and explore new areas of collaboration including the impact of COVID-19, emergency response and preparedness, science and innovation, neglected tropical diseases, health and migration.
“The Government of Qatar is an important partner and supporter of WHO's mandate and programmes,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “I thank the State of Qatar for its commitment to global health and its commitment to flexible funding for WHO, which is so critical to our mission to promote health, keep the world safe and serve the vulnerable.”
Her Excellency Dr Hanan Mohamed Al-Kuwari, Minister of Public Health said: “under the leadership of His Highness Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani the Amir of the State of Qatar, Qatar is proud to provide flexible funding to support WHO’s work on COVID-19, and to contribute towards humanitarian responses in emergencies as well as the new partnership on sport and health.”
“We are keen to strengthen the existing partnership between WHO and the State of Qatar to enhance efficiency actions and establish essential health services as part of our push to achieve SDG3,” Mr Khalifa Al Kuwari, Director General of Qatar Fund for Development.
The strategic dialogue follows a number of enhanced collaborations and developments within the partnership between Qatar and WHO partnership. This includes the signature of the multi-year Memorandum of Understanding focusing on the promotion of health and safety, launched ahead of the 2022 FIFA World Cup that will take place in Qatar. A Memorandum of Understanding for the period 2020-2023 in support of the Organization’s Thirteenth General Programme of work 2019-2023, was also signed in March 2021.
Read more about the strategic partnership between Qatar and WHO.

- While there is a real proposal to build an underwater data center in the Bay of Fundy near Maine, the company behind the idea, DeepGreen Western Passage SPV, has not yet determined whether the proposal is even feasible.
- The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has accepted the company's application for a preliminary permit, which gives DeepGreen priority status for any development in the area for the next four years. The permit does not grant the company permission to build the center, nor does it give the company permission to conduct on-water studies within the area.
- If the data center is indeed built, it's possible it will affect endangered whale species, as there is overwhelming evidence that noise and ship activity can harm whales. However, it's not yet known exactly how impactful underwater data centers are to whale habitats, given that the idea is so new.
- DeepGreen's developer on the project, Louis Wolfson, confirmed to Snopes that it has no concrete construction plans as of this writing. To figure out whether the project is possible, DeepGreen must eventually apply for permits at various federal and state agencies to begin extensive environmental and technical studies in the area, which it has not yet done.
- The proposal has already faced steep opposition from environmentalists, the city of Eastport, which is adjacent to the bay, and the Passamaquoddy Tribe, whose ancestral territories span the area in question. It's not clear whether any of these parties has the jurisdiction to stop the project entirely, however.
In fall 2026, social media users circulated rumors about an alleged proposal to build an underwater data center off the coast of Maine.
According to posts on Facebook, YouTube (archived) and Reddit, construction of the supposed data center could harm endangered North Atlantic right whales, which are found in the Bay of Fundy, which is off the coast of Maine's city of Eastport.
A Snopes reader asked us to verify the facts behind this rumor after receiving a link to a Change.org petition to "Stop the Underwater Data Center Planned in Maine's Right Whale Waters."
Petition · Stop the Underwater Data Center Planned in Maine's Right Whale Waters
by u/forchewbap in whales
A company called DeepGreen Western Passage SPV did, in fact, file for a preliminary permit with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission because it wants to explore the idea of building an underwater data center in the Bay of Fundy. This bay is also home to endangered North Atlantic right whales, which could be affected. FERC approved DeepGreen's permit application in August — despite strong opposition from Eastport's city council and the Passamaquoddy Tribe, whose ancestral territories span the area in question.
As such, we have rated this claim as true. 
However, it is worth noting that this preliminary permit does not grant DeepGreen permission to actually build the center, nor does DeepGreen have any immediate concrete plans to do so. Instead, the permit gives the company "priority to pursue development of this project at this location for up to four years."
Louis Wolfson, DeepGreen's developer on the project, said in an email that the company cannot actually do any on-water testing without detailed study plans and approvals from various federal and state agencies, including FERC, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the Army Corps of Engineers. The city of Eastport has said this project "will require significant additional permitting or licensure from the State and Federal governments" in order to get moving, and there's no evidence that's happening as of this writing.
We reached out to FERC to ask for more details about the process and will update the story if we hear back.
What the documents say
DeepGreen's preliminary permit application documents are all available on FERC's eLibrary website under docket number "P-15424."
A document dated Aug. 19 states FERC's approval of the permit:
Dear Mr. Wolfson:
Your preliminary permit application for the DeepGreen Western Passage Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project has been accepted by the Commission for filing as of February 11, 2026.
FERC's public notice about the permit makes it clear that it does not give DeepGreen the right to build the data center or even enter the waters in question (emphasis ours):
On February 11, 2026, and supplemented and amended on June 8, 2026 and July 30, 2026, DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC, filed an application for a preliminary permit, pursuant to section 4(f) of the Federal Power Act (FPA), proposing to study the feasibility of the DeepGreen Western Passage Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project No. 15424-000 (project), to be located in the Western Passage of the Bay of Fundy in the North Atlantic Ocean near the Town of Eastport, Washington County, Maine. The sole purpose of a preliminary permit, if issued, is to grant the permit holder priority to file a license application during the permit term. A preliminary permit does not authorize the permit holder to perform any land-disturbing activities or otherwise enter upon lands or waters owned by others without the owners' express permission.
In other words, the permit "holds your place in line so you can spend private capital" to study whether the project is possible "without a competitor jumping your spot," Wolfson said. He added that "basic research" does not require special permits, however.
While DeepGreen's application does include proposed specs — the data center would use up to 50 tidal turbines to generate a maximum of 15 megawatts of power — Wolfson said there are no "concrete construction plans" yet.
The company also said its activities under the permit "will remain strictly independent, non-invasive, and focused purely on information gathering, data synthesis, and scientific modeling to provide transparent details to the wider local community" (Page 2).
An Aug. 3 notice from the city of Eastport to residents is also clear that DeepGreen cannot begin construction without further proceedings:
In order to proceed to construction, DeepGreen would need to apply for a license. This would be a much more involved, much more expensive process that the City will need to be prepared for, but which is not yet underway.
The City has received no applications for building permits, earthmoving permits or anything else that would be required to start any sort of construction. The City Council has already expressed its dislike of the project to DeepGreen by a unanimous vote.
Wolfson said whether DeepGreen actually does apply for the license to build "comes down to whether the tech proves technically viable, environmentally safe, and economically feasible."
Potential impact on endangered whales unclear
On Sept. 24, the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmentalist group, filed a motion to intervene in opposition to the permit proceedings. The center has argued that even preliminary studies and monitoring "may increase vessel traffic and noise pollution," which could affect prey, increase pollution and cause other issues for right whales, fin whales and other wildlife.
Both North Atlantic right whales and fin whales are protected under the Endangered Species Act. There were about 6,800 North Atlantic fin whales in 2023, according to the most recent NOAA count as of this writing. Per a 2026 NOAA report, there are only approximately 380 North Atlantic right whales remaining.
It is, of course, impossible to know the actual effects on whales until further studies for this specific data center are underway,. There's also little to no data on the general impact of underwater data centers because the concept is so new, although it's widely accepted that ship noise and vibrations harm whales.
Wolfson said concerns from the communities and environmentalists involved are "completely valid." Proponents of underwater data centers argue that the idea is more environmentally friendly than the average data center, in part because the ocean is a natural heat sink and can possibly neutralize the centers' warming effects. Microsoft, for example, said in 2020 that its pilot projects show the idea is "feasible, as well as logistically, environmentally and economically practical."
"Marine sound, fisheries, and local ecology are the bottom line. We're currently vetting hardware partners and looking at their raw performance data. If the equipment can't run safely within federal acoustic and environmental limits, it will never get licensed or deployed," he said.
Jurisdiction questions are complicated
While opposition from the communities in the area is steep, it's unclear whether any of them can halt the project alone — although efforts are already underway.
The project area itself is within U.S. boundaries. However, Passamaquoddy tribal members on both sides of the U.S.-Canada border have reportedly expressed concerns that potential environmental and community effects would not arbitrarily stop at the border, making it a potential point of contention for Canada and Indigenous people who live there, as well.
The proposed project area for the DeepGreen underwater data center in the Bay of Fundy, per DeepGreen's FERC filings. (DeepGreen Western Passage SPV/FERC)
The Passamaquoddy Tribe — a federally recognized tribe in the United States — has already "explicitly expressed that it is not interested" in any kind of collaboration with DeepGreen.
Wolfson told CBC that his "commitment to respecting tribal sovereignty is non-negotiable," but Aaron Dana, a Passamaquoddy tribal representative in the Maine Legislature, is skeptical that's the case.
"What they're doing is that they're only checking a box, saying that they consulted with the tribal nations here in the state of Maine," he said to CBC. In an August statement in front of Eastport's City Council, Dana said the long-term effects of such a project have not been proven and that the city "should not entertain gambling with an ecosystem that cannot be replaced" (at 2:28).
DeepGreen states in the filings that there are at least four other tribes, aside from Passamaquoddy, that have "historical, cultural, or geographic ties to the project boundary and surrounding waters."
The city of Eastport also filed a Sept. 29 motion to intervene in opposition to the FERC preliminary permit. The city's motion states that the data center "would connect to and be located adjacent to the City." The filing notes that Eastport's City Council unanimously passed a citizen initiative to prohibit large-scale data centers, including underwater data centers, and it hopes to "undertake additional work to strengthen and clarify the City's protections."
However, a second citizen initiative aimed at opposing the data center was rejected after a legal analysis found it likely to be unenforceable. That initiative would have required voter approval for certain commercial and industrial development over a certain size, including underwater development.

Pope's health should not be taken 'for granted', says top Vatican diplomat
- Published
Pope Leo XIV's health should not be taken "for granted", a British senior Vatican official told the BBC.
Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican's foreign minister since 2014, said the news of the Pope's ill health was "a bit of a game changer", adding "it's going to make things a bit different".
The Pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma following surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung.
Speaking on Tuesday after the Pope's operation was announced, but before his cancer diagnosis, Archbishop Gallagher said: "I think we were maybe taking him a little bit for granted."
The 71-year-old had surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
Speaking to Radio 4's the Sunday Programme, due to air this weekend, the Archbishop said: "It's in some ways I think going to be a bit of a game changer after having the latter years of Pope Francis when he was in the wheelchair.
"And Pope Leo comes along and he's sporty and he seems to be in excellent health, and now we're told that he's not in excellent health and things have got to be sorted out."
Asked how it will make things different going forward, the Archbishop said church figures might have assumed "that he was not quite like the rest of us who are very aware of our vulnerabilities and the ageing process".
He went on: "But lots of us have been through similar experiences at different times in our lives, and we've got through them, and so we hope it's going to be the same case with Pope Leo.
"I am concerned. I think we've got to ask the question: how was it discovered? What happened?"
The Vatican has said the Pope is showing steady improvement in hospital, and he was expected to lead Sunday prayers.
They had stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.
The Angelus prayer is traditionally recited at the Vatican, overlooking crowds in St Peter's Square but has sometimes been given from a hospital window by previous popes when necessary.
No date has been given for Pope Leo's hospital discharge, but recovery was expected to take around a week.
Leo himself announced the news of his operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said.
Archbishop Gallagher, who is from Liverpool, also said he expected the Pope to visit the UK at some point.
"We have exchanged a little bit," he said. "He's just beginning to think about what he might do in 2027, but it's still very much at the examining the possibilities (stage)".
He would "bring a spirit of renewed hope", said the Archbishop, after the Pope received a rapturous welcome in France and Spain earlier this year.
"But these things do take quite a lot of planning, and so you don't just do it overnight."

Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen its lowest level since records began, new government data shows.
But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed is on a knife edge ahead of a presidential election run-off on 25 October between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest and how that affects relations with the US under Donald Trump.
The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.
The Prodes satellite data series, which is considered the most accurate measure of deforestation, showed forest clearance in the Amazon fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest value since the start of such measurements in 1988.
This beats the previous record low by 1,236 sq km, equivalent to an area the size of Rio de Janeiro.
Since the start of the Lula administration in 2022, the deforestation rate has slowed by 71.2%, according to the data collated by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. This was largely as a result of stronger enforcement measures and state investments in environmental agencies.
The Brazilian states with the worst records in 2026 were Pará, which registered 33.9% of all Amazon deforestation in the year, Mato Grosso (25.5%) and Amazonas (15.7%). However, even in those places the figures were down by more than 45% on the previous year. The state where the problem grew worse (up 0.4%) was Roraima, which is a Bolsonaro stronghold.
Outside the Amazon, the neighbouring biome of the Cerrado – an area of savanna – registered its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km. This is significant as the Cerrado has long been treated as an area of environmental sacrifice, where soy and beef producers could clear more forest than they were allowed to do in the Amazon. Over the past four years, Cerrado deforestation has fallen by 48.4%.
These spectacular results, which brought some conservationists to tears, stand in sharp contrast to the 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro, who oversaw a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes, and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers.
Bolsonaro was then convicted for attempting a coup but his son has vowed to release his father and let him take any position in government that he chooses.
The younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto.
The former environment minister Marina Silva, who has arguably done more than anyone to defend the rainforest, has warned that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to finish his father’s “perverse project” to destroy the Amazon.
The stark contrast between the two candidates is evident in the electoral results map in the Amazon, where Bolsonaro secured the most votes near areas of degraded forest, mines, ranches and soy monocultures, while Lula’s support was higher in big cities or areas of forest where the vegetation was relatively intact.
It is also evident in their very different relations to the US. Lula has warned that Trump is trying to colonise the country and capture its resources. He defends the Amazon as a sovereign asset for Brazil, an important home for Indigenous peoples and an essential element in global efforts to stabilise the climate.
The Bolsonaro family, by contrast, has close ties to the US. Flavio’s brother Eduardo has lived in Texas since last year and called upon the Trump administration to impose punitive tariffs on his own country. Jair has saluted the US flag and led chants of “USA, USA”. If the family secure power, they are expected to shift Brazil’s trade priorities, particularly when it comes to critical minerals, from China and Europe to the US.
The biggest difference, however, is likely to be the far right’s willingness to exploit natural resources in the Amazon and elsewhere in Brazil and then sell them to the highest bidder, regardless of environmental and social concerns.
Conservation groups said the new deforestation data showed how much was at stake in the presidential run-off.
Marcio Astrini, the executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, said: “The figure makes it clear that putting an end to forest destruction in Brazil is entirely possible. However, everything depends on the election result. The country will decide whether we move toward the end of deforestation or toward the end of the forest.”

Trump signed an executive order allowing federal permitting agencies to ignore environmental protection laws in an effort to increase domestic timber and lumber production. The executive order also calls for expanding domestic logging production on federal lands. Following that executive order, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced that the USDA would attempt to roll back the Roadless Rule, which, at its height, prohibited logging on approximately 59 million acres of land.
The order and proposed repeal of the Roadless Rule would not open 59% of national forests to logging. Rather, by Snopes' calculations, it would allow logging on an additional 24% of national forestland.
In October, posts on social media suggested that U.S. President Donald Trump signed an "emergency order" opening up 59% of U.S. national forests for logging. Snopes readers wrote in asking whether the rumor was accurate.
The claim resembled one we fact-checked in March 2025. Then, we investigated a Trump executive order that social media posters claimed would result in 280 million acres of forest being clear-cut. We found the claim to be a mixture of true and exaggerated information.
We came to the same conclusion on this new variant. While the claim is based partly in truth (the referenced "emergency order" is the same executive order we investigated in 2025), it also exaggerates the facts. We therefore rate it a mixture of true and false.
Here's a breakdown:
The order is real
On March 1, 2025, Trump signed an executive order aimed at fast-tracking logging on federal lands. The order, titled "Immediate Expansion of American Timber Production," directed the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management, two of the largest caretakers of federal lands, to update guidelines in order to "facilitate increased timber production," among other things.
Trump's executive order specifically asked those agencies to investigate and implement ways to increase both the speed and quantity of timber produced by cutting environmental regulations.
It asked the Fish and Wildlife Service to streamline approvals for forestry projects that could potentially be halted by the Endangered Species Act within 60 days of the order. It also asked the Agriculture and Interior departments (which control the Forest Service and BLM, respectively) to exempt "timber thinning" and "timber salvage activities" from the National Environmental Policy Act. That act, signed into law by President Richard Nixon in 1970, requires the federal government to consider the environmental effects of its proposed actions through environmental impact statements.
The executive order also encouraged the Agriculture and Interior departments to use the emergency regulations of the Endangered Species Act "to the maximum extent permissible under applicable law." Those regulations allow the act to be bypassed in situations where time is of the essence, such as "acts of God, disasters, casualties, national defense or security emergencies." (Trump's executive order was issued alongside another order declaring that importing timber and lumber poses a risk to national security.) Under the emergency regulations, the Fish and Wildlife Service provides "strictly advisory" recommendations for how to protect endangered species that can be "implemented at the discretion of the emergency response personnel."
In other words, the executive order would allow the logging industry to bypass environmental restrictions found in the Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act.
The acreage
The Forest Service manages 193 million acres of land across the country (about 188 million acres of national forest). Unlike national parks, national forests were established with the purpose of permitting logging and resource exploitation as well as wildlife conservation and recreation.
If the 59% claim were accurate, then using the 188 million total acres figure from the Forest Service we would expect to find that the order opened up about 110 million acres for logging. But this wasn't the case.
The Forest Service deems just 49 million acres of its land "suitable for timber management," far less than the 110 million acres suggested by the claim.
Social media posts said NPR was the source of that figure, yet when we searched NPR's archive for stories suggesting that either 110 million acres or 59% of national forests would be opened up to logging, we found no results.
Instead, we found that the posts appeared to misinterpret or misrepresent NPR's reporting regarding a real policy change implemented by Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, who was tasked with carrying out the 2025 executive order. 
According to an August 2026 news release, Rollins announced that the USDA would roll back the 2001 Roadless Rule, a policy that prohibits the construction of new roads on national forestland. Because roads are required to transport the raw materials, the Roadless Rule effectively places a limit on the number of timber and mining operations on national forestland. The news release noted the USDA would take public comment on the proposed change until Sept. 21, just before the claim began spreading.
When the Roadless Rule was first implemented, it applied to "nearly 60 million acres" of land, according to the Forest Service. We suspect this was the origin of social media users' claim that Trump's executive order would open up 59% of national forests to logging. Various sources, including NPR, reported 58 million to 59 million acres would be opened up. People may have mistaken the acreage for a percentage.
Even then, the social media posts dwelled on the wrong acreage figure, because the Roadless Rule no longer covers the original acreage. Colorado and Idaho enacted state-level Roadless Rules offering higher levels of protection for some land, and those stricter protections effectively supersede the federal rule. According to the Forest Service, taking those restrictions into account means the federal Roadless Rule now applies to only around 45 million acres of forest.
Using the correct, up-to-date acreage, Snopes calculated the rule's recision would open up approximately 24% of Forest Service land for logging. (We were unable to determine how much of that land is actually suitable for the purpose, however.)
Rollins' repeal is supported by the logging industry and several Republican governors, who claim it will prevent wildfires by allowing humans to more directly access and manage remote forestland.
The repeal is opposed by several groups, according to reports from Pew, NPR and Cal Matters. Environmental groups cite scientific research showing 80% of wildfires are caused by human activity, and therefore more human access would increase, not decrease, fire risk. This is backed up by the Forest Service's own environmental analysis on the repeal, according to Pew. Meanwhile, tribal nations claim the repeal undermines tribal sovereignty, and a spending watchdog notes that the Forest Service already has a $6 billion backlog in road maintenance. Repealing the Roadless Rule would only make that worse.
(In fact, during an phone interview for a different story on the Forest Service, Associate Chief Chris French told Snopes the maintenance backlog has been around for decades, and was part of why the rule was implemented in 2001. That detail didn't make it into the final story.)
A bipartisan group of 164 senators and representatives wrote a letter to Rollins and Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz in September pointing out all of those factors and noting that the Roadless Rule has immense public support.
The USDA is expected to make its final decision on the repeal in early 2027.

President Donald Trump’s main legal fund is nearly out of cash and carrying more than $1.9 million in debt, according to a new Federal Election Commission filing.
Save America PAC, the political fundraising organization Trump established in 2020, disclosed the debts in its quarterly report this week. The report covers July 1 to September 30.
The PAC spent more than $5.4 million in the third quarter, bringing its annual spending to over $14 million. Its cash reserves fell from roughly $1.2 million at the beginning of the year to $32,256 by September 30.
Trump has used Save America to cover a large share of his legal expenses, including payments to attorneys who represented him in his New York “hush money” trial, his classified documents case and his Georgia election interference case.
The PAC lists its outstanding debts as legal consulting fees and reimbursements for legal expenses. It owes about $239,000 to Brito PLLC, whose founder, a Florida-based attorney, represented Trump in his defamation lawsuit against ABC News.
Another $761,000 is owed to Sullivan & Cromwell LLP, a white-shoe law firm that has represented Trump in several major cases, including his appeal of the defamation judgment won by E. Jean Carroll.
Dhillon Law Group Inc., meanwhile, is owed about $34,000. The group was created by Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division.
Trump has spent upwards of $100 million on legal expenses since he left office in 2021, The New York Times reported in 2024.
The president has faced a total of four criminal prosecutions over alleged hush money payments, his retention of classified documents and his efforts to overturn the 2020 election. Only the hush money case reached trial, resulting in 34 felony convictions. The other three cases were dismissed.
His legal battles have also included civil fraud proceedings in New York and lawsuits brought by Carroll, a writer, whose jury awards totaled more than $80 million.
Trump has denied wrongdoing on all counts and the product of legal “weaponization.” He has long used “witch hunt” to describe the court cases against him.
In 2023, after being indicte din the hush money case, Trump blasted the prosecution saying; “This is political persecution and election interference at the highest level in history."

Rusty or something more? South Africa's concern after Australia loss
- Published
First Test, Durban (day five of five)
Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56
South Africa 284 & 206: Markram 75; Hazlewood 6-49
Australia won by 214 runs
South Africa's 12-match unbeaten run came to a shuddering stop with defeat against Australia in Durban, but were they simply rusty or is there more to read into a Test match in which they were outclassed across the five days?
The world champions held on until an hour into the afternoon session on the final day – Aiden Markram fought admirably for 237 deliveries – but Australia, led by Josh Hazlewood with career-best figures of 6-49, eventually broke any lingering resistance to go 1-0 up in the three-match series.
"I would like to see more fight," said Proteas coach Shukri Conrad. "I don't know if it is alarming [but] it is concerning."
So should South Africa be worried at the start of an eye-catching few months which includes the visit of England over Christmas?
Rusty batters or something more?
Much was made of South Africa's run to the 2025 World Test Championship final at Lord's.
They played only 12 Tests – no team played fewer – and qualified after drawing at home against India and losing in New Zealand, before beating West Indies, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Pakistan.
Mitigation for this latest Test also comes from the fact this is their first in almost a year and the majority of their batters played one domestic red-ball match to prepare.
Australia recently came off an eight-month break of their own and lost to Bangladesh in home conditions, as Conrad was keen to point out.
And last summer's famous win over Australia and a 2-0 success in India proves they can beat the world's top teams.
However, this Test only reinforced a worrying trend among South Africa's batters.
Tristan Stubbs and Ryan Rickelton are fine white-ball players, but Stubbs' two Test centuries have come against Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, and Rickelton's against Sri Lanka and Pakistan.
This was an obvious step up.
In the first innings, Stubbs, two overs after Wiaan Mulder had been bounced out, top-edged a pull to fine leg, and in the second he played a loose drive on one.
Opener Rickelton drove and edged at a wide ball late on day two and nicked through a pull in the fourth over on day four.
Similarly, Mulder scored 367 not out against Zimbabwe last year, but Bangladesh are the only other side he averages more than 30 against. His 110-ball stay for 29 on the final day before being strangled down the leg side was at least encouraging.
Wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, in contrast, lasted only three balls before nudging Matt Renshaw's part-time spin to slip. His Test average of 30.14 drops to 28 against Australia and 15 against both England and India.
Conrad said that "a few of the guys need to step up".
"The real disappointment was the batting in the first dig on a really good wicket," Conrad said.
"Yes, a world-class attack, but quite a few guys getting starts and not kicking on."
Markram & Nortje the positives
Aiden Markram's defiant knock in the fourth innings, in which he batted for almost six hours for 75 runs before edging Mitchell Starc through to Alex Carey in the afternoon session, was one positive for the Proteas.
David Bedingham also looked comfortable in his new position of number three, albeit he was one of those guilty of failing to make the most of starts after reaching 49 and 46.
This defeat was not solely on the batters, either.
Bavuma, who tasted defeat as captain for the first time in this match, allowed the game to drift on day two as Australia extended their score from 124-6 to 390 not out.
Australia's Matt Renshaw played brilliantly for his 190 but was not challenged as he casually farmed the strike and protected Nathan Lyon in their ninth-wicket stand of 134.
And while judging them against Australia's fearsome attack, the most successful quartet Test cricket has seen, is hardly fair, South Africa's bowlers lacked the relentless pressure of their counterparts.
Anrich Nortje was impressive in taking four wickets in his first Test since March 2023. His last spell was quicker than his first as he brought pace and hostility, hitting Steve Smith on the helmet with a bouncer on day four.
But Mulder offered little after his new-ball spells and Marco Jansen was quiet after dismissing Nic Maddinson and Steve Smith on day one.
The return from injury of their premier quick Kagiso Rabada, who was seen bowling at lunch on day five, cannot come soon enough.
Spinners Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj did not escape Conrad's gaze either.
"Anrich's return was phenomenal and really pleasing," Conrad said.
"If we were brutally honest, our spinners were not as sharp as they normally are."
With the second Test starting in only five days' time in Gqeberha, South Africa must hope this Test has removed the rust.
The alternate takeaway would be far more concerning.

ముందుగా, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దీనికి సంబంధించిన అసలు వీడియోను (ఆర్కైవ్) “Ruhul vlog” అనే బంగ్లాదేశీ ఫేస్బుక్ పేజీలో 24 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ పేజీలో మొహమ్మద్ రుహుల్ అనే వ్యక్తి సామాజిక అవగాహన, వినోదం కోసం ఇలాంటి వివిధ స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోలను రూపొందిస్తుంటారని తెలిసింది.
ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, ఒక వీధి వ్యాపారి చెరుకు రసంలో స్యాకరిన్ (Saccharin) అనే కృత్రిమ స్వీట్నర్ (Artifical Sweetener) కలిపి ప్రజలను అనారోగ్యానికి గురి చేస్తున్నాడంటూ మొహమ్మద్ రుహుల్ అతనితో వాగ్వాదానికి దిగి దాడికి పాల్పడతాడు. అయితే, వీడియో చివర్లో రుహుల్ మాట్లాడుతూ, ఇది కేవలం అవగాహన కోసం తీసిన స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో అని, తాము సామాజిక అంశాలపై ఇలాంటి వీడియోలు చిత్రీకరిస్తామని స్పష్టం చేశాడు. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ అవుతున్న వీడియో నిజమైన ఘటన కాదని, కేవలం అవగాహన కోసం తీసిన స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో అని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
అయితే, ఆహార పదార్థాలు, పానీయాల్లో స్యాకరిన్ వాడకంపై భిన్నాభిప్రాయాలు ఉన్నాయి. ఆరోగ్యంపై దీని ప్రభావం గురించి మరిన్ని అధ్యయనాలు జరగాల్సిన అవసరం ఉందని నిపుణులు చెబుతున్నారు. FSSAI దీనిని పరిమిత మోతాదులో మాత్రమే వాడటానికి అనుమతిస్తుంది. అయినప్పటికీ, భారత్, బంగ్లాదేశ్ వంటి దేశాల్లో ఎలాంటి నాణ్యతా పరీక్షలు లేకుండా, పరిమితికి మించి దీనిని పానీయాలు, ఆహార పదార్థాల్లో వాడుతున్నట్లు పలు మీడియా కథనాలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పేర్కొన్నాయి.
చివరిగా, ఫుడ్ జిహాద్ పేరుతో వైరల్ అవుతున్న ఈ వీడియో నిజమైన ఘటన కాదు, ఇది బంగ్లాదేశ్లో రూపొందించిన ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో.

Indian woman and boyfriend get death sentence in 'blue drum' murder case
- Published
Warning: This story contains details that some readers may find distressing.
A woman and her boyfriend have been sentenced to death for the murder of her husband in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.
Muskan Rastogi, 26, and Sahil Shukla, 28, were convicted on 30 September by a court in Meerut city for the 2025 murder of her husband Saurabh Rajput.
Rajput's body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum - leading to the case being dubbed as "the blue drum murder".
Wednesday's death sentences have to be confirmed by the high court. Rastogi and Shukla have the option to challenge the verdict.
The prosecution said in court that Rastogi and Shukla had been classmates in school and had grown close in the absence of Rajput who worked in London.
When Rajput first came to know of their affair in 2021, he had wanted to get a divorce but was persuaded against this by his family since the couple had a young daughter.
Rajput was murdered on 3 March 2025 when he was visiting Meerut. Police said he was given food laced with sedatives by Rastogi before he was killed.
Rastogi and Shukla fled to Himachal Pradesh state but used Rajput's mobile phone to send text messages to his family to make it seem like he was alive and travelling for business, they added.
A few days later, however, Rajput's family lodged a complaint with the police saying that he was missing.
On 17 March, when Rastogi visited her parents after returning from Himachal Pradesh, her six-year-old daughter asked about her father.
Rastogi initially blamed her in-laws for her husband's murder. Unconvinced, her parental family took her to the police station.
Rastogi confessed to the crime during interrogation and she and Shukla were arrested and charged with the murder.
"My brother was killed by cruel people," Rajput's brother told BBC Hindi.
Rastogi's parents also demanded strict action against her.
"My daughter, along with a friend, murdered her husband in her own home. She is not fit for this society and is a danger to others," her father told ANI news agency.
Rastogi gave birth to a second child while in jail.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta spoke highly of striker Viktor Gyokeres on Friday, commending the forward’s “incredible will and determination” as he continues his search for a first goal of the campaign for the Premier League champion.
The 28-year-old has played a limited role so far this season and remains without a goal in any competition, even though he has scored regularly for Sweden.
Arteta has preferred Germany international Kai Havertz as his main striker, meaning Gyokeres has yet to start a league match this term.
Ahead of Sunday’s fixture at Nottingham Forest, the Spanish manager was questioned on whether Gyokeres was lacking confidence.
“That’s a very personal question,” replied Arteta. “I think what he transmits is an incredible will and determination and work-rate to improve and help the team, that’s it.
