Trump pauses sanctions package targeted at Russian economy
Citing U.S. national interest, White House doesn't immediately explain that rationale
U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest.
Trump personally signed the legislation last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, it had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling the war against Ukraine.
Trump's unexpected move comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president's handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump's approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress on Election Day on Nov. 3.
Graham, a close ally and friend of the president, had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. He had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine.
His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday.
The package had been meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbour more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100 per cent tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15 per cent of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Democratic Virginia Rep. Don Beyer noted on social media shortly after the announcement of the sanctions being suspended that he and others had "warned" Trump might make such a move. The veteran congressman, who spoke out against the bill as it was debated, called on Congress to "fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine."
The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest.
The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.
Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.
The Trump administration has remained mostly quiet since the recent passage of the bill with large bipartisan majorities in the U.S. House and Senate after Graham's sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy.
Follows deal after Putin call
The U.S. president's latest action also followed him announcing last week that he had reached an agreement with Putin.
Trump said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.
Trump's decision to strike a deal with Putin on diesel on the world market has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a different to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran.
The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centrepiece for Sen. Darline Graham, the late senator's sister appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term, who is also running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.
In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump's endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been "so proud" to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was the president's purview as to how he implemented it.
"It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions," Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia, S.C.
"So, that's up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall."

Coastal homes burn as hot winds fuel California fires
A fast-moving fire fueled by high winds burned at least six homes in Southern California on Friday, engulfing expensive coastal properties and prompting thousands to evacuate.
Black smoke — visible from miles away — billowed over tennis courts and swimming pools while firefighters doused blazing homes in San Juan Capistrano in Orange County. Some homeowners sprayed water on their properties before heeding evacuation orders.
Two firefighters were taken to the hospital with heat-related injuries, officials said. Authorities have not said how the blaze, which was less than a square mile as of Friday evening, started.
"Had these winds been a little bit stronger, a little bit different direction, this could have been a whole lot worse," said San Clemente Mayor Rick Loeffler.
Howard Hart, a councilmember for San Juan Capistrano, said he and his wife doused their roof with water and moved propane tanks away from their home before they evacuated Friday with a to-go bag.
Laura Hart hasn't had to evacuate due to fire in the more than five decades she's lived in the community, she said.
"This doesn't usually happen to us, we usually see it on the news," she said. "We always pray to God it's not us, but yeah, it was today."
The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente, and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano. An evacuation shelter has opened in each city. By Friday night, about 16,000 residents had been ordered to evacuate, said Fire Chief TJ McGovern, of the Orange County Fire Authority.
It was one of several fires in the region hit by dry, warm gusts known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior and toward the coast. The strongest winds were expected through Friday afternoon, but conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday night, with a heat advisory in effect until 8 p.m. Saturday on the Orange County and San Diego County coast, the National Weather Service said.
Tens of thousands of people in the state are without power after their electricity was turned off. A separate fire by the Marine Corps base Camp Pendleton shut down for hours a section of Interstate 5 that is a major artery connecting Orange County to San Diego. That added hours to commutes throughout Southern California.
The coastal cities are surrounded by hillsides. San Juan Capistrano, a city of 35,000, is known for horse trails and the historic Mission San Juan Capistrano. San Clemente, which is home to 62,000 people, is known as a "Spanish village by the sea" and popular with beachgoers and surfers.
"The fire is right up on the city," said Victor Cabral, a San Clemente Council member. "It's on the perimeter of our homes on the north end."
Nine schools were also closed Friday in San Juan Capistrano, the Capistrano Unified School District said.
Nearby residents were also on edge as smoke darkened the sky.
Wyoming resident Shannon Needham was visiting her mother at her assisted living facility in Dana Point just north of San Clemente when she learned about the fire.
The facility director told her that two buses would be on standby in case they needed to evacuate, Needham said.
"You could hear the fire trucks, you could hear the helicopters and everything above. And it was so smoky, it was just dark smoke," Needham said.
Some of California's worst wildfires have been sparked by power equipment, and utilities in recent years have begun proactively shutting off power in dry winds. More than 118,000 customers in California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.
The weather service also issued a red flag warning for parts of central and Northern California through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.

‘Crypto King’ spent $16.3M of investor funds on cars, credit cards, jets, security, accountant testifies
Aiden Pleterski paid $16.1M to investors, but no funds went to trading platform named in contracts: accountant
Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski spent nearly half of the $36.3 million investors gave him on himself and paid out about the same amount to investors as returns between 2020 and 2022, according to a senior forensic accountant who testified at his trial in Toronto’s Superior Court on Friday.
Albert Ciorma, who works for the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC), told the court that none of the funds Pleterski received from investors were ever sent to FXChoice — the trading platform their contracts said he’d use on their behalf. And only about $113,000 was ever sent to other foreign exchange and cryptocurrency platforms.
Instead, Ciorma said his forensic audit found Pleterski spent about $5.6 million on luxury vehicles, $4.9 million on credit card bills, $870,000 on travel and private jets, $598,000 on security, and Pleterski gave nearly $3.7 million to his parents. He also took $609,000 in cash advances from a credit card. Altogether, those expenses total more than $16.3 million.
Pleterski also paid out another $16.1 million to investors from the funds he received, according to Ciorma.

- Real estate developer testifies he gave 'Crypto King’ Aiden Pleterski $4.5M to invest
The 27-year-old has pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and money laundering. Pleterski was charged in May 2024 after a lengthy investigation by the OSC and Durham Regional Police.
Albert Ciorma, a senior forensic accountant, testified about self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski's bank accounts at his fraud and money laundering trial on Friday. (Pam Davies/CBC)
Since the start of Pleterski’s jury trial last week, the Crown has alleged that he guaranteed the money his investors gave him for trading, but never actually invested the funds, instead spending the money on himself. Ciorma’s testimony on Friday was the first detailed evidence presented in court to support that aspect of the Crown’s case.
Previously, nearly a dozen investors testified to giving Pleterski more than $6 million collectively. They all shared similar stories of providing Pleterski funds to trade in foreign exchange, and in some cases cryptocurrency, with weekly gains of about two to 10 per cent. They received texts from Pleterski updating them on these returns.
Most of them said they never got any of their money back.
Millions flow in, and then out
Crown prosecutor Scott Patterson went through dozens of pages of records Ciorma compiled summarizing Pleterski’s bank accounts with the forensic accountant in court.
“We see the same pattern, money in and expenses to credit cards,” said Patterson, referencing transactions from the spring of 2021.
The records showed millions of dollars of investor money flowing in, and then flowing out of Pleterski’s bank accounts to pay for credit card bills, cars, hotels, designer clothing and jewelry.
Other expenses include more than $84,000 for a luxury property rental in Miami in October 2021 and $95,200 to the Toronto Blue Jays baseball team in April 2022.
The jury in Aiden Pleterski's trial was shown this photo last week of Mitchell Learning holding his own phone with a screenshot he testified Pleterski sent him of Pleterski's trading account with a balance of more than $311 million. (Ontario Superior Court of Justice)
Two investors who previously testified spoke about seeing a video of Pleterski’s FXChoice account showing a balance of $311 million in the spring of 2022.
- 'Crypto King' investor recounts the moment he learned $311M investment fund didn’t exist
- 'Crypto King' investor who lost $890K recounts visit to Aiden Pleterski’s lakefront mansion
One of them, Mitchell Learning, later gained access to Pleterski’s email account and found an email showing the same FXChoice account had been closed. He then testified that Pleterski confessed to him that he’d lost investor funds and then started using new money from investors to make payouts to others.
“Did you see $311 million in either of those accounts?” Patterson asked the accountant about the FXChoice accounts he reviewed.
“No, just what we’ve seen today,” replied Ciorma.
Pleterski’s trial is expected to continue Monday with further testimony from the forensic accountant.

California's ultra-rich are reportedly preparing their legal strategy to fight the world's first billionaire tax if voters approve it in early November. If approved, it will be the world’s first billionaire tax.
Tech billionaires have raised more than $340 million to defeat 'Proposition 40', a one-time 5 percent wealth tax that will fund healthcare and education, the Guardian reported.
The campaign they’re funding is reportedly spending more than $1 million a day to defeat the measure, according to state financial disclosures
Californians will vote on the ballot measure, Proposition 40, in early November. If passed, it would require a one-time 5 per cent tax on the state’s billionaires, with the proceeds mostly funding healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance.
Proposition 40 “imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion.”
The proposed California tax would go considerably further than taxing income. It targets an individual’s entire net worth and applies to billionaires who have resided in the state at any point since Jan. 1, 2026, Bloomberg reported.
The measure has divided Democrats in the state, with some giving enthusiastic support and others rejecting the proposal because it’s just a one-time levy and the bulk of it would only fund certain healthcare programs
Proponents and opponents alike are casting the billionaire tax as a potential first step toward wealth taxes in more states. With California having more billionaires than any other state, Prop 40 is seen as setting the stage for more referendums on wealth inequality throughout the country.
California has roughly 250 billionaires, according to the New York Times.
The state’s major unions and progressive politicians such as the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders and California congressman Ro Khanna back Prop 40. Supporters include: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
But both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, as well as organisations like Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, a lobbying branch of the healthcare group, oppose it. Opponents include: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
Among its fiercest critics are the tech billionaires it would most directly apply to.
The California Business Roundtable, a lobbying group representing some of the state’s most powerful companies, would take point on the legal challenges, Chief Executive Officer Rob Lapsley was quoted by Bloomberg as saying.
The group, which represents technology, energy and other corporate interests in the state, has retained Elizabeth Prelogar, the Biden Administration’s top lawyer at the US Supreme Court, to help lead the efforts, Lapsley said.
“Our approach to defeat Proposition 40 is based on a comprehensive strategy that includes both the ballot box and the courts,” Lapsley said in a statement to Bloomberg News. “We will be fully prepared to file a legal challenge immediately after the election should we need to defeat this measure in the courts.”
The group is working closely with the billionaires affected by the tax to formulate a legal strategy, sources told Bloomberg.
Opponents of wealth taxes had reportedly hoped the Supreme Court would use the case, Moore v. United States, to establish constitutional limits on the taxation of unrealised gains. The court ultimately upheld the tax while avoiding a sweeping ruling that could have broader implications for wealth taxes.
The California Business Roundtable has raised at least $700,000 to oppose Proposition 40 through its political arm, according to campaign filings cited by the report.
Earlier, the campaign fighting the billionaire tax placed an ad on television, digital and streaming platforms across California. It starts with quiet, foreboding music and the president of the California Medical Association, René Bravo, dressed in a white lab coat, saying: “The people pushing Prop 40 say it’s supposed to improve healthcare. That’s not true," according to The Guardian.
The campaign reportedly debuted similar ads claiming that teachers, carpenters and firefighters also oppose the wealth tax, calling it “a dangerous experiment”.
The messaging around the campaign centers on how the tax would hurt “doctors, teachers, small businesses, working families and public safety”, without mention of the state’s billionaires. The no on Prop 40 campaign calls it “an everyone tax”.
The three campaigns against the wealth tax, however, draw nearly all of their funding from Super Pacs loaded with Silicon Valley money, according to campaign finance filings.
Since July, the committees opposing Prop 40 and supporting Props 41 and 42 have received a total of more than $297.8 million, most of that from a Super Pac called Building a Better California, the report added.
The three campaigns are spending much of their fortunes on an army of consultants tasked with everything from lobbying politicians to working on media strategy.
The consultants include the Republican-leaning law firm Nielsen Merksamer, known for fighting on behalf of tobacco companies, and the political consultancy PCI Campaigns, known for battling propositions that sought to repeal the death penalty and require condom use in pornographic films.
The donors to the 'No' campaign are the who’s who of Silicon Valley, including the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, crypto magnate Chris Larsen and several prominent venture capitalists, The Guardian reported.
The biggest donor, by far, is the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who has contributed at least $102 million to fight the tax, according to campaign finance filings.
The runner-up is Schmidt, who has donated more than $42m.
For comparison, the yes on 40 campaign has raised a total that’s just shy of $33 million, mostly from the healthcare union sponsoring the measure.
According to the Guardian, recent polling on Prop 40 shows that it’s favoured to pass, but its lead has shrunk over the last few weeks as the opposition campaign has increased spending.
A late-September poll by the University of California shows 45% of voters likely to vote yes on the tax with 42% voting no. Just a month earlier, the proposal enjoyed a 7% lead.
There are two separate countermeasures that Prop 40’s opponents successfully placed on the November ballot. These are Proposition 41 and 42.
Prop 41 directly targets the billionaire tax, while Prop 42 is more of a general proposal to protect individuals from certain new taxes.
If either of these measures receives more yes votes than Prop 40, they will stop the billionaire tax from taking effect – even if it passes, the report added.

Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after five days on the job, officials confirmed on Friday.
The lawyer-ish-person-turned-White House spokesperson had a rocky debut at the podium on Tuesday, during which she stumbled over prepared remarks and later raised eyebrows after she told a reporter that she passed the bar in China.
President Donald Trump said on Friday that he told Zacharia to reconsider the role. Later that day, a White House official told Business Insider that Zacharia was "transitioning out" of the position.
By standards of the Trump White House, which had a notorious revolving door during the first go-round, that's pretty short.
There are a lot of other things that lasted longer than Zacharia's tenure. Here are 10 of them.
Anthony Scaramucci as White House comms director: 10 days
Scaramucci's firing in July 2017 became a spectacle, not least in part because of his notably short tenure.
First came a profanity-laced call to a New Yorker reporter, in which Scaramucci badmouthed some of his colleagues in the White House. Then came John F. Kelly, laying down the law in the West Wing by firing Scaramucci and making an example of him on his first day on the job as chief of staff.
Sally Yates as acting attorney general: 10 days
Sally Yates lasted exactly One Mooch.
Yates was a holdover from the second Obama Administration, taking on the AG role after Loretta Lynch stepped down at Trump's inauguration in 2017.
Her position as attorney general was expected to be short. Still, acting AGs from the previous administration typically held on to their roles until the incoming president picked a new attorney general, who would then be confirmed by the Senate.
Yates was fired after she told the Justice Department not to defend Trump's first travel-ban executive order.
Jerald TerHorst as WH press secretary: 31 days
After Zacharia, TerHorst takes the record for the second shortest-serving White House press secretary.
TerHorst served under President Gerald Ford from August 9, 1974, to September 8, 1974. He resigned in protest after Ford granted Richard Nixon a full pardon.
Liz Truss as Britain's prime minister: 49 days
An opinion piece in The Economist quipped that Truss' premiership will have the "shelf-life of a lettuce."
The comment came after Truss's economic package immediately unnerved investors, sending the pound and government-bond markets spiraling.
Thus, the lettuce meme was born. On October 14, 2022, Daily Star, a tabloid newspaper, was inspired by The Economist's comment and set up a livestream of a lettuce wearing a wig: "Will Liz Truss outlast this lettuce?"
She didn't. Truss resigned six days later. She was the PM from September 6 to October 25, 2022.
A hard-boiled egg in the fridge: 7 days
Keeping in theme with the foods that last longer than political positions: The US Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service says a hard-boiled egg can be stored in the fridge for up to seven days.
Lady Jane Grey as Queen of England: 9 days
Lady Jane Grey was proclaimed queen on July 10, 1553, but her half-sister, Mary — the eldest daughter of Henry VIII — gathered enough political support to overthrow her. Mary would claim the crown on July 19, 1553.
Grey became known as the "Nine Days Queen" and was executed by beheading in 1554.
Apollo 11: 8 days
The Apollo 11 crew spent more time in space than Zacharia did as the press secretary: 8 days, 3 hours, 18 minutes, and 35 seconds to be exact.
We can dig in more. Zacharia's first press briefing lasted about 14 minutes, according to recordings. Neil Armstrong spent more time walking on the moon: 2 hours, 31 minutes, and 37 seconds, a NASA report said. Buzz Aldrin was on the moon for about 40 minutes less, according to the report.
Six-Day War: You can guess
The 1967 conflict between Israel and neighboring Arab states was so short that its duration became its namesake. The war lasted from June 5 to June 10, 1967.
Apple TV+ free trial: 7 days
You have more time to binge-watch "Severance" or "Ted Lasso" on Apple TV than Zacharia had time in the White House.
Maybe we shouldn't point this out unless we want Apple to realize there are shorter things than the company's free-trial policy.
Kim Kardashian's marriage to Kris Humphries: 72 days
Reality TV star Kim Kardashian married NBA player Kris Humphries on August 20, 2011. She filed for divorce on October 31, 2011.
To be fair, this may still be more of a reflection on Kardashian than on Zacharia. You would hope a marriage lasts longer than five days, right? Then again, this is the longest thing on the list, so you go, Kim!

Apple has finally announced its long-rumored foldable: the iPhone Duo.
The new phone has a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch inner display, a “nano‑texture” finish on the inner screen, and barely any visible crease. Instead of Face ID, it uses Touch ID on the power button. It has two cameras, a main lens and a wide-angle lens. Apple completely revamped iOS 27’s controls and apps for the foldable, including putting the dock on the side of the phone. And it has a flashy opening animation when you unfold the phone.
The iPhone Duo a big new bet from Apple, though one that’s a little late to the game compared to competitors like Samsung and Google. The phone isn’t cheap: it starts at $1,999 for the base 256GB model, and the prices only go up from there. Still, Apple said that preorder demand was “extraordinary,” so it could have a hit on its hands.
Here’s everything unfolding about the iPhone Duo.
- Pinned Hands-on with the foldable iPhone Duo The first foldable iPhone is finally here, and following its announcement, we got the chance to try the phone for ourselves. We’ve long been told that Apple would make a foldable iPhone once the tech was good enough — has it been worth the wait? It definitely feels like something different. The inner screen has a decidedly matte finish that handled even some glare from the windows above the hands-on area well. The folding mechanism is smooth, and even IP68 rated, and the crease is almost impossible to find with my finger. The 5.4-inch outer screen looks petite by modern slab phone standards. Read Article >

Bloomberg reports that Apple said: “The pre-order demand for iPhone Duo, our first foldable iPhone, has been nothing short of extraordinary. The foldable is slated to launch in stores on October 23rd, and Apple typically reserves some units for in-store availability. - Skulkers are commonly seen in the new Pendola Pass map in Arc Raiders.
- Players can immobilize Skulkers by shooting their wheels and then eliminate them.
- Skulker Targeter, ARC Thermo Lining, Advanced ARC Powercells, and Heavy Ammo are the loot you can get from a Skulker body.
The Frozen Trail update brought three new ARC enemies to the top side in Arc Raiders. Among the three, Skulker has quickly become a headache for players. It can retreat and catch them off guard at unexpected times. So, if you are worried about facing the new ARC threat head-on, here is how to defeat and kill Skulker in Arc Raiders.
ARC Raiders Skulker Location
Fortunately, the Skulker ARC can be found more often in the new Pendola Pass map in Arc Raiders. Skulker usually roams the outskirts of the new map as well as right outside buildings and shelters. So, whether you are playing the new map normally or during a map condition like Frigate or Redirection, you will often encounter the new ARC threat whether you like it or not.
Skulker Health, Weaknesses and Attacks in Arc Raiders
Like all the ARC enemies in Arc Raiders, Skulker has a big weakness players can exploit. It is none other than its legs. Thankfully, you don’t have to wait for its weakness area to be exposed. Its legs are visible all the time, so players can target them right away. That said, here is a list of details you must learn about the new Skulker enemy in Arc Raiders:
| Category | Details | 
|---|---|
| Threat Level | Moderate | 
| Armor Plate | Light | 
| Primary Attack | Tail-mounted Weaponry Firing | 
| Special Abilities | None | 
| Weakness | Wheels (Legs) | 
Best Loadout to Kill a Skulker in Arc Raiders
Wondering what’s the best loadout to take down the Skulker? Here is our recommended loadout to kill a Skulker in Arc Raiders:
- Shield and Augment: Since this is a moderate threat, players can freely equip the Looting Mk. 1 augment in Arc Raiders along with a light shield.
- Weapons: Any weapon with strong ARC penetration is good against Skulker. So, Renegade, Bettina, Anvil, Osprey, or even a basic Ferro are good picks to deal with Skulker.
- Healing Items: Basic bandages and a couple of shield rechargers are more than enough, just in case.
- Grenades and Gadgets: The Seeker Grenades work like a charm against Skulkers. So, make sure to bring at least a couple of Seeker Grenades.
Tips and Tricks to Kill a Skulker in Arc Raiders
Thankfully, the new Skulker is neither a gigantic ARC threat like Bully nor a rapid-firing enemy like Hydra. So, one can easily deal with this elusive ARC enemy if they can remain patient in battle. That said, here is the best strategy to defeat a Skulker in Arc Raiders.
- Aim for the Wheels: As mentioned earlier, Skulker’s main weakness is its wheels (legs). So, once you notice a Skulker, always aim for its wheels and shoot them one by one.
- Stay on the Move: Do not stand in front of the Skulker. It fires in a burst-fire mode from its tail-mounted weapon. So, keep moving and dodging when necessary to avoid all its incoming attacks.
- Go for the Head: Once you shoot down all four of Skulker’s wheels, it will be incapacitated. It’s your time to strike back and simply keep shooting at its head.
And that’s pretty much everything you need to do while fighting against a Skulker in Arc Raiders. Just remember to always aim for its wheels first and then its head.
Arc Raiders Skulker Loot and Rewards
Once you successfully defeat a Skulker in Arc Raiders, its body gets broken down into multiple parts. You can loot its tail to get its special ARC part and the rest to obtain the more common loot. So, here is a list of all loot and rewards you get from a Skulker’s body in Arc Raiders:
- Skulker Targeter (special loot)
- Heavy Ammo
- Advanced ARC Powercell
- ARC Thermo Lining
- ARC Coolant
- ARC Data Module
Skulker Targeter material is needed in the new Weapon Amplification System in Arc Raiders. In addition, you can set up the targeter on the ground to shoot anyone who steps into the area.
That’s everything you need to know about killing a Skulker ARC in Arc Raiders. Although Skulkers are annoying, they are very easy to deal with and can be killed in minutes. Let us know if our tips helped you defeat a Skulker in the comments below.

La Bola Negra star Milo Quifes has never acted before, but now he is all in
As an out and proud author who has published a gay romance novel, Spanish actor Milo Quifes can't quite believe his luck at making his screen debut as an actor in Cannes-feted film and Oscar-contender, La Bola Negra.
The sweeping historical fiction is extrapolated from an unfinished fragment by revered Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca and written and directed by Los Javis — Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi — and casts Quifes as Carlos, the beating heart behind one of three intertwined stories.
"All those months creating Carlos and La Bola Negra with Los Javis, it was an honour," he tells ABC News. "This opportunity to scratch the surface of an unfinished work, and to bring Lorca's writing to life."
He found resonance in Lorca's writing.
"My belief is that acting is a way to explore myself," Quifes says of recognising the fraught trials of coming out or not. "I could feel all these little things, in reading Lorca, that helped me play Carlos."
Seeing is believing
At school, Quifes studied Lorca alongside other members of Spain's celebrated Generation of '27 writers, including Jorge Guillén and Rafael Albert. But it was only after landing the part of Carlos following six auditions across two months that he set about devouring everything available.
"It was amazing, rediscovering Lorca," he says. "I spent all summer reading the unfinished works, the poetry, the theatre, everything."
And yet all that research couldn't prepare Quifes for his first day on a major film set.
Quifes's character Carlos is a handsome young man from a well-to-do family in Granada. He has the world at his feet, even as distant drums beat inexorably towards the Spanish Civil War. And yet, all his privilege cannot open one door: that of the luxurious local club, or casino, of which his domineering father is a long-time member.
Why? Because this is 1932, and Carlos's closeted homosexuality, a poorly kept secret, is a black mark against his name in unaccepting times.
On Quifes's first day on set, he was overwhelmed by the throng of cast and crew and dazzled by the baroque-inspired casino set, realised by production designer Roger Bellés, art director Oriol Guardiola and set decorator Judit Ferrer.
"I'm in the middle of that lavish casino set and you cannot imagine all the little details," Quifes says, wide-eyed once more.
"I mean, you read the script, and you imagine that space, but you cannot grasp it until you are actually there. The art team were amazing."
The baroque palace is crowned by a great glass dome from which hangs a glittering crystal chandelier. Elegantly looping brass tracks cup this astonishing space, along which the titular back balls roll, the voting method used to block Carlos's membership.
It was almost too much, but once Quifes donned his immaculately tailored suit, as visualised by costume designer Ana López Cobos, his confidence grew exponentially.
"As soon as I pulled on that jacket, my back straightened," he says. "From there, it was step-by-step, little-by-little, day-by-day, but I had very good directors, in Los Javis, and a great team around me."
Face the Cruz and dance
The filming took novice actor Quifes from the lofty world of a casino to the astounding beauty of Granada's snow-capped Sierra Nevada mountain range.
He loved it, even if Carlos's stylish suits were hardly suitable attire for diving into snowdrifts.
"Sometimes you have to suffer for your art," he chuckles, thinking back to how freezing he was, shooting take after take, damp and shivering.
"My mind was so chaotic, but you have to focus and get it right. I remember lying in the snow, looking at the sky, and thinking, 'This is amazing.'"
Each of La Bola Negra's three storylines, set in different locations and timeframes, were filmed separately.
Quifes didn't meet many of his fellow cast members until it premiered at Cannes, where it was nominated for the Palme d'Or and the Queer Palm, with Los Javis taking home best director.
Quifes was in Madrid when co-star Carlos González was filming a key scene with Glenn Close, but the hectic schedule prevented him from meeting the American legend. Sadly, Close couldn't make the Cannes premiere, so he's still patiently waiting to meet an actor he admires and adores.
"I don't know if she's aware of my existence," he laughs.
You lose some, you win some.
Quifes did get to meet another of his heroes, Spanish superstar Penélope Cruz, when she shot her spectacular club sequence in an abandoned theatre in Sigüenza.
"Penélope was amazing," he beams. "She was very down-to-earth, caring, loving and funny all at the same time."
Like Cruz, Quifes also delivers a show-stopping dance number in the movie, revealing it was one of the trickiest days on set.
"I don't have any sense of timing," he says of his clumsy footwork. "So my amazing choreographer Belén Martí Lluch had to teach me how to feel the freedom with my body, and I practised a lot."
It turns out Lluch was the perfect teacher. "We shot that scene three times, but the one that's in the film is my first take."
And the Oscar goes to …
While voting for the Oscars is yet to begin, with the shortlists announced mid-December, the buzz around La Bola Negra is hard to ignore, with the streamer Netflix throwing its campaign muscle behind its horse in the race.
As far as Quifes is concerned, it's too soon to talk awards season potential. "I can't think about that," he insists, covering his eyes bashfully.
It was wild enough going to Cannes with Los Javis, Cruz and co. "I was disassociating."
While he may be modest, Quifes hopes that this is just the beginning, with his passion for acting flourishing on set.
"If I can take this space to ask directors to call me, I will," he says, flashing a wide smile. "Now that I have discovered this world, that makes me so happy, I want to do it again. I want to be this happy again."
La Bola Negra is in cinemas now.

New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested on “felony charges related to AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM),” Bucks County Detectives said in a press release Thursday.
In the US, cops have vowed to crack down on AI CSAM since at least 2024, when the Department of Justice made one of the earliest arrests. After charging a Wisconsin man with spreading “thousands of realistic images of prepubescent minors” across Telegram and Instagram, the DOJ clarified to law enforcement that “CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM.”
On Thursday, New Jersey officials accused 51-year-old Fitzgerald of using AI to make photos from social media of real minors into sexualized images that he then distributed on social media.
Fitzgerald was charged after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received a tip that a Discord user shared an illicit image in July. Cops then used “digital forensics and subscriber records” linked to the Discord account and “associated Internet protocol addresses” to track the user to Fitzgerald’s home address.
After a search Thursday, cops “recovered prompts and scripts used to create artificially generated child sexual abuse material using an AI program,” the press release said. They also found Discord chat logs where Fitzgerald, under the Discord username “thegentlemanpervert_2160_07833,” allegedly “admitted to making multiple illicit images using artificial intelligence and sharing them with other users.”

'We're living with wars behind our doors': Jayda Allen Bonner remembered at Melbourne vigil
In short:
Hundreds of mourners have gathered in Melbourne to pay tribute to a young Indigenous woman one week after she was killed in an inner-suburban apartment.
Jayda Allen Bonner was remembered as "a beautiful soul" by her mother and aunt, who have called for Australians to do more to prevent violence against women.
What's next?
Police investigations are continuing.
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.
Hundreds have gathered in Melbourne to pay tribute to a young Indigenous woman killed at an inner-suburban apartment complex last weekend.
A smoking ceremony was held in honour of 21-year-old Jayda Allen Bonner, who was remembered as "a beautiful soul" by her mother and aunt.
This week, a 31-year-old man was charged with murder and appeared briefly in the Melbourne Magistrates Court.
Police say he was known to Ms Allen Bonner.
Supporters of the Bonner family then marched to Victoria's Parliament to demand changes to domestic violence procedures and reform to better prevent violence against women.
Ms Allen Bonner's mother, Jade Allen, took part in the vigil, wearing a t-shirt emblazoned with an image of her daughter and the phrase 'Justice for Jayda'.
"Jayda loved her family fiercely. She had a heart of gold — she would do anything for anybody," Ms Allen said.
"I want everyone to stand up and stop keeping all of this quiet.
"I want to make sure Jayda's name isn't forgotten. She was one-of-a-kind."
Ms Allen Bonner's aunt Kellie Carter Bell said all Australians need to do more to speak out against violence against women.
"We're living with wars behind our doors,"
she said.
"We need recognition, we need people to understand what this stuff looks like.
"The question should be: What can I do to help (victim-survivors) get out safely?"
Questions raised over police response
Antoinette Braybrook, chief executive of Melbourne-based Aboriginal family violence service Djirra, said the 21-year-old's death was "devastating".
She said it was "outrageous" and "shocking" that Ms Allen Bonner could "fall through the cracks".
Ms Allen Bonner's family has previously said the young woman had made a complaint to police about her safety which she later withdrew.
Her family has also said they tried to contact police themselves, but were told that because Ms Allen Bonner was an adult, there was nothing they could do.
Ms Braybrook said that wasn't true.
"They have the power to investigate violence in the home and initiate their own intervention orders and charge people; my question is, why didn't they do that?"
Ms Braybrook added that it was not uncommon for women experiencing violence to withdraw their complaints to police, even if they were still in danger.
Speaking generally, she said women experiencing violence might be pressured into doing so or be threatened with further violence by their abusers.
"The perpetrator has absolute control, power and control over her in that situation,"
Ms Braybrook said.
"It's a consistent issue in our work."
While Djirra was now in contact with the young Yagera woman's family, Ms Braybrook said given the history of concern for Ms Allen Bonner's safety, it was "extremely disappointing" police or other authorities had not connected her with the service before her death.
"That's one of the concerns that we have as a specialist Aboriginal community-controlled organisation working on the frontline of Aboriginal women and children's safety," she said.
"I am just at a loss — I sit at the table, many tables, with police, with corrections, with courts and others, talking about how we can improve the safety of women.
"When things like this happen to women, it just makes those talks that we participate in all of the time seem like a joke."
A Victoria Police spokesperson said the death of a young woman in Carlton on October 10 was suspicious.
"The investigation is being led by the Homicide Squad," the police spokesperson said.
"As part of investigations, Victoria Police will thoroughly examine any interactions between police and the victim in the lead-up to her death.
"We are unable to comment further while the investigation remains ongoing."

Republicans’ nearly $1 billion war chest was expected to help the party overcome a difficult political environment ahead of the US midterm elections. But despite a massive spending blitz, polling trends have barely shifted, forcing the party to divert funds from potential victories to defending vulnerable seats.
Republican groups spent more than $740 million on congressional races between Labor Day and October 14, including at least $220 million from groups linked to President Donald Trump, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. Billionaire Elon Musk has separately donated more than $276 million to Republican groups since July.
Yet Democrats continue to lead in several competitive Senate races, while the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter favours Democrats to flip the House and remain competitive in the Senate.
“Money is an amplifier, not a magic wand,” said Neil Newhouse, partner at Republican polling firm Public Opinion Strategies. “You can buy all the airtime in the world, but if the political climate is blowing 30 miles an hour in your face, ad volume alone isn’t going to turn the weather around.”
Republican groups entered the final stretch with roughly $1 billion available, compared with $579 million for comparable Democratic groups, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings.
Musk has contributed more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, including $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund super PAC and more than $76 million to his America PAC. His known federal political contributions during this election cycle total roughly $366 million.
The spending comes amid an unprecedented expansion in political advertising.
However, Republican groups have struggled to translate their financial advantage into proportionate advertising exposure. Across nine key Senate battlegrounds, Republicans outspent Democrats on broadcast television by 26% through September 30 but secured only 7% more ad airings, according to CNBC's analysis.
Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonprofit that tracks campaign spending, said, “We are watching an unprecedented concentration and scale of political influence and wealth this election cycle.”
Late spending and higher advertising costs have limited the effectiveness of the Republican cash advantage. Candidates receive broadcasters' lowest unit rates during the final 60 days before a general election, while outside groups such as super PACs do not enjoy the same protection.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico continued to lead Republican Ken Paxton despite more than $113 million in negative advertising targeting Talarico since the primary.
Repeated exposure to political advertising may also be delivering diminishing returns as campaigns target the same pool of undecided voters.
“When an undecided voter has already seen 20 negative ads today, the 21st ad doesn’t persuade them. It just gets tuned out,” said Michael Beckel, money in politics reform director at Issue One. “Their eyes glaze over.”
Republicans, however, argue that spending has helped prevent vulnerable candidates from falling further behind. In Texas, the party spent $121.5 million on the Senate race in September, compared with just $5.5 million over the previous three months.
“The spending hasn’t put Paxton ahead, but it kept a messy race and flawed candidate from becoming an unwinnable one,” said a Republican operative involved in the Texas Senate race, who requested anonymity.
The clearest indication of Republican difficulties is the shift towards defensive spending. Since September 1, the Senate Leadership Fund and affiliated groups — according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data — have spent or committed roughly $180 million across those three states, all of which Trump carried by double digits in 2024.
Michael Beckel said outside groups were “diverting millions into deep-red territory to build defensive moats, leaving pickup opportunities starved for cash in the final stretch.”
In North Carolina, the Senate Leadership Fund initially pledged $71 million to back Republican Michael Whatley. On 2 October, however, the group pulled most of its remaining ad reservations after spending about $32.8 million, as Democrat Roy Cooper continued to hold a double-digit lead in FiftyPlusOne’s polling average.
The same strategy is unfolding in the House, where the Congressional Leadership Fund has withdrawn support from two vulnerable Republican incumbents and shelved efforts to flip two Democratic-held seats.
The redirection points to the central problem facing Republicans: a financial advantage that once promised to expand their electoral opportunities is now being used to limit potential losses.

A winter of hunger looms for residents trapped in Russian-occupied city in Ukraine
Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro River that separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers
Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro River that separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. There’s no electricity, heat or running water. Roads leading from town are mined and dotted with burned-out cars. Menacing drones buzz overhead.
One desperate resident watched the front-line city slide further toward a humanitarian crisis as its trapped population dwindled to fewer than 2,000 people. She decided it was time to escape via what's been dubbed “the road of death.”
So the 40-year-old former hairdresser walked -- for 20 kilometers (12 miles), along the partially mined road — fearing that “every step could have been my last," she said.
Once a city of about 24,000, Oleshky was captured by Moscow’s forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. Further calamity struck in June 2023 when floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military, killing hundreds of residents.
And now those still left in the battered city along Ukraine's southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms, with no agreement in sight for even a humanitarian evacuation.
“There is nothing left in Oleshky,” said the woman, who fled in August and spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because she feared for her security. “No food, no supplies, no medical care, no aid whatsoever.”
Both sides blame each other for the catastrophe. Russia says Ukraine deliberately blocks supplies and evacuations; Kyiv counters that Moscow is effectively holding civilians hostage.
Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. Russia, which as the occupying power is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive, has made no commitment.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy mentioned Oleshky’s suffering at the hands of Russia on Oct. 12 at an international forum in Poland, saying the city had been “razed to the ground.”
Ukraine is "trying to help these people, but they are under occupation,” he said. “Unblock the city of Oleshky and bring our citizens back.”
In a phone call Friday with President Vladimir Putin, Pope Leo XIV urged a ceasefire to allow food and medicine deliveries to Oleshky and to safely evacuate civilians, the Vatican said. The Kremlin said Putin voiced support for the Vatican efforts to help protect the population and secure vital supplies, and voiced readiness to cooperate.
Remaining residents reportedly scrounge for food amid destroyed buildings, or try to grow vegetables in garden plots. Water is drawn from wells. Firewood is used for warmth. Bodies at the city morgue decompose with no electricity.
Another 100 bodies fill the basement of Oleshky's hospital, said Tetiana Hasanenko, the exiled head of the city's Ukrainian military administration.
The U.N. human rights office said the last regular food delivery by road was May 26. Oleshky's Russian-installed officials said this month they delivered 2 tons of aid, although they admitted it was hardly enough.
The U.N. office said Oleshky's hospital lacks medicine and basic supplies, drone attacks prevent ambulances from reaching patients, and it's unsafe to take them elsewhere.
“It is impossible to live in Oleshky, there is no life left there,” said another resident who fled to Russian-held Mariupol and spoke on condition of anonymity because he feared for his security.
Even the Russian soldiers have moved deeper into the occupied part of the Kherson region, farther from the Dnipro, according to the former hairdresser. The Moscow-appointed authorities seemed to have "given up on us a long time ago,” she said.
She considered herself lucky to have survived the journey from Oleshky to the village of Radensk, also occupied by Russia but farther from the front line and thus better off.
She said an acquaintance who tried to bring food into Oleshky was killed on the road when his car came under fire, adding that she saw a photo of him “covered in blood, with bread and chicken legs scattered around him.”
Hasanenko said the route from Oleshky to Radensk is known as “the road of death” because "corpses lie on this road and no one is taking them away." She cited an explosion this month that killed four people and left an 86-year-old man badly wounded.
Russian troops were driven out of the larger city of Kherson across the Dnipro in 2022 but mined the roads around Oleshky, said Lt. Yevhen Voronetskyi, a spokesman with Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade. Kyiv's drones also remotely mined forest paths used by Russian troops, he said.
Some evacuees who make it to Radensk try to return to Oleshky with food “because they have children waiting at home, or immobile elderly parents," Hasanenko said, saying at least 35 children remain there.
Ksenia Arkhipova, who fled Oleshky in 2022 and now helps others leave, said nearby occupied towns and villages in a zone along the Dnipro face similar dire conditions and mined roads.
It takes six to eight hours to walk or cycle from Oleshky to Radensk, she said, because evacuees might be older and weakened by hunger, or they have to wait out attacks or carry their bikes to avoid the mines.
Travel is only possible in dry weather, Arkhipova said, and "I'm terrified at the thought of the coming winter, when many people in Oleshky will be simply doomed."
Some of them don't want to leave their homes or risk a dangerous journey, Voronetskyi said.
Russia and Ukraine have discussed a possible temporary ceasefire and humanitarian corridor but reached no agreement, the U.N. human rights office said. “With winter approaching, the issue is urgent,” it said.
While communications with Moscow continue, "Russia has not provided clear, verifiable guarantees for conducting a humanitarian operation,” according to the office of Ukrainian human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets.
The mined roads make an evacuation impossible, and not all residents want to leave, according to the city's Russian-installed officials.
Vladimir Saldo, who was appointed by Moscow as governor of the occupied part of the Kherson region, promised earlier this month to help anyone who wants to leave the town. The former hairdresser told AP that residents have appealed to local authorities several times for a humanitarian corridor and submitted lists of those hoping to leave, but nothing came of it.
The International Committee of the Red Cross was ready to assist an evacuation but only if both countries agree and there are security guarantees for civilians, said ICRC spokesperson Sarah Davies.
Voronetskyi, the Ukrainian lieutenant, said the food shortages in Oleshky have persisted for months and are getting “worse and worse.”
His brigade has flown drones capable of carrying at least 20 kilograms (44 pounds) each over the Dnipro into the city with food aid for at least a year, he said, adding that more than 7 tons were delivered since September.
The parcels contained canned food, ingredients for baking bread, along with buckwheat, rice, sugar and candy for children. along with hygiene kits and medicine, including insulin, he said.
But Voronetskyi cautioned that these supplies weren't meant to get people through the winter but to help them "gather their strength, pack their things ... and still try to leave Oleshky.”
Russia should “come in and take the people out,” he said. "No one will stop you.”

Outstanding sound quality. Premium build materials. Highly customizable EQ. Most comfortable Nothing headphones. Great ANC and transparency.
TIRED
Love-it or hate-it case. ANC is great, but not the best.
Nothing headphones have always stood out from the competition, and the Headphone (1) Pro is no different. It’s the brand’s most premium option yet, putting it up against the best from Sony, Bose, and Apple. After nearly a month of testing, I’d say these headphones belong among those top-tier choices, while bringing a few unique ideas to the table.
Exquisite Materials
Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz
Nothing Headphone (1) Pro Specs
Wireless connectivity
Bluetooth 6.1 with Multipoint, Auracast
Wired connectivity
USB-C (supports lossless up to 24 bit/192 kHz), 3.5-mm aux (supports lossless up to 24 bit/96 kHz)
Battery life
Up to 30 hours (ANC on), up to 68 hours (ANC off)
Weight
327 grams
Codec
LDAC, LC3, SBC, AAC
Water/dust resistance
IP52
Design is the first standout in the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro. On the outside, it follows the same formula as the Nothing Headphone (1) and Headphone (a), with a distinct square shape and two-tone, transparent outer shell.
The Headphone (1) Pro pushes this design to 11, largely by using premium materials instead of plastic. The square cans are made from a solid aluminum block. The arms are made of titanium. The transparent outer window is made of glass. There’s very little (if any) plastic to be found, yet they actually weigh 2 grams less than the Nothing Headphone (1).
The case is … interesting. It’s basically a hard-shell version of the purse-like case for the Apple AirPods Max 2—a near universally loathed case, I might add. The Headphone (1) Pro case offers better ear cup protection, but the headband remains exposed. It’s something you use once, then promptly forget.
All that being said, these are Nothing’s most comfortable headphones yet. The softer, thicker padding, wider headband, and reduced clamping force make these noticeably more comfortable than the Headphone (1).
Mixing It Up
Noise canceling and transparency are also great, thanks to extra microphones and impressive sound isolation. It’s not quite as bulletproof as Sony and Bose, but it was more than enough for any New York City situation I threw at it.
Inside, things get even more interesting. The headphone uses a triple-driver design—a bass dynamic driver, a precision dynamic driver, and a treble xMEMS driver. The idea is that each driver handles a different frequency range, delivering clearer, fuller, less distorted sound. When every other major ANC headphone brand uses a single dynamic driver for the full frequency range, this triple-driver design is a big risk. Fortunately, sound quality is outstanding.
I’m not going to pretend I’m an audio engineer (I’m not). But songs I’ve listened to for years came back to life with the Headphone (1) Pro, with added emphasis, clarity, and energy in the midrange and treble I didn't expect.
I don’t usually make the stank-face to “Staring at the Sun,” by TV on the Radio, but I did pretty consistently with these headphones. Stevie Wonder’s “Another Star,” with its dense mix of vocals, hi-hat, trumpet, and guitar, sounded more spacious on the Nothing headphones than on the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen). Bass is clear, but not as punchy as headphones like the Sony XM6. I didn’t mind, but it was a little less fun with artists like Bad Bunny and Kendrick Lamar, or anything in the EDM genre. A simple EQ adjustment changed this (more on that later).
This focus on engaging mids and highs meant that music on the Nothing headphones commanded my attention more often. I actually had a harder time achieving deep focus at work with these headphones than with more bass-forward mixes on the Sony XM6 and Bose QC Ultra 2nd Gen.
That was a lot of sound talk, and everyone has different ears, different hearing, and different taste. Luckily, you don’t have to settle for one sound profile with these headphones.
The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro has some of the most customizable EQ settings I’ve ever seen in consumer ANC headphones.
First, there’s a physical “FLAT” switch tucked away on the left ear cup. When you turn it on, it changes to a neutral EQ designed for “reviewing music, producing, or mixing,” according to the brand. As someone who does none of those things, I still had a lot of fun using this mode. I even started to prefer Flat with certain songs and certain genres. One quirk: It increases the volume—I consistently had to lower the volume by two steps.
Second, the Nothing X app offers ample EQ settings. There are two EQ modes: simple, with a familiar three-band EQ (bass, mid, and treble), and advanced, where things get a little crazy. In advanced, you can dial in a +6 dB to -6 dB change for individual frequency bands on both the main driver and precision driver. This level of control is rare in consumer over-ear ANC headphones and will frankly overwhelm some people. That’s why I think more people will enjoy the Explore tab, where Nothing has curated five EQ presets to try out.
Add spatial audio modes on top of that, and you’ve got plenty of options to find your ideal EQ. Though I suspect many people will be happy with the sound out of the box.
Playing in the Big Leagues
The $400 price tag puts these headphones squarely in competition with the established, well-regarded $450 Sony WH-1000XM6, $450 Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen), and $550 (but always on sale for $450) Apple AirPods Pro Max 2. Those are three of the best ANC headphones you can buy.
I think the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro fit in that mix nicely. No, they don’t win in ANC or transparency performance (though both are solid). But it stands out with a unique design, tactile on-ear controls, an excellent sound profile, and in-depth EQ customization. It’s a toss-up whether I’ll use these or the Sony XM6 as my daily driver, and that’s high praise for Nothing's first take on premium over-ear headphones.

Jon Rahm will give up a reported £75m owed to him by LIV Golf after reaching a separation agreement that will secure his exit from the league.
The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its multibillion-dollar backing.

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.

Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.
The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.
