The Impossible ‘Whalefall’: Director Brian Duffield Wanted a Challenge, So He Discovered a Way to Crush Austin Abrams in a Whale Stomach That Left Onlookers ‘Baffled’
Turns out that it’s tough to shoot in a whale’s stomach.
“Whalefall” director Brian Duffield is gleefully outlining some of the biggest hurdles while shooting his new movie. The premise for the film, in theaters now via 20th Century Studios, is simple: A young diver named Jay (Austin Abrams) is accidentally swallowed by a whale, ends up in its stomach and must escape before his tank of oxygen runs out. It’s a lean idea, but required an innovative and energetic leader like Duffield to get the claustrophobic shots done on practical sets.
“It’s such a small space and essentially a 360-degree set,” he says. “There’s a couple portals you can kind of shove a camera through, but it’s also somewhat full of water. All the lighting of the coil is inside the set. Basically everything that you would have on a normal movie set, we’re putting inside of a very small space. It’s also on a gimbal that’s rocking and rolling. So you take your normal film set footprint and then you put it into a bag. And then you also put Austin Abrams into the bag, and then sometimes other animals. If Austin’s wrong an inch, it doesn’t really work. Everyone’s cramped in this little doorway. But he can’t hear us, because the rubber is so thick inside.”
Popular on Variety
Duffield smiles at the outrageous setup.
“I was talking to a director,” he says. “He had a question and I sent him pictures of the set. And he was just like, ‘You’ve got to be joking.’ From when the whale is chewing Austin, it’s just a bunch of big, burly men jumping on the set and crushing down on him. And he’s in there, screaming and drowning with a real oxygen tank. I’m looking at this little monitor and if he needs help, it’s going to sound the exact same. Every time you call cut, you’re just hoping that the screaming stops. We had the studio come to set and watch this thing. From the outside it just looked so silly. I remember Disney safety reps would come and just be watching it, saying, ‘I genuinely don’t know if this is safe.’ But we worked hard, really hard to make sure Austin was safe.”
Everyone made it out of the shoot unharmed, but the finished product is filled with harrowing set-pieces that are sure to push audiences to the brink. Duffield understood the vision early on, as he reached out to novelist Daniel Kraus on social media when he first heard the premise of the novel of the same name, before it was even published. He read an advance copy of the 2023 book, and was quickly swept away with the cinematic promise it held. Duffield ended up co-writing the “Whalefall” script with Kraus.
“You get the initial ‘boy inside a whale’ story, which definitely tickled all the genre parts of my brain,” Duffield says. “The idea of making a movie that had never been made before is always really appealing to me. It’s instantly clear how challenging that was, and I was really looking for a challenge. I was hungry to just keep pushing myself and the crew that I had consistently been working with. I think we just had the appetite at the time to take a big swing.”
Duffield is no stranger to ambitious projects. He began his Hollywood career as a writer with a disparate group of scripts, including a big-budget sequel (2015’s “The Divergent Series: Insurgent”), a Western (2015’s “Jane Got a Gun”), a slasher (2017’s “The Babysitter”) and a sci-fi action movie (2020’s “Underwater”). He transitioned into an idiosyncratic directing career with 2020’s “Spontaneous” (logline: a romance is shaded by the fact that people start spontaneously combusting) and 2023’s “No One Will Save You,” a nearly dialogue-free alien invasion movie.
Beyond their high concepts, Duffield’s works are marked by an emotional heft, which is no different in “Whalefall.” Jay’s diving trip is prompted by him trying to locate the body of his estranged father Mitt (Josh Brolin) after he dies by suicide. He’d never be able make amends with, or come to an understanding with his father, a theme that resonates through much of the story.
“I don’t think I was looking for a father-son story, but I think I needed a father-son story,” Duffield, a parent himself, says. “As soon as I was reading it, I couldn’t stop thinking about … not the whale, but about Jay and Mitt in that relationship. I thought, ‘That was the magic trick of the book.’ You’re forgetting about squids and acid and you’re thinking more about how these two guys are thinking they want nothing more than to spend time together, but they can’t quite express how they need to spend time in a different way.”
While Abrams and Brolin were able to bring the emotional gravitas to flashback scenes chronicling key moments in their frayed relationship, shooting the in-whale scenes was the overarching creative challenge.
“I had plenty of directors come and visit and all of them just looked so baffled,” Duffield says. “I had general confusion about how we were doing what we were doing. The thing I’ve learned the most is the joy of making movies for me is the crew and getting to hire a lot of the same people over and over again. I think if I have any gift as a director, it’s hiring people that are extremely talented, Oscar winners and whatnot. I like spending time with them and feel comfortable asking advice. I trust them if I feel like they have a note or an idea — it’s probably good.”
It’s part of a larger ethos Duffield brings to every project.
“I want to feel the effort, and I want to feel like I’m becoming a better filmmaker because of it,” he says.

- Snopes found no evidence new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia was a lawyer in the U.S. or in China.
- The rumor stems from Zacharia herself, who, asked Oct. 13 about where she passed the bar (the examination that allows people to practice law), responded "when I moved to China." She did not say she passed the bar in any U.S. state.
- Snopes reviewed lawyer directories from the bar association and supreme courts of all 50 U.S. states and Washington, D.C., and found no evidence she had passed the bar examination in any of them.
- A review of Chinese rules suggested she could not have passed China's equivalent of the bar exam as a U.S. national, or practiced as a lawyer, even by the current requirements, which are looser than they used to be.
- A spokesperson for Pepperdine University confirmed in an email to Snopes that Zacharia graduated with a Juris Doctor degree in 2011.
- John Ohnesorge, an expert in Chinese law from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told Snopes in an email "There's no possibility that she passed the Chinese bar exam, ever."
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the White House for more details and are waiting for a response.
In October, social media posts questioned new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia's claim that she passed the bar examination in China.
The posts emerged after several reports asked whether Zacharia had the credentials to practice law anywhere in the U.S., though she has repeatedly identified herself as a lawyer in the past, including in an archived version of her X profile and during a television interview.
When asked Oct. 13 where she passed the bar (the examination that allows people to practice law), Zacharia responded, "When I moved to China." She did not say she passed the bar in any U.S. state.
People on Facebook and Reddit expressed doubts, while Rep. Ted Lieu, a Democrat from California, wrote on X, "Are Katie Zacharia and trump lying when they say she is an attorney?" (archived):
Meanwhile, Snopes readers emailed and searched the website, asking us to examine whether Zacharia could have possibly passed the bar in China.
An extensive search turned up no evidence Zacharia was a member of any state bar in the U.S., nor in Washington, D.C. In addition, current Chinese law made it unlikely that she was ever in a position to pass China's examination to practice law, as she is not a Chinese national. There was no evidence that she could do when she lived there between 2011 and 2013, though China only formalized rules about foreign lawyers in 2017.
For this reason, we have left the claim unrated.
"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Katie Zacharia told Snopes in an emailed statement. Neither she nor the White House press office answered follow-up questions, nor did they share any documentation showing she could practice law as an attorney in good standing in any jurisdiction.
"Katie graduated with a JD [Juris Doctor, a law degree] from Caruso School of Law in 2011, and with a bachelor of arts in political science from Seaver College in 2007," a spokesperson for Pepperdine University wrote in an email to Snopes.
Asked whether Zacharia could have taken and passed China's law examination before 2017, John Ohnesorge, a law professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who researched Chinese regulations of lawyers, said in an email to Snopes, "There's no possibility that she passed the Chinese bar exam, ever." 
"What she did in China was to work in an elite Chinese law firm on international business matters, and doing that kind of work does not really require being a member of a bar anywhere," he added.
We also searched lawyer directories across the U.S. and found no record of Katie Zacharia — also searching by her maiden name, Black — in any of them.
Zacharia's resumé and Chinese rules
Zacharia's LinkedIn profile indicates she worked in China between 2011 and 2013, at Zhong Lun Law Firm.
In 2020, the Chinese Justice Observer — a consulting platform and analysis outlet about the Chinese legal system — said foreigners cannot practice law in China. In 2019, China established a pilot program to allow foreign lawyers to act as legal consultants in China, not lawyers, though one condition is that the person should have practiced as a lawyer in their home country for at least two years.
Even under this program, Zacharia could not have practiced as a legal consultant as she had not practiced law in the U.S. long enough after she graduated.
Zacharia's LinkedIn indicates she later worked as "general counsel" for Fix California, a conservative organization that aims at ensuring "election integrity." It is unclear how she could hold this position without having passed the state's bar examination. We reached out to Fix California asking for more details.
A sheet of advice for French lawyers seeking to work in China from 2017 confirms that only Chinese nationals can practice law in China. In other words, any foreign lawyer practicing in China can do so only with credentials from the countries where they obtained their degrees.
However, China's current rules were implemented in 2017. Ohnesorge, who wrote a research paper in 2023 about the history of the regulation of lawyers in China, said this measure was most likely protectionistic. 
"It's true that the 2017 regulation started requiring two years of practice in a home jurisdiction in order to qualify as a foreign legal consultant, but that's best understood as a protectionist measure used to keep Chinese firms from hiring too many foreign lawyers, not a requirement that actually makes any sense," Ohnesorge said via email. "People doing the work she did aren't really practicing the law of their home jurisdiction anyway, so why require that at all?"
For further reading, Snopes covered several rumors about Zacharia's predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, including the claim that she said the war in Iran would be over if President Donald Trump had "better intelligence."

According to The Washington Post, Omar said that requests to change her birth year were due to it being incorrect, not to cover up the truth. We found evidence to support that she was 17 in the year 2000.
As U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., entered the final weeks of her reelection bid in October, federal agents searched her home in a criminal investigation reportedly related to claims that she or her father may have lied on immigration paperwork when she sought to secure legal status in the U.S. decades earlier.
In an Oct. 12 statement on X, Omar said called the search "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." It is unusual for a federal agency to publicly investigate someone running for office so close to Election Day.
Following the search, numerous social media posts claimed Omar was not a minor in 2000 — the year she reportedly became a U.S. citizen after her father naturalized — saying that official records indicated her birth year was originally listed as 1981 before it was later changed to 1982. Some of the posts said this indicated citizenship fraud.
We looked into the evidence and found that while her birth year was changed in official records, according to The Washington Post, she said this was to fix incorrect information rather than cover up the truth. We found other pieces of evidence indicating she could've indeed been a minor in 2000, including her high school yearbook and reports by reputable news outlets in 2018.
Omar has long maintained that she was 17 when she became a citizen in 2000 — receiving citizenship by default, according to U.S. law, after her father was naturalized.
In 2018, two years after she first ran for public office, articles by The Associated Press and The New York Times reported she had become a U.S. citizen in 2000, when she was 17.
In addition to the 2018 news reports, we found a high school yearbook showing Omar was a junior in 2000 and that she was in the graduating class of 2001. While not definitive proof, it supports the claim that Omar was not yet an adult when her family applied for citizenship.
Omar attended Edison High School in Minneapolis. As a member of the class of 2001, she was listed under the "Juniors" section in the 2000 yearbook.
(Classmates.com / Snopes illustration)
Her family fled Somalia in the early 1990s during the country's civil war, eventually arriving in the U.S. in 1995 before applying for citizenship five years later.
Archived versions of her profile in official records, such as the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, show that at one time, Omar's birth year was listed as 1981 — which would have made it unlikely for her to be a minor in 2000.
The circulated posts above took screenshots of an archived version of that website along with the current version (archived), noting that her birth year was changed from 1981 to 1982.
A note on the current version of her profile read:
Her birth year is correct. It is incorrectly reported as 1981 in other sources. As of May 24, 2019, Rep. Omar's congressional staff are working with Wikipedia and the U.S. House to correct her birth year in those sources.
In a emailed statement to Snopes, David Schmidtke, deputy director of the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, confirmed that "congressional staff contacted the library regarding her birthdate."
"However, we do not have supporting documentation, as the information was 'self-reported,'" he wrote. "The library does not independently verify birthdates before publishing or updating them."
We contacted Omar's office seeking comment on the speculation surrounding her birth year and have not yet received a response. We will update this story if we do.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Hardik Jagda, 35, the CEO of Proximity Works, who lives in San Francisco. The following has been edited for length and clarity.
In 2017, I wanted to build my own company, but I couldn't jump into it full-time because of my financial obligations at home.
Instead, I'd spend the mornings and evenings outside my full-time job working on my side projects. That time was foundational for building my company, Proxmity Works, which I launched in 2019. My aim was to help broadcasters scale their live sports streaming platforms worldwide. In 2020, we started building AI infrastructure for live sports.
Those years made me aware of how my body clock works. I read a lot of autobiographies from entrepreneurs and athletes to understand what allowed them to build what they achieved. I noticed athletes would talk about starting their day early to train and work, in time for rest and recovery throughout the day. I started modeling my days after this, waking up early so I could have four to five hours to build my company before work started. I still stick to this lifestyle now that I'm a full-time founder and CEO.
I want to structure my day to function like an Olympian
In the early stages of Proximity, I performed pretty much every role in the company. Today, I have a team of roughly 45 people, five in the US and the rest spread out globally. My cofounder is based in India.
After 7 a.m., my time isn't mine anymore because I have requests coming in from employees in different time zones.
I like to start the day early, so I'm protecting the first three hours as time for myself. I usually wake up between 3 a.m. and 5 a.m. Between 3 and 6 a.m., I don't touch my emails or look at messages.
I use these early hours to focus on strategic decisions. There was one point, roughly two years ago, when we had to interview a lot of engineers quickly for a new project. I sat down with my talent acquisition team and found a way to redesign our recruitment workflow to take place within 72 hours. That wouldn't have been possible if I didn't give myself the three-hour morning block.
In the mornings, I work out and write my goals down. These are usually measurable and trackable goals for my company, as well as goals for myself and my fitness.
Most of my team calls don't start before 7:30 or 8 a.m. I usually take my first couple of meetings at home before driving to the office. During the day, I try to minimize Zoom calls and take meetings as audio calls so I can move around during them. I try to wrap up my meetings by 2:30 p.m., work out at 3 p.m., and then focus on more creative tasks, like speech-writing, after that. I spend my evenings with loved ones before going to bed around 9 p.m. and trying to get seven hours of sleep.
It's not like I start my day at 4 a.m. and just work through the next 12 hours. I build in slots for "recovery" throughout the day. On my calendar, I put in 15-minute slots before important meetings, where I remind myself of my goal for the call.
For the most part, I work six days a week, spending my Saturdays focusing on a key skill I want to develop, like public speaking.
'996' misses the point. I don't run my team with this schedule in mind.
For the most part, I work six days a week.
I work more than 40 hours a week, but I don't keep track of the time. I listen to my body.
We don't keep track of how many hours the team works. It's more about a culture of ownership, where people really care about the problem they're working on.
Even though I've become a morning person, we're fine with engineers who are more productive at night, as long as they maintain a five-to-six-hour overlap with the other engineers.
"996 culture," working six days a week from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., has gained traction in Silicon Valley. I think it misses the point. It's more about volume than it is about structure. You want to structure your day towards putting in your best work by thinking about when you'll spend time training, recovering, and learning new skills. I'd rather focus on the right structures than on volume.

Canada's Carney makes final appeal against Alberta separation ahead of referendum
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters in his home province of Alberta warning that a referendum that could put the oil-rich province on a path toward independence is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’...
EDMONTON, Alberta -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters considering a path toward independence in his home province of Alberta on Friday, warning that a referendum is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’s sovereignty.
With U.S. President Donald Trump waging a trade war and threatening to make Canada the 51st state, Carney warned that the referendum comes at the “worst possible time” and urged Albertans not to take the outcome for granted.
“Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome,” Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, where he grew up.
“This is not a game. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he said.
Monday’s vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada’s proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation.
Carney’s closing appeal came after two days of campaigning against separation in the province. Earlier Friday, the Liberal prime minister joined Alberta’s conservative premier Danielle Smith in a show of unity against independence.
Smith praised Carney for improving relations with a province that frequently clashed with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, over his carbon tax and other energy policies.
“I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months,” Smith said alongside Carney in Red Deer, Alberta.
Smith noted that Carney grew up in Alberta and remains an Edmonton Oilers fan.
“He can’t be all bad, right?” she joked.
“Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us. Never. Never,” Carney warned Friday in Edmonton, repeating a warning he made a day earlier in Calgary.
At Thursday’s Calgary rally, the crowd erupted in its loudest applause when Carney spoke about reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the United States.
Carney acknowledged Alberta’s longstanding resentment of federal energy policies.
“Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” he said.
But he also emphasized his deep ties to the province.
“Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he said.
Outside the Edmonton rally venue Friday, Alberta independence supporters waved flags and held a sign reading “Say no to Carney’s new world order.”
Smith called the referendum despite opposing independence herself. She recently cited a poll showing 22% of Albertans support separation, a figure she said was still too high.
Smith also faces pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party. Former Premier Jason Kenney said the independence movement gained influence within the party as activists angry over COVID-19 restrictions, some influenced by conspiracy theories, embraced separatism.
But some Albertans who want to remain in Canada are angry with Smith for calling the vote.
“I think it’s a travesty really to be putting our province and our country through this when such a small portion of people are rabble rousing and saying they want to separate from Canada,” said Deb Lee, a retired Calgary resident who voted in advance to remain in Canada.
Smith said Carney had substantially addressed seven of nine federal laws Alberta opposed. She also cited cooperation on a proposed oil pipeline.
Independence advocate Tanya Clemens dismissed the agreements between Carney and Smith as “basically pinky promises” that came with too many conditions.
Carney’s chief political rival, federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, also urged Albertans Friday to remain in Canada.
“Don’t leave your fellow Canadians behind. Lock arms with them,” Poilievre said.
Despite their agreement on keeping Alberta in Canada, Carney and Smith remain divided over nine other questions on Monday’s ballot involving immigration and provincial powers. Smith wants voters to approve them, while Carney has urged their rejection.
“For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said.

Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken her vote for granted. That was, until it was suddenly taken away. She presented officials with her Indian birth certificate and family land documents from the village going back to 1962.
Both her parents had been on the electoral roll going back decades, so she showed proof of that too. But when the final revised voter list came out in April, Fakir was not on it.
The 38-year-old migrant worker, born into a poor Muslim family, was not alone. Since last year, 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – have been removed from India’s electoral roll through a process known as SIR, or special intensive revision. In the nearly eight decades since India’s independence, never have the voter rolls shrunk by such a huge amount over such a short time.
The Narendra Modi government has called SIR a legitimate exercise to clean up the electoral rolls. Overseen by the election commission, tens of millions of dead and duplicate names have been removed. Yet so have the names of millions of living Indian citizens.
Critics allege that the pledge to “purify” India’s voter roll of illegal immigrants has instead been used for more sinister purposes – disenfranchising tens of millions of Muslims, other minorities, and poor and lower caste communities, who are largely not BJP voters.
In a matter of weeks, nationwide anger at SIR has boiled up and spilled out on to the streets of India’s biggest cities, presenting a formidable challenge to the government. Over the weekend, Delhi was transformed into a high-security fortress of barricades, roadblocks and tens of thousands of police and paramilitaries who detained thousands of people, as they attempted to stop youth-led protests calling for the man who oversaw SIR, the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down immediately.
On Monday, opposition parties – who have decried SIR as a “weapon for vote theft” by the Modi government – drew tens of thousands of supporters as they marched through the capital and presented a petition to the supreme court, demanding Kumar’s resignation. The youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, who were behind the call for Saturday’s action, have vowed to “fight on” in their protests against SIR.
Opposition and civil society leaders allege that SIR has already given the BJP an electoral advantage in states such as Bihar and West Bengal, claims the party denied. Others say the exercise has had even more concerning implications: under changes to SIR unilaterally implemented by Kumar, the election commission has become the arbiter of Indian citizenship, a sweeping overreach of its remit.
The consequences are already playing out in West Bengal, where Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) recently came to power and began a crackdown on “illegal” immigrants, complete with several new detention centres. Civil society groups say Muslims excluded by SIR are being targeted.
Fakir was among them. Just three months after the voter list was published – and while her hearing to challenge her exclusion was pending – she was picked up by police and accused of being an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant.
In July she was pushed over the border to Bangladesh, a country she had never been to nor had any connection with, and remains stuck there. “I have all the documents to prove I am an Indian citizen,” she said in a tearful phone call from the Bangladesh border village where she has been sheltering. “I fell on their feet and begged the police not to send me to Bangladesh but they pushed me over the border.”
A Bangladesh border guard officer confirmed Fakir’s account. “We checked all her documents and are convinced that she is an Indian citizen,” they said. In September, her family submitted a petition to the supreme court challenging her deportation. The Indian government was given a month to respond.
“All I want is to return to my family and my home in India. I am waiting desperately for that day,” she said. The backlog of millions of voters in West Bengal challenging their exclusion means it could be years before Fakir’s case is heard.
Those across West Bengal who have been stripped of their votes speak of their terror of being accused of being an alien in their own land. Some have had benefits taken away. Mohammad Hedayet Ullah Siddiqui, 80, from the North 24 Parganas district, said his grandfather had been a freedom fighter for Indian independence and three generations of his family were on the voter rolls. Yet after SIR, Siddiqui described his “humiliation” on finding his name gone.
“With my name erased from the voter list, I am in constant terror. What if they send me to a detention camp?” he said. “I cannot bear to think about being separated from my children and grandchildren at this age, especially when all my ancestors have been buried in India.”
Critics say the problems began in 2023, when the Modi government changed the process for appointing the three-body election commission, giving majority control to the government for the first time. Within a matter of months, the Modi-led panel had appointed Kumar as the election commissioner in spite of opposition objections.
“For decades, the election commission was one of our more credible, independent bodies, but now that has been eroded,” said Ronojoy Sen, a senior fellow at the South Asian Studies Programme, National University of Singapore.
By the following year, the new election commission body had begun SIR, starting in Bihar, where it immediately raised concerns among human rights groups after more than 6 million names were removed. Not long after the revisions, the BJP won a landslide victory in the Bihar state elections.
Despite concerns over SIR rumbling on for months, it did not spark national protests until the Indian Express newspaper last month revealed that two members of the election commission had raised 14 objections to how voters were being excluded from the rolls, but they were unilaterally overruled by Kumar.
“India has always been a flawed democracy but at least citizens felt they had the right to vote and that elections were regular and fair,” said Sen. “SIR has taken away that right. From how it has been conducted, it’s difficult to see how the motive was anything other than to enhance the election prospects of the BJP.”
Three former election commissioners have openly criticised SIR as a “hostile exercise” that has undermined the sanctity of the country’s electoral rolls by focusing on the exclusion – rather than inclusion – of voters. OP Rawat, a former chief election commissioner, described changes to the voter registration form as “wrong and illegal”.
Ashok Lavasa, who was an election commissioner between 2018 and 2020, called for the SIR to be scrapped. “An unfair procedure has been imposed on millions of people in the country, and you have the judiciary which has validated that,” he said last month. “How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?”
None have been more vehement in their opposition than SY Qureshi, who was chief election commissioner between 2010 and 2012. “This is a national harassment exercise designed to throw Muslims off the electoral roll,” he claimed. “The only way to restore the credibility of India’s elections is to restore those deleted voters.”
The BJP has denied any political involvement or motive in the SIR process, accusing the opposition Congress party of “jealousy” over its recent electoral victories and saying any deleted voters can simply re-enrol. The BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the allegations were “disinformation” and part of an opposition campaign “being orchestrated to create an atmosphere of division and anarchy”.
Nonetheless, the election commission has appeared to accept some flaws in the process. Late last week, it belatedly put a cap on the number of voter deletion forms – which allow people to submit objections on behalf of others – after incidents in which people submitted thousands of forms targeting legitimate Muslim voters.
Public anger, meanwhile, has continued to build. In Delhi, where the SIR exercise left millions of people off the draft list, protests are expected to continue this week.
A Delhi resident for 30 years, Prashant Tandon, 60, said he could not believe it when a notice came to his door, questioning his life as a voter. “If someone doubts my citizenship, they should produce evidence against me,” he said furiously, adding that he would be protesting alongside the young people. “I should not have to prove that I am an Indian citizen.”

India rejects US lawmaker Pramila Jayapal’s remarks on voter roll revision as ‘unwarranted’
India rejected US Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal’s criticism of the voter roll revision, calling her remarks “unwarranted and uninformed” and interference in electoral practices.
India on Friday rejected senior US Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal’s criticism of the revision of the country’s electoral rolls as unwarranted and tantamount to interfering in the “electoral practices of a fellow democracy”.
Jayapal, an Indian-origin lawmaker from the Democratic Party who has been a vocal critic of the Indian government, said on social media on Thursday that she was concerned about actions that appeared aimed at purging 130 million people from voting rolls.
When external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal was asked about the matter at a regular media briefing, he replied: “We find the remarks of the Congresswoman unwarranted and uninformed and tantamount to interfering in the electoral practices of a fellow democracy.”
He added, “This is an approach that undermines democracy itself.”
Jayapal, who was born in Chennai and moved to the US in 1982, said on social media that she was “deeply concerned about the actions of the Indian government to purge 130 million people from the voting rolls”. The move “appears to be a similar playbook to what the Trump Administration is doing [in the US] to undermine voting rights in a democracy”, she said.
“Protecting democracies everywhere is essential work, and the Indian people — like the American people — deserve free and fair elections. Non-violent resistance movements are essential in these moments and I stand with the Indian people who are engaging in non-violent protests to counter anti-democratic efforts in India,” she said.
Jayapal’s comments came against the backdrop of protests in India by young people and opposition parties over alleged irregularities in the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which has led to the striking off of millions of voters’ names.
In December 2019, external affairs minister S Jaishankar had called off a meeting with US lawmakers after they reportedly declined to exclude Jayapal from the gathering. At the time, Jayapal had criticised restrictions imposed by the government in Jammu and Kashmir after the region’s special status was scrapped.
“I have an interest in meeting people who are objective and open to discussion but not the people who already made up their minds,” Jaishankar had said at the time, after Jayapal introduced a resolution in the US House of Representatives that urged India to lift all restrictions on communications in Jammu and Kashmir.

For more than a decade, Apple has told other companies to build smart home devices for its platform. This week, Apple launched its own. The Apple Home Collection is a lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. They arrive alongside HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.
Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices
Apple’s new smart home lineup promises easier setup, tighter integration, and data privacy. But with steep competition and steeper prices, can Apple convince more people to adopt its vision of the smart home?
Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices
Apple’s new smart home lineup promises easier setup, tighter integration, and data privacy. But with steep competition and steeper prices, can Apple convince more people to adopt its vision of the smart home?
Even after 12 years of HomeKit, Apple’s smart home ecosystem still feels underdeveloped, especially compared to the competition. Amazon’s and Google’s ecosystems support more products, and both have popular in-house brands: Ring and Nest. Apple had nothing of its own to point customers to as an Apple experience — and now it does.
But why now? And does Apple actually add anything new here, or is this mostly packaging? At Apple’s “Welcome home” event in New York this week, I spoke with Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, about the company’s new approach to the smart home and what this means for Apple’s commitment to Matter, the interoperable open smart home standard it helped found.
Why now?
Drance says the big reason was the development of the right technologies. The first was Matter, which provided the ecosystem. The second was AI, which brought a more conversational Siri voice assistant. Both were necessary to create a dedicated home device in HomeView. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” Drance says. “That’s been a really critical piece of bringing this all together.”
The bigger play is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home.
The bigger play here is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home for Apple’s users. Buy one for playing music, guided cooking recipes, and checking your calendar, and you might soon want a camera or smart lock to go with it. Drance says they’ve seen that once people try a single smart device and find it easier than they expected, it “unlocks this delightful understanding of what’s possible once you bring these products into the home.” She argues that most people just don’t know what a smart home can do.
She’s not wrong. The biggest barrier to buying smart devices is that people don’t see any value in the products, according to research from Parks Associates. Privacy and security concerns and complexity also rank high, along with cost. While Apple isn’t addressing the cost concern here — the products start at $200 — the other elements are part of its pitch: one-tap setup, your data stays yours, one app to run it all. Apple’s stamp of approval also carries a lot of weight. “People who own Apple products are very, very loyal, and there is a large user base,” says Elizabeth Parks, president and CMO at Parks Associates.
From a choose-your-own adventure to a tailored solution
Until now, Apple Home has been a bit like a buffet: You can pick from any brand that supports HomeKit or Matter and hope it all goes together. The Home Collection is more like the chef’s choice, a short list of dishes Apple promises will pair well. Drance says that’s what some customers were asking for. “There is a lot of choice with Matter, and there’s a lot of great products out there,” she says. “But sometimes we do get asked, ‘Hey, what product should I put in the home?’”
Rather than build devices itself, Apple chose to codevelop the lineup with partners that “have their own expertise in the home.” Both have a global footprint and home experience, she says, “LG more so in consumer products, Schneider through home build and home installations.” Drance says it was a ground-up collaboration with Apple bringing “the design aesthetic that would be suitable for the home and suitable to go with our family of products.” The company is also partnering with ADT through Apple retail stores to help people install the devices.
Drance says setup and ease of use were a big focus. “The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app,” she says. “We just wanted that simplicity to be at its core, and of course, the privacy that we’ve developed together with our partners.” She says everything integrates through Apple Home; you don’t need to create an LG or Schneider account, and all data is end-to-end encrypted, so only you can access it.
Drance was clear that the Apple Home Collection isn’t replacing the buffet — the hardware ecosystem that has grown up around Apple Home. “We still have this incredible ecosystem with Matter, and with Works with Apple Home, that is going to remain,” she says. “We know that homes are not a one-size-fits-all solution, so our customers will continue to have that choice, and we remain committed to building that ecosystem as well.”
The hardware mostly backs that up. The lock, thermostats, and sensors are Matter-compatible; the lock supports Aliro and works entirely locally, and every device supports Thread. The exception is the cameras, which use Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, not Matter. That’s the biggest lock-in. I was surprised Apple didn’t announce Matter camera support. But the Thread radios suggest the hardware might be Matter-ready, and Apple may be waiting for the Matter camera standard to support encrypted uploads, something HKSV already does.
So, what’s the benefit?
Does the Home Collection do anything other Apple Home devices can’t? In theory, no; in practice, yes. “What we’ve done with Apple Home Collection is we’ve added another layer on top of that, that deeper integration,” says Drance. There aren’t features exclusive to the Home Collection; it’s more that Apple is saying all the features will be here. It’s a bit like Google making a Pixel phone to show Android developers what Android can do: Apple’s products come with the full suite of capabilities the platform offers.
“The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app.”
— Kaiann Drance, Apple
According to Apple, setup is as simple as tapping your iPhone to the device, like pairing AirPods, with no extra account or app needed and no scanning required. Every device uses Thread to stay connected if Wi-Fi drops, and Apple says each can update its own network credentials when you change your Wi-Fi. This could address the offline-device problems that plague Apple Home. Everything is end-to-end encrypted, and the cameras keep recording to onboard storage if your Wi-Fi drops.
The devices also support Apple Home features other manufacturers have been slow to adopt. The LG lock is only the third to offer hands-free Home Key unlocking over UWB, and both thermostats work with Apple’s Clean Energy Guidance and Adaptive Temperature, which adjusts around your location and sleep schedule.
At least that’s the promise. We’ll have to test these devices to see how well they deliver.
A curated garden path
Together, Apple’s new devices form a polished, cohesive starter kit for the smart home — albeit an expensive one. The cameras, lock, and thermostats cost $200 to $400, and camera history requires an iCloud Plus plan. As Drance said, the smart home isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution, so this won’t work for everybody. If you already have a Ring doorbell or Google Nest Hub, this probably isn’t for you. Instead, Apple is trying to guide its existing customers who haven’t bought a video doorbell or smart lock yet down a curated path into the smart home.
However, Apple faces a tougher challenge in the broader market: It’s arriving late. The smart display category is already mature; millions of homes have Echo and Google smart displays. Millions more have Ring or Nest doorbells, neither of which will work with HomeView at launch.
As a smart home platform, Apple Home ranks third in adoption, behind Google, with Amazon holding a big lead, according to Parks Associates research. But customer loyalty to those platforms isn’t guaranteed. Four in five smart-home households would consider switching, Parks says, especially if another platform lets them control everything in one place. “Interoperability will be critical, but the bigger prize is owning the consumer relationship,” she says.
With its Home Collection, Apple isn’t reinventing the smart home; it’s trying to make it easier to get into one.

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.
Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.
A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.
Police authorities didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.
The CJP said that among those detained was a group of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being taken away in a bus to an unknown location.
The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.
The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.
The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.
The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.
The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.
Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.
“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture student who attended the Bengaluru protest.
There were also protests over police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.
On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of using “brute force” to briefly detain party leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Vadra, and other lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.
Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.
BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.
Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

The Supreme Court has declared access to and use of the internet a fundamental right for every individual, including children, under Articles 21 and 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. And further noted that a blanket ban on children's internet access is not the right way to approach the safety concerns
A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran noted, “We have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.”
“Our children, irrespective of their age enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing,” it added.
“The safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other. Our children are entitled to both,” the Bench said.
The court observed that the internet, in its present form, is far from safe for children. However, it said that keeping children away from the internet because platforms fail to identify and remove harmful content would amount to “mistaking the victim for the problem”.
The Bench also warned that children could migrate to unregulated and potentially more dangerous websites if prohibited from using certain platforms.
“Any blanket restriction on the access of internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality,” the court said.
While rejecting blanket bans, the Supreme Court said proportionate safeguards were necessary to protect children online.
The measures suggest parental consent and supervision, dedicated “child mode” accounts, private-by-default profiles, restrictions on messages from unknown adults, and stronger moderation of advertisements and content accessible to children.
The Bench also pointed out that the internet is particularly important for children in remote areas, for whom it may be the only source of learning and information.
It added that, for children with special needs, the internet was often the only place where they could find companionship with others like them.
The bench also noted that in the 2020 judgment in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India held that "the freedom of speech and expression and the freedom to carry on any trade or business through the medium of the internet is constitutionally protected as a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution." It refrained from expressing any view on whether the right to access the internet is, by itself, a fundamental right.

(Bloomberg) -- At least one firefighter has been injured and hundreds more are scrambling to contain a Malibu wildfire before dangerous winds ramp up again Friday.
The Bryson Fire in Los Angeles County had burned just 147 acres (59 hectares) as of 10:39 a.m. local time Friday. With more than 7,200 structures threatened and just 17% of the perimeter under containment, county officials said at a briefing Friday morning that they were mounting a large response before a multi-day Santa Ana windstorm causes conditions to deteriorate further.
Gusts near the Bryson Fire footprint may reach 60 miles (97 kilometers) per hour by Friday afternoon, according to the US National Weather Service. At higher elevations through the San Gabriel Mountains, winds may top out closer to 80 mph.
“This morning through this afternoon is our most critical period of time during this red flag event,” said Kevin McGowan, director of the Los Angeles County Office of Emergency Management. “Strong winds and very dry conditions will continue to cause fire starts to spread rapidly.”
The Bryson Fire sits within 10 miles of major burn scars left behind in recent years. The fast-moving Franklin Fire destroyed 20 structures around Malibu just before Christmas 2024. A few weeks later, in early January 2025, the devastating Eaton and Palisades fires killed 31 people and inflicted billions in damages in the region.
Though Santa Ana winds also fueled those blazes, weather service forecaster Rich Thompson said current fire conditions in Southern California are nowhere near as severe. Some areas have recently received rain that may limit fire spread.
Ahead of the 2025 fires, “we’d had no rain for months,” Thompson said. “It’s not the same level at all, though it’s still very concerning.”
As of Friday morning, more than 400 personnel had been deployed to fight the Malibu blaze. One had been transported to the hospital with minor injuries, according to Los Angeles County Fire Chief Anthony Marrone.
The largest blaze currently active in Southern California is the Henderson Fire in San Diego County, near Camp Pendleton. Almost 2,100 acres had burned as of midday Friday. The fire prompted the closure of northbound lanes on Interstate 5 in the city of Oceanside, according to the California Department of Transportation.
In a bid to avoid starting new fires, PG&E Corp. and Edison International’s Southern California utility — two of California’s biggest electricity providers — have shut down circuits serving tens of thousands of customers this week. Edison had turned off power to about 132,000 customers as of 12:25 p.m. local time.
Edison said restoration work may begin as soon as Saturday.

Kenya must be 'clean' to be credible, says Wada chief
- Published
Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility as it prepares to stage the 2029 World Athletics Championships, according to Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), .
Banka was speaking at the end of a three-day visit to Nairobi where he held talks with President William Ruto, government and sports officials, the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya (Adak), athletes and representatives of law enforcement.
Wada said the visit was intended to build on recent progress in Kenya's anti-doping programme at a critical time following Nairobi's selection to host the 2029 World Championships.
"Kenya calls itself probably 'home of champions', but every home has to have a good host and has to be clean to be credible," Banka told the BBC.
"We absolutely need to instill the culture of clean sport."
Kenya was awarded the 2029 championships in September, making it the first African country selected to host the event.
The decision has increased scrutiny of its efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem.
More than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit since 2017.
The Polish former sports minister said he had received a clear commitment from Ruto's government to a policy of zero tolerance towards doping, but warned promises would have to be matched by results.
"Wada will monitor this situation and observe the dynamic. Action speaks louder than words," he said.
Banka said his discussions with Ruto also focused on strengthening an independent Adak, and ensuring it has sufficient government support.
- How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships 
  - Published15 September
2029 will be the real test
Nairobi 2029 could provide a global test of Kenya's ability to protect its sporting legacy.
For a country whose distance runners have helped define global athletics for generations, the stakes extend beyond staging a successful championship.
"The problem with anti-doping is not with rules and standards," Banka said. "The problem is with implementation."
Another challenge is testing infrastructure.
Africa currently has no Wada-accredited doping control laboratory following the loss of accreditation of the facility in Bloemfontein, South Africa.
Wada initially suspended the laboratory in March 2024 because of multiple failures to comply with its International Standard for Laboratories.
Its accreditation was formally revoked in May 2025 after those problems were not satisfactorily resolved.
Banka said Kenya has shown political interest in establishing its own facility, but cautioned against expecting a laboratory to be accredited in time for the 2029 championships.
The process, he said, takes years because the consequences of laboratory error can be enormous for an athlete.
That leaves Kenya facing a more immediate priority: strengthening the system around testing rather than relying on a new laboratory as a solution.
'Doping has no colours and flags'
Banka also rejected the idea that doping should be viewed as an exclusively Kenyan, or African, problem.
"Doping has no colours and flags," he said, pointing to cases across established sporting nations including the United States, Germany and his native Poland.
"The problem would be to ignore this issue, not to tackle, or to pretend that there is no doping here."
Wada, he added, can investigate sport but cannot dismantle the criminal networks supplying prohibited substances.
"We are not a superpower. We are not law enforcement," he said.
"They have tools to really go after those who are destroying the credibility of the sport and the country."
He said intelligence indicated performance-enhancing drugs were being produced in Kenya and described Africa as a significant market.
According to him, athletes are often the "weakest points in the ecosystem", arguing that anti-doping authorities need to pursue not only competitors who break the rules but also the coaches, doctors, managers and suppliers who enable doping.
Some athletes, he suggested, are being exploited by people "who have money, who have power" and see them as a route to profit.

Trump’s plan to deport a member of Congress
The investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar just became more alarming.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump wants to deport a member of Congress.
What’s happening? On Monday, Homeland Security officers raided the Washington, DC, home of US Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) in an investigation reportedly tied to immigration paperwork filled out by her father when she was a minor.
That was, at the time, more than enough cause for alarm. Trump’s animosity toward Omar, who is Somali-American and an outspoken critic of the administration, is well-known, and the raid is an extraordinary violation of the Justice Department’s usual rule to avoid taking visible action around politically sensitive cases within 60 days of an election.
On Wednesday evening, however, we learned more about the raid from the Wall Street Journal. The Omar investigation, the Journal reported, is explicitly aimed at stripping Omar of her citizenship — and thus her ability to hold office — and deporting her.
How would they do that? Omar came to the US as a refugee when she was 12 and became a US citizen when she was 17. The Trump administration’s investigation is said to focus on whether she or her family misrecorded her age in order to more easily gain citizenship.
The government cannot unilaterally denaturalize a citizen, however; it would have to ask a court to do so.
What’s the context? Historically, it’s rare for the US to strip citizenship from naturalized US citizens. But doing so at volume has been a major, if less visible, priority for the second Trump administration.
As of earlier this year, NBC News reported, DOJ was targeting hundreds of people for possible denaturalization, and has reportedly hoped to put forward hundreds of new cases per month (though successfully stripping them of citizenship is another matter).
Why does this matter? Trump’s campaign to bend the traditionally nonpartisan DOJ into a tool to punish and harass his enemies has been one of the major stories of his second term.
Even if it never advances beyond Monday’s raid, an investigation targeting Omar’s citizenship with the eventual goal of deporting her from the US represents a new and even more dangerous evolution of that effort — and it threatens to move the US to a far darker place, where citizenship and the rights it guarantees are predicated on the president’s goodwill.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993
- Published
Rwanda has signed a 10-year deal with Formula 1 to host races in the African country, starting "in the early 2030s".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali and next to the city's new international airport. It will be the first F1 race in Africa since 1993.
A statement from F1 said the project came as a result of "years of collaboration to ensure the right foundations, with the best partner, are in place to deliver a successful, sustainable and world-class grand prix for generations to come".
The circuit, designed by the former F1 driver Alex Wurz, has been "designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans," the statement added.
F1 hopes the race will provide an opportunity for the sport to expand its profile in Africa, a relatively unexplored market compared to Europe, Asia and the Americas.
It has not yet been established where the race may best fit into the schedule during the year.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published7 hours ago
The sport is likely to want to avoid holding the race in the main rain season of March to May. There is a shorter, less disruptive rain season from October to November.
F1 is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: "For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement.
"Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.
"The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."
F1 president Stefano Domenicali said the new contract was "a landmark moment for F1", which would mean the sport was racing "on every inhabited continent".
Domenicali added: "Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."
Sportswashing controversy
The race is likely to lead to opposition from human rights groups accusing Rwanda of sportswashing, as has been the case with its sponsorship of Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa.
Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
A spokesperson for F1 said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."
The track's build process will be overseen by three companies, with long-time F1 track architect Tilke and DAR working alongside WurzDesign as the creator of the circuit.
It is designed to be fast and flowing, with significant elevation change, using the natural contours of Rwanda's hilly landscape.
The first grand prix in Africa was the final round of the World Championship in Morocco in 1958.
South Africa hosted a race during the apartheid era - from 1960-66 in East London, now known as KuGompo City, before the race moved to Kyalami near Johannesburg from 1976-85.
Kyalami returned for two races in 1992 and 1993 as apartheid was coming to an end.
The country has held talks with F1 in recent years about a return at various venues, including Kyalami and Cape Town, but a deal has not proved possible.

Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging’s ₹852.1 Cr IPO continued to receive healthy investor interest on the second day of bidding. A video is circulating on social media (here, here) that purportedly shows a young woman criticising the ongoing Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a young woman criticising the ongoing CJP protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
Fact: The video is AI-generated and does not show an authentic recording of a young woman criticising the ongoing CJP protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed a watermark bearing the Instagram handle @sifatsangh. A Google search for the handle led us to the same video (archived), which was uploaded to the account on 07 October 2026. We also observed that the speech patterns throughout the video resemble those commonly found in AI-generated audio.
To further verify the video, we analysed it using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive, SynthID, and Hiya. Hive and SynthID indicated that the video was AI-generated, while Hiya identified the audio as likely to be a deepfake.
We then analysed the photos and videos posted on the profile using Hive’s AI detection tool, which indicated that the content appeared to be AI-generated. This suggests that the profile may be entirely AI-generated and could be fake.
To sum up, this viral video of a young woman criticising the CJP protest demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation is AI-generated.

No, Rome was not built in a day, but it was built at breathtaking speed, its temples, amphitheaters, and aqueducts rising with the help of a magical blend of volcanic ash and lime. Today, that miraculous mortar has a less than enchanting name: concrete.
The surprisingly hopeful quest to fix concrete
Scientists are racing to reinvent concrete before we pour millions more tons of it.
“Romans lived through a true architectural revolution, and at the foundation of this revolution, literally, was a concrete discovery,” said Admir Masic, a materials science professor at MIT who made waves a few years ago for unearthing the fast-hardening secret sauce for why Roman concrete is so durable. “They were able to take a pile of dirt and mix it together, add water, and turn it into solid rock of any arbitrary size. It literally changed everything.”
And yet, for a millennia after the fall of Rome, the world largely forgot about concrete, until, in the 18th century, an English mason found that mixing limestone and clay could form a paste that hardened underwater. Another few decades later, concrete as we now know it was reborn, and once again, it changed everything.
In the centuries since, concrete has come to reshape our way of life, with disastrous results for the climate. What early concrete evangelists didn’t realize was that the modern way of producing the substance released giant amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. As it has become increasingly central to modernity, it has helped fuel environmental catastrophe.
Today, however, a new generation of concretophiles like Masic have pored over the poured mixture in search of another miracle, a greener, more durable kind of concrete. And they’ve found multiple answers, from concrete that can heal its own cracks — as the Pantheon has for millennia — to electroconductive concrete capable of storing energy to a blend that allows concrete to soak up more CO2 than it emits.
Together, they suggest that in a not-so-distant future, concrete — yes, concrete — one of the dirtiest substances ever concocted, could help save the planet, transforming our built environment while actually intervening in the climate for the better.
How concrete built (and polluted) the modern world
It’s no wonder that luminaries of the neo-concrete age, Thomas Edison among them, marveled at the stuff just as their Roman predecessors had. They saw it as a harbinger of utopia, of a world in which anything and everything — a home, an interstate highway, a water pipe, a subway system, or a grand piano — could be molded and poured for a fraction of ordinary costs.
“As to concrete dogs to stand warningly in the front yard and concrete cats to purr stonily under a concrete kitchen range,” the New York Times teased Edison in 1911 when he described his plans for a concrete home finished with concrete furnishings, “he made no announcement.”
The beguiled inventor’s utopian vision of a world remade by concrete would come true in more ways than he realized. Yes, it changed the way we build forever. Muddy roads and rotting wooden sidewalks gave way to smooth gray pavement, and newly cast sewer systems saved millions of lives in the deathly dirty cities of the early industrial era. Concrete, when poured over rods of steel, proved strong enough to prop up colossal skyscrapers that Julius Caesar could only have dreamed of.
But there was a trade-off: Every time Edison fired up his trademark 150-foot kilns, scorching the limestone inside into blistering pebbles of cement clinker, he released hundreds of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Yankee Stadium was built not by Babe Ruth’s swing alone, but with around 30,000 cubic yards of Edison concrete, whose creation released at least 5,400 tons of CO2, the equivalent of driving a gas-powered car 12.5 million miles, or to the moon and back more than two dozen times. But this is nothing compared with the roughly 30 billion tons of concrete the world now uses each year, enough to have turned the gluey gray goo into the second-most used material on Earth. (The first is water. Glug glug.)
The Anthropocene has been built atop a foundation of concrete, its weight eclipsing the biomass of all living things, and its annual carbon tab responsible for up to 8 percent of global emissions, the equivalent of the entire country of India. Critically, unlike the astonishingly enduring remnants of Rome, our modern concrete decays quickly, so it must be repoured time and time again, which only makes it more environmentally catastrophic.
But it doesn’t have to be this way, not anymore.
“The future of concrete is to think differently, to go away from claiming that cement is bad,” Masic told me. “Our goal is to turn this around and make concrete part of the solution instead of being a problem.”
This is why we can have nice concrete
Per ton, concrete actually emits far less CO2 by volume than other materials like aluminum, steel, plastic, or glass.
The problem is that we use so much of it, even a slightly negative footprint can quickly become enormous. But “the upside is,” said Sabbie Miller, a professor at UC Davis who focuses on sustainable concrete, “if you’re able to come up with some small change, then those small changes will also scale” in ways “that could have a huge effect on modern society and its burdens on the environment.”
One of those solutions takes a cue from the Romans, who made concrete differently than we do today. Their once-mysterious method ensured that hulking structures like the Colosseum or the Aqua Virgo, an aqueduct built during Augustus’ reign and still in use today, could survive for millennia while New York City’s Brooklyn-Queens Expressway or the Washington Bridge crumble after just a few decades of use.
It’s not just that we drive cars over our concrete freeways while the Colosseum has been mostly free of even the bulkiest chariot wheels for millennia. The answer, according to Masic’s research, lies in the Romans’ ingenious recipe for cement, the glue that binds concrete together. When the ancients brewed a batch of cement, they left big white chunks of dormant lime in the final mixture. Later, if a crack formed, any water would react with the idle lime, filling the fissure with new stone. Our modern concrete has no such lime clasts, meaning that if water seeps into a crack, it degrades the structure from within, rusting the rebar that made our big towers possible, leading to a grim condition known as “concrete cancer.”
Masic has recently turned his research into a startup called DMAT that reserves unreacted lime in concrete, giving it self-healing properties he says could extend a structure’s lifespan by about 50 percent, which in and of itself would reduce its carbon footprint by 40 percent. If the construction industry normalized such concrete or other mixtures that emit, say, half as much CO2 as usual, it would keep hundreds of millions of tons of it out of the atmosphere each year.
But why stop there? Some startups have gotten much better in recent years at producing concrete capable of quite literally breathing in more CO2 than it emits in a process that takes advantage of concrete’s natural porousness. It could, in theory, turn our cities into concrete rainforests by turning the material into a storage reservoir. As Miller put it, “what if we can use our concrete to undo some of our environmental damages that we’ve already caused?”
In the Bahamas, the startup Partanna has already built what it’s called the world’s first carbon net-negative home, an unassuming 1,250-square-foot abode that the company claims will sequester 182.6 tons of CO2 in its lifetime, the equivalent of hundreds of trees. Meanwhile, Masic’s lab has been piloting ways to turn concrete into a giant battery, capable of storing solar power during the day and releasing it at night, a green innovation that could cancel out its own carbon footprint within a few years of use.
Masic believes that electroconductivity could be key to catalyzing a new era of concrete — more so even than his neo-Roman ventures. “It might hold the secret,” he said, “for turning a bad guy into something amazing.”
But as promising as these innovations are, it will take time for them to ripple out from model homes and into the concrete that actually surrounds us. American concrete startups have lost billions of dollars in federal funding and expected procurement contracts under the Trump administration. Some states, most notably California, are helping to pick up the slack, but investment still lags behind potential. There’s also the challenge of convincing builders running on paper thin margins that their old ways of doing things might fit better in a new mould.
But concrete’s staggering scale means that we can’t afford to keep pouring it without considering its ugly trade-offs. More importantly, perhaps, we can’t afford to miss out on the opportunity that such a mammoth, transformative material presents to change everything yet again.

A fast-moving wildfire destroyed multiple homes in Southern California as hot, gusty weather swept the region on Friday, prompting mandatory evacuations and widespread power outages.
Television footage from KTLA showed several residences engulfed in flames in the Orange County community of San Juan Capistrano.
Aerial coverage captured emergency crews directing water streams onto two-story suburban homes as fire breached their roofs, sending dense black smoke billowing across backyard swimming pools and tennis courts.
The wildfire ignited in the coastal city of San Clemente before quickly moving into San Juan Capistrano.
It was one of several blazes fueled by dry, warm northeast Santa Ana winds blowing from Southern California's interior toward the coast. Forecasters warned that the strongest wind gusts would continue through Friday afternoon.
The conditions forced local evacuations and left tens of thousands of residents without electricity following precautionary power shutoffs.
Both communities are situated near the southern Orange County coast and surrounded by hillsides.
San Juan Capistrano, home to 35,000 people, is recognized for its horse trails, while neighboring San Clemente, with a population of 62,000, is known as a "Spanish village by the sea" and attracts beachgoers and surfers.
The Orange County Fire Authority confirmed that two evacuation shelters were opened, one in each city, and urged residents subject to evacuation orders to "leave now."
To the west of Los Angeles, a separate coastal blaze in Malibu triggered evacuation orders and warnings across a wide section of the Santa Monica Mountains.
A heavy plume of dark smoke rose over the ridgelines, visible from surrounding cameras and several miles away.
The National Weather Service projected sustained winds of 20 mph to 35 mph (32 kph to 56 kph) on Friday, with peak gusts reaching between 50 mph and 70 mph (80 kph to 112 kph) in certain areas.
As humidity levels plummeted, "this will favor a critical fire weather threat," the service stated early Friday.
Meanwhile, more than 400 firefighters worked overnight to contain the Bryson Fire, which stood at 250 acres (100 hectares) by Friday morning.
That blaze threatened a Los Angeles County juvenile detention and rehabilitation facility, forcing an evacuation on Thursday night.
Kevin McGowan, director of the Los Angeles County Office of Emergency Management, noted that the most severe fire conditions would occur through Friday afternoon during the peak wind event, though elevated risks would persist through Saturday night.
"Strong winds and very dry conditions will continue to cause fire starts to spread rapidly, so we’re urging everyone to remain vigilant," he said.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who faced criticism for her city's response to deadly fires in 2025, directed the fire department to deploy personnel and equipment ahead of the winds.
The fire department also requested assistance from the state’s office of emergency services.
"It’s a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert," said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
