For corporate recruiters like Martha Heller, asking questions about a job candidate's credentials — like the kind that swirled around now-former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia this week — is par for the course.
When a background check failed to verify an executive candidate's college degree a few years ago, Heller inquired about the discrepancy. The candidate, who was being considered for a job at a California insurance company, claimed a flood at his school had destroyed the records from the year he graduated. Skeptical, Heller called the college and learned that no such event had occurred.
"It was like detective work," she said, adding that the problem wasn't whether the candidate had a college degree. It was that he misrepresented his education and then doubled down when questioned, she said.
White House controversy
Zacharia's self-described legal career has been the subject of intense scrutiny in recent days following her appointment as White House press secretary. When asked by a reporter what state she passed the bar exam in, she responded, "When I moved to China."
Business Insider reviewed records for all 50 states and the District of Columbia and found no evidence that Zacharia had been admitted to any state bar in the US after she graduated with a law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011.
Zacharia later defended calling herself a lawyer, saying that after failing the bar exam the first time, she did not take it a second time. On Friday, a White House official confirmed that she is "transitioning out" of the role.
Vetting résumés
One of a recruiter's jobs is to vet a candidate's background. Research suggests it's not uncommon for candidates to exaggerate their credentials.
Some 37% of Americans said they've put inaccurate information on their résumés, according to a June report from Novorésumé, an online résumé-building service. Nearly 7% said they'd claimed a degree, certification, or other credential they didn't possess, while 6.1% said they'd listed a job that didn't exist or was substantially fabricated. The findings are based on a May survey of 2,000 US adults.
Brian Fink, a managing partner at tech recruiting firm The ReWork Group, can relate. Last year, a candidate for a senior marketing job at a cybersecurity company was on the verge of being hired when a background check failed to confirm that he'd worked for a company listed as a past employer on his résumé and LinkedIn profile.
Fink said he gave the candidate an opportunity to provide evidence supporting his claim, but the man refused.
"I had no choice but to rescind the offer," said Fink. "If you're willing to lie about your education, what else are you willing to lie about?"
Background checks
Recruiters typically wait until a job candidate is a finalist to conduct a background check because the task is time-consuming and costly. They also tend to hold off contacting references early on to avoid tipping off the person's current employer that they're job hunting. Early in the process, though, some recruiters will look for potential red flags by probing inconsistencies or gaps in candidates' work histories.
Doug Johnson, CEO of executive search firm Valor Partners, said he asks candidates at the end of an interview if there's anything embarrassing or potentially damaging in their past that might come up during a background or reference check. He tells them that disclosing it now gives them a chance to address the issue with a prospective employer, while discovering it later could cost them the job.
Most candidates say there's nothing to be concerned about, said Johnson. But some subsequently fall off the radar, and others suddenly report receiving a raise or finding a better opportunity elsewhere.
"It worries people who have a conscience," he said.
Update: October 16, 2026 — This article has been updated to reflect Friday's news that Zacharia is out of the role.

As KJ Apa navigates life after Riverdale, he’s up for a return to the upcoming Afterlife with Archie series adaptation.
Following his performance as Archie on the CW series for its seven-season run from 2017-’23, the actor expressed his excitement for series creator Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa, the Archie Comics chief creative officer who also co-wrote the Afterlife with Archie comics.
“I spoke to Roberto, who was our showrunner for Riverdale, who’s also showrunning that show,” he told Entertainment Weekly. “And I’m really excited. I can’t wait to see who they cast as Archie and the gang.”
Apa admitted it would “be cool if we could do some cameos or something,” noting, “I asked him!”
Watch on Deadline
“I would think that would be really fun if I could come in for a scene,” added Apa. “Maybe I’m not even [Archie], I don’t know who I’d play, but it’d be fun to do it.”
Set for a Halloween 2027 premiere on Disney+, Afterlife with Archie received a script-to-series order from the streamer last October, with Berlanti Productions (Riverdale, The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina) and Warner Bros. TV producing.
Penned by Aguirre-Sacasa based on his and artist Francesco Francavilla’s comics, Afterlife with Archie turns the all-American town of Riverdale into a zombie-overrun apocalypse — where the only thing scarier than the undead is trying to survive your teenage years. When a supernatural spell from a certain teen-witch backfires, unleashing an army of the possessed dead upon Riverdale, Archie and his friends must fight to stay alive, testing the friendships, romances and loyalties that have always held them together.

EXCLUSIVE: J.K. Rowling‘s agent Neil Blair has claimed that a trans rights protest at the gala performance of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child put people at risk.
During an event celebrating a shortened version of the West End stage show at the Palace Theatre on Thursday night, a number of protesters stormed the red carpet.
Wearing masks to conceal their identities, the individuals lay down on the carpet before being removed by security. One was wearing a shirt featuring the words: “Rowling money kills.”
Rowling has been staunchly critical of transgender rights activists, funding legal efforts to protect women’s rights and attacking trans people on social media.
Watch on Deadline
In a statement provided to Deadline, Blair said: “We respect peaceful activism and the right to express different views. But those rights must be exercised without putting others at risk, including audience members, performers and theatre staff, as we saw yesterday evening during the protests outside the Palace Theatre in London ahead of the gala performance of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.
“Above all, we want to continue bringing the magic of Harry Potter to the wonderful fans who have supported and embraced this world for so many years. Every fan deserves to enjoy the magic of Harry Potter in an atmosphere of respect and security, and we remain committed to keeping live theatre a welcoming and safe experience for everyone.”
The new version of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child has been cut from a five-hour show performed across two parts to a single three-hour performance.

It’s about to get a lot colder very quickly. Here’s how to stay safe
Dangerously cold weather kills more than 1,000 people in the U.S. each year

It’s about to get a lot colder across the U.S., with forecasters projecting a 40-degree temperature drop for the East Coast this weekend.
Freeze warnings were issued across the central U.S. Friday, as a cold front shifts southward from Canada.
Cold is one of the nation’s top weather-related killers, leading to more than 1,000 deaths each year, per federal data.
Though the strengthening El Nino climate pattern is expected to bring above-average temperatures throughout the U.S. this winter, that doesn’t mean there won’t also be life-threatening lows.
Experts say people can protect themselves this year by staying indoors, being prepared and making informed decisions.
“Take weather warnings seriously,” Stephen Cheung, a professor of kinesiology at Canada’s Brock University, told The New York Times earlier this year. “You can still do most things safely - just plan ahead, be prepared, know the risks.”
What are the risks?
Being in the cold can lead to hypothermia and frostbite, as well as raise blood pressure in just 20 minutes.
Blood pressure is typically higher in the winter because low temperatures cause blood vessels to narrow, the Mayo Clinic says, with more pressure needed to force blood through veins and arteries. This raises the risk of cardiovascular events, such as heart attack and stroke.
The cold also increases the risk of hypothermia, a condition that occurs when core body temperature drops below 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 degrees Celsius), affecting a person’s ability to think or move.
And frostbite is an injury that occurs when body tissue freezes in low temperatures, leading to tissue death known as gangrene - and even amputations.
How do you stay safe?
“To prevent hypothermia, follow Grandma’s advice,” instructs Dr. Jennah Morgan, an emergency medicine physician at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. Bundle up - including a hat, scarf, gloves, a warm coat and warm and waterproof shoes.
And avoid going outside with wet hair or clothes, she says. It can make you feel a lot colder.
Make sure not to ignore shivering, too. It’s a sign that the body is losing heat and could be at risk, the New York Department of Health explains.
Much of the same advice works to stave off frostbite - but knowing the physical signs of the condition can help avoid a trip to the emergency room. In the first stages of frostbite, the skin is often red and painful before turning a grayish-yellow. Then, the area may start to feel waxy or numb.
In the worst cases, the skin blisters and turns black as tissue dies. This is known as gangrene.
“In most cases, the person is unaware of frostbite because the frozen tissues are numb,” Johns Hopkins Medicine says. “The symptoms of frostbite may look like other health conditions or problems.”
Lastly, be sure to avoid smoking or drinking. People who drink alcohol or smoke are more sensitive to the cold because the substances make blood vessels narrow.
What if you are already cold?
People with hypothermia or frostbite should seek out medical attention immediately. But if you can’t access medical attention right away, there are several quick ways to warm up a bit.
Using heater packs and heated blankets and drinking hot, non-alcoholic beverages can help raise body temperature, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
So does skin-to-skin contact under loose, dry layers of blankets, clothing, towels or sheets.
“After body temperature has increased, keep the person dry and wrap their body, including their head and neck, in a warm blanket,” the CDC says.

India's 'cockroach' party founder detained ahead of protest
- Published
The founder of India's "cockroach" protest movement, Abhijeet Dipke, has been detained in Delhi ahead of a planned march in the heart of the capital.
His detention follows a police warning against holding Friday's march, with thousands of security personnel deployed across the city to prevent the gathering.
Dipke's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is demanding the resignation of India's election chief over allegations of voter list manipulation. The Election Commission denies the charge.
The group had asked its supporters to come to a park in Connaught Place, one of Delhi's busiest commercial districts, to wave the Indian flag.
The turnout was smaller than at earlier CJP demonstrations though the crowd seemed to be swelling. The BBC saw some young protesters being detained and shoved into a bus which already held some female detainees - there were about 50 female police personnel in the bus, vastly outnumbering the protesters.
Dipke had just left home and was moments away from reaching his vehicle when the BBC saw police officers surround him and force him into a police car. Some CJP supporters tried to block the vehicle from leaving.
Anish Gawande, the opposition politician at whose house Dipke had been staying, questioned why police had detained him. Police have not yet publicly confirmed the grounds for the detention.
"Detaining a lone man walking with the national flag in his hand is a bit of a joke," Gawande said.
It was the second time in less than a week that Dipke was detained. Last Saturday, police boarded his plane shortly after it landed in Delhi and took him away before he could reach a planned demonstration.
Police barricades and mass detentions prevented thousands of other protesters from reaching the venue. Dipke was released the following day, but two other CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were later jailed for five days after entering Jantar Mantar, a protest site recently declared off-limits by police.
Friday's march was partly intended to show solidarity with the two jailed leaders.
Dipke had acknowledged the possibility of being arrested again. In a video message on Thursday, he urged supporters unable to travel to Delhi to raise the Indian flag in their own towns and cities.
"I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said.
Earlier on Friday, police had served Dipke with a notice warning him against holding the march without permission.
Authorities also closed Central Park for two days, citing "administrative reasons". Police offered to let a small group wave the national flag and sing the anthem at another location.
The CJP responded by changing its plans, urging supporters to enter Connaught Place in groups of fewer than five, unfurl the flag, take a photograph and leave.
"Waving the Tiranga is not a crime," the group said in a social media poster, using the Hindi name for India's tricolour flag. It encouraged supporters to share their photographs online.
By the time the protest was due to begin, around 200-300 people had gathered near Central Park. Prevented by police from entering, they moved around the park, waving flags and shouting slogans.
Among those detained was Neha Bora, a prominent leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) who has emerged as one of the faces of the recent protests. She was also detained during last Saturday's crackdown.
Security personnel, meanwhile, continued to arrive. More officers emerged from buses stationed around Connaught Place, joining the thousands of police and paramilitary personnel already deployed. Journalists also crowded the streets, with police and media in much larger numbers than the protesters.
Barely five months old, the CJP began as an online campaign in May after India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches. Dipke embraced the insult and turned it into a rallying cry.
By July, the group had become a formidable force, drawing thousands of young people into protests over leaked examination papers. A march towards Parliament in July descended into clashes with police, bringing the movement wider attention and intensifying pressure on the government. The unrest eventually forced the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.
Police cited earlier demonstrations in their warning against Friday's march. In the notice served to Dipke, they accused the CJP of defying restrictions and said previous attempts to march towards Parliament had led to violence and damage to property.
They also warned that a large gathering in Connaught Place could disrupt traffic, affect businesses and obstruct emergency vehicles.
The CJP wants Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign, accusing the poll panel of favouring Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the commission and the government deny the allegations.
At issue is a sweeping revision of electoral rolls, known as Special Intensive Revision (SIR), that critics say has removed more than 130 million names, putting legitimate voters at risk of losing their right to vote.
Friday's march comes less than a week after police prevented the movement's last mass demonstration from taking place, detaining its leaders - Das, Dipke and Ranka - and putting the city under a sweeping security lockdown.
Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel had fanned out across Delhi, sealing roads, shutting metro stations and intercepting protesters long before they could reach Jantar Mantar, where the CJP had planned its mass demonstration.
The BBC witnessed dozens of people being detained, including journalists and students. In footage from across Delhi, protesters could be seen shouting as police seized them by the arms, dragged them across the pavement and pushed them into waiting buses.
Those who managed to gather elsewhere were swiftly dispersed. There were also reports of protesters being assaulted by police.
The BBC captured footage, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.
The scale of the crackdown drew widespread outrage, with the CJP likening the police action to India's Emergency, when civil liberties were suspended between 1975 and 1977.
Delhi police defended the measures as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings.
Dipke, Das and Ranka were released on Sunday after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour.
Police then took Jantar Mantar off Delhi's list of approved protest sites, designating three alternate venues. Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory sits near parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent. The CJP accused the authorities of pushing protesters away from the seat of power to make their demonstrations less visible and easier to ignore.
On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned with a handful of supporters, unfurling the Indian flag and shouting slogans against Kumar.
Police said they had entered the restricted site without permission, some by climbing over a locked gate, and breached the conditions of their release.
The following day, the two were sent to jail for five days in judicial custody. Another organiser, Ajinkya Shinde, was released on a bond to maintain peace and good behaviour.
The CJP's campaign is unfolding alongside a separate wave of protests by India's opposition parties, which have also accused the Election Commission of manipulating voter rolls to benefit the BJP.
Last week, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other lawmakers attempted to march to the commission's headquarters in Delhi but were stopped by police and detained. Opposition politicians have since taken their grievances to President Droupadi Murmu and marched towards the Supreme Court.
Although the CJP, student organisations and opposition parties have largely protested separately, their demands have increasingly converged. Gandhi has condemned the arrests of CJP organisers and called for Jantar Mantar to be reopened to peaceful demonstrators.
Home minister Amit Shah, meanwhile, has accused opposition parties of spreading falsehoods about the voter-verification exercise and defended the Election Commission's independence.

Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours falls in Caulfield Cup won by Kingswood
Last year's Melbourne Cup winner, Half Yours, has gone down in a nasty fall late in the Caulfield Cup, which was won by Gavin Bedggood's Kingswood.
With about 200 metres to go in the 2,400m race, Half Yours was in the middle of the pack when there appeared to be contact with Kings Valley.
Half Yours went down hard, sending jockey Mark Zahra into the turf, with New Zealand's Ohope Wins also coming down after Jye McNeil was unable to avoid the fallen McEvoy Racing product.
Half Yours returned to his stall after the race and was "all OK", according to Racing.com, while stewards said Zahra and McNeil were both "conscious and alert" and transported to hospital for further assessment.
The condition of Ohope Wins, the New Zealand mare that won the Oaks at Randwick in April, was still not known.
Trainer Tony McEvoy said after the race that Half Yours had suffered some abrasions but looked OK, all things considered.
"That was terrible to watch," McEvoy said.
"The horse, he's got a couple of lacerations, he seems bright, he seems composed in himself.
"He's got a laceration under his arm, he's got a laceration on a hind leg. They look superficial."
The final race of the day at Caulfield was delayed.

Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.) has some advice for fellow lawmakers: unapologetically support the biotech industry, vilify insurance companies, and focus on making America a biotech research haven, instead of relying on protectionism.
Right now in Washington, it’s popular to support protectionist policies against China in industries like tech. China is rapidly gaining on the U.S. biotechnology industry, and there is bipartisan support to extend those protections to the biotech sector.
Auchincloss said that approach hurts America’s competitiveness.
“Washington needs to fix itself and worry less about what China is doing because China is going to be excellent,” he said at the STAT Summit in Boston on Thursday. “But we can be even better.”
That attitude aligns with the views of the biotech industry and its investors. America cannot stop China from becoming a biotech powerhouse, the thinking goes, so Congress should invest in the domestic biotechnology industry and speed research and development.
Auchincloss plans to introduce a bill that would adopt the approach taken by the Australian government, which has sped up the clinical trial regime in part by allowing early-phase trials to bypass pre-approval evaluation by the national regulator. It will never be as cheap to conduct early-stage trials in the U.S. as it is in China, Auchincloss said, but it should be as fast.
He said he’s also interested in cracking down on pharmacy benefit manager business practices, reforming the 340B hospital drug discount program, and creating small business grants.
Although drugmakers have become a popular target of lawmakers, Massachusetts lawmakers should boldly promote the industry, which plays a crucial role in the state’s economy, Auchincloss said.
“Some advice from a six-year veteran of Washington, D.C.: You do need a villain, and the villain is the insurance company,” he said during the conversation with STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo.
Another villain, in his eyes: Russ Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, who Auchincloss said considers science a “blue state subsidy.” The OMB proposed empowering the White House to override the recommendations of peer reviewers, terminate grants at will, and exercise more latitude in the type of research federal agencies support.
Auchincloss also took issue with the Food and Drug Administration’s Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher program. Former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary created the program, and it has come under scrutiny from industry stakeholders and public health advocates.
Auchincloss said it politicizes decisions that should be guided by transparent, well thought-out standards. For example, Makary awarded vouchers to psychedelics after podcaster Joe Rogan texted President Trump about research around ibogaine.
“If Washington behaves that way, there’s nothing that we’re going to do about Beijing that’s going to save our biomedical leadership,” Auchincloss said. “Because ultimately, what makes us great is high, clear, transparent standards paired with the world’s best talent getting funded to pursue curiosity-driven research.”

A ‘Wall of Hope’, a youth-led initiative by the Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF) and its Department of Youth Mental Health, was unveiled at the IIT-Madras Research Park in Taramani on Saturday, a press release said.
With young people facing increasing mental health challenges and suicide remaining concern, creating spaces for expression, connection, resilience, and help-seeking is vital.
The mental health campaign, which began on October 10, 2025, encourages young people aged 10-25 to express, share, and reflect upon their personal reasons for living, through brief messages of hope.
Adolescents and young adults across the country were invited to write the purpose of life on colourful post-it notes.
The activity is completely youth-led through peer leaders and trainer modules, where young people played a central role in leading and facilitating the campaign.
More than 20,000 responses from across six States have been collected.
Additionally, 400 volunteers have been trained to conduct this activity, which is voluntary and anonymous, to initiate and foster conversations around mental health.
Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, Madras High Court judge, and Lakshmi Vijayakumar, founder of suicide prevention organisation SNEHA, participated in the event, besides SCARF vice-chairperson R. Thara and director Sridhar Vaitheswaran.
(Assistance for overcoming suicidal thoughts is available on the State’s health helpline 104, Tele-MANAS 14416, and Sneha’s suicide prevention helpline 044-24640050)

Merz stresses urgency of getting political agreement on EU budget
Finally, Merz gets another question on the next EU budget and competing interests, claims and demands from various countries, including from Marine le Pen, who leads the polls ahead of next year’s presidential elections in France.
Merz says it has been a good practice to agree the financial deal “roughly a year before” it kicks in, and says this time is needed to prepare its implementation at the technical level – more so than political discussions linked to various elections.
Aaaand with that, he’s gone.
He is off to Bonn next I think, where he is expected to attend a big meeting of the youth arm of his CDU party as he continues to face domestic criticism over his style of governance.
Merz gets asked if he had any words of advice for Zelenskyy.
He says he wouldn’t offer any advice publicly as the two talk regularly to each other.
He says he is aware that the Americans have other interests as well, but the Russian invasion on Ukraine is “an assault on the political order across all of Europe.”
He also takes note of Russia’s own actions to place European companies in Russia under state-mandated administration, and says the government will examine these cases closely.
But he says the leaders also discuss a further restrictions on “a very large number of visas still being issued to Russian citizens travelling to the EU.”
“There is certainly room for us to restrict this type of travel … If Russia chooses to respond, we will be ready with a reply,” he says.
He also gets a question on migration, and he says this discussion is still ongoing – but reveals that other leaders, including the Greek PM, noted “enormous progress” made in recent years.
Back to the question of further financial support to Ukraine, he says no decision has been made on the form in which this could be offered.
Merz backs Ukraine's strikes on Russia's communications, energy infrastructure in response to attacks
Merz gets asked about the fallout between Zelenskyy and Trump, and what can be done about it.
He says he is in regular contact with Trump by phone, and will see him in person “by December at the latest.”
But focuses on saying that he sees “no willingness on the Russian side to end this war,” with all indications actually going in the opposite direction as “the escalation continues.”
“Against this backdrop, I believe it is appropriate, logical, and understandable for Ukraine to strike targets within Russia that hinder the war effort of the Russian government and the Russian army – including both communication and energy supply systems.”
He says that’s “the only means Ukraine has to signal to Russia that it is prepared to defend itself.”
'Broad consensus' to keep supporting Ukraine, but details on funding yet to be agreed, Merz says
Germany’s Merz gets asked about the discussion with Zelenskyy and his request for more money for Ukraine.
He says it was more of a discussion with no formal decisions, but says “we are all very concerned about the situation in Ukraine.”
He says there is “a broad consensus” to keep supporting Ukraine “through the winter and into the coming year,” with the commission “assessing the financial requirements,” acknowledging the €90bn loan from last year may not be enough.
He says further discussions on this are expected in November and December.
'Significant differences' on EU budget, but broad support for new trade instrument, new proposals for automotive industry, Merz says
German chancellor Friedrich Merz is the first national leader to leave the room, and he’s now briefing reporters on today’s talks.
He begins by saying the talks are “not quite finished yet,” but gives a bit of a readout from the discussions.
He says the leaders discussed the issue dear to his heart, namely how to improve the bloc’s competitiveness, and agreed that “only an economically strong and sovereign Europe can hold its own in today’s world.”
He says the leaders will meet to discuss in again in early February.
He also says there was “unanimous, unequivocal” support for a proposal put forward by Macron and Merz on trade policy, with a new instrument to “allow for rapid response” to any imbalances (as covered on the blog on Wednesday).
On the EU budget, he says there are “significant differences” in how countries look at this issue, as “a smaller group” calls for the budget to be reduced, and “a larger group” want it to be expanded further.
“We are all facing the need for substantial fiscal consolidation at home; it is simply not tenable for the European budget to increase by around 50% during the same period,” Merz says.
He says there will be likely an extra council in November with a “multi-day session” in December to discuss this further. He hopes for a deal before the end of the year, but is not sure if that’s going to happen.
Merz also welcomes a new German-French deal on the future policy on automotive industry, concerning certain technologies and climate targets.
“To put it simply: the phaseout of internal combustion engines is now off the table. We are receiving a great deal of support for this,” he says.
The focus is on “technology neutrality,” he says, adding that Italy is “largely in agreement” with the proposals, too.
“This now needs to be integrated into the formal legislative process, but I believe we will be able to reach a final decision at the European level quite quickly. If the European Parliament follows this path, then we will have solved this major problem together,” he says.
EU talks move on from Ukraine to migration and Ceuta
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
EU leaders have finished their talks on Ukraine and hybrid threats in Europe in the last half hour, according to an EU source. They now move to the topic of migration, where sudden influx of arrivals in Ceuta is likely to be in focus.
“And we need at least €70 bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount.”
The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.
The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.
Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan went wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.
“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war.”
The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s failed frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.
Ahead of the summit Belgium’s prime minister Bart De Wever said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say, thank you for the 90 billion, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.
De Wever said:
“So are you, as a European family, still willing, ready and able to put your money where your mouths are and support Ukraine and keep Ukrainian society and Ukrainian defence up and running?”
Zelenskyy warns against Putin using energy to 'tempt the world into looking the other way'
The full text of Zelenskyy’s address, released by his office, also includes some further interesting nuggets.
Describing Putin’s Russia as an existential long-term threat to Europe, he explained:
“Some of today’s European leaders, some of today’s people running in elections and taking part in politics in your countries were still at school when Putin was already waging war. And even back when Bill Clinton was still President of the United States, Putin was already waging war. Against the Chechens. And that war taught Putin a lesson.
If he uses oil and gas to tempt the world, many politicians look the other way – even when cities are turned to rubble and villages are burned to the ground. That is exactly how Putin has been running things ever since. And he always has some “excuse” for why he can’t live in peace with one country or another.”
He also tried to set out a pan-European logic for fighting Putin, saying:
“That is why the EU – and your unity, and every truly independent European country – is a target for him.
Not because you are doing something wrong. Not because someone once offended Russia or failed to give Putin something he wanted. Putin only gets along with those who want to wage wars themselves and have no respect for human life. If he wins, everything that holds you together and keeps your people living in peace will simply be gone. Look at what he has been saying all these years. He has a problem with everything that happened after 1985. We don’t want to go back there.
It’s important that people understand this across the whole European Union – from Poland and Finland and all the Nordic countries to France, Spain, and Italy.
We may argue and disagree on politics. Sometimes we have serious disagreements over decisions. And that’s normal for democracies – I’m sure.
Despite all our differences, we all want the same thing – a security system that really works and can deal with today’s threats.”
There is also a nice touch as Zelenskyy paid tribute to Italy’s Giorgia Meloni – although she is not mentioned by name – after she delivered a rousing speech in the Italian parliament, explicitly warning about Russia.
Speaking in the Senate on Wednesday, Meloni said:
“If Ukraine stopped defending itself tomorrow, as many are hoping and proposing, we would not have peace. We would be discussing the occupation of a European nation and the return of the Soviet-style imperialism that Europe has known for half a century.
Personally, I don’t miss those years. I don’t miss the Russian tanks that repressed the uprisings in Prague and Budapest. I don’t miss the Berlin Wall.”
Zelenskyy responded to that in his speech:
“I am grateful to every one of you who does not miss the tanks that crushed the uprisings in Prague and Budapest – or the Berlin Wall.”
You may think it’s a small detail, but be in no doubt: everyone in that room knew what he referred to.
“Unity in defence is always built by many, many standing together, and without a determined European Union capable of making strong decisions, Putin would have gone much further by now.
The European Union has not fallen apart, and it has not backed down or given in to fear when it came to defending the European way of life, and that mattered just as much as the courage of Ukrainians.”
… before turning to the most controversial issue of Ukraine’s relations with the US under Trump, and seemingly making a direct reference to the upcoming midterm elections in the US.
“I am grateful to all of you who are trying to keep Europe and the United States together. There are so many people with good hearts in America who sincerely want evil to lose and Ukraine to stand strong, and these are the very hearts that helped Europe defend its freedom and that fought on D-Day, won the Cold War and won want is best for Europe, Hearts that want to be allies, not to divide or humiliate Europe, and I believe most Americans still feel this way.
And at the end of the day, the American people will have their say.
Putin will listen to America if America really turns up the heat on him and makes one thing clear: either he chooses peace or he gets no more money for his war.”
Zelenskyy also specifically criticised the US-Russia diesel deal once again, warning that lifting any sanctions anywhere will create incentives for Russia to try and get them removed elsewhere – just as what is needed is exactly the opposite.
“We warned that if sanctions are eased … anywhere in Europe, others will quickly … take advantage of it, and now we can see how cash will start flowing back into Russia through the diesel deal.
This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets, but it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.
And we need a strong 22nd package, EU sanctions package, please. And please, we need real sanctions against every company and every person involved in making Russian ballistic missiles, advanced communications systems, and drones, and those involved in Russia’s financial system.”
He also laid bare Ukraine’s pressing financial needs, asking for this issue to be included in planning for the EU’s next budget:
“The war will cost 155 billion euros next year, and we need at least 70 billion euros more from you for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic, yeah, a realistic amount.
And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.
And there are some very simple facts. We stop most Russian assaults on the frontline thanks to drones, and we cut Russian supply lines with these technologies. Our drones are helping to weaken Russia’s economy.
Right now, we could produce two or three times more drones, depending on the type. But we simply, simply, don’t have enough money for that. It’s true. Just imagine if we could put two or three times more pressure on Russia than we do today.
We believe this war will be over as soon as possible, but Putin plans to stick around much longer.
He is building a Russia that looks like North Korea, where children are raised from an early age for war and to die for their leader.
So Russia will not stop being dangerous, and it’s our Ukrainian strength, our army, our technology that help guarantee also European security, your security.
These security guarantees are not yet reflected as we think in your budget from 2028 onward. So let’s get serious about it. Let’s work out exactly how Ukraine’s defence capabilities should be included in that budget.”
Putin 'wants to destroy us' as he questions Ukraine's 'existence,' Zelenskyy warns
Asked again if he’s feeling some pressure among European leaders or fearing potential changes in European politics with big elections coming up next year, he says that he “feels full support from Europe now.”
“Europe is very united and it’s cognisant of all of the risks,” he says.
He says the war clearly shows “major risks for Europe” as he recalls recent incidents in Bulgaria, Germany, Poland, Romania.
“Europe understands as long as Ukraine stands, there will be fewer escalation with Russia,” he says.
He says Russia’s demands are not about Donbas or any part of its territory, but about “our country’s existence.”
“We’re now standing and fighting. What’s the alternative? Annihilation.”
He says Putin “wants to destroy us,” and “does not respect our sovereignty and territorial integrity.”
“So you really trust that he needs only a part of our country?”
He also warns that any further progress in Ukraine could also trigger a wave of Ukrainian migrants in Europe.
Zelenskyy says that he often hears from Trump that he just wants to “stop the killings.”
“Yes, [but] Russia is killing us, on our territory. They came on our land and further pushing further. They don’t want to stop. They even don’t want to freeze [the conflict], as you see. And what will be after that? On what borders will he [stop]?”
Visibly frustrated, he says that more than 1,000 drones were sent to Ukraine yesterday, but the American side “said that it’s difficult to speak with Zelenskyy.”
'I’m only standing up for Ukraine’s interests,' Zelenskyy says after Trump's comments comparing him with Putin
Zelenskyy gets asked about Trump’s comments that he is more difficult to deal with than Putin (11:09).
He says that in his meetings with Trump he always found topics for discussion and decisions.
“I’m only standing up for Ukraine’s interests,” he says, responding to Russian attacks.
“And no matter how Russia would like to limit all of our rights, it’s clear that we do have a right to defend ourselves.”
He says Putin “does not seek negotiations in any format,” but only “playing these games of words.” “He does not want the war to end,” he says, saying Putin’s actions are a “parody” of efforts to end the war.
He says that’s why he cannot accept any diesel deals with the US, because they will then be followed by gas agreements or other attempts to lift sanctions on Russia or its frozen assets, banking system, chemical industry, certain Russian individuals.
“If I don’t stand up to this, if I don’t defend it, who else will do this diplomatically?”
Zelenskyy says he heard 'only support' from EU leaders despite his clash with Trump over diesel deal
Zelenskyy gets asked if he heard any criticism from fellow leaders to his response to the US deal with Russia on diesel.
He says he “heard … only support,” and he is “grateful to them for this.”
He says the diesel deal caught Ukraine by surprise, and he believes Ukraine “should be aware of these things.”
He says despite all of that Ukraine is ready to support an energy ceasefire, but “it all depends on Russia and they do not want it.”
“And if there is no energy ceasefire, give us anti-ballistic missiles so that I can protect my energy facilities – … not too many, but for the period … of the diesel deal.”
He says Ukrainian negotiators are in touch with their US counterparts, and “in the coming days, they will arrange a meeting at a certain level,” and they will keep discussing it.

Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez apologised on Thursday for criticising the club’s hierarchy following its Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid, after holding talks with manager Michael Carrick and senior officials.
Martinez met with Carrick and club executives after training, two days after saying the club needed greater investment to help the team compete at the highest level following Tuesday’s 2-0 loss.
“Today I met with the club’s leadership and the manager,” Martinez said in an Instagram post, in his second statement since the interview.
“It was a very positive conversation where we were able to exchange views and speak openly about what happened after Tuesday’s game.”
A club source said that any internal disciplinary action would remain private, adding that it had been Martinez’ decision to apologise publicly and that all parties considered the matter closed.
Martinez acknowledged that his frustration following the defeat had got the better of him and apologised for choosing the wrong moment to air his feelings.
“Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity,” he said.
“The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise.”
The Argentina international had singled out director of football Jason Wilcox in the post-game interview, saying United needed more signings to compete with its rivals and build a squad capable of challenging in Europe.
Martinez said his comments had not reflected the unity required at Old Trafford and stressed his belief that everyone at the club was working towards the same goal.
“Our club is at its best when we are all united, and I recognise that my words in that moment did not come up with that,” he said.
“I know that every single person at Manchester United is doing everything possible to achieve our shared ambition, bringing the success that this club and its supporters deserve.”
Martinez finished his statement by drawing a line under the episode.
“With this situation now behind us, we are fully focused on winning together.”
United is 13th in the Premier League after six games in its worst start in 40 years. It travels to seventh-placed Leeds United on Sunday.

I was reporting on the ground near Connaught Place, close to Rajiv Chowk metro station, when Delhi Police detained me and several other journalists at around 11:20 am on October 10, 2026.
Delhi Police and central security forces had cordoned off the area around Jantar Mantar, preventing protesters and journalists from approaching the designated protest site. I was filming the police action and speaking to people present at the scene when officers began pushing and shoving individuals standing at the intersection of Connaught Place and Kharak Singh Marg. Several people were holding placards to express their dissent when police arrived and began detaining them.
While I filmed the detentions, one officer thrust his hand towards me and attempted to grab me. I showed him my press card. He backed off but continued gesturing aggressively. On camera, I asked him what legal guideline or constitutional provision allowed him to detain or attempt to assault a journalist on duty. He became enraged, and a heated exchange followed. The police then detained several journalists, including me.
We were shoved into a bus and driven across the national capital. When we repeatedly asked the officers which legal procedure they were following to detain us, they did not respond. They also refused to tell us where we were being taken.
The journey lasted around two hours. We travelled along Deen Dayal Upadhyay Marg, crossed the Yamuna, passed Shahdara flyover and Burari, and eventually reached the Delhi-Karnal highway. We became increasingly concerned about our destination. At 8 am, when I had begun reporting on the ground, I had noticed several police vehicles bearing HR and UP number plates. Our apprehensions grew as the bus continued along the Karnal expressway for another 20 minutes or so.
During the two-hour journey from Connaught Place towards neighbouring Haryana, we were not provided with sufficient drinking water or other basic necessities in the scorching heat. We managed to get some water only when a truck driver passed his bottle through the bus window. However, packed food, including bananas, biscuits and kachori, were already available on the bus.
Around 2 pm, we arrived at Rajiv Gandhi Stadium in Bawana, Delhi, approximately 65 km from Connaught Place. The stadium had been converted into a detention centre, where around 100 people detained from different parts of Delhi were being held.
I began documenting the situation inside the detention centre, speaking to detainees and trying to understand the circumstances in an area that had been without internet connectivity since the previous night.
A Cockroach Janta Party coordinator, reportedly picked up from his residence in Burari around 3 am on October 10, described his experience to me. “No food, no proper water, and a contingent of police officials who were not cooperating with anything since I was detained,” he said.
The stadium, usually filled with the sounds of athletes and cheering fans, now echoed with protesters’ slogans. “Vote Chor, Gaddi Chor” (The vote thief needs to resign) rang out across the premises.
A few minutes later, another bus brought in a group of protesters. They alleged that the police had shoved them into the bus and assaulted them. Despite this, they continued raising slogans against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the BJP-led Union government. Those detained included supporters and activists of the Muslim Students’ Federation (MSF), the All India Students’ Federation (AISF), the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), and leaders of the Communist Party of India (Marxist).
CPI(M) leaders Sujan Chakraborty and Manik Sarkar, the former chief minister of Tripura, were also at the detention centre, along with several other leaders from across the country. Sudip Dutta, general secretary of the Centre for Indian Trade Unions (CITU), a prominent national trade union affiliated with the CPI(M), had also been detained and brought to the stadium.
I spoke to a student from Delhi about how they intended to pursue their demands. Aman, an AISF member, said voter deletions and irregularities in Form 6 could affect future generations of voters.
“See, this issue of voter deletions is going to impact the upcoming generations who are going to vote tomorrow. As college students, it is our responsibility to make our peers aware about these issues. After today, we would hit the classrooms, reach out to our friends and make them aware of how this issue of ‘vote Chori’ that has come to light is going to impact them and the generations to come,” he said.
Another student, Ali, spoke about police brutality and the use of central security personnel to curb the right to protest.
“We were picked up from Minto Road. The police had barricaded the entire area. Around ten police officers were charging at a single protester, and dragging them to the police van. CRPF, BSP, ITBP, CISF, and even Uttar Pradesh Police are on duty. Why is the government acting like this to curb the voices of the students,” he said.
I spent another hour documenting events at Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, where protesters continued raising slogans despite being detained. Around 3:30 pm, after repeated negotiations with police officers, I was released along with another journalist.
As we left the premises, we were asked to provide our personal details. When we identified ourselves as journalists, several officers appeared astonished and initially thought we were lying. They believed us only after we showed our press cards.
The exchange lasted around ten minutes. It became clear that the officers at the detention centre had received no instructions or communication informing them that journalists were also being detained.
During the four to five hours I spent under detention, the same ort of resentment came up in every conversation: Allegations, an investigation and protests against Gyanesh Kumar had prompted the Union government to take preventive measures in the name of maintaining law and order. These measures were so extensive that people seeking reforms to Indian democracy were being detained. The scale of the restrictions was equally alarming.
Metro services, railway stations, roads and shops in parts of Delhi were directed to be shut down, affecting daily commuters, roadside hawkers and shopkeepers. Internet services were also suspended within a four-kilometre radius of the Janpath-Kartavya Path area and in and around makeshift detention centres across Delhi. Internet connectivity was suspended in the area surrounding Rajiv Gandhi Stadium as well.
A shopkeeper in Bawana, near the stadium, told me that the internet shutdown had caused significant losses because customers could not make online payments. The preventive measures affected not only protesters but also ordinary people, disrupting the lives of commuters, daily-wage labourers, shopkeepers, railway platform-based workers, auto drivers and others going about their daily routines.
Why was Delhi being subjected to what resembled a state of emergency?
Article 19(1) of the Indian Constitution guarantees individuals the right to express their opinions and protest, subject to the applicable constitutional restrictions and the rights of others. The government can also take measures to maintain law and order. But how far can such measures legally and constitutionally extend?
I continued to think about these questions as I travelled to Samaypur Badli metro station, approximately 17 km from the detention centre. The 30-minute journey offered no concrete answers.

Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
- Published
Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades.
Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too.
So what is happening?
How big and unusual are these protests?
Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë and Vlora in the west, Gjirokastër in the south and Korçë in the east.
The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.
Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.
Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.
Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.
Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.
A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.
Every evening, throughout the summer for some 135 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign.
The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead.
The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder.
One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue.
- Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania 
  - Published1 day ago
- Kushner-backed luxury resort plan sparks protests in Albania 
  - Published4 June
So has the Flamingo movement radicalised?
The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.
They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.
But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.
The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.
Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.
Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."
Another called Brunela told the BBC's What in the World programme she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."
An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.
After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.
How is the government handling the unrest?
Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.
"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.
The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".
Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.
But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.
So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.
On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.
Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.
Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.
"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."
Is Albania safe to visit?
Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being.
The UK government has urged visitors to check media, external for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities.
Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path.

Delhi HC allows activist Natasha Narwal to travel to UK for academic work
The Delhi high court has allowed Natasha Narwal, an accused in the 2020 Delhi riots conspiracy case, to travel to the UK from November 2 to December 1 for academic work.
The Delhi high court on Friday allowed activist Natasha Narwal, an accused in the larger conspiracy case relating to the 2020 Delhi riots, to travel to the United Kingdom from November 2 to December 1 for an academic conference and research work, observing that the right to travel abroad cannot be curtailed under Article 21 of the Constitution.
A bench of Justice Amit Bansal allowed Narwal to travel subject to furnishing a personal bond of ₹1 lakh, with her brother, who resides in Haryana, standing as surety.
“We cannot restrict the right to travel under Article 21. Your hands are not tied, you are the government of India. The trial will take 20 years. You cannot keep the person here. It is a renowned university and she wants to travel for academic pursuits,” the bench remarked.
The court directed Narwal and her brother to furnish an undertaking before the trial court that she would return to India and would not seek asylum in the UK. She was also directed not to make any public statements on the merits of the pending case during her stay in the UK and to surrender her passport before the trial court within 48 hours of returning to India.
The court took note of a letter from Narwal’s supervisor stating that her physical presence was required for supervisory meetings, presentations of her research work before academic staff and researchers, and participation in doctoral training on campus.
Narwal had approached the high court challenging the trial court’s October 6 order denying her permission to travel abroad. While rejecting her plea, the trial court had noted that the case was at the stage of consideration of charges and that the offences under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) for which she had been chargesheeted carried punishments ranging up to life imprisonment and, in some cases, the death penalty.
It had observed that the right to travel abroad was not absolute and that the pendency of proceedings under the UAPA was a relevant consideration.
Opposing the plea, Additional Solicitor General SV Raju, appearing for the Delhi Police, argued that the UK’s stringent extradition laws could make it difficult to secure Narwal’s return if she failed to come back to India. Raju further submitted that, according to an email from the university, a co-author could present the academic paper in her absence. He argued that Narwal’s physical presence was not necessary, pointing out that she had been pursuing her course virtually for the past three years.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia leaving her role a week after starting it: official
U.S. President Trump said Zacharia was 'brutalized by the media' during her first week
U.S. President Donald Trump's press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her role a mere week after he put her in it, a White House official confirmed to CBC News.
The news broke on Friday, shortly after Trump signalled to reporters that Zacharia may be on her way out.
Trump said he'd spoken to Zacharia and that he felt she didn’t deserve what he called negative media coverage.
"I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy,'" Trump said while speaking to reporters on the White House lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia.
"I want her to have a good life. I don't want her to have a life like she's led the last three days," Trump said.
Trump added, "I said, 'Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this.'"
The president initially said he'd make a final determination later — perhaps after his campaign travel.
"When I get back, we're going to talk," he said.
Trump also said, "I told Katie, in my opinion, she was treated very unfairly," Trump said, noting that Zacharia has been "brutalized by the media."
Anthony Scaramucci, a former White House communications director who served for a short time in Trump's first presidency, posted a note of support that was addressed to Zacharia on social media.
"Speaking as the world's leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family," he said in a post on X.
"In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favour."
Zacharia's short tenure has been defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists.
She was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9. She was the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump’s inner circle for years.
Zacharia came under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments.
She took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes.
Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand.
She later travelled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings.
In an appearance on Fox News Channel earlier Friday, Zacharia was asked if she had the president's confidence and responded: "I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me." But she also wouldn't say when her next press briefing might be.
Questions about why Zacharia called herself a lawyer
Zacharia, a Pepperdine University law graduate, also faced criticism for describing herself as a lawyer when appearing as a commentator on conservative television outlets. Zacharia said the term was a proper one to use when she was offering legal analysis, and said she had worked as a lawyer in China.
Zacharia said Friday on Fox News that she wasn't asked about passing the bar before becoming press secretary, and Trump noted in his subsequent comments that she was hired as a spokesperson for the White House, not as an attorney.
Before joining the White House, Zacharia had been working in communications for Trump Media, the company that oversees the president's social media site, Truth Social. She also briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security during the second Trump administration.

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

Centre seeks Punjab govt report on activist Jhota’s murder, measures to prevent drug trafficking
The MHA has called for the implementation of key measures to support the national goal of a drug-free India.
The Centre has sought a report from the Punjab government on the killing of anti-drug activist Parwinder Singh, alias Jhota, and the steps taken to strengthen the state's anti-narcotics operations.
The Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has asked the state government to submit a detailed account of the October 13 killing in Mansa, PTI reported. It has also sought details of measures taken to combat drug trafficking and substance abuse.
The MHA has called for the implementation of key measures to support the national goal of a drug-free India. These include setting up a dedicated Anti-Narcotics Task Force (ANTF), conducting financial investigations in drug-related cases and strengthening prosecution under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act.
Deep Dive
The ministry has also stressed the need for better coordination through the Narco-Coordination Centre (NCORD) mechanism. Other priorities include designating special NDPS courts, appointing nodal officers and taking action against transnational drug networks.
How Parwinder Singh (Jhota) died
Jhota was shot dead in broad daylight in Mansa on October 13 during a confrontation at a medical store over the alleged sale of addictive substances. He had been campaigning against drug abuse and the alleged illegal sale of habit-forming medicines at chemist shops.
Jhota was known for confronting suspected sellers and recording videos of such encounters for social media, according to reports.
On the day of the incident, he and his associates allegedly confronted a medical store owner over the sale of addictive drugs. The confrontation reportedly turned violent, with the shop owner allegedly opening fire. Jhota was killed, while others were injured.
Protests, demand for CBI probe
The killing triggered protests in Mansa and other parts of Punjab. Jhota's family refused to cremate his body and demanded action against those responsible. His supporters and several farmer organisations also called for a statewide bandh on October 16.
Opposition parties and farmer groups backed demands for a Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe.
Punjab Congress president Pargat Singh and Congress MP Amrinder Singh Raja Warring criticised the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) government over the state's law-and-order situation and its handling of the drug menace.
Punjab BJP chief Kewal Singh Dhillon demanded a CBI probe into Jhota's killing, while Shiromani Akali Dal leader Bikram Singh Majithia called for the dissolution of the state government and the imposition of President's Rule.

A Mexican judge has sentenced three men to 158 years and nine months in prison each for the murder of two Australian brothers and their American friend during a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California.
The defendants were declared guilty a week ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence, crimes committed against Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their American friend Carter Rhoad.
Rhoad and the Robinsons were shot dead in a suspected robbery while travelling through Mexico.
They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on 27 April 2024.
Their bodies were found days later in a clifftop well with gunshot wounds to the heads.
Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons.
Two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were also found guilty and have been sentenced.
The families of the victims followed the sentencing hearing via video link.
Prosecutors had requested damages of more than $100,000 but the judge ruled against it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings.
The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.
They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy.
The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.
Callum, the older of the two brothers, moved to the US as a professional lacrosse player and has been remembered for his loving nature and passion for the environment, having been involved in coastal cleanups.
Jake, a doctor, was set to take up a position at Geelong hospital after returning to Australia.
He has been remembered for his academic success, his passion for sport, particularly cricket and surfing, and his compassion.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
- Published
An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class.
As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander ran inside. Armed with a .40-caliber pistol, he opened fire and killed the teen.
The bystander, a dad of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend when he saw the suspect firing in the car park then shooting through a window to enter.
The details of the Thursday attack were confirmed by police, who said the 16-year-old suspect was a prior student at the school.
Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.
"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday.
Police offered more information on the attack at at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there.
A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but police are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear.
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.
The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside.
Police said he had a legally concealed .40 caliber in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.
In a statement to the BBC's partner CBS News, Giamanco's family said he is a "lifelong resident of Bend" and that he "is not seeking recognition".
The family said Giamanco wants to express his "gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support". He and his family "respectfully ask for privacy".
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander's actions on Friday, calling him a "great hero".
Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.
Without naming the bystander, Governor Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".
