Kota (RJ) Oct 17: Around eight people were killed and 15 others injured -- eight of them critical -- after a minibus carrying around 23 passengers veered off the road and plunged into a 15-foot-deep drain along the Delhi-Mumbai Expressway in Rajasthan's Kota district at around 6 am on Saturday.
The accident occurred near pole number 384 on the Expressway. Authorities suspect the driver fell asleep at the wheel or felt drowsy, causing the vehicle to veer off the eight-lane road.
Emergency personnel immediately launched rescue operations. Mud and water accumulated inside the drain initially hampered their efforts, prompting authorities to deploy cranes to fish out the damaged vehicle and recover the individuals trapped inside.
Kota Rural Superintendent of Police Sujeet Shankar said most of the passengers belonged to extended families from Bhopal and Betul districts of Madhya Pradesh, and had set out on a four-to-five-day pilgrimage in Rajasthan. They began the journey from Bhopal on Friday evening, he said.
An injured passenger, Anshika, said she was travelling with her extended family, consisting of her uncles, aunts and other relatives. She said they departed from Bhopal at 7 pm on Friday and were headed for a darshan at Khatu Shyamji temple, when the accident happened.
There were around 23 passengers inside the vehicle, and most of them were asleep when the accident happened, Anshika said, adding that the driver must have dozed off.
The injured were rushed to the New Medical College Hospital (NMCH) and the MBS Hospital.
NMCH Principal Dr Nilesh Jain said treatment and required investigations, such as CT scans, were promptly initiated for the injured.
Dr Ashutosh Sharma, Superintendent of NMCH's Super Speciality Block Hospital, verified that the facility received 15 patients. Seven were brought dead, while eight others who were injured were immediately given primary stabilisation and comprehensive medical care, he said.
SP Sujeet Shankar said eight individuals lost their lives, while the rest of the passengers received medical treatment. Authorities are continuing to clear the site and verify details of the passengers, he said.

Penélope Cruz had been a muse to Los Javis — the moniker for Spanish filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo — for years before they met for lunch to persuade her to play a singer (more a force of nature, really) in La Bola Negra, an electrifying sensation at Cannes that’s now Spain’s entry for best international feature film Oscar.
“I saw her in a clip of Jamón Jamón,” says Ambrossi, referring to Bigas Luna’s 1992 picture, in which Cruz appeared for the first time opposite her now-husband Javier Bardem. “I was young, and I thought, ‘Who is she?!’ ”
Calvo was similarly enchanted when he saw Cruz in Pedro Almodóvar’s 1999 Oscar winner All About My Mother. “She’s got that material of the stars,” he says. “When you put a camera in front of her, she can do anything, and she doesn’t even realize what she’s doing. There’s a power, there’s a force guiding her, and that’s amazing to see first-hand.”
Watch on Deadline
Los Javis wanted Cruz for a small but pivotal role in their epic tale La Bola Negra, the intertwined story of three gay men who exist in three different time periods in Spain. In 1932, Carlos (Milo Quifes) is a young man in Grenada at a time when Spain is lurching uncomfortably towards an ever-increasing spiteful intolerance of homosexuality. In 1937, against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War, Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) and Rafael (Miguel Bernardeau) are soldiers from opposing political divides brought closer by the conflict. And in 2017, Alberto (Carlos González) is a playwright from Madrid who engages with an eminent Federico Garcia Lorca scholar (played by another Hollywood star, Glenn Close, speaking fluent Spanish) in a storyline that links the characters in the prior timelines.
RELATED: Netflix Unveils U.S. Market Rollout For ‘La Bola Negra’ Theatrical Release
Cruz’s character, one Nené Romero, performs for the troops in a series of beautifully choreographed, risqué numbers that the boys, far from home, lap up with hunger in their eyes. Los Javis say that Nené was inspired by La Fornarina, a cupletista, a Spanish singer of cuplé songs — bawdy numbers about “sex and drugs,” as Calvo explains it — who performed in theaters in Madrid around the turn of the last century.
Their research included the study of the erotic novels penned by Spanish writer and fashion designer Álvaro Retana, who also wrote lyrics for saucy songs of the type that Cruz performs in La Bola Negra. “They would be singing all over Madrid. They were so funny, they were unleashed — and they thought they were going to be free forever,” says Calvo when we meet in a suite at the swanky Corinthia Hotel during the London Film Festival. “But these singers and their gay friends, all the people in that circle, they were all incarcerated, persecuted, killed or disappeared. They’re forgotten, kind of. So we wanted to bring them back.”
Cruz was already a fan of Los Javis having been gripped by their outrageously captivating 2023 TV drama miniseries La Mesías, a hit for Moviestar+ in Spain, which is now available via Mubi in the UK, Canada Turkey, the Netherlands, Germany and Australia, and will soon be streaming in France. “They are so talented,” I recall an ecstatic Cruz telling me at the closing-night party in Cannes. “I saw their first television show Veneno as well,” she said, “and now they’ve won the directing prize at Cannes.”
The next time they work with Cruz, says Ambrossi, they plan to create “a whole film around her,” but that will be be after what they hope will be their next feature project, a movie that they claim will be “90% in English.” That movie, whenever it’s made, will likely have a larger budget than Los Javis spent on La Bola Negra. Ambrossi says that its roughly $15 million budget was tight but it’s “big for a Spanish movie.”
With time and the right people on La Bola Negra, Ambrossi adds, “we knew we could do it big. The scope is not always about big landscapes; it’s about how you position people, so you get the sense that it’s bigger, and taking the time to find the right locations, because these are all natural locations.“ They also insisted on making time for proper rehearsals before the 12-week shoot (“Because it’s a deep story and the actors needed time”).
Calvo explains that with the purse strings being so tight they had to find “creative solutions.” They didn’t, for example, have a room in which to shoot all the soldiers having dinner. “We’re like, “OK, then we’ll compose a beautiful shot with everyone outside with tables, and we’ll just imagine they went out to have dinner there,” he explains.
They also turned to “the godfathers of cinema,” as Calvo refers to such legendary directors as Thodōros Angelopoulos (Alexander the Great) and Andrei Tarkovsky (Solaris), who, “with just with a landscape, mist and composing the humans in a proper way” were able to conjure up scenes of movie magic.
Working with the sublime cinematographer Gris Jordana — a frequent collaborator, as are the film’s editor, production designer, hair and makeup designer, costume designer, composer, and many other key creatives — Los Javis sought to bring some of that “godfathers of cinema” magic to their own film. “They’re part of our team,” Amborossi says. “We have been growing together. In every project we learn together. So that’s why the movie is so big, even if the budget is not. They put a lot of effort because it’s a collective experience. It’s like they put in their souls.”
“This is a movie about poetry,” says Calvo, “and there’s also a poetry in images. You don’t have to show everything. You can give something, and the viewer will leave it to their imagination.”
Ambrosssi jumps in. “If you don’t have the money, just don’t do it badly,” he says. “Cut it, and someone can talk about it in the next scene. Sometimes we needed a natural beauty location. For example, we didn’t have an office for the general lieutenant featured in the film, so we found an empty space with a nice view — you can see the sea — and we composed it with people and a table and a small framed picture of Franco, and that was it. And that’s not expensive.”
The main point, Calvo believes — as the likes of David Lean found while directing Lawrence of Arabia — is that it was necessary to find intimacy within such an epic story.
Los Javis were helped in that endeavor, Calvo adds, because the film is loosely based on Alberto Conejero’s one-act play La Piedra Oscura, which deals only with the relationship between Rafael and Sebastian, a play that is “so intimate and delicate” that they wanted to expand it into a triptych. ”Like, a big movie,” says Calvo, spreading his arms wide, “and an intimate movie at the same time. You have the fragility and the the war, so it’s about contrast. And it was so nice to create that, because sometimes it’s more difficult to create the relationship of Rafael and Sebastian, with all the tension, than a bombing scene.”
Countless meetings with key creatives were held in pre-production to map out the movie, and the more mistakes they made the better, because it meant they’d go out and get it right during the shoot, says Ambrossi. “It’s like, work, work, work, work, make a mistake, then try again,” he says, smiling. The work, however, didn’t feel like work. ”I always go back and say, ‘Oh, wow, it was the journey of our lives,’” Calvo declares.
Ambrossi contends that the film is proudly gay, whether that puts it in a niche box or not; it’s “a gay movie” and “I love to keep it that way,” he says. “I want people to have an experience that is universal. But I don’t want them to miss that it’s gay.”
It’s certainly unusual to see a gay story against the backdrop of war. Calvo cites Tarkovsky’s classic Ivan’s Childhood, Elem Klimov’s harrowing Come and See and Francis Ford Coppola’s Apocalypse Now as being amongst his favorite war movies. “So, I have those references,” he says, “but my emotion is another thing, and my sensitivity is what we’re portraying. Why shouldn’t I make a movie the same way the people that made war movies I admire made, but telling my own story and using my own feelings? For me, it was natural to just talk about myself through my references. And why can’t we have it all?”
Ambrossi laughs. “It’s great that we told everyone it is a gay film with — mostly — gay actors portraying gay characters, directed by gay people about the queer experience, and it’s hitting the No. 1 spot at the box office every single night in Spain. I like that. I think it’s cool, because it really represents two things; one, that the world is going in a direction that we are not always aware, and also that the industry has to understand that gay stories are not niche.”
La Bola Negra is a starting point for the next conversation, Ambrosssi continues, and that “once we try, once we prove them wrong, then we can have the conversation about universal stories. But we had to tell them, ‘You don’t have to change the lead and put a straight star in it to get the audience.’ They just go, “Ah, it’s a gay story.’”
Were they pressured in any way to compromise? “They don’t even try to do it with us, because we write, direct and produce. It’s our movie,” Ambrossi responds with gusto. He allows, however, that they encountered difficulties making the 2020 miniseries Veneno. “It was a show with trans actresses, and everyone was like, ‘You won’t find that many trans actresses to put in a show in Spain.’ And we were like, ‘We’ll do it.’ And we did.”
During their travels promoting the movie — at Cannes (where Los Javis shared the best director prize with Fatherland’s Pawel Pawlikowski), Telluride, Toronto (where it won the People’s Choice Award for best film), San Sebastián (where the film was honored with the festival’s Audience Award) and here in London — the reaction has been overwhelmingly positive. “The feedback from non-gay people, non-LGBTQ people, is the same. This idea of wanting to be yourself, being rejected, a lot of women get that. It gets everyone. At some point, it’s about family, about motherhood, about brotherhood, about friendship. It’s a war movie. It’s about being different, but it’s about art and the power of art.”
Calvo, listening intently, jumps in, pointing out that the film is “about understanding and seeing the other as a human being. Which is, I think, important.”
xxx
When it came to casting the male leads, they chose singer-musician Guitarricadelafuente because they were drawn to the “magnetism, the sadness” in his eyes. “He had to be the eyes of the viewer,” says Calvo, “and he has eyes that you can rely on, and he had this shyness, but also this bravery, this strength, but then this subtleness. We just knew it was for him.”
Ambrossi, meanwhile, hails Bernardeau (Elite) as being “one of the best of his generation.” “We needed his technique,” he explains, “because Guitarricadelafuente is new, so we needed the balance to play off each other.” The same goes for González. “He’s so flamboyant and fun in real life,” Ambrossi says. “Here, he’s doing a job that you cannot imagine. If you were to meet him, you would be like, ‘Are you the same person?’”
Indeed, I spoke with González at a soirée following a special screening of La Bola Negra at Tate Modern, and he was an absolute hoot. He vowed to do anything for the film “with its big black balls.” My eyes widened at that remark and our dirty laughter nearly got us turned outta the party.
As for Carlos, they were looking for Andalusian guys, and the moment they saw Quifes’ audition, they shut down the search.
The roles played by Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau are the heart of the film, providing its most tender, heartfelt moments. They met for the first time at rehearsals, where Guitarricadelfuente, who’d never acted before, says he felt “100 percent safe” because he was working opposite a professional actor. “It was a very special moment meeting Miguel,” he says.
Having someone like Miguel “really helped me out in this in this journey,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “There was something very special about the way that our characters grew up together, and the development of that intimacy, that way of nonverbal communication, those gestures that communicated so much. I’m grateful for the time that we spent at that room rehearsing.”
Los Javis were “democratic with us,” he notes, because “they let us express ourselves freely, and if there was maybe sometimes in the dialogue something that maybe didn’t resound that much in ourselves, they would say, ‘What would you say? What would you do?’ They let us roll on and magical things happened.”
Were they able to improvise? Bernardeau shakes his head and notes that it wasn’t so much improvisation because of how much thought went into every scene, what with how the three stories intertwine. “You need to be careful with what you change. There’s a lot of detail, so you cannot improvise. But they were very free with us in changing smaller stuff. I did feel very free to try different ways and paths into the scenes.”
I remember covering the film’s ecstatic 20-minute ovation at Cannes in the Grand Théâtre Lumière and watching the faces of this new generation of filmmakers and actors. Bernardeau was holding back tears. “I knew that once I start crying I would not stop,” he admits.
In front of him, he recalls, was the festival’s camera team “and Tilda Swinton clapping and looking at us.” Swinton introduced Bernardeau to her agent Christian Hodell, chief executive of Hamilton Hodell, who now represents him. Now the actor will soon be moving from Spain to live in London.
Guitarricadelafuente remembers looking up to the Lumière’s second tier to see so many young people who’d clearly connected with the film: “That made me feel as if we were at a concert.” He notes that he’s been astonished by how audiences in Spain have flocked to see the picture. Los Javis were known to young people, he says. “Like, there are people in my family that haven’t been to the cinema in 10 years. They feel like they’re missing out on something, because there’s been like a consensus between everybody to see it. It’s not a film about civil war, it’s not a film about Lorca. It’s is a film about life.”
It sure is.
Culturally, Spain’s on a roll. Singer-songwriter Rosalía took the International Artist of the Year at the Brit Awards; La Bola Negra won a major prize at Cannes; and, of course, Spain won the World Cup. Calvo beams a full-wattage smile. “We’re just getting out there.”

During my years as a clinical pharmacist, I thought I understood why patients stopped taking long-term medications — one of the biggest challenges in medicine. They forgot to take them, became frustrated with side effects, or didn’t fully understand their conditions. But over time, my clinical experience showed me that these explanations only told part of the story.
I first noticed this pattern across very different medical specialties. In psychiatry, I saw patients with schizophrenia experience psychotic episodes after stopping their antipsychotics. Patients who abruptly discontinued their antidepressants often suffered withdrawal symptoms. Later, when I worked in a kidney transplant center, I encountered a surprisingly similar situation when patients stopped taking one or more of their immunosuppressants and developed acute rejection of their new kidneys. Colleagues in cardiology, primary care, and other specialties described similar experiences.
The patients’ initial explanations were often familiar. After longer conversations, however, especially when patients’ guilt and shame lessened, they gave other explanations. I started to realize that “I forgot” was sometimes an easier answer, both for the patient and for the health care professional.
Some people worried that they would become dependent on medication — not necessarily in the pharmacological sense, but because needing treatment every day felt like losing control over their own bodies. Others stopped medication temporarily to prove to themselves that they could still function without it. Research suggests that many factors leading people to discontinue treatment take root before the first dose, when they are still trying to understand what their illness and their medication will mean in their lives.
In mental health care, I encountered people who believed that medication changed who they were. They didn’t mean the common adverse effects, such as sleepiness or weight gain. They described something harder to define: a feeling of being disconnected from themselves, as if an important part of their personality had changed.
One case, in particular, stayed with me. He was a young man who had received a kidney transplant as a teenager. For years, he had taken his immunosuppressants correctly. At 23, he experienced his first episode of acute rejection.
His initial explanation seemed simple. He had traveled for work and said he had forgotten to bring his medications. Later, during an informal conversation as we walked through the hallways of the hospital, a different explanation emerged. His girlfriend was pregnant, and he told me he felt he needed to “become a man.”
At that moment, it became clear that the medication had taken on a meaning beyond its pharmacological function. For him, depending on a daily treatment seemed to conflict with the image of strength, autonomy, and responsibility that he associated with adulthood.
This conversation changed the way I understood adherence. Medication can become entangled with the way people see themselves, and the kind of people they believe they need to be.
Specifically, for men and younger patients, I noticed that needing a treatment could feel like admitting vulnerability, weakness, or limitation. And stopping it could become an attempt to regain a sense of control over the body and over one’s own life.
Only later did I find research that helped explain what I had been seeing in practice. Studies on medication adherence have shown that people’s beliefs about medicines influence whether they take them as prescribed, including how they weigh their perceived need for treatment against their concerns. A 2024 systematic review on illness identity added another layer to this picture, showing that the way people integrate chronic illness into their sense of self was associated with whether they could manage their health problems and how they adapted to treatment. Research on preventing nonadherence likewise suggests that these beliefs need to be recognized early, potentially before the first prescription is written.
These findings helped put words to something I had repeatedly observed in clinical practice. A patient can fully understand that a medication is necessary and still struggle with what taking it means. It can become a daily reminder that they are living with chronic illness, a symbol of dependence on something external to function, or a challenge to deeply held ideas about strength, control, and personal identity.
Perhaps the problem is partly in the questions we ask. When we ask only “Did you have side effects?” or “Did you forget a dose?”, we may receive answers that are true but incomplete. We need to create space for more difficult questions: What does this medication mean to you? How do you feel about needing it every day? Is there a part of you that resists the idea of depending on this treatment?
If we want to improve adherence to long-term treatments, we may need to change not only the answers we provide, but also the questions we ask. Explaining how a medication works will always be essential. But understanding what that medication has come to represent may be just as important.
Sometimes, the biggest barrier between a patient and their treatment is not pharmacology.
It is how they see themselves.
Marcela Gottschald is a Brazilian journalist and pharmacist based in Argentina.

At the EU-WHO Strategic Dialogue on Health between the European Commissioner for Health and Food Safety Stella Kyriakides and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, the European Commission (EC) and WHO agreed to enhance strategic cooperation in global health security and architecture. They will also cooperate on the implementation of major initiatives, such as the new European Union’s Global Health Strategy launched this week, the European Health Union and the WHO priorities for the 2022-2026 period.
The partners will mutually reinforce their work across areas of common interest, as called by the EU Global Health Strategy, to further bolster a strong multilateral system with the WHO at its core, powered by a strong EU.
Addressing together the challenge of global health security
Many significant elements of global health security will be under discussion in the coming two years. These include the currently ongoing negotiations of a future pandemic accord and of amended International Health regulations, shaping a permanent pandemics platform, top leadership engagement in global health issues, and financing global health.
The EC and WHO will coordinate closely throughout these discussions to shape an effective multilateral system that considers the lessons of the COVID-19 pandemic and provides comprehensive health security for citizens across the world.
“Our citizens expect a step change in global health security, and the new EU Global Health Strategy is our contribution to this process. Combatting health threats effectively requires a strong multilateral governance with a more effective, accountable, and sustainably financed WHO at the center and where the EU has a seat at the table. Reinforced strategic cooperation and alignment between the Commission and the WHO will be essential to deliver better health for all in a changing world.”, said Stella Kyriakides, Commissioner for Health and Food Safety.
Other areas of cooperation include cross-border threats to health and digital health. To ensure mutual reinforcement across areas of common interest, both sides will review all current joint projects and actions by May 2023 and identify further areas of collaboration and specific projects to support. Both parties will meet in June 2023 to take stock, define the lines of future joint work, and provide the political impetus as and when necessary.
“A healthier Europe is stronger and more prosperous Europe, and a stronger and more prosperous Europe is a stronger and more prosperous world. We look forward to scaling up our cooperation with the European Union in the years ahead for a healthier, safer and fairer world.”, said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General at the launch of the Strategy in Brussels.
Background
The new EU Global Health Strategy offers a framework for EU health policies leading up to 2030. It sets policy priorities and guiding principles to shape global health, and it identifies concrete lines of action. It outlines what the Commission will do and what it invites the 27 EU Member States to do, each strictly within their respective competences and institutional roles. The strategy builds on contributions received during a wide public consultation with a broad range of key stakeholders in Europe and beyond.

Bangkok – Inflation in the Asia-Pacific region may persist and worsen amid global uncertainty, Asian Development Bank (ADB) President Masato Kanda has warned.
“The global economy is facing unprecedented uncertainty,” Kanda, a former Japanese vice finance minister for international affairs, said in an interview.
Inflation in the Asia-Pacific region may “continue and even deteriorate further,” Kanda said, citing risk factors such as soaring energy prices stemming from turmoil in the Middle East, the worsening El Nino phenomenon and the increasing severity of natural disasters linked to climate change.
He is visiting Bangkok to attend ongoing 2026 annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group.
According to the ADB’s economic outlook, growth in emerging economies in the Asia-Pacific region is projected to slow to 5.0% in 2026 from 5.5% in 2025.
Given Asian countries’ heavy reliance on the Middle East for crude oil and natural gas supplies, the ADB has provided $5.6 billion in financial support.
“As world leaders are keenly aware of the importance of energy security, we have the opportunity to promote reforms, including strengthening resilience through regional cooperation,” Kanda said.
Rising long-term interest rates, mainly in developed economies, have increased repayment burdens for developing nations with large amounts of dollar-denominated debt, Kanda said.
“Developing nations are facing heightened inflation risks amid rising energy prices and transportation costs, as well as concerns over fiscal sustainability,” he added.
The ADB’s next annual meeting will be held in May next year in Nagoya.
That gathering “will be a very important opportunity for international cooperation at a time when the world is turning inward and societies within countries are becoming more divided,” Kanda said. He expressed hope that the meeting will encourage more Japanese companies to expand into Asia.
On Japan’s economic and fiscal management, Kanda said that maintaining a sound macroeconomic policy is extremely effective for any country. He added that such a policy is the “best weapon” against speculators.
He also said that a “timely interest rate adjustment” would help protect the Japanese economy.
Known as the “Mr. Yen of the Reiwa Era” for overseeing massive yen-buying foreign exchange interventions while serving as Japan’s vice finance minister for international affairs, Kanda assumed the post of ADB president in February 2025 after stepping down as the country’s top finance diplomat. He will begin his second term as head of the Manila-based multilateral development bank in November this year.

Gone are the days when South Indian films were watched only by those who understood the language. With the rise of the pan-India phenomenon, audiences are now willing to wake up before sunrise and catch 6:00 am or 7:00 am shows of major South releases, even if they don't understand a word of Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam or Kannada. Several of these films also feature Hindi film stars in significant roles or special appearances, further attracting audiences from the North. Moreover, thanks to the growing consumption of international content on OTT platforms, viewers have become accustomed to watching films and shows with subtitles. All these factors have encouraged audiences to experience South films in their original language rather than wait for the dubbed version.
Jailer 2 exposes the UGLY truth of pan-India cinema: Audiences wake up at 4:30 am for Rajinikanth, but theatres can’t even guarantee English subtitles!
However, for such moviegoers, watching a film in a cinema hall can still be a gamble. The reason is simple: the uncertainty over English subtitles!
This was one of the biggest talking points among moviegoers in North India who were eager to watch Rajinikanth's much-awaited Jailer 2 in its original Tamil version. This writer attended a screening of Street Fighter on Wednesday, October 14, a day before the release of Jailer 2. Interestingly, one discussion that dominated conversations among journalists at the screening was whether Jailer 2 would be released with English subtitles and, if so, which theatres would provide them. Even on social media, several people were seen asking where they could watch Jailer 2 with subtitles. One of them was filmmaker Navjot Gulati, known for Pooja Meri Jaan.
Anyone reading this if you have seen Jailer 2 in Movietime mumbai then please let me know if they have subtitles or not. @sunpictures #Jailer2 #Thalaivar
— Navjot Gulati (@Navjotalive) October 16, 2026
This writer watched the 6:05 am show of Jailer 2 on the day of its release at Mumbai's popular MovieTime Hub in Goregaon. Before the film began, the writer and his friends were desperately praying that the screening would have English subtitles. After all, the whole gang had woken up at 4:30 am to catch the show, and without subtitles, understanding the film would have been a challenge. It was only when the first dialogue was spoken and the English subtitles appeared simultaneously, that we heaved a collective sigh of relief!
Ticketing platforms like BookMyShow often indicate whether a particular show has English subtitles by displaying 'ENG' beneath the show timing. However, this information was missing for Jailer 2 at the time of booking. There have also been instances in the past when audiences have booked tickets for South films, only to discover that the screenings did not have subtitles.
One might argue that viewers can simply check with the theatre manager before the show begins. But for the first-day, first shows of such films, even the cinema staff may not have complete information about subtitle availability.
Exhibition expert Amit Dadhich explained, "Certain cinemas are non-2K or non-DCI. These cinemas definitely won't have subtitles. Examples of this are MovieMax in Andheri East, Gold Cinema in Malvani, Tilak in Dombivali, etc. But even in multiplexes, it is possible that not all screens are 2K. For instance, if your film is playing in Screen 2 and 3 in MovieTime Cubic Mall in Chembur, subtitles definitely won't be available as these screens are non-2K. Now you can't expect people to know all this."
He continued, "Ideally, BookMyShow and District should clearly mention which theatre and which show will have subtitles. The producers also need to step up. Agreed that for the producers of these South films, business coming from Mumbai is minuscule. However, it is still significant and videos of people enjoying and dancing in theatres in Mumbai for their films also get spread far and wide, ultimately benefiting the film. Hence, they should definitely look into it as a priority."
@sunpictures Not everyone has access to a good theatres nearby (With Subtitles) For many, national multiplex chains are the only option to watch a major release on the big screen. Keeping a film away from these cinemas means limiting audience choice over a business disagreement. #Jailer2
— amit dadhich (@amit12354) October 16, 2026
Interestingly, Amit Dadhich is one of the people behind a social media handle called Mumbai Subtitles Database, which has attracted followers on X from the film industry, including Anurag Kashyap, Milap Zaveri, Gulshan Devaiah, Raj-DK, Sanjay Gupta, Aditya Sarpotdar, Varun Grover, etc. Anurag Kashyap has even praised the page in an interview.
The team behind Mumbai Subtitles Database regularly contacts cinema halls to find out which South Indian films are being screened with English subtitles across the city. The information is then shared with moviegoers, helping them make an informed choice before booking their tickets. However, Amit admitted that collecting complete information for a film like Jailer 2 was particularly challenging.
He explained, "Jailer 2 has been released only in non-national chains. This means that it's not playing in PVR, Inox, Cinepolis and Miraj in the North market. It's easier to get the info on subtitles from the national multiplexes. Also, almost all their screens are often 2K. With Jailer 2, it became a struggle to get the information."
Ultimately, this is an issue that requires the entire film industry to work together. Producers, distributors and exhibitors need to ensure that accurate information about subtitle availability is communicated well in advance, while ticketing platforms such as BookMyShow and District should prominently display it against every show. The makers could also consider providing versions with English subtitles embedded directly into the film, ensuring that even cinemas with technical limitations can screen the film with subtitles.
After all, watching a Rajinikanth film in its original Tamil version, surrounded by hundreds of cheering, whistling and dancing fans, is an experience in itself. Audiences across India should be able to enjoy that experience regardless of whether they understand the language.
In an era when Indian cinema is proudly celebrating its pan-India reach, something as basic as English subtitles should not remain a matter of luck.

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.
Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.
The charity Reprieve says Manasif was tortured and coerced into signing a false confession and only met his state-appointed lawyer for the first time in 2022 – five years after his arrest.
Manasif’s death sentence has now reportedly been upheld by the Saudi supreme court, which was likely to be his last hope of avoiding execution.
His family have not spoken in public about the case and could face harassment or arrest if they do so. “There is nothing they can do now but wait,” said Duaa Dhainy, a consultant for Reprieve and the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights.
Saudi Arabia has seen what activists describe as a “horrifying” surge in executions under the rule of the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. Last year saw a record 356 people put to death in the country. Most of those executed are foreigners convicted of minor and non-violent drug crimes.
At least 17 people, who were children at the time of their alleged offences, have been executed in Saudi Arabia since 2015, according to Reprieve.
Saudi Arabia issued a royal decree abolishing the death penalty for children in 2020, stating that individuals would not be sentenced to death for crimes committed when they were minors.
However, it has since upheld the death penalty in a number of cases involving child defendants. In April, it executed Ali al-Subaiti, along with his uncle, Mustafa al-Subaiti, for non-lethal “terrorist” offences committed when he was 12 years old.
The UN’s independent human rights experts have previously expressed concerns about Manasif’s case. It said Saudi Arabia should immediately halt planned executions of people convicted of offences allegedly committed when they were under 18.
 
“They are using execution as a tool to show how powerful they are and how they can threaten anyone who does not follow their rules,” Dhainy said of the Saudi regime. “We think he should be treated as a minor and not sentenced to death as his charges relate to when he was under 18.”
Human Rights Watch said executing Manasif for a non-violent crime committed as a minor would be “an unconscionable new low”.

Desperate to clear toxic haze, Indonesia to douse its skies with dry ice
- Published
As toxic smog continues to billow from wildfires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands, authorities are looking at an experimental way to disperse the haze.
A trial on Thursday will see an aircraft scatter pellets of dry ice - solid carbon dioxide - in the air above South Sumatra province, one of the regions worst hit by the haze.
Indonesia is battling its most dire wildfire season in a decade, as an unusually strong El Niño has exacerbated drought conditions and made flames harder to put out.
Amid increasingly urgent efforts to clear the hazardous air, authorities in Indonesia and neighbouring Malaysia have turned to various weather modification methods.
These include cloud seeding, a technique that speeds up the natural process of water vapour condensing inside of clouds by dispersing compounds such as silver iodide to form ice crystals.
Authorities have been carrying out such operations for weeks.
But Thursday's dry ice trial is different.
Rather than interacting with clouds to trigger rain, the dry ice is meant to "break down" haze in the lower atmosphere "so that it can rise upward", said Dudung Abdurachman, the coordinating minister for political and security affairs.
"If this trial is successful, we will continue with other areas that are central to the haze, such as Central Kalimantan and its surroundings."
The trial will involve 1.5 tons of dry ice, according to authorities.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for agencies to step up efforts to extinguish the wildfires and mitigate the impact of toxic smog billowing from the hotspots.
New cloud seeding operations are also set to take place in Central Kalimantan - another haze-stricken area - on Thursday and Friday.
Meanwhile, firefighters on the ground are continuing to tackle out-of-control blazes and authorities have deployed dozens of helicopters to extinguish the wildfires - though these operations have at times been disrupted by poor visibility in the haze.
Residents across Kalimantan and South Sumatra are bearing the brunt of the toxic smog, with air in many cities turning a dusty amber.
Pollutants have also drifted across borders to neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia, raising public health concern as air quality scores soar to unhealthy levels.
In parts of Malaysia with particularly hazy air - including its capital Kuala Lumpur and the city of Johor Bahru, near Singapore - local authorities have conducted their own cloud seeding operations.
Last month, Indonesia granted permission for Malaysian agencies to enter its airspace for cloud seeding operations along the countries' shared border.
More than one million wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia this year, burning almost 900,000 hectares of land, according to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas.
Much of the public frustration is directed at agricultural companies that burn vegetation as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.
Indonesian police have named more than 200 individuals and nine companies as suspects in connection with the fires.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Saturday declared access to and use of the internet a fundamental right for every individual, including children, under Articles 21 and 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, observing that “The safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other.”The bench of Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice K Vinod Chandran also suggested that children’s online safety should be strengthened through measures such as a ‘child mode’ for social media accounts, rather than denying them access to the internet altogether, LiveLaw reported.A bench comprising Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice K Vinod Chandran made the observations while issuing directions to strengthen mechanisms for detecting and removing child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) from social media platforms and other online services.According to LiveLaw, the bench said: "..we have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. Our children, irrespective of their age enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing.
The safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other. Our children are entitled to both."Blanket restrictions are not the answerThe bench acknowledged that the internet, in its present form, poses safety risks to children. However, it said restricting children's access because online platforms had failed to detect and remove harmful material would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem.The court examined whether children should be completely shielded from the internet and social media in the interest of their safety. It noted that the right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas.Describing the internet as a marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information, the court said its value extended beyond the material available online to the opportunities it provided for learning, communication and access to information."For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information," the court observed.It also noted that the internet could be particularly important for children with special needs, for whom online platforms might be the only place to find companionship with others facing similar circumstances.
Building on earlier rulingsThe bench referred to the Supreme Court's 2020 judgment in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, which held that "the freedom of speech and expression and the freedom to carry on any trade or business through the medium of the internet is constitutionally protected as a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution."In that judgment, the court had refrained from expressing a view on whether the right to access the internet, by itself, constituted a fundamental right.The bench also referred to the 2025 judgment in Pragya Prasun & Ors. v. Union of India, in which the court recognised the right to digital access as a fundamental right under Article 21.

Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India’s election chief on Sunday, as a court ordered the release of the “cockroach” movement founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and two other senior leaders.
Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday, as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi.
Indian authorities on Saturday deployed a sweeping crackdown across Delhi and detained thousands of protesters as the youth “cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fuelled anger at the prime minister, Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Reuters reported police detained more than 2,000 people to thwart Saturday’s protest. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.
Most detained on the first day of protests were released on Saturday night, police said.
Opposition parties and critics of Modi’s government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters.
The UN human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said: “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled.” He urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
India’s foreign ministry said the UN’s approach was “selective” and its statement constituted “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
The protests are calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years.
Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party.
Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
The BJP and the commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The “cockroach” movement, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi’s education minister.
The CJP has called its protests against Kumar “Season 2” on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India’s election system was reformed.

The rapid rise of a former art dealer to Europe's hottest young manager
- Published
When Brighton lost at home to Crystal Palace in February, Fabian Hurzeler was booed by his own supporters and subjected to chants of "you're getting sacked in the morning".
"There are only two options," said the German after the 1-0 defeat by their fierce rivals left his team floundering 14th in the table with one win in 12 Premier League matches.
"Give up or keep pushing harder, and that's always the option I choose in my life."
Eight months on, Brighton are reaping the benefits of keeping faith with the man who became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in June 2024 at the age of 31.
Palace return to Amex Stadium on Sunday (14:00 BST kick-off) to face opponents who are third in the table after statement wins over defending champions Arsenal and Europa League winners Aston Villa.
Hurzeler's stock has rocketed after 11 wins in 18 top-flight games, a run that has propelled the Seagulls back into Europe and left fans - who shouted "you don't know what you're doing" at him just a few months ago - worried that he could be lured away.
Following last Saturday's win at Sunderland, there was chat on the post-match phone-ins that Hurzeler, rewarded with a new long-term contract before the end of last season and given £150m to spend on signings in the summer, could be a prime target for a big club looking for a manager.
"You learn more about yourself and the people around you when you are losing games," former Brighton striker Glenn Murray told BBC Sport in reference to last season's poor run.
"Hurzeler has come out the other side and the way he has got this group of players performing is exceptional."
Scott McCarthy, from the We Are Brighton fan site, said Hurzeler appeared to have lost the crowd to such a degree at one stage last season than even a few wins would not be enough to turn it around.
"He looked like a manager who was out of ideas," McCarthy told BBC Sport.
"Leaving the stadium after losing at home to Palace, the only conversation fans were having was: 'he has got to go'.
"It's totally different now. It's worked out phenomenally."
Will Brighton manage to keep hold of Hurzeler, who has gone from managing in Germany's fifth tier to reported interest, external from Manchester United?
- Hurzeler signs to 2029 as Brighton rival elite clubs 
  - Published7 May
'Wet behind ears' to Champions League?
The determination Hurzeler demonstrated in the face of anger from fans following last season's defeat by Palace has been evident throughout his 10-year coaching career.
In 2016, after one injury too many following spells in the reserves at Bayern Munich, Hoffenheim and 1860 Munich, the former midfielder gave up playing professionally to accept a player-manager role at German fifth-tier side Pipinsried at the age of 23.
It was the start of a coaching journey that has led to the Premier League.
To make ends meet at village club Pipinsried, which is about 30 miles from Munich, football-obsessed Hurzeler worked for an art dealer selling paintings to wealthy Bavarians.
In an interview with the Guardian, external in 2024, he revealed he was fired from that job because he was spending too much time watching games.
"If you want to sell something to a person, you have to try to convince them by doing something," he said when comparing selling pictures to managing Premier League players.
"And you can't go there and say: 'Look at this picture, it's an amazing picture'. You have to understand the needs and the wishes from the clients.
"That's a little bit similar to being a coach.
"The most important thing is to understand the person behind the player. What are his needs? What are his values? How is he educated? How was his past? Where does he get education?"
Hurzeler's obsession to succeed runs deep.
While managing St Pauli - who he left in 2024 to join Brighton after guiding the Hamburg club back to the Bundesliga following a 13-year absence, external - he was invited to Tottenham's training ground to watch Ange Postecoglou's side train.
Hurzeler - who was born in Houston, Texas, before moving to Germany at the age of two - asked so many questions that Postecoglou had to ask another member of his coaching staff to step in and take over.
He also picked up tips from Roberto de Zerbi at Brighton, a few months before replacing him after Kieran McKenna,, external who had been heavily linked with the job, opted to stay at newly promoted Ipswich.
Despite respectable back-to-back eighth-placed finishes, Hurzeler's time at Brighton has not been without its difficult moments.
In addition to fans calling for his dismissal last season, the Seagulls were thrashed 7-0 at Nottingham Forest in his first season in charge, while former Arsenal and England defender Martin Keown labelled Hurzeler "wet behind the ears", external on the BBC's Final Score following Brighton's 4-2 defeat at Chelsea in September 2024.
So what is the reason for the shift in fortunes since his own fans called for his dismissal?
"It's partly because Hurzeler went back to basics," adds McCarthy.
"He relied on an experienced core in the side to get out of the hole, which is testament to him because it shows his pragmatic side. You get managers who are wedded to their philosophy and won't change.
"Hurzeler realised what he was doing was not working and that it could cost him his job, so tried something else. You can now see this is a team more in his image, because they press insanely."
Will Hurzeler leave Brighton if another club comes for him, or stay and attempt to write his name in club folklore by qualifying for the Champions League?
"I personally don't think he will go," says McCarthy.
"The money would obviously be tempting but he is a very intelligent guy. He didn't become a Premier League manager at the age of 31 without having his head screwed on.
"Does he want to go to another club where he isn't going to get time? What has happened at Brighton has shown he needs two-and-a-half-years to build a squad."
Back in Pipinsried, Hurzeler's name is still revered - and he has not forgotten where his coaching journey began.
"Yes, he does enjoy coming back every now and then - to see if everything's in order," Sepp Ankner, their chief finance officer, told The Athletic, external in 2024.
"When he does, he talks to everybody. He's really retained that connection with Pipinsried."
But his rapid ascent means gilded surroundings might not be far away for Europe's hottest managerial property.

The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) has decided to suspend the Equestrian Federation of India (EFI) from December 1 over a prolonged governance crisis. This move shall bar Indian riders, officials, trainers and horses from participating in international competitions during the period of suspension.
In a letter dated October 15, addressed to members of EFI’s ad hoc committee, Lt. Col. (retd.) Sandeep Dewan and advocate Vidushpat Singhania, the FEI said its board had taken the decision at an online meeting on October 13.
“Further to the FEI Board online meeting of 13 October 2026, please kindly note that the FEI Board decided to suspend the Equestrian Federation of India, with the suspension taking effect on 1 December 2026,” the letter, a copy of which is in the possession of PTI, stated.
Explaining the reasons for the decision, the FEI said the dissolution of EFI’s executive committee by the Delhi High Court in February, combined with the absence of fresh elections, had resulted in a prolonged governance crisis.
“However, the dissolution by the High Court of Delhi in February 2026 of the Executive Committee of Equestrian Federation of India, whose elected tenure had expired in September 2023, coupled with the absence of elections to date to elect a new Executive Committee, has resulted in a prolonged governance and leadership irregularity that is no longer sustainable,” the letter said.
The FEI acknowledged the explanation submitted by the ad hoc committee on September 27 and said it appreciated the work undertaken by the panel since its establishment by the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) on March 27.

The international governing body noted that elections to the EFI executive committee were expected to take place by January 31, 2027, but made clear that the suspension would be reviewed only after the elections had been held and evaluated.
“The suspension will be reviewed once elections for the Executive Committee have been held and have been evaluated by the FEI,” the letter said.
The restrictions during the suspension are comprehensive and extend beyond the national federation itself.
“In accordance with Article 8.4 of the FEI Statutes, during the period of suspension, the Equestrian Federation of India may not attend or be represented at any session or meeting of any FEI body, nor may it organise international events,” the letter stated.
It added: “In addition, its members (including athletes, officials and trainers) and horses may not participate in international events organised by the FEI or any other National Federation, whether under the Indian flag or the FEI flag.”
The decision will disrupt India’s international equestrian participation until the governance issue is resolved and the FEI completes its evaluation of the electoral process.
The FEI has also highlighted the implications for Indian endurance trainers whose horses are registered with other national federations.
According to the letter, Indian endurance trainer Hari Singh Aam is registered with EFI. Horses trained by him but registered with other national federations will require a change of trainer to remain eligible to compete from December 1.
Citing Article 828.3 of the FEI Endurance Rules, the FEI said a horse whose registered trainer changes cannot participate in a competition for 14 days from the date the change is notified.
Any such change must therefore be notified by November 17 for the horses to remain eligible from December 1.

As Diablo Cody prepares to resurrect Megan Fox‘s teen succubus one more time, she’s adding a more human element to the demonic role.
While discussing the “imminent” sequel Jennifer’s Body 2, the Oscar-winning writer explained that the followup will “explore even more about why Jennifer is sympathetic and what she’s been through” after she was sacrificed in a satanic ritual in the 2009 horror comedy, which turned her into the boy-eating entity.
“Jennifer is a sympathetic character for me, before and after the transformation,” she explained on the Petticoat Revolution podcast. “I mean, she is very isolated, she’s very lonely, she’s very insecure. Everybody remembers Jennifer when she’s like, ‘I am a god,’ or when she’s at her most radiant and at her most powerful. But people forget about these moments in the movie where she’s like a shell of herself, she’s just exsanguinated almost. And to me, Megan played both of those sides of Jennifer so well.”
Cody continued, “And one fun thing—I can’t talk about it too much—but you know we’re doing a sequel to this movie, like imminently, and I felt like in the new movie, I was able to explore even more about why Jennifer is sympathetic and what she’s been through. And there is absolutely, to me, a loneliness and a poignancy to that character that people don’t always recognize.”
Watch on Deadline
Deadline previously confirmed that Cody is developing the sequel for 20th Century Studios, with the movie’s original director Karyn Kusama teasing that she’s “very excited to hear what comes” of the follow-up, for which Megan Fox and Amanda Seyfried have both expressed interest in returning.
“I know some of the bones of it, so I’m not going to give anything away, but it sounds fun and crazy like the first film,” Kusama told Deadline last year. “And I have no doubt that Diablo will do something absolutely incredible with it.”
	In Jennifer’s Body, Needy (Seyfried) is BFFs with the titular mean girl played by Fox, whose body becomes possessed by a succubus with a taste for teen boys after a botched sacrifice by a devil-worshipping boy band (led by Adam Brody).
This is how you do horror completely wrong at the completely right time.

'Onion cartel' in Philippines fined $28m for price shock
- Published
Filipino authorities say they have fined six companies 1.76 billion pesos ($27.9m; £21m) for forming an "onion cartel" that caused the price of the vegetable to skyrocket.
In 2022 the price of onions, a staple of Philippine kitchens, surged to a record 800 pesos per 1kg, surpassing the country's daily minimum wage and overtaking the price of meat.
The crisis put pressure on then newly-elected President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, who had promised to bring down surging food prices.
The Philippine Competition Commission (PCC) said Wednesday the fine against the companies, comprised of onion importers and storage and shipping firms, was the largest since its formation in 2016.
For months between late 2022 to early 2023, onions disappeared from restaurant menus and became the object of smuggling attempts.
The bulbous vegetable even became something of a status symbol, having been used on at least one occasion as a wedding bouquet.
Authorities approved the emergency import of onions and Marcos vowed to go after those behind the shortage, saying there were "Filipinos dying from starvation and poverty because of what they are doing".
The crisis ended as local bumper harvests entered the market later in 2023 and prices stabilised.
A parliamentary committee tasked to investigate the price crisis said a cartel was behind the "artificial" surge in onion prices.
The PCC said evidence retrieved during raids on the companies showed that the six firms had collectively controlled nearly 50% of all approved import clearances for onions in 2020 and 2021.
The companies were involved in an "illegal market allocation scheme in the importation, cold storage, and whole sale distribution", the commission said.
The hefty fine shows a "commitment to holding cartels accountable across all sectors of the economy and protecting consumers from the harmful effects of anti-competitive conduct", the PCC said.
The commission also said that offenders may also be criminally prosecuted by the Department of Justice.
