Tesla’s long-delayed Roadster finally made an entrance — by flying off a ramp.
At a livestreamed event Thursday night, the sports car climbed a curved ramp until it was upside down, launched into the air, flipped, and landed on its wheels, apparently aided by thrusters beneath the vehicle.
“Well, it worked,” Elon Musk said during the livestream.
Musk said Tesla and SpaceX engineers collaborated on the car, which uses high-pressure air and thrusters to lift itself off the ground. Tesla also showed a recorded demonstration in which the Roadster reached 60 mph in 0.81 seconds.
While the legality of such a device on public roads remains in question, the tech world is reacting to Musk's new creation with awe.
Here is what the leading voices in business and tech are saying about the new Roadster.
Jason Calacanis
Angel investor Jason Calacanis said in an X post that the videos of the flying car looked like "science fiction," and they're real, although they don't seem to be.
He seemed enthused by the demonstration, asking that while the car was only airborne for a couple of seconds, "what if it could keep you in the air for five minutes? Or ten? Or 30?"
Gene Munster
Gene Munster, the managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management and a longtime tech analyst, wrote his two takeaways from the Roadster event on X.
First, that "it was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers."
And the second, that it signaled Musk's ambition to merge his two publicly traded companies, SpaceX and Tesla.
John Carmack
John Carmack, the former CTO of Meta's virtual reality division, politely rejected the flying car.
"That demo involved a non trivial chance of embarrassing failure!" he wrote on X. 
He added, "I'm only going for the baseline model. At this point in my life, rocket bunny hops are out of my comfort zone."

The Liberty Bell, with its famous crack, hasn’t been rung in 180 years, but that hasn’t stopped scientists from pondering what the bell might have sounded like when tolling. In honor of the nation’s 250th anniversary, researchers at Penn State University have modeled its acoustic properties, drawing on data collected from one of the bell’s replicas. The work was first presented at a meeting of the Acoustical Society of America in Philadelphia earlier this year, followed by an article in Physics Today.
Historians aren’t sure when exactly the Liberty Bell acquired its distinctive crack, just that it occurred sometime between 1817 and 1846. An 1846 account in the Public Ledger described the ringing of the bell on February 23 that year and mentioned that the bell had developed a crack, which someone had attempted to fix by filing the sides down. But it didn’t work: The February 23 ringing extended the crack even more, so much so that “the old Independence Bell… now hangs in the great steeple irreparably cracked and forever dumb.” Nobody has heard it ring since.
This wasn’t the first time the bell had cracked; the rim cracked shortly after it arrived in Philadelphia in 1752, the very first time the clapper struck while testing the sound. It was recast by two local foundry workers, John Pass and John Stow, not once but twice, because the first recast produced a sound that one bystander likened to coal scuttles banging together.
The second recast’s sound was deemed acceptable, and the bell was typically used to summon the Assembly, among other purposes, until it fell into disuse after the American Revolutionary War. As for why the bell was so prone to cracking, a 1975 study of the bell’s chemical composition revealed that the metals used formed “an extremely brittle alloy” that also made it easier for souvenir collectors to chip off pieces from the rim.

Istanbul's worst floods in 80 years leave 4 dead
Turkey’s interior minister says catastrophic flooding in Istanbul has been the worst in more than 80 years as the death toll rises
ISTANBUL -- Catastrophic flooding in Istanbul was the worst in more than 80 years, Turkey’s interior minister said Friday as the death toll rose to four.
Istanbul, Turkey’s largest city with 16 million residents, was hit by more rain in the 48 hours up to Thursday morning than the combined historical average for September and October, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.
“We are trying our best to help our citizens, but we are also experiencing the biggest flood disaster since 1942,” Mustafa Ciftci said during a visit to one of the areas hit hardest by Wednesday night’s downpour.
The body of a 66-year-old man was found Friday under a bridge in Istanbul’s Sariyer district. Three other deaths were previously reported, including a teenager who was electrocuted in the storm.
Homes and businesses were flooded as water covered streets and parks across the city. Vehicles were washed away and many ended up piled up at the bottom of hills.
Before the discovery of the body on Friday, Ciftci told reporters in Sariyer’s Ayazaga neighborhood that four people remained missing.
He said there were 9,850 reports of damage and other issues related to the floods and that 46,000 personnel were working to clean up debris and help residents in Istanbul.
Murat Kurum, the minister for the environment, urbanization and climate change, accompanied Ciftci to the flood-hit neighborhood.
Addressing concerns that the floods were exacerbated by urban development close to waterways, he said that dealing with the problem was “essential.”
Kurum, who will chair the U.N. climate change conference, COP31, next month in the Turkish city of Antalya, also linked the floods to the effects of climate change. “Combating climate change is not a choice, but a necessity,” he said.

Feel-good Koumas story something for Liverpool to smile about
- Published
The first player to celebrate with Lewis Koumas in front of the travelling supporters in Linz was Liverpool's hat-trick hero in Bradley Barcola.
This time last season, Koumas was on loan at Birmingham in the Championship while Barcola was at Paris St-Germain, who went on to win the Champions League for the second season in a row.
Quite a chain of events led to the pair starting together for Liverpool in their 6-3 win over LASK.
And as Barcola left the Raiffeisen Arena with the match ball after a superb hat-trick, the Frenchman knew that he wasn't the only player who put the ball in the net three times on Wednesday in Austria.
Koumas had his first two strikes ruled out for offside, but thankfully it was third time luck for the 21-year-old Wales international.
And so, just three days after making his first Premier League start against Manchester City - with Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Hugo Ekitike all injured - Koumas became the youngest Liverpool player to score and assist in a Champions League game.
Previously, the youngest to achieve the feat had been Steven Gerrard in 2001.
When that was put to him, Koumas wanted to know "Is that official?".
"It's not a bad stat, is it?" he said. "And it's not a bad name to be alongside. Wow. What a legend. I just want more of this."
He is enjoying his run in the first team but staying level-headed about it all, keen to point out: "This is my job."
"I need to get goals and assists," he said. "I hadn't had any before Linz so it was really important to get them."
In a Liverpool side where attention tends to be directed towards big-money names, Koumas provides a real feel-good story.
He joined Liverpool aged 11 and scored on his first-team debut as an 18-year-old under Jurgen Klopp.
After spells on loan at Stoke, Birmingham and Hull, where he helped the Tigers win promotion last season, Andoni Iraola decided in the first week of pre-season that Koumas was part of his Liverpool plans.
He made his Premier League debut at Newcastle before coming on against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League. He was man of the match on his first start of the season against Tottenham in the Carabao Cup after an energetic performance which left Iraola describing his playing style as "contagious".
That night, Koumas went straight on a video call with his family after the game and it was the case again in Austria after he scored his first goal of the season.
"It was probably the best feeling in my career, 100%. I'm just really grateful to have the opportunity again," said Koumas.
"I would not have been a happy man [if I didn't score], I would have been gutted. I just kept going because I knew the more the game was going on, it was opening up.
"Going over to the fans at the end meant absolutely everything. They are the reason we do this and that we want this job. I wish I could have got in there with them, but there was a big metal cage in the way!"
'I couldn't sleep after the Man City game'
It has been quite a week for the son of former Wales midfielder Jason Koumas.
Young Koumas has started two Liverpool games in a row, and on Sunday he nearly scored his first Premier League goal.
At 0-0 against Manchester City, Barcola played him through and Koumas connected sweetly but Gianluigi Donnarumma kept his effort out in front of the Kop.
Koumas was "absolutely gutted" the ball did not ripple the back of the net.
"I couldn't really sleep [on Sunday]. I just kept thinking about the chance all night. I feel like I couldn't have hit it any better. The keeper is huge and he was just in the right place and I think in normal circumstances it goes in."
While Koumas has an important role for now, he knows the likes of Isak and Gakpo will soon be back in first-team contention.
"You never know when your last game is going to be," Koumas said. "I know that sounds like a cliche, but it is true.
"I have got to keep pushing, every chance I get."
Koumas could lead Liverpool's attack for the third time in seven days when Liverpool travel to Brentford on Saturday.
Iraola said on Thursday that it was "too early" to tell whether Isak or Gakpo would be available.
The fact it would not be a surprise if Koumas starts again is testament to the impression he has made on Iraola. The manner in which he is seizing his opportunity is inspiring others too.
Liverpool's under-19s beat LASK's youngsters 4-2 in their Uefa Youth League game on Wednesday, with 18-year-old Will Wright scoring a hat-trick.
"You see Koumas with the first team and the energy he brings to the front line - that's from being in the academy, and Will has a similar identity," said Rob Page, Liverpool's academy boss.
"We have a manager who has come in and has an identity about how he wants to play which suits a lot of the players. And they've seen a pathway there now: Rio [Ngumoha], Trey [Nyoni] and now Koumas.
"My message was 'where is the next one coming from? So go and show the manager what you are capable of doing'," Page said.
For Koumas, confidence is only growing.
"We are getting chances but, ultimately, it is because we are good enough. Trey and Rio are unbelievable and, if you're good enough it doesn't matter how old you are," said Koumas.
First-team duty for the 20-time English champions could become the norm for the academy graduates.
"Hopefully that is the case and that's how I would love it to go," said Koumas, "but you just have to keep working hard, keep my head down and doing what the gaffer asks of me and make it last as long as we can."
Right now, Koumas is doing all he can.

After she descended from a B-stage in the middle of the stands at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday night, Miley Cyrus sat hunched over on the main stage, visibly sapped by the 200-foot trek back to the spotlight. “You guys gave me so much energy, but you also took a little energy out of me, too,” she said. “It is a lot for me, if you could imagine walking from where I was through each of you and feeling how much passion and how much love each of you radiates to me. And I appreciate you so much. But it is a lot for me and it is a little bit overwhelming.”
It’s an admission that a seasoned pop star — one of our biggest and brightest, mind you — would rarely deign to make at their first major show in years. And yet, it felt like the thesis for the first of two concerts Cyrus is performing in Los Angeles in support of her latest album “Bass Persuades,” a record with a few bright moments but lacking the singular vision that defined some of her strongest work. Across the nearly two-hour set, Cyrus appeared at odds with the pressures of being a generational talent, proudly chasing her muse with full-throated renditions of fresher, more opaque material while letting the audience carry the vocals on her biggest hits. It was confounding, oftentimes bizarre and, in the end, strangely entertaining, a snapshot of a megastar who, after all this time, is still figuring out what artist she wants to become.
Popular on Variety
That’s the thrill for anyone who has followed Cyrus’ career since she emerged as a Disney star with “Hannah Montana,” trying on different styles while navigating the mercurial sound of mainstream pop. She’s shape-shifted at a moment’s notice, chasing massive hits with pivots into deeply unconventional genres and sounds, beginning with her reinventive “Bangerz” era in 2013 and its subsequent global trek, her last extensive tour. Since then, she’s remained prolific and expansive, traipsing from psych-pop (“Miley Cyrus & Her Dead Petz”) to glam rock (“Plastic Hearts”) and, perhaps not accidentally, stumbling into a few massive hits along the way, with songs like “Wrecking Ball” and “Flowers” that she let the audience carry during the Bowl show.
On Friday night, Cyrus hewed closely to her new material with tracks from “Bass Persuades” and a few from 2025’s wildly ambitious “Something Beautiful.” She’s performed so rarely that nearly half the songs on the setlist were live debuts: Over the past few years, Cyrus staged only two fans-only shows in Los Angeles and Paris, appearances that reinforced her strengths as a performer without heeding to the pressures — interviews, TV appearances, radio drops — that come with it.
Yet Cyrus was quick to ground the show in her reality, one where she’s learned to balance her public and private lives. “For somebody that likes to keep life fun, and likes to jump out of airplanes and be spontaneous, doing the same thing for your entire life can lose its shine if you don’t continue to give yourself that pressure and polish to create something beautiful, which is the life that I’m living,” she said, leading into the title track from “Something Beautiful.”
For Cyrus, that’s meant stretching the boundaries of pop music and, by proxy, pop stardom. All bets were off as she opened with “Orbit,” a very languid ballad about the magnetism of romance. Already the pace was unpredictable, giving way to the zapping synth-pop of “Different Religion” (with featuring and opening act Model/Actriz) and Fentanyl-rejecting “Bass Persuades.” She let her freak flag fly with Flaming Lips’ frontman Wayne Coyne on the B stage for the group’s “Do You Realize??” and their collaboration “Karen Don’t Be Sad,” and strutted across the catwalk at the lip of the stage for “Walk of Fame,” one of the more supermodel songs in her discography.
Amid her musings on fame, she struck a truly emotive moment in remembrance of her godmother Dolly Parton, recalling that the only time she had seen her perform was at the Bowl some years back. “Like so many things Dolly did that I didn’t understand at the time, sitting here with you all right now, feeling her all around me, knowing that she’s right here beside me every day, all the time, more than she could be when she was here, I feel her more than ever,” she said, choking back tears as she led into a cover of “Jolene.” “And knowing that I get to share this story with you all, it makes that night very worth it. This memory is gold to me. Me and Dolly, we are eternal. Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart. And I’m going to see her again, and I can’t fucking wait because I miss her.”
That’s where she felt most at home, belting out those familiar notes of “Jolene” as she’s done so many times before. So it was strange that she largely held the mic towards the crowd for her bigger hits, “We Can’t Stop” and “Party in the U.S.A.,” where Coyne reemerged with a gigantic assortment of balloons that spelled “Fuck Yeah Hollywood Bowl.” Cyrus seemed removed from those tracks, aware of the power they held over the attending crowd while recognizing they had become so woven into the cultural fabric that they no longer belonged just to her.
Perhaps that’s why the first of Cyrus’ shows at the Hollywood Bowl felt so possessive, so intrinsically tied to her recent eras and willing to explore them. There were no traditional dance breaks or wild set pieces to accent the songs; here was Cyrus, 33 years old, coming out on the other end of the hit factory with the freedom to be who she’s meant to be. Whether that’s satisfactory is of little significance when, across two sold-out nights, 18,000 fans are still pining to witness it.

Outstanding quality. Great noise control at lower volumes. Autofocus improvements are noticeable, if short of life-changing.
TIRED
The massive case desperately needs a redesign. Still very expensive. Poor streaming quality.
This fall, hearing-aid manufacturers have been busily rolling out new and improved devices en masse, including Jabra, a leading maker of direct-to-consumer, over-the-counter devices. The brand has replaced its entire product lineup with all-new gear, swiftly retiring the Jabra Enhance Select 700, 500, 300, and 50R, all of which were only a year or two old. Three new models replace them: Enhance Select M3, M2, and M1. Each of the M-series hearing aids looks and works about the same as the models from last year and the year before that. Most of the updates here happen under the hood—but even those changes are hardly extreme, as I learned with the M3 pair I tested.
Historically, a more expensive device has meant a slightly smaller chassis—not so with Jabra's new hearing aids. Each of the three new models weighs the same: 2.12 grams, give or take a few hundredths of a gram, depending on the ear tip you choose. While the M2 and M1 share an identical form factor, the M3 is a bit squatter in design, measuring a few millimeters shorter than its siblings. Even so, all three are virtually indistinguishable unless you look at the fine print. That is, unless you select the red model; it's an M3 giveaway, as the M1 and M2 aren't available in that color.
Jabra M1 on left, M3 on right
Photograph: Christopher Null
Taking the traditional form of behind-the-ear teardrops, the M3 aids feature a single button on the back. Various presses and holds let you use these buttons for power, volume adjustments, and environmental mode changes that work to varying degrees of usefulness. Even so, the device is among the best available right now.
Within Earshot
Photograph: Christopher Null
Jabra calls its audio enhancement system SoundScape, which launched last year and claims to reduce noise and improve overall speech clarity. SoundScape features are variably available across the three devices in the M line, and two new capabilities are exclusive to the M3. These include a revamped autofocus tool that “locks onto” speech in complex, noisy environments, like restaurants, which I found to be moderately effective. I experienced clean dialog, even when a conversation partner walked fully around me in a circle.
INSERT GROUP ASSET: IMG_3735 and IMG_3734
ScreenshotSoundScape app via Christopher Null
ScreenshotSoundScape app via Christopher Null
The other new SoundScape feature for the M3 is an advanced adaptive listening mode that's responsive to a given environment (whether a restaurant, outdoors, or several other options) in real time to optimize noise reduction. The environmental modes weren’t very useful; keeping the hearing aids in “all around” mode, then tweaking levels manually (especially noise reduction) was the best way to improve the hearing experience.
I tested the M3 hearing aids in a variety of settings and am pleased to report that they work just as well as previous Jabra generations. Clarity in quiet environments (like having a one-on-one conversation or watching television) was just about perfect. Keeping the volume at 30 percent maximized hearing improvement while minimizing hiss, which grows geometrically louder with each upward tick of volume level.
Bluetooth streaming quality has never been Jabra’s strong suit, and while these new devices support Auracast—which lets various audio sources broadcast directly to the hearing aid—I don't expect I’d use any of the streaming modes much. Overall streaming audio quality on the M3 offers a slight improvement from previous generations, but music and movie audio are both too washed out at any level below the highest volume. And any amount of ambient noise still kills the experience completely.
Programming on Demand
Photograph: Christopher Null
The app and other features in the new lineup remain remarkably similar to previous Jabra models. Jabra has a history of offering great customer service: All purchases include three years of access to on-staff audiologists who can make tuning adjustments live over video chat and train new users on their hearing aids. Jabra’s built-in self-test system also remains top-notch, allowing you to create an audiogram from scratch in just a few minutes.
Its massive case unfortunately hasn’t changed, providing three recharges of your spent hearing aids before it also needs to be plugged in. A fully charged pair of hearing aids still lasts for 24 hours, as specified. In fact, I got closer to 26 hours in my testing before I needed to power up.
Notably, pricing also remains consistent, with the M3 starting at $1,995—the same launch price as the Jabra 700 last year. If history is any guide, a few months of patience are likely to reward you with a $200 price cut, and Jabra coupons are available fairly regularly. It's still a big ask for a nonprescription product. But to be fair, you’d likely pay twice as much for a prescription aid that can match the quality of these latest M3s.
My bottom-line recommendation? If you can afford the two grand for the Jabra M3 hearing aids, you'll get the most advanced over-the-counter devices available. That said, those with more modest means will do nearly as well with the $1,695 M2 or $1,195 M1 hearing aids—or one of the even more affordable options featured in my Best Hearing Aids buying guide.

Karnataka HC recalls order in land grab case linked to Kharge family, fresh hearing on Oct 30
The Karnataka High Court recalled its earlier order in the Siddhartha Vihara Trust land case linked to the Kharge family and scheduled a fresh hearing for October 30.
The Karnataka high court on Friday recalled its earlier order in a case involving the alleged illegal allotment of government land to the Siddhartha Vihara Trust, associated with the family of All India Congress Committee (AICC) president Mallikarjun Kharge, and scheduled a fresh hearing for October 30.
A bench headed by Justice M. Nagaprasanna passed the order after Mallikarjun Kharge’s son Rahul sought recall of the court’s August 18 order. The respondents will be heard before the court takes a fresh decision.
The court’s latest order withdraws its directions to the 82nd City Civil and Sessions Court, reopening consideration of the proceedings concerning the alleged allotment of land by the Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) and the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB) to the trust.
On August 18, the Karnataka High Court had set aside proceedings initiated under Section 223 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). It had also allowed the complainant to rectify defects in the affidavit and said the question of a police investigation could be considered subsequently.
The case arises from allegations that the Siddhartha Vihara Trust received government land illegally.
The complaint alleges that the BDA allotted about two acres of civic amenity land in the second block of BTM Layout Fourth Stage to the trust in 2014. About a decade later, another five acres near Bagalur were allegedly allotted to the trust through the KIADB, also citing educational purposes.
The complainant has estimated the combined value of the two parcels at more than ₹240 crore.
Mallikarjun Kharge, wife Radhabai Kharge, son Rahul Kharge, son-in-law Radhakrishna, Karnataka minister Priyank Kharge and INC leader M.B. Patil are among those named in the complaint.
The land was subsequently reportedly returned. The complainant, however, alleged that no effective action was taken on a complaint submitted to the Lokayukta police.
Lanchamukta Karnataka Vedike’s president Vijay Raghava Marathe later filed a private complaint seeking action in the matter.
Marathe s advocate Lakshmi Aiyangar told HT that the withdrawal of the earlier order meant that the proceedings would now be reconsidered. “The High Court’s decision to recall its earlier order means the proceedings will be reconsidered. The next hearing on October 30 is expected to focus on the submissions of the parties and the further course of action in the case. The allegations remain subject to judicial consideration,” she said.

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
- Published
"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.
Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.
The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.
Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.
At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”
Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.
When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.
Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.
“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.
The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.
In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

After public school teacher Gary Keblish was diagnosed with melanoma in 2019, a surgeon cut out the tumor. But he wasn’t out of the woods. In some patients, melanoma aggressively recurs after surgery, so his doctors referred him to a new trial: for Merck and Moderna’s personalized mRNA cancer vaccine.
Speaking by video at the STAT Summit on Thursday, Keblish compared the journey — in all its physical and emotional turbulence — to a trip on Ms. Frizzle’s Magic School Bus. “Seatbelts, everyone!” he said, quoting the iconic line.
He’s glad he went. Today, he is still teaching, and Merck and Moderna are preparing to file the vaccine for approval, after announcing in August that it significantly delayed both cancer recurrence and the development of metastatic disease in melanoma patients like Keblish, in a large Phase 3 trial.
It’s a landmark moment for a cancer vaccine field that has long struggled to live up to its hype. But the two companies’ work is far from complete. They are now looking to prove the vaccine isn’t just a powerful tool for certain melanoma patients but that it can also transform a sea of other tumors, as an early generation of immunotherapies did.
It is careful and costly work.
“We have a lot of exploring to do and need to prioritize where we explore,” Moderna President Stephen Hoge said on stage at the summit.
Beside Hoge, Merck R&D chief Dean Li outlined an exploration strategy. The vaccine, known chemically as intismeran autogene, works in combination with Merck’s blockbuster immunotherapy Keytruda, which has been tested in thousands of trials over the last 15 years. Keytruda works better in some tumors — so-called hot tumors, which often have lots of mutations — than other so-called cold tumors.
“We know exactly where I-O [immuno-oncology] works, where a checkpoint inhibitor works, where it doesn’t, where it almost worked and didn’t make it,” said Li.
The pair has largely focused to date on settings where Keytruda has worked best, such as an adjuvant — add-on — therapy for melanoma patients whose visible tumors have already been removed by a surgeon. They are already running trials in adjuvant lung, kidney, and bladder cancer.
Li and Hoge suggested other settings they may explore or where trials are just beginning, including in tumors where Keytruda failed but another kind of immunotherapy worked, or as a standalone therapy in very early-stage tumors. “There’s an incredible opportunity to think about how we bring immunotherapy into earlier interventions and really intercept cancer so that we don’t present with stage 3, stage 4 disease later,” said Hoge.
Li contrasted their approach with “other people” who “may not have the advantage” of their expertise and have chosen to go after cold or metastatic tumors — an apparent nod at Moderna’s mRNA rival BioNTech, which has some early promising early data but also notable failures.
“We have chosen not to do this,” Li said. “But I can tell you: Anyone has positive data and it’s out there, you will never see Moderna and Merck pivot [so] fast.”
Small tests in adjuvant pancreatic and gastric cancer are underway, to test the possibility. Li also floated the possibility of using the vaccine in patients whose metastatic tumors have already been shrunk by other treatments.
In the meantime, they continue to try to improve the technology. The vaccine is made by looking at individual tumors and using an algorithm to select up to 34 mutant proteins, in hope that you can then flash those as a “wanted sign” to the immune system.
The algorithm is imperfect. But by closely analyzing the immune systems of patients in their trials, Moderna and Merck could in theory build even better software.
“It’s a real privilege to have all that information across the now several thousand people in our Phase 3 program,” Hoge said. “I’m looking forward to digging into it.”

In the 53rd episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu, Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, and Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, discuss medicine pricing, drug safety and dengue surveillance.
The episode examines the Supreme Court’s concerns over the difference between the supply price and maximum retail price of essential cancer medicines. In one instance, the court was told that a cancer drug with a price to retailer of about ₹2,700 carried a maximum retail price of ₹27,000. The Bench described the difference as “broad daylight dacoity”.
The discussion also covers the court’s concerns about hospitals requiring patients to buy medicines from their own pharmacies, its suggestion of a uniform 16% margin and questions around generic prescriptions and the implementation of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order.
The episode also covers the risks of indiscriminate painkiller and antibiotic use, including kidney disease and antimicrobial resistance. While prolonged or inappropriate use of painkillers can cause kidney-related complications, unnecessary or incorrect antibiotic use can make infections harder to treat. The discussion highlights the importance of appropriate prescribing and responsible medicine use.
The final segment focuses on a Dengue Early Warning System being developed by researchers at the Institute of Advanced Virology in Keralam. The system combines disease surveillance data with rainfall, temperature and humidity to generate weekly, district-level forecasts using machine learning.
Trained on six years of data, from March 2020 to February 2026, the system aims to help health authorities anticipate increases in dengue transmission. If validated, the forecasts could support earlier surveillance, mosquito-control measures, healthcare preparedness and public alerts. The system is still under development and evaluation.
The episode ends with a fun fact about dengue mosquito eggs, which can remain dormant for months in dry conditions and hatch when water becomes available. Even seemingly dry containers can harbour eggs that may contribute to future mosquito populations.

Ontario toddler survives rattlesnake bite, partly thanks to 18 doses of antivenom
Wells Gladwish, 15 months, was treated at 2 hospitals after being bitten by an eastern massasauga rattlesnake
A 15-month-old boy from Sarnia, Ont., is recovering at home after being bitten by a rattlesnake at a family cottage on the Thanksgiving long weekend, requiring treatment at two hospitals and 18 doses of antivenom.
Wells Gladwish was bitten on the thumb around 12:45 p.m. on Sunday while spending the afternoon with family at their cottage in Cape Chin North, on the Bruce Peninsula.
His father, Matt Huggett, said the toddler was walking near a family bonfire when he came upon a snake and tried to pick it up. The snake bit Wells on the thumb, which began to turn white within about five minutes.
“We knew right away we were in a pretty bad situation,” Huggett said. “The nearest hospital was Lion's Head, and we did everything we could to get him there as fast as possible.”
Staff at Lion's Head Hospital needed multiple attempts to start an IV in the active toddler. After a test dose to check for a potentially severe allergic reaction, the team administered 10 vials of antivenom. The hospital had 14 vials in total.
A family member photographed the snake, which was identified as an eastern massasauga rattlesnake, Ontario's only venomous snake species, which lives along the eastern shore of Georgian Bay and on the Bruce Peninsula.
A family member photographed the snake that bit Wells Gladwish. It was identified as an eastern massasauga rattlesnake. (Matt Huggett)
Transfer from Lion's Head to London
Huggett said doctors and toxicology specialists co-ordinated an emergency response and decided Wells needed further treatment at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), Victoria Hospital.
Ornge air ambulance planned a transfer, but Huggett said repeated delays and cancellations left the family waiting as the swelling continued. A nurse at Lion's Head advocated for Wells to receive the hospital's remaining four vials of antivenom and to be transported to London by land ambulance.
“We could no longer wait for Ornge to make a decision,” Huggett said. “They ended up putting him in an ambulance.”
After a three-hour ambulance ride, Wells arrived at LHSC’s Pediatric Critical Care Unit.
Wells Gladwish was eventually taken to the Children's Hosptial in London, Ont., for additional treatment for a rattlesnake bite (Matt Huggett)
Dr. Rishi Ganesan, a pediatric critical care physician at LHSC's Children's Hospital, said his first priority when he received the call was to support Wells and secure antivenom, as they don't keep it in stock in London.
He credited the Lion's Head team for having antivenom available and administering it quickly. Ganesan said they sourced additional antivenom and brought it to London under a police escort from the Toronto region to be available when Wells arrived.
Wells received two additional double doses under care in London, bringing the total to 18.
Ganesan said he had not treated a venomous snakebite during his decade in Canada, but his training in India proved valuable.
“I trained in India, many, many years back, and I have managed snakebites of every kind: cobra, viper, krait,” he said. “Some of those things kicked in from the back of my mind, and I felt very comfortable.”
Ganesan said antivenom is derived from horses and can cause a severe allergic reaction, which is why the initial dose must be administered carefully with appropriate monitoring.
He said children do not necessarily need less antivenom than adults. Treatment targets the amount of venom, rather than the patient's size, and children can become seriously ill more quickly because the venom has a greater impact relative to their body size.
Doctors treated Wells for a rattlesnake bite with 18 doses of antivenom. (Matt Huggett)
Doctors monitored Wells's swelling and blood tests to determine whether more antivenom was needed. The venom can damage tissue and interfere with blood clotting, while severe swelling can also restrict blood flow to the affected limb.
“Antivenom doesn't fix all the problems with snake envenomation,” Ganesan said. “It is definitely the cornerstone.”
He said timely treatment generally leads to a good outcome, and he does not anticipate significant long-term complications for Wells.
'Incredibly thankful'
Huggett said many of the medical staff had never treated a case like Wells's before, but worked together and consulted specialists to guide his care.
Ganesan also praised the collaboration between hospitals, pharmacists, the Ontario Poison Centre and other specialists who helped secure the medication.
“This was a remarkable experience,” he said. “You had so many people come together and contribute in many small ways to make sure that he got the best care that he deserved.”
Wells was transferred to the children's inpatient unit before being discharged and returning home to Sarnia.
His father said Wells appears to be using his thumb normally, although a blister remains at the bite site. The family is continuing to monitor his recovery and watch for possible serum sickness, a delayed reaction to antivenom.
“We don't want to say we're 100 per cent out of the woods yet,” Huggett said. “But he's using it right now, he seems happy, and it seems to be looking better.”
What to do if you're bitten
Ganesan said anyone bitten by a rattlesnake should treat it as a medical emergency and call 911 immediately.
Although not every bite injects venom, he said it is not possible to confidently determine that in the field.
“With timely care, full recovery is a normal outcome in these situations,” he said. “The danger is actually the delay, not the snake.”
Eastern massasauga rattlesnakes generally avoid people and typically bite when provoked, attacked or accidentally stepped on, Ganesan said.
He advises people hiking or spending time outdoors in areas where the snakes live to watch where they step, avoid reaching into bushes or concealed spaces without checking, and leave any snake they encounter alone.

Is Leamington still Canada's 'tomato capital' with Chatham-Kent producing more?
Leamington has long dubbed itself the 'Tomato Capital of Canada'
As we're in the middle of October, the tomato harvest is winding down across southwestern Ontario.
Leamington has long dubbed itself the "Tomato Capital of Canada."
But did you know that neighbouring Chatham-Kent actually produces the most outdoor-grown tomatoes, anywhere in the country?
A handful of companies in Essex County and Chatham-Kent process them, while the vast majority of Ontario's output is from area fields, according to agricultural specialist Kim Cooper in the region.
A southwestern Ontario tomato farmer makes their way across a field in this file photo. (CBC)
He says the tomato pendulum swung east of Leamington over the past 12 years or so.
"The grower base has shrunk, and a lot of that was because when Leamington closed up their Heinz plant in 2014, that really threw the tomato sector into a spin," Cooper said.
Vehicles drive past the former Heinz plant in Leamington, Ont., in 2014. (Geoff Robins/The Canadian Press)
"It affected 50 growers back then … so some of those growers kind of packed it in and some of those growers were absorbed by other companies. Then, Highbury Canco came into the picture in Leamington. So they got a lot of those acreages back. That's why Leamington was always referred to as the 'Tomato Capital of Canada' — just basically because of Heinz."
Cooper says the climate in southwestern Ontario makes it the perfect place to grow outdoor tomatoes.
"People don't realize if you look at a map of North America, southern Ontario … Windsor-Essex, Chatham-Kent is the same latitude as northern California. Heat units is the key … and the soil."
Tomatoes grown in southwestern Ontario are shown in a large pile after being shipped to a processing facility in this file photo. (CBC)
According to Cooper, he’s not debunking Leamington as Canada’s tomato capital. Instead, he says, he's stating the fact that Chatham-Kent grows more now than in Essex County.
"Not because we [Chatham-Kent] tried to, but I think it was really because of the Heinz situation."
- Article How Leamington got caught up in one of Canada's greatest food fights
- Inside the ketchup war: what happened after Heinz closed in Leamington
Agricultural economist Philip Shaw says tomatoes are one of the most important crops grown in Chatham-Kent and Essex County.
But historically, he adds, it hasn’t proven to be overly lucrative.
"I wouldn't call it a cash cow because tomato production is incredibly and capital intensive," said Shaw, who’s based out of Dresden in Chatham-Kent and primarily farms corn, wheat and soybeans himself.
"In other words, it takes an awful lot of money to grow tomatoes and to be able to farm tomatoes in terms of land and equipment and dedication."
A worker tends to tomatoes being processed at the Highbury Canco processing plant in Leamington in this file photo. (Dale Molnar/CBC)
Whether the tomatoes are processed into things such as juice, soups, paste or cocktail mixes, a lot goes into growing them.
"You could put all the tomato farmers in a school bus and drive down the road because over a period of time the industry has changed and there's less producers. It takes an awful lot of money and an awful lot of risk to get into tomato production."
- It took nearly a decade. But this man thinks he's perfected Ontario tomatoes
- Tomatoes cost how much now? Why inflation has come for Canada's produce section
Shaw referred to farming tomatoes as "more of a closed shop" to those who’ve been in the business for many years with existing relationships with processors.
"Then there's negotiations between Ontario vegetable growers and these processors, and the processors also constantly change over a period of time. But also you just can't grow tomatoes every year."
A tomato harvesting machine picks and deposits tomatoes into a trailer being pulled by a tractor in southwestern Ontario. (Brent Hodge)
Trucking is another huge cost, says Shaw, which limits the geography of where they’re grown and processed.
"It's just not an economic panacea. There's a whole bunch of moving parts that have to fit together to have profitable tomato production in southwestern Ontario."
Capital of what then?
Just because Chatham-Kent produces more outdoor-grown tomatoes, doesn’t mean Leamington can’t continue to stake claim as the "Tomato Capital of Canada" — a slogan more than anything else — based on its history with the red fruit-vegetable.
But let’s just say it did lose the moniker. What else should the southwestern Ontario coastal municipality along Lake Erie be known for?
Leamington’s Cherise Charron was quick to respond when asked.
"I think it is the greenhouse capital for sure," she said. "I was looking at a map on Google, and you can see at night how lit up it is from all of the greenhouses we do have."
Greenhouse lights from the area of Leamington and Kingsville, Ont., are seen in a photo taken from the International Space Station on March 13, 2026. (NASA/International Space Station)
Nick Klym, also from Leamington, agreed with Charron.
"The greenhouse capital of Canada," he echoed.
Others told CBC News the municipality’s “beautiful waterfront” should be in the running.
Whereas Dave Brown from Leamington focused his attention elsewhere.
“It's the [retirement] capital of Canada, which serves diversity in labour and retirement … because of our climate. I've lived here all my life. It's a great place to live. I've seen a lot of people retiring here now and … from Toronto and bigger cities.”
Mayoral candidates have their say
The two people running for mayor in Leamington have also weighed in on what Leamington should be known — aside from tomatoes.
Incumbent Hilda MacDonald, who’s seeking a third term in the chair, says it would "100 per cent" be her community’s waterfront.
"With the with the amphitheater and now the stage, it's a wonderful place," she told CBC Radio’s Windsor Morning on Friday.
Hilda MacDonald, left, and Cris Biron are running for mayor in Leamington in 2026. (Peter Duck/CBC)
"It's not just for tourism, it's for our residents as well. And to me that's [the] quality of life that makes people come, work, play and stay … I'm very proud of that," MacDonald added.
Cris Biron is challenging MacDonald for a second straight election.
“Thanks to Ms. MacDonald, we have a beautiful waterfront – it’s fantastic,” he told CBC Radio’s Windsor Morning on Friday. "[But] what we did was to paint the vehicle before the fixing the engine. I mean we should have taken care of the downtown first … solidify our tourism … that is not really happening right now."

As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice.
Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday.
“This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman, was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.
“We will first observe the results, and if effective, there is a possibility that this method could be implemented in other regions.”
Since January, almost 900,000 hectares have been burned Indonesia-wide in the worst fire season in more than a decade, exacerbated by this year’s “godzilla” El-Nino and as the practice of “slash and burn” to clear land for crops such as palm oil persists.
For months, millions of Indonesians have been subject to thick smoke and an apocalyptic tangerine haze, with criticism mounting of the government’s response, including a class action lawsuit filed last week accusing it of “gross negligence”. Tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to the haze.
Air quality has also plummeted in neighbouring countries, shuttering schools, grounding flights and driving a spike in respiratory illness.
The haze has drifted into neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and as far afield as the Philippines. Timor-Leste has said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday and urged families to keep children indoors or to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment starting on Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes occurred. The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents.
In the past week, the financial hub of Singapore was listed among the most polluted cities globally. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected, was at number two.
On Thursday, a Cessna aircraft will reportedly disperse 1.5 tons of dry ice over the South Sumatran city of Palembang, a move the government hopes will ease the smoke and improve air quality and visibility.
The technique was first deployed in the 1940s to promote ice formation in clouds, Bloomberg reported.
But experts say the use of dry ice, or solid carbon dioxide, might only offer local, and limited relief.
“It’s got some potential for local relief that might work for a while,” says Rick McRae, an adjunct professor from the University of New South Wales’ (UNSW) bushfire research group.
“Weather systems are all moving from east to west. So if you’re in a town under that and you clear the smoke, there’s gonna be more blowing all the time,” he says, “So it’s a constant … It’s not going to be simple and it’s not going to be a permanent fix in any way.”
In the Indonesian province of central Kalimantan on Wednesday, the ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200 – or four times the “hazardous” level of 300 – environment ministry data showed.
Local news footage showed thick haze blanketing the provincial city of Palangka Raya, cutting visibility for motorists to a minimum.
Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto has ordered firefighting efforts to be stepped up, and called for a crackdown on those suspected of starting fires.
But the government has struggled to combat the fires, the worst of occur in peatland areas, which can burn for weeks underground and are difficult to extinguish.
“As time goes by and climate change kicks in, I think it could become a global problem, not just the fix that one country needs to find,” said McRae, of the widening regional issue. “There’s a lot of interconnectedness on a global scale.”

As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian.
Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.
The potential goals of the Russian campaign, according to an assessment seen by the Guardian that Ukrainian intelligence said it intercepted from Russia last month, range from “degrading the quality of life” of Ukrainians through power outages to fully shutting off the water supply, which the document cooly predicts would cause the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.”
The document does not specify which Russian agency developed the assessment, which is titled Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy, Housing and Utilities Sectors, includes vulnerable Ukrainian energy grid targets and even contemplates strikes against high-risk sites, including the switchyards at several nuclear power plants. But several European officials familiar with the document have said it is likely to have been produced by analytical departments linked to the Russian military or intelligence agencies, and that copies have circulated in Ukraine in previous years.
This year, however, Russia appears to be putting those plans into practice. On Tuesday night, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region – Combined Heat and Power Plants 4 and 5, and the Trypillya Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region – as well as a major electrical substation that transfers electricity from two of the country’s main nuclear power plants to the capital. Those, along with other substations that make up the “Kyiv energy ring” that helps bring electricity from across the country to the capital, have all been targets of a Russian barrage that, if it succeeds, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in a city of 3 million people.
Ukraine’s energy minister first briefed European allies last month about the plan, a copy of which was first reported on by the New York Times. Russia has stepped up its attacks on the Ukrainian power grid precisely as Washington and Kyiv are embroiled in a major political quarrel. The Guardian is withholding some specifics of the military assessment at the request of Ukraine’s energy ministry, which said it could aid in further strikes against the country.
“There are two large documents, written very coldly and very clearly, with tables showing the number of weapons needed for each facility to destroy it,” Ukrainian energy minister Denys Shmyhal said last month. “The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones. We understand how they are going to act.”
The leaked documents identify bottlenecks and prescribe the number of ballistic and hypersonic cruise missiles and jet-powered drones needed to knock out power plants and substations with brutal efficiency. If that was done, it could destroy more than 90% of the power that Kyiv is budgeted for each winter, the document predicts, plunging the city into the dark and cold. A worst-case scenario could lead to blackouts lasting up to 20 hours a day until damaged equipment is repaired, according to expert projections.
The strikes on Ukraine’s energy system have become the country’s new frontlines – and the country is badly outgunned, as its stocks of US-provided PAC-3 missiles have dwindled. Zelenskyy this week castigated city authorities for poor planning for the winter and for failing to protect the city’s energy infrastructure. Protests over heat and electricity blackouts are also planned for Saturday, highlighting how the difficult conditions in winter could provoke a political crisis for the wartime government.
Economic Pravda, a leading Ukrainian news site that covers business, reported on Thursday that the three major power plants in Kyiv no longer have the ability to generate electricity, leaving the city more reliant on electricity brought from elsewhere in the country (the government generally does not confirm specific damage to critical infrastructure). The outlets’ experts predicted that, given a moderate winter and quick repairs of damaged substations, Kyiv residents could face up to eight hours of blackouts a day. Its worst case scenario of frigid temperatures and frequent attacks would leave Kyiv in the dark for up to 20 hours a day.
This is no accident for the Kremlin, which has increasingly turned to punishing Ukraine’s population in major cities as the frontlines of the conflict have frozen. “Last year, we were really on the brink,” said Volodymyr Fesenko, a Ukrainian political analyst. “But the risk this year will be even worse, so the plan [to attack Ukrainian infrastructure] does seem realistic. There’s a very high chance that Russia tries to break us this winter.” If the Kremlin believed in the chance of a clean military victory before now, he added, it may now believe that not to be possible, and focus on destroying Ukraine’s remaining infrastructure rather than trying to capture it.
The secret plan, which officials here say was intercepted by Ukrainian intelligence and then briefed to senior European diplomats by Shmyhal last month, sets itself several goals: to destroy electricity generation, heating, water and sewage systems in such a way as to to make life in Ukrainian cities unliveable. Destroying electrical generation alone, it says, would lead to a “significant decrease in the quality of life of the population.”
To do so, it specifies the number of weapons that should be allocated – Geran 4/5 jet-powered drones and hypersonic or cruise missiles – in order to destroy key infrastructure such as thermal power plants, substations, water pumping stations and more.
Considering strikes against the basis of Ukraine’s water, sewage and heating systems, the document says it would create a “large-scale municipal infrastructure crisis.”
When contacted by the Guardian, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said that the document contained information that could aid in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. It did not reply to questions on how the current Russian bombing strategy matched with the proposals made in the document, or which Russian agency had developed the plans.

Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back on front line where Starlink plays a key role
- Published
A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.
Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.
This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.
The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.
While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September – and suffered few casualties in return.
The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".
Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.
He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.
This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.
Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.
Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.
Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.
Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.
Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.
The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.
An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."
He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.
Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".
"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."
Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.
In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.
"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."
"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".
That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.
"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.
"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."
All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.
This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.
Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.
But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.
The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.
I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."

“Street Fighter” is back on the big screen for a new take on the popular fighting game video series that started back in arcades in the 1980s and is still popular today.
Paramount and Legendary’s live-action movie takes place in the ’90s and follows a worldwide fighting tournament that brings together challengers from around the world. The roster includes Ken Masters (Noah Centineo) and his childhood friend and training partner Ryu (Andrew Koji), who have appeared in every “Street Fighter” video game. There’s a colorful cast of fellow characters like Chun-Li (Callina Liang), M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), Cammy (Mel Jarnson), Vega (Orville Peck) and more. The cast also has several real-life martial arts fighters, WWE stars and wrestlers, like Roman Reigns as Akuma, Cody Rhodes as Guile and Oliver Richters as Zangief.
Kitao Sakurai, who’s helmed episodes of “Beef,” “Dave” and the “Eric Andre Show,” directs the movie, which previously had Danny and Michael Philippou (“Talk to Me,” “Bring Her Back) attached. Bison, Michael Clarke Duncan as Balrog and Black Eyed Peas singer Taboo as Vega.

Nine years after first trying to resurrect the Roadster, Tesla is apparently trying again. CEO Elon Musk might have relocated its HQ to Texas, but yet again he has returned to California’s showbiz industry to hawk his wares; last time it was a Hollywood back lot for the remote-controlled Cybercab demo, last night it was decades-old stunt technology to make a show car do tricks in the air.
The new Roadster, we’re told, will be unlike anything else, although the angular, wedge-shaped styling owes more than a little to Giorgetto Giugiaro’s original Lotus Esprit—Musk is known to own a James Bond prop car—as well as the more recent Lamborghini Gallardo. At the rear are four giant exhaust pipes; these do not signal Tesla’s sudden embrace of hydrocarbons beyond those emitted by private aviation.
Rather, it’s where 100,000 psi jets of compressed nitrogen shoot out. It’s early in the morning and the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Statutes are dense reading, so I am yet to find the section where it explains how and when it’s legal to use such a thing on the road.
Unusually, Tesla says it stuck with rear-wheel drive for the new electric vehicle. The battery pack uses the troubled 4680 cells it has been trying to scale up in-house; customer complaints of poor performance were presumably the driving force behind developing what the company says is a special battery chemistry just for this model.
Some of the performance claims are even more grandiose than nine years ago. Now, Musk claims a planned top speed of 383 mph (616 km/h), with a 0-60 mph time of 0.8 seconds. And as with the last time this happened, there are already other EVs on sale that are more capable than Tesla’s vaporware claims.
You want to drive upside down?
And right now, that’s the McMurtry Spéirling, which looks like a miniaturized Batmobile (the good Michael Keaton one) and which is capable of generating up to 3.5 lateral Gs. The best Tesla claims for the new Roadster is 2 Gs. Oh, and the Spéirling will most definitely drive upside down.
it’s so disappointing once again to wake up to an entire industry being gaslit, and willingly so.
for all intents and purposes, Tesla sells three models of cars, and they are all entirely conventional EVs. no groundbreaking technology, no flying, nothing special at all.
