Amid talk of public execution, public opinion on death penalty is split
U.S. public sentiment about the death penalty has come to the forefront after President Trump gave his blessing, then backtracked, to livestreaming an execution via firing squad.
That planned execution comes after two botched Tennessee lethal injections this year, where the state struggled to find veins to administer death-inducing drugs to Christa Pike and Tony Carruthers.
Speaking at a press conference a day after Pike's failed execution, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said Tennesseans were disappointed about what happened.
"The people of Tennessee have determined that the death penalty is an appropriate penalty for the most heinous crimes in this state," he said. "The people of Tennessee make that decision and my job is to make sure that those sentences are carried out."
Those Tennesseans join some two-thirds of Americans who support the death penalty for people convicted of murder, according to a Pew Research Center poll from this summer. According to PRRI, a nonpartisan nonprofit, people that favor the punishment tend to be Christian, white and vote Republican.
Daniel LaChance, a history professor at Emory University, says the overall numbers mask a wide range of opinions.
" Support for the death penalty in the United States is a mile wide and an inch deep," says LaChance, who also wrote the book "Executing Freedom: The Cultural Life of Capital Punishment in the United States."
That's because the polling is incredibly nuanced, LaChance said. When polls offer more variance in the questions, such as life without parole, 60% of Americans support that over the death penalty. The number drops even further when monetary support to the victims' family members is an option.
And separate 2025 polling from Gallup — which has been tracking support for the death penalty since 1937 — shows that 52% of Americans support the death penalty if a person is convicted of murder, the lowest share in more than 50 years.
The change in public opinion
The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit that tracks the use of the death penalty but does not take a position on it, has counted 203 people since 1972 who were exonerated after being wrongfully convicted and sentenced to death.
"Those are just the ones we know about," says Robin Maher, the nonprofit's executive director. "We don't know how many innocent people were executed before we learned about their claims."
The wrongful death sentences, plus the moral efficacy, are what is swaying the public's opinion, Maher said.
"For the public to realize that the death penalty system was fallible, that it made serious mistakes, raised a lot of issues in people's minds about whether this very costly public policy, that was nonetheless rather inaccurate and unfair, should be used," Maher said.
The Pew Research Center study from July also found that while most people support the death penalty for crimes like murder, some 59% of respondents in the survey said the death penalty does not deter people from committing serious crimes – versus 39% who believe it does.
Six states were responsible for the 31 executions in 2026 — even though 27 states still legally allow the most severe form of punishment in this country. Florida led the way, with more than half of the executions this year.
Maher says that the fact that more than half the states allow capital punishment, but are issuing fewer death sentences, shows that the American people are disenchanted with the use of the death penalty.
" More often than not, they are finding it is not the right answer to violent crime," she says. "Executions on the other hand, are the result of what a handful of elected officials in just a few states are doing."
Texas accounts for the most executions since the 1970s, while Michigan holds the title for the longest-running death penalty abolition in the U.S., after banning the practice in 1847.
Out of public sight
The planned execution by firing squad is of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist stationed at Fort Hood, Texas, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 in 2009. It's slated for December but appeals could delay it further.
While 52% of Americans support Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's execution, 80% say his death should not be livestreamed, according to an October poll from ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos.
When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced earlier this month that Hasan would be executed publicly, the U.S. also hadn't conducted a high-profile public execution in 90 years.
In certain parts of America, quasi-public executions drew up to 10,000 viewers in the past, said LaChance, the Emory history professor. But the growing use of medicine such as anesthesia began a negative shift in public executions.
" Pain, especially in public spaces, starts to seem scandalous," LaChance says. "It's preventable now. It starts to seem barbaric."
LaChance also said the public, especially in immigrant communities, would turn the executed into heroes. "They would claim the body and conduct little parades in Lower Manhattan, celebrating the life of the person who had been put to death," he said.
One U.S. official who spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution said President Trump was talked out of a livestream execution because it was against American values — but also because there was concern the tape would show up on Jihadi websites, leading to an increase in recruits and possible danger to U.S. forces in the Middle East.
" That's the story of the death penalty," LaChance says. "People didn't want public executions to disappear when they did. Elites did because they were becoming embarrassing carnivals."

A fight over a bandana might have led to a cold-case murder in rural West Virginia, cops say
The victim’s skull was found with three bullet wounds to the back

A fight over a bandana in West Virginia may have kicked off a series of events that led to a murder and now an arrest, a decade later.
Richard William Nichols, 65, was arrested in connection to the 2016 murder of Ivan “Vanya” Perlis, 25, last month. He was taken into custody in Indiana and extradited to West Virginia to face charges.
Perlis’ remains were found on November 12, 2016, after a hunter discovered them near Maysville, West Virginia. Authorities found a skull with three bullet holes in the back, West Virginia State Police wrote in a criminal complaint.
A state medical examiner determined that Perlis was killed about a month before the remains were found.
Early in the investigation, police focused on an argument between Nichols and Perlis over a bandana.
In 2016, Perlis and Nichols lived on the same property but in different areas. One day, Nichols accused Perlis of taking a bandana and using his camper, police noted. That led to a fight where Nichols picked up Perlis by the neck and shook him, according to police.
Nichols, however, told authorities in 2017 that he and Perlis patched up their dispute and got along after the confrontation.
Throughout the investigation, Perlis’ story kept changing. At one point, he told troopers that he took Perlis to meet another man. He then changed his account saying that other man threatened both with a gun and demanded Nichols leave.
Nichols also wrote an apology letter to Perlis’ family and friends saying he gave Perlis a ride and the victim never returned. Nichols added that he wished he had done more to help Perlis.
Police continued to conduct interviews and the case remained open over the next decade.
In July 2024, police again interviewed the man who owned the property where both Nichols and Perlis lived. He said he saw the two leave together and Nichols returned wearing different clothes. The witness said Nichols claimed he changed because he had blood on his clothing and Perlis would not be coming back.
Police say there was a possible motive in a separate burglary where Perlis was reportedly pictured at the scene. It was speculated that Nichols might have wanted to prevent Perlis from identifying other people involved.
Nichols is now being held in a West Virginia jail until his next court appearance.

Legal experts are sounding alarms that Meta will soon update its commercial terms to require business accounts to allow Meta to train AI on their linked website content, not just their social media posts.
Kicking in on October 30, the TOS update won’t allow businesses to opt out, instead suggesting that businesses stop using Meta services if they won’t agree to let Meta bots freely crawl their linked content.
As Nieman Lab reported Thursday, this will affect all business accounts but is particularly shocking for news publishers who could perhaps charge Meta millions in licensing fees to continually access their articles for AI training. Currently news organizations are fighting a battle with OpenAI over whether such training without licensing is fair use, and Meta’s terms seemingly risk granting it sweeping permissions, no matter which way the court leans.
“While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab,” the lab said.
Specifically, the updated terms say:
You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.
Notably, there is no mention of AI, but it’s inferred from a single use of the word “train” and references to automated scraping and crawling.

It started with a dinner.
Peter Rice and Ynon Kreiz met for a meal in late September, days before Kreiz surprised the industry by jumping from the CEO job at Mattel to become co-chief executive of Skydance with David Ellison.
The report of the Kreiz-Rice meeting came in the New York Post’s Page Six after Kreiz’s role at Skydance was announced. That set off speculation that he was recruiting Rice for a big role at the enlarged studio. It turns out Kreiz had been trying to persuade Rice to take a board seat at Barbie’s house.
Rice, however, was not destined to advise on matters of Uno and Matchbox cars. The former Fox Searchlight and Fox Networks Group chief — who went to Disney in 2019 as its top TV executive only to be unceremoniously axed during the Chapek regime — has vaulted back to one of the town’s most powerful posts: chief content officer of Netflix.
Popular on Variety
Media coverage of Kreiz’s courtship of Rice is one of the spurs that pushed Netflix to make the move on a hire that will have ripple effects across its expansive film and TV operations. The ouster of Bela Bajaria from the role that Rice now occupies was messy, and angered many inside and outside of Netflix.
“We don’t live in Hollywood right now. We live in Silicon Valley,” said a prominent agent, citing the general mood of the creative community. The brusque treatment of an executive of Bajaria’s stature is a sign that no one is safe from scrutiny, and no one should ever count on making a graceful exit.
“It feels like more of a tech approach than a studio approach to letting someone go. It’s shameful, it sucks and it adds to the feeling that we’re all working by Silicon Valley rules,” the agent said.
The source noted the irony of Bajaria getting the ax just two weeks after the executive that she replaced at Netflix — Cindy Holland — was also hastily ousted from her new role at Skydance. Holland’s role was sacrificed to make room for Casey Bloys, the HBO chief who is taking over all streaming now that the Warner Bros. Discovery merger is completed.
The bombshell executive upheaval at Netflix, coupled with signals that insiders are reading from the layoffs that Netflix implemented this week, has set off renewed speculation about the streaming giant getting back in the hunt for a major studio or some other significant content assets. NBCUniversal is a logical target, given that the company will be spun out from Comcast next year and thus would make for a much smaller and more manageable acquisition than the entirety of Comcast.
The switch to Rice also raises questions about whether Netflix will remain as aggressive in its local-language content strategy as it had been under Bajaria. Rice’s reference in his first memo to Netflix staffers to the need to deliver more buzzy hits for the “UCAN” market (Netflix’s wonky term for the United States and Canada) did not go unnoticed.
Bajaria, according to multiple sources, learned the harsh reality of her fate on Wednesday evening when she cornered Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos before the screening at a private residence in L.A. for the Season 3 premiere of comedy “Nobody Wants This.” (Notably, neither Sarandos nor Bajaria are seen in any of the publicity photos that have been shared from the event.)
At the event, Bajaria asked Sarandos point-blank whether there was truth to the rumors gaining stream — and Sarandos, who it’s believed was originally going to break the news on Monday, told her right at that moment.
Rumors about Bajaria’s fate have swirled in recent months. As the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger saga soldiered on, there was much speculation about HBO chief Bloys jumping ship for a big role at Netflix or to launch a well-funded prestige label for the streamer. But once Bloys was confirmed as the new top boss of streaming for Skydance, the Bajaria speculation cooled off. On Monday, Bajaria was on stage at the Mipcom content conference in Cannes, where she accepted the Vanguard Award for contributions to the global marketplace as bestowed by Variety and Mipcom.
But even as top European content industry insiders gathered to hear Bajaria speak, chatter about her future fired back up in Hollywood this week. It turned out to be a perfect storm of events, with Netflix bracing for its largest-ever layoffs and its third-quarter earnings report coming on Oct. 20. The layoffs, amounting to 6% of the company’s workforce, or about 1,000 positions, were implemented Tuesday and Wednesday. That meant Netflix staffers were already on edge when the shock of the Rice news hit just after lunchtime in L.A. on Thursday.
Meanwhile, as recently as two weeks ago Rice was telling friends that he had no interest in becoming an executive again — which is a sign that Sarandos acted fast as soon as he learned Rice was available.
Bajaria is understood to have received an outpouring of support from her wide network of contacts in the creative community, at home and abroad. Multiple sources say the executive has been telling friends outright that she is shell-shocked, in keeping with her reputation for candor. Bajaria declined to comment.
The microscope now turns to Bajaria’s two top vertical lieutenants — Dan Lin in film, and Jinny Howe in original TV series.
Lin has been a steady hand in Netflix’s film operations for two-and-a-half years, ushered in to stop the lavish spending of the streamer’s formative Scott Stuber era. Slashing budgets carries an emotional price, though, and Lin has been forced to ensure talent delivers quality product without a widely perceived blank check signed by Sarandos.
In addition to making cheaper movies, Lin also backed some high-profile acquisitions (“Emilia Pérez” and Netflix’s current best-hope Oscar contender “La Bola Negra”). Yet, numerous reports have suggested that Lin will exit the company as Rice comes into power. It couldn’t be a more sensitive time, as Netflix will launch Greta Gerwig’s anticipated “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” with a full theatrical release in February. As Bajaria got the boot, the rumor mill instantly offered forth Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy — the ousted Warner Bros. Pictures chiefs — as potential replacements (which actually started a month ago, as Paramount and WBD finally found a path to combine).
According to insiders, with Rice likely to kick off his tenure by focusing on the film side of things, U.S. and Canada scripted head Howe appears to be safe in her role. With whispers in Hollywood that Netflix has struggled recently to produce another megahit in the vein of “Stranger Things” or “Bridgerton,” Howe, who took over in August 2025, has a hefty slate on her plate and is just starting to see some of her own development come to fruition.
That includes Meryl Streep in “The Corrections,” Adam Driver and Michael Fassbender in “Rabbit, Rabbit,” Martin Scorsese’s “The Roman” and the live-action/CGI “Scooby-Doo: Origins.”
“They want her to stay,” said one source. “If she left, that’d be a disaster for them.”
Meanwhile, given Rice’s experience, some also wondered whether Sarandos just hired someone who could ultimately be a candidate to replace him — should the stock continue to suffer and the company see a need to make more changes.
The week has indeed offered more drama than anything Netflix will put on its service this year.

Amritsar: SGPC president Harjinder Singh Dhami on Saturday said a portrait of anti-drug activist Parvinder Singh Jhota, who was killed by a medical store owner in Mansa on October 13, will be displayed at the Central Sikh Museum located within the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar.
The initiative would serve as a symbol of remembrance of Jhota's struggle against drugs and his commitment to saving Punjab's youth, said Dhami, who met the slain anti-drug crusader’s family on Friday.
The Sikh community will always remember the sacrifice of Jhota, who lost his life while fighting to save Punjab's youth from the deadly grip of drugs, Dhami said in a statement.
Carrying forward the struggle he launched against drugs and for protecting the younger generation from substance abuse is the crucial need of the time, the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC) president said.
“Jhota’s portrait will be displayed at the Central Sikh Museum within the Sri Harmandar Sahib complex. The courage and commitment of young people who contribute to movements against drugs cannot be overlooked,” he said.
Assuring the family of the SGPC's support during this difficult time, Dhami said the Sikh body stood firmly with them and would honour any request made by the family.
“Sikh institutions have a duty to stand by families in such circumstances. They are not alone,” he said.
The SGPC president also inquired about the health of the four men who were injured alongside Jhota, and announced that the SGPC would provide financial assistance of Rs 5 lakh to each of them.
On Friday, Akal Takht Jathedar Giani Kuldip Singh Gargajj had accorded the status of martyr of the Sikh community to Jhota.
Known for raising his voice against the illegal sale of addictive substances at chemist shops, Jhota was shot in broad daylight inside a medical store at a busy marketplace in Mansa on Tuesday.
Ashwani Kumar, the store owner who opened fire on Jhota after he questioned him for selling addictive drugs to an elderly man, was taken into custody from Salasar in Rajasthan.
The incident, which took place while Jhota was hosting a Facebook Live, triggered a political slugfest in Punjab, which goes to polls early next year.

My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed.
Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD.
While there he became involved with Operation Omega, a group that smuggled humanitarian aid across the border from India to Bangladesh during its war with Pakistan in 1971. This led him to cut short his studies so that he could begin work as a consultant economist and project planner. Over the years he worked on many projects, including for the University of New South Wales from 1984 to 1986 in the Solomon Islands on a smallholder project and a post-cyclone survey.
In 1989 his work took him back to Bangladesh, where he was employed by the World Bank to develop a flood action plan. Fourteen years of his life, from 1992 to 2006, were then spent with the Department for International Development, working on ways to help tackle the social and economic problems related to rural poverty in India.
He was also particularly proud of a cyclone recovery and reconstruction project he worked on in 2007 for the World Bank, which led to the building of cyclone shelters in Bangladesh.
In 2006 he became a trustee and then chair of trustees of the Humanitarian Centre in Cambridge, which later became the Centre for Global Equality. Two years later he had to leave work after being diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, but eventually he was lucky enough to receive a lung transplant that prolonged his life considerably.
That allowed him to focus on being a trustee, chair and patient president of the charity Action for Pulmonary Fibrosis, giving over the last decade of his life to fighting on behalf of people with the disease so that they can be provided with better diagnosis, care and treatment. He was also president of the European Pulmonary Fibrosis Federation.
In 1976 he met Hilary Gretton, a nurse, and they married five years later. She survives him, along with their children, Rosie, David and Euan, and seven grandchildren.

Reliance said it welcomed competition and that every player, including Jio, must comply with the country’s laws and policies. It also noted that Jio’s own satellite services were awaiting clearances.
"In light of recent remarks about Reliance and the Indian market, we wish to place the facts on record.Like every Indian enterprise, Reliance has grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international, that improve the lives of the people. 
That openness rests on the rule of law. As the Government of India has stated, it applies the same process to every applicant, Indian or foreign. Jio's own satellite services await clearances," Reliance had said.
Musk had accused “certain oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s entry into India before naming Reliance chairman Mukesh Ambani in a series of posts.

“Bacchon, police ki maar ka bura nahi maante. Yeh aapko samjhane ke liye kari gayi hai” (Translation: Children, don’t take offence at being beaten by the police. This was done to teach you a lesson.)
This is what a Delhi Police official had to say after protesters were allegedly subjected to a vicious assault inside a prison van fitted with ‘cages’, while being taken to a detention centre at Pandwalan Khurd, a village in the Kapashera tehsil of Najafgarh in South West Delhi, on October 11.
One detainee was called in. Then came the screams. Another followed, and the screams came again. Inside the pitch-dark van, protesters were allegedly punched, kicked and beaten by police personnel before being shoved into cramped, grille-enclosed compartments. They could hear the violence unfold but could barely see who was inflicting it.
Two detainees who were in the same van spoke to Alt News, recounting what they described as a nightmare that would haunt them for the rest of their lives. Each detainee, they said, was made to board the vehicle one at a time, assaulted and then forced into one of the cages inside.
Their offence: Joining a protest on the streets of Delhi against alleged electoral malpractices and supporting the call for the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
An Evening of Unspeakable Horror
Twenty-three-year-old Tarang Balani, who works at an e-commerce startup, saw a video posted by Neha Bora urging people to reach R K Ashram at 2:30 pm. “I saw that post at 2. So I reached Connaught Place (CP) directly because I thought if they’re marching from R K Ashram towards Jantar Mantar, and if I’m reaching late, I should definitely find the march somewhere around CP. I reached around 3:30 pm,” he said.
With several routes blocked in the area, Balani had to take multiple detours. He eventually came across a group marching towards Jantar Mantar and joined them. “We were told to form a human chain in case the police came to detain us,” he said.
The group was marching past Chilli’s restaurant and about to turn left when the police moved in to detain them. “As soon as police came, half the crowd had dispersed around, trying not to get detained, and 10-15 people sat down and locked hands with each other to form a human chain. I saw male police officers pulling the women protesters. Then women police officers arrived and did the same thing.”
After a tussle with the police, the protesters were forcibly made to board a Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) bus.
In the video below posted by BBC, as Hemansh speaks, a policeman inside the bus can be seen slapping or punching a young man in the face.
View this post on Instagram
“Soon after, they stopped outside the Pind Balluchi restaurant in CP and some police officers started asking us to deboard,” Balani said. The protesters refused to get off the bus since the area was teeming with security personnel and there were no media persons around. “We felt that the media should be able to document what was happening.”
“But if three people are trying to get hold of one person, there’s not much you can do,” he said. According to Balani, police officers began pulling a female protester by her wrists, breaking her bangles and leaving her wrists bleeding. She then clung to the window grille as the officers pulled at her trousers and shoes, leaving her almost suspended in the air. Two women police officers approached her from outside the window and pulled her hair, forcing her to let go. “I saw it happen in front of me,” he recounted.
Outside Pind Balluchi, the protesters were separated by gender. The women were made to sit in a van and taken away, while the men were made to sit on the street for at least half an hour before the next ordeal began.
“If anyone took out their phones, it was immediately snatched, even if they were not recording. They were asking them to open their gallery and delete all media files from the day, even from the recently deleted files. We were told that if we just co-operated, nothing was going to happen to us. So most of us were just sitting quietly,” Balani said.
A Journey that Turned into a Nightmare
Half an hour later, another police van arrived, and the men were asked to board it. Twenty-seven-year-old IIT graduate Hemansh Kashyap recounted how the police allegedly assaulted detainees one by one as they entered the vehicle.
“Some of the policemen started playing good cop, saying that nothing would happen to us if we boarded it. People were taken in one at a time. An official was collecting our phones at the entrance. The first person went in, and then came blood-curdling screams. Then the second person went in, and the same thing happened. We realised that they were being assaulted.”
“We said we wouldn’t board, but the cops said: ‘Aur nahi marenge’ (We won’t hit anymore). But it obviously wasn’t true, and there wasn’t a lot we could do. When I went in, I was immediately slapped very hard, repeatedly, so hard that my glasses flew off. I was shoved into my compartment, and the cops gave me my glasses back,” he said.
Balani said the van had four compartments separated by grille partitions, with a narrow aisle that could accommodate only one person at a time. The vehicle was completely dark, making it impossible for him to see clearly.
“I was beaten up right there in the narrow passage by three policemen. Initially, two of them started beating me up; they punched me and kicked me. And then somebody said, ‘Iska chashma utaar’ (Take off his glasses), and so they took out my specs and started beating me again. I couldn’t even see their faces in the dark; I just saw policemen without name tags,” he recounted.
“I really thought they had confused me with someone else because I was quiet from the start. I was protesting peacefully. As I tried to save myself from the blows, they kept beating me, and beating me, and I just kept pleading with them (to stop). Once they realised that the regular punches and kicks were not working, they started using their elbows. One of them kicked my knee, and I fell in the aisle, and then they hit me more.
“Once I started screaming, that is when they opened the compartment where they pushed me in and just threw my specs. They closed the door behind me and locked it. As soon as I sat down, another person came; he was not wearing glasses, so they literally just took his face and smashed it into a pole in that aisle. I saw it because I was sitting right next to the division between the aisle and my compartment. There was one guy who refused to surrender his phone, and he was beaten by the police as if they had a personal grudge against him,” Balani recounted.
Both Balani and Hemansh Kashyap told Alt News that each of the blocks or cages inside the police van could accommodate six people at most. Each had two benches facing each other, with space for three people on either side. However, 10–12 detainees were crammed into each block, forcing some to sit on the floor and others to sit on fellow detainees’ laps.
The van was completely dark, making it difficult for detainees to even check the time on their watches.
What emerged from both testimonies was the methodical nature of the violence — perhaps its cruellest aspect. One detainee was taken in, beaten and shoved into a cage; then the next was called. The screams were followed by more screams. There was no frenzy, no confusion, but a grim, repeated sequence, with each person left to await their turn, knowing what awaited them in the darkness of the van.
Families Lose Contact as Detainees’ Phones Go Dead
Both detainees had shared their live locations with family members. Kashyap had shared his with his partner, Barshana, who is currently in the United States.
“At 3:45 am Pacific Daylight Time (4.15pm IST) on October 11, Hemansh called me and said he had been detained. He had been detained the day before as well and was held at a farmhouse in Chhattarpur for about six hours before being released. There wasn’t much explicit violence then, so I wasn’t too worried.
“We texted for a while as he told me he was on a bus, and he even sent me a few videos from it. But soon there was complete silence from his side. After two hours of no contact, my calm gave way to worry. I kept checking his location, but it stayed parked at CP for a long time.
“Soon, I received a message request on Instagram from an unknown account. It was Hemansh sending a message from someone else’s phone informing me that he was in a police van and had been assaulted. He told me that his phone was possibly with the cops, and also asked me to track his location. I noticed that the van was moving very fast, heading towards the Haryana border. At around 7 am PDT, the location stopped updating. I had checked, and his battery was at 40%, so it couldn’t have died. I guess the phone was switched off. His friend, who was with him in the van, was also not getting his WhatsApp messages delivered, so both phones seemed to have met the same fate.”
“I kept texting the Instagram account, which, I later found out, belonged to a detainee who had managed to sneak in a phone, but I couldn’t bombard it with messages, as the same phone was being used by thirty others. At around 7:27 am PDT, he called me for a minute, told me they had been brought to a detention centre in the middle of nowhere, and shared the location with me. That is when I mobilised my lawyer and activist friends, who reached the spot to get him out.
“The entire ordeal, from the time he was detained to the time he returned home, lasted about eight hours. It was extremely worrying for me,” Barshana recounted.
Tarang Balani, too, said his brother, with whom he had shared his live location, lost track of him when the police van reached Raota in Delhi. “I’m guessing it was because someone switched it off. An app installed in my phone still shows 70% battery in brother’s phone. The location update was stopped between 6:36 pm and 6:40 pm,” he said.
Kashyap also recounted the assault of a young man, around 19–20 years old, inside the police van. The man allegedly screamed that the police had assaulted him on his private parts and manhandled him. “(He) fell on the ground while being assaulted, and the police started hitting him in between his legs. He told his cellmates after the van started moving. He was probably the first or second detainee to be taken into the van, and he was beaten up brutally. We told him, ‘Don’t get too agitated; they’ll beat you up even more.’ It was very scary,” Kashyap said.
Neither Kashyap nor Balani has got back his phone yet.
Both of them told Alt News that four minors were inside the police van and that all four were assaulted.
Locals Come to Detainee’s Aid at Pandwalan Khurd
The van dropped them at the detention centre around 7:30 pm. The detainees expected their phones back but were told by CRPF personnel that Delhi police had not handed over the phones.
One detainee with a fractured arm received medical attention only at 9:15 pm. “There was just one canister of water, and it ran out pretty quickly. There was no food or medical help. An AIIMS doctor finally came after someone contacted them through their connections,” Hemansh said.
Initially, lawyers were not allowed to enter the detention centre. Meanwhile, a crowd began gathering outside, with some villagers, including children, reportedly protesting the detention.
“They were recording us from outside the gate. We told them to go away or they would get beaten up, but they seemed quite aware of their rights and started asking questions like, ‘How can they beat us up?’ They went away for a bit and came back with their parents, I think. These were ordinary people from the neighbourhood. They came back with water and fruits. Later, when we were released, a man was going around giving everybody 100-rupee notes if they needed to get home,” Kashyap said.
At around 9:30 pm, another van arrived, and some detainees, including 51-year-old journalist Raj Shekhar, were offered the chance to leave. The detainees unanimously refused to go without their phones. The police allegedly told them they could collect their phones from Connaught Place, offering no accountability for their confiscation. Lawyers who had reached the detention centre advised the detainees to call the emergency helpline 112 and submit written applications and complaints.
Between 10:30 pm and 11 pm, buses were arranged to take the protesters to Dwarka More metro station. Unsure whether the buses would actually drop them at Dwarka More, Balani chose not to board one. Instead, he left in a car provided by volunteers, who had been sent sent by journalist Meghnad S to help detainees return home. Kashyap, too, left with lawyers who were present at the scene.
Balani also noted that most Delhi Police personnel involved wore no name tags; only officers with two or three stars had them. He identified one officer as Ashutosh Bishnoi, who, while the detainees waited outside Pind Balluchi, had repeatedly assured them that nothing would happen to them.

Hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia – OB-GYNS set new rules for menopause treatment
For the first time since 2014, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its guidelines for the treatment of symptoms commonly associated with menopause. The doctor's group, known as ACOG, recommends hormone replacement therapy alongside certain antidepressants, nonhormonal medicines, and other treatments to address symptoms like hot flashes, insomnia and mood swings.
"What's changing is the breadth of options that we now have … And the benefit of that is that we are better equipped to be able to take an individualized approach for patients," said Catherine Cansino, MD, MPH, an obstetrician/gynecologist, chair of ACOG's Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines and co-author of the new guidance.
The guidance, released Thursday, focuses on specific menopausal symptoms and underscores that the safety of hormone replacement therapy is now "well-established," Cansino said.
In 2002, the Women's Health Initiative suggested that hormone replacement therapy increased the risk of heart disease, breast cancer, stroke and pulmonary embolism.
However, as researchers revisited that data years later, they noticed certain limitations, (including that a majority of participants were 60 years or older) making it difficult to generalize the findings to younger women experiencing menopause or perimenopause.
With more and better quality studies, physicians are able to review the evidence and make better-informed recommendations, Cansino said.
"Hormone therapy is probably the best option for symptomatic, newly menopausal women within 10 years of the final menstrual period or before the age of 60," said Robert Kauffman, MD, MSCP, a co-author of the guidelines, during a press briefing on Thursday.
In addition to hormone replacement therapy, the guidelines highlight new nonhormonal options for treating menopausal symptoms, including the drug fezolinetant, brand name Veozah, which the Food and Drug Administration approved to treat hot flashes in 2023 and elinzanetant, brand name Lynkuet, which was approved in 2025.
"What's so exciting about these treatment options is they were specifically studied based on the understanding that we have of the physiology of thermoregulation and sleep," Cansino said.
The medications work by blocking certain chemical messengers in the part of the brain that regulates body temperature and manages sleep/wake cycles, according to the guidance.
About 2 million women begin menopause each year. The average age of a woman experiencing menopause is 49.9 years, according to the guidelines. However, symptoms of menopause can begin years before a woman's final menstrual period.
The new recommendations support the use of systemic hormone replacement therapy, or HRT, with a combination of estrogen and progestogen in women with a uterus who have no contraindications to hormones.
Reasons to avoid hormone therapy include undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, and current or past histories of certain gynecologic cancers, blood clots, stroke, heart attack, liver disease or a known or suspected pregnancy.
The reason progestogen is recommended in women with a uterus is because estrogen can stimulate growth of the uterine lining and increase the risk of endometrial cancer. Progestogen therapy helps mitigate that risk, Cansino explained.
Around half a million women have hysterectomies each year, and for women without a uterus, ACOG recommends estrogen alone.
As an alternative to estrogen-progestogen therapy, ACOG also recommends a pill, sold under the brand name Duavee, that combines estrogen and a drug called bazedoxifene. Bazedoxifene is a "selective estrogen receptor modulator," which blocks the estrogen from working in certain areas of the body, such as breast tissue, while mimicking estrogen's benefit for bone density, for instance.
Another drug recommended in the new guideline is gabapentin, an anticonvulsant typically used to treat seizures. It can also manage menopause symptoms for people who can't tolerate hormones or the other new medicines.
Cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based interventions, exercise, clinical hypnosis, and acupuncture can all improve some symptoms, ACOG says, however the guidelines also note that the evidence for these interventions is weaker than the evidence for HRT.
Still, patients may have their own preferences and goals, Cansino said.
"I live in California, and I have a practice where many patients don't necessarily want pharmacologic therapy," Cansino said. So, she tends to have a lot of conversations about non-pharmacologic treatment options with her patients.
"A healthy diet and regular physical exercise is going to go a long way. So let's start with that," and then discuss what other interventions to add to the regimen, she said.
Asked, in a follow-up email, whether Cansino recommended one medication or tool over another, she warned against "over-simplifying treatment based on tiers."
Just like with contraception, she noted that patients may choose a certain method, knowing that it's less effective. "As long as they understand the pros and cons, such a decision is perfectly OK."
Meanwhile, demand for HRT is already rising. Last year, the FDA scrapped the "black-box warning" on labels for certain estrogen therapies.
In recent months, estrogen products like transdermal patches have been hard for pharmacies to keep in stock.
"I think the shortage of transdermal estrogen therapy highlights the fact that we have all of this attention about hormone therapy, and not necessarily enough about other treatment options," Cansino told NPR.
She also stressed the need for patients to talk to trusted clinicians about the pros and cons of treatments and to avoid having "tunnel vision" about a single option.
The level of care that OB/GYNs provide by helping individual patients find the right treatment is one of the most important aspects of the new guidance, Cansino said.
"There's a lot of misinformation out there and exaggerated claims about hormone therapy, and so some people end up taking risks when they shouldn't," she added.

The UK may expand the BBC license fee, charging residents to watch streaming services
If the proposal is enacted, it could cost $240 a year to watch YouTube in the UK.
The UK government will consider charging residents a national fee to access video streaming content, meaning it may cost almost $240 a year just to watch YouTube in the region. The Independent reported that later this year, UK leaders will propose extending the BBC license fee to cover streaming video platforms.
For our non-UK readers, the license fee is responsible for a large amount of funding for the BBC. It is levied on all residents who watch content on a television, whether or not that content includes BBC programming. The standard fee is currently £180 (~$239) a year. Paying the fee grants viewers access to all domestic TV channels, several pay TV services, live TV shown via streaming platforms and on-demand content via BBC iPlayer.
The proposed changes would expand the license fee and apply it to several streaming services such as Netflix, Amazon, Disney+ and YouTube. Proponents of the change argue that people can use those platforms on their mobile devices or computers rather than their TVs to evade the tax. "It's not fair that people are essentially able to watch television content but avoid the license fee," an unnamed source told The Independent about the proposed changes.
The additional funding from expanding the license fee would reportedly be put toward supporting local journalism and combatting misinformation campaigns. The UK's national broadcaster is also facing budget issues, with a 2 million decline in the number of license fees paid over the past five years, according to The Independent. Despite that decrease, YouGov data suggests the BBC remains the most popular media platform in the UK.
The BBC recently announced that it would begin streaming a 24/7 news channel on YouTube for viewers in the UK and the US. The broadcaster already has similar channels active in Australia, Kenya, Nigeria and Poland.

Chicago-area law enforcement officers took part in an undercover probe by Immigration and Customs Enforcement into Minneapolis mutual aid networks last spring as part of the feds’ conspiracy investigation into 15 Twin Cities activists facing federal felony charges for resisting Operation Metro Surge, according to newly released documents reviewed by WIRED.
An April report by ICE’s investigations wing, Homeland Security Investigations, titled “Antifa Roadshow,” details in-person and electronic surveillance by a joint task force of an April 2 talk. The task force was made up of 14 law enforcement officers—six local cops and eight HSI Chicago agents. The talk included self-described anarchists in Minnesota who spoke about their organizing experiences during the three-month immigration surge, which resulted in the killings of two US citizens.
The document, released by the 15 Minnesota activists’ defense team as part of the ongoing federal case against them, exposes close cooperation between local police, sheriffs, and HSI agents on a prosecution that critics say crosses the line into political repression. The Chicago HSI task force, which included officers from Chicago, Aurora, Downer’s Grove, Cook County, and Kane County, used two undercover agents, unspecified electronic surveillance, audio recordings, license-plate-reader data, and surveillance cameras from Chicago’s sprawling CCTV network to identify the April 2 event’s attendees and build connections to other anti-ICE protests in Illinois and other states.
Records produced by the Kane County Sheriff’s office show the unit in question is the Chicago-area Homeland Security Investigations Task Force. Local cops who join the unit are accepted on either a full- or part-time basis for two years, with the sign-off of their superiors.
Since Operation Midway Blitz in Illinois last autumn, residents in Chicago and surrounding communities have pressed elected officials for answers about cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE. While Illinois state law prevents local law enforcement from participating in immigration enforcement operations, criminal investigations by HSI appear to fall outside those restrictions because they pertain to ICE’s other law enforcement functions.
Chicago police have substantial approval requirements for surveilling and infiltrating protests or public gatherings, per a 2017 departmental order. It is unclear how these regulations apply to Chicago Police Department agents participating in joint task forces with federal agencies.
In response to questions from WIRED, the CPD claims that no First Amendment notifications to CPD’s chain of command or the department’s general counsel were made for the April 2 investigation, and says its work with HSI is permitted under Illinois law because it pertained to criminal enforcement, not immigration. A source with knowledge of the matter stated that CPD believed the early April surveillance operation was in service of a federal racketeering investigation. The only financial element mentioned in the report is a GoFundMe account to support the Crimethinc speaking tour. There is no mention of funds solicited or received at the April 2 event.
The Chicago Mayor’s Office did not provide comment ahead of publication. In response to queries from WIRED, ICE would neither confirm nor deny details of past or present investigations and said individual agents are not authorized to speak to the media.
HSI is also emerging as the point agency for Trump’s war on internal dissent and opposition politicians: Its agents, not the FBI, conducted the Minnesota 15 investigation and served a search warrant earlier this month on congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.
The targeted April 2 event was held at Co-Prosperity, a Leftist gallery in the Southside Chicago neighborhood of Bridgeport. Several speakers from the Twin Cities area attended the event to share information about resisting federal immigration surges. This was part of a national tour last spring that was organized by the longtime anarchist collective Crimethinc, whose meetings have been infiltrated by federal informants repeatedly over the decades and contributed to the convictions of Eric McDavid, as well as 2008 Republican National Convention protester Matthew DePalma.
Per the four-page HSI report, a plainclothes cop from suburban Aurora was dropped off at the Co-Prosperity event by Officer Mike Xu from the wealthy village of Downers Grove; HSI undercover agent #9147 walked in five minutes later, once the undercover cop from Aurora confirmed no security checks were done at the door.
The undercover HSI agent transmitted a live recording of the event to the rest of the surveillance team for an hour, until transmission was lost. The recordings of the incident were uploaded and shared with HSI agent Kenneth Popovits, a financial crimes investigations supervisor who was working on a temporary assignment in Minneapolis.
Remarks by defendant Callum Robinet from the April 2 talk in Bridgeport about building rapid-response networks are included in the federal conspiracy indictment brought against the Minnesota 15, implicating the Chicagoland law enforcement that participated in surveillance in the controversial prosecution.
The Aurora Police Department, Downer’s Grove Police Department, and Kane County Sheriff did not respond to requests for comment.
The HSI Chicago surveillance team logged 219 vehicles parked in the vicinity of Co-Prosperity. Several subjects already under investigation, including some of the speakers on the tour, were identified by ICE. Ryan Wasson, a Kane County Sheriff’s deputy, spotted a hooded, masked man outside the venue removing an object from his trunk. Running the license plate, Wasson identified the man as the subject of an October 4 arrest during Operation Midway Blitz whose prosecution had been declined by assistant US attorney Christopher Veatch.
Outside the venue, agents Joel Sullivan and Michael Finerty spotted an unnamed subject already under investigation for running “an anti-ICE Signal chat and group called ‘ICE Cream Patrol’” and noted an orange Hyundai had been documented near two March 2026 protests outside the ICE detention center in Broadview, Illinois. The surveillance lasted for roughly two hours until 8:30 pm local time on April 2.
Nick Nunez, a veteran Chicago Police detective detailed to the joint task force, filed a request to obtain surveillance footage from a CPD camera outside the venue; the request would take a week to complete, and it is unclear whether he received footage. All information obtained during the April investigation in Chicago was shared with HSI St. Paul/Minnesota, according to the agency’s report.
Ed Yohnka, a spokesman for the American Civil Liberties Union of Illinois, calls the surveillance of the Bridgeport gathering “very troubling,” adding that local law enforcement should make a full accounting of their role in the incident and participation in joint task forces with federal agencies.
“No one should be subjected to surveillance and infiltration by law enforcement simply for engaging in constitutionally protected activity, including the ability to gather together and express dissatisfaction with public policy,” Yohnka says. “It is also a moment for local law enforcement to reexamine their participation in task forces with the Trump administration, especially any group focused on combatting ‘terrorism.’”
The April 2 meeting in Bridgeport is not the only out-of-state gathering spied upon by HSI during the Minnesota 15 investigation. Reports obtained by defense attorneys through discovery show that events on the same Crimethinc tour in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and Seattle, Washington, were monitored in person by local HSI agents, who reported the speech’s contents back to their colleagues in Minneapolis.

Who's to blame for the toxic haze choking South East Asia?
- Published
As Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic smog is choking millions of residents in the region.
The air on the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra has turned an ominous amber, with air quality recorded at hazardous levels.
The smog - or haze - has drifted beyond Indonesia's borders to neighbouring countries, raising public health concerns. It has obscured Singapore's skyline and forced some schools to close in Malaysia.
Now, anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning farmland, as well as the authorities who have struggled to stop them.
The annual dry season wildfires have been especially intense this year because of an unusually strong El Niño: a natural climate phenomenon which changes weather patterns around the world.
According to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, 1,043,377 wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia, burning a total of 900,000 hectares of land.
Slash and burn
Many of these fires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands are caused by the razing of vegetation to clear land - a practice known as "slash and burn".
This is an agricultural method that has traditionally been employed by farmers in Indonesia to create nutrient-rich soil for new crops.
But today, many of these fires are associated with commercial farming and are taking place on a much larger scale - and are harder to control. Activists and government investigations have repeatedly accused some companies of using fire as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.
While slash-and-burn farming is illegal in Indonesia, enforcement of a ban has long proven tricky.
But persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offenders.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for tougher sanctions against slash-and-burn farming, describing the practice as "ecological terrorism".
Last month, Indonesian authorities announced they had suspended the operating licences of 26 companies linked to the wildfires and launched investigations into others. Cases involving criminal elements would be taken to court, officials vowed.
But it's not just Indonesian companies that have been embroiled in controversy over the haze.
A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia which are linked to plots of land in Indonesia where wildfires are burning.
This includes First Resources, a Singapore-based palm oil company. Between August and September more than 30 haze source points were recorded on land managed by its two Indonesian subsidiaries, according to Greenpeace.
First Resources told the BBC in a statement that it maintained a "strict zero burning policy across all planting activities and implements robust fire prevention, monitoring and firefighting measures throughout our operations".
Greenpeace also named Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, whose subsidiary PT Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana managed land in Indonesia where 19 haze source points were recorded.
Kuala Lumpur Kepong said in a statement that a "majority" of the fires originated from beyond its concession area and had all been extinguished.
"We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations," it said.
'When there is no smoke, we send oxygen'
It remains to be seen how effective governments can be in sanctioning offending companies.
In 2014, Singapore passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act which allows the government to take action against local and foreign firms found to be contributing to the haze.
The following year when Singapore saw a bad bout of haze, authorities issued summonses to several Indonesian companies thought to have cleared land by burning, in a bid to prosecute them under the new law.
But that drew sharp ire from Jakarta, which said the move harmed bilateral ties. And with Indonesia refusing to cooperate, Singapore authorities said they could not obtain information about the suspected companies.
Also in 2015, Indonesia's then-vice-president Jusuf Kalla angered Singaporeans when he said that "for 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us... they have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset".
Similar tensions surfaced again last weekend when Syahganda Nainggolan, who leads the Indonesian government's communications agency, said the raging wildfires were beyond human control and added that the oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
"When there is no smoke, we send oxygen," he added, in a video that has been widely circulated on social media, triggering criticism and ridicule from Malaysians and Singaporeans.
But in the past Indonesia has also apologised to its neighbours for causing the haze.
This year, Indonesian officials have thanked Singapore and Malaysia for offering to help tackle the wildfires, though Jakarta has not officially requested international support.
In Indonesia, there have been efforts by civil society groups to force the government to take action.
In Pontianak in the West Kalimantan province, several groups have filed a class action lawsuit against the Indonesian government and Prabowo, accusing them of "gross negligence" over recurrent toxic haze.
They want the government to declare the haze a national disaster, which would allow for recovery measures such as the covering healthcare costs.
A similar case was filed last year in South Sumatra but was dismissed.
Meanwhile, on the ground in Kalimantan and Sumatra, air pollution levels have been at dangerous levels for weeks.
There are many who have no choice but to brave the toxic smog every day.
"I'm short of breath and have a headache from breathing this air. But I still have to work," Imrayedi, a 63-year-old motorcycle taxi driver in Pekanbaru city, on Sumatra island, told BBC Indonesian last week.
"The government must also think about common people like us. Please take action to find a solution so that this haze problem can be resolved immediately."

A total of 2,390 Gram Panchayats in Tamil Nadu have been declared tuberculosis (TB)-free for 2025.
Asha Frederick, State TB Officer, said the ‘TB Free Panchayat’ initiative aimed to make TB elimination a community-owned movement at the grassroots level, with panchayats supporting prevention, early identification, diagnosis, treatment, and patient support. After verification under the national framework, 2,390 gram panchayats in the State were declared TB-free for the year 2025. These panchayats were felicitated in their respective districts recently, and the collective efforts of panchayat representatives, health teams, and communities were acknowledged.
The criteria for declaring a panchayat as TB-free included — achieving a target of examining 30 or more presumptive TB persons through NAAT and/or microscopy per 1,000 population in the year, a TB notification rate of one or fewer per 1,000 population for the year, and a treatment success rate of 90% or more among notified drug-sensitive TB patients.
Recently, the JOSH Team (Joint Squad for Health) was launched nationally by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, in collaboration with the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports and Ministry of Defence. In Tamil Nadu, Thoothukudi, Tiruchi, Cuddalore, Dharmapuri, and Theni were the five districts selected for the phase-I implementation of the JOSH teams’ field activities.
TB-free panchayats
The teams are being introduced at the block level to strengthen community participation. Each team is led by a designated Class-I Nodal Officer and supported by five “MY Bharat” volunteers and five NCC cadets. These teams will support TB awareness, regular community outreach, identification, and referral of persons with TB symptoms, mobilisation for screening, and other field-level TB elimination activities in coordination with the National TB Elimination Programme.
Dr. Asha Frederick said that at the block level, the JOSH Team would mobilise communities to spread awareness about TB, early symptoms, and available free diagnostic and treatment services, conduct village/ward-level awareness drives, and youth-led campaigns. They will be involved in patient support and handholding by acting as local “support buddies” for TB patients adopted under the Ni-kshay Mitra initiative and will also encourage treatment adherence, provide psychosocial support, and reduce stigma. The teams will build a cadre of young TB Champions to strengthen “TB Mukt Bharat” movement.
She added that the JOSH Teams would also facilitate the distribution of nutritional kits provided by Ni-kshay Mitras (donors) to patients and link patients to additional welfare schemes (ration, social security, health benefits).

Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring contacts of an employee at a plague research institute in Siberia who contracted pneumonia of an “unknown” cause. Local state TV said the woman died last week.
Russian authorities said they found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with. But the case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
The woman worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, southeastern Siberia. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported on Monday (October 5, 2026) that she died last week in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk.
The hospital has been placed under quarantine, Mayor Maxim Modin said on Friday (October 2, 2026), no longer admitting or discharging patients, and its laboratory halted carrying out routine tests. The hospital’s outpatient clinic kept operating as usual, he said.
Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk and met with Gov. Igor Kobzev and other officials on Friday (October 2, 2026).
Mr. Kobzev said everyone who came into contact with the woman is under medical supervision. He didn’t identify the infection and called it a suspected case of “a particularly dangerous infection.”
Rospotrebnadzor was implementing “a full range of anti-epidemic measures,” he added.
Rospotrebnadzor said on Sunday (October 4, 2026) the woman was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” or origin, and said “extensive” testing found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities.”
The agency also said it didn’t uncover any incidents at the institute “involving pathogenic microorganisms.”
Two people who were in contact with the woman tested positive for a virus that causes a common cold and two others for COVID-19, the agency said, adding that others who were tested were all negative.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday (October 5, 2026) he doesn’t think there is cause for alarm, but the U.S. is watching the case closely, aware that “it could spread quickly” despite the quarantine and other public health protocols.
Independent local news outlet Lyudi Baikala quoted sources it did not identify as saying the 28-year-old lab technician died from pneumonic plague and that several Irkutsk hospitals were placed under quarantine.
Asked on Monday (October 5, 2026) to comment on the case, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumours or speculation.”
Rospotrebnadzor did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Irkutsk Aluminum Plant in Shelekhov required staff to wear masks as a precaution, its director Artyom Fominykh said on Saturday (October 3, 2026) on Telegram, calling for calm and adding: “Better be safe than sorry.”
The World Health Organization describes pneumonic plague as a less common but severe form of plague — a disease caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals and their fleas.
“In the event of a potential laboratory exposure, it would be normal to identify individuals who might have been exposed and to monitor them according to the assessed level of risk,” said Dr. Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology at the Imperial College London.
The scale of any monitoring program would depend on “the circumstances of the exposure and the number of people potentially affected,” Dr. Gibani said in a written comment.
Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, said that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia,” although because of modern living conditions and antibiotics, “its potential is therefore limited.”

Anyone purchasing an Apple iPhone Duo online as a Christmas gift may want to find a backup plan.
Expected shipment dates for new orders of the highly anticipated smartphone model have been pushed back to January 25, 2027. That includes iPhone Duos across all available carriers, colors, and storage sizes. For those who pounced on preorders when they went live early Friday morning, shipments will start arriving as early as October 23.
For latecomers, there is always the Hunger Games that is lining up early outside an Apple store on launch day to try to snag in-store inventory. The cheapest version of the foldable phone, with 256 GB of storage, costs $1,999. The model with 2 TB of storage is priced at $3,199.
While early demand for the iPhone Duo is certainly a factor in pushing back shipping dates, it's not unusual for new Apple products to see extended shipment times. Apple is also navigating "limited" supply due to supply chain constraints, Bloomberg previously reported.
Then-CEO Tim Cook talked about general supply constraints on Apple's broader product lineup during the company's third-quarter earnings call in July.
"If you look forward into the current quarter, the September quarter, we continue to expect high levels of demand," Cook said, speaking of broader product demand. "However, with less flexibility in the supply chain, we expect the impact from the supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially."

Cloud infrastructure company E2E Networks’ operating revenue jumped 411% to ₹223.8 Cr in the second quarter of FY27 from ₹43.8 Cr in the year-ago quarter. The company posted a consolidated net profit of ₹72.7 Cr during the quarter under review, reversing a net loss of ₹13.5 Cr a year earlier. Sequentially, revenue increased 42.7% from ₹156.8 Cr, while net profit rose 65.7% from ₹43.9 Cr. Including other income of ₹9.9 Cr, total income stood at ₹233.7 Cr, compared with ₹52.1 Cr in the September quarter of FY26 and ₹168.2 Cr in the preceding quarter. The company attributed Q2 growth to contributions from Blackwell GPUs, better utilisation, and higher average realisation across its GPU fleet. During the quarter, E2E also signed a multi-year cloud GPU contract worth ₹1,000 Cr with an undisclosed sovereign AI company for NVIDIA Blackwell cloud GPUs and allied services. Speaking on the earnings call, MD Tarun Dua said the contract runs through June 2029 and covers existing B200 capacity previously offered on a pay-as-you-go basis. He added that the company’s existing flagship Blackwell capacity will be fully utilised under the contract. E2E expects to complete another deployment of 1,024 B200 GPUs during the December quarter, Dua said. However, management declined to provide revenue or capital expenditure guidance. Founded in 2009 by Tarun Dua, E2E Networks is an AI-focused cloud provider offering GPU computing infrastructure, AI/ML cloud services, and managed hosting. It positions itself as a domestic alternative to global hyperscalers such as Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud for AI workloads. Its offerings include B200, H200, and H100 GPU infrastructure. CFO Nitin Jain said customers under the IndiaAI Mission accounted for roughly 13-15% of quarterly revenue, while international customers contributed around 20-25%. Management cautioned that these proportions could vary significantly between quarters. Total expenses increased 93.4% to ₹136.6 Cr from ₹70.6 Cr a year earlier. Sequentially, expenditure rose 24.7% from ₹109.6 Cr. The company recorded an EBITDA of ₹171.5 Cr, with its margin increasing to 76.6% from 41.1% in Q2 FY26. On the earnings call, Dua said the company sees EBITDA margins of 70% or more over the medium to long term. Dua said E2E is investing in its AI platforms and retaining some GPU capacity for internal research and product development. The company also added a chief revenue officer, a field CTO, and a founders’ office team during the quarter. Alongside its Q2 disclosures, E2E announced the appointment of Crane Venture Partners’ MD Anandamoy Roychowdhary as its strategic advisor. It also appointed Krishnan Mahesh, a nominee of Larsen & Toubro, as an additional non-executive, non-independent director, subject to shareholder approval. E2E Networks listed on NSE’s SME platform, NSE Emerge, in 2018 before migrating to the NSE mainboard in 2022. In June this year, it took the direct listing route to debut on the BSE mainboard. The listing involved no fresh capital raise or issuance of new shares, with existing shares becoming tradeable on the BSE. Shares of E2E Networks ended today’s trading session 2.41% lower at ₹693.7 apiece on the BSE.

In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.
Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.
Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.
So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.
Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.
Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.
Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.
Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.
Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.
Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?
What else we’re reading about
Flydubai incident | Indian pilot Smit Machchar is being hailed as a hero for helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.

South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a $15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
13,626
This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.
Vibe check
Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.
The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”
