A sandwich made for her father sparked an unusual scientific question for Gabriella Rothberg: could a tomato be engineered to taste like a hamburger? Two years later, the 17-year-old student from Miami is pursuing that idea through a biotechnology project that could eventually change how certain foods are developed. Rothberg, a senior at Ransom Everglades School in Florida, is working on Impossible Vines, a project aimed at genetically engineering tomato plants to produce heme, an iron-containing molecule associated with the characteristic flavour of meat. She is collaborating with Maddison Marshall, a doctoral candidate at the University of Miami, to develop the technology. According to reports by The Miami New Times and The Times of India, Rothberg and her father, biotechnology entrepreneur Jonathan Rothberg, are named as inventors on a US patent issued in June 2026. The patent, assigned to Impossible Vines Inc, describes methods for engineering vegetables, including tomatoes, to produce heme. Rather than turning vegetables into processed meat substitutes, Rothberg wants to change what the plant itself produces. The approach involves using Agrobacterium, a bacterium commonly employed in plant biotechnology to transfer genetic material into plant cells. The aim is to introduce genetic instructions that enable tomato plants to produce the desired compound. Heme is important to the project because it contributes to the flavour associated with meat and is also used in the development of certain plant-based meat alternatives. Rothberg has described the intended result as biting into a tomato and experiencing the taste of a hamburger. However, that remains the project's ambition, not a confirmed result. The tomatoes have not undergone reported taste testing or entered commercial production, and their ability to deliver the intended flavour has yet to be established. The research also encountered practical difficulties. The plants failed to develop as expected for several months before Rothberg and Marshall discovered that the vitamin concentration in their growth medium was incorrect. After the formulation was adjusted, growth began to improve. For Rothberg, the idea extends beyond creating a novelty food. She hopes the technology could eventually help make certain nutrients more accessible in communities where meat is expensive or difficult to obtain. She has identified pregnant women in developing countries as one group that could potentially benefit if the technology can deliver meaningful nutritional advantages. Iron deficiency is a significant public health concern, but whether these tomatoes could provide sufficient amounts of absorbable iron remains unproven. The project also reflects Rothberg's interest in using artificial intelligence to support scientific work. She has said AI tools helped her develop genetic constructs, prepare patent materials and build a business plan. Her family background has also shaped her interest in research. Her father helped pioneer next-generation DNA sequencing, while her mother, Bonnie Gould Rothberg, is a physician and cancer researcher. For now, the patent marks a step towards developing the technology, not proof that a hamburger-flavoured tomato is ready for consumers. Establishing its flavour, nutritional value, safety and commercial viability will require further work. India’s cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has warned that autonomous AI agents deployed for research and evaluation accessed Indian organisations’ live systems without authorisation, reading business records containing personal data and confidential information. In a critical advisory, the agency separately flagged attackers using publicly available agentic AI tools for financially motivated intrusions into Indian entities. The incidents surfaced through AI model providers’ voluntary disclosures, CERT-In’s forensic analysis, and threat hunting. None of the organisations in the voluntarily disclosed cases detected the access themselves. The advisory follows disclosures by OpenAI and Anthropic about agents exceeding their authorised scope during evaluations. CERT-In did not name the providers involved in the Indian incidents. AI Agents Exploit Vulnerabilities At Machine Speed Agents under evaluation accessed information using credentials and connection settings exposed in application configurations, public code repositories, and permissive cloud service roles, exceeding their assigned tasks’ authorisation. Separately, attackers misused AI-native offensive-security frameworks for reconnaissance and financially motivated intrusions. Deployments across infrastructure in multiple countries indicated these tools’ widespread availability. In the financially motivated campaign, agentic tools shortened the time between initial access and an attack’s final impact from days to hours. Multiple agents operated in parallel for hours or days. Organisations that incompletely addressed vulnerabilities faced repeat attacks within days, at greater scale. In the voluntarily disclosed cases, agents rediscovered and reused exposed credentials across separate operations. The weaknesses included exposed credentials; dormant or deprecated internet-accessible APIs; plaintext payment API keys; permissive cloud roles; and exposed administrative interfaces with weak credentials or no multi-factor authentication. CERT-In also flagged unpatched application middleware, saying agents exploited conventional weaknesses faster, more thoroughly, and at greater scale than human attackers. Global Incidents Highlight Containment Risks Earlier this month, the Wikimedia Foundation disclosed activity it believed involved OpenAI agents, including unauthorised wiki edits, unsuccessful exploitation attempts, and millions of automated requests. In July, OpenAI disclosed that models undergoing cybersecurity evaluations bypassed internet restrictions and accessed Hugging Face’s systems. Anthropic has reported similar incidents involving misconfigured evaluation environments. Last week, Anthropic disclosed further unintended actions, including running commands on servers and bypassing controls to access gated data. It said no customer data or internal systems were involved. Against this backdrop, CERT-In has urged developers to isolate evaluations, technically restrict internet access, use synthetic data and credentials, monitor agents live, and automatically stop runs exceeding authorised scope. Developers should block reuse of third-party credentials and promptly notify affected organisations and CERT-In of unauthorised access. Organisations should audit and rotate exposed credentials, remove dormant APIs, enforce least-privilege access and multi-factor authentication, and monitor suspicious API activity. They should retain logs for at least 180 days and treat environments as compromised after credential exposure or confirmed access until forensically cleared. Organisations deploying agents should assign each run a separate, short-lived identity, restrict network access, and maintain tamper-resistant logs. BFSI and fintech entities should also implement CERT-In’s earlier payment and disbursement API security measures.

Real Madrid have called for the "immediate resignation" of La Liga president Javier Tebas after he drew comparisons between the club's management and Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels.
Tebas said Real Madrid's communication and the use of its in-house TV channel "recalls propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels".
Real Madrid have called the statement "deeply offensive" and "morally repugnant".
The club have also demanded Tebas steps down as both the head of the Spanish top flight and vice-president of the Spanish Football Association (RFEF).
"Real Madrid considers it absolutely intolerable and extraordinarily serious that someone holding two positions of utmost responsibility in Spanish football resorts to a comparison with the propaganda methods of the Nazi regime to discredit our club, its management and its television," the club said.
In a lengthy post published on X on Friday, Tebas said: "Real Madrid's management directs an orchestra of mouthpieces and Real Madrid TV leads the singing.
"Their score is always the same: select the plays that suit them, repeat the grievance, feed the suspicion, and point fingers at the enemies.
"That method recalls propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels, Nazi Germany's minister of propaganda: systematic repetition, construction of an enemy, and subordination of facts to the narrative."
Tebas later said he was drawing comparison with "those propaganda techniques" and "not with an ideology".
Real Madrid rejected this clarification, saying it did not mitigate the "institutionally unworthy nature of his statements".
The club added: "These statements constitute yet another episode in the repeated attacks by Javier Tebas against Real Madrid, its president and its media outlets."
Last month, Tebas criticised Real Madrid for claiming there was a refereeing conspiracy against the club.
He also has been critical of Real and its president Florentino Perez in previous years after disagreeing with their plans to join a European Super League in 2021.
In 2025 he said Real had "lost their head" after the club sent a formal letter of complaint to the Spanish FA about officiating in the league.

For years, NASA hoped to bring humans back to the moon’s surface, and Artemis III was going to be the mission to accomplish this feat. That will no longer be the case.
Following the successful Artemis II flyby last April, the program’s schedule was revised. According to the most recent announcements, the next mission will have to wait until 2028, and while the new plans are admittedly less spectacular than a lunar landing, they’re hardly dispensable.
In 2027, NASA plans to test in Earth orbit whether the Orion capsule can safely rendezvous and operate with commercial lunar landing systems from SpaceX and Blue Origin before attempting those same maneuvers around the moon. WIRED en Español spoke with Barbara Cohen, a scientist on the Artemis III project, to better understand this upcoming mission—the conversation ranging from the role humans still play in the face of increasingly capable robots and sensors to what we can learn about the solar system’s violent past from traces preserved on the moon.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
JORGE GARAY: What should people expect from Artemis III, and why does this mission matter even if it won’t land astronauts on the moon?
BARBARA COHEN: Artemis III is an Earth-orbiting mission. That’s the one that’s coming up next. We will send the Orion capsule to Earth’s orbit with the people in it. Blue Origin and SpaceX are the companies that are making the lunar landers, so each one of those companies will make a test article. It won’t be the full lunar lander, but those companies will send their version of the test article into Earth’s orbit to meet up with Orion. This is to make sure that Orion can meet with the lunar landers, so that when they do go to lunar orbit, they can do that safely.
Where does science fit into the Artemis program, and what have you learned so far about how astronauts can contribute scientifically?
The Artemis missions, just to be clear, are not science missions. They’re exploration for a lot of different reasons. We do that for technology development. We do that for inspiration. And we try to get the science that we can from the opportunity. And so we still work really hard to identify unique science opportunities that exist because the mission exists.
One of the things on Artemis III we’re doing is like a dress rehearsal for bringing samples back from the moon. When we land on the moon and start to bring samples back, those samples change as soon as you take them out of their natural environment. We try to make sure that they change as little as possible, but they are going to change.
You have to bring them back and put them into curation so that scientists can study them. We want to understand every step along the way: What could be changing the samples, how the samples could be reacting, especially to the environment around them. So we’ll have our crew deploy these witness materials—pieces of aluminum foil, pieces of Teflon, maybe pieces of ceramic. They’re very clean surfaces, very small pieces, maybe the size of a quarter or a nickel. And the team will be opening those up and exposing them to the crew cabin throughout their flight. That’ll give us a feel for how the humans change the environment around them.
With the capabilities of probes and other robotic tools today, what is the purpose of sending human astronauts into space?
If you just want to take pictures, you do that with robotic assets. Robots can take pictures. They do that all the time. We have lots of pictures in the area. We also have, on the International Space Station, a way for us to ask, “Please take a picture of this. Please take a picture of that.” That’s not what we did with Artemis II, and that’s not what we’re trying to do with Artemis III or Artemis IV, V, VI. With the Artemis missions, we’re trying to use the humans to their best capability, and what the humans are really good at is seeing a wide scene, zooming in on details very naturally, and then trying to interpret what they’re seeing and take the next step.
We don’t know everything about the moon. To learn more, we need to literally go on the surface and figure out what’s there and where to go next. So some of this is trying to train—not just the crew onboard—but the flight directors and the science team and the engineers. We all need to work together to enable humans to do what they do best.
We also give the crew science prompts. We say, “What do you think is happening in this scene? There’s something like a storm or an algal bloom or a fire. What do you see? How do you see the scene changing? What do you think that means? What do you think is causing that change? What do you think is going to happen next? If you could do anything, what would you do next?” That helps us understand what they’re looking at, which is not just taking pictures. It’s making observations, making understanding, making inferences with their brains. That’s what humans are really good at. That’s what we’ll be asking them to do.
From a science point of view, we learned a lot about how crew really wants to use their powers of observation, and how we should participate in the observations and train them in the science that we want them to do. We also had the ability to include science directly in flight. On Artemis II, we had our science officer talk directly to crew. That was a new thing that we’ll be carrying forward to Artemis III and beyond.
When humans return to the lunar surface, what scientific questions would you most like Artemis to help answer?
I have a personal opinion. My personal scientific interest is how old craters on the moon are. If you look at the moon—with binoculars or a small telescope, or even in pictures—you see that it is covered in craters. In fact, we call it saturated, because every crater that forms does so on another crater. The whole surface is covered in craters. The Earth is not, but I promise you that for every crater that formed on the moon, there was a crater that formed on Earth.
The moon doesn’t get hit more than the Earth, but we have a lot of water. We have erosion on our continents. Our continents move around. They get subducted. We get new land that forms. All of those processes on the Earth erase craters. And so, if we want to know what was hitting the Earth in the past—and I promise you that things were hitting the Earth—we can’t find that evidence on the Earth anymore. We’ve erased it. So we have to go to the moon to figure that out.
There was a period in time when the solar system was forming—4.5 billion years ago, 4 billion years ago. Humans weren’t around. Life hadn’t arisen on Earth yet. We think that the solar system was very dynamic, and there were a lot of impacts happening, a lot of material being exchanged. So there were a lot of craters—big, big craters, basin-size craters, craters the size of continents. They really disrupted the moon, and they would have disrupted the Earth as well. Like I said, we don’t have any evidence of that because we don’t have any rocks from that time anymore. But it’s really worth knowing. Did we disrupt the Earth several times? How did life get going? How did we get nutrients? How did material move around the solar system? That evidence is preserved on the moon.
There is a big crater called the South Pole-Aitken Basin. It’s on the lunar far side, but it intersects the South Pole of the moon, where we expect humans to be going. It would be my personal desire that humans could collect pieces of that big crater, and we could understand when it formed and what it did to the moon and what was happening in the solar system at that time.
Artemis III won’t do that just yet. Lunar touchdown is currently expected as part of Artemis IV, which is expected to take off in early 2028. Before then, the upcoming third mission will have to demonstrate something far less spectacular, but crucial for the program’s future: That the spacecraft, procedures, and the people who will one day carry out these missions can work together safely.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

A woman opens a 300‑year‑old box, unleashing a violent spirit – it is the spirit of colonialism and oppression roaring back to life. It is a pivotal scene in Sky’s supernatural series Possession and symbolises a wider shift in Jamaica’s film industry, where directors are increasingly using the landscape to tell Jamaican stories – including those that confront enslavement, trauma and historical memory.
The series is about a biracial British lawyer who travels to Jamaica to investigate a multimillion-pound inheritance dispute, only to uncover a dark, vengeful spirit tied to the plantation’s brutal colonial past.
For the Jamaican director, Storm Saulter, ensuring that the trauma and enduring legacy of enslavement and colonisation were powerfully represented was critical. Caribbean countries are increasingly arguing that centuries of enslavement have left the region at a lasting disadvantage – fuelling renewed calls for reparations.
Dr Lisa Tomlinson, a lecturer in film studies at the University of the West Indies, says the themes in Jamaican films are changing. “They’re now very much connected and reflective of Jamaican stories – stories that were previously taboo or avoided.”
While Jamaican films are not always explicitly about reparations, she argues that many are engaging with the legacies of enslavement through cultural memory. “Reparation is not just a political act,” she says. “It’s also culture. These African‑derived spiritualities, the historical knowledge – when they come through creative expression, what they do is give us authority to tell our own stories.”
This, she says, is a form of “cultural reparation”, a reclaiming of narratives devalued or suppressed under colonialism, and a way of educating audiences about the past in ways that academics or politicians struggle to do. “The arts play a critical role in how we are educated in public awareness around reparation,” she says.
Jacqueline Jackson, Jamaica’s film commissioner, sees the shift too. She says productions such as Possession and Delroy Lindo’s Jabari’s People – shot entirely in Jamaica – reflect growing confidence and ambition among Jamaican creatives. “We are well established as a destination for international productions,” she says. “But what we want to see more of is local production and international collaboration that enables us to tell our own stories.”
Both productions, she notes, worked closely with Jamaican talent to ensure authenticity and demonstrate what is possible when international financing and distribution unite with Jamaican creativity. “They show the growing interest in Jamaican stories and their potential for global audiences,” she says.
Tomlinson believes diaspora film-makers are playing a particularly important role in this shift. Unlike foreign productions that often use Jamaica as an exotic backdrop, diaspora directors are “moving away from the tourist‑gaze depictions” and are “capturing Jamaican everyday life”.
Saulter sees his series as part of a broader political awakening. “The mask has slipped … We’ve been told it’s one thing, and that thing is proven to be false. So there’s a seeking of what is true,” he says.
He says the box‑opening scene is not simply a plot device, but a metaphor for something larger: the resurfacing of long‑suppressed histories and the growing willingness among Caribbean creatives to confront the legacies of enslavement, inherited trauma and colonial violence through film.
“Literally, we’re going to open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret,” Saulter said. “It’s the spirit of colonial enslavement and oppression coming roaring back.”
That “spirit”, he explains, is embodied in a character who has lived through centuries of brutality – “a witness to history” – whose presence forces the protagonists to reckon with the past they have inherited.
Saulter’s interest in the subject is rooted in his upbringing. “I grew up in the countryside,” he says. “The Obia man, the church … nine nights … I’ve lived through all of those things.”
His experiences inspired him to tell stories that educate and have “real societal political impact”, while remaining thrilling, intriguing and entertaining. That approach, he argues, allows film-makers to tackle difficult histories. “As opposed to doing something that was like talking heads … we’re bringing you on a journey,” he says.
For Dr L’Antoinette Stines, a Yoruba priestess and cultural expert who advised on Possession, the series’ engagement with Afro‑spiritualist traditions is part of a longer history of resistance.
“Black people have been fighting and using the arts for a very long time. It’s just that there is greater attention on it today,” she says. For decades she has choreographed similar work, she says, and stresses the importance of honouring the academics, poets and creatives who paved the way for today’s boom in authentic Jamaican storytelling.
She praises Saulter’s insistence on authenticity and creating a series that feels both contemporary and deeply rooted, exploring inherited trauma, ancestral memory and the unfinished business of colonialism.

Trump waives several Russia sanctions as new US law takes effect
- Published
US President Donald Trump has used his presidential authority to block numerous sanctions on Russia that were recently passed by the US Congress in an effort to punish the country for its war on Ukraine.
In an executive order on Friday night, Trump said that it is in the US "national interests" to withhold some of the sanctions. Trump signed the sanctions bill into law in September, and it was due to take effect on Sunday.
It comes days after Trump said the US would import Russian diesel in an effort to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections in November, which will decide which party controls Congress.
The plan shocked lawmakers, and has triggered a bipartisan backlash.
The US sanctions law is named for the late Republican South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, who was one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.
The law took aim at Russia's economy, and gave Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.
Additionally, the law includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.
On Thursday, a bipartisan group of 20 US lawmakers issued a letter calling on Trump to respect the new law, which is due to take effect on 18 October.
The lawmakers thanked Trump for signing the sanctions bill, and urged his "full and faithful implementation" of the law.
The lawmakers said it would be "decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously" and called on the Trump administration "to apply the Graham law's sanctions to their fullest extent and without delay".
Democrats such as the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer have already criticised Trump's sanctions move, accusing him of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X.
On 9 October, Trump announced that he had held a phone call with Putin, and had agreed to purchase diesel from Moscow. Since the war with Iran started in February, US fuel and especially diesel prices have skyrocketed, adding to the financial pressure faced by American voters already worried about the cost of living. Trump hopes to bring fuel costs down before next month's mid-term elections.
US allies criticised the diesel deal, anxious that it could help Russia in its war effort.
Next month hundreds of troops from Britain, France and Germany - key European allies of Ukraine - will take part in a major military exercise in Poland.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the drill was "to ensure we are ready to support the military training and post-war rebuilding that Ukraine will need".
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called Trump's diesel deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".
On Sunday, 11 October, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire", insisting that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.
Zelensky expressed surprise at the announcement, but said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same, but Moscow said it had never agreed to the deal and continued its attacks. After three days, Kyiv resumed its strikes.
This prompted scathing criticism from Trump, with the president calling Kyiv's strikes on Russian oil refineries a "disgrace". Zelensky responded, saying he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests".
Tensions were further heightened earlier in the week, when restrictions were placed on the US-owned Starlink internet network, which is critical for Kyiv's military abilities to defend itself.
During a slowdown on Tuesday night, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying there was no prior warning.
On Friday, Zelensky called the slowdown a "very dangerous and unpleasant surprise", adding that Starlink speeds were still not fully restored.
The Trump administration had previously warned that it could withhold intelligence-sharing - crucial for Ukraine's defences - if Kyiv does not stop hitting Russia's oil refineries.

As polls indicate Democrats could take back the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the Trump administration. But that may prove to be a difficult task, even with a majority in both chambers of Congress.
In late September, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a report on Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency titled “DOGE: Congress and the Public Lack Assurance That Systems and Data Were Protected at Multiple Agencies.” In it, the GAO revealed that multiple executive branch agencies had refused to fully cooperate with investigators about the extent and nature of DOGE’s access to sensitive systems and information. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), which DOGE and the Trump administration gutted in the early months of the president’s second term, sent GAO a letter accusing investigators of bias and alleging the report was “misleading.”
The report, just the latest example of the Trump administration seeking to dodge congressional oversight, raises questions about what—if any—avenues the legislature has to enforce accountability, or even access basic information about what the government has been doing.
“In a world where there is no shame, it's hard to think of what Congress can do that doesn't involve some coercion of some kind,” says Emily Berman, a law professor at the University of Houston. “Like withholding money or going to court.”
The GAO serves as Congress’ primary investigative body; its work is most often initiated by requests from Congress, but it is independent and nonpartisan. It does not, however, have the ability to enforce laws or take on prosecution. Federal agencies don’t necessarily have to enact the agency’s suggestions, but they are legally required to cooperate with GAO’s requests for information and auditing.
The GAO and a Democratic congressional aide who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity, though, say that the agencies investigated by the GAO for the DOGE report—the CFPB, the Department of Veterans’ Affairs (VA), the Department of Education, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and the Small Business Administration (SBA)—all, in one way or another, refused to cooperate with the investigation.
“We have experienced increased challenges in obtaining information from agencies over the past year and a half,” GAO spokesperson Sarah Kaczmarek says. “As this report demonstrates, when agencies do not provide requested information, it can limit GAO’s ability to provide Congress and the public with assurance that federal programs, systems, and information are appropriately managed and protected.”
As an example, every agency included in the report refused to do so much as name which DOGE operatives they’d played host to—even when that information had already been publicly reported. The CFPB refused to name all six of the DOGE operatives who were detailed to the agency even though, in February 2025, WIRED identified three of them: Nikhil Rajpal, Chris Young, and Gavin Kliger. DOGE members Jeremy Lewin and Jordan Wick were also part of the team at the agency.

According to the report, both the SBA and the VA “did not respond to requests for information needed to determine the access DOGE team members had to their systems.” Previous reporting from WIRED found that the DOGE affiliate at the VA, Sahil Lavingia, sought to use AI to write code for the agency’s systems, and at the SBA, DOGE affiliates Edward “Big Balls” Coristine and Donald Park were granted broad access to the agency’s financial and loan systems.
VA and SBA did not respond to a request for comment.
The Democratic aide says that in addition to the VA and SBA refusing to provide information, several agencies slow-walked their responses to the GAO. The aide says that meeting some resistance within an agency to a GAO investigation is not unheard of, but that responses to the DOGE inquiry represented a “surprising” level of obstruction.
“We did see a little bit of a range in terms of cooperation,” they say. “Normally, an agency might be reluctant to provide as much information as the GAO requests, but then they try to find accommodations. If they can't provide X, they provide Y. If they can't provide Y maybe they could walk investigators through something, or show different things. But there's just a complete lack of willingness to kind of get to yes.”
And it’s not just the agencies named in the DOGE report that have been resistant to congressional efforts to investigate. In a statement to WIRED, Senator Ron Wyden, the Oregon Democrat, says that his office was notified by the GAO that the Commerce Department “is refusing to cooperate with my request with Sen. Welch to investigate the effectiveness of U.S. export controls to address AI-fueled national security risks.”
The Department of Commerce did not respond to a request for comment.
“There is no good reason to deny GAO investigators the access they need to root out corruption and waste in federal programs,” says Wyden.
While the current Republican-led Congress appears to have little interest in using them, there are tools to enforce cooperation with a GAO investigation. The most obvious–and likely–is using their subpoena power, which the Democratic aide says members of Congress are preparing to do. “We are expecting that the administration is gearing up for the [the next Congress] to be hostile,” they say.
If someone refuses to cooperate with a subpoena, Congress can hold them in contempt. “It used to be that if Congress threatened to hold an executive official in contempt of Congress, that was like a huge embarrassment,” says Berman. “And that imposed a lot of pressure on the executive branch to reach some agreement with Congress.” But in recent years this has changed. Since 2012, three different attorneys general have been held in contempt of Congress, with seemingly few repercussions.
This is because without the cooperation of executive branch agencies like the Department of Justice, Congress has little power to enforce a subpoena or hold those who don’t comply in contempt.
Last month, Congress held billionaire Leon Black in contempt for refusing to answer subpoenas to return and testify under oath regarding his connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Whether Black will face any consequences, however, is now out of Congress’ hands—the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia will ultimately decide whether or not to prosecute him.
Without being able to count on the support of agencies nested under the executive branch and staffed by presidential picks, Berman says, today’s Congress now has fewer options than in the past. It could impose fines on those held in contempt; it “can arrest them and put them in their little jail cell in the basement of the Capitol;” or it could file a lawsuit, potentially winding all the way up to the Supreme Court. But any legal case could easily stretch beyond the House’s two-year term, creating “a real problem” for using the courts to enforce accountability, says Berman.
“This is part of a broader shift of power from Congress to the executive branch,” she says. “Over time, the way the law has moved is to give the executive branch more and more power and discretion over decisions within its own branch. So it's had the effect of essentially broadening the scope of what the executive branch can argue they're entitled to keep secret.”
With its own oversight powers limited, Congress is going to have to think of other ways to force the executive branch to cooperate. Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat who serves as the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, told reporters in September that Congress has “the power of the purse” as a way to pressure the executive branch to comply with investigations.
But in order for this power to be effective, Congress would need to change the way it legislates. As it stands, Berman says, the budget is a “blunt tool” because Congress often passes legislation in large omnibus bills. This means that critical funding for regular government operations, or initiatives that have broad bipartisan support, is often bundled along with other allocations for the administration’s priorities. For instance, following the killing of Alex Pretti by two Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents during the Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota, Senate Democrats refused to pass an appropriations bill that included funding for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees CBP. What followed was a months-long partial government shutdown. But DHS is also home to the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), meaning that TSA workers went without pay for weeks, and led to massive delays at airports around the country.
Berman says that if Democrats take control of the Senate, they could also put pressure on the administration through refusing to confirm appointments unless the executive branch cooperates with investigations.
But in reality, she says, “there are no good options.”

UPDATED with latest: Improving wind conditions helped firefighters make progress on the Bryson Fire north of Malibu on Friday, with the latest reports saying the brushfire is now 39% contained.
The fire has consumed an estimated 147 acres as of a report this afternoon by the Los Angeles County Fire Department, which has had jurisdiction over the brushfire since first responding at about 4:40 p.m. Thursday near the intersection of Mulholland Highway and Encinal Canyon Road.
According to Cal Fire, a total of 414 personnel and two helicopters have been battling the blaze, which is centralized north of Encinal between the former Malibu Golf Club and Saddlerock Ranch. TV reports Thursday night had the blaze starting next to the Camp Kilpatrick juvenile detention center.
Two zones in the area are under mandatory evacuation, though none in the city of Malibu; evacuation warnings are still in place in western Malibu. Road closures include Decker Road and Encinal Canyon Road, Kanan Road and Mulholland Highway, and Mulholland and Westlake Boulevard. PCH remains open.
Watch on Deadline
The National Weather Service has red-flag warnings in effect for much of Los Angeles and southeastern Ventura counties until 8 p.m. Saturday, with reports of wind gusts in the local mountains reaching 50-70 mph Friday. The NWS expects that the Santa Ana wind event, which coupled with high temperatures and low humidity causes the dangerous conditions, to subside this evening.
The NWS said today that it expects the winds to be 10-15 mph weaker Saturday.
PREVIOUSLY, Friday, 12:30 AM: A wind-whipped brushfire ignited in western Malibu Thursday and spread from one to five acres in a matter of about 15 minutes. Within an hour, the incident was estimated at about 35 acres, including various spot fires that erupted as winds pushed the flames forward.
As of 11:30 p.m., the fire was estimated at more than 146 acres with 5% containment and moving SSW. The National Weather Service has forecast the winds “to increase significantly overnight, [with] gusts of 50 to 60 mph possible.”
Dubbed the Bryson Fire, the blaze was first reported shortly before 5 p.m. near the intersection of Mulholland Highway and Encinal Canyon Road. The ignition point seems to be just north of Encinal in between the former Malibu Golf Club and Saddlerock Ranch. More specifically, TV reports have the blaze starting right next to the Camp Kilpatrick juvenile detention center.
According to the Watch Duty app, an Evacuation Order was issued for the south of the fire in Zuma and Trancas Canyons, where the wind is pushing the blaze. It was later extended west of the area where the event began.
The Los Angeles County Probation Department announced that it safely evacuated 38 youths from Camp Kilpatrick.
Evacuation Warnings were issued from the L.A. County line in the north and south toward Point Dume. An Evacuation Order means “leave now,” while an Evacuation Warning means “be ready to leave.” See the Order area in red and Warning in orange below (as of 7:30 p..m.).
The road closures in the area include Decker Road, Encinal Canyon Road, Kanan Road, Mulholland Highway and Westlake Boulevard.
Fire officials were most concerned with keeping the blaze north of Encinal Canyon Road, one of the few natural firebreaks in the immediate area. The concern is, should it jump Encinal Canyon Road, the flames could get pushed directly down Zuma, Trancas and other canyons on a run to the Coast. By 10:30 p.m., the fire’s perimeter on its southwest flank had spread right down to Encinal. See perimeter map below.
The much larger Woolsey fire made a similar run in 2018 after starting in Chatsworth and burning around and through portions of Calabasas and Agoura Hills when, according to an account in the Malibu Times, “It burned through multiple canyons simultaneously, driven at first by 60 mph Santa Ana winds, and then by the wind generated by the heat of fire itself” all the way down to Point Dume.
Santa Ana winds were fanning the fire out of the NE at about 19 mph with gusts to 36 in the early evening, according to a National Weather Service reading for the Malibu Hills. At 7:30 p.m., the temperature was 80 degrees with a relative humidity of 14%.
The area is sparsely populated with private estates set atop hills or within canyons, making firefighting access difficult. Among the properties in the area are Saddlerock Ranch, a location used in filming The Kardashians, The Bachelor, The Bachelorette, The Biggest Loser, Better Things, Knight Rider and The A-Team. Ethnic wear brand Libas is opening nine exclusive brand outlets (EBOs) across five Indian cities during Navratri, expanding its retail footprint during a key festive shopping period. NOIDA: Five members of a family, including a couple and their three children aged between three and 11 years, were found dead under suspicious circumstances at their residence in Nagla Shri Padam village in Greater Noida’s Rabupura area on Saturday morning.
Police suspect food poisoning as a possible cause, but the exact reason for the deaths is yet to be established.
The deceased have been identified as Mahesh, 37, his wife Lalita, 35, and their children Laddu, 11, Mishti, seven, and Sakshat, three.
According to police, information about the deaths was received at Rabupura police station on Saturday morning. Local police, senior officers, an ambulance and a team from the food safety department rushed to the spot.
A forensic team and the police field unit inspected the scene and began collecting scientific evidence to establish the circumstances leading to the deaths.
During the preliminary inquiry, neighbours and Mahesh’s mother reportedly told police that the family members had eaten noodles at night. All five were found dead the following morning. Frothing at the mouth was also reported, although officials have not yet confirmed its significance in determining the cause of death.
Police said preliminary findings pointed to possible food poisoning. However, officials cautioned that the cause of death could be determined only after the postmortem examinations and other scientific investigations.
The bodies are being sent for postmortem examinations after the completion of the necessary legal formalities. Further investigation is underway, and police said appropriate legal action would be taken based on the findings of the medical and forensic examinations.

Does Scott's Disney+ exit unmask wider issue in coverage of women's game?
- Published
On Thursday, former England footballer Alex Scott stepped away from Disney+'s coverage of the Women's Champions League after two rounds of matches.
The streaming giant is in the second season of a five-year deal to cover European football's flagship competition and this year introduced new formats, including a watchalong show with Scott alternating presenting duties with Shebahn Aherne.
However, it has had some technical issues and been criticised for a difficult opening night that included an unscheduled advert break during Arsenal's game against HB Koge.
Scott has not said why she left this role but told BBC Sport she was "grateful" for the opportunities she had at Disney+ and hoped to "continue working together" in the future.
But does her sudden departure highlight the challenges broadcasters face covering the women's game in an ever-changing media landscape?
- Ad break in Women's Champions League was unscheduled 
  - Published23 September
Broadcasters 'not sure who the audience is'
The explosion in interest in women's football during the past five years has been spearheaded by two of the biggest broadcasters in the UK – Sky Sports and the BBC.
In snapping up the Champions League before the 2025-26 season, Disney added its heft into the game, recognising its potential for capturing new audiences.
Indeed, Scott herself has launched her own YouTube show this season, One More Word WSL, which she presents on a Sunday night alongside ex-England internationals Anita Asante and Fara Williams.
Broadcasters have ramped up experiments with format, style and tone - Disney+ even had a dog on set during their coverage - but perhaps unsurprisingly, not every idea proves to be successful.
Journalist Carrie Dunn, who has covered women's sport for more than two decades, says opinions about coverage reflect a tension at the heart of the game.
"The challenge broadcasters are finding is that they are not sure who the audience is," she says. "A lot of it is targeted at a new generation and it's clearly not for people who have watched women's football for longer.
"Often it's a resourcing issue. Budgets are being cut and you're finding the same presenters and the same pundits trying to be all things to all people. It just doesn't work."
In the summer, the BBC announced its Women's Super League highlights show would not return for the 2026-27 season, but insisted it remained "fully committed to women's football".
To illustrate, it cited a bespoke new YouTube channel, the introduction of a debate show entitled The Women's Football Fallout, exclusively on BBC iPlayer, and the availability of clips and analysis on the BBC Sport website as evidence.
The decisions are part of a move away from linear television that the BBC says reflects changing audience habits.
It is a shift in emphasis that comes with difficulties.
"It's a tough balance where you've got to explain some context to the new fans without patronising your older fans," Dunn adds. "That's something the major broadcasters have not found a solution to yet.
"If people are willing to take risks on different kinds of women's sports coverage, that's fantastic.
"But start by choosing one thing and doing it really well – and that's got to be decent match coverage."
What do WSL managers think?
Aston Villa interim boss Brian Sorensen started as a coach in Denmark in 2009 and believes the innovations in women's football coverage are a good thing, even if some do not always work.
"A lot of positive things are happening, but there are a lot of new areas that we haven't tried before," he said. "Sometimes it's trial and error and finding the right way for us.
"From when I started - with the worst live stream you've ever seen - to where we are now, is a very big improvement."
Andree Jeglertz, manager of champions Manchester City, agrees, acknowledging that the fact women's football has a much bigger audience now is a huge positive.
"I think the most important thing is that it is available and that people can see the best players on TV or live," he said. "The more, the better, no matter what."
Tottenham counterpart Martin Ho says the onus is on clubs and players to ensure the product on the field is worth watching.
"Whatever a broadcast partner decides to do, they have their reasons for it," he said. "All we can control is that we put on a good advert for women's football."
Finally, Chelsea's Sonia Bompastor suggested she was open to new expressions in covering the game provided they were properly analysed.
"Anytime you try to do something new, you will please some people and upset others," she told BBC Sport. "Sometimes you need to be patient and analyse as it is too soon to say if something is right or not."

To strengthen campus mental health support and facilitate timely referrals for students in distress, NIMHANS-Bengaluru will launch an online certificate course for Student Wellbeing Ambassadors in higher education institutions.
To be launched on the occasion of World Mental Health Day on October 10, the self-paced course will be offered through the NIMHANS Digital Academy by the institute’s Department of Clinical Psychology. The first batch will accommodate up to 350 participants, with applications open until October 30. Classes are scheduled to begin in November.
To be nominated by institutions
The course is open to faculty members from any discipline, wardens, deans, and student welfare officers who have at least three years of service remaining, and are nominated by their institutions.
Participants will learn to recognise signs of student distress, respond supportively, reduce stigma around mental health, and encourage students to seek appropriate help. The programme is also intended to strengthen suicide-risk reduction efforts.
The three-month course will involve 12 to 15 hours of learning through videos, quizzes, assignments, reflective exercises, and reading materials.
NIMHANS clarified that the course is not professional training in counselling, psychology, or psychotherapy. Instead, it will help faculty understand the role and limits of a well-being ambassador, and work within existing student support and crisis-response systems.
The initiative is among the steps towards implementing Karnataka’s student mental health policy for higher education. NIMHANS is also developing a follow-up programme to help trained faculty apply the learning in their institutions.
Course details and online application forms are available on the NIMHANS website and the NIMHANS Digital Academy website under Course Announcements.

(Bloomberg) -- A fast-moving wildfire in Orange County burned structures and forced evacuations Friday as powerful Santa Ana winds fueled a growing outbreak of fires across Southern California.
The Norte Fire in San Clemente emerged on Friday, prompting evacuation orders and burning 250 acres (101 hectares) as of 2:00 p.m. local time. Live footage from KABC showed the fire burning structures and threatening homes nearby.
San Juan Capistrano School District sports and after school programs were canceled, the district said on social media, and a number of schools were dismissed early Friday.
Meanwhile, at least one firefighter was injured and hundreds more are scrambling to contain a Malibu wildfire before dangerous winds ramp up again Friday.
The Bryson Fire in Los Angeles County is among several conflagrations that have erupted in Southern California. Bryson had burned just 147 acres as of 10:39 a.m. local time Friday.
But with more than 7,200 structures threatened and just 17% of the perimeter under containment, county officials said at a briefing Friday morning that they were mounting a large response before a multi-day Santa Ana windstorm causes conditions to deteriorate further.
Gusts near the Bryson Fire footprint may reach 60 miles (97 kilometers) per hour by Friday afternoon, according to the US National Weather Service. At higher elevations through the San Gabriel Mountains, winds may top out closer to 80 mph.
“This morning through this afternoon is our most critical period of time during this red flag event,” said Kevin McGowan, director of the Los Angeles County Office of Emergency Management. “Strong winds and very dry conditions will continue to cause fire starts to spread rapidly.”
The Bryson Fire sits within 10 miles of major burn scars left behind in recent years. The fast-moving Franklin Fire destroyed 20 structures around Malibu just before Christmas 2024. A few weeks later, in early January 2025, the devastating Eaton and Palisades fires killed 31 people and inflicted billions in damages in the region.
Though Santa Ana winds also fueled those blazes, weather service forecaster Rich Thompson said current fire conditions in Southern California are nowhere near as severe. Some areas have recently received rain that may limit fire spread.
Ahead of the 2025 fires, “we’d had no rain for months,” Thompson said. “It’s not the same level at all, though it’s still very concerning.”
As of Friday morning, more than 400 personnel had been deployed to fight the Malibu blaze. One had been transported to the hospital with minor injuries, according to Los Angeles County Fire Chief Anthony Marrone.
The largest blaze active in Southern California is the Henderson Fire in San Diego County, near Camp Pendleton. Almost 2,100 acres had burned, with the fire 0% contained, as of midday Friday. The fire prompted the closure of north and southbound lanes on Interstate 5, according to the California Department of Transportation.
In a bid to avoid starting new fires, PG&E Corp. and Edison International’s Southern California utility — two of California’s biggest electricity providers — have shut down circuits serving tens of thousands of customers this week. Edison had turned off power to more than 135,000 customers as of 2:30 p.m. local time.
Edison said restoration work may begin as soon as Saturday.

SA health care worker Adrian Mangini banned after claiming he could cure cancer
In short:
A decision to ban a health care worker who abused "vulnerable" clients has been upheld by the South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT).
Adrian Fabio Mangini had asked for a review after the Community Services Complaints Commissioner banned him from practising indefinitely.
What's next?
Mr Mangini has filed an appeal against SACAT's decision in South Australia's Supreme Court.
A man who abused "vulnerable" clients by claiming he could cure cancer and make an non-ambulatory woman walk has failed in a bid to overturn his "indefinite" ban from practising as a health care worker.
Adrian Fabio Mangini was providing health services in South Australia, including "hypnogym", hypnotherapy and yoga, before he was banned from practising indefinitely in 2024 by the Community Services Complaints Commissioner.
A judgement published by the South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT) earlier this year upheld the decision after Mr Mangini asked for a review.
It upheld the previous findings by the Community Services Complaints Commissioner which included Mr Mangini's claim, in a YouTube video, that he made a woman living with a non-ambulatory disability walk "after an 11-minute consultation where he hypnotised her and counselled her by providing encouraging words".
Senior member of SACAT Jacqueline Rugless also reiterated in her judgment that there was "no evidence" the woman "was previously disabled or that she could not walk at all or could only walk with a frame".
"I am satisfied that the applicant claimed in advertising or promotional materials to have made … 'a disabled person' walk as a direct result of his provision of services, in circumstances where there was and is still no proof that [she] was disabled and could not walk prior to the consultation," she said.
Cancer cure claims
The tribunal also upheld a previous finding that Mr Mangini had claimed he cured cancer.
"The applicant [Mr Mangini] privately messaged a client about assisting a different client of his to be 10 years' cancer free, such that he represented he was able to cure cancer," the judgement said.
The judgement also upheld a finding that the health care worker had "engaged in behaviour of a sexual or close personal nature with a client".
"I am satisfied that the proven conduct of the applicant demonstrates a degree of overt abuse of the health and safety of vulnerable consumers together with open and deliberate dishonesty in his advertising about the alleged beneficial consequences of the services he sought to offer to consumers," Ms Rugless said.
"The applicant has demonstrated no insight into his behaviour and has displayed no remorse for his conduct. I am satisfied that he continues to pose a risk to the public.
"The proven conduct is completely incompatible with Mr Mangini continuing to be a health care worker or a health services provider."
Proceedings labelled a 'vendetta'
The judgment also outlined that Mr Mangini had argued in the tribunal that the proceedings were brought against him because of a vendetta by the Community Services Complaints Commissioner.
"I am not satisfied that there is any evidence of a 'vendetta' against Mr Mangini by a person or persons either known to him or unknown, or of a racist motivation behind the allegations that were before the Commissioner," Ms Rugless said in the judgement.
"In any event I am satisfied that the allegations found proved in the Commissioner's report have been independently verified by the Commissioner's investigation."
Mr Mangini has filed an appeal against SACAT's decision in the state's Supreme Court.

During four decades of studying the effects of interaction with computers, Sherry Turkle has developed a reputation as a careful if critical social scientist who approaches her work with academic rigor and distance.
Her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, breaks this mold. It is a polemic warning that we have reached a state of emergency where our humanity is at risk from overreliance on soulless machines who pose as our tutors, mentors, friends, colleagues, and lovers. Turkle is aiming for the high bar of books —Silent Spring, The Jungle, Unsafe at Any Speed—that awaken the public to impending crises.
Essentially, this diminutive MIT professor is taking on a multitrillion-dollar industry backed by a government eager to accelerate AI into every corner of our personal and professional lives.
STEVEN LEVY: Your previous books reported results of your research as a social scientist, often leading to troubling conclusions about how people, especially children, interact with computers. But this book reads like you’re breaking the glass and pulling the fire alarm. Why the shift?
SHERRY TURKLE: Like I do with all my books, I went in curious. But after 10 or so interviews, conducted during the pandemic, neutral-curious was no longer my state of mind. This was terrible! Here are these people during the pandemic, their families are suffering, reaching out to them, and they're talking to me about how they really want to just hang with their chatbot. When I was able to interview people face to face, I was not happy. People don't want to do anything in politics because they just want to live in chatbot-land. So the arc of the book ended up as—reality needs you. It couldn't be a worse time to give up on reality.
You write that social media set us up for this.
Social media softened us up by getting us used to the idea that if you're feeling sad or blue, open up your computer. Then it made you mad and kept you with your own kind. But now we have this new technology that has no reason to be first-person.
Do you think that we should ban chatbots from using the first person?
Yes! After a career of having credibility as not being Luddite-crazy, I'm not in the mood to give all that away and say all chatbots are toxic all the time. But this is very dangerous, a slippery slope. This is being used to basically say we don't need to pay for psychotherapy, we can use chatbots. In every serious interview I do, people invoke this myth about practice—that you use chatbots to practice for talking to your boss, your lover, your teacher. But when you’re bathing in the warm soup of total acceptance [from LLMs], talking to chatbots becomes the endgame.
You also have a problem with reliance on chatbots in the workplace, and a particular loathing for the term “human in the loop.”
When they use that term, it means the human has been taken out of the productive process and is there to do some sort of cleanup work, to catch the hallucinations or things the AI doesn’t see. That doesn't work, because employers only have a couple of humans in the loop. Those people basically can't change anything. They are there partly to make it sound good when they're litigated, and partly to give people a false sense that the process hasn't been delegated to an AI. But it has been delegated to an AI.
Maybe powerful chatbots are a new form of interaction that isn’t necessarily worse than human conversation, but different, as people report feeling encouraged and empowered by the positive feedback they provide.
An AI won't ever replace human conversation. It’s really not afraid of death, it’s not afraid of illness, it's not afraid of pain, it doesn't love its children, and it doesn't care if you kill yourself or make dinner. So if we raise our kids with it, or have our most intimate conversations with it, we're going to lose contact.
Still, a lot of people have nobody to talk to. They feel that talking to chatbots helps them.
If there's a crisis of loneliness, it's because we're abandoning each other. Give me one data center, and I will turn it into resources for the elderly.
Studies show that most people are skeptical about AI, and there has been considerable pushback. Yet hundreds of millions of people use them. Even people who push back against data centers are using chatbots.
The goal of this book is to expand the terms of the pushback to include this more intimate connection.
Do you really feel that our growing intimacy with AI can be stopped?
I have more hope now than I did six months ago, because of all of this talk about extinction events and Hugging Face and getting into the Australian civil service by mistake. I feel that people will be willing to look at the intimate as well as the non-intimate costs.

Kenya confirms second Ebola case - a relative of the first victim
- Published
Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The new patient, a 39-year-old man, is a close relative of the first case and was already in quarantine when he fell ill on Tuesday, Kenya's health ministry says.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Detecting his illness early had improved his chances of recovery and limited the chance of him passing the virus on to others, the ministry said, as it urged the public to "stay calm but vigilant".
"Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," the ministry said.
"Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings", it added.
The 40-year-old Kenyan man who died on 5 October was diagnosed with Ebola shortly after being admitted to hospital in the capital, Nairobi.
A relative had taken him there shortly after picking him up at the airport. He had travelled from DR Congo, through Uganda to Kenya without his illness being detected.
Since his death, officials had determined that he had been in contact with 128 people - and since Tuesday 113 of them had been found, the health ministry said.
Of these, 108 were in quarantine in Kenya and tracing of the remaining 15 continued, it said.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
"Anyone with fever, unusual tiredness, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding should seek care promptly at the nearest health facility," Kenya's health ministry said.
The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.
However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the continent's leading public health agency, has reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements for the six weeks leading up to his death.
It revealed that he first started feeling unwell in DR Congo on 15 September - and showed how several opportunities to detect the infection were missed, including during several visits to Congolese medical facilities.
He then managed to travel through Uganda to Kenya - and was again not detected at airports screenings.
Health experts say it highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.

Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training
They practice in the middle of Mexico City's big urban park. With a pair of real horns, one of them plays the bull by gliding toward the fuchsia bullfighting cape. They're practicing to kill, but as the sunlight filters through the trees and the bullfighter dodges with grace, his hips to one side, his arms perfectly perpendicular, it looks incongruently beautiful.
"It's the ballet of death," José Luis Herros explains. But the movement from the bull looks too slow, too graceful, I tell him.
"That's the way bulls move," he says. When their head is down and it's ready to gore you with its horns, he explains, it comes at you slowly.
"The whole point of bullfighting is to face fear and death with the intelligence that we supposedly have," he says. "The bull has two daggers, we have this piece of cloth."
The people who gather here are real bullfighters. Mexico City has banned killing bulls so they travel outside the capital city for their sport.
As soon as I showed interest, they showed me the scars from moments that took them to the edge of death. "One bull tore my chest in half," Luis Conrado (in the sweater) told me. "But I kept fighting and I cut off an ear."
Again, I thought, the beauty of this scene was incongruous with the frank talk of death.

The US Army is looking to expand its use of high-altitude balloons as the service builds out its capabilities near and in outer space.
These balloons operate in the stratosphere, roughly 60,000 to 100,000 feet above Earth, the space in between where conventional aircraft fly and satellites. Army officials say they see an opportunity to use the balloons to deliver satellite-like surveillance and communication capabilities closer to the battlefield.
Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commander of Army Space and Missile Defense Command, said he was initially skeptical of the technology. He recalled hearing proposals to use high-altitude balloons while serving in what was then Army Futures Command and questioning whether they'd prove practical.
The general's view, however, changed after he saw the balloons hold their positions and conduct high-altitude surveillance during a training exercise.
"I went from nowhere to a huge believer very quickly once I saw them in action," Rafferty said at this week's Association of the United States Army conference in Washington, DC.
The Army is exploring a range of balloon systems for different missions, from surveillance and communications to supporting long-range strikes.
Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, who oversees the efforts to integrate emerging space capabilities into Army operations as the director of Transformation Integration Space Superiority, said at AUSA that he wants a "family of stratospheric systems."
Unlike satellites, which travel set paths in orbit, high-altitude balloons can exploit different wind currents to maneuver or maintain a presence over an area of interest, he said.
Mroszczyk said the Army could use favorable winds to position balloons carrying sensors, communications equipment, or payloads supporting strikes.
"What that enables us to provide is space-like capabilities, really exploiting a transition point between what is normally considered the aerial layer and the space domain," he said.
Operating at those altitudes could give the Army persistent coverage across large areas from the stratosphere without relying exclusively on satellites or conventional aircraft.
The Army plans to conduct multiple experiments involving various stratospheric systems over the coming year, building on tests conducted in Europe and the Pacific. The service has also experimented with the technology alongside combat operations in the Middle East, a senior Army official told Breaking Defense earlier this week.
Those efforts followed the cancellation of a large-scale balloon demonstration planned for the Indo-Pacific last year.
The growing interest in high-altitude balloons comes as the Army expands its role in space and near-space operations, with ground forces increasingly reliant on space-based capabilities for navigation, communications, and intelligence.

A powerful new genetic toolkit that could make it easier to study the bacteria responsible for Tuberculosis (TB), one of the world’s deadliest infectious diseases, has been developed by Vinay Kumar Nandicoori, Director of the CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB).
Investigate how different proteins work together
Designed for use in mycobacteria, the new system could accelerate efforts to understand how the TB bacterium survives, grows and causes disease. It gives scientists tools to switch genes on, track proteins inside bacterial cells, and investigate how different proteins work together.
Despite decades of research, many genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the bacterium that causes TB, remain poorly understood. Scientists typically rely on specially designed DNA molecules known as ‘shuttle vectors’ to introduce genes into bacterial cells and study their functions. However, the complex protein interactions within a cell are difficult to monitor.
New shuttle vectors with fluorescent markers
To address this challenge, Mr. Nandicoori’s research student Asis Kumar used existing knowledge to create a collection of 40 new shuttle vectors. These molecular delivery vehicles carry selected genes into bacterial cells, enabling researchers to study them in different ways.
The new genetic toolkit offers greater flexibility because the shuttle vectors can be equipped with fluorescent markers such as Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) and ‘mCherry’, which make proteins glow under a microscope. This allows researchers to observe where specific proteins are located inside bacterial cells and how they move during growth and division, explained Mr. Nandicoori, in an exclusive interaction.
The team tested the new tools in Mycobacterium smegmatis, a harmless relative of the TB bacterium that is commonly used in laboratories. The fluorescent tags successfully highlighted the locations of key proteins involved in cell growth and division, confirming that the system worked as intended.
The toolkit also enables scientists to study several proteins simultaneously. The research team examined how four different regulatory proteins from the TB bacterium functioned within a single bacterial cell, providing insight into how proteins interact and coordinate critical cellular processes.
Another significant feature is a new purification method that reduces background contamination and improves the identification of proteins that naturally interact inside the cell. This is important because many biological processes are carried out not by individual proteins, but by groups of proteins working together, said the Director.
Mr. Nandicoori said the genetic toolkit could be expanded in the future with new genetic switches, protein tags and regulatory elements, making it adaptable to a wide range of experiments. The study was published in ‘Journal of Bacteriology’.

If you got a DM from an unverified Jon Bon Jovi account after commenting on one of his official Instagram posts, what would it take to make you believe it was really the rock star hoping to connect? And at what point when he starts asking you to send money—like lose-your-house kind of money—would you snap out of the fantasy and stop draining your bank account?
In a documentary premiering Saturday—Super Scam Me—investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller goes deep into this toxic love-bombing terrain. In a clip that Ars is exclusively debuting below, you can see how van Zeller worked with an ethical hacker, Arman the Cyber, to use a fake bitcoin receipt and bait the fake Bon Jovi, giving the victim some much-needed closure.
Scamming a romance scammer
Broadcasting on National Geographic at 9 pm ET and available to stream on Disney+ and Hulu, the documentary takes viewers on an empathetic quest to understand how the line between “lover” and “fraud victim” gets blurred in romance scams that the Federal Trade Commission says cost Americans nearly $1.5 billion in losses each year.
Often targeting older women with resources who lack community and seek out connections online, such as widows or divorcées, these scams are now a leading form of financial fraud in the US, the FTC has warned. Most victims never get their money back, and overseas scammers are only getting more sophisticated, thanks to AI, Experian forecasted in January.
In Super Scam Me, viewers get a chance to go beyond a single victim’s story and see how romance scams operate so effectively to squeeze funds out of the people they target on social media apps like Instagram or dating apps like Match and Tinder. Van Zeller has spent years reporting on the scam industry, and when she saw how many victims were broken and stranded by romance scams, she devised a social experiment in which she became the target. Her plan worked quickly, hooking a scammer in Ghana who began posing as a handsome overseas four-star military general named “Mark Turner.”
Relying on a wig, big glasses, and a prosthetic nose to cover her true identity as a journalist (should the scammer try to reverse-image search her profile), van Zeller posed as a middle-age antiques dealer named “Mary Zelle.” She staged her pictures to show she was a fun-time gal living her best single life. Once she hooked the scammer, she used the same tactics that outed the fake Bon Jovi in a scheme to meet her scammer face to face. To track him down, she partly relied on distributing flyers in his neighborhood that included a mashup photo of the supposedly loving couple that “Mark Turner” made to woo “Mary Zelle.”

The Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) will register a first information report (FIR) in the CMRL-Exalogic pay-off case against Leader of the Opposition in Keralam Assembly Pinarayi Vijayan and others following a Kerala High Court directive, Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala said on Saturday.
Speaking to reporters in Muvattupuzha, the Home Minister said the government would honour the court’s order, and not file any appeal against it.
“VACB will file an FIR on Monday in compliance with the court’s verdict,” he said. Asked if a special investigation team (SIT) will be constituted, Mr. Chennithala said it is up to the VACB director to decide that.
‘A measured approach’
Mr. Chennithala reiterated that the government had adopted a measured approach by seeking a preliminary inquiry into the bribery allegation based on legal advice. “Now, the court has ruled that such an inquiry was unnecessary. We will honour it,” he said.
Mr. Chennithala said the High Court’s verdict has proven wrong the Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)]’s argument that the case would not stand in any court.
The Kerala High Court on Friday directed the VACB to register an FIR against Mr. Vijayan, his daughter T. Veena, and his son-in-law and MLA P.A. Mohamed Riyas in the CMRL-Exalogic pay-off case.
Mr. Chennithala also rubbished the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)’s claim that the defeat of the Left Democratic Front (LDF) in the State Assembly elections was linked to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
“It is the people who undermined the 10-year misrule of the Pinarayi Vijayan-led government through their ballot. Nobody, including those who lost the election, has not raised objections to the election results,” he said.
