Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Amazon's premium tablet gets almost everything right
This tablet is a great value, even if Android apps still aren't great on a big screen.
Amazon has long followed the same formula for its tablets. Fire tablets are known to be cheap, durable devices good for watching video and doing casual tasks like browsing, playing basic games and checking out Facebook. They're more limited than the average Android tablet, without access to the Google Play Store and its wealth of apps. Amazon's own app store has received plenty of support from developers over the years, but it's still missing plenty of crucial options like Whatsapp and YouTube, just to name a few.
This year, however, Amazon is changing up its strategy. Its new series of Alexa tablets may highlight the company's services and assistant first and foremost, but they're also full-fledged Android tablets with plenty of Google's own apps and access to the Play Store. The Alexa Tablet Pro 12 is easily the most intriguing of the new lineup (which also includes non-pro 8- and 11-inch options). While Fire tablets have always focused on media consumption, the Tablet Pro 12 is clearly squaring off with the iPad Air and Pro. At first glance, it looks nearly identical to Apple's tablets, with a fairly thin bezel surrounding a lovely and large display, and an aluminum unibody design that's relatively thin (6.5mm) and light (1.21 pounds).
Its optional keyboard and stylus accessories complete the look and signify that the Alexa Tablet Pro 12 isn't just meant for watching videos. This is a tablet meant for getting things done — and while it isn't quite as capable as Apple's iPad lineup, mostly due to software limitations, its $499 starting price means it's much easier to forgive the places it falls short.
Hardware
You'll be forgiven if you mistake the Alexa Tablet Pro 12 (from here out I'll just call it the Alexa Tablet) for a recent iPad Air or Pro, because they look very similar. The shorter sides of the Alexa Tablet have speakers on them; one end has a power button with a fingerprint sensor for unlocking the tablet, while the other has a lone USB-C port for charging and data transfer (it recognized my SD card reader and a USB-C flash drive without issue). I'm bummed not to see a headphone jack anywhere, but not surprised.
On the Alexa Tablet's top edge, you'll find volume up and down buttons as well as a groove where you can magnetically attach the Alexa Tablet Pro Pen for charging and storage. The bottom side meanwhile has a four-pin port where the Alexa Tablet's keyboard connects. The back of the not-quite-pitch-black tablet has a single 13-megapixel camera and the word "alexa" in a charming cursive font — the word Amazon doesn't appear anywhere on the device.
The Alexa Tablet sits comfortably between the 11- and 13-inch iPad Air in terms of thickness and weight. It's slightly thicker at 6.5mm (compared to 6.1mm) and a bit heavier than the 11-inch iPad Air (1.21 pounds compared to 1.02 pounds). Regardless of these minute differences, the Alexa Tablet's aluminum unibody design feels study, premium and well-balanced. It's a huge step forward from most Fire tablets I've tried over the years.
Nanomatte display
As with all tablets, the Alexa Tablet Pro 12 is dominated by its screen. The 12-inch screen may not be an OLED, but it's still a very nice display with 500 nits of brightness and a 2,800 x 1,840 resolution. That works out to a very dense 280 pixels per inch, and the 3:2 aspect ratio is definitely preferable on a tablet to something like 16:9. The tablet is primarily designed to be used in landscape mode, but the on-screen keyboard is a bit cramped from a vertical space perspective. And when you use the Alexa Tablet in portrait, it feels just a bit too tall to be comfortable. Apple's tablets have always used a 4:3 aspect ratio, and that just feels right to me at this point. But 3:2 still offers a decent amount of vertical height while still giving widescreen movies plenty of space.
And while I might prefer the iPad's aspect ratio, the Alexa Tablet's screen is superior to what you'll get on an iPad Air in a few significant ways. First, it has a 120Hz refresh rate – to get that on an iPad, you'll need to spend at least $1,199 for an 11-inch iPad Pro. Unfortunately, the Alexa Tablet software isn't as well optimized as iPadOS, so things often felt jerkier than you'd expect given that high refresh rate. More on performance in a bit.
While the higher refresh rate is nice, the Alexa Tablet really sets itself apart from basically every other tablet out there with its so-called nanomatte display finish. This is an optional feature that adds $50 to the tablet's price — but it is well worth it. Nanomatte is Amazon's term for the anti-reflective etching that does a remarkable job of minimizing glare. Placing the Alexa Tablet next to my iPad Pro (with its standard front glass) on my desk in the early morning light made it immediately obvious how effective the nanomatte display is at reducing glare from strong light sources to nearly nothing.
Not to harp on the pricing, but the cheapest iPad that Apple sells with its nano-texture glass is the 11-inch Pro with 1TB of storage, which costs $1,799. iPad Pro prices, which were already hard to stomach, hit the positively bonkers level over the summer when Apple jacked up prices on nearly all its products. This makes the Alexa Tablet look all that much more compelling by comparison. Yes, the iPad Pro's tandem OLED screen is one of the nicest screens I've ever seen, but Amazon has done a seriously excellent job with the screen on the Alexa Tablet considering its price.
My only real complaint about the nanomatte screen is that colors feel a bit washed out when there's a strong light source shining on it. It's still much easier to use than it would be without the nanomatte texture, but things don't look quite as vibrant. Of course, having this option makes a ton of sense, given the inherent portability of a tablet. You're likely to use this screen in a wide variety of places with shifting and unpredictable lighting conditions, and the nanomatte option means you see the screen clearly in nearly all settings.
Alexa Tablet is a surprisingly good reader
The nanomatte display feels particularly well-suited to a few of the Alexa Tablet's more noteworthy features. The first is a new Kindle app experience that makes this probably the best tablet with an LCD display to read on. The Alexa Tablet has dark mode on by default, and I typically haven't loved reading books with a black background and white text, but it looks great on this device. There are some smart software tricks here to enhance the reading experience, as well. Amazon says the Kindle app automatically reduces blue light from the display when you open a book and notifications are muted while you're reading (assuming you turn these features on).
There are also three different display profiles for when you're reading. "Standard" makes the display warmer while keeping bright colors (if you're reading a book with images), while "color paper" makes everything a lot less saturated. Finally, "ink paper" is purely greyscale. I don't have many books with color to test this with, but the cover and first few drawings in a Sailor Moon collection I downloaded looked great in the "color paper" theme — the reduced vibrance seems like it would definitely be easier on the eyes for long reading sessions.
Combine these features with the extremely sharp display and lack of glare and you've got a tablet worth reading on for long periods of time. It doesn't match the comfort of an E Ink Kindle — but it provides a great reading experience for people who prefer a multi-function device over a dedicated e-reader.
Alexa Tablet as a tablet
When you first start up the Alexa Tablet, it's obvious that this is an Amazon-first affair. The home screen has shortcuts to a variety of the company's apps like Kindle, Luna, Prime Video, Audible and Amazon's own Silk browser. But there's also a folder with a bunch of Google apps like Gmail, Maps, Meet, YouTube and more ready to go. And as a full-fledged Android tablet, I was able to quickly download Chrome and a variety of other apps from the Play Store. So while Amazon's services are right up front, it's easy enough to swap them out with your apps of choice.
There are a few other UI tweaks that make this tablet more Amazon than Android, as well. There are two widgets on the home screen; one in the upper-left corner shows content you've interacted with recently on Amazon's apps. I can quickly tap to resume reading my last Kindle book or playing an album on Amazon Music, for example, or continue searches that I was doing with the Alexa+ app. Speaking of Alexa+, there's a widget in the bottom right corner of the home screen that automatically pulls up a chat window with Amazon's virtual assistant. Naturally, you can also say "Hey Alexa" to initiative requests with your voice, as well. Surprisingly, there's also a Google search widget in the top-right corner of the home screen, too. So while Amazon clearly wants to feature Alexa+, it's not against giving Google some screen real estate too.
Going beyond the reading experience I described earlier, the Alexa Tablet is more than capable of doing most things people expect from a tablet. The lovely screen makes it an excellent choice for watching movies or binging YouTube, and the speakers support Dolby Atmos. That only means so much on a small device, but I definitely got a semblance of dialog moving through physical space in a few of the movies I checked out. Music sounds surprisingly solid as well, certainly good enough for casual listening sessions in a small space. I generally prefer to use headphones or a more capable speaker, but the audio quality certainly beats many tinny laptop speakers I've heard over the years.
Other apps I installed from the Play Store worked well, for the most part. The inescapable fact that has always held Android tablets back is that not many developers optimize apps for larger screens, and that's still the case here. So while something like Slack is functional enough, it doesn't have multiple columns so you can see your channels on the left and a chat window on the right, for example. There's no other way to say it: It still feels like a blown-up phone app rather than something designed to use the entirety of a large screen.
While that's certainly a bummer, plenty of the most popular apps people use work just fine. Adobe's Lightroom is nicely optimized for tablets at this point, as is my go-to task manager Todoist. And Google's apps were all redesigned for bigger screens back when the company tried to make the Pixel Tablet a thing of the past, so using things like Gmail, Keep, Docs and other essential apps works nicely on the Alexa Tablet.
Amazon built in some pretty solid multitasking capabilities here, as well. When an app is in fullscreen mode, you can tap a bar at the top of the screen to put it in a split view with a second app, or send it to the "desktop." The desktop view lets you resize and overlap multiple apps however you like — I've had a half-dozen open at once with no real issues, but the Alexa Tablet's screen isn't so large that it makes a lot of sense to run more than a handful at a time.
The MediaTake Dimensity 8400 processor powering the Alexa Tablet was more than capable of keeping up with everything I did, as well. The model I'm testing has 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, but you can double both of those if you think you'll need it. I'd personally choose to upgrade to the nanomatte display before maxing out RAM or storage, but that's just me. That said, there were a handful of times apps went unresponsive on me, and alt-tabbing through different apps was a bit laggier than I'd like.
As for the battery, I haven't had time yet to test Amazon's claims of 16 hours of video playback, but I'm getting closer to eight hours off the charger when using it for a variety of work-related tasks like editing stories, chattering away in Slack, browsing with Chrome and writing this review in Google Docs. I'll update this story with more concrete battery benchmarks soon.
Pro accessories
A big part of what makes the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro "pro" are its optional keyboard and pen. On their own the Pro Keyboard and Pro Pen cost $150 and $90 respectively, but you can save money by bundling the pen and keyboard (or just the keyboard) with the tablet when you buy it. The Alexa Tablet I tested with 8GB RAM, 128GB of storage and the nanomatte display costs $550 on its own, but you can bundle it with the keyboard for $650 or the keyboard and pen for $700. (That's less than an iPad Air on its own, if you were keeping count.)
The keyboard folio is a two-piece accessory — there's a kickstand that attaches to the tablet's back, while the keyboard itself snaps to the bottom side. I don't love the tablet/ keyboard/kickstand combo personally, as it's very difficult to use on your lap. But for the cost, I will absolutely cut Amazon some slack. Apple sells its two-piece keyboard folio for the basic iPad for $249; chopping $100 off that price, or more if you get a bundle, makes its wobbly nature more forgivable. The combo feels fine on a sturdy surface like a desk.
The keyboard itself is compact but not cramped, with most of the main keys being close to the same size as what you'll find on a typical laptop. The main issue is that the key travel is rather shallow, an unavoidable compromise with such a thin keyboard. So while it wouldn't be my first choice for extensive writing sessions, it still feels quite nice for such a small keyboard. I wrote this entire review on it without any major issues.
The biggest problem I had was the prominent Alexa key where I'd usually expect a control key — I found myself frequently trying to use it for standard keyboard shortcuts only to bring up the Alexa+ chat window instead. I get Amazon's thinking here, but Alexa is already easily accessible throughout the tablet. There's also a search key on the left of the space bar; I would have preferred this be where the Alexa key was placed, but that's just me. The search key could have gone in the top row of function keys instead of a "find" key that doesn't work in a lot of apps. And while the trackpad is unsurprisingly rather narrow, it's otherwise smooth and responsive.
The Pro Pen is a capable accessory, as well. I'm no visual artist, but the Alexa Tablet picked up my scribbles from the Pro Pen in apps like Keep and Concepts. The Pro Pen has both pressure and tilt sensitivity, which should make it a pretty capable drawing tool. And Amazon put an "eraser" on the other end, so if you want to clean things up you can just flip the pen around. That's a trick I wouldn't mind Apple stealing for its own stylus.
Bang for the buck
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is not a perfect device. While the hardware is well-designed and the nanomatte screen is outstanding, the inherent limitations of Android on a large screen hold the device back a bit. I can't say I expect that to change — Google and its partners have repeatedly tried to make Android into a proper tablet OS that can rival the iPad, and it just hasn't happened.
However, it's far easier to forgive this when you consider the things that the Alexa Tablet does well and its price. For $550, the Alexa Tablet is a great couch computer and travel companion. I wouldn't use it to do my job for 10 hours a day, but I'd happily work on a story draft or bang out some emails for a few hours. And the nanomatte screen makes it an excellent reading tablet and a solid option for watching movies on a flight.
I think most people who want a tablet will still probably be happier with an iPad, but Apple's entry-level tablet is sorely in need of an update. Plus, it only costs $50 less than the Alexa Tablet. Stepping up to an iPad Air will cost you at least $750 before buying accessories — and for that kind of money you need to be really committed to getting as much as you can out of it. The Alexa Tablet, on the other hand, sits in a sweet spot of price and capability, even if I wish the Android app situation was better. At a time when hardware prices are going through the roof, Amazon's Alexa Tablet is a compelling option.

National Sports Federations (NSFs) can receive financial assistance of up to Rs. 30 lakh to organise National Championships in high-priority sports disciplines, while the ceiling for priority and general disciplines is Rs. 25 lakh, according to the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports’ revised guidelines for assistance to NSFs.
The guidelines prescribe different funding limits depending on the categorisation of the sport and lay down participation requirements that federations must meet to qualify for assistance.
For National Championships in high-priority disciplines, the maximum admissible assistance is Rs. 30 lakh each for senior, junior and sub-junior/youth/cadet categories. The ceiling is Rs. 25 lakh for the corresponding categories in priority and general disciplines.
However, the amount a federation receives depends on the participation of its affiliated units. Federations that secure participation from 75% to 100% of their affiliated units are eligible for the full admissible grant. If participation falls between 50% and 75%, the scale of assistance is reduced by 25%. No grant is provided if fewer than 50% of affiliated units participate.
The guidelines also stipulate that the participation requirement applies separately to men’s and women’s championships. For sports federations catering to persons with disabilities, including those affiliated with the Paralympic Committee of India and the All India Sports Council of the Deaf, the maximum assistance for National Championships is Rs. 20 lakh for each discipline across all categories.
The Ministry has also provided for financial assistance of up to Rs. 25 lakh per tournament for organisers of selected prestigious tournaments conducted in India. These include events such as the Subroto Cup, Durand Cup and Jawaharlal Nehru Hockey Tournament.
The assistance forms part of the Ministry’s broader scheme to support the activities of recognised National Sports Federations, including competition and athlete development.
The guidelines state that financial assistance to NSFs is supplementary in nature. Federations are expected to generate their own revenue to support their operations, while using government assistance alongside other funding sources, including sponsorships and support from public and private institutions.

Actor and investor Varun Dhawan is highlighting biofortification as a way to improve the nutritional value of everyday staples such as atta, rice and dal. On the occasion of World Food Day, the actor has spoken about his investment in Better Nutrition, a brand working with biofortified staples, and his efforts to explore the process on his own farm.
World Food Day 2026: Varun Dhawan backs biofortification after joining Better Nutrition as investor and brand ambassador
Explaining what drew him to the concept, Varun said, “I feel really proud to be part of something that could make a difference to India. When I first learnt about biofortification, I found the idea amazing. What if we could grow more nutrition into the atta, rice and dal we eat every day, right from the seed?”
He added, “I believed in this enough to invest in Better Nutrition and start biofortifying my own farm. Imagine if this could reach millions of Indian homes. I’d be really proud to have played a part in that.”
The actor has also shared a video on social media to explain the concept and encourage more people to learn about its potential role in improving nutrition.
View this post on Instagram
What is biofortification?
Biofortification involves increasing the levels of specific nutrients in crops as they grow. Unlike conventional food fortification, which adds nutrients during processing, biofortification focuses on improving the nutritional content of crops themselves.
The approach can be applied to staple crops such as wheat, rice and millets, which form a regular part of diets across India. The idea is to improve the nutrient content of foods people already consume rather than requiring them to make significant changes to their eating habits.
In 2020, Prime Minister Narendra Modi dedicated 17 biofortified varieties across eight crops to the nation on World Food Day, highlighting their potential contribution to the country's nutritional security.
Varun Dhawan invests in Better Nutrition
Varun has invested in Better Nutrition, which offers biofortified staples, including atta, rice and dals, through its website and quick-commerce platforms. His involvement also extends to exploring biofortification on his own farm.
The initiative comes amid wider conversations around food quality and nutritional security. By drawing attention to the process, Varun hopes to encourage greater awareness of how the nutritional value of staple foods can be improved.

In October 2026, social media users spread an image that claimed to show a woman being punched in the face at one of U.S. President Donald Trump's rallies.
The person in the picture was wearing a shirt that said "RELEASE THE EPSTEIN FILES." (The Justice Department has released millions of files related to its investigation of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, but critics allege the agency made redactions to obscure information.)
The image circulated on platforms such as X and Facebook. Many users sharing the image appeared to believe it was authentic.
"If there's one photo to sum up the Trump era, this is it," one X post aid.
While a protester wearing a similar shirt was, in fact, attacked at an Oct. 12 Trump rally in Youngstown, Ohio, the image above was created using generative artificial intelligence, according to OpenAI's detection software. As such, we have rated this image as fake.
OpenAI's verification tool detected an invisible watermark on the image called SynthID, which the company's AI tools, like ChatGPT, embed in generated images. (As such, the service can only detect images generated with OpenAI's software and does not detect AI generation via other large-language models, such as Google's Gemini.)
(OpenAI)
SynthID detectors are largely accurate but can still be fallible. However, a review of credible footage taken from the Trump rally indicated that the actual protester was wearing slightly different clothing, including an open flannel layered on top of the T-shirt. The T-shirt the real person wore also had variations in the lettering style and coloring, unlike the more uniform version in the AI-generated image.
A reverse-image search could not determine the original creator behind the AI-generated picture.
Numerous reputable news organizations, including NBC News and an ABC affiliate, have published legitimate footage of the event.
NBC News' video shows rally attendees chanting, "USA, USA, USA" as a man in a gray shirt and a baseball cap appears to push down the protester. Another man in a dark blue or black shirt appears to tackle the protester, hit her and put her in a headlock. Security officials then escort the protester away. 
Another clip posted by WKBN, a Youngstown television news station, shows that the same man pulled on the protester's hair:
Images of the incident are also available via credible photo repositories, including Getty Images and Reuters.
NBC News reported that there were no arrests "because deputies didn't see the beating and the woman elected not to file a report, Sheriff Jerry Greene said."
Trump, meanwhile, mocked the protester's weight while watching the attack unfold. "You know they're paid protesters," Trump said, without evidence. "That's a very low-class protester."
The protester has not publicly shared their identity with the media as of this writing.

October 2022 - Geneva, WHO signed new agreements with a variety of civil society, political and community stakeholders in October at the World Health Summit in Berlin, a three-day hybrid event that reached some 60 000 participants worldwide.
For the first time, WHO co-hosted the Summit, which drew 4,100 in-person participants from 141 countries to more than to more 60 sessions with a common goal: improving health for everyone, everywhere. At the event, WHO expanded partnerships with civil society and advocates, and formalized strategic engagements with non-traditional stakeholders - relationships critical to reaching global health goals.
Read on for highlights from the Summit:
International Association of National Public Health Institutes (IANPHI)
IANPHI and WHO signed a memorandum of understanding outlining ways the two agencies intend to work together to strengthen public health functions and health emergency preparedness.
WHO and IANPHI share the vision that essential public health functions are a comprehensive and cost-effective approach to advance universal health coverage, health security and healthier populations. The strengthened alliance between WHO and IANPHI is critical to ensure that global and regional structures are designed to support national and local capacities and provide the right avenues for collaboration and coordination.
Read more: International Association of National Public Health Institutes partners with WHO
UNITE, Parliamentarians Network for Global Health
Showing the diversity and wide reach of the Summit, WHO also signed a memorandum of understanding with UNITE at an event attended in person by more than 40 parliamentarians from 30 countries.
The agreement represents a new step in strengthening WHO engagement with parliaments; UNITE committed to support WHO in raising awareness and building capacity of parliamentarians in three strategic areas of global public health:
- equitable access to health, with a focus on universal health coverage;
- health system strengthening, with a focus on supporting sustainable financing for global health; and
- efficient global health architecture and security and the promotion of the pandemic treaty.
Read more: Parliamentarians commit to support global health (18 October 2022)
Dr Ricardo Baptista Leita, President and Founder of UNITE and Dr Tedros, Director-General, WHO
King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief)
WHO and UNICEF signed US$ 10 million in funding agreements with KSRelief to bolster polio and measles programmes in eight countries.
The new funding - providing US$ 5 million each to WHO and UNICEF - comes in response to an emergency call to action by the two agencies to avert major polio and measles epidemics. Both Organizations have urged countries to prioritize childhood vaccination following global disruptions to immunization programmes caused by COVID-19.
WHO plans to co-organize the 2025 World Health Summit.
Read more: UNICEF and WHO welcome KSRelief funding for measles and polio epidemics prevention
From left to right: Catherine Russel, Executive Director, UNICEF; Dr Abdullah Al Rabeeah, Supervisor General of King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief); Dr Tedros, Director-General, WHO
A global consortium to help smokers quit
WHO also launched a business coalition to support the Organization’s work on tobacco cessation and bring more smokers the tools and medications they need to quit. The Tobacco Cessation Consortium is a public-private partnership fighting tobacco dependence.
An estimated 1.3 billion people use tobacco products, 80% of whom live in low- and middle-income countries. In Germany, where the Consortium was launched, 23% of the adult population smokes.
Latest numbers show that 60% of tobacco users worldwide have expressed a desire to quit, but only 30% have access to comprehensive tobacco cessation services.
The Consortium will focus on solving challenges in collaboration with partners, across five pillars: pharmacotherapies and steady delivery of products and medicines that help people quit tobacco; strengthening health systems; speaking to people in power and advocating for increased investment in cessation; identifying innovations and research ideas, reaching more people through digital channels, and promoting the tools developed by partners.
Pledging to end polio worldwide
ermany co-hosted a global polio eradication fundraising drive at the Summit that yielded pledges of US$ 2.6 billion.
The money will help the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) carry out its 2022-2026 strategy to overcome the final hurdles to eradicating polio, including vaccinating 370 million children over the next five years and continuing disease surveillance across 50 countries.
GPEI is seeking US$ 4.8 million to end polio, which would become the second disease after smallpox to be eradicated by human intervention.
Pledges came from Australia, France, Germany, Japan, Republic of Korea, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Spain, Turkey, United States, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Bloomberg Philanthropies, the Islamic Food and Nutrition Council of America, Latter-day Saint Charities, Rotary International and UNICEF.

Nvidia's communications organization has been reshaped as the company became the face of the AI boom, with multiple teams brought under new leadership and a string of departures.
Business Insider identified roughly 15 communications employees who have left Nvidia since 2025, based on LinkedIn profiles and interviews with former employees.
The organization now numbers roughly 70 to 80 people globally, and has more than doubled in size since Mylene Mangalindan joined as vice president of corporate communications in 2023, according to a person close to the company.
The departures have also included newer hires. Anna Soellner, who was recruited to lead corporate communications, left after roughly four months, Business Insider previously reported.
Nvidia is known for high retention. It reported companywide turnover of 3.7% in fiscal 2026, up from 2.5% the prior year, and well below the tech industry average of 21.9% cited in its latest sustainability report.
Mangalindan succeeded longtime communications chief Bob Sherbin, who retired in 2024. She previously worked at the advisory firm Brunswick Group.
She was brought in to "bring fresh blood" and "upgrade the team" to meet Nvidia's growing profile, one former employee said.
At the end of 2024, Nvidia restructured its communications organization. It brought enterprise public relations under Mangalindan's leadership alongside the corporate communications team she already led, according to two former employees.
Corporate communications focuses on Nvidia's reputation and major media outlets, while enterprise handles product and industry messaging, including for its data center business.
One former employee said the consolidation reflected the growing importance of Nvidia's data center business, which sells chips and systems that power AI and had become its biggest revenue driver.
Analyst relations, social media, and influencer marketing also moved under Mangalindan's remit this year, another former employee said.
Three former employees said Nvidia's communications team had long operated with relatively lean staffing, even as workloads grew alongside the company's public profile, leaving staff juggling multiple responsibilities.
These employees said they experienced long hours, difficulty taking time off, and pressure to respond quickly to emails and Slack messages.
A person close to Nvidia said the company's lean staffing allows employees to move quickly and also requires long hours. The person said Mangalindan encourages staff to take vacation, though the team's small size can make scheduling time off difficult, particularly in the summer.
Nvidia is widely known for its demanding work environment. CEO Jensen Huang has emphasized operating at the "speed of light" and is known for fostering a culture of constant accountability.

In the last few months, a number of attacks against health-care workers, medical transports and facilities have taken place in several countries, like Afghanistan, Syria and Yemen to mention a few. These incidents are taking place in countries with fragile health-care systems that are already struggling to treat the numbers of people affected by the ongoing conflicts there. In some cases, the situation is made yet worse by the restrictions placed on aid workers, preventing them from getting to the people who need them.
Both the attacks themselves and their consequences are of serious concern. These were attacks on medical personnel and facilities protected under international humanitarian law, leaving death and destruction in their wake and disrupting vital health-care services. All those involved with the Health Care in Danger initiative are alarmed by the long-term impact these attacks may have on people’s health.
These are not isolated incidents. The International Committee of the Red Cross, through the Health Care in Danger project, has been gathering data in 11 countries since January 2012. By December 2014, 2398 attacks against health-care personnel, facilities and vehicles had been recorded. This alarming situation highlights the urgent need for measures to prevent future violence.
The Health Care in Danger initiative, with the support of experts and professionals from different backgrounds, including from governments, the armed forces, humanitarian agencies, international professional associations and health-care services, as well as the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, has formulated a substantive body of recommendations and identified practical measures that, if implemented by all those concerned, would increase the protection of health-care services in armed conflict or other emergencies.
As members and partners of the Health Care in Danger initiative, we call on States, weapon bearers, international and national humanitarian agencies and health organizations to give urgent attention to the recommendations resulting from the Health Care in Danger initiative.
In particular, we urge States
- to make every effort to investigate and condemn attacks against health-care personnel, facilities and medical transports that violate international law, including international humanitarian law;
- to revise their domestic legislation and its implementation to ensure that it is in line with their obligations under international law, including international humanitarian law;
- to ensure that the military are properly trained to know, abide by and respect the applicable legal framework for the protection of health care as well as ethical duties of health-care personnel;
- to cooperate with health and humanitarian organizations to ensure that health personnel are specially trained to know, apply and uphold their legal and ethical duties;
- to actively seek to raise awareness of the proper use of the red cross/red crescent/red crystal emblems by armed forces and by the population at large;
- to take the opportunity of the forthcoming International Conference of the Red Cross and Red Crescent to further their commitment to implementing recommendations and measures on protecting health care in armed conflict and other emergencies and to consider submitting specific voluntary pledges on this issue.
We urge State armed forces
- to respect in all circumstances, in particular in situations of armed conflict or other emergencies, health care workers, facilities and medical transports and to allow patients to receive adequate care, regardless of their affiliation;
- to revise military rules of engagement and operational practice and procedures to ensure that recommendations and measures for the protection of the delivery of health care are included therein and that military personnel are adequately trained in them.
We urge all non-state actors
- to respect in all circumstances, in particular in situations of armed conflict or other emergencies, health care workers, facilities and medical transports and to allow patients to receive adequate care, regardless of their affiliation;
We encourage international and national humanitarian and health organizations
- to continue to advocate for the preservation of principled humanitarian action, the respect of the "Ethical Principles of Health Care in Times of Armed Conflict and Other Emergencies”, endorsed by civilian and military health-care organizations in June 2015, and the protection of patients, health-care personnel, facilities and medical transport in armed conflict or other emergencies and to join ongoing efforts or to start their own initiatives to those ends.
- To ensure that health facilities they govern are taking necessary actions to reduce the risk of violence within the facilities’ premises.
Signatory organisations 1
International Committee of Military Medicine; International Committee of the Red Cross; International Council of Nurses; International Federation of Medical Students’ Associations; International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies; International Hospital Federation; International Pharmaceutical Federation; World Federation for Medical Education; World Health Organization; World Medical Association.
Health Care in Danger
Health Care in Danger is an initiative of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement to make access to, and delivery of, health care safer in armed conflict or other emergencies. This initiative calls for the respect and protection of health-care workers, facilities and vehicles and the implementation of a series of recommendations and practical measures to safeguard health-care services and their humanitarian mission. This initiative is supported by a number of partners, individuals and organisations, members of the Health Care in Danger Community of Concern.

Brazil says Amazon deforestation fell to the lowest level since 1988
Brazil’s government announces that annual deforestation in the Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since 1988
SAO PAULO -- SAO PAULO (AP) — Brazil’s government announced Friday that annual deforestation in the Amazon fell to its lowest level since records began in 1988. Official satellite data showed the rainforest lost 3,335 square kilometers (1,300 square miles) from Aug. 2025 through July 2026, the period used to calculate the annual rate.
The data released Friday underscore the success of Brazil’s renewed efforts under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to curb Amazon deforestation, reversing a surge under his predecessor, far-right President Jair Bolsonaro.
During Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency, from 2019 to 2022, Amazon deforestation surged by about 60%, with more than 45,000 square kilometers (17,400 square miles) cleared, according to official data. Under Lula, deforestation has fallen 71% since 2023, the government said.
One of Lula’s first moves after taking office in January 2023 for a third, non-consecutive term was to revive the Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Deforestation in the Legal Amazon, known by its Portuguese acronym, PPCDAm. Launched in 2004 during his first administration, the plan had been shelved under Bolsonaro.
Lula brought back the environmental officials who developed the blueprint two decades earlier, appointing environmental champion Marina Silva — who led the Environment Ministry until she resigned in April to run for Congress — and João Paulo Capobianco, her former deputy and the current minister, to help carry it out.
The plan has four pillars: strengthening monitoring and enforcement; promoting a sustainable economy; managing protected areas and determining how undesignated public forests should be used; and using regulations and financial incentives to curb deforestation.
Measures included restoring sanctions for illegal forest clearing detected by satellites, a practice seen as the most effective tool to curb deforestation that was halted under Bolsonaro. The government also proposed barring properties with illegal deforestation from receiving bank loans and allocated more funding to priority Amazon municipalities that demonstrated reductions in forest loss. It also funded efforts to fight environmental crime and develop subsidized credit for sustainable businesses in the Amazon.
“The formula is always the same, and it works. We saw it work in Brazil years ago and we’re seeing it again now: determination, enforcement on the ground, fighting crime and enforcing the law," said Márcio Astrini, executive director of the Climate Observatory, a Brazilian network of environmental groups.
Astrini added that the deforestation rates announced Friday show that Brazil's pledge to reach zero deforestation by 2030 is achievable without compromising the country's economy.
" Agriculture has been setting production and export records while deforestation has fallen. Today’s figures disprove the false narrative that protecting the environment holds back Brazil’s development,” he added.
Deforestation and other land-use changes are Brazil’s largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions, which drive global warming. The stakes are especially high in the Amazon, which stores vast amounts of carbon dioxide and generates atmospheric moisture that helps regulate weather far beyond South America.
Despite progress curbing deforestation, the Amazon faces threats from climate change, proposed legislation and a possible change in Brazil’s presidency.
Degradation from wildfires, logging and drought affects about 40% of the Amazon and has outpaced clear-cutting in recent years. A strong El Niño, a periodic warming of the equatorial Pacific, could intensify those threats in 2026 and 2027 by bringing hotter, drier conditions that fuel wildfires.
Fire counts across the biome were near historic lows this year but have tripled since Oct. 4, when Brazilians voted in the first round of national elections. Authorities are investigating whether fires were deliberately set for political reasons ahead of this month’s presidential runoff.
Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, won 47% of the vote, while President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva received 45%. The two face an Oct. 25 runoff.
The candidates offer sharply different visions for the rainforest. Climate and conservation experts warn that a Bolsonaro victory could reverse policies to curb deforestation. He has pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year ahead of Brazil’s current target. Lula’s reelection pledge goes further: zero net deforestation by 2030, with restoration offsetting all forest loss, legal or illegal.
Former Minister Silva said in a statement Friday that the deforestation reduction was a “historic achievement” for the Brazilian people and that the election outcome would be crucial to sustain it.
“Jair Bolsonaro’s administration approached environmental protection and climate change with denial and a sweeping dismantling of environmental policies. Flávio has inherited those views and practices and intends to perpetuate them, as he has indicated on several occasions,” she said.
“Those who deny the problem exists will certainly do nothing to address it.”
Bolsonaro has denied climate change while portraying himself as an environmental defender, without detailing plans to protect the Amazon or support forest financing. He has called for modernizing environmental laws, which many environmentalists interpret as weakening them.
“Flávio Bolsonaro is a defender of the environment and of those who preserve standing forests and clean rivers,” his campaign said.

Actor Imran Khan ordered to leave India after participating in protest
- Published
Authorities in India have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by 28 October after he participated in a protest, seeking electoral reforms.
An American citizen, Khan holds an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which allows people of Indian origin to visit and stay in the country. But an OCI cannot vote or contest elections.
"Imran Khan participated in the agitation at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar," police said in a statement on Thursday.
Khan's lawyer has said the actor will challenge the order in the Bombay High Court.
Police said the Foreigners' Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had served Khan a notice for violating laws by protesting.
But the actor's lawyer said that no provision of the law or any rule for OCI cardholders prohibit him from participating in a protest.
The Press Trust of India reports that the actor's petition against the Mumbai police notice termed it as "drastic".
Khan is known for the 2008 hit romantic comedy Jaane Tu... Ya Jaane Na.
He first appeared as a child actor in popular films such as Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak in 1988 and Jo Jeeta Wohi Sikandar in 1992.
Since his debut as a lead actor in 2008, he has starred in a number of films like I Hate Luv Storys, Mere Brother Ki Dulhan and Delhi Belly.
The notice to leave the country comes as Khan returns to acting this year with the Netflix film Adhure Hum Adhure Tum after a hiatus of over a decade.
On 10 October, the actor participated in the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a wider GenZ-led movement that has been holding demonstrations for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud. India's poll panel denies these charges.
"Imran Khan had participated in the agitation despite not being an Indian citizen," police said in their statement.
The complaint against Khan was lodged by Kirit Somaiya, a leader of India's and the state's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who accused the actor of being "involved in a conspiracy to spread anarchy in India".
Khan did not address Somaiya's allegation directly, but had spoken to reporters about his participation in the protest.
"I don't have demands. I'm here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I'm here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted, why people's voices are being suppressed," he'd said.
He added that he was not at the protest as the representative of any organisation.
Following the protest, Khan was briefly detained by the police along with other protesters.
He posted a photo of himself inside the police detention van on Instagram with the caption, "Apparently I'm going for a drive." The post received more than two million likes on the social media platform.
Over the weekend, thousands of protesters had marched in Delhi, Mumbai and other parts of India, demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar ahead of crucial state elections in response to the CJP's call.
On Monday, leaders of many of India's main opposition parties, including Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, led thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place to the Supreme Court in Delhi.
On Wednesday, two top CJP leaders were sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi.
The CJP has called for another protest on Friday evening in the capital.

France has released its Global Health Strategy for 2023-2027, in Lyon today, in the presence of three French Ministers, the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, the Minister of Health and Prevention, the Minister of Higher Education and Research, and WHO’s Director-General.
As a lead player for shaping global health policies, France has called on national and international stakeholders to support building a new global health architecture towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and in particular SDG3, focused on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all, at all ages.
The new Health Strategy aims to help reduce health inequalities and strengthen the One Health approach to better prevent and prepare for future global health emergencies. It urges the global community to address the health consequences of climate change and the environmental impact on health systems.
To underscore WHO’s and France strong collaboration and in recognition of France’s pivotal global health role, Dr Tedros travelled to France to join the launch event.
“France was a founding member of WHO in 1948 and has been a strong friend to WHO throughout the 75 years since then,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health, and the new Global Health Strategy will enhance that role. It aligns well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, empower and perform for health.”
France shares key health priorities with WHO, adopting a crosscutting approach and prioritizing universal health coverage (UHC) as part of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. France also provides support for transformative initiatives at WHO such as the WHO Academy and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) which the Ministers visited today.
Dr Tedros addressed the audiences at the Academy and IARC together with Ms Catherine Colonna, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention, and Ms Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research.
"The World Health Organization, whose 74th anniversary we are celebrating today, must continue to play a central and driving role,” said Ms Catherine Colonna, the French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “France will continue to support the WHO and its ambitious governance and financing reforms."
"France is also committed alongside the WHO Academy through several partnership with universities, research institutes, and public health institutions," remarked Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research. "Our goal is to enrich the learners' experience through a diversified training portfolio within the Academy."
"The launch of this Global Health Strategy is the perfect opportunity to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the WHO. The Organization plays a central role in global health, and we must continue to support it," said Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention. "This is why, I am announcing today, France is keen to host, in the first quarter of 2024, in partnership with the WHO, the first international financing conference for the fight against meningitis."
The 2023-2027 French Strategy for Global Health is the fruit of collaboration involving a wide range of French actors: public agencies, civil society organizations, higher education and research organizations, scientific institutions, foundations, organizations of human, animal and environmental health specialists, local government bodies and the private sector. They will all be represented within a monitoring committee to track the Strategy’s implementation and progress.
From left to right: Minister of Health and Prevention H.E. Aurélien Rousseau, WHO’s Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs H.E. Catherine Colonna, and Minister of Higher Education and Research, H.E. Sylvie Retailleau.

"Back home when we play in front of our own fans, just to see the fans, the crowd get behind us, singing the national anthem... it makes me cry every time."
Edwin Ipape gets emotional when travelling with his Papua New Guinea team-mates to the national stadium.
Children, so mad about rugby league that they will fashion a ball out of anything they can find, run alongside the team bus, eager to catch a glimpse of their heroes. Players are mobbed wherever they go.
The buzz around rugby league in Papua New Guinea can sometimes be daunting for visiting teams. In the past, passion has boiled over to the point where police have fired tear gas into the crowds.
But the national game – and in particular its men's national team, the Kumuls – is also a powerful symbol of unity in a land that can be torn apart by tribal fighting and where more than 800 different languages and dialects are spoken.
When the PNG fans are at their best and noisiest, a 15,000 crowd can sound like twice that number and is so loud that the players on the field cannot hear each other.
They will be at full volume this month when the island's capital Port Moresby is the venue for four Rugby League World Cup matches, as PNG co-hosts the tournament with Australia and New Zealand.
"People in Papua New Guinea probably don't know who the prime minister is, but they know all the NRL [National Rugby League] players," joked Elsie Albert, a prop who plays for PNG's women's side – the Orchids – and for Parramatta Eels in Australia's NRL Women's Premiership.
So, how has an island perched off Australia's northern tip become so obsessed with the sport?
Rugby League World Cup
15 October - 15 November
Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand
Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app
The seeds were sown by Australian miners in the 1930s, who introduced the game, one with deep roots in New South Wales and Queensland, to the local population.
It took hold as the devotion spread. The ferocious physicality of rugby league sat easily with the Papuans, who had long fought battles without a ball on their soil.
These days, the people of PNG are among the most knowledgeable and passionate. Only the Cook Islands can lay similar claims to an all-out obsession with the game in terms of national importance.
Sometimes that fervour spills over, with violence souring matches in their domestic league,, external something the authorities are keen to stamp out. In the past, tear gas was needed to quell over-excited crowds, such as when Great Britain came to tour in the early 1990s.
Generally though, rugby league is more of a peacekeeper. Villages will settle around a television set to watch rugby league, whether it is the NRL or Super League.
Participation levels are high. There are thousands of would-be Edwin Ipapes across the island, running about on bits of grass, on gravel, on the scrawniest patch of clear land somewhere, anywhere they can get the ball out and play.
The games can be rough, bordering on brutal. They are the perfect breeding ground for talent. But kit can be basic.
"If you're lucky enough, you play with a rugby league ball," Ipape recalled of his childhood, growing up in Mount Hagen, in the Highlands of Papua New Guinea.
"Otherwise, you play with containers, you put stuff in it, fill it up and then make it like a ball and whatever... whatever we can get our hands on, we may pretend that it was our rugby ball.
"I remember saving up my lunch money to buy myself one of those American footballs and using it as a rugby ball so we could play."
The Highlands of Papua New Guinea were a testing place to grow up - there is a long history of brutal tribal rivalries. Today, violence in those parts of the country has escalated - as access to increasingly sophisticated weaponry has brought deadly consequences.
Ipape, though, only ever had eyes for rugby league. Larsen Marape and Menzie Yere were the heroes of his youth: the faces on the posters adorning his walls in Mount Hagen.
The sport not only brings unity to the country - for those who make it to the top, it also offers a chance to cross the globe.
Ipape, 27, has played for his country, and travelled worldwide. The hooker now plays in Super League for Leigh Leopards.
The 'Birds of Paradise' - as Kumuls translates - have been life-transforming.
"Rugby league has given me pretty much everything," he said. "It's instilled discipline and it's taught me a lot of lessons about life.
"I've welled up with tears a few times on our way to the stadium in Papua New Guinea, just looking at the young kids running alongside the bus.
"I'm so blessed and privileged to be in the position to represent my country. It's a dream I'm living right now."
For any young hopeful looking to become the next Ipape, the first goal is to play for a village, then a province. Then it is the PNG Hunters, who play in Australia's Queensland Cup.
That can be the ticket to the big leagues, whether that be the NRL - as it was for former Melbourne Storm centre Justin Olam - or Super League, as it has been for Ipape.
From 2028 onwards, there will be an NRL team based on the island, the PNG Chiefs.
While much of their initial recruitment has been high-profile, such as Samoa half-back Jarome Luai, compatriot Brian To'o, and New Zealand international Joey Manu, Papuan players have also been sought to bolster the ranks.
Visiting teams can sometimes find the excitement around rugby league in Papua New Guinea unsettling. Any familiar face from the sport draws attention - but the fans only want to show affection and respect.
"We went to a little market and people were recognising us," Leigh Leopards' Papuan hooker Liam Horne told BBC Sport. "We actually needed a lift to go to one of these shopping centres, so we just hitchhiked.
"We got this random guy to pick us up and he couldn't believe it. He had two Kumuls in his back seat and he was freaking out.
"The people over there, they love it. They're welcoming."
Some of the Kumuls of today are second-generation Papuans born and raised in Australia, such as Leigh back-rower Jacob Alick-Weincke.
Being a PNG international is a chance to connect with the culture, understand more about their heritage, upbringing, and the people.
"People there just want to be around you in your presence," Alick-Weincke added.
"We always go to the shops or go to local villages. We went to one of the markets last time we were over there. That was a really cool experience. Just people everywhere."
The rise of the women's team - chronicled in the 2019 documentary Power Meri,, external which followed the Orchids to their debut World Cup in 2017 - has been helped by Elsie Albert's star power.
Albert is PNG's first female superstar - but that meant challenging some old values back home.
"Women were supposed to stay at home and do household chores, so when this great game came over [for women], it was seen as a threat to the culture," Albert said in 2023 as part of an NRL storytelling campaign.
"The pioneering girls had men throwing bottles at them into the stadium, but in 2019 everything changed for us when we played England."
In that two-Test series, England won the first match 24-10 in Goroka. But the second, in Port Moresby, brought a memorable - and defining - 20-16 victory for the hosts.
"You could feel the atmosphere," Albert recalled. "The crowd was there and to get a win in front of everyone, especially the men... for them to see that women could do what men can do, was a great feeling.
"You could feel it was going to change. Rugby league is a great way for us to to advocate for change."
Even well-known rugby league family names of the past are growing new branches, with Fleur Ginn Wagambie following in the footsteps of elders John and Richard when she made her PNG debut in 2025 - and now hopes to make a World Cup debut.
"I've always wanted to represent the Orchids and I was really lucky last year to make my debut in the Pacific Cup," Wagambie, a Parramatta team-mate of Albert, told ABC Pacific.
"Being lucky enough to play in a World Cup, in Port Moresby, in front of my family is really exciting."
Papua New Guinea's rugby league influence can be felt at Championship club London Broncos.
Jason Demetriou, the Kumuls head coach, is in charge at Plough Lane, and his influence persuaded a host of Papuan players to come over.
Championship player of the year Gairo Voro, full-back Morea Morea, prop Epil Kapinias, centres Alex Max and Robert Mathias, hooker Finley Glare and back-rower Jeremiah Simbiken were all recruited by the Super League aspirant Broncos.
Together, they steered the club to a treble - the Championship League Leaders' Shield, the 1895 Cup and the divisional Grand Final title.
Their progress alerted the PNG Chiefs, who have signed Voro, Glare and Morea for the 2028 season onwards.
"There's going to be eyeballs on every player in the World Cup," Demetriou added.
"We're playing against Lebanon, which will be stacked full of NRL players, playing against England that are full of Super League and NRL players, and Samoa, which is one of the top international sides in the world at the moment.
"We know what's in front of us, but on the flip side of that, they're going to play against PNG as well. We have to make sure that when they go out on the field, they understand that there's some elite level players out there.
"If we want opportunities, we want to be respected, then we need to start with beating teams on the world stage."
Santos National Football Stadium - where the co-hosts will play the four Rugby League World Cup matches they are staging - has a capacity of just under 15,000. It will seem a lot more than that on Saturday, though, when the Orchids face France and the Kumuls take on Lebanon. And that will be thanks to the atmosphere.
"Loud" was how Horne put it. "It sounds like 30,000." Kumuls stalwart Lachlan Lam - forced to miss this World Cup because he needs wrist surgery - likened the atmosphere to "a proper scream".
Team-mate Alick-Wiencke said: "I've not experienced anything like it. You can't hear yourself talking to other team-mates and things like that.
"And, just the heat - you can't believe the whole stadium is packed out. It's like 40C and they're up there singing and dancing and carrying on. So the atmosphere is unbelievable."
Whatever happens at this World Cup, rugby league shows no signs of losing its appeal in Papua New Guinea. And the passion of those supporters might yet give Ipape reason to shed a few more tears.

Blue Origin announced a major expansion of its already considerable Florida launch facilities on Friday morning with the intent of eventually flying 150 rockets a year from there.
The company said it would add two additional launch pads for the New Glenn rocket, in addition to two already under construction at Cape Canaveral. The company is also investing heavily in a new manufacturing facility that will produce up to 150 upper stages for a larger variant of the New Glenn rocket.
Additionally, the company plans to procure two additional landing ships to catch and return the first stage of the New Glenn rocket (it currently has one, named Jacklyn). Finally, Blue Origin said it would add a new customer integration facility, built in conjunction with the US Space Force, that will feature four payload bays to process multiple missions at the same time.
“These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently,” wrote Ian Richardson, senior vice president of operations at Blue Origin, in an update on the company’s website this morning. “As we look ahead, this infrastructure is designed to support multiple flights per week by the end of the decade.
$3 billion and counting
To date, Blue Origin has invested about $3 billion in facilities and infrastructure in Florida, largely to support the construction and launch of the heavy-lift New Glenn rocket. The company now has more than 5,000 employees working in Florida and 500 suppliers in the state.
“Our manufacturing and operations footprint has more than doubled in the last couple of years, now spanning more than 20 sites across Brevard and Orange Counties,” Richardson wrote. “Blue Origin is the only company—and the largest employer—to manufacture, launch, and refurbish rockets on the Space Coast.”
That would seem to be a reference to superseding the 800-pound gorilla on the Florida Space Coast, SpaceX, which has launched hundreds of rockets into orbit over the years from Florida. Blue Origin has launched to orbit twice.

Convicted killer attending McGill law school divides students over safety, 2nd chances
Despite violent past, offender’s lawyer says reintegration is ‘what rehabilitation is about’
Students in McGill University’s law faculty say they are concerned about the presence of a convicted murderer on campus and at faculty events.
The man, Jeffrey George Ewert, was convicted of second-degree murder and attempted murder for two attacks committed in 1984: he sexually assaulted and killed one woman and, less than six weeks later, beat and choked a 15-year-old so severely that she was paralyzed and disabled for life, according to a summary of his case in his parole board file.
Ewert is serving a life sentence and was granted day parole in 2025. He’s been attending law classes at McGill and going to faculty events since August.
His parole was extended for another six months in June 2026. While various clinical assessments ranked Ewert’s risk of reoffending as moderate to high, official parole documents say with close supervision at a halfway house and clinical follow-up, that risk “seems to fall more into the moderate risk category.”
Although Ewert’s case management team did not believe he posed an undue risk to society, the parole board did express concern about his interactions with and attitudes toward women.
Some students, who asked not to be named for fear of repercussions, approached CBC after they learned of Ewert’s criminal past and are upset that the university did not disclose their peer’s violent history.
“For me, it’s really the lack of transparency,” said one of the students.
Whether or not McGill was legally obligated to alert students, she feels the school had a moral obligation to let them know.
“More than half of the students are women, we’re young,” she said, adding she feels Ewert’s presence places them in a “vulnerable and dangerous position.”
Jeffrey George Ewert began attending law classes at McGill University in August. Some students are upset his violent criminal past was not disclosed. (Name withheld/Instagram)
Another student also resented being left in the dark.
“Not knowing made it more scary for us,” said the student, who pieced together Ewert’s past through their own research. “It got me worried and I was panicked.”
If the school had warned them and explained what precautions were in place, she said she would have felt safer and could have decided if or how she wanted to interact with him.
The students told CBC they were aware other students had made a formal complaint to McGill’s administration.
University cites privacy laws
CBC asked McGill University whether the institution was aware of the nature of Ewert’s criminal past and current parole status and what security plans, if any, had been conducted before allowing Ewert to attend campus.
In a statement, a university spokesperson declined to answer questions about Ewert’s specific case, citing privacy laws, but said that “criminal background checks are not typically part of Canadian universities' admissions processes.
“McGill would act quickly and decisively should concerning information be brought forward about a student’s background or behaviour on campus,” the spokesperson wrote.
The statement continues by saying the university “would liaise closely with all relevant government bodies” and use the policy tools at its disposal “to remove the individual from campus” to ensure a safe environment.
“The university would also actively review its admissions processes to ensure a similar situation never happens again.”
In a statement to CBC, McGill said it would act 'quickly and decisively' if concerning information about a student’s background or behaviour on campus was brought forward. (Kolya Hubacek-Guilbault/CBC)
The students who spoke with CBC have not seen Ewert on campus since Oct. 6.
Ewert declined an interview, but his absence at McGill was confirmed by his lawyer, Nora Demnati, who spoke on his behalf.
“He applied to McGill law with the help of many students, of law professors and McGill University was fully aware of his history and his status and where he comes from,” said Demnati in an interview.
Although Ewert had not disclosed his past to everyone at the university — and was not legally obligated to — Demnati said Ewert has never hidden who he is.
“He’s been very honest about his history, his parole status and his conditions,” said Demnati, adding she and Ewert are “completely in the dark” about what specific concerns were raised at McGill.
Although she understands some students are worried, she notes Ewert was in his 20s when he committed his offences.
Now in his 60s, Demnati says he’s a different man and she’s “disheartened” Ewert was not given a chance to hold a meeting with students to address their concerns.
Parolees continuously monitored
The extension to Ewert's day parole was granted under a variety of conditions, including not to enter a drinking establishment, to immediately report all sexual and non-sexual relationships with women and to allow his case management team access to all his telecommunication activity.
The parole board added the latter condition because Ewert had been viewing women's profiles on social media, starting discussions with them, and exploring a dating site without notifying his case management team.
The McGill students who spoke to CBC question how closely the university or his parole supervisor can monitor such a condition.
They say students often work closely on group projects and the teaching assistants — many of whom are also women — meet students one-on-one.
“It was more a fear of potentially women not knowing what he’s done in the past and then having interactions with him that could put them at risk potentially,” one of the students told CBC.
While the Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) is unable to talk about the specifics of Ewert’s case due to privacy, it said in an email that supervising an offender “includes ongoing monitoring of their activities, including educational opportunities.”
CBC was contacted by other students in McGill's law faculty who reported positive experiences with Ewert. They admired his efforts to improve his life and go back to school and value the perspective he brings. (Kolya Hubacek-Guilbault/CBC)
This includes regular meetings with the offender as well as assessing their personal and professional environments. Social media use is also monitored.
“We carefully monitor all aspects and if an offender's risk increases or there is a change in their behaviour or compliance with release conditions, we take immediate action, which can include suspending their release and returning them immediately to custody,” a spokesperson for the CSC wrote.
CBC was contacted by two other McGill students who supported Ewert.
They spent time alone with him and described the experience as positive. Both were aware of his past convictions and said they never felt threatened or unsafe.
“I think there’s a difference between feeling uncomfortable and being in danger,” said one student in reaction to other students’ unease. “I think sometimes those two things feel really similar, but they’re not similar.”
The student, who asked not to be named for fear of repercussions, admired the efforts Ewert had made to improve his life and go back to school. She felt it would be unfortunate if his experience and perspective were lost.
Navigating reintegration can be difficult
Ewert’s day parole — first granted in February 2025 — was temporarily suspended in May 2025 because he had contacted and collected the phone numbers of multiple women, and after the counsellor at his community residential facility took issue with his attitude and behaviour.
The parole board decision also noted that Ewert continues to assert that his interactions with women do not constitute a risk factor and that he denies a sexual element in his crimes, despite what court records say.
Demnati says they may request his file be corrected to show “there is no evidence of a sexual offence.”
CBC found Ewert’s Instagram and Threads accounts, which he operates under a different name. CBC confirmed it was Ewert’s.
On the Threads account, Ewert is actively communicating with women, commenting on images of women, many of which appear to be altered or created by AI. Below one image, he commented “hotties like you drive us crazy.”
Demnati told CBC she was not aware of the specifics of what Ewert wrote on social media, but she said occasional breaches are expected after nearly four decades in prison.
Nora Demnati, Ewert’s lawyer, says her client is still trying to settle into life as a student and is urging people to 'give the man a chance.' (Nora Demnati/LinkedIn)
She said she has countless clients with a life sentence who are working, studying and going about their daily lives.
“This is the choice we have made as a society, to believe in rehabilitation,” said Demnati, who is also the president of the Canadian Prison Law Association.
Alysha McDonald, an assistant professor in the department of sociology at MacEwan University, said that, while she can’t speak to the specifics of Ewert’s case, this situation reflects a tension present in many reintegration cases.
McDonald said education can help offenders reintegrate and provide a “structure, purpose, and the chance to build a new social identity.”
But as this situation shows, there is often no framework as to how an institution will navigate that reintegration and manage students’ concerns.
Universities “rarely have clear, consistent processes for how reintegration intersects with their communities and it needs thoughtful attention if we’re going to see real progress in people’s experiences with reintegration.”
Demnati said Ewert is still trying to settle into life as a student and adjust to the rhythm of taking classes, studying and tackling new technology.
“Like give the man a chance,” said Demnati. “This is what rehabilitation is about and it’s not making people feel like they’re alienated from society and an outcast and they have to run around the city with something on their forehead saying, ‘Hey, I just got out of prison.’”
Neither the parole board nor CSC responded to questions about whether they were aware of Ewert’s current online activities.
‘He’s not the same person’
The details of Ewert’s crimes, reported by newspapers in B.C. at the time, recounted in various court documents and summarized in the parole board decisions, indicate that in a two-month span, he attacked two women.
In May 1984, he met Corrina Lea Makiev, who was hitchhiking outside of a nightclub. He choked her unconscious, sexually assaulted her and beat her before dropping her in the Fraser River, where she was later found dead.
On June 17 of the same year, Ewert arrived late one night at his adoptive parents’ home and found a 15-year-old family friend asleep on a couch.
Ewert forcibly removed the teen from the home and beat her so severely that she suffered permanent serious brain damage and physical injuries that left her paralyzed. He left her in a ditch, but she survived. She has been unable to live independently since the attack.
He was convicted of second-degree murder for Makiev’s killing and attempted murder for the attack on the 15-year-old.
Jeffrey George Ewert was in his 20s when he attacked two women in British Columbia. He was convicted of second-degree murder and attempted murder. (The Province)
Ewert first applied for parole in 2022 but his application was denied. The parole board concluded he still posed an undue risk to society. He challenged the decision, however, and won in Federal Court, when a judge agreed that the board had failed to consider Gladue principles — his Indigenous background and his traumatic upbringing.
It was not Ewert’s first litigation. He has been involved in numerous lawsuits that deal with prisoners’ rights and the rights of Indigenous prisoners.
Notably, in 2018, the Supreme Court of Canada agreed with Ewert’s contention that risk-assessment tools used by CSC were not valid for assessing Indigenous offenders.
Ewert also leads the Canadian Prisoners’ Labour Confederation, a group that advocates for labour rights for inmates.
According to the Parole Board of Canada’s decisions about Ewert, he has partially attributed his past violence to his upbringing. Parole documents say his birth mother was Métis, but he was adopted by a white B.C. family. His adoptive father was an alcoholic and his mother was psychologically ill and, he alleges, abused him physically, mentally and emotionally.
“He was such a broken individual at the time, full of self-hatred, who didn’t know love,” said Demnati.
She said Ewert has worked hard to understand his triggers for violence and has been sober for decades.
“He’s not the same person... at all,” said Demnati. “We just need to remember that and maybe find some reassurance that he is not that broken person anymore. That he not only changed, but he healed.”

Katie Zacharia mocked for only lasting a week with Trump: ‘At least she has her career as a lawyer to fall back on’
Everyone was making the same jokes about Katie Zacharia, while MAGA pundits defended her
