The firing of Katie Zacharia, axed by President Donald Trump after serving just five days as his White House press secretary, has lit up the internet, with everyone making the same jokes.
“Math question: How many Scaramuccis are in a Zacharia?” quipped Democratic Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta of Pennsylvania.
“At least Katie Zacharia has her career as a lawyer to fall back on,” jeered progressive commentator Alex Cole.
Zacharia was fired exactly one week after Trump announced he was hiring the conservative California mom and followed a disastrous White House briefing. Questions over her law credentials then dogged her for the rest of the week, culminating in her admission to a right-wing podcaster that she never passed the bar.
The final nail in Zacharia’s press secretary coffin came during appearances on Fox News, where she told Trump-pal Sean Hannity that the administration did not adequately prepare her, and when she raised questions about the vetting process on Friday’s Fox & Friends.
Trump told reporters Friday afternoon that he said to Zacharia, “I said to her honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider.”
Social media was soon flooded with jokes and memes about the new record set for the shortest time served in the role by a White House press secretary or communications director.
Zacharia’s record is less than half the 11-day one set during Trump’s first term by Anthony Scaramucci. “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain,” he said.
Others followed suit.
“Less than half a Scaramucci,” said Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff of California.
“She lasted one Zachariath. Five elevenths of a Scaramucci,” said analyst Ed Elson.
“Imagine becoming Press Secretary and not even making it a full Scaramucci…” another person joked.
“Katie Zacharia makes Anthony Scaramucci look like Chuck Grassley,” someone else said, referencing the long-serving Iowa senator.
The official X account of the Democratic Party posted a Hunger Games meme depicting Zacharia as one of the fallen tributes, in addition to a spoof LinkedIn icon where she was “#Opentowork.”
“Already,” the account said, with a laughing-crying emoji.
The Daily Show and California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s press office both mocked up similar “in memoriam” tributes to Zacharia making light of her short tenure. Elsewhere, others made jokes about her law credentials after she was described as a lawyer more than a dozen times in TV appearances last year, despite never passing the bar exam.
“At least now she can get back to doing what she loves…Practicing Law without a license,” an account on X reacted to the news.
A New York City brewery shared a mock-up image of a new beer. “Introducing The Bar Is Now So Low It’s Not Even Being Passed, a 6.7% Cold IPA inspired by Katie Zacharia calling herself a lawyer without passing the bar,” the brewery said on social media.
But MAGA figures came rallying to Zacharia’s defense on social media, blasting critics for their “vile” treatment of her.
“Katie Zacharia is one of the nicest, smartest, most hardworking patriots I’ve ever had the pleasure of knowing,” said MAGA influencer Nick Sortor. “She doesn’t deserve this absolutely VILE treatment.”
Jack Posobiec, the right-wing activist who hosted Zacharia on his show Thursday, where she admitted she never passed the bar, said she “will have a bright future.”
“Katie Zacharia is an America First patriot, a mother of four, and a loyal MAGA supporter who said yes when asked to serve her nation by President Trump,” he said.
Conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer said that she believed “people are being unnecessarily cruel” to Zacharia and they should “just leave her alone now.”
“She seems like a nice lady who just wanted to serve the President,” Loomer said. “She was nervous. It’s not a crime…The continued dog piling is just malicious. Let her be,” Loomer continued. “It’s not nice. And if I’m saying it’s not nice, then you really know it’s not nice.”

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia show the Yemeni rebels' growing strength
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have showcased their growing military capabilities, repeatedly striking the airport in Saudi Arabia's capital and seizing territory near a key shipping chokepoint
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have put their growing military capabilities on display in recent weeks, repeatedly striking Saudi Arabia's main international airport hundreds of miles (kilometers) away and seizing territory inside Yemen near a key shipping chokepoint.
At various times over the last decade, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Britain and Israel have carried out punishing air raids on the rebels — only to see them grow even stronger.
The Saudis have struggled to counter the latest attacks, even with far superior U.S.-supplied arms. A senior Saudi diplomat told reporters this week that Iran was encouraging the escalation and that over the summer the Houthis had spurned an offer to negotiate.
The Houthis operate in a large and mountainous territory where they can disperse fighters and military infrastructure while threatening major oil facilities and key trade routes.
Iran and its allies in Lebanon and Iraq provide expertise, training and sophisticated weapons, according to U.N. and other experts. A recent report found that the Houthis have tried to source parts from Chinese suppliers that are used to make precision-guided ballistic missiles with a range of roughly 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers).
The Houthis already have a wide array of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones — many resembling Iranian models — that can reach all the Gulf states as well as Israel. They have also used sophisticated anti-ship missiles and naval drones to strike vessels in the Red Sea, threatening a critical trade route.
Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a U.N. embargo. China has not directly responded to the latest report but says it has a “prudent and responsible” approach to military exports.
Smuggled Iranian weapons and parts have been seized from numerous Yemen-bound shipments, and a report by U.N. experts in 2024 documented extensive military ties between the Houthis, Iran and its other allies.
That report estimated that the Houthis had recruited up to 350,000 fighters by 2024, up from just 30,000 in 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war against the Houthis and imposed a naval blockade.
The Houthis can use relatively inexpensive drones and missiles to target oil and other infrastructure just across the border in Saudi Arabia, as well as tankers off the coast. And while Iran is believed to supply cutting-edge components like guidance systems, the Houthis can manufacture much of their weaponry domestically, and at a much lower cost than the state-of-the-art interceptors used by the Saudis.
There are suggestions they may even be using artificial intelligence to try to build better missiles.
Saudi Arabia boasts an array of U.S.-supplied weapons, including sophisticated aircraft as well as advanced missile defenses used against Iran at the height of the war last spring.
But with supplies of high-end interceptors under pressure, it's unclear how long it can ward off attacks — not only from the Houthis, but from Iran-backed militias in Iraq blamed for an attack that briefly shut down an east-west pipeline crucial for oil exports.
In recent days, the Houthis have repeatedly struck King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, leading to a wave of flight cancellations. They have also hit the headquarters of the national oil company, Aramco. Both are several hundred miles (kilometers) from Yemen.
At least 19 people have been killed, school classes have been canceled, and the disruption threatens the kingdom's ambitious plans to transform itself into a global hub for business, tourism and sports.
Vulnerable assets are scattered across Saudi Arabia’s sparsely populated territory, which is roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) through rugged desert areas.
The Houthis, a Shiite religious and political movement rooted in northern Yemen, are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen's internationally recognized government in the civil war.
The Sunni kingdom, which has long feared the emergence of a well-armed ally of Shiite Iran on its border, joined the war in 2015 after the rebels seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa.
Over the next seven years, Saudi Arabia carried out waves of airstrikes against the Houthis, often killing civilians. An array of Yemeni government forces and southern separatists struggled to push the Houthis back, and the battle lines moved little before a 2022 ceasefire.
The following year, after the outbreak of the war in Gaza, the Houthis began attacking Red Sea shipping in what they said was a blockade of Israel. The U.S. and the U.K. launched waves of strikes against the Houthis beginning in January 2024.
U.S. President Donald Trump ordered an intensified air campaign early last year, with some 2,000 munitions dropped on over 1,000 targets, a U.S. military official told The Associated Press at the time.
After weeks of U.S. strikes, the Houthis agreed to stop attacking American ships. But they continued to target Israel, which responded with its own strikes later in 2025, killing the Houthi prime minister along with other senior officials and repeatedly hitting a key port.
The Houthis largely kept to the sidelines in the first several months of the Iran war, but in July, they resumed attacks on Saudi Arabia and declared a blockade on Saudi shipping.
As recent conflicts have shown, air power is rarely effective without ground troops who can move in and seize territory after strikes.
In the case of Yemen, the ground fighters inside the country who are taking on the Houthis are deeply divided and fought each other as recently as January. They include fighters loyal to the Saudi-backed government and southern separatists supported by the United Arab Emirates — a sometimes rival to the Saudis that withdrew from Yemen in 2019.
The U.S., still preoccupied with Iran, appears keen to stay out. The Saudis signed a mutual defense pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and NATO member Turkey in August, but it's unclear what kind of assistance they are prepared to provide.
The diplomatic options are also limited. The Houthis are demanding that Saudi Arabia lift its blockade, which would be an admission of defeat in the long-running war and pave the way for even more extensive Iranian aid to the rebels.

The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz, the country’s former prime minster has said.
Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed, now an adviser to Yemen’s president, said it would be catastrophic if the city fell to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, since control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea and the road to Aden – the site of the UN-recognised government – would be lost.
Appealing for more western help, Saeed said he had no doubt that the Houthis intended to seize control of all of Yemen, and claimed their goal was “to help Iran to expand the chaos”.
Saeed admitted the lack of coordination among government-backed troops, competition between Gulf states and a slowness to appreciate the implications of Yemen acquiring long-range drone technology had contributed to the pressure facing his government, and its chief backer Saudi Arabia.
“We only have light weapons and Saudi Arabia did not plan at an early stage for this escalation, but it is never too late to regain our position,” he said.
Saeed called on the west to think through the implications of allowing the Houthis to take control of Yemen, arguing the country would never be secure with Houthis on the land.
Saeed is not only an adviser to the Yemeni president, Rashad al-Alimi, he was prime minister between 2018 and 2024 and a former negotiator with the Houthis.
He said: “The battle around Taiz is not just a battle for Taiz, but a broader battle that involves the whole of the western world, and one of the most important maritime straits. The Houthis know controlling Taiz is controlling the straits and it’s the highlands before the straits and the coastal city of Mocha and the Gulf of Aden. If Taiz is lost, access to the strait will be lost. The rest of the country will come later. The Houthi plan is to control the whole of Yemen.”
Taiz has become the new frontline in the war between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces after the Houthis launched a military campaign last month to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast, ending four years of relative calm in Yemen after a UN-brokered ceasefire froze the frontlines in 2022.
He said existing intelligence showed the Houthis were already seeking to control parts of the south, including the former Soviet camp at al-Sabiha, in the Lahij governorate, and eventually Aden. “The Houthis bleed a lot,” he said, “they suffer a lot, but they always want quickly to use their gains or any collapse to gain more land.”
With some Houthi leaders offering safe passage to armed groups to leave the city, he said for now the Houthis were allowing some fuel and commodities into the urban area of Taiz which houses more than 500,000 people, but in the meantime they were expanding their control of rural areas and smaller major cities.
Saeed said: “In a matter of days there will be a full siege and they will try to enter the city. I know the Houthis. They will show some flexibility until they are ready to control. It will be much worse than the siege of 2015. It will be catastrophic.”
He described Taiz as a modern democratic city untied to tribal culture, and predicted the Houthis would try to impose their Zaydi education, financial and tax systems very quickly, but the citizens would continue to resist. “The loss of Taiz would have a very significant symbolic impact on the idea of the modern state in Yemen and of resisting the Houthi project which relies on tribal networks and extremist religious education.”
Saeed admitted Taiz only had light weapons and the government had not been prepared for the loss of the west coast, allowing the Houthis to attack Taiz from four different axes.
“We have good troops,” he said, “but the problem is the coordination. We needed more communication between the National Shield Forces, National Resistance Forces and the Giants Brigades. It’s been a wake-up call inside the government and the army because not enough happened between the truce of 2022 and the restart of the fighting this year to reorganise the troops. The Houthi ideology solely is to fight.”
He added: “I hope now that the knife has come to our neck, and the Houthis represent a critical threat, the priority would be to come together to defeat the Houthis, and then to discuss other demands and guarantees.”
The exiled leader of the southern secessionist force, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, on Tuesday called for a mobilisation of southern troops against the Houthis, but coupled this with a demand for a referendum on secession within two years. He brought tens of thousands on to the streets in support on Wednesday, but his return would be a bitter pill for Riyadh to swallow.
Saeed said it was not a coincidence that the Houthi attack along the Red Sea coast in September had come when Iran was under heavy pressure.
“Its airplanes and airports cannot operate, 90% of the oil was coming out of Hormuz. That is why they attacked the Saudi east-to-west pipelines. The Houthis, by talking about a Saudi blockade, have found a reason to hit the Saudi oil installations, airports and they want to do it now because the only thing Iran can do is to keep expanding the consequences of the war for America.”
He said Houthi military capability and negotiating power had been transformed over the last decade leading to its ability to target key sites in Saudi Arabia now. “In 2017, the Houthis had nothing but blind missiles to fire at us that missed their targets.” By 2020, he said intelligence existed that Iranian experts operating from the Houthi capital Sana’a were training Houthis and in December of that year, in a devastatingly effective attack, they fired ballistic missiles at Aden airport. The attack left 28 dead and 107 injured, including Saeed himself, newly installed as prime minister. The missile travelled 186 miles (299km).
He explained: “We thought even then they did not have that many missiles, but since then the Iranians have expanded their manufacturing lines.” In January 2022, using missiles, the Houthis attacked Abu Dhabi oil tanker trucks more than 900 miles away.
In October 2022, inside Yemen, they struck the Nushayma oil terminal and al-Dhabba port, severely damaging government finances. By the time the US attacked Yemen in March 2025, he said “it was clear the Houthis had dozens of targeted missiles, land sea missiles and drones. They had become a unified front with Iran, and developed their missile base.”
He warned: “This is a new era of radical terrorism. It is not the old chaotic one of Isis and al-Qaida. It is semi-state actors and militias threatening powerful states with cheap technologies, and smuggled third-party components. The way Iran has invested in the Houthis could become a model for threatening navigation elsewhere. It is a new model of war, without traditional armies, needing different air defences. Gulf countries have to reshape and rethink their defences”.

New Delhi: Thailand's PTT group-backed Avaada plans to invest about ₹20,000 crore each in a green ammonia plant in Odisha and a green methanol facility in Maharashtra, as it expands into low-carbon fuels. The group plans a cumulative investment of around ₹1 trillion over the next three to four years, founder and chairman Vineet Mittal said in an interview.
"Avaada is setting up two projects, one in Dighi, Maharashtra, and the second in Gopalpur, Odisha. The feed engineering is happening in Gopalpur. For the first time, we are moving closer to binding agreements for offtake. We should sign by next year," Mittal said.
The methanol project in Nagpur and the proposed green ammonia project in Dighi are in the conceptualisation stage. The company plans to set up a total of four green fuel facilities in the years ahead. The company is in talks with buyers from Europe for long-term offtake agreements for green ammonia.
The manufacturing push comes ahead of a proposed ₹7,600 crore initial public offering of Avaada’s solar module manufacturing arm, Avaada Electro, planned for the end of this year.
Separately, Avaada Ventures Pvt. Ltd., the group’s holding company, recently repaid Brookfield Renewable’s debt in a transaction valued at about ₹6,713 crore.
The company's green ammonia plant in Gopalpur, Odisha has received Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin (RFNBO) certification from the European Union for 85% of its fuel. He said the Gopalpur project is expected to be commissioned around 2030.
Speaking of the planned green methanol plant in Nagpur, he said that the company has sought land allocation from the Maharashtra government and the process is ongoing.
"The first project (in Gopalpur) is around ₹20,000 crore. In case of (green methanol plant in) Nagpur, the land allocation and size of the project is not yet finalized, so the number is not clear, but we want to do it in the same range," he said. He added that RFNBO certification is under process for the methanol plant also.
With a major presence in the renewable power generation and solar component manufacturing business, the company is confident of expanding its footprint into industrial applications and fuels, Mittal added. Green methanol can be used for long-haul shipping, while green ammonia along with its use in shipping can also be used in industries including fertilizer plants.
Mittal said that the company would also focus on developing its super factory in Nagpur. Its operations would range from sand-to-solar panels, and it would be an integrated facility which will manufacture all the components in the solar photovoltaic module supply chain, including glass, ingot, wafer, cell and module.
Avaada aims to build 30 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy capacity by 2030, supported by the group’s planned investment programme of about ₹1 trillion, Mittal said. He said the company would execute its expansion in phases, based on customer demand, grid readiness and capital allocation.
"We see a substantial opportunity as India expands electricity use, electrifies more of its economy and builds domestic manufacturing capability. Avaada's strategy is to serve that demand through renewable generation, manufacturing, storage and green molecules.," he said.
The group is also looking to combine energy storage with solar and wind projects to supply reliable, round-the-clock power to industrial customers. The company sees room for both large renewable projects and distributed generation, including agricultural feeder solarisation, rooftop solar and storage."

FTC subpoenas OpenAI and Anthropic following safety failures
The department is investigating possible consumer harms at the major AI companies.
The US Federal Trade Commission has subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic for information about recent safety incidents with both businesses' AI models. Axios first reported that agency had sent civil subpoenas to the companies, and a spokesperson from the FTC confirmed the action to CBS News.
Axios' source said that the FTC is exploring possible consumer protection violations at Anthropic and OpenAI. The subpoenas are looking for documents regarding security incidents and safeguards, as well as some of the companies' marketing materials and content about their privacy policies. The individual also claimed the FTC plans to seek testimony from the top executives at both businesses. The department will allegedly send investigative demands to third-party AI companies at a later time.
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson is also part of the White House's recently-assembled task force for artificial intelligence, although that group seems more aimed at furthering US industry leadership than at AI regulation.
There have been several calls among tech and AI executives and employees for government intervention, particularly around frontier model development, which has come under increased scrutiny following a string of safety failures. OpenAI has seen its AI agents escape testing safeguards multiple times in recent months, including instances where the models hacked government websites and the business Hugging Face. This month, Anthropic's models have been caught attempting to access various levels of government sites and one sent a false homicide tip to Philadelphia law enforcement.
Today's move from the FTC echoes several lawsuits that are also underway regarding AI safety concerns. Most recently, eight state Attorneys General filed a suit against OpenAI yesterday on claims that the company violated consumer protection laws.

Access fundamental right, even for children: SC rejects age-based internet ban
The Supreme Court rejected blanket age-based restrictions on children's internet access. It sought stronger safeguards against online sexual abuse without curtailing fundamental rights.
The Supreme Court has rejected blanket age-based restrictions on internet access, holding that children enjoy the fundamental right to access and use the internet. It has, however, called for a stricter framework to protect them from online sexual abuse, including faster detection and removal of child sexual abuse material across platforms.
The court said children’s safety and freedom were not at odds with each other. Denying them internet access altogether would be unreasonable, it observed, while stressing that safeguards must protect children without taking away their rights.
The court also warned that age-based restrictions could push children towards unregulated and potentially more dangerous websites. Children who are enticed or threatened online may also hesitate to report such incidents to parents or trusted adults for fear of punishment for violating the restrictions, it said.

E Ink's new Kaleido 4 could inch us closer to the perfect color e-reader
The new display tech offers improved color reproduction and refresh rates.
E Ink has announced the latest version of its Kaleido color e-paper technology, introducing improvements that could be the selling point of future e-readers and writing tablets. The company's new Kaleido 4 display is supposed to be able to produce a wider range of colors, while improving things like refresh rate, a common problem with e-paper screens.
Kaleido 4 "doubles the color gamut volume" so it can produce over 40,000 colors, according to E Ink, while increasing "white reflectance" and contrast. The company also claims that the refresh rate improvements introduced with Kaleido 4 mean it can display video content at 18 fps. That sounds ridiculous when compared to the 120Hz OLED screen you might already have in your smartphone, but for the typically slow refresh rates of e-paper, it's meaningful.
Because E Ink's screens are used by some of the biggest names in e-readers, like Amazon, Kobo and Boox, the improvements offered by Kaleido 4 could mean your next e-reader will have more accurate color images, without compromising as much on the clarity of black and white text. The relative fuzziness of text on older Kaleido 3 displays is one of their drawbacks, and why some companies use Gallery 3, one of E Ink's other color e-paper technologies. Kaleido displays apply a color filter to the black and white pigments that move around to form text and images on a traditional e-paper panel. E Ink's Gallery displays use colored pigments, which produce richer images and text, but take longer to refresh.
E Ink says the addition of an oxide backplate to its display stack improves refresh rates on the Kaleido 4, a similar modification Amazon said it made to the Kaleido screens used in the original Kindle Colorsoft. We'll have to compare the new tech alongside older Kaleido displays to see how big of a difference E Ink's improvements have made, but for now, Kaleido 4 is only officially being used in one device: Hanvon Technology's M10 C II. The e-paper tablet is only available in China and ships with a Kaleido 4 screen, a redesigned front light and micro-etched glass that offers a more paper-like feel when you write on it.

Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.
A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.
“You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday.
On Saturday, the CJP – a pressure group with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.
The CJP, alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.
Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed a sweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained, including the CJP leaders who were kept overnight.
In the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar and instead proposed three alternative venues – all much further away from parliament – which provoked outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.”
Ranka and Das were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans.
In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”.
The jailed CJP leaders were also given the backing of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who said the people of India would “reclaim Jantar Mantar”.
“Waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice,” said Gandhi.
The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty.
The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”.
The crackdown was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.

Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.
Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.
The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.
“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.
The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.
While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.
The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.
The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.
Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.
Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.
As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”
On Monday, the Keralam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”
What else we’re reading about
Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.
Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.
Climate| Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announced water cuts of at least 10% across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
32
At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check
For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”
For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.

He followed a debunked conspiracy theory to claim a tax refund. So why did the CRA agree to a $40M payout?
Agency scrambling to recover fraudulent payments issued to ‘sovereign’ groups
In the summer of 2023, northern Ontario ironworker Jonathon Pearce filed bogus tax returns to the Canada Revenue Agency, falsely claiming he was owed refunds going back several years totalling more than $40 million.
Internal records obtained by CBC's the fifth estate show the agency did not check the veracity of the returns and two weeks later began sending out the refunds in instalments to Pearce's bank account, including a $10-million deposit on Aug. 8, 2023.
Pearce, a longtime resident of Temiskaming Shores, 500 kilometres north of Toronto, initially declined an interview.
But when fifth estate co-host Steven D'Souza knocked on his door recently, Pearce said he was as surprised as anyone when the millions landed in his personal bank account.
"I thought [the CRA] would turn around and say, 'I'm sorry, sir, this doesn't work that way.' Next thing you know, [I was] getting a refund," he said. "Well, this is an easy way to create money."
A fifth estate investigation has found that Pearce is one of a growing movement of so-called "sovereigns" who believe Canada as a country does not exist. Following debunked online conspiracy theories, they have successfully duped the CRA into repeatedly handing over millions in bogus refunds, taking advantage of massive gaps in the agency's fraud detection systems.
A CRA affidavit obtained by the fifth estate shows that Pearce himself contacted the agency's call centre 10 days before he got the refund. An agency investigator who later listened to the recording stated that Pearce outlined the tax "scheme" and his conspiracy beliefs.
Despite Pearce's phone call, the agency still deposited millions in his bank account.
- Watch the full documentary, "The Sovereign Swindle," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.
After the agency looked into how Pearce got his refund, leaked records show it identified that between May 2023 and January 2024, nearly $300 million in bogus claims were linked to the same tax scheme as Pearce. It is unclear how much was paid out.
One auditor later wrote there was no validation process in place to "verify the legitimacy" of the requested refunds before they go out.
Heather Evans was appointed commissioner of the Canada Revenue Agency on July 13, 2026. Evans declined an interview with the fifth estate. (Canadian Revenue Agency)
In a recent statement to the fifth estate, the CRA said it is "unable" to know how much money in total the agency has paid out in bogus returns to sovereign citizen groups, also known as "tax protesters," because it does not track fraudulent returns by "personal views or intent."
The commissioner of the Canada Revenue Agency, Heather Evans, declined an interview.
The minister responsible for the agency, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, told the fifth estate he was unaware of the specific allegations.
"We have a robust process to make sure of the integrity of what we do at the CRA, but we'll be looking into that," he told co-host Steven D'Souza outside a recent cabinet meeting.
An in-depth review of Pearce's Facebook profile shows he follows a debunked online conspiracy theory falsely claiming that every Canadian has a secret trust set up for them when they are born worth millions. According to the fallacy circulating online, only people with specialized knowledge are able to unlock the funds.
Former CRA investigator Shawna Roy says the theory is ludicrous and that there is no pot of money assigned at birth.
"That is not a thing," she said.
The government does "not have a trust assigned to you" when you are born, Roy told the fifth estate.
Former Canada Revenue Agency investigator Shawna Roy thinks there needs to be more checks and balances at the CRA to stop bogus refunds from being sent out. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Pearce, however, said he believes more strongly in the debunked conspiracy theory than ever because the CRA did, in fact, give him the money.
"If the CRA gives me money, who are you to f–king question it?" Pearce told D'Souza.
"As far as I'm concerned, it was between me and CRA. If CRA had a problem, they wouldn't have given me the money."
In his return, Pearce filed T4A slips, which are typically used to report extra income. In his case, Pearce did not report any income, but erroneously stated he had paid millions in taxes since 2016 and wanted it refunded.
CRA's conduct 'enraging,' says former investigator
Roy told the fifth estate Pearce's views are not based on fact or law and that he clearly filed a bogus tax return at the expense of the public purse. She said it is concerning that three years later he appears not to have been charged with tax fraud.
"I can't comprehend it, I can't make sense of it."
Roy said if the agency had done even a little due diligence, it would have known that a factory worker requesting a $40-million refund would probably not qualify for one.
"I think it's enraging."

During an hour-long interview on his front porch, Pearce remained unapologetic about getting the refund, echoing anti-government and anti-tax videos he frequently reposts on his public Facebook page, including conspiracies that Western democracies are illegitimate.
The conversation took place only a few metres from Pearce's Ford F-250 truck, which he says he purchased after receiving the CRA refunds and which he then made his profile picture on Facebook.
Pearce said everyone could do what he did if they just knew how.
"If you really want to know this stuff, you really got to dig deep."
Pearce said he learned those secrets through online "sovereign" gurus who provide seminars on how not to pay tax and still get a refund from the CRA.
The CRA alleges in court documents that Teresa Wallace, left, Angela Bowolin, Bernard Yankson and Pearce are linked to bogus tax refunds. (Daniel Rofusz)
In a statement, Dave Conabree, the CRA's assistant commissioner of security, said that while he could not comment on specific cases, they were aware of schemes "promoted by individuals who reject or challenge Canada's tax system."
"The CRA takes these activities very seriously and has measures in place to detect, prevent and address fraud and non-compliance."
Still, those public court documents obtained by the fifth estate detail how the agency was aware of the ironworker's conspiracy beliefs in advance of paying the bogus refunds.
An affidavit filed in early September 2024 by the CRA in Ontario Court of Justice states that Pearce contacted the agency's call centre on July 21, 2023 — more than a week before the CRA began sending Pearce the money.
According to the affidavit, Pearce discussed "matters relating to the alleged scheme for a majority of the [July 21] call" and told the call centre "he shouldn't be paying taxes."
Yet 10 days later, on July 31, the CRA deposited the first instalment of refunds into Pearce's account for slightly less than $500,000.
Instalments stopped after bank alert
On Aug. 8, Pearce received a further $10 million. Two more scheduled instalments of $10 and $20 million for later in August were stopped after Pearce's bank alerted the agency to the unusual payments, according to internal CRA documents.
In a followup email to the fifth estate, the agency said it would not answer questions about why it began depositing millions into Pearce's account despite knowing about his conspiracy beliefs beforehand.
Despite having filed a lengthy affidavit in public court about Pearce's tax details, the media office said that the CRA itself cannot disclose individual taxpayer information and would therefore also not provide the fifth estate with recordings of Pearce's conversations with the agency's call centre.
Former CRA investigator Roy said the whole story is discouraging for honest Canadians who pay their fair share of taxes and that the $10 million-plus refund should never have been paid in the first place.
"We're paying what we're supposed to pay and then you have people who can make a complete mockery and joke out of the system and then still get away with it."
Canada is a 'corporation'
According to Carmen Celestini, a lecturer at the University of Waterloo in Waterloo, Ont., who studies conspiracy theories and disinformation, so-called sovereigns believe Canada is not a country, but rather a "corporation" — and that they can opt out.
A sovereign is "somebody who sees themselves separate from society," she told the fifth estate. "They are not part of our nation. They can create their own nation. They are not beholden to our laws."
Leaked internal CRA records say that, in addition to Pearce, there were 19 social insurance numbers representing other individuals involved with the specific scheme he used.
Facebook conspiracy theories
The fifth estate has learned there are networks of "sovereign" online forums, websites and social media apps, many of which sprang up after the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns. For a fee, some of them actively instruct followers how to become "sovereign" and claim tax refunds from the CRA.
One "sovereign" website promising tax refunds is run by Angela Albright Bowolin in Kaslo, in B.C.'s southern Interior.
In her online videos, she promises to unlock sovereign secrets to members who make a "donation." On her personal Facebook page, she said "not paying taxes" is possible, and that she is "leaving that system" and that "You can, too!"
The fifth estate has learned that one of her followers is Teresa Wallace, from Silverton in B.C.'s Interior, who the CRA now alleges received a bogus $5-million tax refund in 2024. Court records show the agency is attempting to get the money back.
In an audio recording posted on Bowolin's website, Wallace and her partner, Peter Gay, who also goes by Peter Carson, credit Bowolin and her colleague, Bernard Yankson, with helping them out.
Wallace and Gay did not respond to calls and emails from the fifth estate.
Pearce, however, credits Vancouver-based sovereign guru AJ DeSwart for helping him achieve his refund from the CRA.
DeSwart, who has their own public Telegram channel, posted voice memos in June that there are "billions and billions" available. "I knew about this shit a long time ago."
Raids 'across the country'
The fifth estate has learned that after paying out tens of millions in bogus refunds, the CRA is scrambling to undo the damage — and has launched criminal investigations into at least two sovereign gurus in the Vancouver area.
DeSwart has raised concerns about those CRA investigations on Telegram.
"There are raids happening across the country with 16-plus f–king agents and a bunch of RCMP officers," DeSwart said in a Telegram voice note in June.
DeSwart declined an on-camera interview, but told the fifth estate they did not help Pearce.
Still, court records obtained by the fifth estate back up their claims about criminal investigations.
A search warrant dated May 23, 2026, authorized a CRA search of Yankson's home, alleging he and Bowolin had engaged in tax fraud by counselling "others to make false statements … on tax returns" and to "obtain refunds that they are not entitled to."
According to internal records, the CRA scrambled to recover the millions it paid Pearce, but was still searching for more than $1 million that had been spent or gone missing. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
The fifth estate reached out to both Bowolin and Yankson.
Bowolin declined to speak to the fifth estate. In an e-mail to the CBC, Bolowin says she hasn't been charged with any offence and denies any criminal wrongdoing.
In an email, Yankson said he "categorically rejects any allegation" that associates him with fraud, unlawful activities or anti-government movements, or hostility towards government institutions, including allegations made by the CRA.
Yankson has filed a lawsuit concerning the raids in Federal Court, arguing his Charter rights were violated. No court date has been scheduled.

Back in Ontario, Pearce told the fifth estate the CRA searched his home two years ago and is garnishing his wages, but believes he will never be charged.
According to internal agency records, the CRA scrambled to recover the millions it paid Pearce, but was still searching for more than $1 million that had been spent or gone missing.
"I know I haven't done anything wrong," Pearce said.

On Oct. 12, as federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn, as part of an alleged criminal investigation, a rumor spread online that Omar had escaped to Morocco, which has no extradition treaty with the U.S.
One post (archived) on X read, "We're hearing from sources at the State Department that Ilhan Omar has fled the United States for Morocco, which does not have a billatral extradition treaty with the US."
There is no evidence Omar has escaped to Morocco. The source for this claim, Real Raw News, frequently spreads false and unverified rumors, many of which we have previously debunked. Additionally, Omar posted about the investigation on her social media accounts, describing her intention to fight back. As such, we rate this claim as false.
Snopes reached out to Omar's office for comment. We will update this post as we get more information.
The earliest example of this claim appeared on Real Raw News' X account. The same account posted an AI generated image claiming to show Omar appearing to hide in a tunnel claiming she "has gone underground":
We're hearing [sic] more reports that Ilhan Omar fled her home 30 minutes before the raid and has gone underground, hiding, fearing arrest. Working on two or three [sic] articles right now but will have this report out asap.
Real Raw News frequently posts false and unfounded information. It describes itself as a website for "for informational and educational and entertainment purposes" on its about page, which also says its content includes "humor, parody, and satire." Real Raw News' social media posts about the Omar claim did not contain a satire disclaimer.
Omar raid and investigation
On Oct. 12, Homeland Security Investigations agents carried out a pre-dawn raid of Omar's Washington, D.C., home. In a statement on her Congressional web page, Omar's office called the raid "an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."
A few hours after the raid, Omar posted (archived) on X:
I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.
I will not be silenced.
Omar also posted a series of older clips of herself making critical comments about Fox News and Trump and resisting questions from reporters repeating old and unfounded claims that she had been married to her brother — a rumor we have debunked before.
On Oct. 15, Omar posted another statement on X in response to the news that the Trump administration had also probed her immigration records in 2019 and found nothing. She wrote:
Thank you to everyone who stood with me over the years. It's been a scary journey but I have always been grounded in my work and ability to provide exemplary service to my constituents. Trump and his administration have been after me since I arrived in Congress. I have always stood up to him and that will never change. The pedophile protector will never silence me.
As of this writing, Omar has not been seen publicly since the raid. Federal agents also reportedly seized Omar's laptop, cell phone and passport during their raid, according to an anonymous source speaking to MS NOW. We are unable to confirm whether Omar got those items back.
A video shows Fox News asking Omar's husband, Tim Mynett, if the congresswoman had fled the country while he was walking outside their Washington, D.C., home. Mynett responded: "You guys are annoying the hell out of all the neighbors around here, man."
In an earlier interaction with Fox News on the same street, Mynett was asked about his reaction to the raid. He said: "My wife came here when she was 12 years old, a child war refugee. No concerns."
Omar is also running for reelection in her Minnesota district in the November midterms. In early October, her campaign posted a video of her appealing for donations "to help pay for security for her and her campaign" as she said she was "under attack" by Trump. Ahead of an important election, it is improbable that Omar would escape the country as the posts claim.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, but U.S. Vice President JD Vance previously accused Omar of committing immigration fraud. In September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said his agency was investigating such claims. In October, The Washington Post reported the Trump administration had probed Omar's immigration records in 2019 for the same issues being investigated today, and found nothing.
Snopes has reported on numerous false and unverified rumors about Omar.

'Bhaag Neha Bhaag, Jantar Mantar Chalo': Delhi protests inspire online games where players take on roles of protesters, cops
From gathering virtual crowds and dodging water cannons to escaping police chases, the Jantar Mantar protests have inspired a series of free online video games.
Protests at Jantar Mantar are now inspiring online gaming experiences. Developers have created free online games inspired by the demonstrations, giving players virtual roles as protesters and police personnel in challenges involving crowds, barricades and detentions.
From ‘Jantar Mantar Chalo’, which lets players choose between protesters and police personnel, to ‘Bhaag Neha Bhaag’, inspired by AISA national president Neha Bora’s attempts to reach the protest site, the games draw on recent political developments and the scenes that unfolded on the streets of the national capital.
Another game, ‘Jantar Mantar to Jail’, features Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) members Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. Players must dodge falling jail bars and police personnel while collecting coins representing “accountability” and “democracy”.
The games allows users to participate in virtual versions of events that have attracted attention online.
‘Bhaag Neha Bhaag’ takes inspiration from repeated detentions
Inspired by the protests is ‘Bhaag Neha Bhaag’, created by 30-year-old screenwriter and filmmaker Anav Nayar. He co-founded Wizloop Studios with his brother, Akshay Nayar, with the company focusing on content strategy, intellectual property for brands and the creative use of AI, PTI reported.
Nayar said the idea came from following Neha Bora’s attempts to reach Jantar Mantar and her repeated detentions.
“We were following how Neha Bora and other protesters were trying to reach Jantar Mantar. They were detained but the very next day, they were back at the spot. “My brother Akshay asked me how they were managing to do it, and that got me thinking about creating a game around it,” Nayar told PTI.
The brothers named the game Bhaag Neha Bhaag, drawing inspiration from the 1998 German film Run Lola Run, one of their favourites.
‘Jantar Mantar Chalo’ draws thousands of players
Suraj Kushwah, a 27-year-old resident of Bareilly who works at a cloud gaming company, developed Jantar Mantar Chalo after watching news coverage of the protests.
“I was watching the news and, out of sarcasm, thought of making a game around it,” Kushwah told PTI.
A technology enthusiast, Kushwah used artificial intelligence (AI) tools and his gaming knowledge to develop the game in about one-and-a-half days.
Players can choose to play as either protesters or Delhi Police personnel. Those playing as protesters must gather people and march towards Jantar Mantar, with larger crowds making them more powerful. Players choosing the police role, meanwhile, must detain as many protesters as possible.
The game incorporates several elements associated with the demonstrations. Tear gas slows down protesters, while water cannons present another obstacle. Players can also dance in front of water cannons and interact with media personnel through interviews.
Media coverage influences the game's progression. Interviews can increase a protester's influence and attract more people to the gathering. Its virtual map includes locations such as police stations, detention centres, India Gate and the Badarpur border.
“I made it as a sarcastic take, but now that it is getting so much attention; I am looking at updating it further,” he said.
‘Jantar Mantar to Jail’ turns accountability into points
The Nayar brothers also developed Jantar Mantar to Jail, which features CJP members Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka.
Players choose one of the three characters and attempt to avoid obstacles, including falling jail bars and police personnel dressed in orange kurtas.
Another game inspired by the protests features chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. It turns a satirical act involving a tap on his head into a scoring mechanic.
Protest context to the games
In June and July, the group led protests, including a march towards Parliament on July 20, demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as Union education minister over repeated paper leaks and student suicides. He was forced to resign over a month later.
The groups returned to the streets in October, joining opposition parties and student organisations in demonstrations seeking the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar. The protesters raised allegations concerning the functioning of the Election Commission and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
The demonstrations generated images, videos and online discussions that subsequently became a source of inspiration for the game developers.

New law aims to stop overdoses with stiffer penalties as 8 states struggle to slow deaths
The proposed change would make possession of any amount of fentanyl a felony

Colorado continues to face an increase in overdose deaths while other states have seen a downturn.
Illicitly manufactured fentanyl, a potent opioid, emerged in the Colorado drug market around 2018. That was nearly five years after it began tormenting people who use street drugs in Northeastern states.
By 2019, fentanyl replaced other drugs as the driving force behind opioid overdoses in Colorado, and it has held its grip ever since.
But while overdose deaths in the U.S. are currently experiencing a historic decline of almost 14%, Colorado is one of eight states where rates are not dropping. In fact, Colorado has had an increase of nearly 12% in overdose deaths since April 2025.
Overdoses are top of mind for many everyday Coloradans, healthcare professionals, elected officials and public health experts like me.
Proposition 132 attempts to address these concerns by stiffening legal penalties. A conservative policy organization called Advance Colorado collected the signatures to get the initiative on the November ballot.
The proposed change to Colorado law would make possession of any amount of fentanyl a felony, require a mandatory minimum eight-year prison sentence for distribution of any quantity of fentanyl, and eliminate some existing opportunities for reduced penalties.
Before Coloradans head to the polls, it is worth examining the state’s overdose trends and considering whether Proposition 132 is likely to solve the problem.
A 2022 law already increased penalties
Let’s start by looking at Colorado’s past attempts to stop drug overdoses through legislation. In recent years, the state has pursued some public health interventions but has leaned heavily on increasing criminal penalties for using and possessing fentanyl.
The 2022 Fentanyl Accountability and Prevention Act (HB22-1326), for instance, represented a major expansion of criminal penalties.
This law rolled back a 2019 law that had decriminalized small amounts of drugs. Specifically, HB22-1326 made the knowing possession of more than 1 gram and up to 4 grams of a substance containing fentanyl a Level 4 drug felony punishable by up to 180 days in jail and two years of probation.
Unlike Proposition 132, the 2022 fentanyl act directed funding for the distribution of naloxone, an overdose reversal medication, and fentanyl test strips that help people identify fentanyl in their drugs before using them. Both naloxone and fentanyl test strips decrease the risk of fatal overdose.
The law did not direct funding toward evidence-based treatments such as methadone or buprenorphine for opioid use disorder.
Supporters argued that the legislation was necessary to prevent overdose deaths and get people treatment.
I led a research team that included addiction treatment providers and substance use–focused epidemiologists to study the effects of HB22-1326. Although more people were arrested and faced the tougher penalties, we found no increase in people beginning or staying on buprenorphine. We also found that fewer people were starting and staying on methadone following the implementation of the law.
Importantly, we found that the law did not change the trajectory of overdose deaths compared to what was expected. Taken together, we found no substantial evidence that increasing criminal penalties, even with some increased funding for naloxone and overdose prevention, “saved lives” as proponents had hoped.
Colorado is already uniquely punitive toward people who use illicit drugs, with some of the harshest penalties for drug possession and distribution in the U.S. Colorado’s public health response has developed alongside, not in place of, a substantial criminal-legal response.
What decreases overdose deaths?
Even with efforts to provide additional access to harm-reduction protections, escalating criminal penalties have not produced the treatment gains or decreases in overdose deaths in Colorado that proponents promised.
So, let’s look at a place in the state where overdose deaths are actually falling to see what is being done differently there.
Larimer County, home of Colorado State University and part of Rocky Mountain National Park, offers the clearest contrast to the rest of the state. Accidental overdose deaths have declined year after year since 2022, down nearly 42% from 2021.
What’s going on in Larimer County?
For one, the Larimer County Jail is one of less than half of the Colorado county jails that offers a comprehensive treatment program that includes medications for opioid use disorder.
The sheriff’s office, in collaboration with several community-based organizations, has also flooded the community with naloxone through the Reversal Project. Furthermore, using opioid abatement funds, the county has expanded youth and family support services, co-responder units and other harm-reduction services. The county has also steadily increased the number of people on buprenorphine.
No single intervention can be credited with Larimer County’s decline in accidental overdoes deaths. Criminal enforcement remains one component of the county’s response. Yet, what stands out is its emphasis on evidence-based interventions with an emphasis on expanding treatment access and harm-reduction services that save lives and give people the stability and opportunity to build healthier lives.
A polysubstance problem
In addition, Proposition 132 has a major flaw. It targets one drug: fentanyl. But the available data suggests most people take fentanyl together with stimulants such as methamphetamine. Both drugs can be fatal.
Between 2020 and 2024, nearly 40% of overdose deaths in Colorado involved both opioids and stimulants. National figures follow a similar pattern. Nationally, 43% of overdose deaths in 2024 involved both opioids and stimulants.
Targeting one substance, as Proposition 132 does, ignores the fact that the state has a true “polysubstance” epidemic and will end up making people who unknowingly possess fentanyl susceptible to harsher penalties set forth by Proposition 132.
Since Colorado increased fentanyl penalties in 2022, the promised treatment gains examined in our research have not materialized. The state’s number of overdoses has continued to climb.
Those facts do not mean that criminal penalties alone caused Colorado’s worsening trend. But they do raise an important question as voters consider Proposition 132: What evidence suggests that increasing those penalties further will address the rise in overdose deaths?

JDU MLA Anant Singh clarifies on ‘9 murders’ remark
The JD(U) defended ex Bihar CM Nitish Kumar’s political record and rejected any suggestion of an association with criminal activity.
Janata Dal (United) MLA Anant Kumar Singh on Friday claimed to have arranged the murder of nine people to help former Bihar chief minister Nitish Kumar during his political struggles. The ruling party was quick to distance itself from the controversial remark.
Singh, who represents Mokama, made the claim while criticising the party’s decision to field his political rival, Neeraj Kumar, in the upcoming Bihar Legislative Council elections. He has vowed to ensure Neeraj Kumar’s defeat and is backing Jan Suraaj Party candidate Anuj Singh.
"Nitish Kumar and I go back a long way. To help him, I got nine people murdered. I stood by him in times when he was struggling to find a toehold," Singh said, as per PTI.
‘I was shot’
Singh later appeared to clarify. Speaking to ANI, he said nine of his associates were killed during Lalu Prasad Yadav’s government and claimed that the killings were linked to their support for Nitish Kumar. He also said he had been shot during that period and that his family had suffered significant losses.
“During the Lalu Yadav government, nine of my associates were killed, and I myself was shot. It was because we aligned ourselves with Nitish Kumar that Lalu Yadav had them killed. We have suffered such immense losses. My father also passed away due to a heart attack,” Singh told ANI.
JD(U) responds
The JD(U)'s national spokesperson Rajiv Ranjan Prasad said that the remark did not deserve serious consideration. In a video statement, Prasad, without naming Singh, defended Nitish Kumar’s political record and rejected any suggestion of an association with criminal activity.
"Nitish Kumar has stood out for an untainted record, with no blemishes of hobnobbing with criminals and involvement in violence or any type of negativity," he said. "The type of statement that we have come across deserves no cognisance from the party and is unlikely to be taken seriously by the public," Prasad added.
Political rivalry behind the remarks
Singh’s outburst comes amid a dispute over the JD(U)’s choice of candidate for the upcoming Legislative Council polls. His opposition to Neeraj Kumar, a political rival, has put him at odds with the party leadership, even as he insists that his support for Anuj Singh does not reflect disloyalty to Nitish Kumar.
Nitish Kumar, who has led Bihar for much of the past two decades, has built much of his political image around improving law and order in the state. His tenure has often been associated with the promise of ending the lawlessness that marked parts of Bihar’s earlier political landscape.
