School staff wrestled with 'anxiety and dread' before emaciated teen's rescue
Victim impact statements detail lead-up to discovery of student's shocking confinement
Warning: This story contains graphic details about child abuse and animal abuse.
Staff at an Ottawa school who called on police to do the wellness check that led to the rescue of a severely malnourished 18-year-old earlier this year did so after months of "suffocating anxiety and dread" about the growing absence of the complex-needs student.
They also contacted police because when they had previously reached out to the Children's Aid Society of Ottawa (CASO), when the teen was a minor, the school was "dissatisfied" with CASO's response, a courtroom heard this week.
"I knew something wasn't right," one school employee said in court about the days, weeks and months that passed without the teen coming to school.
Another recalled that after a distressing update from the teen's mother, she lay awake at night "haunted by thoughts of what he was enduring."
"Something in our system needs to change so that there are checks and balances so that [vulnerable students] cannot just disappear," she added.
CASO said it doesn't comment on specific cases or actions taken, citing confidentiality.
"However, we can assure you that every report concerning the safety and well-being of a child is carefully assessed through a child protection and safety lens," the organization said in an email to CBC News on Friday.
"The Society's priority is always the evaluation of potential risk to a child, and all concerns are reviewed and responded to in accordance with applicable child protection standards, legislation and professional practices."
'Difficult to imagine a more vulnerable human'
On Tuesday, the teen's mother pleaded guilty to criminal negligence causing bodily harm, failing to provide the necessaries of life, and failing to care for a family cat that was found dead by the teen's bedside.
The judge sentenced her to nine years in prison for the first conviction and shorter concurrent sentences for the other two.
According to an agreed statement of facts read out in court, police discovered the teen, who is now 19, in January 2026. He was found in what court heard described as a boarded-up "cage bed" in a decrepit basement bedroom.
Though he was 18 and therefore an adult at the time of his rescue, "it's difficult to imagine a more vulnerable human being," assistant Crown attorney Louise Tansey said. The teen was born with a rare genetic disorder affecting his speech, movement and cognitive development. He is also prone to seizures.
"He will forever remain childlike, forever in that vulnerable state," Tansey said.
In the fall of 2025, the teen remained absent from school amid a series of red flags about his family situation. But as detailed in the victim impact statements read out by three school staff members on Tuesday, the concerns about his well-being stretched over years.
And even after the vice-principal shared the good news about the teen being removed from the home, the relief school staff felt was coupled with shock over the teen's condition — and guilt over not having sounded the alarm sooner.
"How I wish I never sent him home the last day of school the previous June, " the first staff member said.
Out of sight
Neither the teen nor his mother can be identified under a publication ban.
The first staff member said she worked with the teen one-on-one for years. He needed help to walk around but loved crawling on the floor during gym time.
"[He] isn’t a complicated guy. He has needs and wants like every other human, but if he’s fed, clean, well-dressed and loved, he is beyond happy," she said.
According to the second staff member, "the decline in the care that [he] was receiving from home," plus the amount of time he was being kept at home, compelled staff to push for a wellness check.
It was an agonizing dilemma that tortured all of us who cared for him, always suspecting the worst but not having any factual evidence. We needed to tread lightly for fear that we would not ever see him again.School staff member
The growing boy who'd been "a smiley, chubby-cheeked [and] active" student began showing up to school with bruises and a "ravenous" appetite, "desperately eating as if every meal might be his last," the third staff member said.
Staff were once told he'd fallen down the stairs at home after his chair locks were disengaged, but there was no damage to the chair, she said.
"A suffocating anxiety and dread took hold of every staff member watching this sweet boy wither away before our eyes," she said.
The school spoke to the mother often, provided the family gift cards and, when the funding for that ran out, staff bought food and other supplies with their own money.
"We would drop them off at his home hoping to catch a glimpse of our smiley friend," the third staff member continued. "Unfortunately, each time we would go to drop off things at home, we were not allowed to see [him]. [She] would always meet us outside the house."
Children's Aid Society contacted
According to the agreed statement of facts, the school contacted the Children's Aid Society of Ottawa in 2024 because the teen had appeared gaunt and pale.
He missed a lot of school that fall, and when a staff member ran into the mother at a store and went to see the teen who was waiting in the family's car, she was horrified by his "shockingly emaciated" appearance, the third staff member said.
It's unclear how CASO responded when contacted in 2024. The school reached out to CASO again at a later point when the teen was now 18, the third staff member said.
"[CASO] stated they could not act because he was [an adult] and suggested a police wellness check," she said.
- Children's Aid Society of Ottawa at breaking point, organization says
- Children's aid workers in Ottawa ratify deal, end strike
According to the agreed statement of facts, "the school was dissatisfied with [CASO's] response to their concerns and so on Jan. 21, 2026, they contacted the Ottawa Police for assistance."
In a statement emailed to CBC News on Thursday, the Children's Aid Society of Ottawa said it can't comment on, confirm or deny any involvement with specific people or families, adding that child welfare records are confidential.
The organization confirmed that once a young person reaches their 18th birthday, they are no longer subject to the child protection provisions of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act.
Not much was shared in court Tuesday about the mother's background.
Oliver Abergel, the lawyer representing her that day, said she was abandoned by her mother and grew up with a father who was not particularly present.
"I can only imagine that the background did not help, and it's not being offered as an excuse," Abergel said, adding that the mother "was not particularly interested in having a violin brought out for her" and has accepted responsibility for her crimes.
Abergel did not say whether the mother struggled as a result of any systemic gaps to getting her son the care he needed.
But in a letter of support filed with the court and which was provided to CBC News on Friday afternoon, the mother's aunt wrote that the mother needed help and still needs help, "not jail time."
The death of the mother's own grandmother hit her hard, according to the aunt.
"Our entire family kept saying ... [she] would not be able to handle it but she kept saying she would never abandon her children like her mother did and honestly she did her best."
"I know she could have reached out to an organization for help but honestly I think she just wanted to prove everyone wrong who doubted her and unfortunately went about it the wrong way," the aunt added. "What she did wasn't malicious. It was a cry for help. I'm not saying it was right but it definitely wasn't intentional."
The mother's guilty pleas spared the court a potentially lengthy trial and witnesses being re-traumatized, the lawyer who represented her Tuesday said. (Guy Quenneville/CBC)
In response to a request to talk about what supports are available for caregivers of complex-needs teens who turn adult, CASO wrote that that transition "can create challenges in situations where vulnerable young adults continue to require significant care, supervision or support but no longer fall within the child welfare system's protection mandate."
"In such circumstances, concerns about an adult's safety or wellbeing may fall under the responsibility of other community systems, including health care providers, developmental services, community agencies, adult protective supports where available or police services when there are immediate safety concerns," CASO added in its written statement.
There is ongoing discussion across Ontario and Canada about the need for strong transition planning and "enhanced services" for youth with complex needs as they age out of the children's systems, the organization added.
Stopped coming to school
For staff at the teen's school, the decision to contact CASO was not easy, according to the third staff member.
"[Some] staff were so worried that we would strain the relationship with the mom and that she would pull him from school," she said, adding that the school later learned the mother was "furious" CASO had checked in on the family.
"[She] had told his support workers that once [her son] turned 18, she wasn’t required to send him back [to school]. This threw my colleagues and I into a panic," she added.
By the fall of 2025, the teen had stopped showing up to school altogether and CHEO had lost contact with the mother, court heard.
The school called and emailed the mother weekly. "In one response, she claimed [her son] refused to come upstairs to eat and that she refused to bring food down to his basement room," the third staff member said.
In October 2025, one of the teen's teachers offered to send a personal support worker to the family's home to help get him ready for school. "There was no response," according to the agreed statement of facts.
Two months later, when hospital staff went to deliver a new stroller, the mother would not let them inside their home. She also refused the school's delivery of a new wheelchair in January 2026.
In arguing for the nine-year sentence on the criminal negligence charge — which was a joint submission with the defence — Tansey, the Crown attorney, described the mother's behaviour as "deprivation being paired with preventing others from rendering life-saving assistance."
'An indelible scar on my soul'
The night before school resumed in January 2026, the teen's mother told staff that he would not be returning to class and that she was placing him in a home.
"Our fears had come true," the third staff member said.
She was no longer on staff at the school, but she and others encouraged the school's vice-principal to call police and ask for a wellness check, she said.
"I wrestled with making that call, terrified of losing the relationship that kept a link to him," she said. "It was an agonizing dilemma that tortured all of us who cared for him, always suspecting the worst but not having any factual evidence. We needed to tread lightly for fear that we would not ever see him again."
The horror of knowing he endured extended starvation, solitary confinement, and severe cruelty in that basement leaves an indelible scar on my soul.School staff member
Police went to the home on Jan. 21 and found the teen in dire condition. The agreed statement of facts lists a host of medical issues, including severe respiratory failure, infestation by bugs and renal failure.
"Police, when they attended, thought they had discovered a body," Tansey said.
The teen is now back at school but can't crawl on the gym floor anymore because his legs suffered substantial atrophy and contractures from his time in confinement, the second staff member said.
When she visited him in the hospital, "I apologized to him for taking so long," she told the courtroom, her voice racked with emotion.
The third staff member said the entire school community is grateful he survived.
But she added, "The horror of knowing he endured extended starvation, solitary confinement and severe cruelty in that basement leaves an indelible scar on my soul."

Tanvi Sharma’s Denmark Open campaign ended in the quarterfinals on Friday, as world champion An Se-young beat her 21-15, 21-13 in Odense.
With the opening game level at 2-2, Tanvi tried to find her rhythm against An, relying on controlled length clears and straight drives. She held her own in the early exchanges, using deep clears to test the world champion’s backcourt and starting rallies with purpose.
However, the longer rallies left Tanvi with little margin for error. She struggled to find openings against An’s tireless retrieving, with her drives down the line often sailing wide or long as she tried to force the pace.
Tanvi ended up on the floor after a punishing, high-intensity baseline exchange, stretching deep to chase down a sharp cross-court placement.

Trailing 17-11 in the opening game, Tanvi fought to close the gap, mixing deep lifts with quick exchanges at the net. However, An’s relentless court coverage continued to frustrate her, and Tanvi struggled to keep her attacking shots within the lines. An eventually closed out the game 21-15.

One of the biggest names in venture capital is looking to hire a new right-hand person.
Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said on X Thursday that he's seeking his next chief of staff, a job that offers a rare opportunity to work in close contact with the billionaire investor whose Silicon Valley firm is known for its early bets on OpenAI, DoorDash, and Instacart.
"What matters is how quickly you learn, the questions you ask, and whether you can think from first principles," Khosla wrote. "You'll help evaluate opportunities and work with founders building consequential companies."
The opening comes as demand for chiefs of staff is growing at a fast clip, with the role offering a potential path to senior leadership. For the person Khosla hires, it also offers a front-row seat to an AI-fueled venture capital boom.
A hot job
Job postings for chiefs of staff on Indeed were nearly 90% above pre-pandemic levels in September, far outpacing management jobs and postings overall. In the San Francisco Bay Area, the median advertised salary for the role is $175,000, compared with about $152,000 nationally, according to Indeed.
Through the first three quarters of this year, US VC deal value reached $516 billion across an estimated 14,199 deals, according to PitchBook. That is already the highest total in the research firm's dataset and roughly 44% above the prior record, set in 2021.
Most chiefs of staff in the US stay in the same profession when they change jobs, but some move into senior leadership roles, according to a March study from LinkedIn. Becoming a chief operating officer was the second most common career move, accounting for 2.9% of transitions. Another 3.7% became founders or cofounders, while 1% became CEOs.
Close contact
Khosla's new chief of staff will work directly with him to evaluate investment opportunities, meet founders, research emerging technologies, and support portfolio companies, according to the job posting. As the person earns Khosla's trust, they'll also lead conversations on his behalf and help determine which opportunities to pursue.
"It will suit someone who wants significant responsibility and is comfortable with ambiguity," the ad says.
Compensation isn't listed. The posting says the position comes with a three-year commitment and long hours. The successful candidate must work in person in Menlo Park, California, generally from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., and be available nights and weekends when needed.
The potential payoff? Previous chiefs of staff have gone on to start companies, launch investment firms, and take leadership roles at Khosla Ventures, according to the listing.
Applicants shouldn't, however, count on becoming a VC. The posting says the job is "not a dedicated investing seat or a guaranteed path to one."

Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence. Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI.
As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.
“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.
Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.
Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.
The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.
Last month, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes, which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU— who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.
OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI, warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.
As with math, Thompson says we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way.
Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science, and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound.
“We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.”

The International Olympic Committee said it is shutting down 12 permanent committees focusing on issues like human rights and gender issues, saying Friday it will instead create expert panels when needed.
The streamlining and cost-cutting move leaves 19 committees in place. IOC President Kirsty Coventry, who is in her second year in the role, has already relied on appointing smaller working groups for key issues.
A review in March of “protection of the female category” in sports was allocated to an expert panel whose membership was kept confidential rather than the in-house commission for Gender Equality, Diversity and Inclusion. That commission will now be shut down, as will the IOC Advisory Committee on Human Rights chaired by the former deputy president of South Africa, Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka.
Other commissions being scrapped include those for sustainability, technology, athletes’ entourage and digital engagement.
They typically would comprise from 10 to as many as 30 members who would gather in the IOC’s home city Lausanne, Switzerland, for annual meetings.
The IOC said in a statement the switch to ad hoc working groups will allow “targeted engagement on key strategic priorities and policy development.”

Apple’s App Store rules now more explicitly ban so-called “nudify” apps that generate intimate images of people without their consent using AI tools.
Apple’s updated App Store rules go after ‘nudify’ AI apps
The terms more explicitly ban apps that create ‘nonconsensual intimate imagery.’
The rule changes follow significant criticism toward Apple after X users used Grok earlier this year to make nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes, including minors. Apple didn’t pull X or Grok from the App Store, though it told senators that it threatened to yank Grok. At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did.
As part of updates announced Friday, Apple says that developers “must proactively prevent and remove” nonconsensual, sexual images as part of its content moderation requirements for App Store apps. Developers who “fail to implement adequate safeguards” or “don’t remedy violations after notice” may be removed from the App Store. Apple also clarified a rule that bars “bait-and-switch” apps, or apps that add or change features, including “nudification,” after they have been approved.
Apple’s rules also more clearly spell out that any apps that “facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children” will be pulled from the App Store and “blocked from alternative distribution.”

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

McNuggets, booze smuggled by drone into Canada's most secure prison: union
Union says it's at 'breaking point' for illegal goods entering Quebec facility
The union representing correctional officers is raising the alarm after it says an inmate had a drone drop off a McDonald's meal and alcohol to what's supposed to be Canada's most secure prison earlier this week.
The union said the drone delivered McDonald's chicken nuggets and fries complete with sauce and some alcohol straight to the inmate's cell window in the special handling unit at the Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, Que., facility at around 3 a.m. on Thursday.
"The inmate found that really funny in the morning when the guards did their rounds," said Mike Bolduc, regional president of the UCCO-SACC-CSN union, in an interview.
But he's not laughing. The union has been growing increasingly concerned about contraband, from cellphones to knives, getting into the maximum security facility via drone.
"We're at the breaking point where an inmate went and delivered himself McDonald's.… What's the next thing? Is that a loaded gun? You know, it's scaring us, it's really scaring us," he said.
The inmate's unit — known as the SHU — houses extremely violent and high-risk offenders. Some of Canada's most notorious killers, like Clifford Olson and Allan Legere, spent part of their incarceration at the Quebec prison along with convicted terrorists.
"It's supposed to be the most secure jail in Canada and he's eating McDonald's," said Bolduc.
The details of the story were first reported on by TVA Nouvelles.
Drones are an escalating problem for Canada's penitentiary system and those who run it.
'What in the heck?' Conservative MP
Correctional Service Canada (CSC) deploys unmanned aerial vehicle detection technology at its institutions, but Bolduc said it's concerning that the radar didn't appear to detect this drone.
He thinks inmates probably get multiple drones sent out to find blind spots.
"So what happened here is that they beat the technology," said Bolduc. "The drones are incredible [with] the damage that they're causing."
The union been pushing for a far more low-tech solution: physical netting
"It's not harder than that," Bolduc said. "This now has to be a cry for help saying that we need that netting as fast as possible."
The entrance of the Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines penitentiary is shown on July 3, 2005. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)
Bolduc said the McDonald's delivery should be a "wake-up call" for federal Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree, whose government cut $132 million from CSC's operational budget.
"I'm scared for Canadians, for their security," he said.
In a social media video Conservative MP Frank Caputo, the party's public safety critic, said the minister has been too slow on the issue of drones delivering illegal goods to prisons.
"What in the heck are we doing in Canada?" he said.
In a statement, CSC said the incident is under review but wouldn't comment on the case further, citing security considerations.
"The introduction of contraband and unauthorized items into correctional institutions remains an important issue that CSC continues to actively address," said spokesperson Kevin Antonucci.
"CSC continues to implement a multi-layered approach that includes staff vigilance, security intelligence activities, searches, detection technologies and collaboration with police and other partners."
Anandasangaree's office referred CBC News to the CSC comment.

Serbian populist leader Aleksandar Vucic returns to tragedy-hit Novi Sad for preelection rally
Serbia’s populist leader Aleksandar Vucic has returned to Novi Sad, the northern city where 16 people died in a train station tragedy almost two years ago that set off a wave of anti-government protests
NOVI SAD, Serbia -- NOVI SAD, Serbia (AP) — Serbia 's populist leader Aleksandar Vucic on Friday staged a preelection rally in Novi Sad, the northern city where 16 people died in a train station tragedy almost two years ago setting off a wave of mass anti-government protests.
Thousands of flag-waving supporters attended the gathering at a central square in Novi Sad, many bused in from other parts of the country. It was Vucic’s first big rally in the city since the protests started in November 2024.
The former Serbian president and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, are facing a major test in the Oct. 25 election after 14 years in power in the Balkan country. The main challenger is the Students’ List candidates supported by Serbia’s protesting university students.
Serbia’s youth led the mass demonstrations demanding accountability for the concrete canopy collapse at the Novi Sad train station that many in Serbia believed was the result of bad construction work during renovation and of corruption-fueled negligence.
Near daily protests rattled Vucic more than ever and protesters forced a government collapse as student rallies drew hundreds of thousands of people.
Vucic's return to Novi Sad was seen as a show of confidence ahead of the Oct. 25 vote that he said his party will win. Without providing evidence, Vucic in a speech said that the student-led protests were organized and financed by unspecified foreign powers.
“A lot of money came from abroad, billions were brought in to destroy Serbia," he told the crowd. "They used the tragedy and moved against our Serbia ... they hate everything that is Serbian.”
A special guest at the rally was Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, who praised Vucic in a speech he held in the Serbian language.
Critics accuse Vucic and his party of clamping down on democratic freedoms, rampant corruption and ties to organized crime, which they have denied. Serbia is formally seeking European Union membership but the effort has stalled under Vucic, who has close ties with Russia and China.
No one has been held responsible for the train station tragedy despite the protests, and the issue remains highly sensitive for Novi Sad. Students have urged residents to stay away on Friday to avoid confrontation with Vucic's supporters.
In his speech, Vucic promised justice for the Novi Sad tragedy. Pro-government media reported that he arrived in Novi Sad by train and then walked through the city flanked by chanting supporters.
Many in the crowd waved flags with the image of the former Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladic, who was convicted of genocide by a U.N. war crimes court for atrocities during Bosnia's 1992-95 conflict. Mladic was buried as a hero in Belgrade in September following his death in the The Hague, Netherlands.
Vucic is looking to return as prime minister after the vote on Oct. 25. He resigned as president last month to lead his SNS party's campaign and boost its chances at the parliamentary ballot.
Novi Sad was the scene of clashes with police and Vucic’s supporters on several occasions during protests. No major incidents were reported Friday.

In his first stint at Mumbai Indians from 2017 to 2022, the 49-year-old guided the side to three titles.

- The upcoming Cyberpunk 2077 live-action movie isn't a 1:1 adaptation of the video game.
- Michał Nowakowski, CD Projekt Red's joint CEO, has revealed that the movie will feature an original story.
- More details about the live-action Cyberpunk 2077 movie will be shared in the future.
CD Projekt Red’s Michał Nowakowski has opened up about the upcoming live-action Cyberpunk movie. In a recent interview with Polish outlet PAP Biznes, CD Projekt Red’s joint CEO has confirmed that the live-action Cyberpunk 2077 movie won’t be a direct adaptation of the popular game. Instead, the live-action team will tell a completely original story set in Night City.
Cyberpunk 2077 Live-Action Movie Won’t Adapt the Game, CD Projekt Red Says
Speaking with Polish outlet PAP Biznes, Michał Nowakowski, joint CEO of CD Projekt, said the company wanted to make a live-action Cyberpunk 2077 movie in a “new formula” following its collaboration with Paramount Pictures.
As a result, the production team decided to go for a fresh story set in the Cyberpunk 2077 world rather than adapt one of the best video games of all time. Michał added that this is all they can reveal for now and that they will share more details about the live-action movie when both parties are ready to.
“At this point, we can only say that we definitely don’t want to make a film adaptation of the game. We want to tell a story in the world of Cyberpunk, but it won’t be a one-to-one translation of the game’s story,” Michał said.
Ultimately, the live-action production appears to be following a similar approach to the team behind the Cyberpunk: Edgerunners anime. The first season of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, one of the best animated shows like Arcane, tells the tragic tale of David Martinez, a street kid from Night City.
Meanwhile, Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2, premiering on October 20, 2026, follows four different characters in Night City whose journeys are intertwined. The anime is solid proof that Night City is full of intriguing and heartbreaking stories, and the live-action Cyberpunk movie could draw inspiration from them.
In the same interview, Michał discussed how interest in the Cyberpunk 2077 game surged when the first season of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners premiered. He hopes for a similar result when the second season arrives on Netflix, potentially driving up game sales:
“In 2022, when the first installment of the anime debuted, we observed increased interest in the game. This was particularly noticeable during the series’ premiere, but equally importantly, in the following months, game sales continued to exceed those observed before its premiere. We hope that this time we will also be able to invite anime viewers to our game.”
The release date of the live-action Cyberpunk 2077 movie remains unknown at the time of writing. Transformers franchise producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura is producing the movie, with CD Projekt Red closely involved in its development.

People who developed an early onset of Alzheimer's disease -- before turning 65 -- displayed symptoms and conditions different to those in late-onset Alzheimer's, accumulating a wide range of health problems, particularly during the five years preceding diagnosis, a study has found.
Researchers from the University of Oulu and the University of Eastern Finland said the group is more likely to experience depression, dizziness, headaches, traumatic brain injuries, epilepsy, cerebrovascular disorders, thyroid diseases and problems related to heavy alcohol use.
Tinnitus (ringing in ears) and hearing loss were already more common six to ten years before diagnosis, findings published in the journal Alzheimer's and Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association showed.
However, cardiovascular risk factors traditionally associated with Alzheimer's disease were found to be no more common among those diagnosed at working age, compared to age- and sex-matched healthy people.
Cardiovascular risk factors, alongside advanced age, are among the best-known risk factors for the neurodegenerative disease, the researchers said.
However, compared to late-onset Alzheimer's disease, high blood pressure and hyperlipidemia were not more common among people with early-onset Alzheimer's disease than among the control group, they said.
"Our findings support the view that early-onset Alzheimer's disease is not simply a younger-age version of late-onset Alzheimer's disease. Rather than the familiar cardiovascular risk factors, we observed a range of other health problems becoming more common as diagnosis approached," lead researcher Johanna Krüger, adjunct professor from the University of Oulu, said.
The researchers also found no significant differences in morbidity 11 to 15 years before diagnosis, suggesting that identifiable changes begin to emerge mainly closer to disease onset.
The findings indicate that early-onset Alzheimer's disease may involve mechanisms that differ, at least in part, from those underlying late-onset Alzheimer's disease, they said.
Healthcare utilisation was found to have increased markedly during the five years leading up to diagnosis, alongside a growing burden of health conditions. The steepest increase in healthcare visits was seen to occur during the final year before Alzheimer's disease was diagnosed.
The study's findings are based on patient data from memory clinics at Oulu University Hospital and Kuopio University Hospital, combined with nationwide health register data.
The study included 407 people with early-onset Alzheimer's disease, whose health records were compared with those of more than 4,000 age- and sex-matched people without the neurodegenerative disease. Diseases and health conditions were examined that occurred during the 15 years preceding an Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
"EOAD (early onset Alzheimer's disease) patients had higher prevalence of vertigo, depression, headache, delirium, brain injuries, thyroid disorders, alcohol-related disorders, epilepsy, strokes, and otorhinolaryngologic diseases 1-5 years before diagnosis," the authors wrote.

Android was designed for phones, but that hasn’t stopped Google from trying to adapt the OS and its apps to larger machines over the years. Googlebooks are just the latest attempt after tablets, Chromebooks, and foldables induced little change in how people interact with Android software. These new Android-powered laptops are designed to pick up where the web-focused ChromeOS left off, offering premium hardware and native support for Android apps.
Google sees Googlebooks as an alternative to Windows and macOS, but these platforms are entrenched with decades of software and UI conventions that keep users locked in. Googlebooks have to offer something very special to steal users away from either of the dominant operating systems.
For devoted Android phone users, there are some cool things in Googlebook OS, but the Android roots of these machines are impossible to miss. Sometimes it feels like using a Chromebook, and sometimes it feels like using a giant phone. It almost never feels like using a premium laptop, and that’s the problem.
OEMs pulling their weight
While there were a few premium Chromebooks, the platform was really only successful in the budget segment. With Googlebooks, the company is almost conspicuously ignoring lower-cost options. And as most of the lineup clocks in at well over a thousand dollars, Googlebooks are not just a new take on budget-oriented Chromebooks.
The Glowbar doesn’t do a whole lot, but it’s kind of pretty.

All of the launch Googlebooks have excellent touchscreen displays, aluminum and magnesium bodies, biometric unlock (fingerprint or face), and big trackpads. There’s also the Glowbar, which doesn’t do very much right now. It lights up in Google colors when Gemini is activated with the wake word and during boot-up. It also shows the battery level when you plug in a Googlebook. The latter is modestly useful, but it’s not really a selling point.
There’s something in the lineup for most premium laptop buyers. If you want a convertible, there’s the Acer machine. Sleek and spendy? Asus and HP have you covered. Want something a little bigger? Lenovo has a 15.3-inch model with an HDMI port and USB-A.

The least-spendy model, the Acer Googlebook 14, starts at $899, and that’s a limited-time deal. Even this one gets a lot of the hardware right. It has a vibrant OLED screen, a metal chassis, and three USB-C ports (all of which can charge the laptop). However, you won’t get a haptic trackpad, just the old-fashioned kind that physically clicks. The supposedly DTS-tuned speakers also don’t sound great. Still, the hardware is at least as nice as any $900 Windows laptop. Acer hasn’t decided when the price will change or what it will be, but it’s at $899 for the rest of the year at least.
The next step up from that is the Dell XPS Googlebook at $999, but this model has an LCD instead of OLED. If you want the most capable Google laptops with OLED and haptic trackpads, you’re looking at spending at least $1,100 for the Lenovo version. This machine is solid, and the larger footprint allows for vents in the hinge instead of on the bottom. But I don’t love the slightly wobbly feel of the keys or the flex in the middle of the keyboard. The HP Googlebook 14 has a much nicer keyboard, a better overall look, and a Snapdragon X Elite chip inside. However, it’s also $1,300.

Ryan Whitwam
I appreciate that Google is pushing for things like haptic trackpads and high-resolution OLED screens, but the more expensive Googlebooks suffer from the same issue as premium Windows laptops—they don’t exist in a vacuum. If you’re spending $1,300 on a laptop, the entry-level MacBook Air is probably a better overall option for most people.
All of the launch Googlebooks have the same keyboard layout, which is a bit different from what you get on other laptops. There’s a G button that works similarly to the Windows button, and the top F-row has been revamped. You get the usual Windows staples like brightness and volume control, but there are also Android navigation buttons and a voice input key that activates the AI-powered Rambler.
The Googlebook keyboard (seen on the Acer Googlebook 14) might take a little getting used to.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
The Googlebook keyboard (seen on the Acer Googlebook 14) might take a little getting used to.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Probably the best change to the Googlebook keyboard is ‘quick insert’ in place of ‘caps lock’ (you can still get caps lock with the Fn toggle). Just press this key to add emoji, recent screenshots, clipboard contents, recently visited URLs, and more. Admittedly, I don’t mind using function layers on a keyboard, so the extra step to access caps isn’t a concern. You may feel differently, and that’s okay.
Googlebooks all perform similarly in CPU tests.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Googlebooks all perform similarly in CPU tests.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Googlebooks come in both Intel and Snapdragon variants. I’ve been using both, and general performance feels about the same. There have been some reports of app issues with Intel-powered Googlebooks, but I haven’t run into any apps that will only run on Snapdragon.
Snapdragon’s GPU performance is better on Android.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Snapdragon’s GPU performance is better on Android.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
The Snapdragon model (HP) seems to have a higher performance ceiling, if you can find a way to reach it. Gaming performance also appears better on Snapdragon, but even the heaviest Android games seem fine on the Intel models (Lenovo and Acer). It can be hard to push these machines when you’re relying on software that was originally designed to run on phones. Unsurprisingly, software proves to be the biggest hurdle for Googlebooks.
Using Android—err, Googlebook OS
Google has flirted with Android on larger screens on a few occasions, mostly with tablets and tablets that impersonate laptops. This is the first time it has totally revamped the OS for a laptop, but it’s still Android under the hood. Sometimes that’s good, and other times not so much.
Setting up a Googlebook is a snap for Android users. Just like configuring a new phone, you can scan a QR code with your current phone to copy your accounts, data, and apps over automatically. You can be up and running in minutes, and your phone will integrate deeply with the OS. Well, provided it runs Android 17. That’s going to be a sticking point, since most phones don’t have that update yet.
With Google’s “Better Together” services, a Googlebook can access files on your Android 17 phone, sync notifications, remember where you left off in apps, and even mirror apps from your phone. This all sounds great, and when it works, the experience can be good. However, there are various limitations and bugs that get in the way.
Googlebooks can stream apps, mirror notifications, and access storage from your Android phone.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Googlebooks can stream apps, mirror notifications, and access storage from your Android phone.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
To remain in contact, the phone and Googlebook need to be on the same Wi-Fi network, and switching to other networks can break the connection in annoying ways. Even when the devices appear to have a solid connection, I have rarely seen any hint of Google’s Continue On feature, which is supposed to let you pick up where you left off in a phone app. Mirroring phone apps on your laptop can also be handy, but the performance is varying degrees of bad, and apps with system-level security features won’t work at all. You are also limited to one app at a time, and they won’t stay open in the background.
Accessing the files on your phone from the laptop is a good idea, but the transfer speed is often sluggish. More annoyingly, the connection only goes one way—the Files app on the Googlebook can see your phone, but the Google Files app on a phone can’t see the Googlebook. Speaking of the Files app, this is emblematic of how far behind Google is with desktop software. The app lacks basic things like tabs and support for network shares. It’s nice that it can access my phone, but it feels very restrictive if you’re used to Finder or Windows Explorer.
Google has at least done a good job of making Android look like a desktop OS. There’s a proper desktop that you can fill with app shortcuts, folders, widgets, and files. There’s a folder in the storage tree where you can manage that content, or you can simply drag things onto it from a file manager. You also get ChromeOS-style split-screen support and multiple desktops. These features work, but they’re not as intuitive or capable as what you get on either macOS or Windows.
Managing multiple desktops on Googlebook OS.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Managing multiple desktops on Googlebook OS.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
AI is a big part of the Googlebook experience. Google talks a lot about Magic Pointer, which you can activate by wiggling the cursor. This allows you to hand any content on your screen over to Gemini, but calling it magic is a little silly. You can have it translate text, make images, create calendar appointments, and so on. You’re basically feeding Gemini screenshots and asking it to do things.
Magic Pointer can be useful sometimes, but it’s hardly revolutionary to streamline the process of feeding screen content into an AI by attaching it to the mouse. You still have to contend with the inaccuracy of Gemini. Even adding calendar appointments can fail, which means you have to double-check almost everything the AI does.
Magic Pointer is an optional feature, and you can adjust the sensitivity of the gesture. However, I never found a level that I was entirely happy to use. Too much sensitivity, and the gesture triggers when you don’t intend it. Too little, and you have to shake the mouse so hard that the cursor is probably going to be nowhere near what you wanted to highlight.
Rambler, which debuted on the Pixel 11 lineup, is included with all Googlebooks. This AI-powered voice input feature works in any text field on the laptop, which is handy if you want to add a lot of text without typing and don’t mind sounding like a robot. This has been popular on phones, and most people using it on a Googlebook will probably be impressed.
Create My Widget is another head-scratcher, though. The pitch is that you can simply describe the widget you want, and the AI will place it on your desktop. It sounds cool, but in reality, the content you can rope in is so limited as to make the feature largely useless. If you want calendar countdowns and sports scores, great. If you want system info or app content, you’re out of luck.
All the mobile apps
Googlebooks come with the Play Store, which is crammed full of all the Android apps you could ever want. But desktop apps? Google says it has worked with devs to optimize apps for Googlebooks, and some software has been newly built from the ground up for a desktop experience. For example, Chrome on Googlebooks is a mostly desktop-class experience. It’s missing a few niche features like split windows, tab groups, and multiple profiles, but it will work with all of your extensions.
On other platforms, I’ve routinely used desktop clients for Dropbox and Drive to sync files. I had hoped something similar would be possible on these Android laptops, but no such luck. Dropbox runs on a Googlebook, but it’s not optimized. The UI is clunky, and even if you save a folder offline, it only updates when you refresh the app manually (just like a phone running the app).
The Play Store highlights the handful of desktop-caliber apps currently available.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
The Play Store highlights the handful of desktop-caliber apps currently available.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Meanwhile, the Drive app isn’t even an Android app—it’s a progressive web app (PWA). So you can’t set it up to sync a folder to the device. All you have is the option to make individual files in Drive available offline. Without a real desktop app experience here, you actually get a lot more functionality out of Google’s cloud storage system on Windows and macOS.
Drive isn’t the only Google web app masquerading as a native app. Gmail and Calendar are also PWAs on the Googlebook, offering the same experience you’d get opening them in a browser tab. Gmail exists as an Android app with a large screen format. Why not adapt that for Googlebooks? Real operating systems have email apps. If you’re just going to end up in a web app, why not buy a Chromebook for a third of the price?
The Play Store uses labels to let you know which apps are best on a laptop, but most apps in the Play Store are very obviously built around a phone experience. Google is in a tough spot here. Developers only build for what people use, and so far, no one has been demanding desktop-style Android apps. As you peruse the Play Store, you’ll see a few of those “optimized” labels, but there are many more “Compatible with desktop” tags, which means you can expect only nominal support for a keyboard and mouse.
The most problematic apps are flagged in the Play Store as “Built for mobile” or even “Better on the website.” Some popular apps fall into these categories. For example, team chat app Slack is an abysmal experience on anything other than a phone. The app runs on Googlebooks, but the web UI is much more desktop-friendly. You are supposed to be able to install Slack as a progressive web app, essentially what Google is doing with Gmail, Drive, and other apps. However, this doesn’t work currently for unknown reasons. Again, you could just use a Chromebook if you wanted everything in a browser tab.
Adobe’s optimized version of Photoshop is still very limited on Googlebooks.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Adobe’s optimized version of Photoshop is still very limited on Googlebooks.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Even apps that have been optimized for desktop can be frustrating on a Googlebook. These apps are aware you have a keyboard, but they can respond to button presses in ways you don’t expect. Photoshop is a major offender here. The app has a poorly scaled mobile UI shifted into landscape, and there are only a few keyboard shortcuts. Sometimes, you’ll see a UI element that looks like it should be controllable with the arrows or enter key, but you just end up moving the cursor around and selecting the wrong thing. In fairness, Android’s Photoshop app is free, whereas the real Adobe suite on other platforms costs money. But calling this a desktop app is a stretch.
You’ll find lots of pbone-first apps that don’t fully understand that you have a trackpad, ignoring hover interactions and right-clicks. Many apps also expect you to frequently trigger the Android back gesture to navigate the UI. On that last count, Google has a solution. Googlebooks have Back, Home, and Multitasking buttons on F1-F3. So you can make phone apps work, but reaching up to mash F1 constantly is annoying.
The Android lineage of Googlebook OS also means that even apps built for desktop may not operate the way you’d expect on a desktop PC. Android was designed for a memory-constrained environment, so the system closes apps in the background whenever it needs to free up RAM. It’s common to come back to an app you left in the background to find that it has lost your place and has to reload. This is a phone-like experience that doesn’t really fit with a real computer.
Can vibes save it?
Google is aware that Googlebook apps may not fulfill all needs. One possible solution to that, say reps, is to simply make what you need with Antigravity. The new Android version of Google’s AI-centric development app is included on every Googlebook, giving you the option to vibe code apps for your laptop. The AI can generate plans, mockups, and line after line of code to bring your idea to life.
Antigravity on Googlebook OS.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Antigravity on Googlebook OS.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Antigravity can autonomously download all the Android developer tools it needs and builds APKs ready for installation on your device. Installing your apps is technically sideloading, as they’re not hosted in the Play Store, but Google gives these special treatment. They get scanned by Play Protect, but you don’t have to enable unknown sources in the settings. Google also confirms these apps won’t be affected by developer verification when that rolls out on Googlebooks next year.
After struggling with the Files app for a few days, I decided the lack of network shares was a deal-breaker. I keep most of my files on a NAS so I can access them from any device, and Googlebooks were cramping my style. I first tried to find an alternative in the Play Store, but the apps with sufficient features were totally unoptimized for a laptop, so I decided to test Antigravity on Googlebooks by making one.
Using Google’s default Gemini Flash model, I was able to get a functional but very buggy file manager installed in a few minutes. Making it work reliably and support all the features I needed took several hours of prompting over a few days, but the result is something I like using more than Google’s default Files app.
My custom file manager is essentially Windows Explorer on Android. While I did not set out with that intent, that’s where I ended up. The app has a desktop-friendly UI, tabs, network share support, expandable file trees, file previews, and more buttons. It has more features than Google’s default app, although it lacks the deep phone and system integration of the default file manager.
Left: Default Files app, Right: My vibe-coded replacement
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Left: Default Files app, Right: My vibe-coded replacement
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
On one hand, it’s cool that you can create your own apps with the included Antigravity software. However, you’ll need to pay someone (probably Google) for enough AI compute to get the job done. It took a lot of iterations and bug hunting with Gemini 3.8 Flash to get my app where I needed it to be, and lighter models will struggle to produce something functional. It’s also not ideal to expect people buying a laptop to spend hours chatting with a robot to make it do basic laptop things. It should do those things out of the box.
The first step on a long road
I keep coming back to one inescapable question that hangs over everything Google is doing with these new laptops: Do Googlebooks need to exist? This seems like a lot of effort just to deliver deeper Android phone integration and more AI features when Chromebooks are already established in the market. True, that’s not a premium part of the market, but going after premium laptops means you need a premium experience, and currently, Googlebooks don’t offer that.
Port location and selection vary across the lineup.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Port location and selection vary across the lineup.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
The hardware is solid—it’s smart that Google is pushing for things like OLED and haptic trackpads on Googlebooks. Its OEM partners have made some very nice-feeling laptops for Google’s software, but the OS isn’t doing its part. I just don’t feel more productive on a Googlebook than I do on a Chromebook.
I’ve been using Android since the beginning—this should be a good laptop for someone like me. However, the rough edges of the Googlebook experience are still wearing me down. It’s great that it talks to my phone, but that conversation is too often one-sided and buggy. It’s good, in theory, that Googlebooks have a deep software library with the Play Store, but too few apps are actually good on a laptop. And it’s cool that Googlebooks have such nice hardware, but they’re too expensive for what you get.
Googlebooks have generously sized touchpads, and most of them are haptic.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Googlebooks have generously sized touchpads, and most of them are haptic.
Credit:
Ryan Whitwam
Maybe Google can fix this—ChromeOS looked a lot different a year or two after its consumer launch, after all. But Google has a lot of work ahead to make the Googlebook experience what it needs to be, and in the meantime, it’s not a viable alternative to macOS and Windows. Does Google have the patience to spend years doing this work? The company’s recent history leaves me feeling skeptical, and that makes it difficult to recommend a Googlebook to even the most ardent Google customers.
The good
Laptop hardware looks and feels great
Extremely quick setup
Deep Android phone integration
Access to millions of Android apps running natively
The bad
High price tags and no budget options
Very few Android apps work well on laptops
Missing features of more mature desktop operating systems

Petite, lightweight, and kind of kicky for a cargo bike. Can fit in a car’s back seat. Fat tires provide stability. Cushy bike seat is comfortable for long rides. So many accessories. Surprising 500-pound payload.
TIRED
Fast braking requires a firm hand. Range is middling. Battery indicator sneaks up on you. Not as petite as other JackRabbits. Technically a scooter, not an ebike.
I am not an obvious target customer for a cargo ebike, as I neither have kids to tote nor a large space for bike parking. But the new JackRabbit MG Cargo is so tiny, it doesn't conjure the dully utilitarian, heedlessly bulky nature that's common to other cargo ebike models. In fact, when I tested the wee, plucky ebike, I found its fat tires and tiny wheelbase make it feel more like a speedy urban dirt bike than anything else.
But despite being a relative lightweight (55 pounds) and petite enough to fit in the back seat of my old Montero, the MG sports a 750-watt motor that can haul nine times the bike's weight uphill. I even threw a grill onto a bike trailer to test this claim, which held up.
Note that likeall JackRabbits WIRED testers have reviewed, the MG is less an ebike than a scooter that looks and acts like an ebike: Instead of pedals, you get pedal-like footrests, plus a throttle. This means when the battery runs out, the bike stops moving. Also, the listed 48-mile range drops considerably when you ride at top speed or haul a large load. Nonetheless, the MG may have converted me to the pannier class.
After testing this MG for a couple of months, I no longer use my car when I need groceries, even when I'm taking a longer trek to the Grocery Outlet for discount steaks or salmon. The same is true when I want to haul a slushie machine across Portland’s steep mid-city ridge to a friend's house for cheeky weekday margaritas. By not acting like a cargo bike, the MG has convinced me to haul cargo on a bike.
Zippy Little Devil
Photograph: Matthew Korfhage
“How exactly is this a cargo bike?” my editor asked when I showed her a photo of the MG Cargo after it arrived. She wasn't asking out of wonderment. As mentioned, the MG flat-out looks less like a bike you'd use to haul stuff and more like a dirt bike.
JackRabbit is known for making lightweight, zippy, fun little scooter hybrids that physically resemble BMX trick bikes. I loved the easy mobility and high-speed capability of JackRabbit's equally powerful XG Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends) when I tested that model last year. I'd worried that the MG Cargo—18 pounds heavier and nearly a foot longer than the XG—would compromise too much on these virtues. I needn't have worried. As I quickly learned, the pleasantly peppy MG rides like an off-road bike when you're not hauling a big load.
Its three throttle speeds max out at about 20 mph, 15 mph, and 7 mph, respectively. The lowest speed is manageable for a sidewalk, while the fastest hits top speed within about 50 feet on flat ground, unless you've got some weight behind (or on) you. The MG advertises a range of 48 miles, though I'll assume this requires being a lighter rider who is gentle on the throttle. As a 200-pound man with an admittedly heavy throttle thumb, I only made it to about 25 miles, even with minimal cargo. Because the bike's battery indicator shows up as at least half-full for the vast majority of this range, you'll need to test and learn your personal range when doing so is not mission-critical.
Note that because JackRabbits don't have working pedals, the bikes exist in an interesting technical gray area in some states in terms of their classification. Specifically, one could debate whether they're really a Class 2 ebike that can ride on bike lanes and trails. Given the MG's maximum speed of 20 mph—aside from an honor-system 24-mph jailbreak speed you can unlock for off-road riding—it mostly looks and quacks like a Class 2 ebike. In my experience, it's also treated as such.
The MG also offers nice customization options for accessorizing. It's easy to add a couple of rear pannier bags to the rear mounting rack or side racks ($75) on each side, offering enough capacity for most small grocery trips or beach excursions without adding much bulk. You could also opt for a rear basket.
Photograph: Matthew Korfhage
While I can't quite stow the MG as easily as other JackRabbit models, it's still small enough that I can slide it into my back seat—as long as I uncork the front handlebars and turn its front wheel backward. (Some sources refer to the MG as “foldable,” but this isn't strictly true: it just has a quick-release wheel and an easily removed handlebar.)
Which is to say, even without the cargo component, I could like the MG just as a fun little commuter, especially with the welcome addition of a cushy Kinekt active-suspension seat post that provides some added give for longer rides.
The Little Cargo Ebike That Could
Despite its petite size, the MG performs well as a true cargo hauler that you could use to move trailers full of groceries or the more precious cargo of your own children. I didn't borrow any kids to test rear child trailers or JackRabbit's mini-me rear seat and handlebar set ($175). But I did use the MG's preinstalled Burley trailer hitch to haul a box containing a 150-pound grill up a hill with a 7 percent grade. While the MG didn't get to full speed on the ascent, it pulled the grill and my 200-plus-pound self surprisingly well.
The MG's stability and cornering capabilities also fared better than I expected, given its short base. Cargo bikes tend to lengthen their frame to add stability and make room for riders to pedal comfortably while carrying loads on the front or the back. The MG Cargo's stability mostly comes from its cushy fat tires, largely thanks to the clever design of the larger front tire, which both adds stability up front on rugged terrain and lowers the center of gravity where cargo hangs. The lack of pedaling also naturally removes some wobble.
You will make compromises, though: Cornering while hauling a large load can yield a jumpy ride, leading to the occasional overcorrection. The range also drops considerably with heavy carries, given that you can't add your own pedal power. Braking is fast but does require a good grip, especially with larger loads downhill.
For the Occasional Hauler
The MG Cargo lives in an interesting middle ground between commuter and cargo ebike. If I were primarily using it to transport children or work gear, I'd probably opt for a bulkier hauler or the Specialized Global Haul ST, WIRED's top-pick electric cargo bike that offers a more reliable long range.
The best use cases for the MG Cargo are as a fun recreational ebike that stows easily into your back seat or as a multipurpose commuter with built-in storage that saves its rider from needing to wear a backpack. In either case, the cargo capabilities function as bonus features as opposed to being the main draw.
It's less a workhorse than a hobby pony: I've slipped books and a blanket into a pannier so I can read at the park, and I've spontaneously brought home six-packs from the brewery a couple of miles down the road. When I grocery shop using the MG Cargo, I'm spared the bother of tightly packed parking lots that make me angry before I reach the aisles. I zip in, I unlock the panniers, pop in my groceries, and zip right back out. In this way, the MG Cargo also doubles as the cheapest therapist I know.
Matthew Korfhage was a staff writer on WIRED’s Reviews team, where he focused on coffee, home, and home office technology. Since her first appearance behind the podium this week, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s past has become murkier by the day.
A WIRED review of deleted social media and professional networking profiles has helped clear up at least one mystery. Zacharia’s online resume shows a gap extending from 2013 to late 2023. For part of that time, she worked as an affiliate of Beachbody, a fitness company that ran a multilevel marketing operation she describes to WIRED as “sort of a pyramid scheme.”
Zacharia’s background prior to her emergence as a right-wing operative and pundit in recent years has been the subject of intense curiosity. Prior to joining the White House’s press team, she was a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, a communications advisor at President Donald Trump’s media company, and a commentator on Newsmax and Fox News.
Other parts of her professional background have come under scrutiny, particularly her legal work. According to her LinkedIn, Zacharia was an associate at the Zhong Lun law firm, known in China as a top tier “red circle” firm, between 2011 and 2013. She also identifies herself on LinkedIn as having worked as general counsel for the nonprofit Fix California. Tax filings reviewed by WIRED, though, show that rather than working as general counsel for Fix California, Zacharia was in fact a fundraiser for the nonprofit.
On Tuesday, journalist Judd Legum reported that Zacharia—who, he noted, was identified as an attorney in at least 18 appearances on Fox News—did not appear to have ever passed the bar. Since then, The Wall Street Journal has reported that she sat for the California bar exam but never passed—a finding WIRED independently confirmed. (On Wednesday, watchdog organization Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California seeking to investigate the veracity of Zacharia’s claims to be an attorney.)
WIRED was able to gain some clarity about other aspects of Zacharia’s professional history using a database of material leaked online created by the open-source intelligence firm District 4 Labs. It contains details from a since-deleted LinkedIn account belonging to Zacharia, which listed Beachbody email addresses as two of her points of contact. A representative for the company told WIRED there was no record of her having worked there. In a phone call, Zacharia confirmed to WIRED that she had never been employed by the company.
Zacharia says she was, rather, an affiliate marketer for Beachbody, following her 2013 return from China. She recalls being brought in by a friend and promoting its Shakeology product, which is promoted as a “superfood nutrition shake.” She stopped using and promoting the product, she says, because of its vitamin A content, which she didn’t feel was good for her while pregnant.
Beachbody, now known as BODi, confirmed in a statement that Zacharia was among its 300,000 “independent Team Beachbody distributors” in 2013. A spokesperson added that they believed it would be “misrepresentation” to conflate Zacharia’s time at Beachbody with “BODi’s current business and operations.”
Perhaps unsurprisingly for a company that relied on a multilevel marketing scheme for decades, the company has run into a number of legal issues over the years. It's been accused of falsely advertising a revolutionary anti-aging treatment (the suit was voluntarily dismissed), and making false or misleading income promises to contractors. It got into a copyright battle with a company called orderlegalsteroids.com, accusing it of stealing an image of Israeli bodybuilder Sagi Kalev from promotional materials for their “BODY BEAST” Program. (Beachbody won a default judgment.)
In 2017, Beachbody, without admitting any wrongdoing, settled a $3.6 million consumer protection lawsuit with the city attorney in Santa Monica, California. Prosecutors alleged that Beachbody made health-related claims about its products, including Shakeology, that were “false, misleading, and not backed by scientific evidence.” They also claimed in filings that Beachbody had been automatically charging customers credit cards for renewals of their products without their consent. As part of its settlement, Beachbody was ordered to pay $1 million to nonprofits that promote health and nutrition.
And in 2023, Beachbody was hit with a class action lawsuit accusing it of scamming its coaches. The lead plaintiff was a schoolteacher who alleged she joined Beachbody with the hope of making a supplementary income, but ended up paying $20,000 in personal funds to cover expenses related to her coaching role—all while making about $50 per month for about 50 hours of work. The following year, the company dropped its multilevel marketing program in favor of a “single-level affiliate” one. In 2025, it reached a settlement in the class action suit that resulted in the dismissal of all claims, and the lawsuit was later formally dismissed.
In a statement to WIRED, BODi says, “Team Beachbody was a peer-to-peer sales and support network” and that the company “helped tens of millions of people pursue their health goals through in home fitness programs like P90X, Insanity, and 21 Day Fix, and nutrition products such as Shakeology.”
This particular notch on Zacharia’s resume puts her in good company with other high-profile Trumpworld personnel, a cadre of professionals who have a great fondness for supplement-related business opportunities. FBI chief Kash Patel previously promoted supplements that promised to help people “detox” from the Covid-19 vaccine. Nicole Saphier, Trump’s nominee for surgeon general, reported receiving nearly $300,000 in business income from her own company that owns a supplement line. And Donald Trump himself once oversaw a multilevel marketing company, The Trump Network, which sold an array of vitamins, home urine tests claiming to test for vitamin deficiency, and children's snacks.

A day after four people were killed at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, police have identified the shooter as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II. According to authorities, John was once a special needs student at Silver Rail Elementary, the same school where he killed three students and a 25-year-old teacher. Authorities added that he attacked a classroom full of special needs students. AP, citing City of Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz, said that the teen shooter fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed. As investigators try to determine the motive behind the shooting and how the 16-year-old obtained the pump-action shotgun, Krantz said, "Everyone wants to know why, including us,” and added, “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.” According to the report, the pump-action shotgun was bought by the teen shooter's mother, identified as Shauntai Nickerson. She told reporters that if she could have done something to prevent the incident, she would have. She said, "I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss," and added, "I miss my boy." However, Nickerson did not reveal how her 16-year-old son obtained the pump-action shotgun. Following the latest shooting, Nickerson's earlier interview with local news station KTVZ in 2020 has also come to light. In it, she identified the boy, who was 10 then, as a participant in a special needs programme called NEST, which stands for Nurturing Empathy, Safety and Trust. The programme aimed to help students experiencing intensive behavioural and social skills challenges. Nickerson said he struggled to learn from home during the COVID-19 pandemic. According to Krantz, a man driving a red pickup truck made the first 911 call early Thursday afternoon after seeing John toss a gun over a fence outside the school and climb over it. When the driver shouted at him, John opened fire, striking the truck three times. The driver escaped injury. Another driver, identified as Kaylub Giamanco, 36, whose children attend Silver Rail school, witnessed the gunfire directed at the pickup and saw John move towards the school. The 16-year-old then fired through the locked doors to enter the building. Giamanco drove into the parking lot, took his .40-caliber pistol and followed him inside. On finding John struggling with a teacher, Giamanco shot him multiple times. On Thursday (local time), three children, aged 5, 8 and 11, and teacher Meghan Lambert, 25, were killed after John fired through the locked doors and entered the school. Bihar: 1.4mn voters added in post-SIR roll in one year
The current electoral roll — last updated on October 1— has 75.5 million voters, roughly 1.4 million names more than the 74.1 million in September 2025 roll.
Bihar’s electoral roll swelled by nearly 1.4 million names since the publication of the post-special intensive revision (SIR) in Bihar on September 30 last year, officials attached with the state electoral officer(CEO) have said.
The current electoral roll — last updated on October 1 this year — has 75.5 million voters, roughly 1.4 million names more than the 74.1 million in the September 2025 roll, published after the end of SIR.
In this period, nearly 1.87 million people applied to be on the rolls using Form 6, the statutory application prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, for a person seeking inclusion of their name in an electoral roll. Out of these, 1.4 million applications have been successful, the officials quoted above said.
“The number of enrolment goes up in an election year and then declines. It happens before the Lok Sabha, the legislative assembly or the panchayat polls,” said one of the officers quoted above on Wednesday.
The additional 1.4 million names comprise people seeking to return to the rolls, new voters and young voters enrolling for the first time, said the second officer.
The number of voters in Bihar went up by 4.19 million in 2023-24 — the year of Lok Sabha elections — and by 4.14 million in 2024-25, the year of assembly polls in the state.
Prior to that, in 2022-23, the voter increase was 1.3 million, while in 2025-26, the increase was 2.45 million, said a second officer.
All the 1.4 million people added to the post-SIR electoral roll, including new or first-time voters, have had to fill Form 6 for new enrolment.
“Most people who enrolled after the SIR have applied online on the ECI portal,” said Kumud Kumari, a booth-level officer of Raja Bazar area in Patna. “At present, there is no electoral activity whatsoever. We as teachers are currently busy with academic activities in schools. Fresh enrolment to the voter list generally happens before elections through online applications.”
The three-month SIR exercise in Bihar undertaken between June 25 and September 30, 2025 — the first in the country in the current series — initially removed 6.56 million people from the rolls, after 2.23 million voters were reported dead, 3.64 million shifted, and 0.68 million voters found to have their names at more than one location, out of the 78.9 million voters reported before the exercise.
After the one-month scrutiny period between August 1 and September 1, 2025, during which aggrieved voters had to submit claims and objections, 2.15 million voters were added to the list and another 0.36 million removed, taking the number of electorate in the state to 74.1 million after the SIR.
Bihar has not had a summary revision of the electoral roll since the 2025 SIR.
In Kishanganj’s Thakurganj nagar panchayat, a booth-level officer received around 3,600 applications over the past year and recommended about 636 names for inclusion after verification. The BLO is also examining seven applications flagged as potential duplicates by the mobile application linked to the EC’s Demographic Similar Entry (DSE) software, which flags entries with similarities in names, fathers’ names and age.
“I try my best to verify the documents of each voter before recommending the name to the ERO. The ERO then scrutinises it at his level before adding the voter,” said the BLO, requesting anonymity.
In Patna, Siddheshwar Kumar Sharma, a government schoolteacher and BLO at booth No. 419 at the blind school in Kadamkuan, received about 24 applications over the past year.
The development comes days after ECI told state election authorities that eligible citizens seeking enrolment need not submit a separate declaration – which seeks details of parental linkage to the previous SIR – along with Form 6.
The Bihar CEO’s office has also been asked to conduct a campaign to identify and enrol first-time and left-out voters, according to a communication issued after a video conference of electoral officers on October 1.
“Video conferences with EROs and district magistrates have been completed. Currently, training and orientation of officials is being done. We will begin the campaign this week itself,” said the second officer quoted above.

Police release details on fiery, fatal bus crash in Calgary
Crash occurred in Calgary's Saddle Ridge neighbourhood on Thursday
Calgary police released more details on Friday about a fiery bus crash and explosion that resulted in three deaths.
Just after 1 p.m. on Thursday, a collision involving a Calgary transit bus in the city’s northeast Saddle Ridge neighbourhood led to a fire. Three people were declared dead at the scene, and 16 were injured.
The bus was travelling north in the 800 block of Saddletowne Circle N.E., toward 80th Avenue, near the neighbourhood's fire station. The driver of the first bus was transported to hospital with life-altering injuries. The driver of the second bus was able to exit the vehicle.
