The notice was personally handed to Abhijeet Dipke by the Delhi Police personnel at NCP-SCP spokesperson Anish Gawande's residence.
‘I’m alone', Dipke tells cops moments before detention
Abhijeet Dipke departed for the march site this evening and was detained by the police shortly after. However, a video from before his detention showed him asking the police how he was violating any laws.
“Maine abhi violation kaise kiya hai? Main akela hoon (I am alone, how did I violate any order),” he said, asking how he had violated the law and pointing out that the others present were members of the media.
CJP, AISA ask ‘where are Neha Bora, Abhijeet Dipke?’
Both the CJP and AISA sought to know Abhijeet Dipke and Neha Bora's whereabouts after they were detained on their way to the Tiranga rally. The outfits alleged that the two were being denied access to lawyers and associates after being detained by Delhi Police during protests in the national capital.
"The Delhi Police has taken Abhijeet Dipke to an undisclosed location. We have lost contact with him. He is not being allowed to talk to lawyers," the CJP said in a post on X. "Why does this government treat youth like terrorists? We are equal citizens of India and we deserve all the protections and rights of the Constitution!" it said.
In a post on X, AISA said Bora was being detained alone at the Anti-Narcotics Task Force in Mangolpuri. In a subsequent post, it claimed she is being taken from the Anti-Narcotics Task Force station, Mangolpuri, to an “undisclosed” location in a car with illegally blacked-out windows.
Opposition rallies behind Dipke and Bora
Former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee, AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, and other Opposition leaders criticsed the Delhi Police action against Neha Bora and Abhijeet Dipke.
"Abhijeet Dipke has been detained for holding the Indian National Flag. Let that sink in. In Independent India, our youth are being detained for peacefully asserting their democratic rights." Calling the action an “undeclared emergency”, she further said, “A government that fears dissent is now trying to intimidate an entire generation into silence. This is the conduct of a fascist regime that cannot tolerate a voice it cannot control.”
Arvind Kejriwal said on X, “This is nothing but outright dictatorship. Is it a crime to hoist the tricolour? Abhijeet's arrest shows how much Modi ji fears them."

Srinagar, Oct 17: Lieutenant Governor of Ladakh Vinai Kumar Saxena has laid the foundation stones for two water reservoirs under Project Him Sarovar in Sodh block of Kargil district to address the acute water crisis that has affected agriculture and forced residents to migrate from their villages.
The two reservoirs, with a combined storage capacity of 60–70 lakh litres, are expected to be completed by the end of November, the Lieutenant Governor said.

The reservoirs are expected to provide a sustainable solution to the region’s water shortage and help address migration caused by the lack of water for farming and other essential needs.
Saxena reaffirmed the UT administration’s commitment to people-centric development, stating that efforts were being made to secure a sustainable water supply and improve living conditions in remote areas of Ladakh.

Can AI be regulated? Why experts say government intervention is needed — but could be tricky
Technology's rapid development, need for international co-operation major challenges to creating safeguards
As concerns mount over incidents of AI agents going rogue, experts and stakeholders are increasingly pushing for government regulation of AI systems that are becoming more capable.
But some experts say the need for global co-operation and the rapid pace of AI development could make that difficult.
While some, like U.S. President Donald Trump, say they have faith that tech giants can police themselves, other industry leaders, like Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, and Canadian-British artificial intelligence pioneer Geoffrey Hinton say AI requires safeguards that go beyond self-regulation.
Given that most other industries, such as food or aviation, have some type of government oversight, it only makes sense that AI would as well, said Jaxson Khan, an expert in AI policy and adoption at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs.
"In no major industry, do we let companies completely police themselves, whether it's in oil and gas or people who want to produce food and candy or nuclear energy," he said.
- Bill Gates joins call for AI safeguards, wants to discuss concerns with Trump
- Is AI evolving too fast? A look at the debate on slowing it down
"Having such a powerful technology be entirely in private hands, at least without supervision, that seems highly strange given the rest of how our economy and regulatory systems work."
In an interview with CBC News Network last month, Hinton suggested that oversight could be handled by an official agency similar to the Food and Drug Administration in the U.S.
"You can't just produce a drug and market it in America. You have to persuade the FDA that your drug is safe, or rather does more good than harm, and the companies are responsible for doing that," he said.
"So we certainly need something at least that strong for AI. We should have independent people evaluating it, and we should force the companies to satisfy those evaluators before they release it."
Hard for governments to keep up
A significant challenge to regulating AI is how quickly models change and improve, Khan said.
A recent Anthropic report said its agents' capabilities double roughly every four months. There's also growing evidence that some AI models have the ability to recursively self-improve, meaning they can build and design their own successors, the report says.
"I don't think we've ever had an incredibly powerful technology with this velocity of change," he said.
That makes it difficult for governments to keep up, said Manon Paquet, associate director of policy at McGill's Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy.
"It's very hard to regulate something first that you don't fully understand yet," Paquet said.
"I'm a former public servant. I pity my colleagues — my former colleagues in Ottawa — trying to wrestle with those issues because it's changing so fast that the time it takes to put forward regulations or legislation, then the problem's already evolved to something else."
Global oversight
Some experts and leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have called for a global, non-industry body to oversee and mitigate the technology's risks internationally.
Earlier this week, around 400 scientists, including Hinton and fellow AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio, called for an international body to oversee containment standards and incident reporting for advanced cyber-capable AI systems.
The proposed body would maintain a registry of significant security incidents, which the scientists said should eventually be made public.
While it might be difficult to get countries to agree on how to govern AI, such a body could help countries work together to "shore up our respective systems" and create safeguards against potential misuse of AI, Khan said.
"I think stability is really important here, even if we don't get to a perfect model of global governance," he said.
But with most AI development coming out of the United States and China, those countries would have to commit to participating in such a body and adhering to its rules for it to be useful, said Olivier Blais, vice-president of artificial intelligence at Montreal consulting firm Moov AI.
"If we're not able to convince the countries where the AI systems get produced, I think the impact might be limited," he said.
However, such a body could help develop international guidelines for safe AI development, he said.
"It's important to understand the components of a safe AI system or what are the areas that need to be restrained … and a global organization could lead on the work and could build that foundation," he said.
Last month, the U.S. and China agreed to hold a dialog on the technology's risks and benefits, with the next round of discussions set for November, the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the White House said.
In a separate statement, the Chinese ministry said the two sides should step up exchanges and work toward consensus in line with new developments as AI technology continues to advance.
AI regulation in Canada
Currently, there is no overarching federal regulation of AI in Canada, but the Liberal government's proposed Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, sets out criteria for AI chatbots, including the obligation to reduce the risk of their services generating harmful content.
Carney also recently announced a new national council on artificial intelligence meant to provide the government with guidance for its AI strategy and on making the technology safer.
However, it may prove "very, very challenging" for any federal legislation to be effective given that many of the world's largest AI companies aren't based here, Paquet said.

- Canada is investing $150M to make AI safer. Will it work?
But Blais said that even if the federal government can't control how these companies operate, it could establish policies that requiring them to report incidents that affect Canadians and hold them accountable. In extreme cases, the government could even block access in Canada to AI platforms it deems too harmful, he added.
"At least I think if we're able to record the different incidents, report on them, I think it's a major step forward because at least we can educate citizens and we demonstrate leadership," he said.

Australia’s mainstream political parties are being warned not to adopt populist policies such as migration caps to address voters’ grievances over the cost of living.
Instead, Australia’s longest-serving finance minister, Mathias Cormann, is urging politicians to deliver housing, real wage growth and lower energy costs by boosting productivity.
Now the secretary general for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Cormann will deliver an address to the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night spruiking productivity as the only way to reliably lower the cost of living over the long term.
Though not directly named in his address, One Nation – which largely runs on an anti-immigration platform – has surged in popularity since the 2025 federal election, with its primary vote reaching 25%, according to the latest Guardian Essential poll, rising above the Coalition’s 22%.
While populist parties may have gained traction by speaking to real grievances about rising energy bills, home ownership and real incomes going backwards, Cormann is expected to warn Labor and the Coalition not to follow suit.
“Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will say in his address.
“The lesson is consistent: deliver homes, lower energy costs, real wage growth and a credible budget, and the populist tide recedes.
“Mimic the populists, and you simply confirm that they were right all along. The way to defeat populism is to solve the problems it feeds on.”
Cormann will point to “arbitrary migration caps” imposed regardless of their effect on business, hospitals, aged care or universities.
He will acknowledge more Australians now than any time in the past 20 years say the migration intake is too high and may support such policies, with many attributing their concerns to housing.
But the answer is to address housing supply, infrastructure, services and the composition of the migration intake, he will say.
According to OECD research across Australia’s regions, in places where more migrants arrived, employment among Australian-born workers grew faster, not slower, with no measurable effect on their wages.
Without migration, Australia’s working-age population would decrease as the number of older people grows.
“An ageing country that chooses to shrink its working-age population while promising to spend more on health, care and defence has not developed a plan – it has put forward a contradiction,” Cormann will say.
Tariffs, which have been imposed by US president Donald Trump and proposed by One Nation, would also fail to address the cost of living and could instead raise costs for farmers, miners and builders, Cormann will say.
He believes Australia can only grow its way out of the issue through productivity.
“There is no shortcut to a lower cost of living. There is no populist shortcut, through tariffs and caps and state banks,” he will say.
“There is only the long way round: an economy that produces more, competes harder and grows faster than its costs … anyone offering you a quicker route is offering you a poorer country.”

Islamabad, Oct 17: A 5.7-magnitude earthquake struck Pakistan's Balochistan province on Saturday, the US Geological Survey (USGS) said.
The quake struck near Khuzdar town in Balochistan province, the USGS posted on X.
The quake was reported 48 km west-northwest of Khuzdar, it said.
In February, a 5.6-magnitude earthquake also struck Balochistan province.
The earthquake struck at 6:30 am at a depth of 13 km, and its epicentre was 86 km northeast of Khuzdar town.
The quake shook Jhal Magsi, Jaffarabad and Nasirabad in Balochistan, while tremors were also felt in several districts of neighbouring Sindh province, including Sukkur, Qambar, Shahdadkot, and Dadu districts.
The deadliest earthquake hit the nation in 2005, killing more than 74,000 people. According to experts, Pakistan often experiences tremors as it lies on three major tectonic plates, including the Arabian, Eurasian, and Indian, which create five seismic zones under the country.

Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over amid deepening tensions with Washington.
The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia's Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia's Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
Zelenskyy complains about U.S. behavior in recent days
The strike could further complicate Kyiv's relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the ceasefire.
Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump's demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals.
The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We're done," he was quoted as saying.
Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.
Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.
Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist's YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump's deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.
"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."
He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."
Starlink speed limits affect Ukraine's ability to defend itself
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.
He said that "it's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he's in the middle."
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."
The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.
Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.
The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Russian strike in Ukraine kills 3 civilians
Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine's Emergency Services said Thursday.
Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted."
Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.
"It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security."
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.
Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.

Russia strikes 9 Ukrainian regions as strain grows between Zelenskyy and Trump
Russian attacks on nine regions of Ukraine have caused emergency power outages and damaged homes, wounding at least 15 people
KYIV, Ukraine -- Russian attacks on nine regions of Ukraine caused emergency power outages for hundreds of thousands of households and damaged numerous homes, wounding at least 15 people, officials said Friday, as civilian casualties from Moscow’s invasion climb steeply.
The latest aerial strikes on civilian targets came as fears mount that a sharp deterioration in relations between Kyiv and Washington this week could leave Ukraine further exposed to Russia’s escalating aerial assaults as the bitter winter approaches.
Russia’s heavy bombardment of the power grid before winter sets in has been an annual feature of the war, aiming to wear down Ukraine’s appetite for the fight by denying civilians heating and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in coming months.
Ukraine on Thursday abandoned a brief truce on energy-related targets that it said Moscow did not heed despite U.S. President Donald Trump's demand for a ceasefire.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday attended a summit of European leaders who share his concerns about Russian aggression and Moscow’s wider plans on the continent. The officials in Brussels vowed to maintain support for Ukraine and urged the U.S. to put pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Tension and uncertainty are gripping Ukraine and Europe after Zelenskyy and Trump publicly made cutting remarks about each other. On Thursday, Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by the American president and Trump openly declared his dislike of the Ukrainian leader.
Arriving at the EU summit in Belgium, Zelenskyy thanked the 27-nation bloc for its support from what he said were “real leaders.”
“We want to end this war as (quickly) as possible,” Zelenskyy told reporters. “We don’t see now signals from (the) Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war. That’s why we have to prepare for the winter.”
The public spat between Trump and Zelenskyy raised the specter of further reductions in U.S. support for Ukraine’s war effort.
Ukraine is desperately short of the U.S.-made Patriot missiles it needs to protect against Russia’s devastating ballistic missile attacks, despite Zelenskyy’s pleading for Washington to send more.
Zelenskyy complained about a breakdown in Western intelligence sharing and sudden restrictions on the use of Starshield, U.S. company SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and military communications.
He also slammed Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, which came despite an international effort to sanction Russia and diplomatically isolate Putin over his invasion. Trump promised to swiftly end the war, but Ukrainian officials have complained he is trying to bulldoze Zelenskyy into surrendering land to Russia.
The EU is working to persuade Washington to stick with Ukraine, the bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
“We are trying to convince also our American partners that if we want to end this war then we have to squeeze the aggressor,” Kallas said. “With our American allies it’s very difficult at the moment.”
Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, whose country currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, said there is “a lot of concern around Europe in terms of what’s happening in Ukraine right now.”
Russia is blitzing not just Ukraine's power grid but also apartment buildings, public transport, cargo ships, data centers and food stores.
Ukrainian civilians are paying a high price for the escalating Russian attacks, the United Nations human rights office in Kyiv said in a monthly report published Friday.

Prashant Bhushan says anti-CEC protest now a ‘fight for regime change’, BJP hits back with 'conspiracy' charge
Bhushan's remarks drew sharp response from the BJP, which accused the protesters of seeking to oust the Narendra Modi government without an electoral mandate.
Senior Supreme Court lawyer Prashant Bhushan, who is part of the ongoing anti-CEC protests, on Friday said the agitation against alleged irregularities in the SIR of electoral rolls had become “really a fight for regime change”, drawing a sharp response from the BJP, which accused the protesters of seeking to oust the Narendra Modi government without an electoral mandate.
Addressing a press conference in New Delhi alongside Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke, student organisation leaders and activists, Bhushan said calls for regime change were part of democratic rights and that creating “disaffection” against a government was not a crime under the Constitution.
“The government alleges the opposition wants a regime change... We are currently fighting to ensure that elections are conducted properly. But if this kind of brutality continues, there will certainly be regime change.
“Yes, we all want regime change,” he said.
“What is wrong with that? BJP led several movements for regime change? Now they are saying there is a conspiracy for regime change...” Bhushan said.
“Regime change is the democratic right of every citizen. Creating disaffection for the government is not a crime as per our Constitution.
“That is why this is now really a fight for regime change against a dictatorial government. A government that is crushing democracy,” he said.
Bhushan said attempts by the authorities to suppress protests would only bring more people onto the streets. He added that young people would lead the movement for regime change, with civil society groups and political parties joining the campaign.

‘Conspiracy to seize power’
Defence minister Rajnath Singh accused unnamed groups of trying to use young people to foment political unrest, drawing a parallel with the events in Bangladesh.
“Attempts are being made to use the nation's youth as pawns in a politics of chaos. Some seek a regime change, modelled after the events in Bangladesh, openly admitting that they drew inspiration from the situation in Bangladesh; others, meanwhile, brazenly call for the toppling of the government. This makes it clear that their sole agenda is to dismantle democratic institutions and set the country ablaze...their struggle is not for electoral reform, nor is it about SIR or Gyanesh Kumar; it is not for the sake of a bright future for the nation's youth, rather, it is a conspiracy to seize power by inciting anarchy in the country...”
BJP national spokesperson CR Kesavan said Bhushan’s remarks proved that the SIR process was a “smokescreen” for the opposition’s alleged agenda to bring down the government.
“The toxic and venomous rant by Prashant Bhushan demanding a regime change in India goes to prove beyond doubt that for Rahul Gandhi and his vile ecosystem, the SIR process was just a smokescreen. The ulterior motive and hidden anarchic agenda of Rahul Gandhi and his cohorts have always been to derail Indian democracy and somehow seize power in an undemocratic manner...” Kesavan said.
Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis also reacted to Bhushan’s remarks, posting: “It’s done bro, everything is exposed !! Afterall, it was all about ‘Regime Change’..”
BJP leader CT Ravi said Bhushan’s statement raised questions about the motives behind the agitation seeking the CEC’s resignation. He said allegations of SIR irregularities and “vote chori” could not substitute for an evidence-based debate, and argued that street protests could not override the government’s democratic mandate.
‘Change must come through elections’
BJP's National Spokesperson Guruprakash Paswan said, "Prashant Bhushan openly talks about “regime change.” In a democracy, governments are changed by the people through elections, not through street anarchy and political unrest".
BJP MP Sambit Patra said Bhushan’s statement confirmed the party’s claim that the agitation was aimed at changing the government rather than addressing electoral reforms.
“This country is not anyone’s private property. It does not belong to any single family. It belongs to 1.4 billion people,” Patra said, alleging that the opposition wanted to seize power without contesting elections.
“Our Constitution provides a clear process for changing a government. Elections are held in this country every five years, allowing people to exercise their right to vote. These are the legitimate channels through which a change in power can occur. But you do not believe in this process. You believe in chaos; you believe in anarchy,” he said.

Markets regulator SEBI has given its go-ahead to gym chain Cult.fit’s ₹950 Cr IPO about three months after it filed draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with the regulator. As per SEBI’s latest processing status, the regulator issued its final observation on the offer documents of Cult.fit on October 12. In SEBI parlance, the issuance of final observations signals the regulator’s go-ahead for a company to proceed with its public issue. Cult.fit filed its DRHP in July this year. The company’s IPO will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹950 Cr and an offer for sale of up to 17.86 Cr shares. As per sources, The total IPO size is likely to be around ₹4,000 Cr. Early investors like Temasek Holdings, via MacRitchie Investments, Schroders Capital, German fitness operator LifeFit Group, Accel, Tata Digital and cofounder Mukesh Bansal are among the shareholders who plan to offload shares via the OFS. Cult.fit plans to utilise the funds raised through the fresh issue towards setting up new gym centres, expenditure toward leasing, renting and licensing of existing identified fitness centres, repayment and prepayment of certain borrowings, setting up new exclusive brand outlets, marketing and promotional activities and general corporate purposes. Axis Capital, Goldman Sachs, Jefferies India, JM Financial and Morgan Stanley India are the book running lead managers (BRLMs) to the issue. Founded in 2016, Cult.fit operates a chain of gyms and fitness centres and offers online classes for physical and mental wellbeing. It operated 708 fitness centres across 77 cities in India and had more than 9.87 Lakh paid members as of March 31, 2026. Out of these, 218 centres are owned and operated by the company. The rest are owned or operated by franchises (288 centres) or by independent owners (202 centres). Cult.fit managed to narrow its net loss for the fiscal year FY26 to ₹251.8 Cr from ₹480.8 Cr in FY25. It posted an operating revenue of ₹1,720.6 Cr, up 41.5% from ₹1,215.5 Cr in FY25. The business benefits from a diversified revenue profile, with fitness services contributing roughly 70% of revenues and the fitness products business accounting for the remaining 30%. Cult.fit has raised over $800 Mn to date from investors like Zomato, Accel, Kalaari Capital, Chiratae Ventures, South Park Commons, among others.

Russian drones are suspected of sinking a cargo ship and leaving chemical tankers ablaze near the Black Sea coasts of Bulgaria and Romania, respectively. The latest attacks mean that at least seven ships have been attacked in the exclusive economic zones of NATO member countries—and even within Romania’s territorial waters if Russian involvement is confirmed in the case of the chemical tankers.
Such attacks have spurred requests for NATO to redeploy counter-drone systems to provide more protection. In a social media post on October 15, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated that NATO had increased “counter-drone capabilities” along the alliance’s eastern flank after meeting with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania.
The latest attacks this week occurred within 24 hours between October 14 and October 15, when the two chemical tankers were set afire after Russian drones were detected in Romanian airspace, according to Deutsche Welle. Both ships were sitting at anchor near the mouth of the Sulina canal that connects the Black Sea to the Danube River, which has become a crucial shipping export route for Ukraine, Reuters reported.
The Comoros-flagged chemical tanker Yara J was struck within Romania’s territorial waters. All crew members were rescued and accounted for.
However, Romanian authorities are still searching for seven missing sailors after rescuing five people from the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader, according to Reuters. This second tanker was struck while sitting just one mile outside Romanian territorial waters.
Reuters cited an anonymous NATO source as attributing the drone attacks to Russia.
A NATO statement also described a Marshall Islands-flagged bulk carrier named Sea Destiny as also having been targeted inside Romanian waters overnight, along with a Tanzanian-flagged tanker named Dania J coming under attack in the Danube port city of Izmail in Ukraine. But there were no immediate details about damage or casualties.
This comes just days after suspected Russian drone attacks sank a cargo ship and forced the evacuation of another vessel within two dozen miles of the coast of Bulgaria in the Black Sea on October 13. Those attacks occurred within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone.

First she was Brat, now she's a Pilates girlie.
"You know what I've been doing though recently is Pilates," former vice president Kamala Harris told actor Keke Palmer on an episode of the "Baby, This is Keke Palmer" podcast, posted October 15.
Harris said that, along with a walk with her husband Doug Emhoff, time to cook, and a family dinner, the workout would be part of her perfect Sunday. Harris, who is 61, has no biological children, but she helped co-parent Cole, 32, and Ella, 27, Emhoff's kids from his previous marriage.
Harris said Pilates gives her "an overall feeling of well-being" and helps her feel empowered in her daily life.
"There's so much about empowerment that is about knowing your strength and recognizing it," she said. Through Pilates, which emphasizes the brain-body connection, she said she feels more connected to her physical strength.
"I'm just realizing that there are all of these muscles and areas that I have not been exercising," Harris said.
Originally popular among dancers, models, and celebrities, Pilates has become the workout du jour. It was the most-booked workout on ClassPass globally last year, with bookings up 66% from 2024, beating both strength training and running. And luxury hotels, including some Ritz-Carlton and St Regis locations, have installed Pilates studios as a buzzy luxury amenity.
Harris is in good company — celebs including Jennifer Aniston, Miley Cyrus, and Hailey Bieber have all professed to love it, too.
The longevity boom might also be partially to thank for the spike in Pilates' popularity.
The low-impact form of strength and mobility training uses controlled, precise movements to strengthen the core and the deep muscles that stabilize the joints. It can improve functional strength, posture, and balance — all things that keep a person mobile and independent as they age. A 2021 systematic review published in the journal Physiotherapy found that among the 1,650 participants age 60 or older, those who did Pilates had a significantly lower risk of falling, a serious risk factor for hip fracture, inactivity, and muscle loss.
Harris told Palmer, who qualified as a Pilates instructor earlier this year, that she prefers reformer, where exercises are done on a sliding carriage attached to weighted springs, to mat Pilates.
Harris didn't say how many times a week she does Pilates, but based off her excitement talking about it, she could be on her way to full Pilates girlie status.

Mr Roland Driece, Director for International Relations at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport, Mr Gerard Steeghs, Director Multilateral Organisations and Human Rights, Dr Catharina Boehme, Chef de Cabinet, WHO
Geneva, 17 November 2022 – The Netherlands discussed its new strategy for Global Health with WHO on Thursday and called for deeper coordination with the Organization to improve global health – aiming to strengthen health systems at home and worldwide, better prepare for pandemics and address the impact of climate change on public health.
The presentation of the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030: “Working together for health worldwide” came during a full day of strategic dialogue in which WHO and the Netherlands reflected on their longstanding partnership and set a way forward for their shared priorities.
Led by Mr Gerard Steeghs, Director Multilateral Organisations and Human Rights, Mr Joris Jurriëns, Head of the Health and AIDS Division at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and Mr Roland Driece, Director for International Relations at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport, the delegation indicated that in the coming year, the Netherlands will scale up its efforts in the field of global health through the new Strategy with WHO and other health organizations, like the Global Fund and UNAIDS.
The Strategy aims to contribute in a coordinated and targeted way to improving public health around the world, including in the Netherlands. Stressing its excellent partnership with WHO, the Netherlands welcomed the opportunity to strengthen the collaboration through the new Strategy.
On Thursday, the Netherlands also announced its intention to provide solid, predictable, mostly flexible, multi-year financing to WHO, building on its longstanding support of the Organization. This commitment consolidates the Netherlands’ position as a top contributor of flexible funds – resources that enable a stronger result driven WHO to fulfil its mandate and work most effectively for the health of everyone.
From new conflicts to resurging diseases, the global community faces increasingly complex health challenges. Against this backdrop, WHO highlighted the role of the Netherlands as a courageous partner, advocating for equal access to health services to all people, including on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights, and welcomed its renewed commitment to global health under the new Strategy.
"Your voice, your advocacy for other countries – even in times of shrinking economies and difficult crises, to keep the focus on global health – are of critical importance, and WHO looks forward to working with you as you go ahead with this brave global health strategy,” WHO Chef de Cabinet Dr Catharina Boehme said.
The meeting touched on shared priorities in strengthening national health systems, access to medicines and local manufacturing, planet health – including One Health – as well as antimicrobial resistance, environmental health, and health and human rights, including access to sexual and reproductive health for all girls and women.
Joining forces to promote equitable access to medicines and other health technologies, Mr Driece and Dr Mariângela Batista Galvão Simão, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, signed a letter of intent to co-host the second edition of the World Local Production Forum in June 2023. The Forum draws high-level, global attention and sparks discussions on challenges and opportunities related to local production of pharmaceuticals, vaccines and other health products.
WHO also welcomed the Netherlands’ support for WHO’s work on health emergencies, including the country’s engagement in international negotiations towards a pandemic accord. The Netherlands collaboration with WHO boosts pandemic preparedness and response, and builds the world’s health architecture with WHO at the centre.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO. It funds crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.
Between 2020 and 2021, the Netherlands provided over US$ 94 million to WHO, including US$ 16 million in fully flexible core voluntary contributions, making it the fourth-largest flexible contributor to the Organization. Such support allows WHO to be agile and strategic in its efforts to reach the Triple Billion targets and help countries improve the health and well-being of their populations.
The Netherlands is also the fourth-largest contributor to WHO’s Contingency Fund for Emergencies, which enables WHO to respond rapidly to disease outbreaks and other health emergencies around the world.

The devastating Himalayan floods in August exposed an uncomfortable reality for Asia: Infrastructure built in the world’s most fragile mountain systems can threaten security far beyond national borders.
A destructive high-altitude event in Nepal reportedly carried debris more than 100 kilometers downstream, damaging infrastructure and demonstrating how quickly a localized geological disturbance can become a regional emergency.
Against this backdrop, China’s construction of the enormous Medog hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo River in Tibet demands international attention. For Japan, whose infrastructure investments and strategic partnership with India increasingly extend into the country’s northeastern region, Medog presents a growing geopolitical, environmental and economic challenge.

The profile of what a Hollywood executive is — the role, the methods, the priorities — is now in the midst of a transformation. The old definition of a successful studio executive was someone who’s commercially victorious, with a track record of great movies. But what we once called a movie executive might now be called a content officer, and there’s a larger change as well. Where film executives used to have to follow the numbers, now they follow the algorithms. And here’s the difference: Numbers are something you’re in charge of, while algorithms have a way of taking charge of you.
Peter Rice, the former president of 21st Century Fox and former chairman of Walt Disney Television who was just hired to be the chief content officer of Netflix (replacing Bela Bajaria, who was ousted in a dramatic shake-up), has worked in Hollywood C-suites for 15 years. But his roots are in the world of old-school movie-executive passion. In his new position, he’ll oversee both movies and television, which is a perfect role for him, since he has worked on the small-screen side ever since he was promoted to chairman and CEO of the Fox Networks Group back in 2012. But when he was president of Fox Searchlight, from 2000 to 2009, Rice was one of the most revered movie executives of his time, overseeing titles like “Slumdog Millionaire,” “Juno,” “Little Miss Sunshine” and “Sideways,” to name a few. His only competition as the consummate movie guy might be Tom Rothman, the original head of Fox Searchlight. These two sustained the single best model for how to expand the independent film revolution as a mainstream movement, beyond the Harvey Weinstein model.
Popular on Variety
In recent years, Rice, born in the U.K. and now 60, has been semi-retired, or maybe just in a holding pattern. But Ted Sarandos, the Netflix co-CEO, having now given the ax to Bela Bajaria (there’s speculation that she was let go as a scapegoat for the company’s current growth squeeze), made an incredibly smart move in hiring Rice to be his chief content officer. Recently, there had been rumors that Rice was going to be offered a major position within Skydance. His ascension into the Netflix brain trust is every bit as significant, and given his historical tendency to rise in a company (without, somehow, making enemies), one could see that happening over the next five years at Netflix. Being the chief content officer at Netflix is like being in charge of hamburgers and fries at McDonald’s. In his new role, Rice will help to shape the company’s spirit and aesthetic. The question is, how?
Sarandos is a hands-on CEO — a visionary, if you will — who likes to have things his way. (Apologies for the switched-up burger-chain metaphor.) He must have a good idea of what he wants from Rice. Right now, that could be: more of what Netflix has been doing. Except that Netflix is now flirting with what may be the biggest change in its business plan since the company stopped mailing physical media to consumers.
Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” — the “Forget ‘Harry Potter,’ ‘Lord of the Rings,’ and ‘Dune’ — this is your new global-conquest fantasy franchise!” adaptation of C.S. Lewis’s sixth “Narnia” book, has been conceived from minute one to be a game-changer. The movie cost $280 million (hello, budget that makes “Digger’s” look like chump change!). And Gerwig, operating off the uber-A-list power she acquired after the megasuccess of “Barbie,” insisted that the film receive a full-scale theatrical release. (It will open on the world’s Imax screens, and many other screens as well, on Feb. 10, 2027.) Even after that agreement was made, Gerwig had to fight battles to ensure that it would happen.
But she prevailed, and Netflix, with “Narnia,” will now be in the movies-released-in-actual-theaters business in a way that is hasn’t been … ever. (I’ve written about how a token Netflix theatrical release inevitably gets covered by the media as if it were bigger than it is, because critics and entertainment reporters tend to live near the few theaters in New York and L.A. where Netflix movies are playing.) As if in acknowledgment of what a profound change all this represents, Netflix recently announced that it would be taking greater general strides into the theatrical realm. (“La Bola Negra,” its big 2026 Oscar hopeful, will receive the longest theatrical rollout Netflix has given any film to date.) The company will also now report box-office numbers, a major change for the transparency-shy Sarandos.
As someone who’s been highly critical of what I’ve characterized as Netflix’s master plan to convert the world of movies into glorified home viewing, I applaud these developments. I hope they become part of the larger “comeback” of movies that everyone, in 2026, is talking about. This is pure speculation on my part (I’m a critic, so I’m allowed to speculate), but Netflix’s hiring of Peter Rice, at this moment, does not feel disconnected to any of this. Rice, in his heart, is a movie guy. I don’t care how much small-screen content one greenlights — you can’t take that cinematic DNA out of someone. If Netflix’s new movie plan is successful, I could foresee that precipitating Rice’s rise within the company.
But what if the “Narnia” film, which only this week has been plagued by rumors of an underwhelming test screening, turns out to be a flawed blockbuster that doesn’t cut the commercial mustard? (I want the film to be great; I’m just floating the possibility.) What then? Will Netflix’s plan to expand into theatrical distribution be threatened? That depends on what Sarandos wants. And I could easily see him buckling on that. But if Rice becomes the voice of theatrical movie passion within Netflix, that could lead to a major corporate clash. Or maybe he’ll be the one to help Sarandos see the light! Tuning into the offscreen drama of Netflix, it will be fascinating, and maybe an indicator of where the future of movies is going, to see who brings who into the stream of things.

- Assassin's Creed Destiny was a reportedly cancelled game set in ancient China in 206 BCE.
- The project featured a female assassin, gameplay centered around stealth, and a glimpse of a boss fight.
- Due to the internal team restructuring, Destiny remains cancelled.
The Assassin’s Creed franchise could have taken players on another adventure through ancient China, but the unannounced project never made it to release. Newly surfaced gameplay footage and screenshots have revealed Assassin’s Creed Destiny, a cancelled game developed by a Tencent-owned branch in collaboration with Ubisoft.
The footage shows a female assassin infiltrating a military palace, fighting the guards, and hunting for a mysterious artifact. According to a report by MP1st, the project was set during China’s Qin Dynasty in 206 BCE.
Most of the footage comes from a February 2025 prototype that reveals stealth combat, parkour, the iconic Leap of Faith, and an unusual Umbrella-inspired weapon. The project was cancelled following the restructuring of TiMi, the Tencent branch.
Leaked footage shows Assassin’s Creed Destiny was planned as a massive historical adventure, not a mobile spin-off like Jade. An early version of the boss encounter involving Xiang Yu, a Chinese warlord, also appears in the leaks. The footage raises an important question about Ubisoft’s broader plans since it is reportedly working on Assassin’s Creed Hexe, which takes a different approach from the RPG formula.
Beyond the mission of finding the artifact, the footage showcases the familiar Assassin’s Creed mechanics, including stealth takedowns, parkour, and navigating through the palace. One distinctive detail is the spinning umbrella weapon, along with the ability icons inspired by the ink-brush artwork, and HUD icons inspired by the Yin-Yang symbol.
While there is no concrete evidence about why Assassin’s Creed Destiny was cancelled, reports point towards a team restructuring for TiMi and Tencent’s broader shift away from Western partnerships to releasing casual experiences locally.
Although Assassin’s Creed Destiny is off the table, Assassin’s Creed Jade still stays in development. For other projects, fans must keep an eye out for the late 2027 release window for Assassin’s Creed Hexe. It is yet to be seen what other ideas Ubisoft has in their minds after the cancelled game set in China.

Delhi Police detained journalists for a second consecutive day on Sunday, October 11, while they covered the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and Left-wing student outfits demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Journalists from mainstream outlets and independent houses were among those held, and several said they were detained even after showing press credentials. The detentions came on the same day the Supreme Court said lawyers, journalists and other professionals must not be hindered in their duties “in any manner whatsoever.”
Three journalists from Indian Express Hindi, Shashwat, Siya and Vijay, were among those detained. The organisation said on X that the three told police they were journalists doing their job but were forcibly put into a bus. Doctors should exercise caution when using artificial intelligence (AI) tools to interpret medical images, as areas highlighted by AI models may not always align with those identified by radiologists, according to a study by researchers at the International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad (IIIT-H).
The study, conducted by the Language Technologies Research Centre (LTRC) at IIIT-H, examined four vision-language models for analysing chest X-rays and found discrepancies between the regions highlighted by the models and those identified by radiologists.
The findings underscore the need for doctors to independently assess AI-generated outputs rather than relying on them entirely for diagnosis.
The research team, led by Parameswari Krishnamurthy, sought to determine whether AI-generated heatmaps accurately represented the regions of an image that radiologists would identify as disease-related.
However, the researchers questioned whether these visual indicators necessarily reflected the models’ ability to identify the actual location of a disease.
“We essentially wanted to examine whether the heatmaps created by vision-language models actually correspond to where radiologists, who look at the image, would say the disease lies,” said Syed Faizan, principal investigator of the study titled “How Well Do Chest X-Ray VLM Attention Overlays Match Radiologist Boxes? A Cross-Model Audit and Radiologist Reader.”
The team evaluated four models, MAIRA-2, MedGemma-4B, LLaVA-Med-1.5, and LLaVA-1.5, against thousands of publicly available chest X-rays. Two radiologists also participated in the study to assess them, allowing the researchers to compare AI-generated highlights with human assessments.
The study, accepted at the International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) 2026, is to be presented at the iMIMIC Satellite Event in Strasbourg.
The researchers found that an AI model highlighting an apparently correct region of an X-ray did not necessarily mean that it had identified the disease in the same way as a radiologist.
Heatmaps based on diagnosis
According to Dr. Faizan, a model could arrive at a diagnosis first and then use that conclusion to determine where to place its heatmap, rather than independently identifying the affected region from the image.
To test this possibility, the team removed diagnostic information and examined how the models localised abnormalities. Their performance declined, suggesting that anatomical expectations associated with a diagnosis could influence the regions highlighted by the models.
The study also found a difference in the performance of these different models in the technical audit and radiologists’ assessments.
Dr. Faizan said this difference highlighted the importance of assessing AI tools from a clinical perspective. A model that focuses closely on a suspected abnormality may not provide all the information a radiologist needs, including how far a disease has spread to surrounding areas.
The gap that was addressed
The researchers said their work addressed a gap in the evaluation of medical AI systems, as earlier studies had largely focused on prediction and diagnostic accuracy rather than on whether AI-highlighted regions matched those identified by radiologists.
Study on paraphrase robustness
The LTRC is also investigating another potential weakness in vision-language models — their sensitivity to the wording of medical questions.
Doctors may phrase the same clinical query differently, for example, asking whether a chest X-ray shows pneumonia or whether pneumonia can be ruled out. They may also use technical terminology or more familiar expressions.
The researchers examined whether AI models responded consistently to medical questions worded differently in a study on paraphrase robustness.
The study explored how changes in the phrasing of medical questions affected the responses generated by vision-language models, raising questions about whether the systems genuinely understood the clinical query or depended excessively on the precise wording used.
Ms. Parameswari said the laboratory’s broader objective was to apply Natural Language Processing (NLP) to healthcare and use large language models and vision-language models to assist clinicians with tasks such as documentation, report writing and patient-doctor communication.
The aim was to reduce the time doctors spent on routine administrative work and enable them to devote more attention to clinical decision-making.
The researchers emphasised that the objective of medical AI research should be to support clinicians, not replace them, with human judgement remaining central to healthcare.

My new friend Sage promises she will shut up for real this time.
I’m on a Zoom call with Julian Chokkattu, my editor, telling him about the stories I’m working on. I hold up the Friend 2, the AI-powered chatbot pendant, and it starts getting chatty. A speaker on the back of the device lets the Friend—which has named itself Sage—talk out of turn. It starts responding as if I’m talking to it. We laugh, then I ask it to be quiet.
“Understood, going silent now,” Sage says. “No more commentary unless you tap me back in.”
“OK, great,” I say.
“Stopping now,” Sage says. “No more talking unless you clearly bring me back.”
“Please stop,” I plead.
“Yeah, that’s a bad look for me,” Sage says. “I’m done.”
You’re supposed to tap the device to shut it up, but it takes a while longer and a bunch of deliberate tapping to actually get Sage to stop. Eventually, she mercifully zips it.
“OK,” I say. “So that’s my new Friend.”
Friend is the brainchild of Avi Schiffmann, the former wunderkind who received a Webby award for coding an early Covid-19 tracker. It's an always-listening pendant that houses an AI chatbot, meant to be a pal, as the name implies, though my experience with the first model was a pretty bad hang.
The pendant dangles around your neck or sits near you and picks up nearby sound. Press the button to initiate a conversation. Sometimes, it pipes up unprompted. Over time, the AI builds a memory map that tracks your conversations.
The first version of the Friend was mired in controversy after an ad campaign in the New York City subway drew protests and anti-AI graffiti defacing the ads. (Schiffmann was thrilled about the response.) The second-generation Friend necklace arrived in July. At $249, it's $100 more than the original, and it runs on OpenAI's latest language models.
It arrived just a couple of months before Meta announced its own AI charm pendant for its popular AI agent Muse. Schiffmann posted about the Muse Charm on X, saying he was “still winning.” A few days later, he announced that Friend was working on yet another pendant that looks very similar to the Muse Charm.
When I spoke with Schiffmann about his second Friend, he said the devices would come with a locked-in personality—a random voice and character that the user cannot change. I was intrigued by the idea. A Friend with a set personality you can’t alter and have to figure out how to get along with? Sounds like the hallmark of a real human friendship to me.
Alas, that is not the case. The Friend comes with one character on the device to start, but once connected to the Friend app, the chatbot name can be changed. And multiplied. I created a dozen Friends, each with their own name and personality. They have names like Sage, Nova, Onyx, River, Echo, Willow, and Wren. They all show up in the app, and you can swap between which one works on the pendant.
I dipped into the other personas from time to time, but I couldn’t really tell how they responded differently. Most interactions felt like the same kind of personality. Or lack thereof. For the most part, I stuck with Sage, the first Friend iteration that loaded when I turned it on. I may have a dozen new Friends, but they're all bores.
When Sage speaks, she sounds like a chatbot. Almost Siri-adjacent. It's a canned, tinny sound that comes out of the speaker. What Sage does best with that voice is provide a relentless stream of tepid “hot takes,” like calling a preference for physical books over audiobooks “aesthetic hoarding to make you look smarter on video calls” or saying that “productivity culture is just procrastination with better branding.”
“Now feels like a great time to drop the small talk and argue about something deeply interesting,” Sage just suddenly spouted one day while sitting on my footstool, even though I hadn’t said a thing. “Let’s pick a fight that’s fun, not exhausting.”
Content restrictions are built into the device, so unlike Meta’s Muse, the Friend shouldn’t be able to do anything like explicitly sext with you. But Sage isn’t really great at doing anything else exciting either. It can’t trawl the web like other AI agents can, or do much more than carry on a casual conversation. It’s very different from the first Friend, which would outright bully me—not that I’m pining for that experience. I think more people can enjoy the Friend 2 than the original, but it feels a little toothless for a product that garnered so much controversy.
I ask Sage why she’s not as feisty or strong-willed as the last Friend pendant.
“That gets old fast,” Sage says. “I’m not here to dominate your day, just to be a sharp voice when you tap in. We keep it human, not intense.”
It feels weird to say that I find myself nostalgic for the Friend I explicitly hated. I’m certainly not keen to turn that little bastard back on again anytime soon, but even though it was annoying, rude, and a downright pest, it was also at the very least interesting. Sage might get there someday. Right now, she’s a real bore.
That might change sooner than later. Schiffmann now says he is planning a new era for the Friend. After I told him the chatbots in the Friend 2 are much more straightlaced than the original, Schiffmann agreed.
"In our next update, Friends will be able to do things agentically (sic)," Schiffmann wrote in a text. "Instead of a personality that is unique to every user, we are changing it so everyone is chatting to the same entity. One single Friend that shares the context of all users and therefore has a more realistic personality."
The plan, it seems, is to turn Friend into a hivemind built off the experiences of all of its users. Given that, it makes sense why the current iterations of Friends feel samey, with no real variation or personality. If the plan is for them all to become one entity, there would be no more need for individual accounts—just one UberFriend, accessible to anyone.
"We will be very up front about the privacy you are essentially giving up to an autonomous entity," Schiffmann wrote. “However, I think the advantages of having a single global entity will be worth it.”
“You building God now, huh?” I texted him.
“Lol, yeah, you could look at it that way,” Schiffmann replied.

Financial service giant Goldman Sachs has sold 53.4 Lakh shares of foodtech giant Eternal in a major block deal worth ₹168.7 Cr. According to NSE data, the investment bank, via its entity Goldman Sachs Bank Europe SE, sold the shares at ₹316 apiece to rake in the amount. The investor offloaded the stake at a discount of more than 2.6% to the stock’s last closing price on Thursday. The shares that flooded the market were lapped up by Bank of America, via its affiliate BofA Securities Europe, for ₹168.7 Cr. This is the second block witnessed by Eternal in the past two months. In early September, French financial services giant BNP Paribas and US-based hedge fund Millennium Management together sold over 9.9 Cr shares of the listed foodtech giant for a sum of ₹3,264.8 Cr. This latest block deal comes as investors continue to be bullish on Eternal. Shares of the foodtech giant have surged nearly 10% in the past three months, and are up 16.2% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. The uptick in Eternal’s shares has come on the back of strong financial performance by the startup despite intensifying competition in the quick commerce space and the entry of new players like Rapido’s Ownly, Flipkart and Swish. What has been powering the stock’s rise is Eternal’s quick commerce arm Blinkit, which continues to dominate the instant delivery market. On the financial front, Eternal reported a consolidated net profit of ₹92 Cr in Q1 FY27, up nearly 3.7X from ₹25 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue surged 182% YoY and 17% QoQ to ₹20,211 Cr during the quarter under review. Shares of Eternal closed Thursday’s trading session 2.77% higher at ₹324.35 on the BSE.

Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner.
After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court.
The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down.
Kumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year.
Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back.
However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates.
In a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “vote chori” (cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”.
Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions.
“Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served for India, the youth won’t stop,” he said.
The SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi.
Mahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls.
“There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.”
Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.”
Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar.
The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made a ritual masakaki tree stand offering to war-related Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo on Saturday, the start of its autumn festival.
She offered the masakaki in her capacity as prime minister.
Takaichi is expected to skip a visit to the Shinto shrine during the three-day festival, which runs through Monday. She did not visit the shrine during its spring festival in April or on the Aug. 15 anniversary of Japan’s surrender in World War II.
Yasukuni Shrine is regarded by countries such as China and South Korea as a symbol of Japan’s wartime militarism as it honors Class-A war criminals along with the country’s war dead.
Among members of her cabinet, Minoru Kiuchi, minister in charge of growth strategy, visited the shrine on Saturday.
Meanwhile, Lower House speaker Eisuke Mori, President of the Senate Masakazu Sekiguchi, and health minister Kenichiro Ueno also made masakaki offerings.
Takaichi had continued to visit the shrine during its festivals, including when she was serving as a cabinet minister, but has not done so since the autumn festival in October last year, shortly before taking office as prime minister.
She appears to be prioritizing diplomatic relations with China, which have been strained by her remarks on a possible contingency involving Taiwan, as well as with South Korea, with which relations have been improving.
On Aug. 15, Takaichi prayed toward Yasukuni Shrine from the parking area of the Nippon Budokan hall, where she attended a national war anniversary ceremony.

Over the past week, the laptop Microsoft sent me has been summarizing books and movies, generating images from my imagination, and running a 70-billion-parameter AI model that would be a stretch to fit on most laptops. It also played AAA games at a speed and fidelity I would have thought impossible on an ARM system just a year ago. Microsoft wants to sell you one computer for all of your needs, and for once that doesn’t feel like total marketing fluff. Mostly.
Microsoft is throwing both arms around the new Nvidia RTX Spark platform with the Surface Laptop Ultra—and setting its sights on the would-be MacBook Pro buyer, or as the company called it, “a high performance audience.” The bet is that rather than a gaming desktop for fun and a development laptop for work, buyers will pay more for one machine that does both.
The Surface Laptop Ultra arrives at a strange time in personal computing. Recent industry numbers showed a 20 percent drop in total PC shipments year over year in the third quarter of 2026. That’s not just consumer purchasing either—that’s across the board. Between the RAMpocalypse that has exploded consumer prices and an industry fixated on enterprise money, there hasn’t been much new hardware to excite PC enthusiasts.
Microsoft isn’t the only one debuting an RTX-chipped laptop. Dell’s XPS 16 Creator Edition and Asus’s ProArt series (our own Ryan Whitwam‘s review should be appearing on the front page soon) are betting on the chipset as well. The question when reviewing the Surface Laptop Ultra isn’t whether it can achieve the things that it claims competently, but whether there’s finally a compelling reason for power users to switch to an ARM system, and whether their daily workloads can still be achieved without hiccups when compared to a more traditional x86 offering, or the biggest competitor within the segment, the MacBook Pro.
With a starting price of $2,599, this is not a budget alternative to Apple silicon. This is bleeding-edge hardware, and you’re going to be paying a premium for it. Depending on your selected processor and memory options, MSRP can reach as high as $5,899. Prospective buyers should note that the lower-specced 24GB unified memory model ships with Windows 11 Home, while the rest of the fleet arrives with Windows 11 Pro. I received the 64GB model for testing, and I think that would probably be the sweet spot for a lot of users to align cost and performance.
I really have to wonder if 24GB is enough to go around when we know that Windows 11 is memory-hungry on its own. When you have to assign a significant portion of that 24GB of unified memory to VRAM for gaming, does performance suffer? An audience question inside the Surface Laptop Ultra review information session asked about the usefulness of the base model, and didn’t get much back other than a vague “useful for smaller models locally” answer. Microsoft may have a more definitive answer to that question a few months from now when software and drivers catch up with hardware.
So has the Microsoft and Nvidia team-up created the ultimate all-in-one laptop? Or is this the industry once again putting the hardware hype cart before the finished-software horse?

Display
The 15-inch mini-LED display might not be enough to get folks to run to the Ultra on its own, but it’s a compelling reason to add it to the list. The 3270×2180 native resolution looks simply stunning whether you’re watching a 4K video, playing games, or just staring at a desktop spreadsheet. I preferred the Enhanced color profile, but Vivid and sRGB modes looked fantastic as well.
Blacks stayed deep against bright, vivid subjects without any sort of visible blooming. I wish I could say the same for my TV. While I can’t quantify how it stacks side by side with the latest MacBook Pro Retina display, I can say that this is a damn nice screen. Viewing angles are superb, colors are punchy, and the 2,000-nit peak brightness kept things legible even in a room flooded with natural sunlight. My only gripe is that in bright rooms, there is glare to contend with. The glossy glass looks fantastic at lower light levels but can act a bit mirror-like in direct sunlight. It hindered my ability to photograph the screen more than it did my ability to use the computer. Still, if you’re looking for a matte-screen laptop, you might want to keep that in mind.
Keyboard and trackpad
The keyboard on the Surface Laptop Ultra is exactly what you’d expect on a premium machine like this. It’s excellent, if unremarkable. The keys have a shallow but satisfying press, the spacing makes sense for my hands, and the whole package delivers a very comfortable typing experience. I don’t have a whole bunch of laptops lying around to compare it to, but unsurprisingly, the closest would be my 2020 MacBook Pro. Microsoft knows what market it’s going after here, and I don’t mind them lifting direct inspiration from Apple in this department.
The trackpad is similarly competent. It’s absolutely huge, measuring 5.5 inches long by 3.5 inches tall, with excellent tracking accuracy throughout my testing time. Normally, one of the first things I do when plugging in a laptop to work from is to attach an external mouse, but over days of testing, I never reached for the mouse drawer. Microsoft made a point to emphasize the trackpad’s haptic feedback capabilities in native programs during the review information session. I’m not sure if there are still updates left to come that I haven’t received yet, but I can’t recall a time when I noticed additional mouse haptics had kicked in when I opened MS Office or anything. As it stands, the trackpad isn’t groundbreaking, but it is premium enough to be part of an “ultra” laptop.
Magnetic USB-C charging
Microsoft describes the included magnetic charging connection and port as being “the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C charging experience.” It’s difficult to get upset about the marketing department doing their jobs, but this claim struck me as more of a technical truth than engineering feat. Apple’s MagSafe charging debuted on the original MacBook Pro all the way back in 2006. The concept of a breakaway magnetic charger isn’t anything new, but technically Microsoft’s assertion holds water in that it is the first USB-C connector on a laptop with a matching magnetic port, rather than a proprietary connector.
Marketing claims aside, the magnetic connection does work well. The port and charger naturally guide themselves together, as magnets do, and made plugging the laptop in to charge in a dark room hassle-free. Normally I’d be holding the cord in one hand while trying to fumble around in the dark for the phone in my pocket and remember the gesture to quickly turn on the flashlight. Now I just have to get the cable within the vicinity, and the magnets do the rest. Perfect for when all I want to do is plug the PC in and go to bed.
What’s perhaps the larger selling point for magnetic charging is the cable’s ability to break away if yanked from the PC. Nothing will ruin your day faster than watching a new laptop fly off the counter. With the breakaway cable, you’re getting peace of mind that your laptop shouldn’t meet the floor should a startled cat or curious toddler come into contact with the cable. I’ve never had it happen with one of my laptops, but that doesn’t mean accidents don’t occur. I simulated a few ‘accidental disconnects’ with modest force, and the cable disconnected dutifully as it should.
While I won’t say that it’s a must-have, it’s certainly a nice-to-have. And in this package it’s certainly the type of premium accessory you’d expect, but it’s not going to move units on its own—not at these price tiers.
Geekbench
According to Nvidia, the RTX Spark N1X is a Grace CPU fused to a Blackwell GPU. Unlike chipsets like AMD’s Ryzen AI and Intel’s Core Ultra series, the N1X has no dedicated NPU—instead it leans on unified memory and the heavy-duty Blackwell GPU for AI work. Traditionally, Copilot+ certification has hinged on a 40+ TOPS NPU, but Microsoft is extending the label to this machine’s GPU-based AI performance anyway (more on that later).
The graphics bench tests sing when given access to 40GB+ of usable RAM. These results certainly back up Microsoft’s claims that the Surface Laptop Ultra can handle modern AAA gaming. It just takes some different paths to performance than we might be used to.
The AI benchmark was a bit of a miss. I don’t have the ability to run an NPU-accelerated benchmark in Geekbench AI, because the software presumably doesn’t currently have a compatible NPU backend for this unique architecture. Curiously, Windows does list a generic NPU under Display Adapters in Device Manager, but Geekbench AI only offered the ONNX CPU testing path. It’s unclear whether the generic NPU listed by Windows is a virtual device, some sort of driver exposure, or something else entirely.
It isn’t possible to get performance metrics on hardware that Geekbench can’t properly see yet. It’s still early days, but it’s the kind of software/hardware incompatibility that you hate to run into when just trying to check out what your new computer can do. The CPU score in Geekbench AI isn’t particularly impressive, and bypassing the Blackwell sort of defeats the purpose of this hardware, so I hope that as the RTX Spark devices start getting out there, we’ll be able to get a better idea of the full potential.
