Steam Achievement Sets will stop DLCs from ruining your 100 percent record
The platform now separates base game and DLC achievements.
Steam can now group together different categories of achievements — and separates ones for base games and ones for DLCs — so that developers' new additions won't affect your completion percentage. The new feature, called Achievement Sets, is now live in Steam Client beta. Developers will have to update their games to add specific collections, each one with a defined purpose, but the platform says there's a growing number of games that already support the feature. They can, for example, group single-player and multiplayer achievements or introduce seasonal sets, like one for a Halloween event.
You'll see achievements grouped together in collections when you browse everything you've unlocked on your profile. Each set has a progress bar that shows how far along you are in completing it, and you'll be able to display a "set complete" trophy on your profile every time you earn every single achievement in a collection. Your progress will still show 100 percent even if the developer adds more achievements to a set later on.
Steam divides collections into two types: Base Game Achievement Sets and DLC Achievement Sets. All base game trophies, as well as their progress bar, appear blue on your achievements page. Meanwhile, DLC achievements and progress bars are displayed in purple. Those sets will not show up in your overall game progress until you have access to the specific DLCs they're connected to, so as to not affect your completion.
The platform has redesigned its achievements page to be able to show the sets and your progress better, as well. This new page will also allow you to compare your progress with up to three friends, including the rare achievements you've earned and the sets you've completed.

Rakuten Group priced ¥400 billion ($2.5 billion) of yen-denominated bonds on Friday, including debt aimed at individual investors, in its largest-ever yen bond sale.
The 5.5-year bonds carry a 4.37% coupon and were priced at a spread of 200 basis points over the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond, with ¥360 billion sold to retail investors and ¥40 billion to institutional investors.
Following SoftBank Group’s ¥1 trillion retail bond sale, Rakuten’s offering highlights the growing role of the retail market as a funding source for large corporate borrowers. As individual investors shift money from deposits into higher-yielding assets, demand for corporate bonds is expanding.
“The recent string of large bond sales is evidence of rising interest and demand among individuals,” said Toshiyasu Ohashi, a visiting professor at Chiba University of Commerce’s Graduate School of Accounting and Finance. “Households are beginning to recognize the appeal of corporate bonds as inflation erodes the value of cash and deposits.”
Japanese companies have sold about ¥3.2 trillion of yen-denominated retail bonds so far in 2026, including Rakuten’s latest offering, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That is already more than 15% above last year’s record.
Ohashi also said the surge in demand could help break the “chicken-and-egg problem” that has long constrained the growth of Japan’s corporate bond market. Stronger demand could spur more retail bond issuance and help broaden Japan’s corporate bond market, he said.
Rakuten returned to a quarterly net profit in the April-June period for the first time in six years, though its mobile business remains in the red. It faces substantial bond redemptions from 2027 onward and has said it plans to meet its funding needs through a range of measures, including bond issuance in Japan and overseas and asset monetization.
According to Daiwa Securities, a lead manager, the institutional tranche was initially marketed at 170-180 basis points over government bonds but priced at 200 basis points amid heavy supply and widening spreads in the secondary market. Final demand was about 1.3 times the issue size.

The F1 pit stop that helped save lives
- Published
When the McLaren pit crew refuelled a car, changed its tyres and relayed information to their driver in less than seven seconds at the Spanish Grand Prix in 2001, they were just doing their jobs.
But 700 miles away in the break room at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), Dr Martin Elliott and his colleagues were watching after completing a life-saving operation on a young child.
The brief glimpse would change how the doctors approached patient care. From surgery-to-ICU handovers and neonatal care to air-ambulance response times, F1's innovations have made an impact far beyond the track.
At Ferrari's factory in Maranello, the medical team studied how pit crews organised roles, communication and handovers.
Doctors and nurses started each procedure with a checklist, setting out specific roles and tasks. This reduced human error and helped ensure key tasks were completed. All patient data was also shared from the operating theatre to the care unit.
Gaps in performance were identified and addressed, while repeated rehearsals helped refine the process.
As a result, the process from surgery to intensive care became more organised, and a 2007 study by researchers at GOSH and the University of Oxford found the F1-inspired handover process reduced technical errors, information omissions and handover time.
Reflecting on the project, Dr Elliott, then a consultant paediatric cardiothoracic surgeon at GOSH, said: "The environment we were working in then and in many ways still do is fundamentally potentially dangerous at every step.
"And of course, fundamentally, that's how F1 doesn't make mistakes. They have created an environment of complete precision, not only in engineering, but also in process, because they simply can't afford financially or from a race perspective to slip up.
"It's the same, you know, the precious parcel on the trolley is the same as the precious parcel in the car. You have to get all of those steps right."
The model was later adopted by other healthcare teams.
From trackside to bedside
Fifteen years ago, Williams worked with the University Hospital of Wales to improve neonatal resuscitation.
Former Williams human performance specialist Gemma Fisher recognised that the organisation of pit-crew equipment to prevent delay could also be applied in a hospital setting.
Video analysis unveiled the chaotic reality of medical emergencies with overlapping voices and misplaced equipment.
Standardising roles - deciding who stood where, who needed to be heard at what moment and where equipment was stationed - allowed for a faster, more efficient response.
Debriefings allowed medical staff to review what had happened and identify what could be improved for future emergencies.
The changes also encouraged junior doctors to raise concerns without fear of blame.
The collaboration extended beyond working practices and into engineering. Advanced Healthcare Technology and Williams have since developed the Babypod: a carbon fibre carrier designed to withstand a 20G crash, which can help prevent injury in the transportation of babies from ambulance to hospital.
Every second counts
F1 continues to find new ways to apply its expertise in emergency medicine.
At this year's race at Silverstone, a collaboration with Air Ambulance Cornwall showed how response times could be improved, with take-off time reduced from five minutes to three and a half.
This was achieved using many of the same methods, including quick and organised starts, having equipment ready for use and clear communication across the team.
David Richards, chairman of Motorsport UK and former team principal of BAR and Benetton, said: "You might not see one and a half minutes in the overall scheme of things, but one and a half minutes when you're lying by the side of the road or you've fallen off a horse or you've fallen down a cliff and you've hurt yourself, those minutes must seem like years for the person who's injured."
Richards said the partnership would continue to look for ways to reduce response times further.
Twenty-five years after Dr Elliott first saw a pit stop that inspired a new way of thinking, lessons from the sport continue to influence healthcare, from neonatal treatment to emergency response.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.

- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and

The Olympic sprinter now bedbound for 22 hours a day
- Published
Beth Dobbin is so determined to raise awareness of the illness that has decimated her life that she is speaking out, despite knowing it could trigger a brutal deterioration in her health.
Five years ago, she ran for Great Britain at the Tokyo Olympics. Now, at 32, she spends more than 22 hours a day in bed.
"I've done little things like attend a blood test at the doctors and been in bed for months after. So doing this interview, chatting away for 30 minutes, that could have an impact on me in 2027," she says.
"But I felt like it was really important to do that to get the message out."
She now only gets out of bed to eat and use the bathroom.
Dobbin has been diagnosed with ME, or myalgic encephalomyelitis - a chronic, fluctuating disease, causing symptoms such as sleep problems, problems with thinking and memory, pain and severe, persistent fatigue that does not improve with rest, and more.
A conversation, or even something so simple as a light too bright or a sound too loud, can cause a "crash" that lasts 24, 48 hours, or in the worst cases, months on end.
This year, Dobbin has left the house on just five occasions.
"It's life-decimating like I can't even put into words," she says. "I feel like I've lost everything.
"I have still got my family, but I've lost my independence, my health, the ability to work, the ability to exercise."
For Dobbin it all started with back-to-back Covid and glandular fever infections in the winter of 2021-22. She had not been unwell with either, only discovering she had contracted both through retrospective tests.
She had been sleeping a bit more and her running times were slightly down, but nothing that raised alarm. As time went on, she noticed soreness in the glands of her neck and armpits and a general sense of not quite feeling herself.
British Athletics doctors ran tests that gave no answers, so she carried on, assuming it was lingering glandular fever that would eventually pass.
She qualified for that year's World Championships, Commonwealth Games and European Championships in what was an unusually condensed season owing to the backlog from the pandemic.
Her health progressively deteriorated. At the Worlds, she struggled with a painful throat and was waking at unusual times in the night. At the Commonwealths, she was dizzy while running and her body was more sore than normal.
At the Europeans, she false-started after losing all feeling in her legs while in the blocks. She spoke of her "year of hell" in an emotional interview with BBC Sport after that race.
"When the Europeans had finished, I had this huge rest and the symptoms were just piling on. Things were getting worse and worse," Dobbin says. "I was struggling to stand up, I was sleeping loads, in bed all the time.
"After six weeks, I went back to training. I managed three weeks.
"[Doctors] were just really shocked that I still wasn't doing well and I'd had these viruses months ago.
"I think I saw four or five different specialists because the symptoms that I was having, they were across multiple [body] systems. All the specialists said 'this is ME' and we don't want it to be that because there's nothing out there for it."
ME has no known cure or specific treatment, with patients often relying on off-label medication to manage a condition that can cause more than 200 symptoms, including nausea, headaches, poor cognitive function and brain fog.
The condition is also known as chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), a label Dobbin strongly rejects. As a former athlete who balanced working eight-hour shifts with training before turning professional, she says she has "known fatigue my whole life" and believes the term fails to capture the severity of the illness.
"I wish it was just fatigue, that would be a walk in the park," she says. "It's so much more than that. If I thought of fatigue in my top 20 symptoms it might just make the cut."
Instead, she says, it feels like her entire body "is shutting down; it feels like you are a few days from death".
More than 400,000 people in the UK are thought to have ME, although the true figure could exceed one million, with severity ranging from people able to work or study to those requiring round-the-clock care and tube feeding.
Despite the length of time she spends in bed, Dobbin often feels too unwell to sleep and requires medication to help her do so.
"Even things like sitting up for a prolonged period of time can take it out of me so I prefer to be just propped up in bed, and that doesn't mean I feel fine. It doesn't get rid of my symptoms, but it makes them less hellish."
For Dobbin's parents and sister Faye, who sit close by to her in support during the interview at the family home in Doncaster, the impact is clear.
"I'm just so desperate to help her but I can't because there is nothing. I'd take her anywhere, I'd take her to America if I had to, but there's nothing," says her father Jim, a former footballer who played for Barnsley, Grimsby and Doncaster Rovers.
Mum Jean adds: "You wake up every day and just feel sad. She should be building her life, living her best life.
"Every day you worry about how she's going to be that day. It's a worry about what our future life's going to be like, who's going look after her if we can't look after her.
"There is nothing out there. There is nowhere to go. You go to the GP and there's nowhere for them to send you to. It's really at the back of the queue as far as research, knowledge, expertise, funding."
There is no specialist service for ME within the NHS and Dobbin says she has found herself educating GPs about the condition.
She had to wait 22 months before she got a face-to-face appointment with a private specialist she sourced herself after her British Athletics funding ended.
On Sunday, Dobbin's younger sister Faye will run the Yorkshire Marathon to raise money for ME Research UK.
"You just feel so helpless and we've been saying this for years now, what can we do?" Faye says.
"It feels like [the marathon] is all I can do other than supporting her emotionally.
"It does feel quite like grief in a way. I'm always worried about Beth. She's always on my mind. I'm worried about what kind of day she is having. What if she never improves? What if she gets worse? What if she gets another virus?"
Asked about her future, Dobbin is straight to the point: "It's very bleak, unfortunately.
"The only positive thing really to say is that Covid happened six years ago now and it's like the whole medical community has woken up."
Since the Covid pandemic and the emergence of long Covid, for which there is a significant overlap in symptoms with ME, there has been a surge in attention and increase in research funding for the condition.
She added: "There will be something, I hope, in the future.
"I said I wanted to speak about it. It's not necessarily that I want to discuss it [but] it's raising that awareness. And unfortunately, athletes are believed a lot more than the average person.
"A lot of people that have this illness that I've spoken to have said to me 'I don't get believed, people think I'm lazy'. I've never experienced one person that doesn't believe me and that's because, why would an athlete just suddenly stop after 20 years?
"I've got a slight platform. If this happened to most people they wouldn't be able to speak about it, so I do feel like I've got a bit of a duty to do that."

Oregon teen gunman was tackled by ‘heroic’ teacher then shot by students’ father
Attacker Griffin J. John II, an ex-student at the school, killed four people and had 44 rounds remaining when he died
A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon junior school, then tackled and fought with him – probably saving lives before he was shot by a father who followed him into the building, police said Friday.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called the teacher’s actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured. He identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II and said all of the victims were shot in the same classroom.
Authorities said John had been a special needs student at the school and had attacked a classroom with special needs students. He fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed, Krantz said.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” he said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.”

England's 41-match unbeaten run ended by Canada
- Published
WXV Global Series
Canada (5) 24
Tries: Bauder, Corrigan, Menin, Seumanutafa Cons: De Goede (2)
England (14) 21
Tries: Feaunati, Harrison, Bern Cons: Harrison (3)
England's 41-match unbeaten streak ended in dramatic fashion as Shoshanah Seumanutafa's late try handed Canada a thrilling 24-21 victory in Toronto.
Canada, who previously snapped England's 39-match winning run with a 26-26 draw in Exeter in September, are the first team to defeat the Red Roses since November 2022, when they lost to New Zealand in the World Cup final.
Playing in front of 18,621 fans, a record for a standalone women's fixture in North America, the result also marks England's first defeat by Canada since 2016 and their first against their hosts on Canadian soil, having won their previous 11 away matches.
Canada's Savannah Bauder took advantage of Zoe Harrison's yellow card to open the scoring in the 15th minute, but it was England who took a 14-5 half-time lead, hitting back late in the first half through Maddie Feaunati and Harrison, with Laetitia Royer in the sin-bin for the hosts.
Sarah Bern cancelled out a stylish solo try from the hosts' Alysha Corrigan early in the second half to preserve England's nine-point lead before Canada's DaLeaka Menin crashed over for a converted score just after the hour mark to set up a tense finale.
Three minutes from time, Canada mounted an attack from halfway after a fumble put Harrison's clearing kick under pressure, and replacement Seumanutafa charged down the left wing to complete the comeback.
"We're not driven by outcome. We're disappointed by the result but there was some very good things in our performance. So we'll stick to our processes," said England head coach John Mitchell, following his first defeat since being appointed in late 2023.
"I guess [the loss] frees us up and allows us to find more. I know this group has got more in them. Sometimes it requires the context that we've just received to dig deeper and find something more."
The two sides will renew their rivalry in Ottawa on Friday, 23 October (in the early hours of Saturday on UK time) before England conclude their 2026 WXV Global Series against the USA in New Jersey on Friday, 30 October (21:15 GMT).
'We're still world champions, we're still number one'
This result has been coming for England, who showcased vulnerability in their three WXV Global Series home matches in September.
Against Australia, the world champions trailed at half-time for the first time since 2020 before roaring back with seven second-half tries for a 48-15 win. The following week, Canada held them to a draw in Exeter while a nail-biting 26-19 win over New Zealand at Twickenham was secured with the clock in the red.
This time, Canada's defensive resilience in the face of repeated attacks kept the world champions off the scoreboard until the 32nd minute, but England also lacked a clinical touch in their opponents' 22, with multiple opportunities going begging. Notably, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald had an early try chalked off for a knock-on in the grounding.
In defence, multiple penalties afforded Canada the freedom to form free-flowing attacks while it was an individual handling error when delivering the ball to fly-half Harrison which gave the hosts field position to score their match-winning try.
The result places England in uncharted territory, with several players in the squad never having tasted defeat on the international stage - winger Jess Breach was unbeaten in her previous 59 caps.
But for captain Meg Jones, it is no time to panic. England are "still world champions" and her message is simple: "Stick together, look out for each other, and we go again."
She added: "We've got to remember, there's a target on our back continuously. Everyone's got that underdog mentality, that underdog fight.
"We've got to be in a position now where we've got to be the quickest to respond. That's the nature of the game.
"What an amazing achievement for us as a group. I think they will go down in history as one of the best sporting teams.
"We're still world champions, we're still number one, and we'll still keep pushing to be the best we possibly can."

Pune: Despite Pune District Collector Jitendra Dudi's directive to immediately halt its two-wheeler aggregator services until the required government and Regional Transport Office (RTO) licences are obtained, Rapido continued ferrying passengers in parts of the city on Friday night.
A ground check by The Free Press Journal after Dandiya celebrations found bike taxi riders accepting passengers.
Speaking to The Free Press Journal on condition of anonymity, one Rapido rider said, "I work at a company and take Rapido rides after my working hours, as it helps me financially. I know there is no government licence yet and the collector has ordered the service to be halted. But when the app provides us with an opportunity to earn extra money and meet our daily expenses, it helps a lot."
He added, "Whenever the app stops the service, I will also stop. Until then, it helps me cover my expenses and supports me financially. I take three to four rides a day, which brings me around Rs800."
The collector had warned that legal action would follow if the company continued operating without authorisation.
Dudi issued the directive during a meeting with cab and autorickshaw aggregators after drivers complained of alleged violations of existing regulations. He clarified that the meeting was intended to enforce existing rules rather than announce a new policy.
FIR registered under seven legal provisions
According to the First Information Report (FIR) registered at Vishrantwadi Police Station on Oct 16, 2026, at 11.11 pm, police registered a case against Rapido's operator, identified in the document as Roppen Transportation Services Private Limited, over allegations of operating bike taxis without the required authorisation.
The FIR lists Section 318(3) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, along with Sections 66, 93, 192A, 193 and 197 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and Section 66(3) of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Prasad Govind Shukre, a Motor Vehicle Inspector at the Pune Regional Transport Office, filed the complaint. The FIR states that the alleged offence occurred between 6.50 pm and 8 pm on Oct 16 in the Kamshet-Yewalewadi area of Pune, as recorded in the complaint.
According to the complaint, the company allegedly facilitated passenger transport through its app using motorcycles without the required permits or authorisation. The complaint refers to provisions governing the use of vehicles without permits and other alleged violations under motor vehicle regulations. Inspector Sampatrao Sahebrao Raut has been assigned to investigate the case.

From homes and hotels to churches, theaters, and cemeteries, there's no shortage of supposedly haunted places across the US.
Nearly every state has its own eerie legends — stories of restless spirits, mysterious footsteps in empty hallways, and unexplained flickering lights that locals swear attest to these spots being haunted.
Many of these sites are also steeped in history, with tragic pasts or notorious events.
Business Insider examined local legends and historic sites to determine the most reportedly haunted locations in every state, with many having reported ghost sightings, strange occurrences, or bloody histories.
Whether you believe in ghosts or just love a good scare, these haunted places across the US have earned spooky reputations.
Madeline Diamond contributed to an earlier version of this story.
ALABAMA: Sloss Furnaces, Birmingham
The Sloss Furnaces are now a historic national landmark, but in the late 19th century, they produced iron, which was then turned into steel.
James "Slag" Wormwood was the boss at the furnaces, and it's said that he subjected his employees to some inhumane working conditions.
Labor laws didn't exist at the time, and furnace temperatures often exceeded 100 degrees. A total of 47 men died with Wormwood as their boss, and even Wormwood himself lost his life in the furnaces when he slipped and fell into the iron ore, causing his body to melt, Travel South USA reported.
Wormwood and his workers are believed to haunt the furnaces to this day.
ALASKA: Kennecott
Kennecott is a remote Alaskan town that's been mostly abandoned since 1950.
The town was a hub for copper mining from 1911 to 1938, but after the area's copper supply was diminished, Kennecott's population dwindled.
Today, many rickety wooden buildings still stand in Kennecott, and many people believe that they are haunted by former miners and railroad workers, the Anchorage Daily News reported.
ARIZONA: Lost Dutchman State Park, Apache Junction
The Lost Dutchman gold mine is believed to be situated in a state park in Apache Junction, Arizona, although its exact location is unclear.
The park is said to be haunted by the spirits of people who died over the years searching for the mine, the Phoenix New Times reported.
ARKANSAS: Crescent Hotel, Eureka Springs
The Crescent Hotel in Eureka Springs, Arkansas, takes pride in its reputation as a haunted hotel.
Guests can join ghost tours and catch a glimpse of several ghosts who reportedly haunt the property, including one known as "the girl in the mist."
CALIFORNIA: Bodie
According to the California Department of Parks and Recreation, Bodie, California, is a ghost town turned state park that offers a taste of life during the gold rush of the late 1800s.
Many homes and other buildings are still standing in the town today. Some people believe that the town is haunted by former residents, Legends of America reported.
COLORADO: St. Elmo
St. Elmo, Colorado, was a thriving mining town in the late 1800s, though it was abandoned as soon as the area's mines shut down, History Colorado reported.
The ghost town has been well-maintained, allowing visitors to get a sense of life in the late 19th century. They might even catch a glimpse of ghosts of former residents.
There's a particularly popular ghost story about Annabelle Stark, a woman from St. Elmo who is said to have continued living there even after the town was entirely abandoned.
CONNECTICUT: Old Newgate Prison, East Granby
Connecticut History reported that the Old Newgate Prison was the first prison in the state of Connecticut, operating from 1773 to 1827. Most notably, it once held prisoners of war during the Revolutionary War.
Many people believe that the site is haunted by soldiers and prisoners who died while trying to escape from the prison.
DELAWARE: Fort Delaware, Delaware City
Fort Delaware is situated on its own island, accessible only by ferry. It was built as a Union fortress during the Civil War and was later used as a prison for Confederate soldiers.
Many prisoners died while held captive, and their ghosts are believed to haunt the property today, the Delaware News Journal reported.
Paranormal tours are currently being offered on Friday and Saturday nights, but visitors need to make a reservation.
FLORIDA: Old St. Johns County Jail, St. Augustine
The Old St. Johns County Jail no longer houses inmates, although the spirits of many of St. Augustine's violent criminals reportedly still haunt the historic jail.
The jail is now a museum, and visitors can go on nighttime "Old Jail After Dark" tours to try to spot the ghosts for themselves.
GEORGIA: Lucas Theatre, Savannah
Aside from being a beautiful Southern city with tons of history, Savannah, Georgia, is also said to be haunted.
The Lucas Theatre is just one of the city's haunted locales.
According to a local tour company, visitors to the historic theater have reported ghost sightings, including shadowy figures and sounds of applause, even when there's no one around.
HAWAII: 'Iolani Palace, Honolulu
The 'Iolani Palace was once home to Hawaii's royalty, although today it serves as a museum of Hawaiian history.
Queen Lili'uokalani and other Hawaiian royals are said to haunt the palace. One room in the museum is notorious for supernatural activity — visitors have reported hearing mysterious music and chanting, Honolulu Magazine reported.
IDAHO: Old Idaho Penitentiary, Boise
According to the Idaho State Historical Society, the Old Idaho Penitentiary housed some of the area's most dangerous criminals for over 100 years until it closed in 1973.
Visitors can now explore the expansive property in Boise, including jail cells that are reportedly haunted by former inmates.
ILLINOIS: Congress Plaza Hotel, Chicago
The Congress Plaza Hotel in Chicago, Illinois, has almost too many ghost stories to count. The hotel was built for the World's Fair in 1893, and there have been tales of paranormal activity ever since.
For example, the serial killer H.H. Holmes is said to have lured his victims to the hotel. Hotel guests have also reported seeing the ghosts of Al Capone and a ghost called Peg Leg Johnny around the property, Choose Chicago reported.
And if all that isn't spooky enough, the hotel is reportedly the inspiration behind Stephen King's short story, "1408."
INDIANA: Indiana Medical History Museum, Indianapolis
The Indiana Medical History Museum is situated in the oldest surviving pathology building in the United States. It is also said to be haunted by the spirits of former patients of Central State Hospital.
The museum, located in Indianapolis, is home to recreations of amphitheaters and laboratories that were once used by the hospital, which treated a variety of different mental-health-related illnesses from 1848 until the late 1990s, according to the museum.
IOWA: Villisca Ax Murder House, Villisca, Iowa
According to the house's official website, six members of the Moore family, plus two houseguests, were brutally killed by an ax murderer who was never identified on June 10, 1912. Their restless spirits are said to still haunt the grounds.
Guests can visit the house during the daytime, but to experience it in its full creepiness, you can make a reservation to spend the night.
KANSAS: Stull Cemetery, Stull
A haunted cemetery? No surprise there. However, Stull Cemetery in Kansas is known to be particularly spooky.
The cemetery is located in a tiny, nearly abandoned town outside of Lawrence. It has reportedly been the site of witchcraft and other supernatural activity over the years.
KENTUCKY: Waverly Hills Sanatorium, Louisville
The Waverly Hills Sanatorium started as a one-room schoolhouse in the late 1800s. The Board of Tuberculosis Hospital later purchased the land and built the sanatorium, which opened in 1910 as a small quarantine for tuberculosis patients.
The large building that now stands abandoned was built in 1926 to meet the need for a larger facility; the sanatorium could house over 400 patients, according to its website.
Waverly Hills was its own community, complete with a ZIP code, post office, and water treatment facility. Everyone in the sanatorium — patients, nurses, doctors — was cut off from the outside world. It closed in 1961 after the discovery of an antibiotic that cured tuberculosis.
However, it's believed that some patients never left and still haunt the grounds. Visitors can participate in ghost tours on the hospital grounds during the fall season.
LOUISIANA: St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, New Orleans
One of the most notable people buried at the St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans is Marie Laveau, a voodoo priestess who died in 1881, according to the New Orleans Historical Society.
Given her unique profession, many people believe Laveau's spirit remains present in the cemetery to this day.
Atlas Obscura reported that actor Nicolas Cage bought a burial tomb in the cemetery, so there's no telling about the cemetery's haunted future.
MAINE: Wood Island Lighthouse, Saco
The Wood Island Lighthouse is one of the many beautiful lighthouses on Maine's coastline. It differs, however, in that it's said to be haunted.
In fact, the television show "Ghost Hunters" visited the lighthouse in 2006 to investigate paranormal activity in the area, according to the official Wood Island Lighthouse website.
MARYLAND: Antietam National Battlefield, Washington County
Many people visit the Antietam National Battlefield in Washington County, Maryland, to learn about the history of the Civil War.
However, others visit to explore the supernatural activity at the site of the bloodiest battle of the Civil War.
Given the site's history, it's understandable why many people believe the battlefield is full of spirits. The area is said to be haunted by the ghosts of the soldiers who were killed there in 1862, the Akron Beacon Journal reported.
MASSACHUSETTS: The Mount, Lenox
The Mount in Lenox, Massachusetts, is a historic estate that was once home to the writer Edith Wharton. Aside from being a beautifully restored architectural masterpiece, the estate also has a haunted history.
When she was alive, Wharton herself often wrote about ghosts, so it's no surprise that her former home may be haunted.
Visitors can see for themselves on one of the estate's ghost tours, both online and, hopefully, in person later this season.
MICHIGAN: Detroit Masonic Temple, Detroit
From cold spots and doors slamming to odd shadows, the Detroit Masonic Temple reportedly has it all.
One ghost in particular said to haunt the 1,037-room building is that of George D. Mason, one of its architects, according to the Detroit Historical Society.
However, while legend goes that Mason, distraught over financial losses and the death of his wife, died by suicide by jumping off the top of the 210-foot building, the historical society says this isn't true.
"While the story makes for a great Halloween horror tale, it is not true," the Detroit Historical Society states on its website. "George Mason died in 1948 at 91 years old in his home in the Wilshire Apartment building on Grand Boulevard."
MINNESOTA: Fitzgerald Theater, St. Paul
The Fitzgerald Theater in St. Paul, Minnesota, is the oldest surviving theater in the city, and its rich history is accompanied by some ghost stories.
The theater is perhaps best known for its production of Garrison Keillor's variety show, "A Prairie Home Companion," which began in 1974.
Over the years, visitors to the theater have reported sightings of a ghost named Ben, who apparently used to work on the site as a stagehand, Minnesota Haunted Houses reported.
MISSISSIPPI: King's Tavern, Natchez
King's Tavern in Natchez, Mississippi, now operates as a cooking school where Chef Regina Charboneau hosts cooking classes and dinners, although it once had many stories to accompany its hundreds of years of history, including some that involve ghosts.
According to one blog, the ghost of the mistress of the tavern's first owner — who is said to have been murdered there — reportedly haunted the restaurant.
MISSOURI: Governor's Mansion, Jefferson City
The Governor's Mansion in Jefferson City, Missouri, is one of the state's most beautiful historic buildings, dating back to 1871.
In 1882, the governor's family experienced a tragedy when their 9-year-old daughter, Carrie, died from diphtheria.
Years later, a construction worker who was renovating the mansion reported seeing a young girl playing in the attic, the News Tribune reported in 2014.
Some people believe that he saw the ghost of Carrie.
MONTANA: Daly Mansion, Hamilton
Now a popular wedding and event venue, the Daly Mansion has a reportedly haunted history.
Over the years, the staff at the estate have reported occurrences of paranormal activity, including a gold picture frame that is frequently found removed from the wall and placed on the ground, the Billings Gazette reported.
NEBRASKA: Ball Cemetery, Springfield
With gravestones in Ball Cemetery dating back to the late 1860s, this historic cemetery is one of the oldest in the state.
Multiple spirits have reportedly been sighted here, including a tall, angry man who has been seen kicking over gravestones and a woman named Mary Mumford, who is said to tug at visitors' clothes, according to Nebraska Haunted Houses.
NEVADA: Bowers Mansion, Washoe City
The Bowers Mansion is a stately home in Washoe City, Nevada, with a spooky history.
The home once belonged to local millionaires Eilley and Sandy Bowers, and, as legend has it, after Sandy died, his wife held seances to try to conjure his spirit, Nevada Ghost Towns and Beyond reported.
It's unclear whether she ever managed to reach her husband, although visitors report seeing mysterious figures around the property to this day.
NEW HAMPSHIRE: Alton Town Hall, Alton
This historic government building in Alton, New Hampshire, is not only a beautiful landmark but also the site of reported paranormal activity, as New Hampshire Magazine reported in 2020.
Locals have reported seeing furniture that moves, doors that open and close on their own, and hearing mysterious voices.
NEW JERSEY: Pine Barrens
The Pine Barrens in New Jersey are one of the state's spookiest locations.
Condé Nast Traveler reported that the forest spans seven counties and is home to numerous ghost towns.
During the colonial era, the area was bustling with sawmills, paper mills, and towns to accompany them; however, these industries were all abandoned when coal was discovered in Pennsylvania.
The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that it's also said to be home to the infamous Jersey Devil, a beast that the Pinelands Preservation Alliance describes as "a kangaroo-like creature with the face of a horse, the head of a dog, bat-like wings, horns, and a tail."
NEW MEXICO: The Luna Mansion, Los Lunas
The Luna Mansion, a historic 19th-century estate near Albuquerque, New Mexico, operated as a restaurant until closing in 2020. In 2026, the property began preparing to reopen as an event venue under new ownership, with a haunted-house experience planned for October, according to a local news website.
When the site operated as a restaurant, visitors reported seeing ghosts from the estate's past, including a woman named Josefina, who was the home's interior decorator.
Legends of America reported that one sighting included a rocking chair — placed under her portrait — rocking without anyone in it.
"I hear things," general manager Farid Himeur told KOAT in 2017. "I see things that aren't supposed to happen."
NEW YORK: Letchworth Village, Thiells
Letchworth Village is a former psychiatric hospital that has fallen into a state of complete disrepair, Hudson Valley Magazine reported in 2020.
Located in Thiells, New York, the campus spans 2,000 acres and features various medical buildings, dormitories, and a synagogue.
Like many hospitals and institutions, Letchworth Village is allegedly haunted by the spirits of former patients, and was even featured on the Travel Channel's popular series "Ghost Adventures."
NORTH CAROLINA: Cape Hatteras Lighthouse, Hatteras Island
The Cape Hatteras lighthouse is an iconic fixture on the North Carolina coastline, said to be haunted by a woman named Theodosia Burr, according to a local travel website.
Burr, the daughter of Founding Father Aaron Burr and a character mentioned in the hit musical "Hamilton," was killed in a shipwreck in 1812.
She is believed to haunt the lighthouse and the surrounding shore.
The lighthouse is closed for climbing through at least the end of 2026, with plans to potentially reopen in the summer of 2027.
NORTH DAKOTA: Fort Abraham Lincoln, Mandan
Fort Abraham Lincoln's history dates back to 1872.
George Armstrong Custer, a lieutenant colonel in the Union Army during the Civil War, built the fort but died just four years after its completion.
People who visit the fort today have reported seeing the ghost of Custer and his wife on the property, local news station KX News.
OHIO: Moonville Tunnel, Vinton County
Now overgrown and covered in graffiti, the Moonville Tunnel is a favorite spot among urban explorers and ghost hunters in Ohio.
The tunnel was once used by the local railroad, although it has been in disrepair for years. According to a local legend, some of the ghosts that haunt the tunnel include an old engineer and a railway brakeman.
OKLAHOMA: The Skirvin Hotel, Oklahoma City
The unique architecture of the Skirvin Hilton Hotel, which dates back to 1911, is striking. The hotel reportedly even offered a private room where guests could drink alcohol during Prohibition, Historic Hotels of America reported.
Opposing NBA teams often stay at the Skirvin Hilton Hotel when they visit the city to play the Oklahoma City Thunder. Over the years, many players have reported ghost sightings, specifically of a woman named Effie who died at the hotel, The New York Times reported.
OREGON: The Shanghai Tunnels, Portland
Travel Portland reported that the Shanghai Tunnels in Portland get their name from the practice of kidnapping and selling men as workers on ships headed to East Asia.
Restless, agitated spirits of men who were drugged and trafficked in the city's ports during the early 19th century are said to haunt the underground tunnels through which they were reportedly sold.
Legend has it that the local saloons had entrances to the tunnels, enabling swindlers to prey on unsuspecting patrons and bring them directly underground before they even knew what was happening.
Visitors can take walking tours to learn more about the dark history of the tunnels.
PENNSYLVANIA: Eastern State Penitentiary, Philadelphia
During its heyday, Eastern State Penitentiary was one of the most expensive and well-known prisons in the world. According to the official Eastern State Penitentiary website, it was built in 1829 and housed notable criminals, including Al Capone and the bank robber known as "Slick Willie."
Up until overcrowding became a problem in 1913, prisoners were kept in complete solitude at all times. Even when prisoners left their cell, a guard would cover their heads so they couldn't see and no one could see them.
Today, the decaying penitentiary offers ghost tours and a museum. Condé Nast Traveler reported that shadowy figures, laughter, and footsteps have all been reported as paranormal activity within the prison walls.
RHODE ISLAND: The Breakers, Newport
The Breakers Mansion is a popular museum for tourists in Newport, Rhode Island, but is said to have paranormal activity.
Alice Vanderbilt, the matriarch of the wealthy Vanderbilt family in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, lived in the mansion for many years after her husband, Cornelius, died.
Her ghost is said to still roam the giant home, Nostalgia Providence reported.
SOUTH CAROLINA: Poinsett Bridge, Greenville
Besides bearing the distinction of South Carolina's oldest bridge, Poinsett is also believed by many to be a particularly spooky spot, Condé Nast Traveler reported.
The bridge, which was built entirely out of stone in 1820, is rumored to be haunted by multiple ghosts.
There's the story of the mason who died while building the bridge; his body is said to be entombed inside it. There's also the story of a man who died here in a car accident in the '50s and an enslaved person who was lynched near the bridge.
SOUTH DAKOTA: The Historic Bullock Hotel, Deadwood
The Bullock Hotel in Deadwood, South Dakota, is reportedly haunted by Deadwood's first Sheriff, Seth Bullock.
According to the hotel's website, guests and staff have seen items "inexplicably moved by unseen hands," and showers turn on out of nowhere.
TENNESSEE: The Orpheum Theatre, Memphis
The Orpheum Theatre in Memphis has survived bankruptcies, a fire, and a threat of demolition since it opened in 1928, according to the theater's website.
Furnished with 2,000-pound chandeliers and gold leafing, its stunning interior seats 2,000 people, but there's also plenty of room for spirits.
A little girl named Mary is one of six ghosts that have been spotted in the theater, according to The Tennessee State Museum. Performers onstage have spotted her in the audience of their shows, and theatergoers have seen her dancing in the lobby.
TEXAS: The Alamo, San Antonio
The Alamo is one of the most iconic monuments in the US.
Given its extensive history, it's understandable why many people believe the site is haunted.
History buffs interested in paranormal activity can go on ghost tours of the site in hopes of catching a glimpse of the spirits of those who died there during the 1836 Battle of the Alamo.
UTAH: Fort Douglas Military Museum, Salt Lake City
The Fort Douglas Military Museum was formerly known simply as Fort Douglas. Located near the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, the military fort dates back to 1862.
The Daily Utah Chronicle reported in 2014 that visitors to the museum spoke of sightings of a ghost named Clem, a soldier who died at the fort.
Reports of paranormal activity include seeing a figure in Civil War military garb and people feeling something — or someone — breathing down their necks.
The museum is temporarily closed but will reopen on November 14th.
VERMONT: Emily's Bridge, Stowe
New England is known for its beautiful covered bridges.
However, Emily's Bridge in Stowe, Vermont, is said to be haunted.
According to the Vermont Historical Society, local legend has it that sometime between 1849 and 1949, a young woman named Emily killed herself on the bridge after she was jilted by her lover.
Local lore holds that her spirit has haunted the area ever since, although the historical society claims there is no evidence to suggest that anyone died at the site.
VIRGINIA: Oak Grove Cemetery, Lexington
This cemetery was originally named after Stonewall Jackson, the Confederate general who is buried on the site, but was renamed to Oak Grove Cemetery in 2020.
Located in Lexington, Virginia, the cemetery is said to be haunted by Jackson and other Civil War soldiers, according to the official Visit Virginia website.
WASHINGTON: Northern State Mental Hospital, Sedro-Woolley
Located in northern Washington, this former hospital was once a fully self-sustaining psychiatric facility.
The Northern State Mental Hospital operated from 1912 to 1976, and although it has been closed for many years, many of its buildings still stand today.
It's said that thousands of patients may have died here, and a graveyard behind the old gymnasium has many unmarked graves.
However, the Seattle Times reported in 2023 that two never-before-released death registers contain information on patients who died at Northern State Hospital between 1911 and 1963.
Some of the hospital's expansive property now operates as a recreational area, although it's said to be haunted by former patients.
WEST VIRGINIA: Trans-Allegheny Lunatic Asylum, Weston
Originally built as a place of healing, the Trans-Allegheny Lunatic Asylum welcomed its first patients in 1864.
According to the hospital's official website, it hit its peak in 1950 when the psychiatric hospital was home to 2,400 patients, many of whom endured lobotomies and electroshock therapy.
Mental health reforms and the building's poor condition led to the hospital's closure in 1994. However, many patients died there during the facility's 130 years of operation. Some are believed to haunt the building's halls, which is why it attracts visitors and ghost hunters.
Visitors interested in exploring paranormal activity can join ghost tours on the site.
WISCONSIN: The Pfister Hotel, Milwaukee
The Pfister Hotel is popular among professional athletes who visit Milwaukee for games, although the hotel's haunted history has made many guests skeptical about staying there.
Guests have reported hearing mysterious knocking sounds and voices.
The Los Angeles Times reported in 2005 that Adrián Beltré of the Los Angeles Dodgers said he couldn't sleep during his stay at the Pfister because of the strange noises.
WYOMING: The Historic Occidental Hotel, Buffalo
A stay at the Historic Occidental Hotel in Buffalo, Wyoming, is like taking a step back in time to the Old West.
Famous figures from the era, like Butch Cassidy, Calamity Jane, Buffalo Bill, and even President Theodore Roosevelt, have visited the hotel over the years.
Given the hotel's rich history, it's no surprise that some people believe it is haunted by former guests, and it was even featured on the Travel Channel's "Dead Files."

They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
- Published
Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum.
"It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia.
Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face.
US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement.
In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account.
The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours.
"At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere."
Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home.
"I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?"
Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees.
Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia.
One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison.
"We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee.
And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere.
Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025.
"Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC.
Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data.
Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns.
Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds.
Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries.
Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face.
"I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me."
He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt.
"I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'".
Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad.
"Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life."
The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them."
The asylum clampdown comes as repression inside Russia has reached "an unprecedented level", according to Nobel Prize-winning Russian human rights group Memorial. Their list of political prisoners grew from 803 to 1,265 during 2025, a record increase.
The Russian Embassy in London did not respond to a request for comment.
Anti-war activist Mikhail says he and his wife Dasha are awaiting deportation from Finland "any day". Their names have been changed to protect their identity, as Mikhail fears for relatives back home.
Russian authorities blocked his social media accounts over anti-war posts, and police visited his mother and accused him of spreading "fake information".
Dasha is a Jehovah's Witness, an organisation banned as "extremist" in Russia. The couple provided Finnish authorities with evidence, seen by the BBC, including a video of Russian police telling his mother that more than 300 posts had violated Russian law. A single post can result in a long prison sentence.
The Finnish Immigration Service has rejected their asylum request five times, deciding there is "no reasonable basis to believe" the couple would face serious rights violations if returned.
"We're sitting here and someone could knock on our door at any moment, take us to the Russian border and simply hand us over to Russian officers," says Mikhail. "We fear for our lives!"
"We came to Finland for help, and they're refusing us," he adds. "My wife cries constantly."
Amnesty International, which is supporting the couple, says they could face a "real risk" of detention, prosecution, imprisonment and torture if returned.
The Finnish Immigration Service said all asylum decisions were based on international refugee law standards, and the share of Russian citizens receiving asylum was in line with EU averages.
For Mikhail and Dasha, the threat of deportation comes as more Russians may be considering leaving.
There are rumours that Vladimir Putin may announce a new wave of mobilisation to boost the ranks of his army in Ukraine, which the Kremlin denies. The last mobilisation in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee, many to ex-Soviet states such as Armenia and Georgia.
Anastasia Burakova's organisation says requests for help from Russians wanting to leave rose tenfold in August compared with May. For those now looking to escape, the question is whether the West will offer them refuge — or send them back.

Leap seconds have driven a raging debate in the metrological community for three decades. Now, that argument has been put to rest: The leap second is officially dead.
Doing away with an obscure metric the average person has been blissfully unaware of may seem like a novelty, but killing the leap second has major ramifications for technology you rely on every day. It also helps stave off what could’ve been a dangerous moment in time: The possibility of the world’s first negative leap second.
The International Bureau of Weights and Measurements (known by its French acronym BIPM) on Thursday said that in May 2027, it would stop issuing leap seconds to adjust what’s known as Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), 32 of which have been added since 1972.
The world implemented the leap second in 1972 due to a growing gap between time measured with atomic clocks and time based on the Earth’s rotation. The reason for the discrepancy? The latter is slowing down due in large part to tidal friction caused by the moon and Earth’s rotation not lining up. The molten core of the Earth as well as oceans and the atmosphere also affect the spin rate.
Leap seconds are a way to keep atomic-clock-driven UTC in line with astronomically kept Universal Time (UT1). Think of it like adding a little extra track for a train to keep running exactly parallel with another one. Rather than happening on a set interval—like a leap year—BIPM uses the average of hundreds of atomic clocks around the world and compares their time calculations to astronomical time to determine when a leap second is necessary. The most recent one was added in 2016.
Of course, adding track is no small effort, and it may seem like a lot of hassle for a measly second. But UTC is vital for all sorts of technology given the number of APIs and databases that rely on it. Introducing a leap second helped keep UTC and UT1 aligned, but it also wrought havoc on various systems running on UTC and forced companies to figure out how to deal with them when they were added every few years.
A number of tech companies like Google and Meta use “a ‘smear’ method of dealing with leap seconds,” Judah Levine, a fellow at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, writes in an email. In essence, they spread a leap second out over the course of a day or so in tiny increments. But leap seconds have thrown off other systems; the airline Qantas, for example, saw its booking system borked by a leap second in 2012.
Adding a leap second is hard enough as it is. But the odds of having to add a negative leap second have been rising in part because the Earth has picked up rotational speed in recent years due to climate change. (There’s always a climate angle.) Melting ice has caused a shift in the planet’s gravity so extreme that a negative leap second may have been required as soon as 2029, according to a 2024 Nature study. Part of the calculus of ditching the leap second altogether was that going negative isn’t worth the risk.
“There are continuing problems with positive leap seconds even after 50 years, and the concern was that the negative leap second would be much more serious because its effects had never been tested,” Levine says.
BIPM time department director Patrizia Tavella confirmed those concerns in an email to WIRED. “The probability of a negative leap second convinced us [to] set the application date in 2027,” she wrote, adding that there was added urgency following tests by an industry standards group that “showed several failures with a negative leap.”
Tavella says the group is waiting until May 20, 2027 to implement it because it's the anniversary of 1875 signing of the Metre Convention, creating BIPM, as well as Metrology Day. In other words, it’s the perfect time to mark the passing of time—or more accurately, the lack thereof.
The death of the leap second makes life easier for everyone now. “The nice fact is that we have nothing to do!” Tavella says. “Just continue to accumulate second[s] and ‘normal’ minutes of 60 seconds.”
Levine concurs, writing that “life will have one less hassle.”
But kicking the can on adding leap seconds doesn’t mean atomic time and astronomical time won’t continue to drift apart. That’s why BIPM also agreed to create a leap hour. Given how long it takes leap seconds to add up, a leap hour is millennia away. (There are, after all, 3,600 seconds in an hour.)
“We do not speak of leap hour yet,” Tavella says. “If systems rely on UTC, they have nothing to do. If they rely on UT1, they have to be able to use the information UT1-UTC which, in [the] future, will be larger than 1 second.”
In other words, not our problem, and good luck to future generations!

NEW DELHI: US President Donald Trump has waived key Russia-related sanctions and tariffs just days before they were due to take effect, offering potential relief to major buyers of Russian oil, including India and China. In an executive order issued late on Friday, Trump said it was in the US “national interests” to withhold some of the sanctions. The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, signed by Trump last month, authorized him to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries importing Russian oil, with the aim of curbing Moscow’s economic might amid its war with Ukraine. The measures were due to take effect on 18 October. The move comes as India and the US negotiate a trade deal that is said to be in its final stages, while crude oil prices remain above $100 a barrel amid the prolonged conflict in West Asia. The price surge poses a risk to India, which imports about 90% of its annual oil requirement, with Russia accounting for a substantial share of those supplies. Earlier this month, Trump announced a decision to buy diesel from Moscow, aimed at curbing rising prices in the US. The waiver could ease uncertainty around the India-US trade negotiations, as New Delhi seeks tariff concessions that give its exporters an advantage over competitors in the US market. On Thursday, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said the first phase of the trade deal had been finalized and was being legally drafted. He expressed confidence that the agreement would be concluded and operationalised soon, but said India needed to secure an export advantage over its competitors in the US market. The threat of US sanctions had introduced fresh uncertainty into the negotiations, leaving India unsure of the tariff concessions it could secure relative to competing countries that were not facing similar threats. On Friday, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman expressed hope that the proposed trade deal would be concluded at the earliest, in the interest of both bilateral and global trade. Earlier this week, external affairs minister S. Jaishankar said the two sides were ironing out differences and moving towards a “landing point” in negotiations. Separately, US ambassador to India Sergio Gor said earlier this week that negotiations were moving at an “incredible pace” and that the “big items are done”. In February, the two countries agreed on a framework for the deal that reduced the punitive tariff on most Indian goods to 18% from 50%. The higher tariff had been imposed in August 2025. The US remains India’s largest export market, accounting for $87 billion in goods exports in the fiscal year ended March 2026. In the first half of the current fiscal year, Indian exports to the US rose 11% from a year earlier to $50.8 billion, according to data from commerce ministry. India is the second-largest importer of Russian oil after China, with Russian supplies forming a mainstay of its crude imports. In the April-July period, Russian oil supplies were valued at $28.33 billion, or about 45% of India’s total oil imports of $63.33 billion, according to commerce ministry data. Although the tariff threat did not significantly affect Russian oil supplies, as refiners struggled to replace those barrels immediately, the waiver could ease supply constraints and moderate prices. This comes amid persistent tensions in West Asia involving the US and Iran, as well as Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi militia. These tensions have disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. For India, which relies heavily on imported crude, uncertainty over supplies and price volatility can have economy-wide consequences. Supply disruptions and geopolitical risks keep prices elevated, increasing costs for major importers such as India. Global benchmark Brent crude traded at $72 a barrel in February, before the US-Iran war erupted, peaking at $130 a barrel in April. Prices are currently at $109.9 a barrel. The country’s crude oil import bill stood at around $123 billion in fiscal year 2026 (FY26), according to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell. A sustained increase of $1 a barrel is estimated to raise the annual bill by ₹18,000 crore, estimates from Bank of Baroda show. India has already imported crude worth $74.85 billion in the first five months of the current fiscal year, equivalent to about 48% of its total import bill for FY26, Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell data showed. A higher import bill could add to inflationary pressures if the increased costs are passed on to downstream products and consumers. It could also weigh on economic growth and widen pressure on the current account. India’s retail inflation rose to a 23-month high of 5.54% in September. In October, the Reserve Bank of India raised its inflation projection for FY27 to 5.2%, from 5% in August, citing volatility in international oil prices, persistent supply-side pressures stemming from deficient south-west monsoon rainfall. All Blacks thump Wallabies in Sydney on the back of brilliant first half
SYDNEY, Oct 17 : The All Blacks rode a first-half try blitz to a 43-21 victory over the Wallabies at Stadium Australia on Saturday, extending their win streak over their trans-Tasman-Sea rivals to 13 matches.
With the Bledisloe Cup already safely in the cupboard for a 24th year after last week's 50-19 win in Auckland, New Zealand exploded out of the blocks and crushed all thoughts of an upset with six tries before the break.
Despite losing Jordie Barrett to a calf injury before kickoff and another centre in Quinn Tupaea early on with a concussion, the All Blacks overwhelmed the Wallabies with power, pace and precision in the opening 40 minutes.
"I'm really proud of the boys, the way we came out on that in that first half," said New Zealand captain Codie Taylor.
"It was a real challenge for us this week to make sure that we backed up a really good performance from last week, and I thought we were awesome in that first 40."
Australia showed some flashes of backline brilliance, particularly in the second half, but struggled to get hold of the ball for prolonged periods and were unable to match the accuracy or clinical finishing of the All Blacks.
In a whirlwind of offloads, winger Josh Moorby, fullback Beauden Barrett, flanker Peter Lakai and replacement back Rieko Ioane all crossed in the first 26 minutes to give the visitors a quick-fire 22-0 lead.
Wallabies flyhalf Declan Meredith did well to get a pass away in the tackle just before the half-hour mark to send Jeremy Williams over for a try but the lock was sin-binned at the other end of the field two minutes later.
All Blacks number eight Wallace Sititi immediately made the extra man count with his team's fifth try and Beauden Barrett added a sixth, his second, off an intercept to send New Zealand into the break with a 36-7 lead.
Moorby faked out the defence for his second five-pointer within three minutes of the restart before the Wallabies finally finished off a backline move for fullback Tom Wright to go over.
Australia were looking stronger with their replacements on the pitch, and Meredith almost scored a try after a scything break up the middle, then saved a try at the other end.
A clever line dropout from Wright did result in a third Australia try in the 66th minute for replacement back Filipo Daugunu that delighted the majority of the crowd of 73,399.
New Zealand were reduced to 14 men after Samisoni Taukei'aho went off injured, and went down to 13 when debutant Chay Fihaki was shown a yellow card but managed to hold out the Wallabies for the last few minutes.
"I'm gutted," said Wallabies captain Harry Wilson. "When you give a team like the All Blacks a head start it's tough, and it's not good enough for this group.
"We've got to be a lot better. It's been a very disappointing series, and we're going to have to regroup."

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

The Tesla Roadster should go into production in 2028, but don't get your hopes up
I drive upside down on the boulevard of broken dreams.
Tesla dominated the headlines on Thursday thanks to a very cool stunt. In announcing the redesigned Roadster at its October 15 event, the electric car company put some jet fuel in the mix. After driving up a C-shaped ramp on a suction rig until it was upside-down, the Roadster floated to the ground on rocket boosters. We also learned that the new sports car is targeting a 2028 production window and that it will cost $250,000 to reserve the "Thrust" trim level with cold-gas thrusters. "We enter production in 2028," Musk said during the event. "Actually, for real."
If you're feeling a bit of deja vu, don't worry — you're firmly within your faculties. This is not the first time Tesla has announced the second-generation Roadster, and the company hasn't exactly drawn attention to that fact with this re-announced version. Still, the question on many minds is whether this is another paper launch for Tesla's embattled second-gen sports car.
The first Roadster was a milestone for Tesla in its early days. Released in 2008 and produced in very limited numbers, the car was ideated by one of Tesla's original founders, Martin Eberhard, before current CEO Elon Musk had bought Eberhard and his partner, Marc Tarpenning, out of the company. It was the idea of the Roadster which initially drew Musk to the fledgling startup in 2004 and prompted his initial investment in the company. He would go on to oversee the production of that sports car. Crammed inside the chassis of a Lotus Elise, it was truly impressive at the time to see a battery-powered vehicle able to reach 244 miles on a charge.
The redesigned Roadster was first unveiled in November 2017, promising to be the apex of Tesla's innovations in electric vehicle manufacturing. Musk called it "a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars." Targeted for a 2020 release, it was shown off alongside the Tesla Semi, a Class 8 electric semitruck which also stalled in production. In Feburary 2018, Musk promised a "SpaceX" package that would "include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around the car" and would "dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking and cornering."
Then the delays began. With Tesla still accepting deposits starting at $50,000 and extending up to $250,000, the initial 2020 production window came and went. In a July 2020 earnings call for Tesla, Musk said production would begin within the following year to 18 months. With the globe engulfed in a public health crisis, the delay wasn't the most shocking of developments. Ironically, Musk noted in an interview with Joe Rogan that same year that he wanted to build the Cybertruck first — a mission accomplished after years of that vehicle's own delays.
But a year and a half after the initial delay, there was no Roadster in sight. Musk delayed the car to 2022 in early 2021, but by the end of the year, that projection had slipped to 2023. The CEO announced further delays in 2023 and 2024.
And those years have been bizarre for Musk and Tesla, to say the least. The CEO has undergone a public transformation from public environmentalist to far-right political kingmaker, a period which culminated in a slash-and-burn of the Federal government as he headed up president Donald Trump's newly formed Department of Government Efficiency. By July 2025, The Lancet had published a study projecting the cuts could lead to more than 14 million deaths by 2030. Musk has disputed those numbers, but the reputational damage his stint in government caused spilled over to Tesla, leading to widespread global protests against the company. As Musk stepped down from DOGE in May 2025, dogged by allegations of substance abuse and family drama, the Roadster may not have been near the top of the billionaire's priority list.
By the time Tesla recommitted to releasing the Roadster this past April, many had given up hope that the sports car would ever make it to market. Tesla's failure to deliver the vehicle had long ago become pop-cultural joke fodder, and even Tesla owners such as YouTuber Marques Brownlee, who had interviewed Musk multiple times on his MKBHD channel, fretted on his Waveform podcast in September 2025, "Tesla has been sitting with my 50 grand for eight years and hasn't done anything with it." Another high-profile figure to complain about their Roadster reservations included Musk's erstwhile business partner and current rival Sam Altman of OpenAI.
It's worth noting that a launch event without a firm launch date isn't much of a launch. Even after Tesla's impressive October event, Musk and company will need to convince potential customers that putting down a deposit for the Roadster is a better investment than burning a pile of money with a Boring Company flamethrower.
