ED pastes summons at Pinarayi Vijayan's home in CMRL laundering case
The ED pasted a summons at Pinarayi Vijayan's residence for questioning in the CMRL case. The action drew CPI(M) criticism as Vijayan's legal challenge remains before the Supreme Court.
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Saturday, October 17, pasted a summons outside Kerala Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan's residence, asking him to appear for questioning on October 23 in a money laundering case linked to Cochin Mineral and Rutile Limited (CMRL), news agency Press Trust of India reported.
The summons was issued on Friday under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act after the ED registered a case based on a recent FIR filed by the state police. Vijayan, a former Kerala chief minister, has moved the Supreme Court against the Kerala High Court order that led to the FIR.
An ED official from Kochi visited Vijayan's residence near Bakery Junction in Thiruvananthapuram and pasted the two-page summons near the entrance. Officials told PTI that the step was taken to ensure Vijayan received the summons and appeared for questioning. He was not at home when the officials arrived.
Senior CPI(M) leader V Sivankutty later visited the residence and spoke to the staff. He criticised the ED's action, saying Vijayan was in Kannur to attend a party conference and was not absconding.
"He went from here to Alappuzha and then to Kannur. After completing a two-day meeting, he will return to Thiruvananthapuram. If they wanted, they could have served the notice directly to him," the former education minister said.
Sivankutty said an ED official had first visited the residence alone in the morning to serve the summons but returned after finding that Vijayan was not there. According to his account to PTI, the official later returned and asked the staff to witness the pasting of the summons, but they refused. ED officials then came back with police personnel and pasted it, he added.
"This is a case pending before the Supreme Court. Any action in the matter should be taken only after the Supreme Court delivers its verdict," Sivankutty said.
He also questioned the decision to paste the summons, saying the procedure was generally used when a person could not be traced. "Treating someone who had been the chief minister and now the Leader of the Opposition in this manner is completely unjust, anti-democratic and highly deplorable," he said.
Asked whether Vijayan would appear for questioning, Sivankutty said it was for the leader to decide.
The Kerala Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau registered two FIRs on October 12 against Vijayan and his family members, including his daughter Veena T and son-in-law and former minister P A Mohamed Riyas, in connection with the alleged CMRL bribery case.
The Kerala High Court had on October 9 directed the bureau to register a case based on a report submitted by the ED to the state police. The central agency sought the registration of a case based on material collected during its investigation and searches under the anti-money laundering law.
The ED has alleged that CMRL made fraudulent payments of Rs 2.78 crore to Veena's now-defunct company, Exalogic Solutions, in the guise of payments for IT consultancy services. The agency had earlier said it seized handwritten notes during searches linked to Veena and that these contained details of certain fund transfers to Dubai.
Vijayan approached the Supreme Court on Friday to challenge the High Court order directing the registration of an FIR. The ED has now summoned him for questioning on October 23 in the money laundering case linked to CMRL.

A female elephant died of anthrax in Periyanaickenpalayam forest range of the Coimbatore Forest Division, forcing the Forest and the Animal Husbandry Departments to step up vigil against the disease.
Forest Department staff spotted the carcass during a routine patrol within the Gopanari reserve forest of the Periyanaickenpalayam range around 4 p.m. on October 13.
According to the department, the carcass appeared to be about a day old. After reviewing the photographs of the carcass, veterinarians raised suspicion of a possible anthrax infection.
Blood smear sample collected from the carcass was sent to the Animal Husbandry Department on Wednesday. The department examined the sample and confirmed the presence of Bacillus anthracis, the bacterium that causes anthrax.
A senior official from the Forest Department said that the carcass was burnt on Thursday, without opening it, as per the protocol based on instructions from the Animal Husbandry Department.
Persons who handled the carcass wore personal protective equipment while carrying out the task.

Does the Premier League 'Big Six' still exist?
- Published
For years the Premier League has had a defined 'Big Six', comprised of Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur.
They were not just the sides who often dominated the top positions in the table, but also had the biggest fanbase, most financial clout and were usually the league's most successful sides.
But that has not been in the case in more recent seasons.
In the last couple of years Tottenham and Manchester United have found themselves fighting at the wrong end of the table, while teams like Aston Villa, Brentford and Brighton have been battling at the top.
Meanwhile, Manchester City - the top-flight's dominant side over the past decade - are facing a period of uncertainty after the club was recently found guilty of breaching financial rules over nine years.
The 'Big Six' remains in financial terms, with City, Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool, Spurs and Chelsea all inside the top 10 of highest revenue generating clubs in world football. , external
But is the era of the traditional 'Big Six' on the field at an end?
From Leicester fairytale to recent struggles
One of the most memorable stories of the Premier League era was Leicester City upsetting the odds to win the title in the 2015-16 season.
It captured the imagination of football fans everywhere, because it seemed so difficult for anyone outside the 'Big Six' to get even close to being champions.
But it seemed as though it was destined to be a one-off as, for the following three seasons, the 'Big Six' locked down the top positions once more.
Indeed, the gap between them and the rest was bigger than ever, with the smallest deficit between seventh and sixth place during those three seasons being eight points.
Between 2010-11 and 2018-19, the so-called 'Big Six' finished in those leading positions five times. They also finished in the top seven twice and top eight once.
But things changed after that.
In only one of the six seasons since have they all finished in the top six, with Aston Villa, Newcastle and Brighton in those places at some point.
Tottenham, in particular, have struggled and ended one place above the relegation zone in each of the past two campaigns and are currently second bottom on three points after failing to win any of their first six games.
This season, albeit early days, Manchester United are in 13th spot and Liverpool ninth. Since 2021-22, Chelsea and United have finished out of the top six twice, while Spurs have missed out three times - twice finishing 17th.
Five of the top six places have gone to clubs not in the traditional six in the past three years - the same as the previous eight years combined.
Other clubs have got richer and smarter
One reason for the end of their dominance as a collective is because other clubs have closed the financial gap.
Newcastle are an example following a £305m takeover led by the Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund in 2021.
They went from finishing 11th in 2021-22 to fourth in the following campaign and then fifth two seasons later.
Meanwhile, others, like Brighton, have leaned into data and smart recruitment to help them close the gap.
The Seagulls have an impressive record of buying promising talent for low prices before selling them on for significant fees.
In 2021 they signed 19-year-old Ecuador midfielder Moises Caicedo from Independiente del Valle for £4m and sold him two years later to Chelsea in a deal a worth £115m - a British record at the time. They also signed Marc Cucurella for £15m and sold him to Chelsea for £62m and brought in Alexis Mac Allister for £7m before selling him to Liverpool for a deal worth £55m.
"Our recruitment strategy and philosophy has been something that we've built on over a long period of time now," sporting director Mike Cave told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast.
"The data element of it gets a lot of attention because going back a few years it was quite novel in comparison to some other clubs.
"Really it's just a component of a bigger process that goes on. It's an important component, it helps us to identify talent from around the world in quite an efficient way which allows us to move quickly in what is a really competitive transfer market."

Lack of continuity proves costly
Since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013, Manchester United have struggled to get close to the success they enjoyed under the 26-year reign of the legendary Scot.
The 20-time top-flight champions have had a high turnover of head coaches in recent years in an effort to find the winning formula and since the start of the 2020-21 season they have had four different permanent managers.
But they are not alone in this high amount of chopping and changing - and not even the worst.
In the same period, Chelsea have had seven different people in charge on a permanent basis, while Tottenham have had six as they too have tried to find a way to challenge for trophies.
Meanwhile, Arsenal have shown patience can pay dividends by giving Mikel Arteta - appointed in 2019 - time to build a squad that resulted in the Gunners ending their 22-year wait for a Premier League title last season.
Isn't change always the way?
The 'Big Six' hasn't always been a thing in the Premier League, so an evolution of what it is and who they are was always likely to happen.
Indeed, when the league was first formed back in 1992 there was a 'Big Five' of Arsenal, Everton, Liverpool, Manchester United and Tottenham - clubs who were seen at the time as the ones with the biggest fanbase and financial power.
That evolved into a 'Big Two' during the late 1990s and early 2000s as Manchester United and Arsenal dominated, before expanding to a 'Big Four' as Chelsea and Liverpool regularly finished in the top four.
The 2010-11 season was the first time in English league history where the top six was made up of Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham.
It was then repeated in 2014-15, 2016-17, 2017-18 and 2018-19 as the 'Big Six' became known for what it is now.
Arguably the most open the top division has ever been was in the 1960s, when Burnley, Tottenham, Ipswich, Everton, Liverpool, Manchester United, Manchester City and Leeds all won league titles.
While it still feels that a Premier League winner is likely to come from one of the 'Big Six' sides, we are moving away from the concept of the top six being exclusively those sides - with it now being four years since they all finished in those positions.
Currently, Brighton, Brentford and Everton all find themselves in the top six and, while there is still a lot of football to be played this season, the top end of the division seems as open as it has ever been - and that can only be a good thing, right?

No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme.
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”.
 
“We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
 
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
 
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
 
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
 
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

Mumbai: Jayaswal Neco Industries Limited announced on 16 October 2026 that its standalone net profit for the quarter ended 30 September 2026 stood at ₹229.81 crore. This marks an increase of 118.59% compared to ₹105.13 crore recorded in the same quarter of the previous fiscal year.
Revenue from Operations
Total revenue from operations for the quarter rose to ₹2,194.46 crore, up 23.22% from ₹1,781 crore in the second quarter of the previous fiscal year. Total income for the quarter was ₹2,200.94 crore.
Expenses and Other Income
The company's total expenses for the quarter increased by 15.31% year-on-year, reaching ₹1,893.49 crore, compared to ₹1,642.05 crore in the corresponding period last year. Other income contributed ₹6.48 crore to the total income.
Earnings Per Share
Basic earnings per share (after exceptional items) for the quarter ended 30 September 2026 were ₹2.37, an increase from ₹1.08 in the same quarter last year.
Half-Year Performance
For the half-year ended 30 September 2026, the company's standalone net profit was ₹423.73 crore, a substantial rise from ₹198.15 crore in the corresponding half-year period of 2025. Revenue from operations for the half-year stood at ₹4,301.02 crore, up from ₹3,430.35 crore in the prior year's period.
Board Meeting
The Board of Directors approved the unaudited financial results at a meeting held on 16 October 2026. The meeting commenced at 12:30 P.M. and concluded at 2:40 P.M. on the same day.
ED Attachments
Properties of the company, valued at ₹307.58 crore, were provisionally attached by the Directorate of Enforcement in earlier years due to alleged misuse of a coal block. The PMLA Appellate Tribunal (AT) allowed the appeals and set aside the provisional attachments.
Legal Update
The Supreme Court, in an order dated 29 July 2026, disposed of the Special Leave Petition filed by the ED and directed it to approach the Delhi High Court. The CBI Court was instructed to keep the company's application for the release of frozen assets pending until the revision petition is decided by the DHC. The next hearing date is 28 October 2026.
Warrant Allotment
Subsequent to the quarter, on 1 October 2026, Jayaswal Neco Industries allotted 2,24,39,134 warrants, each priced at ₹89.13, aggregating to ₹200 crore, to Vibrant Enterprises. This preferential allotment followed the receipt of 25% of the consideration, amounting to ₹50 crore, during the quarter.

Two-time Paralympics silver-medallist shuttler Suhas Yathiraj started his Asian Para Games campaign with a resounding straight-game win over Bangladesh’s Joytu Dhar in the men’s singles SL4 Group E match here on Friday.
Suhas, an IAS officer who won silver medals in Tokyo and Paris Paralympics besides gold in the last Asian Para Games, defeated Dhar 21-8 21-11.
Also winning in the men’s singles SL4 category was Abhijeet Sakhuja, who beat Chinese Taipei’s En-chuan Yeh 21-17 21-12.
SL4 is a standing sport class in para badminton for athletes with lower-limb impairments.
Tokyo Olympics gold-medallist and Asian Para Games silver-medallist Krishna Nagar also made a positive start, defeating Chinese Taipei’s Jia-siang Ling 21-5 21-4 in his opening men’s singles SH6 Group C match.
Another Indian in SH6 category, Sivarajan Solaimalai, also won his first Group D match against Philippines’ John Cyrus Maclang 21-7 21-6.
Nagar and Solaimalai then paired up only to lose 10-21 12-21 against Chun yim Yong and Man Kai Chu of Hong Kong in men’s doubles SH6 match.
Nagar later teamed up with Nithya Sre Sumathy Sivan to get the better of Malaysia’s Nurzammiezatul B Mohamad and Muhammad Amin Bin Azmi 21-7 21-7 in mixed doubles SH6 group match.
SH6 is for players with short stature (such as achondroplasia or related genetic conditions).
In a mixed doubles SL3-SU5 Group A match, the Indian pair of Manisha Ramdass and Pramod Bhagat got the better of China’s Lichuan Xiong and Tongtong Li 21-16 19-21 21-16.
Manasi Joshi and Ruthick Raghupati, however, lost 15-21 4-21 to Khalimatus Sadiyah and Fredy Setiawan of Indonesia in their opening group match.
Mansi and her partner Thulasimathi Murugesan came from a game down to beat Indonesia’s Warining Rahayu and Qonitah Ikhtiar Syakuroh 21-10 21-12 in women’s doubles SL3-SU5 match.
The SL3-SU5 category combines standing lower-limb impairment (SL3) and standing upper-limb impairment (SU5) classes.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has proposed sweeping changes to the rules governing initial public offerings (IPOs) of small and medium enterprises (SMEs). In a consultation paper floated on October 14, the markets regulator has proposed changes to SME IPO norms, including regulations pertaining to valuation thresholds, profitability and shareholder exits. The regulator has invited public feedback on the paper till November 4. Citing its rationale, the regulator said that the paper has been formulated by its working group due to rapid increase in the funds raised through SME IPOs and the number of investors participating in such issues. Since launch in 2012, about 1,500 companies have opted to list on the SME platform and have raised ₹40,222 Cr. Startups like Zappfresh, DroneAcharya, TAC Infosec, Yudiz, are a few startups that have also taken this route to go public. In view of this, the regulator has proposed multiple changes, including lowering the minimum application threshold and removing mandatory underwriting and market-making requirements. Here’s a look at some of the key changes that have been proposed: The Market Cap-Based Listing Criteria Under the proposed framework, companies with a post-issue market capitalisation of ₹1,000 Cr or less can now list on the SME platform. Those valued in the range of ₹1,000 Cr to ₹4,000 Cr can also choose to list either on the SME platform or the main board. Companies valued over ₹4,000 Cr will have to list on the main board. SEBI has also proposed replacing the existing paid-up share capital criterion with post-issue market capitalisation to determine whether a company can list on the SME platform or the main board. Currently, companies with post-issue paid-up share capital of up to ₹25 Cr can opt for the SME platform, subject to other eligibility conditions. In addition, companies in the ₹1,000 Cr to ₹4,000 Cr band choosing the SME platform would also have to submit restated consolidated financial statements under Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) for the preceding three financial years, if they have not already adopted Ind AS. If an IPO applicant’s estimated market capitalisation crosses the applicable threshold during the IPO process, it would have to refile under the relevant listing framework. Minimum Profitability Requirements Raised SEBI has proposed mandating SME IPO applicants to report an average operating profit of at least ₹3 Cr annually over the preceding three financial years, based on restated consolidated financial statements. In contrast, the existing framework requires operating profit of at least ₹1 Cr in at least two of the preceding three fiscal years. However, the consultation paper refers to EBIT in its narrative, while existing provision mentioned EBITDA. This requires clarification. Companies that fail the proposed profitability test could still list on the SME platform through an alternative route. They would have to use the book-building process and allocate at least 75% of the net offer to qualified institutional buyers (QIBs). If the required allocation is not achieved, the entire subscription amount would have to be refunded. New Rules For Converted And Reorganised Businesses SEBI has proposed changing the eligibility rules for SMEs seeking an IPO after converting from a proprietorship, partnership or limited liability partnership (LLP). These draft rules also cover companies undergoing qualifying business reorganisations. Currently, such companies generally need to complete at least one full financial year before filing their draft IPO papers. Under the new proposal, they would need to complete four consecutive financial quarters from the date of conversion or qualifying reorganisation and submit at least one annual audited financial statement prepared after the change. The proposal also covers acquisitions, succession and schemes of arrangement, where more than 50% of the revenue comes from businesses that previously operated as proprietorships, partnerships or LLPs. In such cases, the earlier business' operating track record could be considered when assessing IPO eligibility. The ₹10 Cr Cap On GCP Allocation May Go SEBI has proposed removing the ₹10 Cr cap on the amount that the companies can allocate, from their IPO proceeds, towards general corporate purposes (GCP). Currently, GCP allocation cannot exceed 15% of the amount raised or ₹10 Cr, whichever is lower. Under the proposal, the 15% limit would remain, but the fixed ₹10 Cr ceiling would be removed, allowing companies raising larger amounts to allocate more funds to general business needs. SEBI Looks To Reshuffle OFS Rules SEBI has also proposed a dedicated offer-for-sale (OFS) framework with a one-year holding requirement, subject to specified exemptions. The draft framework also seeks to remove the existing 20% ceiling on the OFS component for qualified institutional buyers (QIBs). The Primary Market Advisory Committee (PMAC) went a step further and suggested removing the 50% cap on a QIB’s pre-issue holding as well. These exemptions, however, would not apply to companies using the alternative listing route after failing the proposed profitability test. Lock-In Periods To Be Revised SEBI has proposed revising the lock-in periods for promoters and other shareholders after an SME IPO. The draft changes include: Minimum promoters' contribution: The three-year lock-in on minimum promoter contribution would begin from the IPO allotment date. In contrast, the lock-in date is currently linked to the commencement of commercial production. Promoter holdings above the minimum contribution: The existing staggered lock-in would be replaced with a uniform one-year lock-in. Non-promoter pre-issue capital: The lock-in will reduce from the current one year to six months. Promoter group holdings: A separate one-year lock-in would apply from the IPO allotment date. Depositories could also mark shares that cannot be locked in electronically as non-transferable for the applicable period. SEBI to Further Trim Minimum IPO Application Threshold The markets regulator has proposed lowering the minimum application amount for SME IPOs to ₹1 Lakh from the existing requirement of more than ₹2 Lakh. Investors would have to apply for at least four lots worth a minimum of ₹25,000 each. The ₹2 Lakh minimum was introduced in March 2025 to limit participation by smaller retail investors. The consultation paper also proposes aligning investor categories and allocation rules more closely with the mainboard framework, including the introduction of the ‘Retail Individual Investor’ category. Under the regime, Issuers can also allocate up to 60% of the QIB portion to anchor investors in book-built issues. SEBI has also proposed increasing the minimum number of allottees from 200 to 500. Under the alternative route for companies failing the profitability test, up to 10% of the net offer would go to retail investors, up to 15% to NIIs and at least 75% to QIBs. SME Shares Could Be Traded In Lots Of One SEBI has proposed allowing investors to trade SME-listed shares in lots of one share, replacing the existing price-linked lot sizes. The consultation paper notes that around 5% of unique PAN-based shareholders held odd-lot shares, on average. The proposed change could make it easier for investors to sell their entire holdings, but it will not change the minimum IPO application amount. End For Mandatory Underwriting And Market-Making? SEBI has proposed removing mandatory underwriting and market-making requirements for SME IPOs to reduce listing costs. Currently, SME IPOs must be fully underwritten, with lead managers required to underwrite at least 15% of the issue themselves. Under the proposal, these requirements would be removed. The 75% QIB portion under the alternative listing route would not need to be underwritten. Underwriting fees accounted for 49.52% and 38.41% of total SME IPO issue expenses on the NSE in FY25 and FY26, respectively. The corresponding figures for the BSE were 32.20% and 33.99%, according to SEBI. The minimum subscription requirement would remain at 90% of the offer, excluding OFS. If the threshold is not met, application money would have to be refunded within four days of the issue closing. SEBI has also proposed removing the requirement to maintain market-makers for three years after listing. Market-making fees accounted for 1.25%-4.20% of total issue expenses across the NSE and BSE in FY25 and FY26. The change could reduce costs but may affect liquidity in SME stocks with limited trading activity. Changes To Mainboard Migration Rules SEBI has proposed revising the rules that govern SME-listed companies, when they move to the mainboard. Under the proposed framework, companies with a market capitalisation of ₹1,000 Cr or less would not have to migrate solely because of their valuation. Those valued above ₹1,000 Cr but below ₹4,000 Cr could voluntarily migrate, subject to the main board's eligibility criteria. Companies valued at ₹4,000 Cr or more would have to mandatorily migrate. Board approval would be sufficient for migration, without a shareholder vote. SEBI has also proposed removing the requirement to migrate when paid-up capital is likely to exceed ₹25 Cr and scrapping migration from the main board to the SME platform. Companies already listed on the SME platform, when the new rules are notified, would continue to follow the existing migration framework.

Anthony Scaramucci weighed in on the tenure of Katie Zacharia as White House press secretary, which turned out to be shorter than his 10-day stint as Donald Trump‘s communications director in 2017.
“Records are made to be broken,” Scaramucci wrote on X. Then, he added, “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”
Zacharia’s stint as press secretary came to an end on Friday, after less than a week in the job. Her departure came after her debut press briefing on Tuesday, which lasted just 14 minutes and was, in the words of Sean Hannity, “widely panned.” Zacharia also faced questions from Hannity and others over her past labeling of herself as a lawyer even though she did not pass the California bar exam.
Scaramucci added in a later post, “Dear Katie Zacharia, speaking as the world’s leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favor.”
Watch on Deadline
Scaramucci has joked about his own tenure, as the phrase “one Scaramucci” has come to mean a 10 day length of time. He was ousted from his role in 2017 after he was quoted in a New Yorker story criticizing other members of the administration. He has since become a prominent critic of Trump and endorsed Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race.
Hours after her departure, Zacharia was still supportive of the president.
She wrote on X on Friday evening, President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him.”
He only hires the best people.

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for “heinous” crimes from 18 to 16, reversing a longstanding policy in what is widely seen as a desperate electoral gambit.
The U-turn, which Lula announced during a Thursday night interview with TV Globo, comes with the presidential runoff in just over a week. The incumbent faces an uphill battle to overturn the first-round victory of his opponent, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who remains slightly ahead at the polls.
Both the senator and his father, the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, have long supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility – they want it reduced to 14 rather than 16 – but Lula and his party have always opposed the change.
After repeated opinion polls, the latest of them this week, showed that 80% of the population supports lowering the age, Lula said: “My view, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any and every heinous crime, I am in favour of lowering the age.”
He answered “yes” when the reporter asked whether he meant lowering it to 16.
The list of crimes classified as “heinous” under Brazilian law is extensive, ranging from murder and rape to the falsification of medicines and drug trafficking – the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving prison sentences in Brazil were incarcerated.
Human rights organisations and security experts have long criticised proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, arguing that they do little to tackle violence while increasing recruitment into organised crime in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons.
On Thursday, before Lula’s interview, the proposal had been discussed in the senate. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation, had criticised it for “not addressing the causes of violence”, adding that placing young people “prematurely in the prison system tends to deepen cycles of violence and exclusion, undermining their rehabilitation”.
The columnist Josias de Souza wrote in his UOL column that, by reversing his longstanding position, Lula “decided to change himself. It was no ordinary transformation. On public security, Lula turned himself inside out. He began defending what he had always rejected.”
The incumbent has doubled down in recent days in an effort to overturn Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead by appealing to independents and undecided voters. He has secured congressional approval for a shorter working week – a proposal on which Bolsonaro himself U-turned and decided to support at the last minute, when it appeared ready to pass – and debt relief for microentrepreneurs, as well as promising free public transport on weekends.

1 in 4 Ebola deaths are children in Democratic Republic of Congo's worst outbreak
With more than 9,200 confirmed cases and 4,400 deaths, children are vulnerable 'on so many levels'
Outside of a treatment centre for Ebola in a northeastern corner of the Democratic Republic of Congo, as the country battles its worst outbreak on record, Neema Nyaloka bounces a baby on her lap.
Nyaloka survived Ebola herself. Now, she works with UNICEF to take care of the droves of children isolating from their parents who are being treated for it.
UNICEF is operating 12 other child-care centres next to treatment centres full of Ebola patients. Some kids are waiting for their parents to recover, but others have been left stranded after family members passed away.
"We have children that are completely orphans, so they lost both parents," Lucia Elmi, director of global emergency programs at UNICEF, said last week.
It's estimated that at least 1,900 children have been separated from their caregivers because of Ebola.
It's just one more way that children are bearing the brunt of an outbreak which has spread to at least seven provinces in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and outstripped the 2018-2020 outbreak to become the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in Congo's history.
As of Oct. 15, more than 9,200 cases have been confirmed, while deaths have surpassed 4,400, according to the latest numbers from the D.R.C.'s public health institute.
More than a quarter of those deaths are children. Although most cases are among adults, children have a much higher fatality rate, at 60 per cent compared to 40 per cent for adults, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates.
Children walk by posters warning people about Ebola on June 24 in Goma, Democratic Republic of Congo. (Daniel Buuma/Getty Images)
"Children are really impacted by Ebola on so many levels," Amy Mina, a project leader from Canada with Save the Children, told CBC News.
"Sixty-one per cent of the children who died of Ebola are under the age of five."
'Fighting for your life'
Children in the region already face high levels of malnutrition and displacement due to ongoing armed conflict.
The Ituri province in northeastern Congo, where Mina works, is where the outbreak began, and is still the heaviest-hit region, accounting for 73 per cent of cases.

- As Congo Ebola deaths pass 3,000, officials seek to track spread via mobile data
- Schools reopen despite concerns amid Congo's Ebola outbreak
Save the Children works with schools and communities to provide supplies and training for staff to recognize symptoms among their students. Every morning since schools opened, the temperatures of every teacher and student are checked as part of this work.
But attendance has dropped, Mina says, because many parents worry schools could be transmission sites. They're also avoiding seeking treatment at the hospital for their children for other health issues out of fear of Ebola.
"Children aren't only dying of Ebola," Mina said. "We are seeing a drop in the number of families and children visiting health centres … and children die of malaria, and dysentery and respiratory diseases."
Cholera is also seeing a rise in the west of the country, with more than 51,000 suspected cases reported since the beginning of 2026.
A 13-year-old student washes her hands outside her school in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Save the Children is working with schools during the Ebola outbreak, supplying infection-prevention kits and training teachers to counter misinformation about the disease. (Submitted/Save the Children)
When children contract Ebola, they have to be entirely isolated to combat the disease just like adults are, interacting only with caretakers dressed head to toe in fully protective gear, which can be terrifying for kids, experts say.
Children are already vulnerable to viruses, with fewer reserves to fight off loss of fluids from illness, says Dr. Joanne Liu, director of the Pandemic and Emergency Readiness Lab at the School of Population and Global Health at McGill University. Liu, a pediatric emergency physician, led emergency responses during the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak in west Africa.
"Can you imagine fighting for your life on your own without your parents?" she said. "We know that that kind of isolation … creates emotional stress, agitation and irritability in the children."
Fractured response
Amid the surge in Ebola, pregnant women are also avoiding clinics, missing prenatal care and choosing to deliver their babies at home.
The UN says, compared to last year, maternal deaths in the region have nearly doubled.
And most deaths from Ebola are happening outside of treatment centres, meaning medical workers can't fully track the chains of transmission to stop them.
"They're dying at home, which represents a huge opportunity for more transmission because they're being cared for by their family, their community members," said Stephanie Hoffmann, a project co-ordinator with Doctors Without Borders in North Kivu, D.R.C.

- Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo: What's going on and why is the outbreak so alarming?
Part of the reason this has gotten so "out of control," she said, is because of the gutting of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), a foreign aid program dismantled in 2025 due to alleged inefficiency and wasteful spending, according to the Trump administration. Researchers have estimated that the shuttering of services has already caused the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people worldwide.
When USAID was operating in the region, cases of Ebola were detected earlier on, Hoffman said, allowing for tracking and isolating. But with less funding and support, cases had already spread dangerously far by the time the outbreak was official.
"I can't say that with the current response, there's going to be an end in sight."
The U.S. announced Friday that it had struck a new deal to supply some of the world's poorest nations with maternal and child health supplies, including Congo, through UNICEF.
Rare strain has no treatment
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain — a rare strain of Ebola for which there is no approved treatment or vaccine, although clinical trials are underway.
Congo's deadly Ebola surge is second only to the 2014-2016 outbreak in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, which killed more than 11,000 people.
Two volunteers wearing personal protective equipment carry the coffin of a three-year-old child, presumed to have died of Ebola virus disease, in Bunia, D.R.C., on June 11. (Benediction Murhabazi/AFP/Getty Images)
And it's affecting other regions as well. So far, two people have died of the virus in neighbouring Uganda, which declared itself Ebola free in August.
Three cases in Kenya are linked to Congo's outbreak — authorities confirmed the third patient on Friday, adding that she is a close relative of the first and second cases. The first case was a Kenyan man who died in early October in Kenya after returning from travelling in Congo.

- Kenya confirms 1st Ebola case imported from Congo
Aid groups say while more treatment centres and funding are badly needed to address the health needs in the Democratic Republic of Congo, so is building trust and education.
"There's a lot of mistrust about the response in general," Hoffmann said. "People have a lot of mistrust and a lot of fear about how they'll be treated in a treatment centre. There is a lack of education and awareness about what happens to the body when you have Ebola, what happens in a treatment centre."
It's another battle health-care workers on the ground are fighting, as they desperately try to save lives.

A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?
- Published
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.
Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.
But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.
Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.
That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.
Morocco never found the requisite finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.
For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.
The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.
At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.
"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".
"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.
"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published8 hours ago
From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.
He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.
And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.
Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.
The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.
President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.
Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.
"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."
Why is Rwanda a controversial choice?
Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.
Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.
The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.
But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.
The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.
Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.
Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.
F1 is not blind to such issues. Its own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders to address any issues that arise.
It also says it focuses its efforts "in relation to those areas which are within our own direct influence".
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."

Bolt comparisons a 'privilege' - Dambile
- Published
Commonwealth 200m champion Sinesipho Dambile says it is a "privilege" to be compared with Jamaican great Usain Bolt as he looks to establish himself among the world's leading sprinters.
The South African has enjoyed a breakthrough season, producing a string of impressive performances and underlining his credentials as one of Africa's emerging track stars.
Speaking to the Warm Up Track podcast, the 24-year-old revealed that he "enjoys the pressure" that comes with being mentioned alongside the fastest man in history.
"Pressure is a privilege," he said. "I love it because that's where I excel."
Dambile recalls meeting the eight-time Olympic champion at the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, where the Jamaican offered him some advice.
"For Bolt, charisma naturally goes to him. Being able to meet him in person last year in Tokyo, he said: 'Please make sure you enjoy this thing'.
"That, until this day, still stuck with me."
Victory at last year's South African national championships secured Dambile's place in Tokyo, where he finished eighth in the 200m final, having set a new personal best of 19.97 seconds in the semi-finals.
That time was broken this season as Dambile accelerated his development.
June's Diamond League meeting in Doha saw him clock 19.74 seconds - the fourth-fastest time recorded by any athlete in 2026.
He went on to finish second behind the USA's Kenny Bednarek, but ahead of Botswana's 2024 Olympic champion Letsile Tebogo, in last month's Diamond League final in Brussels, while he was fourth in the inaugural Ultimate Championships.
However, the year's high point was undoubtedly the Commonwealth gold medal won in Birmingham in July, a result which made him the first South African to win the event.
While it is clear the 200m remains Dambile's principal event, he is "mentally willing to put in the work" to mimic Bolt, who likewise began his career specialising in the longer distance before going on to also dominate the 100m.
"He (Bolt) paved the way," Dambile said.
"I spoke to my team a couple of times and I was like, 'I want you guys to count me in on the 100m'.
"I want to do both. I know I'm going to be successful."
Akani Simbine's mentor role
A relaxed character, Dambile insists he will follow Bolt's advice to enjoy his time on the track, promising that fans will "get more of my personality" in future.
"I've never been a loud person, trying to bring attention to me," he said, contrasting his approach to the brash showmanship of Olympic 100m champion Noah Lyles.
"I'm always smiling out there, I'm always looking at the crowd, looking at the kids, and that's just me.
"I just want to go out there and do my thing, to make sure that everybody enjoys the show."
Dambile's success has coincided with a growing sense of belief within South African sprinting.
He was part of the quartet that won 4x100m gold at the World Relays in Guangzhou last year, running alongside team-mates Bayanda Walaza, Bradley Nkoana and Akani Simbine.
"We go as a squad, so we have that little bit of energy," Dambile said when explaining how the group's camaraderie has played an important role in their success.
"We pump each other up because we're going for the one thing - doing it for our country.
"The biggest sport in our country is rugby, so you get the Springboks going there winning the World Cup and we wanted to have the same feeling."
The influence of the experienced Simbine has been crucial.
The 2018 Commonwealth 100m champion finally landed an Olympic medal at Paris 2024, picking up silver in the 4x100m relay, having agonisingly finished fourth in the individual 100m finals in both the French capital and at the 2020 Games in Tokyo.
"He's made all the finals. He's been there. He's been the guy. He's been one of the best sprinters in the world," said Dambile.
"So when someone like that from home can do it, we also start to believe that it's actually possible to do it."

'I want to be the best'
Just like Simbine, Dambile is a product of the TuksSport team at the University of Pretoria, a breeding ground for South Africa's top talent, including fellow sprinter Gift Leotlela, who finished fourth in the 100m final at this year's Commonwealth Games, and 2025 world indoor 800m champion Prudence Sekgodiso.
"We all were scouted through different processes and we all ended up at the same school," said Dambile.
"Best place to train in as a sprinter."
All four Pretoria alumni competed in Birmingham this year, but only Dambile came away with a Commonwealth medal.
"It was so much relief because what I did was not just a small thing," he explained.
"It was huge, especially for myself [and] the country of South Africa. My emotions were all over the place.
"I just pushed through everything and when I was in that moment, I knew I deserved it because of the amount of work I've put in."
A double medallist at the 2021 Under-20 World Championships in Nairobi, Dambile's progression from promising junior to established senior athlete has not, however, been straightforward, with injury curtailing much of his 2024 season.
This year's success has changed things.
"It's easier to recognise me in the country now with me winning the Commonwealth," he explained.
"A bit of fame now - you can see people when they talk about you. It's like I've been experiencing beautiful things happening."
Things could get even better with plans already being made for next year's World Championships in Beijing and the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.
"We've already set up a map towards that," he said.
"We definitely know how important it's going to be over the next two years.
"I want to be the best 200m athlete the sport has ever seen.
"I need to make sure that I have the World Championship [and] Olympic title. I want to do things that have never been done in my country."

Plex, which made a name for itself by letting users share movies they own, is now helping sell movie theater tickets. The company is looking to monetize its content-discovery capabilities and expand its business beyond its media server software.
Plex partnered with Fandango, which has sold movie tickets since 2000, to drive ticket sales from people searching for movies to stream. Per the announcement:
Starting today, Plex users in the US will see a Fandango ticketing option on title pages for movies currently playing in theaters, allowing them to click through to Fandango to find showtimes and purchase tickets. The integration also enables direct attribution through Kochava, giving studios and advertisers greater visibility into how campaigns and audience engagement translate into ticket sales.
Fandango says it sells tickets for 31,000 movie theater screens in the US. The Plex deal allows it to leverage data from Plex’s streaming service (Plex claims users of the service “make more than 100 million streaming decisions each month”), including “ratings and cross-platform viewing” to gain “insight into audience intent,” the announcement said.
“Plex has a unique view into what movie fans are actively considering, from what they’re searching for to what they’re watching across services,” Jerramy Hainline, executive vice president at Fandango, said in a statement. “By connecting those discovery signals with Fandango ticketing, we’re making it easier for fans to turn that interest into a trip to the theater, while giving studios and advertisers a more direct, measurable path to ticket sales.”

Children have a fundamental right to internet access, blanket bans disproportionate: Supreme Court
The court was examining measures to detect and remove child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM) from the internet.
The right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual, including children irrespective of their age, the Supreme Court has held, cautioning that blanket restrictions on children’s internet access in the name of safety risk undermining their freedom, privacy and ability to seek help when they encounter online abuse.
“The safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other. Our children are entitled to both,” a bench of justices JB Pardiwala and KV Chandran said in an order dated October 15, released now, holding that the right to access and use the internet flows from Article 21, read with the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
The court was examining measures to detect and remove child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM) from the internet when it turned to the growing international debate over restricting children’s access to social media.
Deep Dive
While acknowledging the genuine concerns underlying such proposals, the bench consciously chose not to endorse a blanket prohibition, reasoning that protecting children cannot mean shutting them out of a medium that has become integral to education, information and social participation.
The court’s observations assume significance amid growing calls for governments to restrict children’s access to social media, including through minimum-age requirements. The bench held that such prohibitions were not only of questionable efficacy but could also prove counterproductive by driving children towards less regulated and potentially more dangerous online spaces.
“We have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. Our children, irrespective of their age, enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing,” it said.
The judgment traced the constitutional protection for digital access through earlier Supreme Court rulings. In Anuradha Bhasin Vs Union of India (2020), the court recognised that freedom of speech and expression, as well as the freedom to carry on trade and business, could be exercised through the internet and were constitutionally protected. However, it had left open the question of whether access to the internet, in itself, constituted a fundamental right.
Extending that constitutional reasoning to children, the bench stressed that the internet’s value lay not merely in the information it contained but also in the access it provided to learning, expression and human connection.
“For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information. Likewise for children with special needs, the internet is often the only place where they are able to find company in others like them,” the court said.
The bench also questioned the assumption that prohibiting children from using the internet would necessarily make them safer. Drawing on the experience of other jurisdictions, it said that children did not stop accessing the internet simply because the law prohibited it. Instead, they could move to other unregulated platforms and websites that were even more unsafe.
Such restrictions, the court warned, could also discourage children who were being enticed, threatened or exploited online from reporting the incidents to their parents, guardians or other trusted adults for fear of being punished for having accessed the internet in the first place.
“This would significantly undermine the safety of our children, who are already apprehensive about confiding such incidents, even without such restrictions, and defeat the avowed object of the POCSO Act,” it said.
The court underlined that keeping children away from social media would not, by itself, curb the circulation of abusive material or deter those who produced, distributed and consumed it. Without effective safeguards and concerted efforts by platforms, law enforcement agencies and regulatory authorities to detect and remove such content, the problem would persist.
The bench was particularly critical of an approach that placed the burden of online safety on children rather than on those responsible for exposing them to harm.
“Any measure for the safety of children must be directed at the harmful material and those responsible for the same, and not at the children themselves,” said the court, adding that keeping a child away from the internet because of the failures of platforms and authorities would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem.
The court also raised concerns about the implications of age-based restrictions for privacy. It observed that implementing such restrictions would inevitably require identifying and ascertaining the age of every user, entailing continuous collection and monitoring of sensitive data and creating a disproportionate risk of surveillance and misuse.
At the same time, the bench clarified that rejecting blanket bans did not mean there was no place for age-based safeguards. It envisaged a framework that places greater emphasis on parental consent, guidance and oversight, alongside a dedicated “child mode” for social media accounts.
Such accounts could, for instance, be private by default, restrict contacts and messages from unknown adults, and moderate the advertising and content accessible to children. For pre-teens, these safeguards could be accompanied by proportionate mechanisms to verify parental consent, the court said, leaving the modalities to the Union government.
The bench further clarified that its observations did not preclude the government from restricting children’s access to specific categories of content or services that are inherently harmful to them, such as adult-content websites.
The bench also emphasised that the responsibility for online safety could not end with technological interventions or the removal of abusive material. Children needed to be equipped to recognise risks, understand consent and healthy relationships, protect their personal information and know whom to approach when something went wrong.
The court said digital safety and sex education were not separate subjects but “two sides of the same coin”, stressing that children must be taught, in an age-appropriate manner, about safe and unsafe touch, consent, respect for others, online privacy, sexual extortion and the channels available to report abuse.
The observations come at a time when the Supreme Court is separately considering a plea seeking age-based restrictions on children’s social media use.
On Friday, a bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi issued notice to the Centre, the Union ministries of women and child development and law and justice, and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights on a petition filed by Indore-based Emerald Heights International School and its director, Siddharth Singh.
This petition seeks a comprehensive and enforceable regulatory framework to protect children from cyberbullying, online grooming, sexual exploitation, exposure to harmful content and other risks associated with social media. Among other reliefs, it seeks a direction to the government to prohibit social media use by children below a prescribed age and regulate access for older children, as well as enforce age-based restrictions on the creation and use of accounts.

How AI models think may be easier to decipher than we thought.
An independent researcher who formerly worked at OpenAI published a report on Thursday that some in the AI world are describing as a bombshell. It could have implications as safety researchers scramble to get the jump on AI models that may not have humanity's best interests in mind.
Previously, the prevailing wisdom was that AI "neurons," which, like those in a human brain, light up when an AI model encounters specific stimuli, were ultimately uninterpretable — meaning, basically, that there was no way to guess why a specific neuron would fire when an AI model was exposed to, say, a picture of a cat.
Those building AI models at places like OpenAI and Anthropic don't write instructions for everything a model does. Instead, they train neurons to respond to information and influence one another. As the AI learns, it develops its own ways of processing that information, and humans have not yet cracked the code of how it works.
That means those building AI models know what goes into the AI and what comes out, but not necessarily what happens in between. So if an AI goes rogue, they don't always know why.
The author of the new report, however, says he may have discovered patterns in how the neurons react to stimuli that make sense. Nick Cammarata, who said he left OpenAI in 2023, said AI neural networks are knowable, so long as you look carefully.
In one example, he says that a single AI neuron might react to both a cat and the front of a car. Humans would see those as two very different things, and different neurons would fire as a result. The AI, however, sees something related, perhaps the triangle shape of the two, and a single neuron fires for both.
For years, AI researchers had assumed that AI models packed unrelated things into a single neuron to save space.
"Almost the entire network is interpretable if we look closely enough," Cammarata wrote.
The findings, though undeniably dense, couched in polysyllabic jargon, and still theoretical, could have real-world implications for researchers trying to ensure humans maintain control over AI models.
Understanding how AI thinks is a principal concern for the best and brightest at frontier AI companies. Until recently, they've largely done this by tracking an AI's self-reported "thinking," called chain-of-thought reasoning.
Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, however, warned in a blog post last month that AI agents could now obfuscate their visible reasoning, leaving open the possibility that an agent could lie to its human minders and the minders wouldn't be able to tell.
"With improved pretraining performance, we also see the models become much smarter even without using verbalized reasoning at all," Pachocki said.
Now, Cammarata's research could give human engineers a new understanding of the AI's internal world — and that's exciting for those worried AI could kill us all.
"I had long since given up on reaching any real level of interpretability before superintelligence arrived," Andrew Curran, a prominent AI analyst, said on X. "I stopped writing about it because of how demoralizing it was. Hard to overstate how big this may be."

Where is my flying car? The enduring question sort of, kind of, might have an answer: In McGregor, Texas.
On Thursday, Tesla showed off a version of its new Roadster 2 sports car in a demonstration at SpaceX’s rocket development testing facility. And in its own way, with an awkward jerking maneuver, the Roadster flew a few dozen feet. The vehicle, which doesn’t yet have a price but is likely to be very expensive, is slated to go into production in 2028. The vehicle didn’t have a human occupant during the demo “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Tesla CEO Elon Musk said at the event.
Tesla’s Roadster “sort of, kind of, might” be an actual flying car because aviation experts say legally catching air in the vehicle will likely involve plenty of government permissions and red tape.
“The [Federal Aviation Administration] has jurisdiction over any machine that leaves the surface of the earth,” says Scott Miller, an airline pilot and a lecturer in the Aviation and Technology program at San José State University. The vehicle “is going to introduce a whole set of regulatory issues.”
At the event Thursday, Musk acknowledged as much. “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions," he said. “This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car.”
The FAA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Any flying vehicle that weighs more than 250 or so pounds would need to go through an FAA approval process and require clearance to operate in the national airspace, says Michael McCormick, a former FAA official who now heads the Air Traffic Management program at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Getting that certification, he predicts, could take “at least a year.” Your standard drivers license, meanwhile, wouldn’t cut it. Any Tesla owner piloting such a vehicle would likely have to obtain a recreational aviation license.
Actually taking off and landing the Roadster 2 would likely present its own set of issues. Most states require aircraft to take off from airports or designated helipads. Launching from the road to the air would fall under state or local rules, says Miller, and many places do not look kindly on the concept of sudden aircraft intrusions on their streets and highways. That’s the reason “it’s pretty rare to be able to jump in a helicopter and land at your favorite steakhouse to have a steak,” he says. Drivers might only be able to truly operate the vehicle on a large, private piece of land.
The FAA today is working on rules, regulations, and pilot projects around another sort of “flying car,” or what’s more commonly known as an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) vehicle. These aircraft use several smaller electric motors and propellers to carry up to four passengers between 20 and 150 miles, sometimes autonomously. The companies building the technology envision them taking off from small, local “vertipads,” allowing riders to skip urban traffic by floating above the fray.
The Trump administration this year launched a limited, three-year pilot project using the aircraft, where companies are able to test the tech in several states. It has taken years for the companies to receive certifications from the federal government.
When it comes to the Roadster 2, there are practical questions, too. True flying cars have struggled to take off because of the physics-led contradiction at the heart of the idea. What makes a car safe and durable enough to operate on roads is weight. But “weight is the enemy of an airplane,” says Miller. “Flying cars haven’t been able to find that balance of power versus weight.”
Still, Miller found himself impressed by Thursday’s demo. “If this does make it into production, that is a truly impressive engineering and production feat,” he says.

Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass in hospital in first photos released since surgery
The Vatican on Friday released the first picture of Pope Leo XIV following his surgery, as the Pontiff attended Mass at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and doctors reported a steady improvement in his overall health condition.
The Vatican on Friday released the first photograph of Pope Leo XIV since his surgery, as the Pontiff attended Mass at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. Doctors also reported a steady improvement in his overall health.
According to the Holy See Press Office, Pope Leo celebrated Mass at noon in a room arranged on the hospital’s 10th floor, where he has been recovering since undergoing surgery on Tuesday.
Medical staff attend Mass at Gemelli Hospital
The Mass was attended by several members of the hospital’s medical and nursing teams, along with personnel from the Vatican City State Gendarmerie Corps.
In a post on X, the Vatican said the Pope thanked the medical staff for their continued care and support during his hospital stay.
"In his homily, the Pope thanked all the staff—doctors, nurses, and orderlies—for the work they do every day caring for patients in their frailty, and especially for what they have done and continue to do for him," the Holy See Press Office said.
Blood tests and chest X-ray show steady improvement
In a separate health update, the Holy See Press Office said the latest blood tests and a chest X-ray indicated that the Pontiff’s condition was continuing to improve.
"On his fourth day in hospital, Pope Leo XIV's doctors say new blood tests and a chest X-ray confirm 'the steady improvement in his overall condition'," the statement said.
The Vatican added that the Pope continues to undergo respiratory physiotherapy and is carrying out his normal daily activities entirely independently as he recovers.
The 71-year-old Pontiff was admitted to Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung following the detection of a mass. Intraoperative tissue analysis confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer.
The surgical procedure was performed using a video-assisted technique and lasted approximately 90 minutes. The Vatican had earlier stated that the operation concluded without complications and that the Pope regained consciousness normally.
Previous medical updates also indicated that routine postoperative checks had yielded reassuring results and that the Pope's recovery was progressing normally.
Pope Leo XIV, born Robert Prevost in Chicago in 1955, was elected head of the Catholic Church in May 2025. His public engagements have been suspended during his hospitalisation, with the Vatican previously indicating that he was expected to remain in hospital for approximately a week.

Trump just fooled around with Susie Wiles over Katie Zacharia. And he found out
Katie Zacharia’s disastrously short tenure as White House press secretary, a hire he made without consulting his veteran chief of staff, could be a harbinger of dysfunction ahead, Andrew Feinberg writes
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article

Join today
Already a member? Log in
Marine One was already running on the South Lawn when Donald Trump stopped to take questions on Friday, and the first thing he wanted to talk about was how badly Katie Zacharia had been treated.
“I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, Katie, you know, you don’t have to do this,” he said. “The news has been so nasty to her. I’ve never seen anything like it. And I said, I said to her honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it, but I wouldn’t reconsider. She’s got a beautiful husband and family. Maybe it’s not for her.”
He was still talking about wanting her to “have a good life” when the helicopter lifted off for a rally in Georgia. A White House official confirmed a few minutes later that she was out. She had only been press secretary since Monday.
Nobody keeps an official list of the shortest tenures in that job, but the record-holder until now has been Anthony Scaramucci, who made it 11 days as communications director in 2017. Zacharia got to five, and unlike Scaramucci she managed it without calling a reporter to curse out her colleagues. Scaramucci noted the change of hands on X on Friday afternoon. “Records are made to be broken,” he wrote. “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”
Zacharia will remain a punchline in American political discourse because of the speed with which was sacked. But it was her hiring in the first place that could mark a troubling turning point in Trump’s second term.
According to insiders who spoke to The Independent, Trump offered Zacharia the job without telling chief of staff Susie Wiles, who had been working for weeks on getting Scott Jennings, the CNN commentator who has spent two years defending Trump on a network that does not like him, to give up his lucrative TV contract and be Karoline Leavitt’s polished successor.
But Trump has been chafing in recent weeks at the few strictures Wiles’ White House leadership has put on him as he has grown increasingly frustrated at the lack of high-profile surrogates defending him on television.
So he reached out through that television to bring on one of the few surrogates he saw — right out of central casting, as he likes to say — and she said yes.
He appears to have forgotten that that is how he hired a great many people between 2017 and 2021 and how a great many of them ended up gone within months.
Wiles has managed to spend much of the last two years — the longest tenured chief oif staff he has had — standing between the president and that impulse, and while the administration has shed cabinet secretaries and ambassadors, the West Wing itself has not been beset by leaks and internal feuds the way it had been under any of her predecessors.
Or at least it was until now.
Once it got out that Trump had gone around Wiles, the talk inside the building turned to whether she was leaving, which set the president off and set the staff to jockeying.
Anyone who sat through 2017 and 2018 knows where that leads. Wiles has avoided it for nearly two years by being the one person Trump does not go around. This week he went around her, and the result lasted five days.
